title: Sill Through Glass
oneLiner: From inside, frame the outside window sill and whatever rests on it.
details: Stand indoors and shoot through the closed window so you do not lean out. The subject is the outer sill: paint, dust, or a bare ledge, and a window box only if one is already there. Include the window frame on one side so it is clear you are looking through glass.
tips: Put the lens close to the glass to cut a reflection of the room.
Focus on the sill, not on a speck on the pane.
constraint: Stay entirely indoors for this one.

title: Landing from Inside
oneLiner: From your side of the front door, frame the first edge of outside.
details: Open the door and keep your feet indoors. The picture is the near edge of the entrance, the shared path, or the sidewalk, wherever outside actually begins. Show the line where your flooring stops and the outer material starts. A door that opens straight onto a corridor counts if a threshold strip or a change of floor is there.
tips: Use the door frame as a border along one side.
Keep the phone level so that outer line stays horizontal.

title: Ledge From the Room
oneLiner: From the room, frame an outer ledge through the closed glass.
details: Any outer ledge will do, even a bare one with nothing on it. A window box or a single pot is only one option, and a bare sill is enough, seen from inside. Look for the rim or the point where the ledge meets the frame. Square up so that edge is a clean horizontal.
tips: Hood the lens with your hand to block a reflection of the room.
Tap the rim rather than the glass.
constraint: Leave the window closed.

title: Threshold Materials
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the join of indoor flooring and the outer sill.
details: Stay inside and point the phone down at the threshold. You want both sides large: timber against metal, your floor against a communal floor, or a mat against the sill. If both floors match, the metal strip or the door's bottom edge is the line. That line should cross the picture.
tips: Shoot straight down so neither material is squeezed by perspective.
Tap the join itself.

title: Narrow Outside Slice
oneLiner: Use a curtain or the window frame to crop a thin slice of outside.
details: From inside, make a narrow opening with a curtain or a blind. If you have neither, stand so the window frame itself cuts the view down to a strip. That strip should be the entrance path, a fence along the sidewalk, a planted strip, or a window box if one is already there, and little else.
tips: Focus beyond the cloth or the frame, on whatever sits outside.
Expose for the outside so the interior falls dark.
constraint: Do not leave the room.

title: Leading Lip
oneLiner: Get low and shoot along the front lip of a sill, slab, or low wall.
details: Choose an edge you can reach while standing on the sidewalk or at your entrance: a window sill, the front of a paving slab, a low wall, or the edge of a planted strip. Get low and let that lip run from the near corner away from you. Chips and worn paint are part of the picture.
tips: Brace a hand on your knee so the low angle stays steady.
Focus about a third of the way along the lip.
constraint: The lip must lead from the near foreground into the frame.

title: Two Materials
oneLiner: Find the seam where two outdoor surfaces meet near your entrance.
details: Concrete against stone, a fence post against the sidewalk, timber against tile, or a slab against the planted strip. Stand at your entrance or on the sidewalk by the building and give both materials equal space. A shared path is the right place if that is what lies outside your door.
tips: Shoot straight down when the seam is on the ground.
Tap the seam, not the cleaner surface beside it.

title: Where It Ends
oneLiner: Photograph where a mat or a paving slab comes to an end.
details: If a mat already lives outside your door, use its fringe or bound edge against the bare surface beside it. If your mat stays indoors, leave it there and use the edge of a slab on the shared path, where the stone stops and another surface begins. Show both sides of that ending.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the ground so the border stays even.
Brush aside only what completely hides the border.
constraint: Both the ending edge and the surface beyond it must show.

title: Path Edge
oneLiner: Frame the line where a path or the sidewalk changes surface.
details: A shared path, the sidewalk by your building, or the planted strip beside the entrance is enough. Let the line where the surface changes run through the frame. Keep that change of surface as the subject rather than the building beyond it.
tips: Keep that change of surface level in the picture.
Move closer until the seam is the widest line you can see.

title: Fence or Frame
oneLiner: Shoot where a fence, a gate, or the door frame meets the ground.
details: A fence along the sidewalk is as useful as a gate. If you can reach neither, the bottom of your own door frame is the same kind of edge. Look for dirt, a gap, flaking paint, or a pale line of dust. Crouch and put the meeting of upright and ground near a corner of the picture.
tips: Include both the upright and the ground.
Focus exactly where the two meet.
constraint: Put that meeting point near a third, not in the middle.

title: Rim in Profile
oneLiner: Follow the rim of an outer sill, a low wall, or a fence rail.
details: Use an outer sill, the top of a low wall, or a fence rail you can reach from the sidewalk or your entrance. A window box or a pot already outside is only one option, not a requirement. Look for the lip and the line where it meets the wall or the ground. Do not lean out of an upstairs window.
tips: Shoot from the side so the rim becomes an oval.
Move your head if it is blocking the light.

title: One Chipped Edge
oneLiner: Isolate one chip on an outside edge and make it large.
details: Run your eye along a sill, a fence rail, a paving slab, or the threshold until you find one nick. Photograph that nick close up. Show the broken edge and the intact surface together.
tips: Cup a hand nearby if the mark looks too flat to read.
Tap the rough edge to focus.
constraint: One chip only, large in the frame.

title: Threshold Bar
oneLiner: Photograph the bar or raised edge along the bottom of the outer door.
details: Stand just outside your door, on the shared path or the sidewalk, and make that bar the horizon of the picture. Look for screws, worn metal, a rubber strip, or dirt in the groove. A door with no raised step has the same kind of bar. If yours is a plain bottom edge, that edge replaces it.
tips: Get low so you are not only looking down on it.
Lock focus on the nearest screw or the nearest groove.

title: Three-Plane Corner
oneLiner: Include an outside corner where three surfaces meet.
details: A paving slab has a top, a face, and an end, and a fence post or a window sill can give you the same three planes. Pick a corner you can see from the sidewalk, the shared path, or your entrance, and place that point near the centre. You want three planes, not a flat line.
tips: Move to the side until you can see all three faces.
Keep the uprights vertical on the screen.
constraint: All three planes must be visible.

title: Weed in the Join
oneLiner: Frame a crack at an outside edge first, whether a plant is in it or not.
details: A small plant in the join can stay, but the crack is the subject. Look in the sidewalk, along a planted strip, under a fence, or along a window box if one is already there. If there is no plant, photograph the empty crack or a line of grit in the same kind of join.
tips: Get low so the crack has a little depth.
Focus on the crack edge rather than the tip of a leaf.

title: Slab Groove
oneLiner: Find a groove or a seam in the paving near home and follow it.
details: Many slabs on a shared path or the sidewalk have a narrow groove or a sloped edge. You do not need anything sitting in it. Crouch and let that channel run through the frame. If the paving is plain, use the seam between two slabs instead.
tips: Shoot along the groove rather than across it.
Tap a point a short way down the channel.
constraint: The groove or seam must cross the frame.

title: Grit at the Edge
oneLiner: Photograph grit that has already gathered along an outside edge.
details: Sills, the base of a fence, and the edge of a planted strip collect a line of soil or grit. Find a scatter that is already there and shoot it where it has settled. Include the edge it follows, whether that is a sill, a fence base, or the rim of a window box if you have one. Leave the grit as you found it.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the surface the grit sits on.
Include the rim or the edge in the same frame.

title: Along the Verge
oneLiner: Frame the boundary of a verge, a fence line, or the strip beside the sidewalk.
details: A planted strip along the sidewalk, a narrow dirt edge, or the ground along a fence will do. Let that boundary run from the lower corner upward. You may be looking at the sidewalk outside an apartment building, and that is the right subject.
tips: Make the boundary the strongest line in the picture.
Crouch so the strip fills more of the frame than the building.
constraint: The boundary must run from a lower corner toward the top of the frame.

title: Base Course
oneLiner: Photograph the lowest band of the outside wall where it meets the ground.
details: That band may be brick, stucco, timber, or paint, often dirtier than the wall above. From your entrance or the sidewalk by the building, crouch and fill the frame with the meeting of wall and ground. The base of an apartment building is fair if you can reach it from the sidewalk. A pipe can stay in shot, but the base of the wall is the subject.
tips: Crouch to the height of that band.
Square the wall so the verticals stay upright.

title: Pipe Meets Ground
oneLiner: Photograph where a drainpipe or a cable meets the ground.
details: Many buildings have a vertical pipe or a cable dropping to the sidewalk or a shared path. Crouch and put that meeting in the frame, with the upright and the ground both clear. If you cannot see one, use the point where a fence post or the door frame meets the ground.
tips: Get down so you meet the joint rather than looking only from above.
Tap the exact point where the upright enters the ground.
constraint: The meeting of upright and ground must be sharp.

title: Pipe Along the Base
oneLiner: Follow a pipe, cable, or trim running along the base of the outside wall.
details: From your entrance or the sidewalk, look along the wall beside the shared path. A pipe, a cable, or a timber batten all make a base edge. Let it enter at one side and leave at the other. If the wall is bare, the line where wall meets sidewalk is your line instead.
tips: Crouch to the height of the pipe or the joint.
Tap the nearest bracket, or the nearest chip if there is no bracket.

title: Shared Path Seam
oneLiner: Photograph the nearest seam in the path or sidewalk by your building.
details: A slab joint, a crack, or a change of material close to the entrance is enough. Stand on the sidewalk or the shared path and make the seam large. Your doorway may appear at the edge of the frame, but the seam is the subject.
tips: Shoot along the seam so it widens in the foreground.
Focus a short distance along the seam.
constraint: The seam must run from the near edge of the frame toward the far one.

title: Ridges at the Door
oneLiner: Photograph ridges at your entrance, on a scraper, a threshold, or a mat.
details: A metal scraper, a ribbed mat that already lives outside, or a grooved threshold will do. Get close to the ridges or the worn metal. An apartment door often has a plain metal bar under it, and that bar is enough.
tips: Let light from the open doorway skim across the ridges.
Fill the frame with that texture.

title: Dark Fence Gap
oneLiner: Let one dark gap in a fence or a door frame fill the picture.
details: A fence along the sidewalk is ideal. Come close so a single gap reads as a dark slot, with the board edges on either side. If there is no fence, use the gap between your door and the frame, seen from the entrance side.
tips: Stand so the gap runs top to bottom.
Focus on the edge nearest the lens.
constraint: One gap only, running through the frame.

title: Low Dark Slot
oneLiner: Frame the narrow slot under a fence or under your outer door.
details: If you can reach a fence from the sidewalk, use the gap between its bottom edge and the ground. Otherwise get low at your entrance and shoot the dark slot under the outer door. Solid structure should sit above the slot so the opening reads as an edge.
tips: Expose for the brighter part of the slot.
Stay low, with a hand on your knee for balance.

title: Leaf Already Caught
oneLiner: Find a leaf or twig already caught on an outside edge.
details: Look along a fence base, a sill, a planted strip, or a window box if one is already there, for a leaf or twig that has lodged. Do not move it, and keep both the edge and the caught piece clear. If nothing has caught, photograph a leaf still on a plant at that edge, with the rim or the fence in the frame.
tips: A low angle makes the edge and the leaf both readable.
Focus where the leaf or twig meets the edge.
constraint: The edge and the leaf or twig must both be in frame.

title: Kitchen Shadows in Mono
oneLiner: Turn your kitchen into a black-and-white study of light and deep shadow.
details: Set your phone to monochrome or convert the picture afterwards. Side light from a window or a lamp cuts a mug or a counter into a bright plane and a deep shadow, and the colours of cans and boxes would only fight that split. Frame the brightest area so it draws the eye while the shadow still holds a little detail.
tips: Expose for the highlights and let shadows go deep.
Use a plain background so shapes read clearly.
Tap to focus on the edge where light meets dark.
constraint: Include only one main subject in the frame.

title: Window Light Still Life
oneLiner: Set one object in window light and record the grey gradient around it.
details: Choose a bowl, a book, or a bottle and set it where daylight falls from one side. In colour the object's hue takes over; in mono you can see the light wrapping the form and the soft gradient on the surface behind it. Shoot in monochrome, or remove the colour later, and turn other lights off so that gradient stays gentle.
tips: Turn off overhead lights to keep the mood soft.
Shoot with the window to your side, not behind the object.
Move closer to simplify the background.
constraint: Use natural window light only, with no flash.

title: Close Bark Tones
oneLiner: Find tree bark and fill the frame with its rough monochrome texture.
details: From the sidewalk, move in on the nearest trunk, a thick shrub stem, or a weathered post. Bark is a muddle of similar browns, so colour hides the ridges and cracks. In mono those ridges become an abstract field of light and dark texture. Fill the frame with that surface.
tips: Hold the phone steady and tap to focus on mid-bark.
Try a slight angle instead of shooting straight at the bark.
Look for a zone where light and shadow cross the texture.

title: Stripes and Lines
oneLiner: Hunt for repeating lines indoors and compose them as a bold black-and-white graphic.
details: Blinds, stair rails, tile grout, or stacked books offer repeating lines. Their colours distract from the rhythm; mono leaves the contrast between each line and the gap beside it. Align the lines diagonally or vertically and move until the pattern fills the frame.
tips: Keep the horizon level if lines are horizontal.
Switch to mono so hue cannot compete with the lines.
Try shooting from a low angle to lengthen the lines.
constraint: No curved shapes, only straight lines.

title: Mug and Spoon Portrait
oneLiner: Pair a bright spoon with a duller mug and judge them as tones.
details: Set a mug and a spoon on a plain surface near a lamp or a window. The spoon is a thin bright metal and the mug a broader, duller mass, so the portrait is about tone rather than the colour of the ceramic. Arrange the spoon so it leads toward the handle or the rim.
tips: Place the spoon at an angle for visual energy.
Use a cloth or napkin to control reflections on metal.
Shoot from slightly above table height.
constraint: Both objects must touch the same surface.

title: Urban Geometry Up Close
oneLiner: Find building edges and frames that read as sharp black-and-white shapes.
details: From the sidewalk by your door, look along a wall for a corner, a window frame, or railings that make a clean shape. Stone, glass, and paint often sit close in colour, and mono lets tone alone separate them. Let the corner or the railing occupy the frame, with only a sliver of sky if you need it.
tips: Move until the frame holds only wall, frame, and a sliver of sky.
Expose for bright sky or facade depending on your story.
Use grid lines to align vertical edges.

title: Fabric Folds in Grey
oneLiner: Drape a towel or shirt and photograph the soft folds as a grey sculpture.
details: Lay or hang a towel or a shirt where light can rake across it from the side. Colour and print would turn this into a fabric picture; mono turns the folds into bands of light and dark, like a soft carving. Move until that rhythm of tone fills the frame.
tips: Use side light from a lamp or window.
A plain cloth shows the folds more clearly than a busy print.
Get close enough that seams disappear.
constraint: Fill at least eighty percent of the frame with fabric.

title: Cloud Tones Above
oneLiner: From a window, reduce the sky to a field of grey tones.
details: Stand at a window and point the phone at the sky as it is right now. A sky is already a stack of tones, from a bright patch to a heavier veil, and mono makes those greys the whole subject. Keep the frame on sky alone.
tips: Tap the brightest patch, then lower exposure until it has detail.
Brace a knuckle on the window frame to steady the phone.
constraint: Keep ground and walls out of the frame.

title: Red Beside Green
oneLiner: Set a red fruit beside a green one and watch their colours collapse to grey.
details: Put a red apple or a tomato beside a green apple or a lime on a pale plate. To the eye they are opposites; in mono they may sit much closer in tone. Expose so neither becomes a black blob, and notice which one is actually darker.
tips: Shoot in mono from the start so you judge tone, not memory of colour.
A side window keeps a small highlight on each skin.
constraint: Only the two pieces of fruit and the plate.

title: High Key Bedding
oneLiner: Expose white bedding in mono so the faint creases still exist.
details: On pale sheets or a white duvet, the colour is almost nothing, so the picture only works as tone. Shoot in monochrome and keep the creases a pale grey rather than letting them drop to charcoal. Crop until those folds are the only event in the frame.
tips: Add a little exposure if the phone turns white cloth dull grey.
Smooth most of the bed, then leave three or four creases.

title: Cupboard Highlight
oneLiner: Open a dark cupboard and find one small highlight inside it.
details: Open a cupboard or closet and let the room light fall in from behind you. The picture is one small highlight against a deep surround, which is a contrast study, so any colour on the jars would only weaken it. Shoot in mono and let the rest of the interior go deep.
tips: Tap the small highlight so the phone does not brighten the whole cave.
Lean the door until the light just reaches that one edge.
constraint: Only one bright accent in the dark.

title: Tea Gradient
oneLiner: Pour tea into a clear glass and record the gradient in mono.
details: Pour tea, coffee, or a dark juice into a clear glass by a window. The drink's colour is not the point; the way the tone thickens from the bright rim down through the glass is. Shoot in monochrome so that falloff reads as grey rather than as brown or orange.
tips: Hold the glass up to the window if the tone looks flat on the table.
Focus on the rim where the highlight is thinnest.

title: Foil in Grey
oneLiner: Crumple foil and let mono turn the creases into a range of greys.
details: Crumple a sheet of kitchen foil, then open it partway so the creases stay. Foil is a single metal colour, but each crease faces the light differently, so mono splits it into bright peaks, mid greys, and dark cuts. Shoot under a lamp or a window and fill the frame.
tips: Move the light until the brightest crease is small, not a white sheet.
Fill the frame with foil and leave the table out.
constraint: No other object in the frame.

title: Beads on the Glass
oneLiner: Take a glass from the fridge and shoot the beads before they fade.
details: Use a drinking glass from the fridge, or fill one with cold water until beads form on the outside. The beads have almost no colour of their own, so mono is how they read: soft grey dots on a darker curve. Set the glass against a dark cloth and shoot before the beads join up.
tips: Tap a bead rather than the dark cloth behind it.
Shoot before you wipe the glass, while the beads are still separate.

title: Two Mug Finishes
oneLiner: Place a matte mug beside a glossy one in the same window light.
details: Choose two mugs or bowls, one dull and one shiny, and set them in the same side light. Photograph that pair in monochrome so the finish, not the colour, does the work. The glossy one should carry a hard highlight while the matte one turns in a smoother grey.
tips: Turn the shiny mug until its highlight is a small mark, not a flare.
Keep both rims fully in the frame.
constraint: Same light on both, with no second lamp.

title: Dark Line on Boards
oneLiner: Run one dark cable across pale floorboards and treat it as a line.
details: Lay a dark cable or a headphone cord across pale boards or a light rug. The picture is one dark line on a light field, and any colour in the floor would dilute that contrast. Shoot from above in mono and tuck the spare coil out of frame.
tips: Angle the phone downward from standing height and crop tighter afterwards.
Make sure the line enters and leaves at the frame edges.

title: Flour on the Board
oneLiner: Dust flour across a dark board and rake the light across it.
details: Scatter a little flour on a dark tray or chopping board. Flour against a dark board is already a tone picture, and mono states the texture without the board's colour. Skim a lamp or a low window across the drifts so the brightest dust sits on the dark ground.
tips: Use less flour than you think, so the board still shows through.
Lock the exposure on a bright patch, then darken it a fraction.
constraint: The board fills the frame.

title: Hand at the Pane
oneLiner: Press your hand to a bright window and crop before your face appears.
details: Stand at a bright window and press your own hand flat to the glass. Against the light the hand becomes a shape of grey, which is a tonal picture rather than a colour portrait of skin. Shoot in mono from inside the room, and keep your head out of the frame and out of the reflection.
tips: Expose for the hand if you want the skin tones, or for the window if you want a silhouette.
Wipe a clear patch of glass first so the outline stays clean.
constraint: Only your own hand, with no face in frame.

title: Thin Metal Frames
oneLiner: Lay glasses on a cloth and show the thin metal as a grey line.
details: Set a pair of glasses on a plain cloth near a window. If you wear none, a metal hanger or a thin bangle works the same way. The metal is only a fine bright line with a soft shadow, so mono keeps the eye on that thinness instead of on the colour of the cloth.
tips: Get low enough that the frame is seen from the side, not only from above.
A dark cloth makes thin metal easier to separate.

title: Roll End Spiral
oneLiner: Look into the end of a kitchen roll and frame the grey spiral.
details: Stand a kitchen roll or a cardboard tube on its end and look down into the spiral. The cardboard is a single hue, so only the shadowed grooves separate the rings. Shoot in mono and let those repeating greys tighten towards the middle.
tips: Shade the top with your hand if the cardboard all turns white.
Centre the hole, then rotate the tube until the spiral feels uneven.

title: Scarf Without Hue
oneLiner: Wrap a striped scarf and let mono turn the colours into bands.
details: Coil a striped or checked scarf, tie, or dish towel on a table. Shoot in monochrome so the colours survive only as lighter and darker bands. If two different colours become the same grey, keep that sameness in the picture.
tips: Spread the cloth so at least three bands are visible.
Avoid a busy tablecloth underneath, which adds a second pattern.
constraint: The cloth fills the frame.

title: The Empty Frame
oneLiner: Hang or lean an empty frame and photograph the rectangle of tone.
details: Lean an empty picture frame, or a rectangle of card, against a wall. The border, the wall inside it, and the shadow can be three separate tones, which is easier to judge once the colour is gone. Shoot in mono and leave the centre empty.
tips: Shift the frame until its shadow becomes a third tone.
Square the phone to the wall so the rectangle stays true.
constraint: Nothing inside the frame.

title: Pale Against Dark
oneLiner: Set something pale against dark leaves or cloth and remove the colour.
details: Use a pale flower, the heart of a lettuce, or a folded white tissue against dark leaves or a dark sweater. Strip the colour so you can judge the separation as tone, not as green against white. The pale shape should sit clearly on the deeper ground, with a soft edge rather than a hard cutout.
tips: Side light keeps the pale object from merging with a light wall.
Move the dark cloth if the tones are closer than they looked in colour.

title: Baseboard and Floor
oneLiner: Include the baseboard and the shadow where the wall meets the floor.
details: Stand in a hall or beside any wall and frame the baseboard where it meets the floor. Render that join in monochrome, where the shadow line is the event. The join should be a dark line between two close greys, with a little wall above and a little floor below.
tips: Get low so the baseboard crosses the frame as a strong band.
Turn a lamp towards the wall if the join has no shadow.

title: Cold Oven Mouth
oneLiner: With the oven off and cold, frame the dark mouth and one metal edge.
details: Check the oven is off and cold, then open the door. The mouth of the oven suits mono because you want a deep cavity against a thin metal highlight, not the colour of the enamel. Frame that dark space with one rack or metal edge catching light.
tips: Do not lean on the door, just let it rest open.
Tap the metal edge so the cavity stays dark.
constraint: The oven stays off.

title: Net Curtain Layers
oneLiner: Shoot through a net curtain so the window becomes soft grey layers.
details: Close a net curtain or a sheer and shoot through it towards the window. The cloth already softens the view, and mono turns those layers into grey rather than a faded colour scene. A thin dish towel held taut in front of the lens works if you have no net.
tips: Focus on the cloth if you want the weave, or beyond it if you want the soft view.
Stand back a short way so the phone does not poke the fabric.

title: Greens Become Tone
oneLiner: Reduce a variegated houseplant to tones, ignoring the greens.
details: Choose a houseplant with pale patches, or any plant set against a light wall. Shoot in mono and forget that it was green. Leaf, stem, and wall should separate by tone alone.
tips: A pale wall behind a dark leaf is often clearer than a busy shelf.
Turn the pot until the lightest leaf sits against the darkest background.
constraint: No pot decoration competing with the leaves.

title: Paper Plane Greys
oneLiner: Fold a paper plane and show its planes as separate greys.
details: Fold a sheet into a simple dart and set it on a pale surface. The paper is one colour, so the faces exist only as tone where they turn toward or away from the light. Shoot from a low side angle in mono and let each plane carry a slightly different grey.
tips: A window to one side separates the facets better than light from above.
Keep the background untextured so the small tone shifts read.

title: Door Chain Links
oneLiner: Photograph the door chain as bright links against the door.
details: If the door has a chain, shoot it close against the paint. If it does not, lay a necklace or a short length of chain on a dark cloth. Each link is a small highlight wrapped around a dark hole, a contrast picture, so shoot in mono and let the colour of the door fall away.
tips: A lamp from the side puts a highlight on each link.
Get close enough that three or four links fill the width.

title: Mortar and Brick
oneLiner: Let mortar read lighter than the bricks in a tight mono frame.
details: From the sidewalk, move close to a brick or block wall until mortar and brick fill the frame. Mortar and brick are often close in colour, and mono is what shows the mortar as the lighter line. Let the brick stay the darker mass.
tips: Stand square so the courses stay level.
If the tones are close, move to the shaded side of the wall and lower the exposure slightly.
constraint: No sky, only wall.

title: Leaf Veins in Grey
oneLiner: Lay a leaf vein-side up and let the veins become grey lines.
details: Place one leaf from a houseplant or a cabbage, vein-side up, on a plain board or a sheet of paper. Veins are pale lines in a darker leaf, a tonal drawing that colour only tints. Shoot from above in mono and let those lines carry the frame.
tips: A low side angle, still looking down, gives the veins a little shadow.
Tap the midrib so the finer veins stay with it.

title: Door in the Wall
oneLiner: Frame your front door as a dark shape in a paler wall.
details: From the sidewalk, frame the front door so it sits as a shape in the wall. A door and a wall are often a similar colour, and mono shows whether they actually separate as tone. Expose so the two are clearly different, include the frame, and leave out the wider view.
tips: Move along the sidewalk until the door sits with a margin of wall around it.
If the door and wall are close in tone, include the darker mail slot or handle as the accent.
constraint: The door occupies at least half the frame.

title: Gravel Field
oneLiner: Fill the frame with gravel and let the stones separate by tone.
details: Crouch over gravel, pebbles, or coarse concrete you can reach from the sidewalk. In colour the stones share a narrow range of browns; in mono they separate by tone. Fill the frame and look for stones that do not share the same grey.
tips: Brush dust aside if every stone looks the same.
Shoot from directly above so size is not confused by perspective.

title: Stair Nosing
oneLiner: Show a stair nosing as a bright line between two close greys.
details: Use an indoor stair, or the lip of a hearth or a windowsill if you have no stairs. The nosing is a light edge over a darker face, which mono describes more clearly than colour does. Shoot so that line crosses the frame, with a little surface above and a little face below.
tips: Get the phone near the nosing so the edge runs corner to corner.
Include a little of the upper surface and a little of the face beneath.
constraint: The edge must cross the whole frame.

title: Bars Against Wall
oneLiner: Turn a row of uprights into a black rhythm against a light wall.
details: Use railings you can see from the sidewalk, or a stair rail, a chair back, or a cooling rack indoors in front of a light wall. The bars are a repeated dark rhythm against a pale ground, and mono keeps that beat in tone alone. Move aside until the bars separate rather than stacking into one mass.
tips: Expose for the wall so the bars can go dark.
Crop out latches unless one of them breaks the rhythm on purpose.

title: Ellipse of the Rim
oneLiner: Photograph the ellipse of a bowl rim and make that rim the lightest line.
details: Set a bowl, a plant pot, or a bucket on the floor indoors. Get low and shoot across the rim in mono so the opening becomes an ellipse. The rim should be the lightest line and the interior a darker tone, which is a curve of grey rather than a coloured object.
tips: Kneel rather than tipping the bowl towards the lens.
A plain wall behind the rim keeps the ellipse clean.

title: Faucet and Shadow
oneLiner: Render a faucet or a metal handle as highlight and deep shadow.
details: Use the kitchen faucet or a metal door handle. Metal against a duller ground is a highlight-and-shadow subject, so the colour of the fitting matters less than the shine and the dark beneath it. Come close, shoot from the side in mono, and let one edge shine while the space under the spout or the lever goes deep.
tips: Come from the side so the spout or the lever has a clear profile.
Wipe spots off the metal if they glitter more than the shape.
constraint: The fitting fills most of the frame.

title: Cable Down the Wall
oneLiner: Follow a cable down a pale wall as a single dark line.
details: Hang a dark cord down a pale interior wall, or frame a slim pipe on the outside wall by your entrance. The wall should be a broad even tone and the cable one darker line, so mono states the contrast without the colour of the surface. Shoot from the side and include a single clip, bracket, or piece of tape.
tips: Keep the line near a third of the frame, not dead centre, if the wall is blank.
Move parallel to the wall so the line stays straight.

title: Threshold Strip
oneLiner: Crop to the strip where one floor tone meets another.
details: Stand inside at a doorway and look down at the metal, wood, or carpet strip under the door. Two rooms often differ in brightness more than in colour, so mono shows two greys with the strip between them. Shoot across the join and let the strip be the dividing line.
tips: Angle the phone so the strip runs diagonally.
Include only a hand's width of floor on each side.
constraint: The strip must be the dividing line.

title: Latch and Recess
oneLiner: Move close on a latch so highlight and shadow describe the metal.
details: Use a door bolt, a latch, or a handle on a door indoors. The metal edge should catch light while a recess falls dark, which is the contrast that makes the fitting readable once colour is gone. Shoot close in mono.
tips: Rest a finger beside the latch to steady the close shot.
Turn slightly until the metal separates from the door behind it.

title: Doorbell Disc
oneLiner: Centre the doorbell and treat it as a small disc of tone.
details: From the sidewalk, frame the doorbell, a round button, or a circular plaque by the entrance. Let any numbers fall soft so they are not the subject. In mono the disc should separate into three tones, a rim, a face, and a shadow, and the colour of the plastic is beside the point.
tips: Stand square to the button so the circle stays round.
A fingertip at the edge, then removed, helps you judge scale before the shot.
constraint: The disc sits fully inside the frame.

title: Light Pot Dark Pot
oneLiner: Set a light pot beside a dark one and let tone do the separating.
details: Put a light bowl or pot next to a dark one on the floor or a table. Their colours may shout, but mono asks only whether the tones differ. Shoot from the side and move them until each edge stays separate and the shadows do not merge.
tips: A plain wall behind them keeps the comparison simple.
Leave a gap between the pots so each keeps its own edge.
constraint: Two pots only.

title: Lid Highlight
oneLiner: Move around a lid until the highlight runs along the curve.
details: Use a saucepan lid, a bowl, or a can on the table. A curved lid throws a long highlight and a falling shadow, which is a tone study rather than a colour one. Walk around it and shoot in mono when that highlight runs along the curve, with the background as one quiet tone.
tips: Crouch so the highlight sits on the near rim.
If the whole lid blows out, turn a little until the shine shrinks.

title: Dark Frame Bright Opening
oneLiner: Frame a bright doorway from inside so the surround falls dark.
details: Stand inside and point the phone at an open doorway or a bright window. The surround should fall into deep tone while the opening stays bright, a contrast that mono states without the colour of the walls. Keep both the dark frame and the light in the picture.
tips: Expose for the bright opening so the frame can fall dark.
Include the line where the frame meets the light.
constraint: Both the dark frame and the bright opening stay in frame.

title: Glass Rim First
oneLiner: Focus on the near rim of a glass and let the room soften.
details: Fill a clear glass and set it on a table. Bring the phone close to the near rim, close enough that the rim is large in the frame, and tap the rim. The room behind, much farther away, should fall into a soft wash.
tips: Tap the rim and keep the phone at that close distance.
If the room stays sharp, move the glass nearer the phone and farther from the wall.
constraint: The rim is sharp and the room behind it is not.

title: Only the Near Bottle
oneLiner: Sharpen only the nearest bottle in a row and let the others fall away.
details: Line up two or three bottles, jars or tins with a clear gap between them, each one farther from the phone. Put the nearest one close to the lens, almost filling the frame, and tap it. Turn labels away so nothing can be read, and let the farther bottles fall soft.
tips: A small gap will not do. Separate them by an arm's length if you can.
If the far bottles stay crisp, use portrait mode with the nearest bottle as the subject.
constraint: Only one bottle may be sharp.

title: Discs in a Dim Room
oneLiner: Defocus a cluster of small lights until they become soft discs.
details: Darken the room and switch on a short string of small lights. If you have none, stand where a few indicator lamps already show, such as a charger, a router and the stove clock. Hold a fingertip or a pencil at the edge of the frame, very close to the lens, and tap it so the lights behind become soft discs.
tips: Leave the flash off, or the discs will vanish into a bright wash.
Move the lights farther back if they still look like sharp points.
constraint: No small light may be sharp.

title: A Streak on the Glass
oneLiner: Wipe a damp streak on the window and shoot through the softness.
details: Wring a damp cloth until it is almost dry, then wipe one streak across the inside of a window. Set a mug or a small plant on the sill first. Shoot through the streak so that subject softens, while the dry glass beside it stays clearer.
tips: One wipe is enough. A second wipe just cleans the idea away.
Stand so the streak runs across the mug or the plant, not across empty glass.

title: Nothing Left Sharp
oneLiner: Leave a lamp and a coloured bottle entirely soft.
details: Set a switched-on lamp beside a coloured bottle or a bright mug. Close the curtains and turn every other light off so the corner is dark. As you take the picture, shift the phone a short distance so the glow and the bottle both smear and no edge stays crisp.
tips: Shift far enough that the lamp travels across the frame.
If a night setting keeps the picture steady and sharp, switch that setting off.
constraint: Nothing in the frame may be sharp.

title: Time Out of Focus
oneLiner: Soften a clock until the time cannot be read.
details: Use a wall clock or the digits on a stove. Hold a pen or a fingertip very close to the lens, at the edge of the frame, and tap it. The clock should fall so soft that the time cannot be read, even if the round shape or the glow remains.
tips: Keep the pen small at the edge so the clock still fills the picture.
If digits stay readable, the pen is too far from the lens. Bring it closer.
constraint: The time must be impossible to read.

title: Near Rim of the Shade
oneLiner: Catch the near rim of a lampshade and let the far side soften.
details: Switch a lamp on and turn the other lights off. Bring the phone close to the near rim of the shade, looking across the opening, and tap that near rim. The far side of the shade, and the room beyond it, should fall soft.
tips: Any shade works, paper or cloth.
If both rims are sharp, move closer until the near rim is large in the frame.

title: Cup Against the Clutter
oneLiner: Use portrait mode so a cup stays crisp against a soft kitchen.
details: Set a plain cup on the table with jars, a cloth and the rest of the kitchen farther behind it. Choose portrait mode and tap the cup so the clutter falls soft. If portrait mode will not engage, bring the cup very close to the phone and leave that clutter across the room.
tips: Give the cup space in front of the clutter so the blur has room to show.
Turn a printed cup so any wording faces away.

title: Softened Patch of Glass
oneLiner: Let a hot drink soften a patch of glass, then shoot through that patch.
details: Make a mug of tea or coffee and hold it near a window or a clear tumbler, without touching the glass. Wait until a small patch turns milky. Have a bottle or a bright cup already standing on the far side, and photograph it through that patch before the glass clears.
tips: Keep the mug off to the side so it does not block the patch.
Have the bottle in place first, because the softness fades quickly.

title: Tines Across the Plate
oneLiner: Hold a fork close to the lens so the tines soften across a plate.
details: Set a plate of fruit, bread or a bright cloth on the table. Hold a fork a few centimetres from the lens, off to one side, and tap the plate so the plate stays sharp. The tines should cross the frame as soft shapes.
tips: If the tines come out sharp, they are too far from the lens. Bring them closer.
Keep the fork at the edge so most of the plate is still visible.
constraint: The tines stay soft and the plate stays sharp.

title: The Near Fold
oneLiner: Sharpen the nearest fold of a sweater and let the rest fall soft.
details: Drape a sweater, a scarf or a towel over the back of a chair. Pull one fold towards the phone so it is much closer than the rest of the cloth. Tap that near fold and let the chair and the farther fabric turn soft.
tips: Side light from a window picks out the near fold.
If the whole garment stays sharp, pull the fold closer and push the chair back.

title: Sweep of the Spines
oneLiner: Sweep the phone gently across a row of coloured spines.
details: Stand before a row of books, notebooks or colourful boxes in a dim corner, with the main light off. As you press the shutter, sweep the phone a short way sideways. You want a wash of colour, with the spines no longer crisp.
tips: If the spines stay sharp, sweep faster and switch off a night setting that steadies the shot.
Keep the sweep level so the colour runs in bands.
constraint: The spines must lose their sharp edges.

title: Turn Across the Stripes
oneLiner: Turn the phone slightly while you shoot a striped cloth.
details: Lay a striped dish towel, a striped shirt or any banded cloth in a dim room, away from the window. Twist the phone a little as you take the picture. The bands should smear into soft ribbons.
tips: A small twist beats a wild swing.
If every thread stays frozen, twist a little faster in the same dim room.

title: The Plant in Portrait
oneLiner: Switch on portrait mode and let the room fall away behind a plant.
details: Set a houseplant, or a sprig of herbs in a jar, with clear space between the leaves and the wall behind. Use portrait mode and tap the leaves so the room softens. If portrait mode will not engage, bring one jutting leaf close to the phone and tap that leaf.
tips: A plain wall behind the plant makes the softness easy to see.
Wipe the lens first so a smudge is not mistaken for the blur you wanted.

title: Finger in the Foreground
oneLiner: Hold a fingertip close and soft, with a mug sharp behind it.
details: Set a plain mug on the table. Hold one fingertip very close to the lens, off to one side, and focus on the mug. The finger should be a soft shape and the mug the clear subject.
tips: Use the front of the fingertip, not a whole hand across the lens.
If the mug softens too, you have focused on the finger. Tap the mug again.
constraint: The fingertip stays soft and the mug stays sharp.

title: The Frame Stays Sharp
oneLiner: Tap the near window frame and leave the view beyond it soft.
details: Stand beside a window so the near upright of the frame is close to the phone and the outdoors sits far beyond the glass. Tap the frame, not the view. The frame should stay crisp while trees, walls or sky outside turn into a soft band.
tips: The grid helps you set the upright along one line.
If the view stays sharp, you are too far from the frame. Move closer to that upright.
constraint: The frame is sharp and the view beyond it is not.

title: Shoe Down the Hall
oneLiner: Bring one shoe close and let the hallway behind it fall soft.
details: Set one of your shoes on the floor, close to the phone, and leave the other shoe or the rest of the hall farther away. Get down low and tap the near shoe. The hallway behind it should fall soft.
tips: Shoot from floor level so the hall has somewhere to recede.
If the hall stays sharp, put the shoe closer to the lens.

title: The Chosen Drop
oneLiner: Place one drop on the window and let the view behind it soften.
details: Flick one drop of water onto the inside of a window. Bring the phone close and tap the drop so the drop stays crisp. Whatever is outside, a wall, foliage or another building, should sit as a soft wash behind it.
tips: A single fat drop is easier to lock onto than a tiny bead.
Brace a knuckle on the frame so the phone does not drift off the drop.

title: Words Falling Away
oneLiner: Keep the words unreadable by focusing on a page edge.
details: Open a book, a notebook or a magazine to any ordinary page. Tilt it so the near edge is close to the phone and the far side of the page is much farther away. Focus on that near edge so the words fall too soft to read.
tips: If a line is still readable, steepen the tilt and move closer to the near edge.
A page of ordinary print softens more willingly than a huge headline.
constraint: No word on the page may be readable.

title: Through a Soap Smear
oneLiner: Smear a little soap on glass and soften a bottle behind it.
details: On a window, a clear tumbler or a shower screen, rub a small dab of soap into a patch. Set a coloured bottle or cup on the far side and shoot through the smear. If you already have pebbled bathroom glass, skip the soap and shoot the bottle through that texture instead.
tips: A coloured bottle shows the blur more clearly than a clear one.
Wipe the soap away when you finish.

title: Tip of the Nearest Leaf
oneLiner: Isolate the tip of the nearest leaf and let the plant wash away.
details: Choose a houseplant leaf that sticks out towards you, or a sprig of herbs if you have no houseplant. Bring the phone close to that tip, close enough that the tip is large in the frame, and tap it. The rest of the plant, sitting farther back, should become a green wash.
tips: A leaf near a window gives you a bright edge to tap.
If the whole plant is sharp, the tip is not close enough. Move in.

title: The Next Room Soft
oneLiner: Let the next room fall soft behind a door frame you keep sharp.
details: Stand in a doorway and bring the phone close to the near upright of the frame. Tap that frame. The furniture or the wall in the room beyond should fall soft, well behind the wood.
tips: Shoot through the opening rather than straight at a closed door.
If the far room stays sharp, move closer to the near upright.
constraint: The frame is sharp and the far room is not.

title: Pasta Held Forward
oneLiner: Hold one piece of pasta close and let the pile behind it soften.
details: Pile a handful of dry pasta on a plate. Hold a single piece much closer to the phone, in front of that pile, and tap the piece you are holding. The pile should turn into a soft jumble of the same colour.
tips: Penne, shells or spaghetti all work. Use whatever is in the cupboard.
Prop the phone against a mug if you need a free hand for the pasta.
constraint: Only one piece of pasta is sharp.

title: Front of the Fridge
oneLiner: Open the fridge and sharpen only the jar closest to you.
details: Open the fridge and pull one jar, bottle or carton to the front edge. Bring the phone close to that item and tap it. The packets towards the back should fall soft in the fridge light.
tips: The fridge lamp is enough on its own.
If the back stays sharp, draw the front item farther towards the phone.
constraint: Only the nearest item is sharp.

title: A Warm Streak
oneLiner: Drift the phone so a switched-on lamp becomes a warm streak.
details: Leave only one lamp on in a dark room and frame the shade. Drift the phone sideways during the shutter press so the glow draws a warm streak. If the shade stays a hard shape, drift farther and switch off any night setting that tries to keep the picture steady.
tips: A short drift keeps a hint of the shade. A long one becomes a plain line.
Close the curtains so daylight does not freeze the shade.

title: Edge of the Curtain
oneLiner: Press close to a curtain edge and let the room go soft.
details: Stand so a curtain edge is close to the phone and you are looking past it into the room, not out of the window. Tap the cloth edge. The room beyond should turn into a soft space while the cloth stays crisp.
tips: A pale curtain against a darker room shows the change clearly.
If the room stays sharp, bring the cloth closer to the lens.

title: A Green Ghost
oneLiner: Move the phone during the shot so a plant becomes a soft ghost.
details: Set a houseplant, or herbs in a jar, against a plain wall and dim the room. During the shutter press, move the phone a short distance sideways. The plant should ghost into a soft green shape rather than stay a crisp specimen.
tips: Close the curtains if the first try is frozen sharp.
Move the phone only a little. A long sweep leaves a smear with no shape.
constraint: The plant must not be crisp.

title: The Nearest Slat
oneLiner: Stand at one end of the blinds and sharpen only the nearest slat.
details: Use horizontal or vertical blinds, a slatted drying rack, or a radiator seen from one end. Stand at one end so those repeated lines run away from the phone. Tap the nearest line, very close, and let the farther ones fall soft.
tips: Get the nearest slat almost as close as the phone will focus.
A row of books, shot from one end, works if you have no slats.

title: Loop of the Cable
oneLiner: Hang a cable towards the phone and soften the loops behind it.
details: Drape a charging cable or a headphone lead over a chair back so one loop hangs towards the phone and the rest hangs farther away. Tap the near loop. The farther loops should fall soft, like a loose drawing of the same curve.
tips: A pale chair behind a dark cable helps the loops show.
Shoot from the side so the loops sit at clearly different distances.

title: Copper Wash
oneLiner: Hold an onion skin close to the lens and turn it into a copper wash.
details: Peel a dry outer skin from an onion with your fingers. Hold that thin piece very close to the lens, leaving part of a bright window clear. Tap the clear glass or the frame, not the skin, so the skin sits in the picture as a soft copper or gold wash.
tips: Keep a gap so the skin does not touch the lens.
One thin piece works better than a thick handful.
constraint: The skin must be fully soft.

title: The Zip Pull
oneLiner: Draw a zip pull towards the phone and let the jacket fall soft.
details: Lay a jacket, a bag or a cushion on the bed or a chair. Draw the zip pull towards the phone so it is much closer than the cloth, and tap the pull. The fabric should fall soft behind that small shape.
tips: A metal pull catches the light better than a fabric tab.
If the cloth stays as sharp as the pull, bring the pull closer to the lens.

title: Hem of the Towel
oneLiner: Catch the near hem of a towel and let the bathroom fall soft.
details: Hang a towel on a rail, a hook or the back of a door. Pull the near hem towards the phone so the cloth is close and the bathroom sits well behind it, then tap the hem. The room should turn soft while the hem stays crisp.
tips: A hem stitch or a stripe gives you a clear line to tap.
Stand the towel away from the wall so there is real distance behind it.

title: The Nearest Hanger
oneLiner: Open the closet and sharpen only the hanger closest to you.
details: Open a closet or a cupboard with a rail of clothes or empty hangers. Stand so the rail runs away from the phone, and tap the nearest hanger, very close to the lens. The hangers farther along the rail should soften.
tips: Clothes or empty hangers both work.
If the far hangers stay sharp, move in until the nearest one is large in the frame.
constraint: Only the nearest hanger is sharp.

title: Peg Before the Cloth
oneLiner: Pick out a peg or a clip and let the cloth behind it soften.
details: Use a peg on a drying rack, a clip on a packet, or a hair clip on a scarf. Hold the peg or clip towards the phone so it is much closer than the cloth, and tap the clip. The fabric behind should fall soft.
tips: A bright cloth behind a plain peg makes the softness obvious.
If both are sharp, the clip is not close enough to the lens.

title: Leaf Against the Wall
oneLiner: Tap a leaf close to the phone and let the wall behind it soften.
details: Hold one leaf close to the phone and tap it so the wall behind falls soft. A houseplant leaf works, held in front of a plain indoor wall. If you are already just outside your door, a leaf on a low branch works the same way, with the building wall behind it. Keep your fingers out of the frame.
tips: The leaf needs to be close and the wall much farther, or both will be sharp.
Crouch if you need the leaf nearer the lens, and brace an elbow on your knee.
constraint: The leaf is sharp and the wall is not.

title: Keys Into Softness
oneLiner: Look along a keyboard and let the farther keys fall soft.
details: Use a laptop or a desk keyboard. Keep the screen out of the frame so you are not photographing notes or messages. Get down at one corner so the keys run away from the phone, tap the nearest keys, and let the farther ones soften.
tips: Angle the keyboard so the near corner is much closer than the far one.
If the far keys stay crisp, move the phone closer to the near corner.
constraint: Only the nearest keys are sharp.

title: Drum Behind the Glass
oneLiner: Tap a washing-machine door and let the clothes inside soften.
details: If your washing machine has a glass door, bring the phone close to the near edge of that door and tap the edge, not the clothes. The drum inside should fall soft. If there is no glass door, use a glass-fronted cupboard with something set well back from the pane, and tap the near edge so the inside softens.
tips: A speck or the door rim is easier to tap than a clean pane.
If the inside stays sharp, move the phone closer to the glass.

title: Weave Before the Bottle
oneLiner: Focus on a sheer weave and let a bottle behind it turn soft.
details: Hang a sheer curtain, a net or a thin pale shirt between the phone and a coloured bottle. Put the cloth close to the phone and the bottle farther back. Tap the weave, or a hem if the weave will not lock, so the cloth is crisp and the bottle becomes a soft block of colour.
tips: A bright bottle against a darker room shows through the cloth.
If the bottle stays sharp, move it farther behind the cloth.

title: A Waved Curtain
oneLiner: Wave a curtain during the shot so the cloth smears and the frame stays.
details: Dim the room, then prop the phone on a table so it faces a curtain and the window frame. Give the curtain a quick wave with your free hand while the picture is taken. The cloth should smear and the frame should stay still.
tips: If the cloth freezes, wave faster and shoot the darker side of the curtain.
Keep your hand out of the frame. Only the cloth should move.
constraint: The cloth is smeared and the frame is sharp.

title: A Rolled Frame
oneLiner: Roll the phone slightly as you shoot so the edges streak.
details: Stand before a shelf or a table with a few objects on it, and dim the room. As you press the shutter, roll the phone a short way, as if you were turning a dial. The edges of the picture should streak while the middle stays a little calmer.
tips: Roll more quickly if the first try is sharp.
A small roll is enough. A full spin loses the room entirely.
constraint: The edges of the frame must streak.

title: Pot Rim Only
oneLiner: Settle on a pot rim and let the plant above it soften.
details: Choose a houseplant in a pot, one whose leaves rise well above the rim. Crouch so the near rim is close to the phone and the leaves sit much farther back, then tap the rim. The foliage should fall soft above that sharp curve.
tips: A bright rim against darker compost is an easy edge to lock onto.
If the leaves stay sharp, lower the phone and move closer to the rim.

title: Back of the Drawer
oneLiner: Open a drawer and let the things at the back fall soft.
details: Pull open a kitchen drawer or a desk drawer that holds ordinary things, not private papers. Tap an object at the front edge, close to the phone. The items towards the back of the drawer should soften.
tips: Slide one object to the front if everything is piled at the same depth.
A spoon, a reel of tape or a tin at the front is enough to tap.
constraint: The back of the drawer must be soft.

title: Paper Over the Lens
oneLiner: Hold a thin tissue just in front of the lens and soften the whole room.
details: Choose any room with a lamp or a window for light. Hold a single sheet of tissue or baking paper just in front of the lens, close but not touching the glass. The room should turn into a soft, bright blur, with no crisp edge left.
tips: Do not press the paper onto the lens. A gap keeps the glass clean.
A plain sheet softens more evenly than a printed one.
constraint: Nothing in the room may stay crisp.

title: Through the Thick Base
oneLiner: Look through the thick base of a glass and turn a lamp into glow.
details: Switch on a lamp and dim the rest of the room. Hold a clear tumbler or a jam jar so you look through the thick bottom, not through the open top, and point it at the lamp. The glass should soften the lamp into a glow and bend its edge.
tips: Wipe the glass so fingerprints do not become the subject.
A thin flat base will barely soften the lamp. Choose a chunky bottom.
constraint: The lamp must not stay a hard-edged shape.

title: Hand and a Soft Wall
oneLiner: Soften the wall behind your own hand with portrait mode.
details: Stand a short distance from a plain wall and hold your other hand up, with clear space between your fingers and the wall. Use portrait mode, tap the hand, and keep your face out of the frame. If portrait mode will not engage, bring the hand much closer to the phone than the wall and tap the hand.
tips: A bare wall shows the blur more clearly than a busy shelf.
Spread the fingers slightly so the shape is easy to read.

title: The Front Grape
oneLiner: Fill a glass with grapes and sharpen only the nearest one.
details: Put a few grapes, olives or cherry tomatoes in a clear glass. Bring the phone close to the glass and tap the piece that touches the front. The fruit farther inside the glass should soften.
tips: If they all look sharp, take some out so one sits at the front and the next sits well behind.
Wipe any moisture off the outside of the glass before you shoot.
constraint: Only the nearest piece of fruit is sharp.

title: Crust and a Soft Kitchen
oneLiner: Fill the frame with bread crust and let the kitchen fall away.
details: Set a loaf, a roll or a thick slice on a board. Bring the phone close to the crust so the texture is large, and tap the crust. The kitchen behind the board should fall soft.
tips: Side light shows the crust better than light from straight above.
If the kitchen stays sharp, move the board away from the wall and get closer to the crust.

title: Bristles Before the Cup
oneLiner: Hold a toothbrush close and let the cup behind it soften.
details: Stand a cup on the sink. Hold your toothbrush so the bristles are close to the phone and the cup sits farther back, and tap the bristles. The cup and the tiles should fall soft behind them.
tips: Rinse the brush first so the picture is of the bristles, not the paste.
If the cup stays sharp, move it back and bring the brush closer.

title: Remote Before the Screen
oneLiner: Hold the remote close and let a bright screen melt into colour.
details: Switch on a television or a laptop with something bright on the screen. Hold the remote, or a pen if you have no remote, very close to the phone and tap it. The screen, much farther away, should melt into colour with no readable word.
tips: Turn the flash off so it does not reflect in the screen.
Angle the remote so it does not hide the whole screen.

title: Pale to Deep
oneLiner: Arrange whatever books you have from pale spines to deep ones.
details: Gather the books, notebooks or magazines within reach and stand them in a short row from the palest spine to the deepest. Three is enough, and a recipe book counts. The picture is that simple sequence of tone. Shoot from straight in front so the row reads as bands.
tips: A plain wall behind the row keeps the spine tones honest.
Step back until a little space shows above and below the row.
constraint: Order them from pale to deep, left to right.

title: One Spine Forward
oneLiner: Pull a single book a little forward from a row and make that the subject.
details: In a shelf, or in a row you make on the table, pull one book forward by a couple of centimetres. That slight step is the picture. If you own only two books, stand them together and ease one ahead of the other. Leave the titles readable or not; the step forward matters more.
tips: Shoot from a slight side angle so the forward book casts a slim shadow.
Focus on the spine that stands proud of the others.

title: Page Edge Strata
oneLiner: Photograph a stack from the side so the page edges look like strata.
details: Stack two or more books, notebooks or magazines and photograph them from the side so the page edges become horizontal bands. The covers are only the borders. A single thick paperback still shows a block of pages if that is all you have. Even light from a window will separate the layers.
tips: Get close enough that the page edges fill the frame.
Align the phone so the bands run truly horizontal.
constraint: The page edges, not the covers, must dominate.

title: Tent of Pages
oneLiner: Open a book and stand it like a tent, then photograph the valley inside.
details: Open a book, notebook or magazine near the middle and stand it on a table like a tent. Look into the valley where the pages meet and photograph that hollow. The two slopes of paper should frame a darker centre. A stiff book holds the tent; a floppy one can lean against a mug hidden behind it.
tips: Shoot from low, level with the table, looking into the valley.
Let the far end of the valley go a little darker than the near pages.
constraint: The tent must stand on its own page edges.

title: Ribbon Marker
oneLiner: Follow a ribbon marker or a paper strip where it leaves the pages.
details: If a book has a ribbon, follow it from between the pages out into the air. If it has none, slip a plain strip of paper in as a marker and use that. The line leaving the block of pages is the subject. Choose a printed book or a notebook, and leave private notes closed.
tips: Lay the book on its side so the ribbon hangs or trails in a clear curve.
Focus where the ribbon exits the pages.

title: Endpaper Colour
oneLiner: Open a cover and photograph the endpaper just inside, not the story.
details: Open the front cover of a hardcover or paperback and photograph the paper fixed inside it, before the story starts. Often it is a plain colour, a pattern or a map. If your book has no separate endpaper, use the inside cover of a notebook. Keep any handwritten notes out of the frame.
tips: Fill the frame with the inside cover and a sliver of the board.
Shoot in window light so the paper colour stays true.
constraint: Do not include a page of the story.

title: Tops of the Row
oneLiner: Shoot from above a row so you see the top edge of each closed book.
details: Stand several books or notebooks in a row and shoot from above, looking down on their top edges. You should see a rhythm of paper blocks and cover tops, not the titles on the spines. Two books are enough if you come close. A windowsill or a table both work.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the tops so the edges stay even.
Include the little gap of table between books if there is one.

title: Along the Spines
oneLiner: Look along a row of spines so colour and wear repeat into the distance.
details: Get beside a shelf or a row you have stood on the table, and look along the spines. Let the nearest spine be large and the others shrink away. Notice colour, scuffs and the odd thin volume, not only the line they make. If the shelf is short, three books still show the repeat.
tips: Rest the phone on the shelf so the row stays level.
Focus on the second spine, leaving the nearest one slightly soft.
constraint: Include at least three spines.

title: Cracked Spine
oneLiner: Find a worn spine and photograph the crack or fade along it.
details: Choose the most worn book or notebook you have and come close to the spine. A crack, a faded strip or a softened corner is the subject. If everything you own is new, open a notebook flat and photograph the crease you just made. Do not damage a book to get the picture.
tips: Rake the light from the side so the crack casts a tiny shadow.
Fill the frame with a short stretch of spine.

title: Spiral Rings
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the rings of a spiral notebook or a bound pad.
details: Find a spiral notebook, a reporter's pad or a calendar with rings. Come close so the rings repeat across the frame, with page edges behind them. If you have no spirals, photograph the stitches of a sewn notebook or the elastic loop on a closed journal. The binding is the subject, not the notes.
tips: Shoot slightly from the side so each ring has a highlight.
Keep any written lines too soft to read.
constraint: The binding must fill the width of the frame.

title: Bedside Pile
oneLiner: Photograph the pile of books where you actually leave them, without tidying.
details: Find the place books already gather, a bedside, a chair, the floor by the sofa or a corner of the desk. Photograph the pile as it is, including the crooked one. Do not tidy it and do not add a mug for charm. If you own a single book, that one book where it lives is enough.
tips: Shoot from the height of the pile, not from the ceiling.
Include a little of the surface it sits on so the pile has a home.

title: Kitchen Spine Row
oneLiner: Line up the cookbooks or notebooks in the kitchen and shoot their spines.
details: In the kitchen, stand whatever books live there, cookbooks, a notebook, a magazine you cook from. If the kitchen has none, carry three from another room and stand them against a plain bit of counter, then put them back. The row should feel like it belongs to the room, so include a small hint of tile or wood. Titles can be soft.
tips: Use the window, not the overhead lamp, so the spines are evenly lit.
Stand square to the row.
constraint: Keep food and utensils out of the frame.

title: Leaning Pair
oneLiner: Lean two books against each other and photograph the dark space between them.
details: Stand two books, or a book and a notebook, so they lean together and meet near the top. Look into the dark gap between them and photograph that space, with the covers as the two sides. A hardcover pair holds the lean more easily than two thin paperbacks. If they slip, set them in a corner where the walls keep them up.
tips: Get the phone down to table height so the gap reads clearly.
Focus on the darkest point where the two covers meet.

title: Along the Inner Fold
oneLiner: Follow the inner fold of an open book from near to far.
details: Open a book or notebook fairly wide and aim along the fold where the pages meet. The curve of the pages on either side should lead into that join. Private writing stays out; a printed page or a blank one is the right choice. Come close so the fold runs through the frame.
tips: Hold the covers down with objects outside the frame if the book springs shut.
Focus a short way along the fold, not on the nearest corner.
constraint: The fold must run from the near edge into the frame.

title: Cloth Headband
oneLiner: Come close to the woven band at the top of a hardcover spine.
details: On a hardcover, look at the top of the spine for the small woven band, often a stripe of cloth between the cover and the pages. Photograph that band close up. If you only have paperbacks, photograph the top corner where the cover meets the page block instead. Either way, the joint is the subject.
tips: Rest the book on a table and brace the phone on a mug for the close view.
Side light will show the weave or the paper edge.

title: Band that Shuts
oneLiner: Show the elastic, string or band that keeps a notebook shut.
details: Find a notebook with an elastic closure, a string tie or a rubber band you use to keep notes together. Photograph that band where it crosses the cover. The tension, the slight dent in the cover, is the detail. A paperback with a paper band still on it works too.
tips: Shoot from the side so the band lifts a little off the cover.
Let the cover colour sit behind the band as a simple field.
constraint: The band must cross the frame.

title: One Stands Up
oneLiner: Lay a stack flat and stand one book upright against it.
details: Make a low flat stack of books or notebooks and stand one book upright against the stack. The contrast between the lying books and the standing one is the picture. Two books total are enough: one flat, one upright. Place them on a table with a plain background.
tips: Shoot from the side so you see both the flat page blocks and the upright spine.
Leave a little empty table to the side of the upright book.

title: Nearest Spine Sharp
oneLiner: Focus on the nearest spine and let the titles farther along fall soft.
details: Line up a few books and get close to the nearest spine. Focus there, and let the spines behind fall soft so their titles blur. The sharp spine can be worn or plain. If the phone keeps everything sharp, move closer to the first book and farther from the rest.
tips: Tap the nearest spine and hold until focus locks.
A gap between the first book and the next helps the softness.
constraint: Only the nearest spine may be sharp.

title: Lifted Page Arc
oneLiner: Lift one page into a curve and photograph the arc of the paper.
details: Open a book or a notebook and lift a single page into a gentle curve, holding the corner with a fingertip at the edge of the frame. The arc of paper is the subject, with the pages below it quieter. A blank page or a printed one both work. Let the text go soft if it competes with the curve.
tips: Shoot from the side so the arc has height.
Light from behind the page if you want it to glow, or from the side if you want the curve's shadow.
constraint: A fingertip may show, but only at the edge.

title: Folded Corner
oneLiner: Find a creased page corner and photograph that small wear close up.
details: Look for a page corner already creased. Come close so the triangle of the crease fills much of the frame. If every book is pristine, fold a corner of a newspaper, a magazine or a notebook page you can spare, and photograph that. Do not crease a book you care about.
tips: Low side light shows the crease as a ridge.
Include a little of the flat page around the corner.

title: Uneven Skyline
oneLiner: Stand books of different heights so their tops make a little skyline.
details: Gather a few books or notebooks of different heights and stand them in a row on a table. The rising and falling tops are the picture, so shoot from the side. Three is enough, and a thin magazine can be the short one. A plain wall behind them keeps the skyline clear.
tips: Line the camera up with the table so the tops are easy to compare.
Leave a gap of wall above the tallest book.

title: Fore-Edge Face
oneLiner: Turn a closed book so the block of page edges faces you.
details: Sit at a table and turn a closed book so you face the block of page edges rather than the spine or the cover. Fill the frame with that pale block. A thick volume shows it best, though a notebook still has an edge. Window light from the side should graze the paper.
tips: Turn the book until the light skims the page edges.
Keep the cover to a thin border around the block.
constraint: Page edges fill at least two thirds of the frame.

title: Along the Cover
oneLiner: Shoot along a book cover from one corner so it recedes like a plane.
details: Lay a book or notebook on the table and bring the phone close to one lower corner. Aim along the cover so it becomes a plane receding away from you. The table is only the support. A paperback may curve and a hardcover will stay flat, and either result is honest.
tips: Include the edge of the pages as a pale stripe.
Focus a short way up the cover, not on the nearest corner.

title: Thin beside Thick
oneLiner: Stand a thin magazine or notebook beside the thickest book you own.
details: Choose the thickest book you can find and stand a magazine, a pamphlet or a thin notebook tight against it. The contrast in width is the picture, so shoot from the spine side or from above the page blocks. Two items are enough. If every book is a similar size, stack two of them to make the thicker shape.
tips: Come close so the thin one looks even slimmer against the block.
Use the window so both spines keep their colour.

title: Curling Cover
oneLiner: Photograph the curl of a magazine or paperback cover on the table.
details: Lay a magazine, a thin paperback or a catalogue on the table and lift one corner, or leave it if it curls on its own. Photograph that curl against the flatter rest of the cover. If nothing curls, bend a corner gently upward and hold it at the edge of the frame. Let any large title fall partly out of the picture.
tips: Get low and shoot across the cover so the curl rises.
Focus on the highest point of the curl.
constraint: The curl must be the highest part of the picture.

title: Weave of the Cover
oneLiner: Move in until one closed cover is nothing but texture.
details: Take any book or notebook and come close to the closed cover until the title drops out of frame. Cloth weave, paper grain or a scuffed patch should fill the picture. A plain notebook is a perfect subject. Window light from the side will show the grain.
tips: Angle the light across the cover rather than from straight above.
Tap the texture, not a shiny spot of glare.

title: Empty Seat from Above
oneLiner: Look straight down onto an empty chair and frame the whole seat.
details: Pick any chair or stool and leave the seat empty. Stand over it and point the camera down until the whole seat fits, with the legs starting at the edges. A plain seat is welcome, and so is a seat with a cushion, as long as you can see its boundary. Clear cups and clothes off it first.
tips: Hold the phone level so the seat stays a true rectangle or circle.
Lean over the seat if the back blocks it from a standing view.
constraint: The whole seat must be in the frame.

title: Four Feet on the Floor
oneLiner: Photograph every foot of a chair and the shadows gathered around them.
details: Set a chair or stool on a bare floor and get low so you can see every foot, or the whole pedestal if it has only one. Use window light, or a lamp from one side, so the feet throw shadows. If the daylight is even, move that lamp closer until each foot has its own shadow. The feet and their shadows are the subject, not the seat.
tips: Rest your elbows on the floor to keep the low angle steady.
Move the lamp until each foot throws a separate shadow.
constraint: Every foot must be in the frame.

title: Sweater Over the Back
oneLiner: Hang a sweater or coat over a chair back and shoot the drape from the side.
details: Drape a sweater, a coat, or a scarf over the back of a chair so the fabric falls in one clear shape. Shoot from the side, level with the top of the back, and let the cloth be the reason for the picture. If the chair has no tall back, hang the sweater over a stool and include the stool's edge. Smooth one side and leave the other folded.
tips: Stand to the side so the drape has a clear outline against the wall.
A plain wall behind the chair keeps the cloth readable.

title: Bars of the Back
oneLiner: Crowd the frame with the bars, slats, or spindles of a chair back.
details: Move close to the back of a chair until the bars, slats, or spindles repeat across the picture. Line them up so they run the same way through the frame. If the back is a solid panel, photograph the narrow gap between the seat and the back instead, and let that dark slot repeat only once, large. The chair's structure is the whole subject.
tips: Match the phone's tilt to the bars so they stay parallel.
Focus on the middle bar and let the nearest one soften slightly.

title: Chair Left Askew
oneLiner: Pull one chair away from the table and shoot the awkward angle.
details: Pull a chair or stool out from the table, the desk, or the wall, and leave it at a careless angle. Shoot from a standing height so you see both the chair and the edge it left behind. The awkwardness is the point, so do not tidy the angle. If you have no table, the gap between the chair and the wall tells the same story.
tips: Include a slice of the table or wall so the angle has something to miss.
Stand back far enough to show the whole chair and the gap.
constraint: The chair must not sit square to the table or the wall.

title: Where the Seat Wore
oneLiner: Move close to the worn, stained, or smoothest patch in the middle of the seat.
details: Look at the seat of a chair you use often and find the worn patch, a stain, a seam, or the smoothest spot. Move the camera close until that patch fills the frame. You are recording use, not advertising the chair. If the seat is uniform, the seam or the piping can take the same close treatment.
tips: Tap the worn area so the phone does not focus on the floor beyond.
Side light will show scuffs that flat light hides.

title: Between the Legs
oneLiner: Rest the camera on the floor and look out between the chair legs.
details: Set the phone on the floor under or just behind a chair, looking out through the legs. The legs become a frame for a bit of floor, a rug, or the opposite wall. Use the timer or the volume buttons so you are not holding the phone. A stool with a crossbar works as well as a dining chair.
tips: Use the two-second timer so the phone is still when it fires.
Slide the phone until one leg sits near each edge.
constraint: The camera must stay on the floor.

title: Almost Touching
oneLiner: Place two chairs so their legs nearly touch and shoot the narrow gap.
details: Bring two chairs, or a chair and a stool, close enough that two legs almost meet. If you only have one chair, use the table leg or a desk leg as the second upright. Focus on the narrow gap between them. The rest of the room can fall soft, because the almost-touch is the picture.
tips: Focus on the gap, not on the seat above it.
A low position makes the two legs feel taller.
constraint: The gap must be the sharpest part of the picture.

title: Folded and Leaning
oneLiner: Fold a chair flat, or push it tight to the wall, and shoot the compact shape.
