details: If your chair or stool folds, fold it and lean it somewhere safe, such as against a wall on the floor. If it does not fold, push the back tight to the wall so it looks stored. Photograph the compact shape from the side, including the point where it meets the wall. Do not balance it anywhere it could slip.
tips: Shoot from the side so the thin stored shape is obvious.
Leave a margin of wall so the chair has a plain ground.

title: Cup on the Empty Seat
oneLiner: Set a cup and a closed book on an empty chair and shoot from the side.
details: Place a cup and a closed book, or just the cup, on the seat of an empty chair. Shoot from the side at seat height so the objects and the chair read together. The chair should still feel like the subject, with the cup as a guest on it. Leave the back of the chair visible.
tips: Seat height keeps the cup from looming over the chair.
A plain seat shows the cup more clearly than a busy cushion.
constraint: Nothing else may share the seat.

title: Chair in Profile
oneLiner: Shoot a chair from the side so its outline reads clearly against a plain wall.
details: Place a chair or stool in front of the plainest wall you have. Stand to the side and frame the whole outline, from the top of the back to the feet. Shift until the outline does not merge with a doorway or a picture. The side view should explain the chair in one glance.
tips: A wall lighter or darker than the chair will separate the outline.
Move farther back if the feet are being cut off.

title: Where the Legs Join
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the joint where a chair leg meets the seat.
details: Find the joint, bracket, screw line, or glue point where a leg meets the seat. Move close until that meeting fills the picture. Side light will show the change of material or the shadow in the joint. Any chair or stool has this meeting place, even if it is only a weld or a folded tube.
tips: Use side light so the joint casts a small shadow.
Brace the phone against the seat edge if your hands wander.

title: Dent in the Cushion
oneLiner: Press one dent into a cushion or towel and photograph the hollow.
details: Put a cushion or a folded towel on the chair seat. Press one hollow with your hand, then take the hand away. Photograph the dent from the side so the hollow has a bright rim and a darker middle. If the cushion springs back, use a heavier book for a moment and then remove it before you shoot.
tips: Side light makes the hollow readable.
Shoot as soon as your hand is out of the way, before the foam rises.
constraint: The dent must be the main subject.

title: Under the Seat
oneLiner: Tip a light chair onto its side and photograph the underside.
details: Choose a light chair or a stool you can lower gently onto its side on the floor. Do not wrestle a heavy armchair. Once it is resting safely, photograph the underside: webbing, screws, a label, or plain wood. The raw hidden face is the subject, so fill the frame with it.
tips: Kneel beside the tipped chair rather than leaning it on yourself.
Clean the lens if dust from the floor smudges it.
constraint: The chair must rest fully on the floor.

title: Facing the Wall
oneLiner: Turn a chair to face the wall and shoot the gap between them.
details: Turn a chair or stool so the seat faces a wall, with a small gap between them. Stand behind the chair and frame that gap from the top of the back down to the floor. The wall should be plain enough that the gap reads as a clean slot. A wider gap makes the picture about the room, so keep it narrow.
tips: Line the phone up with the gap so the slot stays vertical.
A darker chair against a pale wall shows the gap best.
constraint: The gap must be visible from top to bottom.

title: Wheels or Glides
oneLiner: Get down and photograph the wheels, glides, or felt pads under a chair.
details: Look under an office chair, a dining chair, or a stool and find the wheels, plastic glides, or felt pads. Get the camera near the floor and fill the frame with one or two of them where they meet the floor. If the feet are bare wood or metal, photograph the end of the leg in the same way. A lamp from the side will separate the foot from the floor.
tips: Move a lamp to one side so the wheel separates from the floor.
Focus where the foot actually touches the floor.

title: Curve of the Arm
oneLiner: Follow one armrest, or the top rail, until that curve fills the frame.
details: If the chair has an arm, follow its curve with the camera until the bend fills the picture. If there is no arm, use the curved or straight top rail of the back in the same close way. You want the line of the chair, not the whole object. A plain background keeps that line easy to see.
tips: Shoot along the curve so it travels from one corner of the frame towards another.
Focus partway along the rail, where the bend is strongest.

title: Light Through the Weave
oneLiner: Backlight a woven seat, or a knit draped over the chair, so the holes glow.
details: Place a chair with a woven, cane, or mesh seat in front of a bright window, or drape a loose-knit sweater over any chair back and do the same. Stand on the darker side so the light comes through the holes. Move until the bright gaps are the clearest part of the picture. A solid seat can sit out of frame if the knit is doing the work.
tips: Expose for the bright holes so they do not burn to white.
Switch the room lamp off so it does not fill the holes with flat light.
constraint: The light must come from behind the weave.

title: A Leg on a Book
oneLiner: Slip a thin book under one chair leg and photograph the small tilt.
details: Slide a thin book, a magazine, or a folded cloth under one leg of a steady chair. The tilt should be slight, so the chair stays planted and cannot rock away. Photograph from the side, low, so you can see the raised leg and the book together. Use only one support, and take it away when you are done.
tips: Choose a slim book so the chair cannot tip.
Get low enough to see a thin gap under the raised leg.
constraint: Only one leg may be raised.

title: Light Across the Seat
oneLiner: Let a patch of window light fall across an empty chair seat.
details: Set a chair or stool near a window and leave the seat empty. Look for a patch of daylight lying on the seat, and frame that light rather than the whole room. A cushion edge may stay if it shows where the light ends. If the patch is bigger than the seat, move the chair until the light has a clear boundary on it.
tips: Turn indoor lamps off so the window is the only light on the seat.
Shoot from the side so the patch has a visible boundary.

title: Shadow of the Back
oneLiner: Cast a chair's shadow on a wall and give the shadow most of the frame.
details: Set a chair near a plain indoor wall. Use window light or a lamp from the side so the back throws a clear shadow. If the daylight is even, move a lamp to the side until the shadow sharpens. Frame the picture so the shadow takes more space than the chair, and let the chair itself be partly out of frame.
tips: Bring the lamp closer to the chair if you want a larger shadow.
Focus on the shadow edge, not on the chair.
constraint: The shadow must take up more of the frame than the chair.

title: Through the Bars
oneLiner: Look through a chair back at one object in the room.
details: Put a chair between you and something simple, such as a lamp, a plant, or a doorway. Look through the bars of the back, or through the gap under the seat if the back is solid, and include that object in the opening. The chair should feel like a frame you are looking through. Move until the object sits cleanly in one gap.
tips: Choose to focus either on the bars or on the object, and stick to it.
A plain wall behind the object keeps the gap easy to read.
constraint: The object beyond must be visible through the chair.

title: Lip of the Seat
oneLiner: Crop to the front edge of a chair seat so that line leads across.
details: Move close to the front lip of a chair or stool indoors. Crop so that edge runs across the frame, with a little of the seat above it and the floor or a rug below. Wear, a chip, or the thickness of the seat can show along that line. The rest of the chair can stay out.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the front edge so the line stays straight.
Side light will mark the thickness of the seat.

title: Strap Over the Back
oneLiner: Hang a bag strap or a belt over a chair back and shoot the line.
details: Drape a bag strap, a belt, or a thin scarf so it makes one line over the back of a chair, not a coat piled on the seat. Shoot from the side so you see the line and the chair that holds it. A plain wall can be the background. Take the strap off afterwards if the chair is in use.
tips: Let one end hang lower so the line has a direction.
Keep the seat mostly clear so the strap stays the accent.
constraint: The strap must hang over the back, not lie on the seat.

title: Tucked in Square
oneLiner: Push a chair squarely under the table and shoot that neat fit.
details: Slide a chair or stool in until it sits square to the table, the desk, or the wall. Shoot from a standing height so the lined-up edges are obvious. The neatness is the point, so straighten it before you raise the phone. If you have no table, push the chair back until it sits parallel to the wall.
tips: Include the table edge so the square angle has something to meet.
Crouch slightly if the tabletop hides the seat.
constraint: The chair must sit square to the table or the wall.

title: Seen from Behind
oneLiner: Stand behind a chair and photograph the back, with the seat hidden.
details: Place a chair in front of a plain wall and stand directly behind it. Frame the back so it fills the picture, and keep the seat out of view or only a hint at the bottom. The shape of the back is the whole subject. Shift if the outline merges with a doorway or a picture.
tips: Fill the frame from the top of the back to just above the seat.
Move closer if the seat keeps entering the bottom of the frame.

title: One Red on White
oneLiner: Place a single red object on a white or pale surface and let it dominate.
details: Use a tomato, a pen, a sock, or a lid, anything red you already have. Clear the surface so nothing else competes with that red. Set the object off to one side so the pale area has room to breathe. The simplicity is the picture.
tips: Use daylight so the white surface does not drift towards grey.
Tap the red object so the phone keeps its colour true.
constraint: Only one red item may appear in the frame.

title: Citrus Slice Burst
oneLiner: Open a lemon or orange and photograph the bright interior on a dark plate.
details: Pull a lemon, an orange, or a grapefruit apart with your hands, or break open a colourful candy if you have no citrus. Set the bright face on a dark plate, a dark board, or a dark pan while it still looks fresh. Window light from behind will make the colour glow.
tips: Fill the frame with the open face rather than the whole fruit.
Pat the board dry if juice makes a distracting shine.

title: Brightest Petal or Leaf
oneLiner: Isolate the brightest petal, leaf, or piece of fruit you can find at home.
details: Use a houseplant, a herb, a piece of fruit, or a leaf from a bunch you already have indoors. Move close until one vivid petal, leaf, or fruit fills most of the frame. Let the background fall soft so that colour stays the subject. Gentle window light keeps it rich without a hard shine.
tips: Get close and let the background fall out of focus.
Draw a curtain across if a hard beam flattens the colour.
constraint: Only one flower, leaf, or fruit may be the subject.

title: Rainbow Book Spines
oneLiner: Stack or line up books so their spines make a stripe of colour.
details: Pull a few books, notebooks, or magazines from a shelf and turn the spines towards the camera. You do not need a full rainbow, because three strong colours are enough. Titles do not matter, and you can turn a spine away if the lettering shouts. Shoot straight on so the colour bands stay upright.
tips: Sort the spines by colour before you shoot.
Leave a small gap between spines so each colour stays separate.

title: Spice Jar Spectrum
oneLiner: Line up spice jars or tea tins so their contents show a run of colour.
details: Choose jars with bold contents, such as paprika, turmeric, tea, lentils, or pasta. Set them on the counter with the contents visible, and turn labels away if they carry a logo. Side light from a window makes the powders and leaves glow. Put the lids back on when you are finished.
tips: Wipe the bases so the jars stand without a wobble.
Shoot from counter height rather than from above.

title: A Door of One Colour
oneLiner: Let one interior door of a strong colour own the picture.
details: Choose a door inside the home that is already one strong colour: a front door seen from inside, a cupboard door, or a closet. Stand square to it so the sides stay upright. Keep the frame simple: the door and maybe a handle. If every door is neutral, hang a bright towel on the inside of one and fill the shape with that colour instead.
tips: Lock the exposure on the door so a nearby window does not bleach the colour.
Include the handle or the towel hem so the colour has a scale.
constraint: The door or the towel must fill at least half the frame.

title: The Bright Small One
oneLiner: Set one vivid small object on a grey or wooden surface.
details: Choose a toy, a game piece, a bottle cap, a hair tie, or a small fruit. Set it on grey carpet, bare wood, or plain paper so the colour sits against a quiet ground. Move in until the object feels large. Turn it until the brightest face is towards the window.
tips: Use side daylight so the object gets a soft shadow and a bright face.
Clear other colourful bits out of the background before you shoot.

title: Three Small Bottles
oneLiner: Line three small coloured bottles up in a simple gradient.
details: Use nail polish, food colouring, ink, or small paint pots, and if you own none of those, tint three small jars with juice. Line up exactly three on a bathroom or kitchen counter. Let the glass and the liquid add shine. The counter can stay ordinary at the edges.
tips: A pale ceiling reflected in the glass gives cleaner highlights.
Wipe the glass so dried drips do not muddy the colours.
constraint: Use exactly three bottles or jars.

title: Colour Canopy
oneLiner: Open a bright jacket or umbrella indoors and shoot from underneath.
details: Indoors, open an umbrella or stretch a bright jacket, tote, or dish towel above the lens so the colour fills the frame. A hem, a seam, or a handle can stay in for scale. Keep the window and the ceiling out. Any strong colour you can hold is enough.
tips: Shoot from underneath the cloth so the colour becomes a canopy.
Lower the exposure a little so the colour stays deep.

title: Yellow Against Grey
oneLiner: Sit a yellow mug on a grey or brown counter and let the yellow lead.
details: Find the yellowest mug, bowl, or sponge you own and set it on a grey, brown, or steel surface. Clear other bright objects away. Daylight from the side should light the yellow without blowing it out to white. Move closer until the yellow is the first thing the eye finds.
tips: If the mug is pale, put it against the darkest part of the counter.
Tap the yellow, then check it did not turn white.
constraint: The mug must be the only yellow object.

title: Blue Sponge, White Sink
oneLiner: Drop a blue or green sponge into a white or steel sink and move in close.
details: Use a sponge, a cloth, or a glove in a strong blue or green. Set it in the empty sink so the bowl stays pale or metallic around it. Shoot from close and slightly above. The colour should read instantly against the sink.
tips: Rinse the sponge if old stains dull the colour.
Leave the faucet out of frame unless it is the same colour.

title: Banana on Blue
oneLiner: Lay a banana across a blue cloth and crop in tight.
details: Put a banana, a lemon, or a yellow pepper on a blue towel, a blue folder, or a blue shirt. The pair of colours is the picture, so crop until little else remains. Window light from the side will model the fruit without hiding the blue. If you have no blue cloth, a blue mug beside the fruit can take its place.
tips: Smooth the blue cloth so wrinkles do not break the colour.
Turn the fruit until the yellow is at its strongest.
constraint: Both the yellow and the blue must be in the frame.

title: Apple on Steel
oneLiner: Set a red apple on a steel sink or a dark tray and fill the frame with it.
details: Use a red apple, a tomato, or a red pepper. Place it on stainless steel, a black tray, or a dark pan so the red separates cleanly. Move close until the fruit is large. A little side light will show the curve without turning the red dull.
tips: Polish the fruit with a dry cloth so the red looks even.
Shoot slightly above the fruit so the dark surface surrounds it.
constraint: The fruit must fill at least half the frame.

title: Fan of Colour
oneLiner: Fan coloured pencils, pens, or markers so the tips make a colour arc.
details: Gather pencils, pens, markers, or crayons and fan them on a pale table. The tips or the caps should make a clear arc of different colours. You only need four or five. Shoot from above so the fan reads in one glance.
tips: Align the tips along a curve before you pick up the phone.
A pale table keeps every colour equally readable.
constraint: At least four different colours must show.

title: Three Tinted Glasses
oneLiner: Tint three glasses of water with juice or food colouring.
details: Fill three clear glasses with water and tint each a different colour using juice, jam stirred in, or food colouring. Set them in a row on a white surface by a window so the liquids glow. Shoot from the side, through the glass, rather than from above. A plain background keeps the three colours honest.
tips: Backlight the glasses with the window so the liquids turn translucent.
Wipe the outsides so drips do not streak the colour.
constraint: Use exactly three glasses.

title: Block of Sticky Notes
oneLiner: Stand a block of sticky notes so one strong colour faces the camera.
details: Use a pad of sticky notes, a stack of coloured paper, or a single bright envelope. Stand it on a neutral desk so the colour faces you. If you only have one note, stick it to a grey folder or a plain wall. Shoot straight on so the colour is a flat shape.
tips: Peel one sheet slightly if you want a thin second edge of colour.
Keep shadows off the paper so the colour stays flat and even.
constraint: The paper must be the only object.

title: Bottle of Green
oneLiner: Stand a bright dish soap bottle against a plain sink.
details: Stand a dish soap bottle, a shampoo bottle, or a cleaning bottle with a strong colour on the edge of the sink or on a white counter. Turn the label away or crop it out. The bottle's own colour is the subject, so the background should stay plain. Side light will show the curve of the plastic.
tips: Crop above the label if the branding is louder than the colour.
Set the bottle away from other bottles so it stands alone.

title: Soap on a White Dish
oneLiner: Place a pink, blue, or green soap on a white dish and shoot from above.
details: Set a coloured bar of soap, a wrapped soap, or a colourful sponge on a white plate or a pale sink. Shoot from directly above so the colour sits in the middle of the pale shape. Dry the soap if water dulls it. If your soap is white, use a coloured washcloth underneath it instead.
tips: Centre the phone over the plate so the rim stays even.
A dry bar keeps a stronger colour than a wet one.
constraint: Shoot from directly above.

title: Red Board, Empty
oneLiner: Clear a red or blue chopping board and photograph the colour field.
details: Use a chopping board, a folder, a tray, or a placemat in one strong colour. Clear it completely and shoot the surface so the colour runs to the edges of the frame. A corner of the board can show against the counter if you want a boundary. Daylight from the side avoids a dull sheen in the middle.
tips: Wipe crumbs away so the colour reads as one field.
Tilt the board slightly if a shiny patch hides the colour.
constraint: The coloured surface must fill the frame.

title: Spatula on a Pale Plate
oneLiner: Lay an orange or red spatula on a pale plate and crop to the colour.
details: Use a spatula, a wooden spoon with a coloured handle, or a bright straw. Lay it on a white or cream plate so the colour has a quiet surround. Crop until the utensil and the plate are the whole picture. Turn the handle until the strongest colour faces the light.
tips: Shoot from above so the plate becomes a simple circle or oval.
Keep other utensils out of the pile.

title: Blue Cover
oneLiner: Stand a vivid notebook or folder against a neutral wall.
details: Choose a notebook, a folder, or a book with a strong plain colour. Stand it against a white, grey, or wood wall and move in until the cover is large. Hide the title with your crop if the words are louder than the colour. Soft daylight from the side will keep the cover even.
tips: Shoot straight on so the cover stays a clean rectangle.
Slide any busy posters out of the background.

title: Glow on the Wall
oneLiner: Hold a coloured glass or bottle to the window and shoot the glow on a wall.
details: Hold a coloured bottle, a tinted glass, or a sheet of coloured plastic against a window. Aim the coloured light onto a plain wall or a white sheet and photograph that glow, not the view outside. Move the glass until the patch of colour is obvious. Clear glass will not work, so tint it with a candy wrapper if you need to.
tips: Keep the glass out of the frame if you want only the coloured patch.
A white wall shows the tint more clearly than a cream one.
constraint: The coloured glow must land on a plain wall.

title: One Loud Cushion
oneLiner: Isolate one bright cushion on a grey or beige sofa.
details: Pick the brightest cushion, pillow, or folded blanket you own and set it on a neutral sofa, bed, or chair. Move the other cushions out of frame. The picture is one loud colour against a quiet ground. Daylight from a window beside the sofa is enough.
tips: Plump the cushion so the colour reads as one clear shape.
Crouch so the neutral furniture fills the background.

title: Jam in the Jar
oneLiner: Shoot the red or purple of jam, honey, or sauce through the glass.
details: Hold a jar of jam, honey, sauce, or pickled vegetables up to the window. Photograph through the glass so the colour of what is inside fills the frame. Turn the label to the back. If the jar is dull, open it and shoot the surface of the jam in the jar from above.
tips: Press close so the label and the lid stay out of frame.
Window light behind the jar makes the colour glow.

title: Lids in a Row
oneLiner: Line up marker lids or bottle caps in colour order on a pale table.
details: Collect lids, caps, or buttons in several colours and line them up on white paper or a pale table. Put them in an order that pleases you, from cool to warm or simply from bright to bright. Five is enough. Shoot from low and along the row, or from above if that keeps the colours clearer.
tips: Space them evenly so no single lid crowds the next.
A low angle makes the colours stack into a skyline.
constraint: At least five lids or caps must be in the frame.

title: One Sock on White
oneLiner: Lay one brightly coloured sock on a white sheet and leave the rest bare.
details: Choose one sock, glove, or small cloth in a strong colour and lay it on a white sheet, a white towel, or white paper. Leave the surrounding area empty. Smooth the white ground so it stays a clean field. Shoot from above and let the sock sit off to one side.
tips: Pull the sock flat so the colour is a clear shape.
Check the white area for other clothes and clear them.
constraint: Only one sock or cloth may be in the frame.

title: Purple Onion Skin
oneLiner: Move close on the purple skin of an onion or a red cabbage leaf.
details: Use a red onion, a red cabbage leaf, a beet, or a piece of purple packaging. Move close until the purple fills the frame, with only a thin pale edge if you need a boundary. Daylight from the side shows the papery skin or the leaf veins. You do not need to cut anything.
tips: Peel one dry outer layer by hand if it is dull, and stop there.
A pale plate under the onion gives the purple an edge.

title: Berries in a White Bowl
oneLiner: Heap blueberries, grapes, or tomatoes in a white bowl and shoot from above.
details: Fill a white or pale bowl with one strongly coloured food: blueberries, grapes, cherry tomatoes, or frozen peas. Shoot from above so the colour sits inside the pale rim. If you have only two or three pieces, push them together so the colour still clusters. Window light from the side keeps the fruit from looking flat.
tips: Dry the fruit so water drops do not outshine the colour.
Keep the bowl's rim visible as a pale border.
constraint: The bowl must be white or pale.

title: Straw in Clear Water
oneLiner: Stand a coloured straw or spoon in a clear glass and crop tight.
details: Fill a clear glass with water and stand a coloured straw, a plastic spoon, or a pen in it. The colour should show both above the water and through it. Set the glass by a window on a pale surface. Crop tight so the coloured line is the subject.
tips: Shoot from the side so you see the colour bend at the water line.
Use a plain background, or the glass will mirror the room.

title: Looking into Colour
oneLiner: Look down into a coloured mug and let the interior colour fill the frame.
details: Choose a mug, a bowl, or a cup with a strong colour inside. Look straight down into it and let that colour fill most of the picture. The rim can show as a thin border. Empty is fine, and daylight from a window beside you will light the inside.
tips: Hold the phone level so the rim stays even all the way round.
If the inside is shadowed, tilt the mug towards the window.
constraint: The interior colour must dominate the frame.

title: One Colour in the Fridge
oneLiner: Open the fridge and frame one vivid item against the pale interior.
details: Open the fridge and choose one strongly coloured thing: a pepper, a jar, a pot of yoghurt, or a drink. Move other bright items aside for a moment so the pale interior surrounds that one colour. Daylight from the kitchen, or the fridge lamp if the room is dim, should light it. Close the door when you have the picture.
tips: Decide the frame before you linger, then shoot and shut the door.
Tap the colourful item so the white interior does not fool the exposure.
constraint: Only one strongly coloured item may stay in the frame.

title: Bath Mat from Above
oneLiner: Point the camera down at the strongest colour on a bath mat.
details: Use a bath mat, or a bright towel laid on the bathroom floor if the mat is dull. Point the camera straight down and crop to the boldest patch of colour. The bathroom floor around it can stay in as a quieter border. Keep your feet out of the frame.
tips: Hold the phone out so your shadow misses the mat.
If the colour is pale, move closer until it dominates.

title: Small Note, Big Ground
oneLiner: Stick one bright note on a large neutral surface and leave the rest bare.
details: Use a sticky note, a square of coloured paper, or a piece of packaging in one strong colour. Stick it on a fridge door, a grey folder, or a plain wall, well away from other colours. The note should stay modest, with a wide quiet area around it. Shoot straight on so the paper stays rectangular.
tips: Let the note occupy about a third of the frame and leave the rest empty.
Keep other magnets and papers out of the crop.
constraint: The note must be a single colour.

title: Cable on the Boards
oneLiner: Lay a bright cable across pale floorboards so the colour crosses.
details: Use a charging cable, a shoelace, a ribbon, or a strip of cloth in a strong colour. Lay it across pale floorboards, a grey carpet, or a plain rug indoors. The ground should stay neutral. Shoot from above and keep that line as the only bright colour.
tips: Pull the cable straight so the colour reads as one clean line.
Brush fluff aside if it breaks the quiet ground.
constraint: The coloured line must cross from one edge of the frame to another.

title: Pot of One Colour
oneLiner: Move close on a plant pot until its colour fills the picture.
details: Find a pot, a jug, or a plastic bowl in one strong colour and set it on a shelf or the floor indoors. Move close until that colour fills the picture, with only a hint of the background. A plant inside the pot is optional and should not take over. Wipe dust off so the colour looks even.
tips: Turn the pot so any printed words face away.
Soft window light keeps the colour from blowing out to white.

title: Tote Against the Wall
oneLiner: Stand a bright tote indoors against a plain wall and crop any logo.
details: Use a colourful bag, a tote, or a backpack and stand it against a plain indoor wall or the inside of a door. Crop or turn it so logos and words disappear and the colour remains. A handle or a fold can stay for shape. Move close enough that the colour dominates.
tips: Turn the printed face to the wall if the words are large.
Prop the bag so it stays still before you shoot.
constraint: Any logo or lettering must be cropped out.

title: Fruit Against the Glass
oneLiner: Set one piece of fruit on the sill so window light fills its colour.
details: Place one orange, apple, lemon, or tomato on an indoor windowsill. Stand on the indoor side and let the window light the colour from behind or from the side. The wall or the window frame should stay plain. One piece of fruit is the whole subject.
tips: Leave a plain margin around the fruit so the colour has room.
Draw a sheer curtain if the highlight on the skin turns white.
constraint: Only one piece of fruit may be in the frame.

title: Scarf on the Handle
oneLiner: Knot a bright scarf on an indoor handle and move in close.
details: Tie or hang a bright scarf, a dish towel, or a sock on a door handle or a hook inside the home. Move close so the colour fills most of the frame and the door becomes a quiet background. A knot or a hem gives the colour a shape. Any interior door will do.
tips: Pull the fabric so the strongest colour faces the camera.
Keep the handle small so it does not compete with the cloth.

title: Pegs Along the Edge
oneLiner: Clip three coloured clothespins along a towel and shoot the row.
details: Clip clothespins, hair ties, or loops of coloured tape along the edge of a towel, a sleeve, or a cushion indoors. Three colours are enough, and they should be easy to tell apart. Shoot along the row so the colours line up. If you have no clothespins, fold three coloured scraps over the edge of a book.
tips: Space them a finger apart so each colour stays distinct.
Use a plain towel or cushion so the clips do the shouting.
constraint: Use exactly three coloured clips or scraps.

title: Green Glass in Daylight
oneLiner: Raise a green bottle to the window and let daylight shine through it.
details: Indoors, hold a green, brown, or blue bottle up towards a window, with a plain wall or a curtain beside it rather than a view outside. The glass should glow with its own colour. An empty bottle works, and so does one with water in it. Turn any label away from the camera.
tips: Hold the bottle in front of a plain wall so the colour separates.
Focus on the glass edge where the colour is deepest.

title: Bright Lining
oneLiner: Open a bag or case and photograph the brightest lining you can find.
details: Open a bag, a pencil case, a glasses case, or a box with a coloured inside. Point the camera into the opening so the lining or the interior colour fills the frame. A zip or an edge can stay as a border. If the inside is dull, tuck a bright sock or cloth in and shoot that colour in the opening.
tips: Stand so window light falls into the opening.
Crop out logos on the outside of the bag.
constraint: A rim, zip, or edge of the opening must stay in the frame.

title: Colander Colour
oneLiner: Move in on a bright colander or sieve until the colour owns the frame.
details: Use a colourful colander, a sieve, or a bright plastic bowl in the kitchen. Move close until that colour fills the picture, and let the holes or the rim give it shape. A plain counter can show at the edge. If nothing you own is that bright, line a plain bowl with a strong-coloured cloth for the shot.
tips: Shoot from slightly above so the inside colour shows.
Wipe water spots off so the colour stays even.

title: Laces in Colour
oneLiner: Move close on brightly coloured laces against a dark shoe.
details: Use a shoe, a sneaker, or a boot with laces in a strong colour. If the laces are dull, thread a bright ribbon or a strip of cloth through a few eyelets instead. Move close so the colour of the laces leads, and the shoe stays dark behind them. Shoot indoors by a window.
tips: Pull the laces loose so the colour makes a clear line.
Tap the laces so the dark shoe does not underexpose them.
constraint: The laces must be the brightest colour in the frame.

title: A Drop of Colour
oneLiner: Drop juice into a glass of water and catch the bloom.
details: Fill a clear glass with water and set it by a window on a pale surface. Add one drop of juice or food colouring, and photograph while the colour is still blooming. You want the moving stain of colour, not a glass that has already mixed through. A plain background keeps the colour honest.
tips: Shoot from the side so you see the colour travel through the water.
Take a short burst, because the bloom changes quickly.
constraint: The colour must still be spreading, not fully mixed.

title: Reading Nook Glow
oneLiner: Capture the cosiest spot where you sit with a book or tablet.
details: Frame your chair, cushion, or corner with a blanket and a side table visible. Include a lamp or window glow, with no need to stage new props. The seat should look ready for you to sit in.
tips: Warm the white balance if the corner looks blue.
Include one personal object, not a crowd of them.
Shoot from the height of the seat.
constraint: Leave the place you would sit empty and visible.

title: Blanket and Pillow Stack
oneLiner: Arrange a blanket and pillow so the pile looks irresistibly soft.
details: Fold or drape a blanket over a pillow on a sofa or bed edge. Shoot close enough to see fabric texture and loose folds. Keep the palette calm, since this is about comfort rather than a tidy display.
tips: Fluff the pillow so the corners look plump.
Use side light to give the folds a little depth.
Crop out busy patterns elsewhere in the room.

title: Lamp Pool of Light
oneLiner: Photograph a table lamp casting a warm pool of light in an otherwise dim corner.
details: Turn off the ceiling lights and let one lamp define the scene. Include the base, the shade, and the lit surface beside it. Let the surrounding shadows stay soft so the corner feels sheltered.
tips: Expose for the lit patch, not the dark walls.
Keep the bulb itself hidden by the shade.
A book or mug may sit in the pool if it already belongs there.
constraint: Only one light source in the room.

title: Mug on Side Table
oneLiner: Place a warm drink on a side table and shoot a small cosy still life.
details: Set a mug on a table near a sofa or bed, with a coaster, a book, or a remote if one already lives there. Steam is optional and not required. Frame tightly so the table feels like a little island of calm.
tips: Shoot while the drink is still hot only if you want a wisp of steam.
Keep the background as a soft sofa or wall.
Try a slightly low angle looking towards the mug.
constraint: The mug must sit on a table, not in a hand.

title: Slippers by the Chair
oneLiner: Photograph slippers or socks waiting where you kick them off at home.
details: Place the footwear where you naturally leave it, by a chair, a bed, or a rug. Shoot from standing height looking down, or from the floor looking across. The scene should feel lived-in rather than arranged for display.
tips: Leave the pair slightly askew.
Include a bit of rug or floor texture.
Soft daylight through a sheer curtain, or a lamp bounced off the wall, keeps the light gentle.

title: Shelf With a Plant
oneLiner: Frame a shelf where books and something green share the same cosy ledge.
details: Choose one shelf or windowsill with a few books or small objects and something green. A houseplant is ideal, and a herb stem or a few leaves in a glass will do if that is what you have. Let the green sit off to one side so it softens the hard edge of the shelf. Keep the shot to that ledge rather than a tour of the room.
tips: Dust the shelf lip before you shoot.
Use light from the window on the leaves.
A vertical frame suits a tall plant.
constraint: Include at least one book and one plant.

title: Window Seat Pause
oneLiner: Shoot the view from a window seat or sill with cloth and glass in frame.
details: Compose so the cushion or ledge occupies the foreground and the glass leads outward. If the sill is bare, lay a folded towel, sweater, or cushion there so the foreground has cloth. Day or night both work, and whatever is outside can stay soft or dark. The cosy part is the seat.
tips: Clean the smudge on the bit of glass you include.
Expose for the interior so the outside may go bright.
A folded blanket on the ledge helps if you have one.
constraint: The foreground must show fabric or cushion texture.

title: Candle and Closed Book
oneLiner: Set an unlit candle or a small jar beside a closed book for a calm tableau.
details: Arrange the candle or jar and a book on a tray or table, and leave any wick unlit. Add a pen or reading glasses only if they are already nearby. Shoot warm and close so the scene feels like the moment before sleep.
tips: An unlit candle or a plain jar still reads as evening and stays safe.
Choose a book and a candle or jar of similar height.
Use a lamp rather than a harsh ceiling light.
constraint: Leave the candle or jar unlit.

title: Radiator Cloth Corner
oneLiner: Drape a towel over a radiator or chair back and include the corner.
details: Any radiator, heated towel bar, or chair back near a lamp will do. Let the cloth hang with one natural fold, and include the wall and a slice of floor so it reads as a place. You are photographing a small waiting warmth, not a study of cloth alone.
tips: Let window light skim the fold from the side.
Crop the rest of the room out past the corner.
constraint: Show both the cloth and the place where wall meets floor.

title: Duvet Corner Fold
oneLiner: Turn down one corner of the duvet and photograph the invitation.
details: Fold a corner of a duvet, sheet, or blanket back so the layers show. Stand at the side of the bed or sofa and include a pillow at the far edge. Keep the rest of the room out so the spot feels quiet.
tips: Shoot from the height of the mattress.
Warm the white balance if the sheets look icy blue.

title: Cardigan on the Chair
oneLiner: Leave a cardigan or hoodie over a chair back and frame the empty seat.
details: Use the chair you actually sit in. Let the sleeves fall as they fall. Include a little of the floor or rug so the chair belongs to a room.
tips: Step to the side so the chair back makes a strong shape.
Expose for the fabric if a window sits behind it.
constraint: The seat stays empty.

title: Headphone Cushion Nest
oneLiner: Build a small listening spot with headphones, a cushion, and low light.
details: Set headphones or earphones on a cushion in the corner of a sofa, a bed, or the floor against a wall. Light the spot with a lamp already in the room, kept low. Shoot from a low seated height.
tips: Tuck the cable into a loose coil that does not cross the cushion.
Tap focus on the headphones.

title: Breakfast by the Window
oneLiner: Set tea or toast on a side table by a window and keep the frame tight.
details: Whatever you are actually having is enough: a plate, a mug, and a napkin. Place it where you would sit, and include the chair edge or the sill. Leave the food as it is, since the picture is the pause.
tips: Shoot before you sit so the chair stays empty.
Use the window as the only light on the table.
constraint: No ceiling light, only the window.

title: Footstool Book Rest
oneLiner: Rest a closed book on a footstool or low box and shoot across it.
details: If you have no footstool, a sturdy box or a low stool is enough. Add a cushion beside it so the spot looks ready. Get down to the height of the book and let the background be only the nearby chair or sofa.
tips: Put the book on a lower third with the grid.
Move closer until the chair behind goes soft.

title: Basket of Wool
oneLiner: Place wool socks or a hat in a basket and shoot down into it.
details: A basket, a bowl, or a tote on the floor by a chair is the corner. Let the wool spill a little over the rim. Shoot from above and slightly to the side so the inside stays dark and soft.
tips: Include a chair leg or the sofa edge for context.
Focus on the rim rather than the darkest wool.
constraint: The basket or bowl must sit on the floor.

title: Sheet Fort Opening
oneLiner: Drape a sheet between two chairs and photograph the opening.
details: Two chairs, a sofa and a chair, or a chair and the side of a bed will hold a sheet or a blanket. Put one cushion inside and leave the rest simple. Kneel at the opening and shoot into the little room, using the cloth edges as a frame.
tips: Expose for the inside so the entrance stays bright.
Smooth only the cloth along the top of the opening.

title: Three Things at Bedside
oneLiner: Clear a bedside surface down to three comforting objects and shoot it.
details: A glass of water, a book, and a lamp are plenty, or any three things already there. Move the rest out of frame. Shoot from pillow height, as if you had just looked sideways.
tips: Turn the lamp on and the ceiling light off.
Shift an inch if a highlight hides the rim of the glass.
constraint: Exactly three objects on the surface.

title: Pillow Hollow
oneLiner: Photograph the hollow in a pillow where a head has just rested.
details: Sit up and leave the pillow as it is, or press a hollow with your hand and take the hand away. Move close so the crease and the shadow inside it fill the frame. Include a little of the sheet so it still feels like a bed.
tips: Use side light so the hollow has a dark middle.
Hold the phone level with the pillow, not above it.

title: Sofa Arm Nest
oneLiner: Pull a throw into the corner of a sofa and shoot that nest.
details: Rumple a blanket into the angle where the arm meets the back, or into the corner of a bed if you have no sofa. Add one cushion and stop. Stand so the lines of the seat lead into that corner, and keep the rest of the room outside the frame.
tips: Shoot at sitting height.
Warm the white balance if the throw looks grey and blue.
constraint: The inner corner of the seat must be in the frame.

title: Robe on the Hook
oneLiner: Frame a robe or towel on a bathroom hook with the door ajar.
details: The comfort is the warmer light on cloth against cooler tile. Open the door a little so the robe has space, and include the hook and a slice of wall. Skip any mirror that would reflect you.
tips: Stand so a mirror cannot see you.
Expose for the robe and let the tile go a little dark.

title: Floor Seat by the Wall
oneLiner: Make a floor seat with two cushions and a book against a wall.
details: Choose a corner where two walls meet, or where a sofa ends. Set the cushions so they look used, not freshly plumped, and lean a book on the wall. Shoot from standing height, including the baseboard.
tips: Include the line where the two walls meet.
Switch off the ceiling light if a lamp is nearby.
constraint: The book must lean on the wall, not lie flat.

title: Curtain Meets Chair
oneLiner: Draw a curtain or towel at the window until it brushes a chair, then shoot.
details: Pull any chair to the window. Let a curtain, a blind, or a towel hung at the side fall in one soft vertical, and include the place where it meets the chair. The corner between window and seat is the subject.
tips: Use only the light coming through the curtain.
Focus where the cloth meets the chair.

title: Hidden Warmth Lump
oneLiner: Hide a flask or a rolled sweater under a blanket and shoot the lump.
details: You do not need to boil anything. A flask, a hot water bottle, or a rolled sweater under a blanket on the bed or sofa makes the shape. Shoot from the side so the bump is clear and the blanket edge leads in.
tips: Side light will describe the bump better than a ceiling light.
Keep the background as the plain bed or sofa.
constraint: The flask, bottle, or sweater stays hidden.

title: Closed Laptop Evening
oneLiner: Set a closed laptop or a notebook beside a folded blanket and shoot it.
details: On a sofa or bed, set a closed laptop, a tablet, or a notebook next to a folded blanket or a cushion. Include a mug if one is already there. Keep every screen dark and the arrangement slight, as if the evening is finished.
tips: Shoot from a low corner of the sofa.
Dim the room to a single lamp.

title: Glasses on the Page
oneLiner: Leave glasses or a pen on an open book in the chair you use.
details: Open a book to any page on the seat or a wide arm. Rest glasses, a pen, or a bookmark on the pages and take your hands away. Shoot from above so the seat fills the frame.
tips: Angle the phone to dodge glare on the lenses.
Focus on the glasses or the pen and let the page go slightly soft.
constraint: Your hands stay out of the frame.

title: Lights Behind a Cushion
oneLiner: Coil small lights behind a cushion in a dark corner.
details: Turn the room lights off. If you have a short string of small lights, coil them behind a cushion where two walls or a sofa arm meet. If you do not, set a lamp on the floor behind the cushion so only a warm rim shows.
tips: Expose for the cushion, not the brightest bulb.
Lean the phone against a book so the lights stay as dots.

title: Tray of Tea Things
oneLiner: Group a tea tin, a mug, and a spoon on a tray in a quiet corner.
details: A tray on a side table, a stool, or the counter where you wait for the kettle is the spot. Keep the group tight and include the wall or tile behind it. Leave the mug empty or full, and keep the kettle out if it would steal the frame.
tips: Shoot at the height of the mug.
Use window light from one side only.
constraint: Three objects on the tray, and no more.

title: Mug Against the Glass
oneLiner: Set a mug on the sill and shoot it against the dim glass.
details: Evening is ideal, though daytime works if the room is warmer than the view. Place the mug where you would stand with it, then take your hand away. Include the window frame as the edge of this small corner.
tips: Expose for the mug so the glass goes dark.
Wipe a circle of the pane behind the mug.

title: Socks Under the Throw
oneLiner: Slide socked feet under a blanket edge and shoot along them.
details: Sit on the sofa or bed and pull a blanket to your ankles. Point the phone along your legs towards the far arm or the foot of the bed. Keep your face out, and let the picture be the warm line of the blanket.
tips: Rest the phone on the cushion so it stays low.
Focus on the blanket edge nearest the lens.
constraint: No face, and no skin above the ankle.

title: Chair Beyond the Doorway
oneLiner: From a doorway, frame the chair that sits in the warm part of the room.
details: Let the door frame border the picture. The chair should sit in lamp light or window light, with the corners of the room falling darker. Tidy only the chair, not the whole room.
tips: Lean on the door frame to steady the phone.
Expose for the lit chair and let the surround go dark.

title: Notebook in the Lamp
oneLiner: Open a notebook beneath a lamp and shoot the page inside the pool.
details: Any notebook or a sheet of letter paper will do. Sit it in the lit patch on a table in a corner, with a pen beside it. If the page is private, turn to a blank sheet and write one ordinary word.
tips: Switch every other light off.
Tilt the page so the lamp does not glare into the lens.
constraint: Only one word on the page may be readable.

title: Three Cushion Lean
oneLiner: Stack three cushions, or folded towels, and shoot the little tower.
details: A corner of the sofa, the bed, or the floor against a wall works. Let them lean rather than lining them up, using folded towels if you are short of cushions. Include both walls or the sofa arms so the stack is clearly tucked in.
tips: Get the phone near the floor.
Focus on the middle cushion.

title: Curtain Stripe
oneLiner: Part the curtains or a blind a hand's width and shoot the soft seat inside.
details: The idea is a thin stripe of daylight on a blanket, a chair, or a pillow. Open the curtains or a blind only a little and leave the room lights off. Stand so the stripe falls across something soft.
tips: Expose for the bright stripe.
Include both the dark cloth and the lit band.
constraint: The room lights stay off.

title: Wide Cup by the Sofa
oneLiner: Sit a wide cup or bowl of a warm drink beside the sofa or the bed.
details: Tea, cocoa, or soup in a bowl or a wide mug is the anchor. A spoon on a napkin may join it, and the sofa or bed edge should appear. Shoot from the seat, the way it looks when you are about to reach.
tips: Focus on the near rim.
A lamp to the side will catch the surface of the drink.

title: Scarf on the Hall Seat
oneLiner: Drape one scarf where you drop it when you come through the door.
details: A hat or a soft sweater works if you have no scarf. Use the bench, chair, or hook where things actually land, and include a bit of wall. Keep it to one soft item so the corner feels like relief.
tips: Use the light already in the hall.
Shoot from the height of the seat or the hook.
constraint: Only one soft item in the frame.

title: Quilt Meets the Sheet
oneLiner: Crop the corner where a quilt or pillowcase meets the plain sheet.
details: The meeting of patterned cloth and plain sheet is enough. If you have no quilt, a printed pillowcase against a plain duvet works. Fill the frame with that junction and a little of the mattress edge.
tips: Shoot from above on a slight diagonal.
Skip the flash so the colours stay soft.

title: Pocket of the Gown
oneLiner: Hang a bathrobe so one pocket gapes, and shoot into that pocket.
details: A hoodie or cardigan pocket works if you have no bathrobe. Hang it on a door or a chair in a corner and move close, including a little of the soft fabric around the pocket. A tissue or a blank folded note peeking out is enough story.
tips: Light the inside of the pocket with a lamp from the side.
Focus on the pocket edge.
constraint: Nothing with private writing may show.

title: Throw on the Rug
oneLiner: Let a throw spill from the sofa onto the rug and shoot along it.
details: Hang a blanket off the seat so a little of it rests on the rug, or on the bare floor if you have no rug. Get down on the floor and shoot along that meeting. Include one sofa or bed edge, or the underside of the seat, so the spot feels enclosed.
tips: Focus on the nearest fold of the blanket.
Keep the top of the sofa out of the frame.

title: Waiting for the Kettle
oneLiner: Frame the counter where you wait for the kettle, mug already set.
details: Put a mug where you actually stand and wait, and include the kettle only at the edge if it shares that corner. You should not be in the picture. A tea box or a spoon may be the third thing, then stop.
tips: Shoot from chest height, square to the counter.
Let the shadow under the cupboard make a dark band at the top.
constraint: You stay out of the frame.

title: Blanket at the Foot
oneLiner: Fold a spare blanket at the foot of the bed and shoot along the layers.
details: A spare duvet, a throw, or a large towel folded once is enough. Stand at the side and look along the fold so the layers step towards the pillows. Keep the head of the bed soft and secondary.
tips: Lower the camera to mattress height.
Let side window light skim the steps of cloth.

title: Mug Cupboard Hideaway
oneLiner: Open one mug cupboard and photograph the shelf as a small hideaway.
details: Frame the mugs with the door edge included. If the shelf is crowded, pull two mugs forward and let the rest fall dark. Use room light in front of the cupboard, and switch the cupboard light off if it has one.
tips: Lean in so the door and the shelf become the frame.
Focus on the nearest handle.
constraint: The cupboard light stays off.

title: Towels on the Stool
oneLiner: Pile a clean towel and a washcloth on a stool after washing.
details: A stool, the closed lid of the toilet, or a chair just outside the bathroom can hold the pile. Turn any bottle labels away. The idea is the moment after washing, when the towels are waiting.
tips: Use the warmest bulb already in the room.
Fill the frame with the stool and the towels.

title: Washcloth on the Rim
oneLiner: Fold a washcloth on the rim of a dry bath and shoot that quiet corner.
details: Use a dry bath or a shower tray, and a small folded washcloth. Include the curve of the rim and a little tile, with the warmest bulb in the room switched on. Leave bottles out of the frame, or turn their labels to the wall.
tips: Stand at the side and look slightly down into the empty bath.
If the tile looks blue, nudge the white balance warmer.
constraint: Keep the bath or tray empty of water.

title: Hoodie as a Pillow
oneLiner: Fold a hoodie into a pillow and set it in the corner of the sofa.
details: Use a hoodie or a soft sweater you actually wear. Fold it so the shape looks used, and tuck it where the sofa arm meets the back. Include a little of the sofa and nothing else, and leave the seat empty.
tips: Shoot from sitting height so the fold looks ready to lean on.
Let a nearby lamp light the fabric from one side.

title: Elbow Crease
oneLiner: Lay a long-sleeved shirt flat and frame the crease at the elbow.
details: Smooth a shirt on the bed or a table and bend one sleeve as an elbow would. The fan of wrinkles at that bend is the subject, not the whole garment. A plain surface keeps the small folds easy to read.
tips: Stand over the bend and keep the phone parallel to the cloth.
Side light from a window will separate the wrinkles.
Smooth the cuff so it does not compete with the elbow.

title: Towel in Thirds
oneLiner: Fold a towel into three and photograph the stacked edges.
details: Use a bath towel or a dish towel and fold it into a tidy third. Prop the bundle on end, against a book if it will not stand, so the layered edges face you like the edge of a closed book. A slightly uneven layer is worth keeping if the cloth still reads as a stack.
tips: Shoot from the end, not from above.
Align the edges so they run vertically.
Use a dark sofa or a plain wall behind the stack.

title: Curtain at the Floor
oneLiner: Show where a curtain or sheet meets the floor in a heap.
details: If your curtains reach the floor, photograph the spare cloth where it settles. If they stop short, drape a sheet or a throw so the extra length lands in a soft heap. Get low so the meeting of fabric and floor fills the frame.
tips: Put the phone near the floor and tilt the screen up to see.
Focus on the nearest fold, not the window.
Leave the heap unstraightened.
constraint: Both the floor and the cloth must show.

title: One Corner Turned
oneLiner: Turn one corner of a napkin down and leave the rest plain.
details: Lay a cloth napkin, a handkerchief, or a clean dish towel flat. Fold a single corner back so a triangle of the layer beneath appears. That one deliberate fold should be the only event in the picture.
tips: Shoot straight down so the triangle keeps its shape.
Let the turned corner point towards a corner of the frame.
Keep the cloth larger than the phone's shadow.
constraint: Only one corner is turned.

title: Duvet Spiral
oneLiner: Roll the duvet from the foot of the bed into a loose spiral.
details: Roll only part of the way, so the spiral sits at the foot and the rest of the bed stays flat. A blanket or a thick towel can stand in if you have no duvet. Shoot from the foot of the bed, looking along the roll.
tips: Keep the spiral tight enough to hold and loose enough to show layers.
Expose for the cloth, not the bright window beyond the bed.
Include a little flat sheet so the roll has a start.

title: Sleeve Over the Edge
oneLiner: Let one sleeve hang off a table and follow the drop.
details: Lay a shirt or a sweater on a table, a desk, or the bed, and send one sleeve over the edge. Gravity will stack the cloth into soft shelves. Photograph from the side so the hanging sleeve has floor or shadow behind it.
tips: Focus on the fold right at the table edge.
A lamp on the table can light the hanging cloth from above.
Step sideways until the sleeve makes an S or a simple drop.
constraint: The sleeve must cross the edge inside the frame.

title: A Frayed Edge
oneLiner: Find a frayed hem and let the loose threads cross the frame.
details: Use an old towel, a frayed shirt, or a cleaning cloth you can spare. If nothing is frayed, loosen a few threads at the hem of that cloth. Lay it so the threads stick out against a plain background, with the tidy cloth filling the rest.
tips: Graze the light across the threads so each one throws a shadow.
Focus on the longest thread.
Keep the phone parallel to the cloth.
constraint: The loose threads must be in focus.

title: Scarf in an S
oneLiner: Drop a scarf so it lands in a loose S.
details: Use a scarf, a necktie, or a long sock. Drop it once onto a sofa or a bed and do not tidy the curve. Shoot from above so the S is obvious and the ends leave the frame or curl inside it.
tips: Drop from a short height so the shape stays simple.
If the first drop is a knot, pick it up and drop once more.
Use a plain cushion or sheet as the background.
constraint: Do not rearrange the cloth after it lands.

title: A Single Crease
oneLiner: Open a stored pillowcase and keep only one fold line.
details: Take a pillowcase or a folded sheet from a cupboard and open it until one storage crease remains. Smooth everything else with your hand. That pale line is the fold you are photographing.
tips: Graze the light across the crease so it throws a thin shadow.
Keep the phone parallel to the cloth.
Crop close enough that the crease crosses the whole frame.
constraint: Only one crease may show.

title: Sleeves Tied
oneLiner: Knot the sleeves of a sweater and photograph the knot.
details: Tie the sleeves once, loosely, and lay the sweater on the bed. The knot should sit as a dense bud of cloth, with the body of the sweater calmer around it. Choose the angle that gives the knot the most weight.
tips: Shoot from a low side if the knot looks flat from above.
Tuck the hem out of the way if it tangles with the knot.
Side light will mark each wrap of the sleeves.

title: Pleat Light
oneLiner: Find pleats or pressed creases and light them from the side.
details: A skirt, trousers with a crease, or a pleated curtain will do. If none of those has enough folds, make four folds in a towel and prop it upright against a book so they run vertically. Window light from the side should put a bright edge on each pleat and a softer dark in each valley.
tips: Let the folds run top to bottom.
Underexpose a little if the bright edges blow out.
Focus on the pleat nearest the window.
constraint: At least four folds or pleats must appear.

title: The Tucked Corner
oneLiner: Tuck a sheet corner and photograph the layers you made.
details: Fold a sheet or a duvet corner under itself as if you were finishing the bed, then stop. You want three or four layers and a clear order. Stand close enough to see which layer is on top, and far enough to keep the corner's shape.
tips: Shoot from the corner, looking back along the bed.
Smooth only the top layer.
Include the mattress edge as a straight line beside the cloth.

title: Cloth in the Bowl
oneLiner: Push a soft cloth into a bowl and shoot the gathers.
details: Press a clean dish towel or napkin into a mixing bowl so it wrinkles where it bends. Look down into the bowl and let the rim frame the cloth. The gathers should feel crowded, soft, and held in a circle.
tips: Use a plain bowl if you have one.
Focus on the deepest gather.
Shift a lamp or stand near the window so the inside is not a black hole.

title: Hills of a Blanket
oneLiner: Look along a rumpled blanket so the folds become hills.
details: Leave a blanket, a throw, or a duvet cover rumpled on the bed or the sofa. Lower the phone until it almost touches the cloth and look across the surface, not down onto it. Peaks near the lens should be clearer than the ones farther along.
tips: Rest your elbows so the phone does not sink into the cloth.
Focus on the first ridge.
Let later ridges soften; that depth is the point.
constraint: Shoot from the height of the blanket, not from above.

title: Cloth Off the Table
oneLiner: Cover a table and let the cloth fall on one side only.
details: A tablecloth, a sheet, or a large towel can be the cloth. Set it so one side hangs and the other sides stay on the top. The vertical fall, with a few broad folds, is the picture.
tips: Stand so the hanging cloth fills the lower half.
Keep objects off the tabletop.
Focus where the cloth turns over the edge.

title: A Twisted Dish Towel
oneLiner: Twist a dry dish towel into a rope and show the spiral.
details: Twist a dry dish towel until a clear spiral forms, then lay it on the counter. Leave it still once the ridges look right. Side light should catch each turn of the twist.
tips: Lay the rope on a contrasting counter.
Focus along the nearest ridge.
Keep both hands out once the twist is set.
constraint: The twist runs from one edge of the frame to the other.

title: Cinched Curtain
oneLiner: Pull a curtain into a tie-back and frame the bunched cloth.
details: Use a tie-back, a ribbon, or a piece of string to hold a curtain in a bundle. The cloth should flare above and below the cinch. If you have no curtain, bunch a sheet in a loose band and hang that over the top of a door.
tips: Put the cinch near the middle, with cloth bursting on both sides.
Focus on the tightest gather.
Step close so the window does not become the subject.

title: The Collar Roll
oneLiner: Stand a shirt collar up and photograph the roll of cloth.
details: Pop the collar of a shirt or a jacket laid on the bed. If nothing has a collar, fold a waistband so it makes the same roll. The curve, and the shadow inside it, are the subject.
tips: Get close so the collar leaves the frame on both sides.
Light from the side to open the shadow inside the roll.
Keep loud buttons at the edge or out.
constraint: The collar or waistband fills at least half the picture.

title: Shoulders on a Hanger
oneLiner: Hang a shirt so the folds under the hanger fill the frame.
details: Use a hanger on a rail, a hook, or the top of a door. The cloth should fall from the shoulders in two soft slopes. If you have no hanger, fold the shirt over the top of a door and shoot the hollow underneath.
tips: Stand so the bar or the door top stays in frame.
Focus on the deepest fold under one shoulder.
Step in until the window or the closet recedes.
constraint: The support and the cloth both show.

title: Sheet Over a Chair
oneLiner: Drape a sheet over a chair and photograph the hollow.
details: A chair, a stool, or the arm of a sofa can be the support. Drop a sheet or a thin blanket over it so the cloth makes a small cave. Shoot from the open side, and keep your face well out of that hollow.
tips: Use a thin sheet so the shape of the chair still tells.
Focus on the rim of the opening.
A lamp behind the chair can glow through the cloth.

title: Turned Cuff
oneLiner: Turn one cuff back and frame the double layer.
details: Use a shirt, a jacket, or a pair of trousers. Fold one cuff so both the outside and the inside of the cloth show. The thickness at the fold, and a slight mismatch of the two edges, are what matter.
tips: Lay the sleeve flat so the cuff is the highest fold.
Shoot from a low angle across the cloth.
Focus on the stitched edge of the cuff.

title: Lining Falling Open
oneLiner: Open a coat so the lining folds out towards the light.
details: Lay a coat or a jacket open on the bed with the inside up. If there is no separate lining, use the inside cloth anyway. Let it slump into its own folds, and use side light to show whether that cloth shines more than the outside.
tips: Include a border of the outer cloth around the lining.
Focus on a fold in the lining, which may be slippery.
Wait until the cloth has stopped sliding.
constraint: Both the lining and the outer cloth appear.

title: Fitted Sheet Gather
oneLiner: Stretch a fitted sheet corner so the elastic bunches into folds.
details: Use the corner of a fitted sheet on the mattress, or lift that corner if the bed is already made. The ruched elastic and the stacked cloth are the subject. A flat sheet with a gathered hem can stand in if you have no fitted sheet.
tips: Get close so the bunched elastic fills the frame.
Side light from the window will separate the little folds.
Hold the corner still with one hand kept at the edge.
constraint: The elastic or gathered hem is in the frame.

title: Napkin in a Ring
oneLiner: Pull a napkin through a ring, a band, or a hair tie.
details: The cloth should flare on both sides of whatever cinches it. A napkin ring is ideal, and a hair tie or a loose bangle works if you have no ring. Set it on the table and shoot from the side so the squeeze is obvious.
tips: Use a plain tabletop.
Focus on the cloth where it is most compressed.
Let the two flared ends leave the frame.

title: Rolled Towel End
oneLiner: Roll a towel tightly and photograph the spiral at the end.
details: Roll it on a shelf, the rim of the bathtub, or the bed. The spiral should be the sharp part, and the length of the roll can leave the frame. Keep the weave quiet so the coil is what you notice.
tips: Face the spiral straight on.
A darker towel shows the spiral more clearly than a white one in bright light.
Brace the phone on the shelf if the spiral is small.
constraint: The spiral fills at least half the frame.

title: Cushion Valley
oneLiner: Press a book into a cushion so the cloth dips into a valley.
details: Any cushion or pillow on the sofa or the bed will do. A book or a remote can hold the dip while you shoot. The valley and the cloth rising around it are the fold.
tips: Get down to cushion height and look across the dip.
Focus on the near rim of the valley.
Keep the book small in the frame if it is only there to weigh the cloth.

title: Outlet Stare
oneLiner: Find a wall outlet whose openings read as eyes and a mouth.
details: Walk the rooms and look at each wall outlet straight on. Two slots or holes become eyes, and a third opening or a switch becomes a mouth. Stand square to the plate so the openings sit level, and crop until the wall falls away.
tips: Tap the plate itself so focus does not jump to the wall.
If the corner is dim, switch on the nearest lamp rather than the flash.
constraint: Keep the outlet plate filling most of the frame.

title: Toaster Slots
oneLiner: Catch your toaster looking back from the counter.
details: Set a two-slice toaster on the counter with the slots facing you. The dark openings work as eyes, and the lever or the crumb tray can read as a nose or a mouth. Shoot from slightly above so the top becomes a forehead.
tips: Brush crumbs off the top so they do not clutter the expression.
Stand on the window side of the toaster for soft light on the metal.

title: Handles for Eyes
oneLiner: Frame a kitchen faucet so the handles become eyes.
details: Stand at the kitchen sink and look straight at the faucet. Round handles sit like eyes and the spout drops between them like a long nose. If there is only one handle, use it as a brow, the spout as a nose, and the base of the spout as a mouth. Clear the basin first so dishes do not break the shape.
tips: Focus on a handle, not the backsplash behind it.
A pale sink makes the metal features easier to separate.
constraint: The spout must appear with the parts you are using as features.

title: Ears on a Tote
oneLiner: Show a soft bag with handles rising like ears.
details: Stand a tote or shopping bag on a chair and let the handles rise on either side. A zip, a seam or a pocket line can become the mouth. Nudge the fabric until the look is calm rather than crumpled shut.
tips: Place the bag against a plain wall so the handles stay readable.
Focus on the seam you have chosen as the mouth.

title: Ports for Eyes
oneLiner: Lay a charger so two ports read as a pair of eyes.
details: Set a phone charger or a power bank on a pale table. Two ports can sit as eyes, and the seam of the case can suggest a mouth. If there is only one port, that opening becomes the mouth and the two lower corners of the block become cheeks.
tips: Angle a lamp so the ports fall dark and easy to read.
Brace your wrists on the table for this close framing.
constraint: Show the charger alone, with pins and cables tucked away.

title: Mesh and a Mouth
oneLiner: Look into a speaker grille and find a hidden expression.
details: Any speaker will do: a radio, a television bar or a small portable speaker. From straight on, two darker patches become eyes and a seam becomes a mouth. Move a lamp to one side so the mesh shows without a hard glare.
tips: Switch a television picture off if you are using its speaker.
Get close and tap the mesh, not the room behind.

title: The Pillow's Fold
oneLiner: Notice a pillow crease that already looks like a face.
details: Leave a pillow as it landed after sleep or after you plumped it. Walk around the bed until two dents and a fold line up on their own. Resist poking them into a cartoon, and shoot in the daylight already on the bed.
tips: Lower the exposure a touch if the white cloth blows out.
Shoot from the side of the bed so the folds keep their depth.
constraint: Do not rearrange the creases before you shoot.

title: Knobs Above a Handle
oneLiner: Pair two drawer knobs with a handle beneath them.
details: Kitchen or bedroom drawers often carry two knobs over a wider pull. Crouch until that trio sits level, knobs as eyes and the pull as a mouth. If your drawers have only knobs, use two of them and the shadow gap between drawers as the mouth.
tips: Step back until the drawer fronts look square, not slanted.
A lamp from the side lifts the knobs off the wood.

title: Ear Cups Looking Up
oneLiner: Lay headphones flat so the ear cups stare upward.
details: Place over-ear headphones on a table, cups up, with the band arched like a brow. The cushions become two wide eyes. If you only have small buds, set them side by side in an open case and let the hinge suggest a mouth.
tips: Shoot from directly above so both cups stay the same size.
Tap a cushion rather than the table when you focus.
constraint: Both ear cups, or both buds, must be in frame.

title: The Oven's Expression
oneLiner: Use the oven knobs as eyes and the handle as a mouth.
details: Close the oven and stand square in front of it. Two knobs sit like eyes and the long handle makes a straight mouth. If there is a whole row of knobs, choose the most even pair and crop the others out.
tips: Put a room light on so the glass door is not a black mirror.
Hold the phone level with the knobs, not looking down.

title: A Potato Watching
oneLiner: Seek a potato whose eyes already suggest a face.
details: Tip a few potatoes onto a board and turn each one under the window. The small eyes are already there, and a scar can finish a mouth. Choose the one that works without a pen mark, and shoot it close on the board.
tips: Side light from the window will model each bump.
Wipe the lens after handling the potatoes.

title: Holes in the Crumb
oneLiner: Hunt two holes in an English muffin or bread slice.
details: Take an English muffin or a slice of bread with an open crumb and look across it for a pair of openings that read as eyes. A split in the crust can be the mouth. Set it on a plate by the window and shoot from a low angle so the chosen holes fall dark.
tips: Move in until only a few holes remain in the picture.
Tap the nearest chosen hole so the focus sits on the expression.
constraint: Only one muffin or slice in the picture.

title: Marks on the Fruit
oneLiner: Pick one fruit whose marks already suggest a face.
details: Look through the fruit bowl for an apple, pear, orange or lemon that already has the marks. A stem and a navel often do the work of a nose and a mouth. Set that single fruit on the table and leave the rest of the bowl out.
tips: Turn the fruit in your fingers until the marks line up, then put it down.
Window light from one side keeps the colour rich without a flat glare.

title: Lenses Left Behind
oneLiner: Rest glasses so the lenses become a pair of eyes.
details: Set a pair of glasses or sunglasses on a table and look from the front. The lenses read as eyes and the bridge is a nose. Choose a quiet background, such as a bare counter or a plain sheet of paper.
tips: Tilt the frames until window glare slides off the lenses.
Focus on the bridge between the lenses.
constraint: Only the glasses appear, with no wearer.

title: The Hanger's Profile
oneLiner: Hang a clothes hanger until its hook suggests a profile.
details: Hang a wire or plastic hanger on a door or a rail against a plain wall. The hook can read as a nose or a curled fringe, and the shoulders of the hanger as a jaw. Shift it a few degrees until the likeness clicks, then shoot hanger and wall only.
tips: Step back so the whole hanger is sharp from hook to tips.
A plain wall matters more here than a clever angle.

title: Spout Over the Drain
oneLiner: Compose a basin faucet above the drain like a face.
details: Look down into an empty washbasin or kitchen sink. The faucet becomes the nose and the drain an open mouth. Handles, if you have them, can sit at the sides like cheeks.
tips: Dry the metal first so highlights do not swallow the shapes.
Hold the phone parallel with the rim of the basin.
constraint: The basin must be empty of dishes and bottles.

title: Two Buttons Watching
oneLiner: Study two toilet tank buttons until they read as eyes.
details: Close the lid and look at the toilet tank from slightly above. Round or oval buttons become eyes, and the gap between them can suggest a mouth. If there is printed branding, angle the phone so only the button shapes remain.
tips: Wipe water spots off the buttons before you frame them.
Stand so your shadow does not fall across the lid.
constraint: Leave any printed branding out of the frame.

title: Antennas and Lights
oneLiner: Discover a router whose lights and antennas form a face.
details: Find the router, often low on a shelf near an outlet, and leave it plugged in. Two antennas can be ears, and a pair of status lights can be eyes. If there are no antennas, use two lights as eyes and a dark port as a mouth, and hide most of the cables.
tips: Leave the flash off so the little lights stay visible.
Tap one status light to focus in a dim corner.

title: Still Fan Hub
oneLiner: Isolate the hub of a switched-off fan or round vent.
details: Switch the fan off and wait until the blades are still. Look through the grille: the hub can be a nose and two darker gaps can be eyes. A round wall vent or a stove extractor works the same way if you have no desk fan.
tips: Let the circular rim run close to the edges of the frame.
Confirm the blades have fully stopped before you focus.

title: Holes in the Bowl
oneLiner: Choose two colander holes that seem to stare at you.
details: Hold a metal or plastic colander near a window, hollow side toward you. Hunt for a pair of holes with a natural mouth nearby, perhaps where the handle joins. Let the other holes fall away toward the edges.
tips: The window behind the colander turns the chosen holes dark and clear.
Focus on the near rim rather than the room beyond.
constraint: The colander fills the frame, hollow side toward you.

title: Grain in the Spoon
oneLiner: Scan a wooden spoon for a face hiding in the grain.
details: Wooden spoons collect dark lines that sometimes sit like brows and a mouth. Turn one under the window until a cluster of marks lines up. Rest it on a pale cloth so the wood is the whole subject.
tips: Look from a low glancing angle so the grain throws tiny shadows.
Tap the wood, then brighten slightly if the spoon looks muddy.

title: Glove on the Counter
oneLiner: Sit an oven glove so the thumb suggests a character.
details: Prop the glove on the counter with the thumb upright and the cuff as a body. A stitched line or a worn patch can be the mouth. Once it is posed, take your hands away so the glove has the picture to itself.
tips: A mug or a small stack of books will prop the cuff.
Shoot from glove height rather than looking down on it.
constraint: Your hands stay out of the frame.

title: Caps at Eye Level
oneLiner: Stand two bottles so their caps sit level like eyes.
details: On a shelf or in the fridge door, find two similar caps at the same height. A label edge or a gap beneath them can read as a mouth. Slide one bottle a little if the spacing feels uneven, then shoot straight at the caps.
tips: If the shelf is dim, open the fridge and use its lamp, then shoot quickly.
Wipe any moisture off the caps so the circles stay crisp.

title: The Tissue Slot
oneLiner: Angle a tissue box until the slot reads as a mouth.
details: A tissue box has a wide opening that can look like a mouth, especially if one tissue rises a little. Two corners of that opening can suggest eyes. Turn the box until the slot is the clearest shape and any wording falls away.
tips: Pull a single tissue up only a short way.
Focus on the edge of the slot.
constraint: Keep any brand name too soft or too cropped to read.

title: One Eye Overhead
oneLiner: Point upward at a smoke alarm and find its single eye.
details: From the hallway or bedroom floor, look up at the alarm disc. Slots around the edge can be lashes and the centre sensor a single eye. If you have no alarm, a round ceiling light with a dark middle works instead.
tips: Tap the alarm, then lower exposure so the ceiling stays a calm tone.
Place the disc near the middle using the grid overlay.
constraint: The disc sits alone against the ceiling.

title: Hooks in a Pair
oneLiner: Line two coat hooks up so they read as a pair of eyes.
details: Look along a row of hooks and choose two at the same height. A rail beneath them, or the shadow of that rail, can be a mouth. Clear those two hooks so the shapes stay simple.
tips: Stand directly opposite so the rail does not slope.
Side light gives each hook a small shadow like a brow.
constraint: No coats or bags hanging in the frame.

title: Lock Under the Lever
oneLiner: See a door handle and lock as a nose and a mouth.
details: Close an interior door and face the handle. A round knob can be a nose and the keyhole a small mouth, with screw heads as eyes. If the handle is a lever, use it as a lopsided smile and let the lock sit above it.
tips: Crouch to handle height so the door is an even background.
Focus on the metal rather than the door edge.

title: Buttons in a Cluster
oneLiner: Tilt a remote until some buttons cluster into a face.
details: Hold a television or lamp remote under a lamp and turn it slowly. Round buttons make good eyes and a longer button can be a mouth. Stop turning at the first accidental expression.
tips: Rest the remote on a dark book so it lifts off the background.
Move close enough that the chosen buttons dominate.
constraint: Use only one remote.

title: Lid Knob Nose
oneLiner: Watch a French press lid and handle settle into a face.
