details: Set a French press, teapot or pitcher on the table with the handle to one side. From a low angle the lid knob becomes a nose and the handle an ear. The dark ellipse of the opening, or the liquid inside, can read as a mouth.
tips: Shoot from just below the lid so the knob leads.
Wipe fingerprints off the glass or metal first.

title: Wells in a Tray
oneLiner: Scan an empty ice tray for two wells that sit like eyes.
details: An ice tray is a field of little hollows. Look along it until two wells feel like eyes and a third, or the end gap, feels like a mouth. Shoot from a low side so the hollows cast small shadows.
tips: One lamp to the side is enough to shape the wells.
Angle the tray so a rim line leads toward the expression.
constraint: The tray should be empty and dry.

title: Pores in the Sponge
oneLiner: Find a face in the pores of a kitchen or bath sponge.
details: Dampen a sponge and squeeze it so the pores open, then set it on a plate. Look across the rough side for two darker holes and a crease. The smooth yellow side is usually less expressive than the scrubbing side.
tips: Move in until the sponge fills the frame and the room disappears.
Brace your elbows and tap a single pore to focus.

title: Magnets on the Door
oneLiner: Let two fridge magnets sit level and become eyes.
details: The fridge door is a ready-made face if two magnets share a height. Use a handle, a vent or the edge of a note as the mouth. Keep lists and names out of the picture, and shoot straight on so the door does not slope.
tips: If the overhead light glares, switch it off and use light from the side.
Focus on the magnets rather than the door skin.
constraint: No readable writing in the frame.

title: Round Door Eye
oneLiner: Let a round appliance door stare back as one eye.
details: Look at a front-loading washer, a dryer or a microwave. The round window is the eye, and a handle, button or vent below it can be a mouth. Stand square to the door so the circle stays round, and crop out any readable name.
tips: Turn off a harsh ceiling light if it flares in the glass.
Tap the rim of the window rather than the room behind it.
constraint: Only one appliance in the frame.

title: Burners from Above
oneLiner: Look straight down at two burners that stare back.
details: Stand over the stove and look down with the burners off and cool. Two rings, coils or printed circles become eyes, and a bar across them or the gap between them becomes a mouth. If you see only one burner, use that circle as a mouth and two control knobs along the front as eyes.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the cooktop.
Crop out any printed name along the front edge.

title: A Knot Watching
oneLiner: Search bark on a sidewalk tree for a watchful knot.
details: From the sidewalk near home, look at the bark of a tree growing along it. A knot can be an eye, a second scar can make a pair, and a crack can be a mouth. Fill the frame with that patch and leave the rest of the tree out.
tips: Open shade on the trunk is kinder than a bright sky behind it.
Focus on the knot, not the bark farther around the curve.
constraint: Only bark in the frame.

title: Two Eggs Watching
oneLiner: Rest two eggs in a carton so they seem to watch.
details: Set two eggs side by side in an open carton on the counter. They become eyes, and the near edge of the carton can be a mouth. If you have no eggs, two round tomatoes or small apples in a bowl work the same way.
tips: Shoot from egg height rather than from high above.
Window light from the side will round each shell.
constraint: Only the pair, with nothing extra crowding them.

title: Rocker Switch Eyes
oneLiner: Read a double light switch as a waiting pair of eyes.
details: Find a double rocker switch and stand square to the plate. The two rockers read as eyes, and the gap or the screws below them can suggest a mouth. A single switch still works if you treat the two screws as eyes and the rocker as a nose.
tips: Light the plate from the side so each rocker takes a slim shadow.
Tap the plate and keep the surrounding wall plain.
constraint: Keep the whole plate in the frame.

title: Grater Hole Gaze
oneLiner: Hunt a face among the holes of a box grater.
details: Hold a box grater near a window, with the largest holes toward you. Look for two openings that sit as eyes and another that can be a mouth. If you have no grater, a slotted spoon or a spatula with slots will do.
tips: Let the window sit behind the metal so the chosen holes go dark.
Focus on the near side of the grater, not the room beyond.
constraint: Fill the frame with the holed metal.

title: Closed Scissors
oneLiner: Lay closed scissors so the finger holes become eyes.
details: Place a closed pair of scissors on a light table, with the finger holes toward you. Those two holes read as eyes and the pivot can be a nose or a mouth. Keep the blades together and let the holes carry the picture.
tips: Shoot from above so both holes stay the same size.
Slide a sheet of pale paper under them if the table is busy.
constraint: The scissors stay closed.

title: The Webcam Eye
oneLiner: Use a webcam lens as one dark eye on the bezel.
details: Look for a small dark lens, such as the camera on a laptop, a tablet or a monitor. That dot is a single eye, and two screws or the curves beside it can finish the look. If you cannot find a lens, use a round dial with a dark centre in the same way, and keep your own reflection out of any glass.
tips: Tap the dark dot, then darken the exposure so it stays a small point.
If it sits on a screen, prop the bezel so it runs level.
constraint: No readable letters in the frame.

title: Shower Head Gaze
oneLiner: Look up into a shower head and find a face in the holes.
details: With the water off, look up at a fixed shower head or hold a handheld sprayer against the wall. The spray holes can cluster into eyes and a mouth. Fill the frame with that disc and leave the rest of the shower out.
tips: Stand so a ceiling light does not glare on the metal.
Wipe drops away if they break up the holes.

title: Front of the Vacuum
oneLiner: Meet the vacuum from the front and find its features.
details: Set the vacuum where you usually store it and crouch to its height. A round opening, a switch or two bumps can line up, with a brush slot or a bumper as a mouth. An upright or stick vacuum works if you look at the floor nozzle from the front. If you have no vacuum, use the front of an iron or a fan, with two screws or switches as eyes.
tips: Clear stray shoes away so the machine has a quiet background.
Tap the body of the machine, not the floor.
constraint: Keep the whole front of the machine in frame.

title: Slot from Inside
oneLiner: From inside, frame the mail slot as a wide mouth.
details: On the inside of your own door, look at the mail slot with the flap closed. The slot is a mouth, and two screws or the corners of the flap can be eyes. If the door has no slot, use the opening of a bread box or a napkin holder the same way.
tips: Crouch until the slot runs level across the frame.
Angle off any gloss so you are not reflected in the paint.
constraint: If there is a flap, leave it closed.

title: Wound Cable Eyes
oneLiner: Coil a charging cable so two loops read as eyes.
details: On a table, coil a charging cable or earphone cord into loose loops. Two rounds become eyes and the gathered middle can be a nose. Tuck the connector underneath so it does not become the subject.
tips: Use a plain tabletop so the loops stay easy to follow.
Shoot from above and keep the coil in the middle.

title: Crack in the Plate
oneLiner: Let a crack in a plate read as a sideways mouth.
details: Look through the plates, bowls or plastic lids for a hairline crack, a glaze line or a worn crease. Two speckles above it can be eyes. Set that one piece on the table in window light and leave the rest of the stack out.
tips: A low side light will throw the crack into a thin shadow.
Tap the crack so the line stays sharp.
constraint: Only one plate or lid in the frame.

title: Mouse Button Eyes
oneLiner: Turn a computer mouse until its buttons look watchful.
details: Set a mouse on a plain desk and look from slightly above. The two buttons become eyes and the wheel becomes a nose. Crop any logo, and if the shell is one smooth piece, use the seam under the buttons as a mouth. If you have no mouse, lay a calculator in its place and use two round buttons as eyes.
tips: Dim a bright screen nearby so the desk is not washed with light.
Focus on the wheel rather than the desk.

title: Leaf on the Table
oneLiner: Find two spots on a houseplant leaf that read as eyes.
details: Look at a leaf still on a houseplant, or lay a herb leaf or a salad leaf on a plate. Two spots, holes or pale patches can be eyes, and a vein can be a mouth. A plain wall or a sheet of paper behind it keeps the marks easy to see.
tips: If you steady the leaf, keep your fingers out of the frame.
Focus on the spots and let the leaf edge soften.

title: Hinge and Screws
oneLiner: Close in on a hinge until its screws suggest eyes.
details: Open a cupboard door, or another interior door, just enough to see the hinge. Two screws can be eyes and the curved knuckle a nose or a brow. Shoot close so the metal fills the frame and the room falls away.
tips: Rest your wrist on the door to steady this close view.
Angle the phone so the metal takes a small highlight.

title: Basket Openings
oneLiner: Look through a laundry basket for two holes that stare.
details: Hold an empty laundry basket toward a window, or set it on a chair against a plain wall. Choose two openings as eyes and a slot below them as a mouth. A dish rack will do if you have no basket.
tips: Let the light sit behind the basket so the chosen holes go dark.
Move in until those holes lead and the rest fall to the edges.
constraint: The basket or rack should be empty.

title: Spring on the Clip
oneLiner: Stand a clothespin so the spring sits like a brow.
details: Stand one clothespin, or a clothes peg, on the table with the pinch toward you. The metal spring can sit as a brow or as two eyes, and the gap between the legs can be a mouth. A clip with wire arms works the same way if you have neither.
tips: Shoot from clip height so you are not looking straight down.
Slide pale paper underneath if the table pattern competes.
constraint: Only one clip in the frame.

title: Window Light on Boards
oneLiner: Find the patch of window light lying on the floor.
details: A window throws a brighter patch on the floor even when the day is dull. Stand in the room and look for that patch on boards, vinyl or carpet. Frame the bright area and the floor around it, and leave furniture legs out.
tips: Crouch so the patch is a shape, not a thin sliver at the edge.
Tap the bright floor, then lower exposure a notch if the patch blows out.
constraint: Keep furniture legs out of the frame.

title: The Dropped Sock
oneLiner: Photograph a sock where it actually fell on the floor.
details: Use a sock that is already on the floor, or drop a clean one and leave it crooked. Include enough floor around it that the picture is about the find. Shoot from standing height, looking down, and do not tidy the sock into a pose.
tips: A single sock reads faster than a pair in this picture.
If the floor and the sock are the same tone, shoot from a lower side angle.

title: Curling Rug Corner
oneLiner: Catch the corner of a rug lifting off the floor.
details: Find a rug, a runner or a mat with a corner that curls or a fringe that splays. Get low, close to the floor, without lying anywhere you cannot get up from easily. Show both the rug and the floor it is leaving.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor and use the timer so you are not in the shot.
Focus on the curl, where the underside of the rug may show.
constraint: Shoot from below knee height.

title: Knot in the Board
oneLiner: Fill the frame with a knot or mark in the floorboards.
details: If your floor is carpet or vinyl, look for a worn patch, a stain or a join instead of a knot. Get close so the mark fills most of the picture. Let the grain or the pile run to the edges of the frame.
tips: Wipe the patch with a dry cloth so dust does not soften the detail.
Macro mode helps if the mark is smaller than a coin.

title: Cable Across the Floor
oneLiner: Follow a cable where it runs across the floor.
details: Use a charger lead, a lamp cable or an extension that already crosses the floor. Do not unplug anything just to improve the line. Frame a length of cable with floor on both sides, so it enters one edge and leaves another.
tips: Shoot along the cable from a low angle rather than straight down.
Hide a messy plug by cropping, not by pulling the lead.
constraint: The cable enters and leaves the frame.

title: Threshold Between Rooms
oneLiner: Stand over the strip where one floor meets another.
details: Find a doorway with a metal strip, a wooden bar or a simple change from carpet to a hard floor. Point the phone straight down. Let the join sit across the frame and show a little of both floors.
tips: Stand with one foot in each room so the phone can hover over the strip.
The grid will tell you if the strip is running downhill in the picture.

title: Slipper Under the Bed
oneLiner: Look under the bed and photograph a slipper half hidden.
details: If nothing is under the bed, slide one slipper or shoe halfway under and leave it. A sofa or a low shelf works the same way if you have no bed. Rest the phone on the floor at the edge, lens pointing into the gap, and use the screen to frame. Turn on a room lamp so the floor in front is visible and the gap can stay dark.
tips: If the gap is too dark to focus, switch on a lamp in the room behind you.
Include a triangle of visible floor so the hidden slipper has a way in.
constraint: Keep your face out of this low shot.

title: Crumb Trail
oneLiner: Photograph a small scatter of crumbs on the kitchen floor.
details: Drop a few dry crumbs from bread or a cookie, or use a pinch of oats. Keep the scatter small, then shoot from above before you wipe it up. The floor should still be mostly clear around the crumbs.
tips: Get close enough that the crumbs have shape, not just specks.
A side light from the kitchen window gives each crumb a tiny shadow.
constraint: No more than a small pinch of crumbs.

title: Light Under the Door
oneLiner: Catch the line of light leaking under a closed door.
details: Close a door onto a brighter room and look at the gap above the floor. Get the phone down near the floor and frame the bright line against the darker boards or carpet. If the gap is tiny, that thin line is still the picture.
tips: Switch off the light on your side so the gap glows.
Rest the phone on the floor and trigger it with the timer.

title: Coin by the Baseboard
oneLiner: Find or place a coin where the floor meets the baseboard.
details: Use one coin already on the floor, or set one against the baseboard. Get down so the coin, the board edge and the floor all show. The picture is that meeting place, with the coin as the small find.
tips: A coin on its edge will fall; leave it flat.
Focus on the coin's rim where it touches the baseboard.
constraint: Only one coin.

title: Bath Mat Edge
oneLiner: Frame the edge of a bath mat where it meets the floor.
details: Look at the bathroom floor where a mat or a towel ends and the bare floor begins. Include both textures in one frame. Shoot from above and slightly to the side so the edge runs across the picture.
tips: Include a hand's width of bare floor beyond the mat edge.
Align the mat edge with the lower third if the grid is on.

title: Laundry Basket Base
oneLiner: Photograph the base of a laundry basket sitting on the floor.
details: You do not need to empty the basket. Frame where the base, the floor and the contact between them meet. If you have no basket, use a garbage can, a bag or a box that already lives on the floor, and shoot from low beside it.
tips: A low side view shows the little gap under the base.
Let the floor occupy the bottom half so this stays a floor picture.
constraint: Show the floor and the base together.

title: Hair Tie on the Boards
oneLiner: Spot a hair tie or button on the floor and shoot it where it lies.
details: If the floor is clear, drop a hair tie, a button or a rubber band and do not tidy it into a perfect circle. Include enough floor to show it is a find, not a studio object. Focus on the small loop or the button holes.
tips: Get on your knees and hold the phone a forearm above the floor.
A hair tie in a colour unlike the floor will survive the wide view.

title: Lamp Pool on the Floor
oneLiner: Aim a lamp at the floor and photograph the pool of light.
details: Close the curtains or switch off the overhead light. Point a desk lamp or a flashlight at the floor so a pool of light appears, and keep the lamp itself out of the picture. Frame the bright pool and the darker floor around it.
tips: Set the lamp on a book so it aims down. A separate flashlight there works if you have no desk lamp.
Expose for the edge of the pool, where light fades into the floor.
constraint: The lamp stays out of frame.

title: Saucer Under the Pot
oneLiner: Look under a plant pot and photograph the saucer on the floor.
details: Find a pot that sits on a saucer, a plate or a drip tray on the floor. Frame the saucer, the pot's base and the floor around them. If every plant is up on a shelf, set one pot on the floor for a few minutes, on a plate.
tips: Shoot from floor level so the saucer becomes an ellipse.
Dust on the saucer can stay; it proves the pot lives there.

title: Toes at the Rug Edge
oneLiner: Include your own toes where a rug meets the bare floor.
details: Stand in socks or barefoot where a rug, a mat or the carpet meets bare floor. If the floor is all one surface, lay a towel down and use its edge. Point the phone down so your toes and a stretch of floor both appear. These are your own feet, and the floor is the subject, so crop at the ankles.
tips: Wiggle once, then hold still, or the toes will blur.
Include equal amounts of rug and bare floor.
constraint: Only your own feet may appear.

title: Leaf by the Door
oneLiner: Find a leaf that has already landed outside your door.
details: Use a leaf, a petal, a scrap of blossom or a bit of grit that is already on the ground outside your door or on a shared landing. Do not arrange a display. Shoot from above with that ground filling the background, and stay beside the door.
tips: Leave the leaf away from the middle so plenty of ground still shows.
Get low if the leaf is the same colour as the ground, so its edge lifts.

title: Crack by the Door
oneLiner: Trace a crack in the paving right beside your door.
details: Look down at the slab, the concrete or the landing just outside your door. Find a crack, a join or a chip, and fill the frame with it plus a little unmarked surface around it. A join between two slabs counts if you cannot find a crack.
tips: Follow the crack so it runs corner to corner.
Focus a third of the way along the crack rather than at the nearest point.
constraint: Keep your feet beside the door.

title: Where Ground Meets Wall
oneLiner: Frame the line where the outside ground meets the wall.
details: Stand beside your door and point down into the corner where the paving, the landing or the threshold meets the wall or the door frame. Show both surfaces. Dust and small marks can stay; they belong to the place.
tips: A portrait frame gives the corner more height.
Tap focus where the two surfaces touch.

title: Corner of the Floor
oneLiner: Point down at the floor where two walls meet.
details: Find a room corner and point the phone down so the floor fills most of the frame and the two baseboards meet at the top. Include the seam where the floor meets the wood. Scuffs and dust can stay.
tips: A portrait crop gives the corner more floor in front of it.
Tap focus on the seam, not on the floor closest to the lens.
constraint: Keep furniture legs out of the corner.

title: Letter on the Mat
oneLiner: Shoot an envelope where it lies on the indoor mat.
details: Use an envelope with any writing turned away so no name shows, or drop a blank envelope on the mat inside the door. Leave it slightly crooked. Include the mat and a bit of the floor around it.
tips: A white envelope on a dark mat needs a little less exposure.
Shoot from the side of the mat so the envelope has a diagonal.
constraint: No readable name or address.

title: Fluff Along the Baseboard
oneLiner: Show the dust and fluff where floor meets baseboard.
details: Look along the bottom of a wall, behind a door or under a shelf, where fluff collects. Get low so the baseboard, the floor and that pale dust share the frame. You can wipe it up after the picture.
tips: Set a lamp low beside the dust, or lay a separate flashlight next to it, and rake that light across the fluff if the room is dim.
Include a length of baseboard so the fluff has a line to sit against.
constraint: Do not tidy the dust before you shoot.

title: Foot of the Chair
oneLiner: Get down beside a chair foot and the floor it rests on.
details: Choose any chair and get down beside a front leg. Show the foot, the little gap or the dent under it, and a stretch of floor. If the chair has no visible foot, use the leg of a table or a stool the same way.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor and use the timer so your hand stays out.
A side view shows the gap under the foot better than a view from above.
constraint: Shoot from floor level, not from standing height.

title: Book Left on the Floor
oneLiner: Find a book lying on the floor where it slid.
details: Use a book, a magazine or a notebook that is already on the floor, or set one down so it looks as if it slipped off a chair. Leave it crooked. Include enough floor that the picture is about the find, and shoot from standing height.
tips: A dark cover on a pale floor, or the reverse, keeps the book readable.
Check your shoes are out of the top of the frame.

title: Under the Cupboard
oneLiner: Look into the gap under a cupboard and photograph the floor there.
details: Crouch by a kitchen cupboard, a closet or a shelf unit and point the phone into the gap underneath. Include the floor in front and the darker floor under the unit. If a bag, a tin or a shoe is already there, let it stay.
tips: Rest your elbow on your knee so the low view stays sharp.
Switch on a room light behind you if the gap is too dark to focus.
constraint: Include plenty of floor in the foreground.

title: Door Shadow on the Floor
oneLiner: Open a door so its shadow or a bright wedge falls on the floor.
details: Stand inside and open a door until it throws a shadow, or lets a wedge of brighter light, across the floor. Frame the floor, not the door hardware. Any difference in brightness will do, even on a dull day.
tips: Include the threshold as a thin line at the top of the frame.
Lock exposure on the middle tone of the floor, not the brightest patch.

title: Door Around the Chair
oneLiner: Stand in the hall and box a chair inside the doorway.
details: Stand back in the hallway, or in the room next door if you have no hall, and look through one doorway. Shift until a chair sits cleanly inside the rectangle, with a little space between the chair and the surround. Keep the door frame sharp so the chair feels placed inside a picture.
tips: Tap the near door frame so the border stays crisp.
Move back a little if the chair spills past the surround.
constraint: The chair must sit fully inside the doorway rectangle.

title: Two Doorways Deep
oneLiner: Line up two doorways so one opening sits inside the other.
details: Find any place where one opening lines up with another, such as a hall looking through a room toward a further door. Move until the far frame sits inside the near one with a margin on every side. If your rooms do not line up, open a cupboard in the room beyond and let that smaller opening sit inside the doorway.
tips: Turn on the grid and check the inner frame is not cut off.
Expose for the far room if the hall is brighter.
constraint: Both openings must appear in full.

title: Handle Around the Spoon
oneLiner: Use a mug handle as a loop around a spoon on the table.
details: Set a mug on the table with the handle facing you, and lay a teaspoon, a tea bag or a sugar cube just beyond it. Lower the phone until the handle becomes a closed loop with that small thing sitting in the opening. A plain mug on a plain table keeps the loop easy to read.
tips: Get level with the handle so the loop looks closed.
Focus on the handle, then shift the mug until the spoon sits in the gap.
constraint: The handle must form a complete loop.

title: The Ajar Slice
oneLiner: Leave a door ajar and frame a lamp in that gap.
details: Leave an internal door open only a few centimetres so the gap is a tall narrow slot. Stand to the side and aim through it at one clear thing in the next room, such as a lamp, a coat or the corner of a bed. The door edge and the frame should make two strong verticals around that subject.
tips: Steady the phone against the nearer door edge.
Switch on a lamp in the far room so the slot has a subject.
constraint: The gap should be narrower than your hand.

title: Keyhole Circle
oneLiner: Let a keyhole or a tape roll circle one mug.
details: A keyhole only works if the phone can still focus with the lens almost touching the hole. Place a bright mug or a pale towel in the next room and try it, so the dark door becomes a border around that one object. If it will not focus, hold a roll of tape so its cardboard hole circles the same mug and photograph that circle instead.
tips: Rest a finger on the door so the hole stays still.
Light the far room and leave your side of the door dimmer.
constraint: The opening must make a complete border around one object.

title: Pane With One Bottle
oneLiner: Set a bottle against a window so one pane holds it.
details: Stand indoors at a window and place a bottle, jar or tall glass on the sill, well inside the outer frame. If the window has glazing bars, keep the bottle inside a single pane so a bar does not cut it. Move back until the frame reads as a border and the bottle is the thing the pane was holding.
tips: Wipe the glass if a smear crosses the bottle.
Lock exposure on the bottle if the glass is much brighter.

title: Carton Handle Hole
oneLiner: Hold a carton so its handle hole circles a lemon.
details: Take a cereal box or any box with an oval handle hole. Hold it so the hole frames something small and bright behind it, such as a lemon, a reel of tape or a tealight on the table, and keep printed lettering outside the hole. Bring the carton closer to the lens until the hole is large and the object sits in the middle of it.
tips: Brace your elbows on the table so the hole does not wander.
Focus on the cardboard edge rather than the lemon behind it.

title: Mirror Boxes the Lamp
oneLiner: Let a wall mirror's edges box a lamp and nothing else.
details: Stand at a bathroom or hall mirror and shift until a lamp, or just its shade, sits inside the glass. Move until the mirror's frame, or the hard edge of a frameless mirror, crops the lamp with a margin of glass around it. Keep your face out of the reflection so the lamp is the only subject the border holds.
tips: Focus on the mirror's edge, not the lamp in the glass.
Step sideways to change what the rectangle contains.
constraint: Your face must stay out of the mirror.

title: Propped Picture Frame
oneLiner: Prop a picture frame so a mug sits inside it.
details: Take a spare picture frame and stand it on the table so you can see through the opening, sliding the backing aside if a picture is still in it. Place a mug or a piece of fruit behind it so the object sits inside the rectangle. If you have no frame, lay four pens or spoons as a rectangle around the object and shoot from above.
tips: Keep the frame edge sharp and let the mug sit a little softer.
Use a plain wall behind the object so the rectangle stays clear.

title: Gap to the Third Jar
oneLiner: Find the gap between two jars that frames a third behind.
details: On a spice rack, a pantry shelf or a bathroom shelf, look for two containers with a gap between them. Shift until that gap frames a third jar farther back, and if everything sits in one row, place one jar just behind the others so the gap has something to hold. The two nearer containers should become the sides of a small window.
tips: Shoot square to the shelf so the gap stays a clean slot.
Aim a lamp past the front jars, or a separate flashlight if you have one, when the back jar disappears.

title: Closet Crack
oneLiner: Open a closet just enough to frame one hanging sleeve.
details: Open a closet or cupboard door only a short way, so you see a vertical slice of what hangs inside. Adjust the door until one sleeve, a belt or a scarf sits in that slice, held between the door edge and the frame. Let the rest of the clothes fall into dark on either side of the gap.
tips: Expose for the sleeve in the gap, not the dark wood.
Aim a bedside lamp inward if the clothes are too dim to read.
constraint: Only one garment should be clearly readable in the gap.

title: Fridge Shelf in a Frame
oneLiner: Open the fridge and let its doorway frame one shelf.
details: Open the fridge and stand square to it so the surround becomes a frame around the lit interior. Choose one shelf and shift until a jug, a row of jars or a piece of fruit sits in the middle of that opening. Let the fridge light carry the picture, with the kitchen around the door falling darker.
tips: Angle your body so the open door blocks a bright window.
Hold the door steady with your free hand at the outer edge.

title: Slot Between Cushions
oneLiner: Slide two cushions until their gap frames a small book.
details: On a sofa or a bed, set two cushions a little apart. Stand a small book, a remote or a glasses case in the gap so the cushions become a soft frame around it. Shoot from straight in front, close enough that the cushions fill the sides and the object has a clear margin.
tips: Focus on the book, not the nearer cushion.
Drop to cushion height so the gap does not taper into a wedge.

title: Inside the Open Bag
oneLiner: Look into an open bag so the rim frames a book.
details: Open a tote, a backpack or a shopping bag on a chair or the floor and look straight down into the mouth. Arrange nothing fancy: let a book, a pair of gloves or a water bottle sit in the opening so the bag's rim becomes the frame. Fill the photo with that rim and whatever it holds, and leave the room out.
tips: Hold the phone above the opening so the rim stays an even oval.
Tap the rim if the phone keeps focusing on the dark inside.
constraint: The bag's opening must touch every edge of the photo.

title: Drawer Sliver
oneLiner: Pull a drawer out a little and frame a spoon inside.
details: Open a kitchen or desk drawer only a few centimetres, enough to see a horizontal slot of the contents. Slide a wooden spoon, a notebook or a plain tin until it sits in that slot, bordered by the drawer front and the cabinet. Shoot from slightly above so the opening is a wide horizontal slot around one object.
tips: Rest the phone on the counter edge to keep the slot level.
A desk lamp over the drawer stops the interior going black.
constraint: Show only a narrow band of the drawer, not the whole interior.

title: One Square in the Back
oneLiner: Frame a shoe through one gap in a banister or chair.
details: Find a repeated opening you already have: a square in a stair banister, a gap in a slatted chair back, or a rectangle in a drying rack. Pick one opening and move until it frames a single thing beyond, such as a shoe, a towel or a patch of floor. The bars around that one gap should be sharper than whatever they contain.
tips: Get close enough that one opening dominates the others.
Focus on the nearest bar so the frame leads.

title: Hanger Around a Button
oneLiner: Hold a clothes hanger so its triangle borders one button.
details: Take a wire or plastic hanger and hold it in front of a shirt, a coat or a cushion that has a button or a pocket. Move the hanger until the triangle encloses that one detail and the hook stays out of the way at the top. A plain shirt makes the triangle easier to see than a busy pattern.
tips: Pinch the hook against a door top so your hand stays out.
Fill the frame with the triangle rather than the whole garment.
constraint: The button or pocket must sit inside the hanger's triangle.

title: Lens on the Pattern
oneLiner: Lay a pair of glasses so one lens frames a pattern.
details: Put a magazine, a dish towel or a patterned plate flat on the table. Lay glasses or sunglasses on it so one rim circles a single motif, such as a flower or a stripe. If you have neither, a bangle does the same job, shot from above so the rim is the border.
tips: Tilt the phone slightly to dodge a white glare on the lens.
Focus on the rim, then nudge it until the motif sits in the middle of the opening.

title: Circle of a Hair Tie
oneLiner: Set a hair tie, bangle or ring so it circles a button.
details: On a table, place a loose button, a coin or a dried bean. Drop a hair tie, a bangle or a ring around it so the circle is complete and the small object sits in the middle, not under the band. Shoot from above with the table filling the background, so the loop is the whole idea.
tips: Use a plain table so the circle does not fight a pattern.
Move a lamp to the side if the band throws a confusing shadow across the button.
constraint: The circle must be unbroken, and the button, coin or bean must sit inside it.

title: One Gap in the Blinds
oneLiner: Tilt the blinds until one gap frames a narrow strip.
details: Close a set of horizontal blinds, then tilt them until one gap shows a narrow strip of wall, tree trunk or the building opposite. Stand close so that one slot fills the frame and the slats become thick borders. If you have curtains instead of blinds, leave a narrow gap between the panels and frame the same kind of strip through it.
tips: Focus on the nearer slat so the borders are hard-edged.
Turn the phone to portrait if the slot is taller than it is wide.
constraint: Only one gap should appear in the picture.

title: Curtain Leaves a Pane
oneLiner: Draw the curtain back until the pane frames a branch.
details: Pull a curtain or a blind across most of a window, leaving a clean rectangle of glass. Shift the fabric until that leftover pane frames one thing beyond the glass, such as a branch, a wall or a plant that already lives on the sill. The curtain edge and the window frame should meet as a border, with the subject fully inside.
tips: Expose for the view in the leftover pane, not the dark curtain.
Smooth the curtain edge with your hand so the border is a straight line.

title: Washer Round Window
oneLiner: Shut the washer door and frame the clothes in its round window.
details: Put a few clothes in the washing machine, ideally a strong colour against the drum, and close the door without starting a cycle. Stand square to the round window so the door's ring frames the bundle. If you have no machine, use a clothes dryer or a cold oven with the power left off and a folded cloth behind the glass.
tips: Wipe the round glass so a smear does not cross the clothes.
Turn off the room light if the glass mostly shows your own reflection.

title: Cup in the Microwave
oneLiner: Leave a cup inside the microwave and frame it in the door.
details: Set a coloured cup on the plate of a microwave, or on the rack of a cold oven, and close the door without switching anything on. Crouch until the cup sits in the door window, with the dark border around it. A lamp behind you helps the cup show through the glass.
tips: Press the phone close to the glass to weaken the room reflection.
Focus on the door frame, then check the cup is still recognisable.
constraint: The appliance must stay switched off.

title: Through the Spout Arch
oneLiner: Crouch by the sink and frame the drain through the spout.
details: If the spout has a high curve, crouch at the sink until the arch frames the drain, a sponge or an upturned glass. The metal curve should read as a border, with the subject sitting in the opening rather than behind the spout. If the spout is a straight pillar, stand a jug with a handle in the sink and use that handle as the arch instead.
tips: Dry the metal first so highlights do not hide the curve.
Get the lens level with the arch so it does not collapse into a line.

title: Rim of the Cup
oneLiner: Look straight down into a cup so the rim frames the drink.
details: Pour water, tea or juice into a cup and hold the phone directly above the opening. The rim should become a circle that contains only the surface of the drink, with the table left outside. A light-coloured cup against a darker table, or the reverse, makes the ring obvious.
tips: Hover until the rim looks round rather than a squashed oval.
Lock exposure on the liquid if the rim is much brighter.
constraint: Nothing but the drink should appear inside the rim.

title: Opening of a Shoe
oneLiner: Point the phone into a shoe so the opening frames the insole.
details: Set a shoe on the floor with the opening facing you, laces loosened if they cross the hole. Bring the phone close until the collar of the shoe becomes a frame around the insole, the stitching or the wear marks inside. One shoe is enough, and a pale insole inside a dark shoe gives the cleanest border.
tips: Shoot in the shade of the room so the opening is not a black hole.
Brace the phone on the floor in front of the shoe.

title: Handle Through Handle
oneLiner: Place two mugs so one handle loops the other handle.
details: Set two mugs on the table and turn them until the opening of the nearer handle lines up with the farther one. Lower the camera until you see handle through handle, two loops nesting. A pale wall or a bright window behind the mugs keeps the holes from merging into the background.
tips: Close one eye while you line the handles up, then match that view.
A spoon left inside a mug will clutter the loop, so take it out.
constraint: Both handle openings must be visible, one inside the other.

title: Border Around the Print
oneLiner: Crop a framed print so its border boxes the picture.
details: Find a framed picture on a wall, or lay a magazine page on a larger sheet so the sheet makes a border. Move in until you can see nested rectangles: an outer edge, a pale border, and the picture itself. Keep the corners of the inner picture visible, and leave any name or digits out of the frame.
tips: Shoot square to the wall to keep the corners honest.
Shade the glass with your body if a lamp reflects in the middle.

title: Between Two Books
oneLiner: Shoot through the gap between two books at the wall.
details: Stand two books upright with a narrow gap between them, on a shelf or held on a table. Aim through that gap at a plain wall, a poster or a third book set farther back. The page edges and covers should become the sides of a tall window, with the far surface sitting inside it.
tips: Pinch the books steady from above so the gap stays even.
Focus on the nearer cover, not the wall in the distance.

title: Doorway Around a Window
oneLiner: Stand where a doorway surrounds a window farther on.
details: Find a view from one room through a doorway to a window, a picture or a mirror in the next room. Move until that inner rectangle sits wholly inside the door frame, with wall visible between the two. A plant or a curtain gives a window something to hold, and a picture works if no window lines up.
tips: Tap the darker door frame, then slide exposure up if the surround sinks to black.
Shift a little left or right until the inner rectangle is not cut by the door edge.
constraint: The inner rectangle must sit completely inside the doorway.

title: Mirror Holds a Doorway
oneLiner: Catch a doorway inside a mirror so the frames nest.
details: Use a hall mirror, a closet door or any mirror you can tilt, and stand so a doorway appears in the glass. Adjust until the mirror's own edge is visible and the doorway sits inside it, a rectangle inside a rectangle. If no door will fall in the glass, catch a window frame the same way, and keep your face outside the reflection.
tips: Include the mirror's physical edge so it reads as a frame.
Wipe a finger-smudge off the glass before you shoot.
constraint: The mirror edge and the doorway or window must both be in the picture.

title: Letter Slot View
oneLiner: Lift the mail flap and frame the mat through the slot.
details: From inside, lift the mail slot flap and look through the slot so its four edges frame the mat, a plain wall or the floor just outside your own door. Prop the flap with a book or a mug so your fingers stay out of the opening. If the door has no slot, lie down and use the gap under an interior door to frame a rug or a slipper in the next room.
tips: Rest the phone on the mat or the floor so the slot stays level.
Wait until the slice shows only the mat, the floor or a wall.

title: Cupboard Door Border
oneLiner: Open a cupboard door so it borders a row of jars.
details: Open a kitchen or bathroom cupboard and stand a little to one side. Let the door on one side and the cabinet edge on the other form a frame around a single shelf of jars, bottles or folded towels. Close the door slightly until the contents feel held by the opening rather than spilling out of it.
tips: Use the cupboard's own light, or stand a lamp so it washes the shelf.
Keep the door edge sharp and let the jars sit just behind the focus.

title: Through the Chair Legs
oneLiner: Lie on the floor and frame a slipper through chair legs.
details: Put a slipper, a sock or a small book on the floor beyond a chair. Lie down and look through the gap between the legs, or under the seat, until that object sits inside the opening. If the chair is a solid box, use the space under a table and frame the slipper between two legs instead.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor so the gap stays steady.
A lamp low to the ground lifts the slipper out of the shadow under the seat.
constraint: The slipper, sock or book must sit fully inside the gap.

title: Ring Around the Bottle
oneLiner: Use a curtain ring or towel ring to circle a bottle.
details: Take one ring from a shower curtain, or use a towel ring, a bangle or the handle of a basket. Hold it in front of a bottle, a toothbrush cup or a small plant so the ring makes a full circle around it. Bring the ring close to the phone and leave the bottle a little farther back, so the circle is the border and the bottle is what it contains.
tips: Hold the ring at the edge with two fingers kept outside the circle.
A plain tiled wall behind the bottle keeps the hole easy to see.

title: Egg in Its Cup
oneLiner: Look into an egg carton so one cup frames a single egg.
details: Open an egg carton and look straight down until one moulded compartment frames a single egg, the cardboard walls forming the border. Shift so neighbouring eggs stay outside that one cup or fall out of the picture. If you have no eggs, set a cotton ball or a wrapped candy in one compartment of an egg carton or an ice-cube tray.
tips: Shoot from directly above so the compartment looks square.
Soft window light from the side shows the rim of the cup.
constraint: Only one egg, or one small object in its place, should sit in the cup.

title: Basket Holds the Apple
oneLiner: Let one basket hole circle a piece of fruit.
details: Hold a fruit basket, a laundry basket or a mesh bag in front of an apple, a lemon or a small jar. Shift until one opening makes a complete border around that object and the weave stays sharp. If every hole is tiny, use the open top of the basket as the frame and shoot down so the rim holds the fruit.
tips: Bring the basket close so one hole grows large.
Focus on the near weave, not the fruit behind it.
constraint: The fruit must sit fully inside one opening.

title: Ring Around a Pen
oneLiner: Stand a pen inside a napkin ring and shoot the circle.
details: Take a napkin ring, a spare curtain ring or a roll of tape and stand it on the table. Slide a pen, a breadstick or a carrot through the middle so the ring frames it. Shoot from the side, level with the ring, so the circle reads as a border rather than a thin line.
tips: Rest the ring against a mug if it keeps tipping.
Choose a plain wall behind the pen so the hole stays easy to see.

title: Colander's Single Hole
oneLiner: Bring a colander close so one hole frames a tomato.
details: Set a cherry tomato, a grape or a wrapped candy on the table. Hold a colander, a grater or a slotted spoon in front of it and choose a single hole. Move until that hole is a round border with the small object in the middle and the other holes fall outside the picture.
tips: If the phone will not focus, move the colander a little farther from the lens.
Turn the colander until the chosen hole looks round.
constraint: Only one hole should appear in the picture.

title: Hood Circles a Spoon
oneLiner: Shape a hood into a circle around a wooden spoon.
details: Hold a hoodie, a coat or a scarf so the hood or a rolled edge makes a soft circle. Place a wooden spoon, a bottle neck or a hanger hook in that opening. Bring the cloth close to the phone and leave the object a little farther back so the fabric is the frame and the spoon is what it contains.
tips: Pinch the cloth at the bottom, keeping your fingers outside the circle.
Put a light wall behind the spoon so the hood does not swallow it.

title: Magazine Tube
oneLiner: Roll a magazine and look through it at a pen.
details: Roll a magazine or a sheet of paper into a short tube and look through it at a pen, a candle or a spice jar on the table. The near end of the tube should reach the edges of the photo, with the object sitting in the far opening. Rest the far end on a book so the tube stays still while you shoot.
tips: Brace your elbows on the table and shoot through the near opening.
Focus on the near rim so the tube reads as the frame.
constraint: The near opening must touch every edge of the photo.

title: Cuff Around a Button
oneLiner: Open a cuff so the stitched ring frames one button.
details: Use the cuff of a shirt you are wearing or a shirt on a hanger. Hold the cuff open so the stitched circle becomes a frame around one button or around the cuff on the other sleeve. Shoot close, with the cloth filling the edges and the button sitting in the opening.
tips: A lamp to the side shows the stitching on the cuff.
Keep your fingers outside the ring.

title: Through the Open Box
oneLiner: Look through an open box at a jar set behind it.
details: Stand a shoe box or a cereal box on its side with both ends open, and set a jar or a mug a little behind it. Move until the near opening holds the jar with cardboard visible on every side. If you would rather use a cupboard, open the door and frame one shelf the same way, with the door edge as one side of the border.
tips: Get the phone close to the near opening so the box becomes the frame.
Aim a lamp at the jar and leave the inside of the box a little darker.
constraint: The jar or mug must sit fully inside the near opening.

title: Slit Beside the Curtain
oneLiner: Leave a narrow slit where the curtain meets the wall.
details: Draw a curtain or hang a towel beside a wall, leaving a narrow vertical gap. Stand so that slit frames a thin slice of the window frame, a plant on the sill or the edge of a picture. The fabric and the wall should be the two borders, and the slice in the middle should stay fully inside them.
tips: Turn the phone so the slit runs from top to bottom.
Focus on the fabric edge nearest the lens.

title: Arch of the Headphones
oneLiner: Rest a headphone band so it arches over a small jar.
details: Set a small jar, a candle or a spice pot on the table. Rest the band of a pair of headphones, or a belt folded into a curve, over it so the arch frames the jar and the ends stay on the table. Shoot from the side, level with the arch, so the jar sits in the opening rather than in front of it.
tips: Get the lens level with the jar so the arch does not flatten into a line.
A plain wall behind the jar keeps the opening easy to see.
constraint: The jar, candle or pot must sit fully inside the arch.

title: Flap as a Window
oneLiner: Open one box flap and frame a mug inside the box.
details: Take a cereal box, a shoe box or any small carton and open one flap. Place a mug, a ball of socks or a piece of fruit inside. Shoot so the flap and the box edges make a border around that object, and turn busy printing toward the outside of the picture.
tips: Shoot from slightly above so you can see into the box.
Tap the flap edge so the border stays sharp.

title: Under the Chair Arm
oneLiner: Frame a cushion through the opening under a chair arm.
details: Set the phone low beside a chair that has an open arm, and look through that opening at a cushion, a folded blanket or a book on the seat. Shift until the cushion sits inside the gap with the arm and the seat as borders. If the chair is solid, set a basket in front of the cushion and use one gap in the weave the same way.
tips: Rest the phone on a stack of books so the opening stays level.
Keep the near wood or weave sharp and the cushion a little softer.
constraint: The cushion, blanket or book must sit fully inside the opening.

title: Lid Inside a Lid
oneLiner: Set a small lid inside a larger one and shoot the rings.
details: On the table, place a bottle cap or a small jar lid in the middle of a larger lid, a plate or a shallow bowl. Shoot from above so you see one ring inside another, with the table as the outer ground. Turn labels face down so the shapes stay clean.
tips: Centre the small lid so the nesting is obvious.
Fill the frame with the outer ring and a little of the table.
constraint: Both rims must be complete circles.

title: Side of the Sill
oneLiner: Stand beside a window and let the opening frame the glass.
details: Move close to one side of any window so you see the inner wall of the opening, the sill and the glass together. The near wall should border the pane, like a short tunnel around the view. If the sill is shallow, open a book beside the glass and let the cover and the pages make the same nested borders around a small object.
tips: Focus on the near wall of the opening, not the view beyond.
Include the corner where the sill meets the glass.

title: Ceiling Light Halo
oneLiner: Hold the phone just above the floor and aim it up into a ceiling light.
details: Find a pendant, a flush light, or a ceiling fan and hold the phone just clear of the floor beneath it. Include a wide circle of ceiling around the fixture so the height is part of the picture. Watch the exposure so the bulb does not blow out entirely unless you want a small burst of rays.
tips: Use the timer and tuck your fingers behind the phone so you are not a dark shape.
Shift the phone slightly off the exact middle.
If dust on the shade shows, include it rather than climbing up.
constraint: The camera must point within thirty degrees of straight up.

title: Houseplant From Ground
oneLiner: Look up through a houseplant from a phone held near the floor.
details: Hold the phone just above the floor, or rest it on a low stool with your hand still on it, and aim through the leaves towards a window or a lamp. Stems should feel tall, and the leaves can turn into dark shapes against the bright. A plant on a stand works as well as one at floor level.
tips: Tap focus on the nearest leaf, not the bright window.
Choose a portrait frame so the plant has room to rise.
Wipe the floor only if a bit of it sneaks into the corner.

title: Under the Table View
oneLiner: Slide low and shoot upward at a table or desk from underneath its edge.
details: Hold the phone on the floor under a table and aim up at the underside and the things on top. Legs, books, or a mug rim can show against the brighter ceiling. Keep the phone fully underneath, where a foot cannot reach it, so the angle still feels clearly from below.
tips: Keep hold of the phone, or rest it fully under the tabletop.
Include at least two table legs for a frame.
Expose for the brighter ceiling and let the underside go dark.
constraint: The camera must be below the table surface.

title: Stairs From the Bottom
oneLiner: From the lowest indoor step, shoot upward, or up a doorway if you have none.
details: Stand on the lowest indoor tread and hold the phone low, still in your hand, pointing up the flight. The lines of the treads should converge towards the top, with a slice of ceiling included. If you have no stairs, hold the phone at floor level in an indoor doorway and aim up the door so the frame narrows overhead.
tips: Turn the grid on and keep the uprights straight.
Wait until the flight or the doorway is clear.
House lights or daylight from the door are enough.
constraint: Keep the phone in your hand, low on the lowest tread or at an indoor doorway.

title: Canopy From Knee Height
oneLiner: From knee height indoors, aim up through leaves or branches.
details: Stand at a window or in a doorway and hold the phone down by your knee. Aim up so stems anchor a corner and leaves break the bright background, whether that is sky through the glass or a lamp behind a tall plant. Use a houseplant if no branches are visible without leaving home.
tips: Take a short burst if a breeze shifts the leaves.
Cup a hand beside the lens if the background is glaring.
Let one stem touch a corner of the frame.

title: Wall From the Ground
oneLiner: Aim up a wall in the room from a phone held near the floor.
details: Crouch indoors and hold the phone just above the floor where a wall rises. Aim up so the wall, a window, or a corner lean together. Keep the picture to that wall and whatever already hangs on it.
tips: Put the corner of the wall near a third.
Expose for the wall when a window is brighter.
A portrait frame gives the wall more height.
constraint: The wall must run off the top of the frame.

title: Sky Gap From the Ground
oneLiner: From a low hold in your doorway, frame a ribbon of sky between two edges.
details: Hold the phone low in a doorway or at a window, with your feet kept indoors, and aim up until two edges border the sky. Two walls, a door frame and a wall, or the window frame itself all count. The sky can be any tone you find.
tips: Rotate to a portrait frame if the gap is a tall strip.
Move a little further back if both edges will not fit.
Expose for the edges if you want them dark against the sky.
constraint: Sky must be bordered on at least two sides.

title: Under-Bed Slats
oneLiner: Slide the phone fully under the bed and look up at the slats.
details: Push the phone fully under the bed frame, where a foot cannot catch it, and aim up at the slats or the base. A little daylight from the far side will separate the boards. If the bed has no gap, use the space under a sofa instead, and draw the phone straight back out.
tips: If the gap is dark, aim a nearby lamp at the far side of the bed.
Focus on the nearest slat edge.
constraint: The phone must be under the furniture, not beside it.

title: Chair From the Floor
oneLiner: From beneath a chair, shoot up past the seat.
details: An empty kitchen or desk chair is ideal. Hold the phone on the floor beneath the seat, with your hand still on it, so the seat becomes a dark ceiling and the legs become columns. A window or lamp beyond the chair will brighten the gaps.
tips: Include at least three legs if they fit.
Expose for the bright gap, not the dark seat.

title: Shelf From the Floor
oneLiner: From the floor, aim up the face of a bookcase or shelf.
details: Hold the phone against the baseboard at the base of a bookcase and tilt it up the shelves. The shelves should stack like floors of a building. One leaning book or a plant on a high shelf can be the only accent.
tips: Keep the uprights of the bookcase parallel to the phone edge.
Tap a book on the middle shelf.
constraint: The top shelf must be cut by the frame.

title: Curtain From the Hem
oneLiner: Look up a curtain from a phone held at the hem.
details: Hold the phone low where the curtain meets the floor, or on the sill if the hem ends there, and aim up the folds. The cloth should fill most of the frame and end at the rail or the top of the window. A narrow slice of window light at the edge is enough.
tips: Focus on the nearest fold.
Shoot in portrait so the curtain can run the full height.

title: Hall at Baseboard Height
oneLiner: Rest the phone by the baseboard and look along the hall.
details: A hallway, a corridor, or the length of one room will do, as long as you have it to yourself. From baseboard height the floor becomes a wide plain and the door at the end looks far away. Hold the phone so it just touches the floor, with your hand still on it, and include the line where wall meets floor.
tips: Keep your hand on the phone so the horizon stays level.
Focus about a third of the way down the hall.
constraint: The phone must stay in your hand while it touches the floor.

title: Under the Sofa
oneLiner: Push the phone under the sofa and catch the light on the far side.
details: There is often a bright gap on the far side of a sofa or an armchair. Slide the phone fully underneath, where a foot cannot catch it, and point it towards that gap, including a leg or the underside. Dust is honest here, so leave it unless it hides the shape, then draw the phone straight back out.
tips: Expose for the bright gap.
Use the timer only once the phone is fully underneath.

title: Tabletop Mug Loom
oneLiner: Put the phone on the table and let a mug loom above it.
details: Set the phone flat on a table or counter, lens aimed slightly up at a mug, a glass, or a jug. Move the cup close so it becomes huge and the room shrinks behind it. A spoon beside it can stay small in the distance.
tips: Tap the near rim so the room falls soft.
Raise the far edge of the phone on a coaster if you need a little more upward tilt.
constraint: The cup must be cut off by the top of the frame.

title: Fridge From the Floor
oneLiner: Shoot up the fridge door from a phone held near the floor.
details: From a low hold on the kitchen floor the fridge is a tower of straight lines. Aim up so the top of it meets the wall or a cupboard. A magnet or a note may stay if it does not show a name.
tips: Keep the fridge edge parallel to the frame.
Expose for the door if a window beside it is brighter.

title: Radiator From the Floor
oneLiner: Skim the phone along the floor towards a radiator or low shelf.
details: Hold the phone just above the floor, about a metre back, and look along the baseboard towards a radiator, a low heater, or the end of a bookcase. The pipes, panels, or uprights should diminish with distance. A towel or a book can break the rhythm, but the low line is the idea.
tips: Keep the baseboard as a level line across the lower third.
Focus on the nearest pipe, panel, or upright.
constraint: Include the radiator, heater, or bookcase and the floor that leads to it.

title: Plant on a High Shelf
oneLiner: Point the phone up from the floor at a plant sitting on a shelf.
details: A plant on a shelf, a closet, or the top of a cupboard is the subject, seen from a low hold. Leaves should overhang and show their undersides. If nothing lives up high, put a plant on a stack of books on a table and shoot up from the floor.
tips: Focus on the lowest leaf that juts out.
Let a lamp or window sit behind the leaves.

title: Runner Towards a Door
oneLiner: Follow a rug along the floor towards a closed door.
details: Choose a rug, a runner, or the edge of a mat in a room you have to yourself. Hold the phone just above the floor so the near edge is wide and the door sits small at the far end. A chair leg can interrupt the line, and you stay indoors.
tips: Tap the rug a short way in front of the lens.
Keep the door near the top third.
constraint: The phone stays close to the floor, still in your hand.

title: Door From the Mat
oneLiner: From a low crouch at the mat, aim up the full height of the door.
details: Hold the phone just above a doormat, or the floor inside the door if you have no mat, and tilt it up the door. Keep the phone in your hand. The bottom rail should be huge and the top of the door small, with the frame on one side so the rectangle converges.
tips: Portrait framing fits the door better than a wide frame.
Expose for the door colour, not the bright room beyond it.

title: Gap Between Two Pots
oneLiner: Hold the phone in the gap between two pots and look up.
details: Two plant pots on the floor, or a pot and a tall bottle, can make a little canyon. Hold the phone low between them and aim up so their rims frame a piece of ceiling or wall. Do not shift the pots into a walkway.
tips: Choose pots of different heights if you can.
Focus on the nearer rim.
constraint: Both objects must enter the frame.

title: Gap Under a Bookcase
oneLiner: Peer through the low gap under a bookcase or cabinet.
details: Many bookcases and cabinets stop a little short of the floor. Hold the phone at that gap and shoot through to the light on the other side. Do not slide the phone under and leave it where a foot goes.
tips: Expose for the bright side beyond the gap.
Keep your fingers out of the near edge.

title: Along a Low Edge
oneLiner: Look along a windowsill or low shelf from just above it.
details: Hold the phone just above a windowsill, a low shelf, or a long counter. The near end should be large and the far end should narrow. A plant, a book, or the frame can close the far end.
tips: Keep the near edge as a strong diagonal or a level line.
Focus on the near corner of that edge.
constraint: The window glass stays mostly out of frame.

title: Mat From Ground Level
oneLiner: Get the phone level with the doormat and shoot across its edge.
details: From this height the mat is a landscape of fibres, and the door is only a wall beyond it. Crouch and hold the phone just in front of the mat. If you have no mat, a rough rug indoors works the same way.
tips: Focus on the near fibres.
Include the mat edge as a horizon across the frame.

title: Courses Up the Wall
oneLiner: Aim upward along an indoor wall from a phone held close.
details: Any wall at home will do, brick, tile, or smooth paint. Hold the phone close to the wall, just above the floor, so the lines race upward and converge. Include the line where the wall meets the floor as the bottom of the picture.
tips: Bring the phone close to the wall, still in your hand, then tilt up.
A portrait frame exaggerates the rise.
constraint: The floor line must appear along the bottom.

title: Under the Drying Rack
oneLiner: Slide the phone under a drying rack and shoot up through the rungs.
details: Set the phone face up on the floor beneath a clothes drying rack, with or without laundry on it. Use the timer, step back, and let the rungs cross the ceiling like a lattice. Socks or towels hanging from the bars become dark shapes against the light.
tips: Use the three-second timer so your hand stays out of the shot.
Switch on the ceiling light if the rungs read as flat grey.

title: Spout From the Floor
oneLiner: Frame the sink spout, or a tall jug, from down near the floor.
details: Hold the phone low in front of the sink so the spout occupies the top of the frame. If the sink is awkward from the floor, set a tall jug on the counter and shoot that from the same low hold. The object should feel larger than the wall behind it.
tips: Focus on the spout or the jug lip.
Keep the counter line low in the frame.
constraint: The spout or jug must touch the top edge.

title: Mail Slot From Below
oneLiner: Aim up from floor level at a mail flap or a hinge.
details: A mail flap usually sits well above a phone held down by your knee. Hold the phone indoors and shoot up so the flap, or a hinge if there is no slot, fills the frame with a little of the door. The underside is the part you rarely see. Leave any envelopes out of the picture.
tips: Wait until the flap or hinge is still.
Include the screws under the flap, or the pins of the hinge.

title: Leaves at Ground Level
oneLiner: Look along low leaves from a phone held among them.
details: The lower leaves of a pot, a trailing plant, or herbs on a low shelf will do. Hold the phone low among the leaves so they tower over the lens. A wall or a cupboard can be a soft backdrop.
tips: Focus on the leaf closest to the lens.
Shade the lens if a bright window sneaks in above the leaves.
constraint: At least one leaf must be larger than the wall behind it.

title: Floor Joints Indoors
oneLiner: Follow a joint in the floor from a low hold towards a door.
details: Tiles, boards, or the seam beside a rug have lines you can follow. Hold the phone low so one joint runs from the bottom of the frame towards a closed door. Kneel where you have room, and do not lay the phone on the floor.
tips: Clean the lens, since it will be near the floor.
Stop the line before it reaches the exact middle.

title: Bright Door Slit
oneLiner: Catch the bright gap under a door from a low hold beside it.
details: With a light on in the next room, the gap under the door becomes a thin glow. Crouch on your side of the door, hold the phone low, and aim at that slit, including the bottom rail. Daylight from a far window in that room is enough if the lamps are off.
tips: Expose for the gap so the door stays dark.
Brace your wrist on your knee so the slit stays sharp.
constraint: The glowing gap must cross the frame.

title: Sill From Beneath
oneLiner: Shoot the underside of a windowsill from a low hold beneath it.
details: An indoor windowsill, or the lip under a high shelf, has an underside you only see from below. Hold the phone low and tilt up until that underside is a dark band. Include a little wall below it and a little of the shelf or glass above.
tips: Portrait framing gives the wall room under the sill.
Focus on the front edge of the sill.

title: Fitting Over the Door
oneLiner: Point up from floor level at the light nearest a door.
details: A ceiling light, a lamp on a high shelf, or a plain fitting above an interior door all work, switched off or on. Hold the phone low and aim up so the fitting is large against the wall or ceiling. If no light sits there, frame the top hinge the same way.
tips: If the lamp is on, expose for the fitting so the glow keeps a shape.
Include a little of the door head so the light has a place.
constraint: The fitting or the top hinge must sit in the top half.

title: Dresser Bottom Slit
oneLiner: Look through the long gap under a dresser from floor level.
details: A dresser, a chest, or a closet door often stops short of the floor. Hold the phone low and look through that long gap, with the far side as a bright slit. If the piece sits flush to the floor, use the gap under the fridge instead.
tips: Align the gap so it runs horizontally through the middle.
Focus on the near lower edge of the furniture.

title: Pitcher Looming Low
oneLiner: Let a pitcher loom over the phone, held low in front of it.
details: Hold the phone low in front of a pitcher, a kettle, or a large bottle on the floor or a low counter. The spout or handle should arc across the top of the frame, and the room can shrink behind it. Keep the phone clear of anywhere a foot might pass.
tips: Focus on the nearest part of the spout or handle.
Wipe spots off the pitcher if they hide the shape.
constraint: The pitcher, kettle, or bottle must be closer than the wall.

title: Coil on the Floor
oneLiner: Peer through a coiled cable, or a rolled towel, from one end.
details: Coil a cable, a belt, or a rolled towel on a clear patch of floor that you are not crossing. Hold the phone at one open end and look through the tunnel. The far opening should be a bright circle or oval.
tips: Shade the near end with your body so the far opening stays the bright part.
Focus on the near rim of the coil.

title: Shoe from Toe Height
oneLiner: Set a shoe indoors and shoot it from the height of the toe.
details: One shoe or boot you already wear is enough. Put it on the floor just inside the door, then hold the phone low in front of the toe and tilt up so the shoe towers. Leave the other shoe out of frame.
tips: Focus on the toe, not the door behind it.
Get low enough that the sole or the toe cap fills the lower half.
constraint: Only one shoe in the frame.

title: Wall Meets the Floor
oneLiner: Frame the joint where an interior wall meets the floor.
details: Find an inside corner where a wall meets the floor. Hold the phone low in that corner so one surface rises and the other runs away. A scuff, a cable, or the edge of a rug can mark the joint.
tips: Put the joint near the lower corner of the frame.
Keep both surfaces in focus by tapping the joint itself.

title: Fibres in Front
oneLiner: Fill the foreground with rug fibres and keep a door small above.
details: Kneel indoors and hold the phone close to the pile of a rug or the grain of the floor, without letting it touch. A door or the far wall should sit small at the top. You are making that texture the main subject.
tips: Focus on the fibres nearest the lens so the door softens.
Wipe the lens after, since the floor is dusty.
constraint: The door or wall may occupy no more than the top quarter.

title: Low Vent From Below
oneLiner: Face a floor vent from below and include the wall above.
details: A floor vent, a low wall grate, or the slots on a heater cover can be the foreground. Hold the phone low in front of it and tilt up so the pattern leads into the plain wall. If you have none of these, use the lowest line of tiles and the grout.
tips: Get close enough that the holes or slots are large.
Keep the wall filling the top half.

title: Below the Shelf
oneLiner: Look up from beneath a high shelf or a wall cupboard.
details: Hold the phone below a wall cupboard, a high shelf, or a pot that already sits up there, and shoot up so the underside overhangs the frame. Trailing leaves can enter if they are already there. Do not move anything into a walkway.
tips: Focus on the rim from below.
Include a little wall or ceiling so the overhang reads.
constraint: The underside of the shelf, cupboard, or pot must be visible.

title: Rod From the Floor
oneLiner: Look up from a low hold at a curtain rod or a cable.
details: A curtain rod, a string of lights, or the top edge of a door frame can cross the upper part of the picture. Hold the phone low and aim up so the line enters from one corner and leaves by another. The door or the curtain below can be a dark base.
tips: Expose so the rod stays dark against the brighter wall or ceiling.
Take two frames if the line is thin, and keep the sharper one.

title: Latch from Down Low
oneLiner: Photograph a latch or handle from below, with the phone held low.
details: A door handle or a drawer pull is usually seen straight on. Hold the phone low and look up to the underside of the lever and the plate. Fill the frame with that hardware and a little of the door or drawer around it.
tips: Focus on the underside of the lever.
Shift so the metal does not mirror the whole room.
constraint: The handle or latch must fill at least half the frame.

title: Grain From One End
oneLiner: Track a floorboard or a wooden sill from one low end.
details: A floorboard, a wooden windowsill, or a timber shelf has a grain line you can follow. Hold the phone at one end, close to the wood, and look along it. The groove or the grain should run into the distance.
tips: Side light will show the grain better than even light.
Focus on the wood nearest the lens.

title: Chair Caster Line
oneLiner: Line the phone up with a chair caster and look along the wheels.
details: From down low, the casters of a desk chair or a small cart make a repeating shape. Hold the phone in line with them so the nearest wheel is large and the next is smaller. If there is only one wheel, let that one sit huge with the chair rising behind it.
tips: Get low enough to see under the chair a little.
Focus on the nearest wheel.
constraint: The nearest wheel must be partly cut off by the frame.

title: Staircase Steps as Lines
oneLiner: Find a staircase and frame it so the steps draw clean diagonal lines through your shot.
details: Use an indoor flight if you have one. If you do not, a low stool or a short stack of books seen from the side can stand in. Get to the bottom so the edges repeat as diagonals in ordinary room light.
tips: Align your phone parallel to the step edges for the cleanest lines.
Include a handrail or wall at one edge to anchor the geometry.
constraint: Shoot from the bottom of the flight or the stack.

title: Window Grid Portrait
oneLiner: Photograph a building facade where windows form a repeating rectangular grid.
details: From the sidewalk outside your home, frame the window frames on your own building so they repeat as a grid, staying on the frames rather than anything seen through the glass. Fill most of the picture with that pattern and keep the lines level. If the windows do not repeat, use a grille, a vent, or a row of identical panels on that same wall.
tips: Tap to focus on the glass, then slightly underexpose to keep reflections crisp.
Crop tight so the grid fills the frame edge to edge.

title: Circle in a Square Room
oneLiner: Spot a circular object inside a square or rectangular space and make both shapes obvious.
details: A clock on a wall, a plate on a table, or a round mirror in a hallway all count. Place the circle where it contrasts with straight edges nearby. Step back enough to show the room geometry around it.
tips: Place the circle in the middle for a calm, graphic look.
Use portrait orientation if the room height helps the square feel.
constraint: Include at least three straight edges in the frame.

title: Shadow Triangle Hunt
oneLiner: Find a triangular shadow cast by a door, a lamp, or a chair leg.
details: A partly open door, a lamp close to a wall, or a chair leg can throw a triangle onto the floor or wall. Move until one triangle is clean and obvious. You do not need strong daylight; a single lamp is enough.
tips: Increase contrast slightly in your editor if the shadow feels faint.
Place the triangle on a rule-of-thirds intersection.

title: Parallel Lines Receding
oneLiner: Frame paving joints so they run parallel from near to far.
details: From the sidewalk by your door, use the parallel joints of the slabs, or the rails of a fence beside them. Crouch a little so the lines run from the near edge towards a vanishing point. Keep the picture on those lines and the slabs around them.
tips: Hold the phone low and level for a stronger perspective.
If something blocks the joints, shift along to another stretch of slabs.
constraint: The lines must run from the near edge into the distance.

title: Shelf Stack Symmetry
oneLiner: Arrange or find stacked boxes, books, or cans that mirror each other across a shelf.
details: A kitchen shelf, a cupboard, or a bookshelf can supply the stacks. Stand square to the shelf so left and right feel balanced. Look for repeated heights and gaps that echo each other.
tips: Shoot straight on to avoid skewed rectangles.
Remove one distracting item if it breaks the symmetry.

title: Corner Where Two Walls Meet
oneLiner: Make a sharp interior corner the subject, with both walls equally visible.
details: Stand close to where two indoor walls meet at a right angle. Include the seam running through the frame. Plain paint or a textured wall both work, because the corner itself is the geometry.
tips: Hold the phone so the vertical corner line stays truly vertical.
Shift a little sideways if one wall looks much wider than the other.
constraint: Shoot within arm's length of the corner.

title: Tile Diamond Repeat
oneLiner: Fill the frame with floor or wall tiles whose grout lines form a repeating diamond or grid.
details: A bathroom floor, a kitchen floor, or the tiled wall behind a counter is enough. Hold the phone flat above the floor or straight at the wall so the grout reads clearly. Even light keeps a diamond layout or a plain grid easy to see.
tips: Use grid lines on your camera to keep grout lines parallel to the edges.
Fill the entire frame with pattern; no floor edge needed.

title: Hanger Makes a Triangle
oneLiner: Hang a coat hanger on a door and frame the triangle it makes.
details: Use a wire or wooden hanger against a plain door or wall. The triangle of the shoulders, plus the hook if it helps, should be the clear shape. If your hanger is only a curve, fold a card into a triangle and lean it in the same place.
tips: A plain door stops the background from competing with the wires.
Tap the hanger so the door behind falls a little soft.
constraint: Nothing else should hang on that door.

title: Rings on the Stovetop
oneLiner: Look straight down at the rings of a stovetop until they read as circles.
details: Stand over the stovetop and frame one ring or several, whatever the stove actually has. Include a little of the metal around them so the circles have a square or rectangle to sit in. If you have no stovetop, use a round trivet or a pot lid on the counter.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the stovetop so the rings stay round.
Wipe the lens if a smudge turns a ring into a blur.
constraint: Shoot from directly above.

title: Circle in the Sink
oneLiner: Point the phone down into an empty sink and make the drain a clear circle.
details: Clear the sink, then look straight into it so the drain sits as a circle in the basin. The corners of the sink can supply straight edges around it. A bathroom basin and a kitchen sink both work.
tips: Dry the metal if a wet highlight hides the rim of the drain.
Tap the drain, not the bright metal rim above it.

title: Radiator Parallel Lines
oneLiner: Use the fins or panels of a radiator as a set of parallel lines.
details: Stand square to a radiator, a convector, or a vent with repeated bars. Fill the frame so the lines run edge to edge. If you have none, a wire rack or an oven shelf leaned against a wall will do.
tips: A side-on lamp, or light from a window, picks out each fin.
Match the fins to the grid so they do not drift.
constraint: Lines must run edge to edge.

title: The Curve of a Banana
oneLiner: Place a banana or a loose cable on a plain surface and photograph the arc.
details: Choose one curve and give it an empty table, a sheet of paper, or a bare floor. Come in close so the arc enters from one side and leaves by another. A wooden spoon or a headphone band can stand in if you would rather not use fruit.
tips: Shoot from above so the curve lies flat in the picture.
Keep the background to one colour.

title: Pencil End Geometry
oneLiner: Show the end of a pencil so its shape fills the frame.
details: Most pencils end in a hexagon. Come as close as the phone allows until that end is large and readable. If your pencil is round, photograph the round end instead and let the circle be the subject.
tips: Rest the pencil on a book and brace the phone on the same book.
Add a lamp if the end falls into shadow.
constraint: The end of the pencil must touch at least three edges of the frame.

title: Rings of a Tape Roll
oneLiner: Stand a roll of tape on end and photograph the concentric rings.
details: Masking tape, washi tape, or a kitchen-paper roll all show rings when stood on end. Shoot from slightly above so you see the hole and the outer circle together. A plain table stops other shapes from intruding.
tips: Focus on the cardboard core.
Rotate the roll until any loose end is hidden underneath.

title: Keyboard as a Grid
oneLiner: Angle a keyboard so the keys become a grid of small rectangles.
