details: Use a laptop or a separate keyboard on a desk. Get low and to the side so the keys foreshorten into a repeating field and the characters matter less than the grid. A phone keypad works if that is what you have.
tips: Glare from a window can wash the letters while leaving the key edges.
Lock focus on the nearest row, then tilt a fraction more.
constraint: Do not let readable words become the subject.

title: Arcs in a Plate Stack
oneLiner: Stack three or more plates and shoot the repeating curves from the side.
details: A short stack on a table or in a cupboard is enough. Put the phone at the height of the rims so each plate adds an arc. Bowls work too if their curves repeat.
tips: A lamp from the rim side draws a line on each plate.
Leave a little dark gap between rims if you can see one.

title: The Machine's Round Door
oneLiner: Frame the round door of a washing machine as a clean circle.
details: Stand square to the door so the rim does not squash into an egg shape. Include a little of the machine's rectangular body if it sets off the circle. If you have no round door, use a large pot lid or a round tin on a square surface.
tips: Tap the rim rather than the dark glass in the middle.
Take a small step sideways until the circle looks round again.
constraint: The circle must be fully inside the frame.

title: Holes in the Grater
oneLiner: Fill the picture with the regular holes of a grater, a colander, or a sieve.
details: Hold the utensil up or lay it on a contrasting cloth. Move until the holes repeat without the handle taking over. The pattern of holes is the geometry; food is not required.
tips: Light from behind the holes makes them read as bright dots.
Keep the phone parallel to the metal so the holes stay even.
constraint: The handle must stay out of frame.

title: Spiral of the Binding
oneLiner: Open a notebook and photograph the wire binding as a spiral.
details: A spiral pad shows a row of loops along one edge. Come close and let those loops run from top to bottom. If your notebooks are glued, coil a tape measure or a ribbon into a spiral and shoot that from above.
tips: Focus on the nearest loop and let the far ones soften.
A vertical frame suits a binding that runs down the page.

title: The V of an Open Book
oneLiner: Open a book partway and frame the V where the pages rise.
details: Set the book on a table with the covers down and the pages up, like a tent, or simply open it halfway. The valley or the peak should make a clear V. Shoot from one end so the V leads into the frame.
tips: Get down to table height rather than shooting from above.
Soft window light along the fold of the book shows the crease.
constraint: The V must be the largest shape in the picture.

title: Cables Along the Baseboard
oneLiner: Follow cables along a baseboard so they echo that horizontal.
details: Look where a cable runs above the baseboard, or where the baseboard meets the floor if no cable is visible. Frame a stretch where two or three lines stay parallel. A cable cover counts as one of the lines.
tips: Crouch so the lines sit across the middle of a horizontal frame.
Exclude plugs with readable labels by cropping tighter.

title: Rim of the Lampshade
oneLiner: Shoot across a lampshade so the rim becomes a clean ellipse.
details: Any shade works, lit or unlit. Hold the phone so you look slightly down on the rim and the circle turns into an oval. If you have no shade, the rim of a mixing bowl gives the same ellipse.
tips: Tap the near rim, where the curve is sharpest.
Step around the lamp until the ellipse is even, not pinched.
constraint: The rim must be a complete oval, not a broken arc.

title: A Paper Triangle
oneLiner: Fold a sheet of paper once and photograph the triangle you made.
details: Fold a rectangular sheet so one corner crosses the opposite edge and a triangle appears. Leave the spare paper visible so the rectangle is still in the picture. Shoot from above on a clear table.
tips: A hard crease reads better than a floppy fold.
Hold the phone flat so the table edges stay straight.

title: Floorboards Running
oneLiner: Stand at one end of the floorboards and let the parallels run away.
details: Boards, laminate, or the long stripes of a rug all work. Stand so the lines start wide at your feet and narrow farther on. If the floor is plain, use the parallel edges of a runner or a long mat.
tips: A low hold, around knee height, strengthens the convergence.
Keep the phone level left to right so the boards do not tilt.
constraint: The lines must converge in the frame.

title: A Square Coaster
oneLiner: Set a square coaster on a plain table and shoot it from above.
details: A coaster, a square napkin, or a spare tile will do. Turn it so its edges are not parallel to the table, and leave plain table around it. The contrast between those two rectangles is the point.
tips: Shoot from directly above to keep the corners square.
Leave empty table around the coaster on all sides.

title: Arch of a Handle
oneLiner: Find an arch in a basket handle, a mug, or the top of a mirror.
details: Look for a curve that rises and comes down again: a basket, a cup handle, or a rounded mirror frame. Frame the arch so the two ends are included. A plain background keeps the curve readable.
tips: Get close enough that the arch spans most of the width.
Focus on the top of the curve.
constraint: Both ends of the arch must be in the picture.

title: The Switch Plate
oneLiner: Treat a light switch or an outlet plate as a small rectangle on a big wall.
details: Stand back a little so the plate is small and the wall around it is large and plain. The rectangle should sit clearly, screws and all. A double outlet gives you two rectangles if that is what you have.
tips: Square the phone to the wall so the plate does not become a diamond by mistake.
Even light avoids a shadow that could be mistaken for part of the shape.

title: Grid of a Cooling Rack
oneLiner: Lay a cooling rack or an oven shelf flat and fill the frame with the grid.
details: Put the rack on a table or shoot it in the oven if it is cool and fixed. Line the wires up with the phone so the grid looks deliberate. A wire letter tray or a fan guard works if you have no rack.
tips: Light from the side gives each wire a bright edge.
Crop until the grid is cut off by the frame on every side.
constraint: No food in the picture.

title: Circle at the Mug Rim
oneLiner: Look down into a mug so the rim is a circle around a darker pool.
details: An empty mug is best. Hold the phone just above the rim and centre it until the opening is round. The inner bottom and the rim should read as two circles.
tips: Brace your elbows on the table.
If the inside is too dark, a window to one side will lift it without flattening the rim.
constraint: The rim must be a full circle.

title: A Complete Circle
oneLiner: Frame a round cover or a circular mat so the circle is complete.
details: Look for a round metal cover set into the sidewalk near your door and shoot straight down, keeping your shoes out of the circle. If you cannot find one there, use a round mat or a circular tray on the floor indoors. Either way, the whole circle should sit inside the frame with a little surface around it.
tips: Hold the phone level so the circle stays round.
Include a little of the surface around the rim for scale.
constraint: The whole circle must sit inside the frame.

title: One Strong Diagonal
oneLiner: Find one diagonal brace or rail and let it cross the frame.
details: A timber brace on a gate or a fence panel works if one is right outside your door. If you have neither, use the diagonal of a chair back, a drying rack, or a picture frame leaned in a corner. Let that single line run from a lower corner of the frame toward an upper one.
tips: Get low so the diagonal runs from a lower corner towards an upper one.
Tap where the diagonal meets another edge.
constraint: One diagonal must be the strongest line in the picture.

title: Rectangles in the Brick
oneLiner: Move close to a brick wall and make the repeating rectangles obvious.
details: Use the wall of your own building, seen from the sidewalk. Fill the frame with bricks and the mortar lines between them. If the wall has no visible bricks, use panels, blocks, or a run of rectangular slabs instead.
tips: Stand square to the wall so the courses stay horizontal.
Even light shows the mortar better than a hard patch of glare.
constraint: The pattern must reach all four edges.

title: Top of a Bollard
oneLiner: Shoot down onto a bollard, a post cap, or a round stool top.
details: The top should read as a circle or a rounded square, with sidewalk or floor around it. Stand close and point the phone down. If no post is near your door, use the round top of a stool indoors.
tips: Include a short stretch of the side so the top has a base.
Focus on the rim of the cap.

title: Curve of the Column
oneLiner: Stand beside a round post or pipe and show its curve against a flat wall.
details: A round post, a thick drainpipe, or a round fence post will do, seen from the sidewalk by your door. The curve should contrast with a straight wall beside it. Frame the bulge against that flat surface.
tips: A side view shows the bulge better than a head-on view.
Leave space on the flat side so the curve has something to push against.
constraint: The curve and the straight wall must both appear.

title: Diamonds in the Fence
oneLiner: Make a field of diamonds from a lattice fence or from brick joints.
details: If a chain-link fence or a lattice stands beside the sidewalk, move close and fill the frame with diamonds. If you have neither, use brickwork, a lattice chair back, or a woven basket until the crossings read as diamonds. The repeat is the subject.
tips: Focus on the nearest crossing so the pattern locks.
Turn the phone until a row of diamonds sits level.

title: Light Between the Slats
oneLiner: Let the gaps in a blind become a row of bright parallel lines.
details: Close a blind, then tilt it until thin bright gaps appear between the slats. Those lines of light are the subject, so fill the frame with them. If you have no blind, use a slatted vent, or hold a dish rack up to a lamp and photograph the gaps.
tips: Underexpose a little so the bright gaps stay thin lines.
Turn the phone until the gaps run truly horizontal.
constraint: Only the slats and the gaps may be in the frame.

title: Wheel of the Can
oneLiner: Isolate one wheel of a garbage can so the circle and the tyre dominate.
details: Crouch by a garbage can or a recycling bin at home and frame a single wheel or round foot. The circle and a little of the can beside it are enough. If the can has neither, photograph a small wheel on a desk chair from the same low angle.
tips: Get low so the wheel looks large.
Focus on the rubber edge where it meets the floor.

title: Arch at the Entrance
oneLiner: Frame an arch at your entrance, or the closest curve you can find at home.
details: Look above your own door, or along an indoor hallway, for a curved head or an arched opening. Include the whole rise and fall of the curve. If every head is straight, use the bend in a drainpipe on the wall or the curve of a shower rod.
tips: Take a pace back until the full arch fits.
Keep the phone upright so the arch does not lean.
constraint: The full curve must be visible.

title: Cable Spiral
oneLiner: Coil a charging cable on a table and shoot the spiral from above.
details: Use a cable you already have indoors and lay it into a flat spiral on a plain table. Shoot from above so the rings read clearly. Tuck the plug under the coil or crop it out so the spiral stays the subject.
tips: Keep the rings from crossing so each circle stays readable.
Stand so your shadow falls off the table, not across the coil.
constraint: Shoot from directly above the spiral.

title: Shelves as Parallels
oneLiner: Face a bookcase or cupboard and let the shelves run as parallels.
details: Stand square to a shelf, a bookcase, or a set of cupboard shelves. Let two or more horizontals cross the frame, with the gaps between them clear enough to read. Empty shelves work as well as full ones, because the lines matter more than the objects.
tips: Keep the phone level so the shelves stay horizontal.
Come closer if a tall unit will not fit, and let the shelves run off the frame.
constraint: At least two shelves must cross the frame.

title: Circle of the Lid
oneLiner: Stand over a garbage can lid and fill the frame with that circle.
details: Use the lid of a garbage can or a recycling bin you keep at home. Shoot down so the lid reads as a circle or a near-circle, with the handle only if it helps the shape. This is the lid, not the wheels.
tips: Hold the phone level with the lid.
If the lid is square, frame the round handle on that lid.
constraint: The lid's outer edge must be fully visible.

title: Rectangles in the Door
oneLiner: Find the rectangles in a door and frame several at once.
details: Use any panelled door in the home and stand square to it. Include the outer frame as one rectangle and the panels as smaller ones inside it. A flush door can give you the frame and a handle plate, or use cupboard doors for the same nested rectangles.
tips: Turn the grid on and line the door up with it.
Move back if the outer rectangle is cut off.

title: Squares of a Trellis
oneLiner: Frame a trellis or a square vent so the grid runs edge to edge.
details: Use a trellis, a fence panel, or an outdoor vent you can see from the sidewalk. Move close until the squares are cut by the frame on every side. If none of these are outside, fill the frame with a square vent cover on an indoor wall.
tips: Match one bar to the top edge of the phone before you shoot.
Focus on the crossings, where the grid is clearest.
constraint: No sky in the frame.

title: The Broken Straw
oneLiner: Stand a straw or a pencil in water and show the shaft appearing to bend.
details: Fill a clear tumbler with water and lower a straw or a pencil in at a slant. Move until the shaft looks bent at the waterline. That kink, seen through the side of the glass, is the picture.
tips: Get the phone level with the waterline so the bend sits in the middle.
A plain background keeps the kink easy to see.
constraint: The bend must be visible at the waterline.

title: Tint at the Base
oneLiner: Tip a clear tumbler and show the colour gathered in its thick base.
details: Many clear tumblers hide a green or blue tint in the thick bottom. Tip one on a light cloth so you look through that thick part. If your glass stays colourless, use the thickest rim you can find, where the material deepens.
tips: A window behind the glass makes a faint tint easier to see.
Fill the frame with the base rather than the whole tumbler.

title: Overlapping Rims
oneLiner: Overlap two drinking glasses so the rims cross in the frame.
details: Set two empty glasses on a table, one partly behind the other. Shoot through the near glass so both rims are visible and they cross. The doubled transparency is the subject, so leave drinks out of them.
tips: A side light draws a bright line along each rim.
Focus on the near rim and let the far one soften slightly.
constraint: Both rims must cross near the middle of the frame.

title: Pooled Light from Glass
oneLiner: Catch the wobbly patch of light a water glass throws on the table.
details: Set a glass of water between a window or a lamp and a plain table or cloth. Shift the glass until a bright, warped patch appears on the surface. Photograph the patch with the glass still in frame, so the cause is visible.
tips: Dim other lamps if a ceiling light washes the patch out.
Focus on the table where the patch is brightest.

title: Oil on the Water
oneLiner: Float a little cooking oil on water and photograph the line between them.
details: Pour water into a clear tumbler, then add a small spoon of cooking oil and let it settle. Look through the side of the glass at the boundary where the two layers meet. A window or a white card behind the glass makes that line easier to see.
tips: Hold the phone level with the boundary.
Tap the glass at that line, not the rim above it.
constraint: The boundary between oil and water must cross the frame.

title: Print Bent by Water
oneLiner: Hold printed type behind a water glass and show the letters bend.
details: Use a book page, a newspaper, or a plain label, and keep any branding out of the story. Hold a glass of water in front of the type and watch the letters swell and curve. The words need not be readable; the bend is the point.
tips: Fill the glass nearly to the top so the lens of water is large.
Steady the glass on the page if holding it wobbles the letters.

title: Hollow under the Bottle
oneLiner: Photograph the inward hollow in the base of a glass bottle.
details: Many bottles have a base that pushes inward. Use an empty bottle and rest it near the table edge so you can see that hollow from the side. If the base is flat, photograph the thick glass where the side meets the bottom instead.
tips: A low lamp or a window from behind lights the thick glass.
Keep the label turned away so the glass stays the subject.
constraint: Include the whole base.

title: Threads at the Neck
oneLiner: Close in on the screw threads at a jar's glass neck.
details: Take a clean empty jar, a sauce jar or a jam jar, and unscrew the lid. Come close to the ridges of glass at the neck. Turn the jar until those threads catch a line of light.
tips: Use the phone's closest focus, then ease back until the ridges sharpen.
A dark cloth behind the jar separates the threads from the room.

title: Beads on Cold Glass
oneLiner: Take a cold glass from the fridge and photograph the beads on it.
details: Fill a tumbler with cold water and leave it on the table until droplets form on the outside. Photograph those beads, not the drink. If the glass stays dry, sprinkle a few drops on the outside yourself.
tips: Focus on a single bead near the middle of the glass.
Side light turns each bead into a tiny highlight.
constraint: The droplets must be on the outside of the glass.

title: Drops on the Screen
oneLiner: After a shower, photograph droplets clinging to the glass screen.
details: Run the shower briefly, then frame droplets on a glass screen before they sheet together. The screen is the subject, so leave the rest of the room out. If you have no glass screen, sprinkle water on a glass lid or the outside of a tumbler and shoot those drops instead.
tips: Turn off the room light and use the window, or a small lamp from the side.
Tap one drop so the camera does not focus through to the tiles.

title: Dust on Picture Glass
oneLiner: Focus on dust sitting on picture glass rather than the picture.
details: Choose a framed picture, a glass cabinet door, or a glass tabletop. Get close and focus on specks on the glass so the image or the room beyond falls soft. You are proving the glass is a surface in front of something else.
tips: A raking lamp from the side wakes the dust up.
Shoot at a slight angle so the glass plane is obvious.
constraint: Whatever is behind the glass must be soft.

title: Mesh in the Oven Door
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the mesh in an oven or microwave door.
details: Make sure the oven is off and cool, then move close to the door glass. The fine mesh or dotted pattern in the glass should fill the picture. If neither door has a pattern, hold a small metal tea strainer against a plain glass and shoot through both.
tips: A light on in the oven, with the door shut, can reveal the mesh.
Keep the phone parallel to the door so the dots stay even.

title: Tint of a Kitchen Bottle
oneLiner: Hold a green or brown bottle to the light and show the tint.
details: Olive oil bottles, vinegar bottles, and some sauce bottles are coloured glass. Hold one up to a window or a lamp and let the tint fill the frame. If every bottle is clear, shoot the faint green edge of a thick tumbler instead.
tips: Turn the label away from the light.
Underexpose a little so the tint stays rich rather than white.
constraint: The bottle or glass must be backlit.

title: An Unlit Clear Bulb
oneLiner: Photograph an unlit bulb if the glass is visible, or a small round vase.
details: Use a clear bulb only if the lamp is unplugged and the glass is cool, or if the bulb is already out and cold. Frame the curve of the glass and the stem inside if you can see it. If your bulbs are coated or plastic, a small round vase or a clear bauble on a table works instead.
tips: Put a dark sweater or cloth behind the bulb so the glass edge shows.
Do not switch the lamp on for this picture.

title: Glass over the Watch
oneLiner: Shoot the cover glass of a watch or a clock, not the time.
details: Lay a watch or a small clock on a table and tilt it until you can see the glass cover as a layer. Look for a speck, a fine scratch, or the rim where glass meets the case. The numbers can fall soft.
tips: A window reflection in the cover, kept small, helps prove the glass is there.
Use close focus and brace your wrist on the table.
constraint: Do not make the time the subject.

title: Curve of the Jug
oneLiner: Fill a glass jug with water and magnify whatever sits behind it.
details: A measuring jug, a vase, or a large tumbler will do if you have no jug. Set a spoon, a coloured cloth, or a lemon behind it and look through the curved water. Move until the object behind is clearly swollen by the glass.
tips: Keep the jug close to the object behind it.
Focus through the glass onto that object, not on the near rim.

title: Glass Around a Candle
oneLiner: Place an unlit candle behind glass, or shoot an empty glass holder.
details: Set an unlit candle in a glass holder, or leave the holder empty if you have no candle. Shoot through the side so the glass thickness and the curve wrap the candle or the empty middle. Do not light it.
tips: A window to one side traces the rim of the holder.
Crop close enough that the glass wall is thick in the frame.
constraint: Leave the candle unlit.

title: Edge of the Glass Shelf
oneLiner: Photograph the thick edge of a glass shelf, a platter, or a tumbler on its side.
details: Find a glass shelf, a glass platter, or lay a thick tumbler on its side. Look along the edge so you see the thickness as a green or clear band. That band is the subject, not the things on the shelf.
tips: A sheet of white paper behind a loose platter makes the edge readable.
Focus on the near corner of the edge.

title: The Pane Seen Edge-On
oneLiner: Open a window just enough to photograph the pane's edge.
details: From inside, open a window a little and look at the cut edge of the glass, not at the view. The edge is often slightly green and brighter than the sheet. If the window does not open, use the edge of a mirror or a glass shelf in the same close way, without climbing.
tips: Keep your hands and the phone inside the room.
Rest a dark notebook just behind the edge, kept out of frame, if the glass vanishes against the light.
constraint: Stay inside, and show the edge rather than the view.

title: Lid over Patterned Cloth
oneLiner: Lay a glass lid on patterned cloth and shoot the pattern through it.
details: Use a pot lid, a glass dish, or a clear plate. Set it on a dish towel, a patterned shirt, or a magazine page. Photograph the way the pattern shifts under the glass compared with the cloth beside it.
tips: Include both covered pattern and bare pattern in one frame.
Shoot from above so the lid does not become a mirror.

title: A Ring on the Table
oneLiner: Set a wet glass down, lift it, and include both glass and ring.
details: Dip the base of a tumbler in a little water and press it on a dark table or a tray. Lift it and leave the ring, with the glass still in the frame beside the mark. The picture is the glass and the print it made.
tips: A dark surface shows a water ring more clearly than a pale one.
Shoot from a low side angle so the ring is an oval.
constraint: Both the glass and the ring must be visible.

title: Bubbles Against the Glass
oneLiner: Photograph bubbles clinging to the inside of a glass of water.
details: Run water into a clear tumbler so a few bubbles sit on the glass, or use sparkling water if you have it. Come close to the side and focus on the bubbles, not the far rim. If they vanish quickly, add a drop of dish soap and swirl gently until a few small bubbles remain.
tips: Side light from a window puts a bright edge on each bubble.
Brace your wrist on the table so the close view stays sharp.
constraint: The bubbles must be inside the glass.

title: A Lens on the Page
oneLiner: Lay reading glasses or a tumbler base on a page and frame the magnified type.
details: If you wear reading glasses, fold them on a book so one lens covers the type. If you do not, press the thick base of a tumbler gently on the page, or use a magnifying glass if you own one. Frame the jump in size where the glass begins.
tips: Shoot from above to avoid reflections of the ceiling.
Focus on the enlarged letters under the glass.
constraint: The glass must cover only part of the type.

title: Shoulders of Two Jars
oneLiner: Stand two jars so their glass shoulders overlap and stay transparent.
details: The shoulder is the curve between a jar's neck and its wider body. Stand two empty glass jars so those curves overlap. Shoot through both so you can see the far jar through the near one.
tips: A window behind them keeps the glass bright and see-through.
Shift one jar a centimetre at a time until the curves cross cleanly.

title: The Doubled Pane
oneLiner: From inside, find the faint second edge in a double-glazed window.
details: Stand indoors and look at your own window for the spacer bar or a ghosted second line near the frame. That doubled edge is the subject, so come close and let the view outside fall soft. If you cannot see a second line, photograph the seal where the pane meets the frame.
tips: Stand to one side so your reflection is not the main shape.
Tap the glass near the frame, not the view through it.

title: Lines Through a Tumbler
oneLiner: Hold a tumbler of water so a window frame bends behind it.
details: Fill a clear tumbler and hold it up indoors, between you and a window. Move it until a straight frame or a glazing bar bows through the water. Keep the bent line recognisable, with the rim of the glass still in the picture.
tips: Fill the tumbler nearly to the top for a stronger curve.
Focus on the frame seen through the water, not on the near glass.
constraint: A straight line must look bent through the water.

title: One Leaf, Plain Surface
oneLiner: Set one leaf on a plain surface and make it the clear focal point.
details: Use the sidewalk or the bare ground just outside your door as a quiet backdrop, or a pale cloth on a table. Pick a leaf with a strong edge or a clear colour against that surface. If nothing has fallen outside, take one leaf from a weed already growing there, or from a houseplant, and lay it on the ground or the cloth.
tips: Stand over the leaf and point the phone straight down so the surface stays even.
Tap the leaf once so the veins, not the surface around it, carry the focus.
constraint: Only one leaf in the frame.

title: Daylight on the Sill
oneLiner: Let daylight settle on a houseplant and include both the leaves and the sill.
details: Choose any pot already near a window, or move a small one there. Daylight from the glass is enough even when it is soft and indirect. Include a strip of sill so the plant is clearly living indoors.
tips: Slide exposure down a touch if the window turns into a white block.
Focus on the nearest leaf edge rather than the buildings outside.

title: Moss in a Brick Crack
oneLiner: Find green moss or a tiny weed growing from a crack in brick or stone outdoors.
details: Check a boundary wall or gaps in the paving near your door. Move close until you can see the texture of the green against the mortar. The picture is a small plant holding a narrow space.
tips: Switch on close-up mode before you lean in, if your phone offers it.
Shade the spot with your body when the stone is glaring.
constraint: Fill at least half the frame with the crack and its green growth.

title: Herb Cluster on a Counter
oneLiner: Group a few kitchen herbs or greens on a counter and shoot them like a tiny garden.
details: Basil, parsley, spinach or a few green onion tops can stand in for a garden. Cluster pots or cut stems on a clear patch of counter near a window. Keep bottles and clutter out so the greens stay the whole story.
tips: Get down to counter height instead of shooting from standing height.
Wet your fingertips and tap a couple of leaves so they catch a small shine.

title: The Bark's Pattern
oneLiner: Fill the frame with ridges on bark or on a thick woody stem.
details: Use a tree you can reach from the sidewalk near home, and move close. Follow ridges, splits and any pale lichen rather than showing the whole trunk. This is the surface, so leave sky and branches out. If no tree is within reach, fill the frame indoors with a woody herb stem or a thick houseplant cane.
tips: Step back slightly and use a little zoom if the frame edges bow outward.
Choose a patch where the light skims sideways across the ridges.
constraint: No sky in the frame.

title: Spiral from Above
oneLiner: Look straight down into a small plant so its leaves make a spiral.
details: A succulent, a tight herb or any houseplant with leaves around a middle will do. Hold the phone parallel to the rim of the pot so the shape stays even. Ordinary room light is enough for this overhead pattern.
tips: Set the pot on a plain sheet of paper or a bare table first.
Tap the middle of the plant, where the newest growth sits.

title: Where the Green Turns
oneLiner: Frame green growth where it turns the corner of an outside wall.
details: Look along a wall you can reach from your own entrance for ivy, a vine, moss or a weed, especially where the growth bends around a corner. Show the leaves and the hard surface together. Move back just enough that both the plant and the wall have room. Moss or a weed at that corner is a complete subject.
tips: If the leaves glare, move until your body blocks the brightest patch.
Let the corner of the wall sit near one side so the turn is obvious.
constraint: Give the wall and the green roughly equal space.

title: A Start in a Cup
oneLiner: Set a seedling, cutting or damp bean in a cup on a daylit ledge.
details: A small cup, a glass or a jar can hold a seedling, a herb cutting, or a dry bean pressed into wet cotton. Put it where daylight comes from one side only. You are photographing a small start on a ledge, not a finished display.
tips: Stand a dark book behind the cup so the stem separates from the room.
Include the soil or the water line so the container has a scale.

title: Leaf Against the Lamp
oneLiner: Hold one leaf up to a lamp and photograph the veins as a bright map.
details: Pick a leaf from a herb, a houseplant you tend, or a fallen leaf brought inside. Switch on a lamp and hold the leaf between the bulb and the phone so light comes through it. Keep your fingers off a hot shade and use a cool lamp, or a bright screen, if the bulb feels warm. Move until the veins read as bright lines and the room behind stays dim.
tips: Tap the leaf surface so the phone does not focus on the lamp behind it.
Turn other lights off so the glow comes through the leaf only.
constraint: The leaf should cover most of the frame.

title: Roots in the Glass
oneLiner: Stand a green stem in a clear glass and show what the water does to it.
details: Use a herb stem, the base of a green onion or a cutting that already has roots. Fill a clear glass with water and place it on a windowsill. Shoot from the side so the stem, the water line and any roots are visible through the glass.
tips: Wipe fingerprints off the outside of the glass before you focus.
A sheet of white paper behind the glass keeps the stem easy to read.

title: The Youngest Leaf
oneLiner: Seek the smallest leaf on a houseplant and give it more space than the old ones.
details: Look at the growing tip of any houseplant, where the newest leaf is still smaller or paler. Frame that leaf with part of an older one beside it so the size difference is obvious. A fresh herb sprig works if the pots are not putting out growth.
tips: Brace your wrist on the pot rim before you come in close.
Approach from the side so the new leaf sits against a darker one.
constraint: The newest leaf stays the sharpest thing in the picture.

title: The Fading One
oneLiner: Let a fading leaf lead the picture while greener leaves sit behind it.
details: Find a yellow, pale or brown leaf on a houseplant, a herb or a bunch of greens in the kitchen. Place that leaf in front and let healthier green recede. The contrast of tired and fresh is the idea, so leave the faded leaf in place.
tips: Daylight from the side shows the colour change more clearly than a ceiling light.
Tap the faded leaf so the green behind it falls a little soft.

title: Dark Soil, Bright Stems
oneLiner: Water the soil lightly, then shoot the dark surface around the stems.
details: Use any potted plant and pour a small splash at the base so the soil turns a deeper colour. Come in close from above, keeping the rim mostly out. The picture is the damp soil, the stem bases and the grit on the surface.
tips: Wait a few seconds so the water is no longer one shiny blob.
Focus where a stem enters the soil.
constraint: Keep the pot rim out of the frame.

title: Down the Trail
oneLiner: Trace a trailing plant from the pot down to its lowest leaf.
details: Use a trailing houseplant or, if you have none, hang a few long herb stems over the rim of a jug. Stand back until you can see the start at the container and the end of the trail. Let the hanging line run from the top of the frame towards the bottom.
tips: A plain wall behind the trail keeps each leaf easy to follow.
Hold the phone upright so the drop has room.

title: Grain and Green
oneLiner: Lay one green leaf on a wooden table and shoot along the grain.
details: A herb leaf, a salad leaf or a leaf from a plant you tend can lie flat on a table or a chopping board. Get low so you look across the surface rather than straight down. Wood grain and the leaf's midrib should cross or follow each other.
tips: A low side light from a window lifts the leaf off the wood.
Focus on the midrib and let the far edge of the table soften.

title: Pressed to the Pane
oneLiner: Shoot leaves that touch the window, from inside the room.
details: Find a houseplant pressed to the glass, or gently rest one leaf against the pane. Include both the leaf and a little clear glass. A faint reflection on the indoor side is fine as long as the leaf stays the subject.
tips: Focus on the leaf, not the view through the window.
Wipe a small indoor patch of glass first if marks compete with the leaf.
constraint: Include both a leaf and a patch of bare glass.

title: Three Greens Together
oneLiner: Compare three different greens side by side on a plain surface.
details: Pick three greens that do not match, such as a herb sprig, a houseplant leaf and a piece of lettuce or cabbage. Lay them in a row on a pale plate or a sheet of paper. Nothing else should compete with those three shades.
tips: Shoot from above so the row reads as a simple line.
Keep the phone parallel to the table so the nearest leaf is not stretched.
constraint: Nothing but the three greens and the surface they rest on.

title: Pale Side Up
oneLiner: Flip a leaf and photograph the paler underside and its veins.
details: Turn over a leaf from a houseplant, a herb or a head of lettuce. The underside is often paler, with veins that stand out. Rest it on a dark cloth or a dark book so the pale side has something to sit against.
tips: Place a lamp to one side so tiny shadows form along the veins.
Come in close and tap a single vein.

title: Green Ends in a Dish
oneLiner: Stand kitchen greens in a shallow dish of water and shoot the cut ends.
details: Green onion bases, herb stems or celery tops can stand in a shallow bowl with a little water. Get level with the dish so you see the cut ends and the green rising out. This is a small restart on the counter, using greens you already have.
tips: A window to one side separates the stems from the background.
Focus on the cut end nearest the camera.
constraint: Keep packaging out of the frame.

title: Inside the Foliage
oneLiner: Tuck the phone into a leafy plant and shoot outward through the leaves.
details: Use any full houseplant, or stand long leaves in a jug if your pots are sparse. Rest the phone low among the leaves, pointing across the plant rather than at the ceiling. Near leaves can be soft as long as one leaf farther in is sharp.
tips: Brace the phone on the soil or the pot rim so it stays steady.
Lift a blocking leaf aside, then take your finger out before you shoot.

title: Bead on Green
oneLiner: Add one water drop to a leaf with your finger and photograph that bead.
details: Dip a finger in a glass and let a single drop fall on a houseplant leaf or a herb leaf on the counter. Wait until the drop sits still. Come in close so the bead and the bit of leaf under it are the whole picture.
tips: Let window light sit in the drop without hiding the leaf beneath it.
Tap the drop itself so the surrounding leaf can soften.
constraint: Only one drop in the frame.

title: A Gap in the Row
oneLiner: Leave a gap in a row of small plants about as wide as one missing pot.
details: Line up three or more small pots or glasses of cuttings on a shelf, sill or table. Take one out of the middle so a clear gap remains. Shoot along the row so the empty space is as noticeable as the plants.
tips: Get low so the pots overlap a little and the gap reads as a pause.
Use a plain wall behind the row so the gap does not fill with clutter.
constraint: The gap should be about as wide as one pot.

title: Lamp on One Plant
oneLiner: Light a single plant with one lamp in a room you have darkened.
details: Close the curtains, lower a blind or work in a room away from the window. Aim one lamp at a houseplant and let the wall behind fall dim. A separate flashlight, stood on a book, can play the lamp if that is the light you have.
tips: Expose for the lit leaves so the background stays dark.
Shift the lamp until one leaf edge picks up a thin bright line.
constraint: The background stays nearly black.

title: Salad Leaf Close
oneLiner: Fill the picture with one broad leaf from the kitchen.
details: Take one leaf from lettuce, cabbage, spinach or a bunch of herbs. Lay it flat or hold it up to the window. Come close until the veins and the crinkled surface fill the frame and the kitchen disappears.
tips: Hold the leaf against the window if you want the veins to brighten.
Tap the middle of the leaf and let the curled edges fall soft.

title: Mark Under the Pot
oneLiner: Show the ring a pot has left on its saucer or on the surface under it.
details: Look under a houseplant for a water mark, a dust ring or a stain on the saucer, sill or table. If the surface is clean, wet the base of the pot, set it down for a minute, then lift it. Photograph the circle it leaves, with a little of the pot still in frame so the cause is clear.
tips: Shoot from a low angle so the ring and the pot share the picture.
Tap the mark itself, which is easier to miss than the pot.

title: Layers of Green
oneLiner: Look through layered leaves so near ones soften and a farther leaf stays sharp.
details: Stand close to a bushy houseplant, or hold two sprigs at different distances from the lens. Focus on a leaf that is not the nearest one. The soft green in front should frame the sharper leaf without covering it completely.
tips: Tap the farther leaf carefully, because the phone will prefer the near one.
A bright window behind the plant helps separate the layers.
constraint: At least two layers of green in the frame.

title: Seed on Wet Cotton
oneLiner: Press a dry seed onto wet cotton and photograph that small setup.
details: A bean, a lentil or any dry seed from the cupboard can sit on a cotton pad, tissue or a paper towel in a saucer. Wet the cotton so it darkens, then press the seed in. Shoot from above or from a low side so both the seed and the damp fibres show.
tips: Steady the phone on the table edge before you come in close.
Stand a dark mug behind the saucer so the pale cotton stands out.
constraint: Use a plain dish, saucer or lid.

title: A Hung Bunch
oneLiner: Hang herbs or long leaves so they fall in front of a plain wall.
details: Tie a bunch of herbs or several long leaves with string, a hair tie or a strip of cloth. Hang them from a hook, a cupboard handle or a wooden spoon laid across a jug. Stand back so the bunch has air around it and the wall stays empty.
tips: Side light from a window will separate leaf from leaf.
Focus on the tie, then check that the lower leaves are still readable.

title: The Lean of the Plant
oneLiner: Turn a plant that leans towards the window and shoot the lean before it changes.
details: Many houseplants bend towards the glass. Photograph that curve from the side and include the pot. If every plant is upright, stand a few herb stems in a glass and lean the glass against a book so the stems angle across the frame.
tips: Get level with the pot rather than looking down on the lean.
A plain background makes the curve easier to see.

title: Pot and Leaf
oneLiner: Match a leafy plant with a pot or cup whose colour argues with the leaves.
details: Set a green plant in, or in front of, a pot, mug or bowl that is red, blue, yellow or any strong non-green. Use something from the kitchen if the plant's own pot is plain. Frame both the leaves and enough of the container that the two colours meet.
tips: Window light keeps both colours honest, without an orange cast from a lamp.
Come in close enough that the background cannot add a third colour.
constraint: Only one container and one plant.

title: Two Leaves Compared
oneLiner: Pair two leaves of different shapes and shoot them together.
details: Use two fallen leaves of different shapes, or two leaves from a houseplant or the kitchen. Place them side by side on paving, bare ground or a table. Fill the frame with the pair so the difference in outline is the point.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the surface and shoot from above.
Brush extra leaves aside so only the chosen pair remains.
constraint: Only two leaves in the frame.

title: Buds at Eye Height
oneLiner: Find a tight bud or furled tip at eye height on a plant you can reach.
details: Check a plant you can reach for buds, new tips or tightly furled leaves. One tight tip is enough. Come close and let that tip sit against a softer mass of green behind it. A weed tip by the door, or a furled leaf on a houseplant, is a fair subject.
tips: Steady your elbow against your side before you use close-up mode.
Shift a little left or right until the bud separates from the leaves behind.

title: Beneath the Leaves
oneLiner: Stand beneath leafy growth and fill the frame with leaves seen from below.
details: Use a tree or a large shrub you can stand under from the sidewalk near home. Point upward into the leaves. If you cannot stand under anything, hold a few leaves above the phone, from outdoor growth or a houseplant, and point up through them. Gaps of sky or ceiling may show, but the leaves should be the larger part.
tips: Tap a leaf, not a bright gap, so the green stays detailed.
Shift until one strong leaf crosses the middle.
constraint: Leaves cover more of the frame than the sky does.

title: Where Root Meets Stone
oneLiner: Include the point where a stem or trunk meets soil or paving.
details: At the base of a tree or shrub you can reach from the sidewalk, look for roots, flared bark or the stem entering the soil. Frame that meeting place and leave the upper growth out. If no trunk is near, photograph where a weed enters a crack, or where a houseplant stem enters the soil in its pot.
tips: Crouch so the camera looks slightly down on the join.
Include a little paving or soil for scale, then stop.

title: A Wall of Green
oneLiner: Make a dense patch of green fill the frame like a living wall.
details: Stand close to a hedge, a bush or any thick plant you can reach, or fill the frame with a bushy houseplant. Move in until leaves cover every edge. If the growth is thin, come closer until moss, a weed or those leaves leave no gap. You are photographing the density of the green.
tips: Open shade, or light off a pale wall, keeps single leaves from turning into black holes.
Focus a little way into the leaves so the green has some depth.
constraint: No sky and no bare wall in the frame.

title: Green in the Gravel
oneLiner: Spot one green shoot in a crack or in the bare soil of a pot.
details: Look in a crack just outside your door, or in the bare soil of a pot you already keep inside. A single shoot is enough. Get close and low so the pale ground or the soil makes the green obvious.
tips: Tap the shoot and let the stones behind it soften.
Keep the phone low enough that the plant has a little height.
constraint: One shoot only.

title: A Hole in Green
oneLiner: Choose a leaf with a hole or a torn edge and make that flaw the subject.
details: Find a fallen leaf, or a leaf on a plant you tend, with a hole, a notch or a torn edge. Hold it up by the stem or leave it where it is. Frame the damage so the missing part shows the window, a wall or your fingers behind it. A houseplant leaf indoors is fine if nothing outside has a flaw.
tips: Keep your fingers at the edge of the frame, on the stem.
Focus on the rim of the hole rather than the middle of the leaf.

title: Tied to a Stake
oneLiner: Show the tie that holds a leaning stem to a stick or a chopstick.
details: If a houseplant is already supported, photograph the knot, the stick and the stem together. If nothing is tied, rest a long herb stem against a chopstick or a pencil and loop string or a hair tie around both. Come in close so the fastening is the subject, not the whole plant.
tips: Let window light from the side give the string a small shadow.
Tap the knot so the stick and the stem are both readable.
constraint: The tie sits near the middle of the frame.

title: Branch from the Corner
oneLiner: Let a branch or long stem enter from one corner and cross the frame.
details: Choose a low branch or a long stem you can photograph without pulling it off. Let it enter from a corner and cross towards the opposite side. A weed or a length of ivy on a wall works, and so does a houseplant stem laid on a pale cloth. Leaves may overlap, but the line of the stem should stay readable.
tips: A plain bit of wall or sky behind the branch separates it from other growth.
Focus where the stem enters, then check the leaves at the far end.
constraint: The stem touches two edges of the frame.

title: Seed Head Close
oneLiner: Close in on a seed head, a grass head or a tight cluster of buds.
details: Look on weeds, long grass or a shrub you can reach without going far. If you cannot find a seed head, use a tight new tip or a cluster of tiny leaves. A chive head, a dried herb or a houseplant tip works indoors if you find nothing outside. Fill the frame and let the background fall smooth.
tips: Hold your breath for the moment the shutter fires at this distance.
Come at the head from the side rather than only from above.

title: Green Across a Line
oneLiner: Show a stem or a vine crossing a straight edge you already have.
details: Rest a houseplant stem, a vine or a long herb across a chair back, a window mullion or a drying rack. The straight line should show through the green. If a rail is right by your door, weeds along it work the same way, from your own side. Move until the plant and the line are both clear.
tips: Line the phone up with the straight edge so it stays upright.
Focus on a leaf that crosses in front of that line.

title: Along the Ground
oneLiner: Lay the phone near the base of a plant and shoot along the ground towards it.
details: Choose a low plant just outside your door, or set a houseplant on the floor. Put the phone on that surface, lens towards the plant, and fire the shutter without lifting it far. The floor or the ground should lead to the green, which sits a little above the middle.
tips: Wipe the lens first, because ground-level shots pick up smears.
Prop the phone on a book if the surface blocks the lens.
constraint: The phone stays within a hand's width of the floor.

title: Flat Against the Wall
oneLiner: Find green lying flat against brick, stone or tile and shoot it straight on.
details: Look for a leaf, moss or a weed pressed against a brick or stone wall near the door. A tiled wall, indoors or out, can stand in, with the plant laid or growing against it. Stand square to the wall so the grid lines stay straight, and let the green interrupt them.
tips: Let the plant occupy about a third of a frame that is otherwise wall.
Choose a wall out of direct glare so the lines stay visible.
constraint: The grid lines of the wall remain visible.

title: Inner Leaf, Outer Leaf
oneLiner: Compare a dim inner leaf with a brighter outer leaf on the same plant.
details: At a bush you can reach, or with a bushy houseplant beside a window, look from the outside into the darker interior. Include both a dim inner leaf and a brighter outer leaf. You are showing how the same plant changes from shaded to lit in the light you have today.
tips: Expose for the brighter leaf, then check the inner leaf is still visible.
Hold a blocking twig aside with a finger, then move your hand out.

title: Light Spilling In
oneLiner: Let light from a bright room spill across the floor of a dimmer passage.
details: Stand in the hall, the lobby, or the space by the front door, and leave a brighter room open. Dim the passage lights if they are on. Photograph the brightness as it crosses the floor, and keep the doorway it comes from in the picture.
tips: Expose for the bright floor so the near boards can stay dark.
Crouch so the spill becomes a wide band rather than a small distant patch.
constraint: The spill on the floor is the largest bright area.

title: Glow Under the Door
oneLiner: Show the strip of light that escapes under a closed door.
details: Close a door between a lit room and a darker hall, lobby or the space beside that room. Get the camera down level with the gap at the floor. A glowing strip, a little of the door and a little of the floor are enough.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor so the strip stays level.
If the gap is dim, turn on a lamp in the room beyond the door.
constraint: The strip runs the full width of the door.

title: Bright at the Far End
oneLiner: Look down the passage towards the brightest point at the far end.
details: Use a hallway, a corridor, or a straight run between two rooms. Let the bright end, whether a window or an open lit room, sit smaller in the distance. The walls can darken as they come towards you.
tips: Hold the phone at the height of the bright opening, not at the ceiling.
Tap the bright end so the near walls are allowed to fall soft.

title: Daylight on the Mat
oneLiner: Catch the light falling on the mat or floor just inside the front door.
details: Open the front door a little, or use glass in the door, so daylight lands on the mat, boards or tiles. If it is dark outside, aim a lamp at that same patch instead. Stay indoors, on your side of the door. Include both the lit patch and the edge of whatever it falls on.
tips: Move to the side so your shadow does not cover the mat.
If the glass is the source, wipe the inside before you judge the light.
constraint: You stay indoors, on your side of the door.

title: One Lamp Only
oneLiner: Switch off every light but one, and shoot the hall it leaves behind.
details: Turn off the ceiling lights and close the curtains if daylight adds a second source. Leave a single lamp, or only the light from one open doorway. Stand where the passage, lobby or space by the door shows that lone brightness and the rest falls quiet.
tips: Wait a moment so your eyes, and the exposure, settle on the single source.
Angle the shade if the bulb is an ugly hot spot.
constraint: Only one light source is visible.

title: Where the Light Stops
oneLiner: Find the soft boundary where a patch of light fades into the dim floor.
details: Use daylight from the front door or brightness from an open room, and look at the floor of the passage. There is usually a place where the brightness gives up. Fill the frame with that boundary, with floor on both sides of it.
tips: Get low so the boundary becomes a long edge rather than a small smudge.
Lock exposure on the bright side, then check the dim side is still visible.

title: A Wall Washed Clean
oneLiner: Watch a passage wall get washed by light from a side door.
details: Open a door off the hall or lobby so light rakes across one wall. The wall should be brighter near the doorway and quieter farther along. A switch or a mark can stay if it is already there, but do not add anything.
tips: Stand close to the opposite wall so the lit one has room to stretch.
Turn the phone sideways if the wash is a long horizontal band.
constraint: The lit wall fills at least three quarters of the frame.

title: Wedge from a Door Ajar
oneLiner: Leave a door ajar and photograph the wedge of light on the floor.
details: Open any door along the passage just enough to throw a triangle of brightness onto the floor. Include the door edge and the shape it makes. Between two rooms, with no hall at all, the same wedge still works.
tips: Adjust the door by a hand's width at a time until the triangle is clean.
Shoot from floor level so the wedge has a point you can see.
constraint: The wedge is wider at one end than the other.

title: Into the Bright Room
oneLiner: Stand in the dim passage and shoot into the brightest open room.
details: From the hall, the lobby or a doorway, look into a kitchen, bathroom or living room that is brighter than where you stand. Let the frame around the opening stay dark. Expose for the bright room so the passage around you falls away.
tips: Brace a shoulder on the door frame to keep the dark edges straight.
Take one step back if the bright room is cut off by the frame.

title: Back Into the Dim Hall
oneLiner: From a bright room, turn back and photograph the dimmer passage.
details: Stand in a lit room and face the hall, the lobby or the darker space by the door. Brightness should sit around the edges of your view, with a quieter passage ahead. Include the door frame so the drop in light has a border.
tips: Expose for the dim passage, even if the room at the edges burns a little.
Switch off a lamp behind you if it flattens the difference.
constraint: The passage is darker than the room you shoot from.

title: Lamp Mixed with Day
oneLiner: Let a warm lamp and a cooler light share one wall of the passage.
details: By day, switch on a lamp in the hall or just inside a doorway and leave the daylight as it is. If it is dark outside, use the lamp for the warm pool and a cooler ceiling light farther along for the pale wash. Find a wall that shows both at once. The warm area and the cooler wash should be readable together.
tips: Set the lamp close to the wall so its warmth has an edge.
Avoid a yellow-tinted screen preview by judging the wall with your eyes too.

title: The Switch in Its Glow
oneLiner: Include a light switch inside the pool of light it controls.
details: Turn on the passage light and find the switch that controls it. Frame the plate inside that brightness, with plain wall around it. If the ceiling light leaves the plate in shadow, switch on a lamp and frame the switch that sits in the lamp's own pool of light.
tips: Come in close enough that the switch is large, but keep some lit wall around it.
Tap the plate so the lettering or the screws are sharp.
constraint: The switch plate is fully inside the lit area.

title: Hooks Against the Light
oneLiner: Place coat hooks or hung coats against the bright end of the passage.
details: Stand so hooks, a coat or a bag become dark shapes against a brighter doorway or window farther along. If you have no hooks, hang a jacket on a door handle in the passage. The light behind them is the reason for the picture, so leave that brightness large.
tips: Expose for the bright end, letting the coats fall dark on purpose.
Shift until a hook or a collar has a clean rim of light.

title: The Turn in the Hall
oneLiner: Record the corner where the passage turns and only one plane is lit.
details: If the hall turns, stand so one wall is lit and the wall beyond the corner is quieter. If the passage is straight, use the corner of an open door frame, where light hits one face and misses the next. The meeting of those two planes is the subject.
tips: Put the corner itself near the middle, with light on one side only.
Square the upright edge so it does not lean.
constraint: Both planes of the corner appear.

title: Frosted Panel Glow
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the even glow of a frosted panel in the passage.
details: Use frosted glass in a door, a bathroom window that faces the hall, or baking paper taped over a bright pane. Stand in the passage and let that even glow fill the picture. A thin line of frame can remain so the glow has a home.
tips: Focus on the glass or the paper, not on a shape guessed behind it.
If the glow is hotter in the centre, step aside until it evens out.
constraint: The glow stays even, with no clear view through it.

title: A Slit by the Door
oneLiner: Use the mail slot, the door edge or a gap under the door as a slit of light.
details: Stay inside and find a narrow slit of daylight at the front door. The mail slot surround, the edge of a slightly open door, or the gap at the floor will do. Come close so the slit is bright and the door around it is darker.
tips: Turn the phone so the slit runs the long way across the frame.
Shield the lens with your hand if the slit flares into a white blob.

title: Along the Baseboard
oneLiner: Follow the baseboard as the light along it fades from one end to the other.
details: Get low in the passage, the lobby or the space by the door. Let the baseboard, or the line where wall meets floor, run across the frame. Brightness should change along that line, from a lit end towards a dimmer one.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor and slide it until the line is straight.
Include a door frame or a corner as the point where the brightness changes.
constraint: The baseboard runs from one side of the frame to the other.

title: Hall from the Floor
oneLiner: Lie in the passage and shoot along the floor towards the light.
details: Lie or sit on the floor of the hall, the lobby or the space between two rooms. Point along the floor towards a bright doorway or the front door. Let the floor carry the light, and keep the ceiling out of the picture.
tips: Tuck your elbows in so the floor line stays low and wide.
A timer helps if your fingers keep blocking the low lens.

title: Highlight on the Edge
oneLiner: Catch the bright edge of a partly open door in the passage.
details: Open a door halfway and stand where the edge facing you picks up light from the room beyond or from a window. That highlight should be a thin line. Show enough of the door to explain what the line belongs to.
tips: Move an inch at a time, because the highlight vanishes when you shift.
Focus on the edge, which is narrower than the door around it.
constraint: The bright edge is the sharpest line in the picture.

title: Two Doors, Two Tones
oneLiner: Frame two openings in the passage that are not the same brightness.
details: Open one door onto a brighter room and leave another closed, or open onto a darker room. If you can see only one doorway, pair it with a closed door, a cupboard or a darker corner. Stand where both are in the picture. The difference in tone is the point, so leave extra objects out.
tips: If the two tones look alike, switch a lamp on in only one room.
Keep both door heads in the frame so the pair reads as a pair.

title: Something in the Bright Patch
oneLiner: Set one ordinary object in the brightest patch on the passage floor.
details: Find the brightest pool of light on the floor of the hall, the lobby or the space by the door. If the floor is evenly dim, aim a lamp down to make a pool. Place a bowl, a key or a single shoe in that brightness. Shoot so the light still dominates and the object is only an anchor.
tips: Choose a low object so it does not block the pool it sits in.
Meter on the floor beside the object, not on the object itself.
constraint: The object stays inside the brightest patch.

title: The Darkest Opening
oneLiner: Include the darkest doorway off the passage beside a lighter wall.
details: Look for a cupboard, a room with the lamp off, or a closed door that reads darker than the wall beside it. Frame that dark opening with some of the lit wall. You are comparing the dark hole with the light the passage already has.
tips: Expose for the lit wall so the opening can stay truly dark.
Include the top of the door frame so the dark shape has a clear end.

title: A Closed Door Glowing
oneLiner: Let a closed door at the end of the passage become a flat field of light.
details: Shut a door that daylight or a lamp is falling on, and stand back in the hall or lobby. Expose for the door so it becomes a quiet, even surface. The frame around it can fall darker and give the flat colour a border.
tips: Stand square to the door so it stays a rectangle.
If the door is busy with notes, use a plainer door or crop in to a clear panel.

title: Soft Edge, Hard Light
oneLiner: Hang a coat or towel so it softens the edge of a hard patch of light.
details: Find a crisp patch of light on the passage floor or on a wall. Hang a coat, a scarf or a towel so the fabric crosses that edge and softens part of it. The picture needs both the clean boundary and the place the cloth interrupts it.
tips: Use a thinner scarf if a heavy coat swallows the whole patch.
Side-step until the fabric edge and the light edge cross at an angle.
constraint: Fabric crosses the boundary of the light.

title: Shine on the Floor
oneLiner: If the floor shines, shoot the reflection of a doorway on it.
details: Look on the hall floor, a tile or a sealed board for a reflection of a bright doorway. Include the real opening and its reflection if both fit. If the floor is dull, lay a dark tray or a glossy magazine in the light and use that surface instead.
tips: Get low, because the reflection appears more strongly at a shallow angle.
Shift the tray until the doorway, not a ceiling light, is what it holds.

title: The Narrowest Stretch
oneLiner: Shoot the narrowest part of the passage, with light visible beyond it.
details: Find the tightest bit of hall, lobby, or gap between a piece of furniture and the wall. Let that narrow stretch lead towards a brighter opening. In an open room, the gap between a door and the wall beside it can stand in for a passage.
tips: Hold the phone in the tight gap rather than shooting the gap from far away.
Let the brighter end sit slightly soft if the near walls need to stay sharp.

title: Hands Kneading Dough
oneLiner: Photograph your own hands working dough on a floured counter.
details: Set the phone on a stable surface and use the timer so both of your hands can work. Knead bread dough or pastry on a lightly floured board, or press and fold a thick piece of bread if that is what you have. Crop at the wrists so your face stays out.
tips: Wipe the lens if flour dusts it.
Use burst mode for the best gesture.
Side light from a window shows texture.
constraint: Only your hands may appear in the photo.

title: Peeling a Vegetable
oneLiner: Show your hands mid-peel over a bowl or board.
details: Start peeling a potato, a carrot or a clementine and photograph the pause mid-strip. A peeler works, and so does your thumb on the clementine. Keep the focus on your fingers and leave your face out.
tips: Rest the phone against a jar for stability.
Shoot before the peel pile gets messy.
Focus on your thumb where it meets the peel.

title: Thread and Needle
oneLiner: Capture your fingers guiding thread through a needle or fabric.
details: Sit by a window with a simple mending task, using a needle or a safety pin if that is what you have. Move in close on the pinch point where the thread meets the eye. The background should fall soft so the tiny action reads clearly.
tips: Use macro mode if available for sharp thread.
Pick a thread that stands out against the cloth.
Brace your elbows on the table for steadiness.
constraint: Keep the phone about a hand's width from the thread.

title: Washing Dishes Motion
oneLiner: Photograph your hands under running water with a sponge or dish.
details: At the sink, catch the moment water sheets over a plate or glass. Your hands should feel active, not posed. Bubbles and splashes add life if they stay in focus.
tips: Prop your wrists against the sink edge so your fingers stay steady.
Shoot from above the sink for clarity.
Keep the tap flow gentle to control splash.
constraint: Capture motion without blur on the hands.

title: Folding Laundry Stack
oneLiner: Show your hands smoothing a folded shirt or towel on a table.
details: Mid-fold, pause with palms flat on fabric and shoot downward or from the side. Creases and alignment matter more than the brand of clothing. Stay cropped tight on hands and textile.
tips: Choose a plain tabletop background.
Align folds parallel to the frame edge.
Use even daylight to show fabric texture.

title: Writing a Postcard
oneLiner: Photograph your hand holding a pen over paper without readable private text.
details: Begin a note or list and shoot from above as your hand moves. Blur or angle away any sensitive words. The pen tip and finger grip should be the sharpest elements.
tips: Use burst mode while you write slowly.
Keep shadows from your phone off the page.
Choose a pen with a visible cap or clip.
constraint: No legible words in the final image.

title: Potting a Houseplant
oneLiner: Press soil around a plant with your hands at the sink.
details: Set a houseplant in the sink or on a tray on the table, with a sheet of paper underneath. Use your fingertips to firm the soil that is already in the pot, or dry oats in a bowl if you have no plant. Lean the phone against a mug and start the timer so both hands can work.
tips: Lay a sheet of paper under the pot for easy cleanup.
Focus on soil texture at the pot rim.
Shoot before your hands get too dirty for the phone.
constraint: Shoot from above the pot only.

title: Opening a Jar Lid
oneLiner: Show the grip of your hands twisting a jar lid on a counter.
details: Choose an ordinary pantry jar and photograph the tension in your fingers and wrist. The jar label can appear but need not be readable. Keep the lid half turned, which reads more clearly than a jar that is already open.
tips: Place the jar on a nonslip mat.
Shoot from counter height at a forty-five-degree angle.
Use continuous shooting for the strongest grip.

title: Buttoning a Cuff
oneLiner: Fasten a cuff with your own fingers and catch the pinch.
details: Lay a shirt or a blouse flat on a table so the cuff is easy to reach. Prop the phone against a book at the table edge, start the timer, and bring both hands in to fasten the button. The picture wants the pinch of finger and thumb on the button, not your face.
tips: A contrasting button and cuff cloth will read more clearly.
Come close enough that the button is larger than a fingernail in the frame.
constraint: Both of your hands must be on the cuff.

title: Stirring the Mug
oneLiner: Hold a mug steady and stir it with your other hand.
details: Stand a mug of tea, coffee or just water on the counter. Rest the phone against a jar looking across the mug, give yourself a few seconds on the timer, and put one hand on the handle while the other stirs with a spoon. Side light from the window should catch the spoon and the knuckles.
tips: Stir slowly so the spoon does not blur into the mug.
Keep the spoon handle visible between your fingers.

title: Turning the Key
oneLiner: Turn a key in a lock with your own hand.
details: Hold the phone in one hand and turn a key in your own door from the inside. Keep your face behind the phone so only the hand, the key and the lock show. If the door has no key, turn the latch or the handle with the same close framing.
tips: Tap focus on the key before you start to turn it.
Shoot from the side so the key sticks out in profile.
constraint: Your face stays out of the frame.

title: Plugging the Charger
oneLiner: Plug a charger in with your fingers close to the outlet.
details: Hold the phone in one hand and the charger in the other, at an outlet you can reach comfortably. Keep your fingers on the charger body as it meets the outlet, never poking inside. Frame tightly so the hand, the charger and a little of the wall are the whole picture.
tips: A side-on view shows the grip better than a view from above.
Turn a lamp on nearby if the outlet sits in a dark corner.

title: Tucking the Sheet
oneLiner: Tuck a sheet with both hands while the phone watches from a chair.
details: Set the phone on a chair or a bedside table pointing at the corner of the mattress, and use the timer. With both hands, tuck the sheet or duvet under the mattress and pause mid-push. The story is the pressure of your palms, so fill the frame with hands, cloth and mattress edge.
tips: A low phone position makes the tuck look more physical.
Smooth the sheet once, then shoot the second push so it looks lived-in.
constraint: Both hands must touch the sheet.

title: Whisking an Egg
oneLiner: Whisk an egg in a bowl and show the working hand.
details: Crack an egg into a bowl, or pour in a little milk if you have no egg, and beat it with a whisk or a fork. Hold the phone in your free hand, off to the side and slightly above the bowl. Time it so the whisk is blurred a touch and the fingers on the handle stay readable.
tips: A metal bowl reflects the window and can confuse the focus, so a plain bowl is kinder.
Short bursts will give you one frame where the fingers are sharp.

title: Turning a Page
oneLiner: Turn a page and freeze your fingers at the corner.
details: Open a book, a magazine or a notebook on a table. Hold the phone above it with one hand and lift the page corner with the other, stopping while the page is still in the air. The lifted corner and the fingertip are the subject.
tips: Daylight from the side will light the page without a hot spot from a lamp.
Focus on the fingertip, not the text underneath.
constraint: The page is mid-turn, not flat.

title: Washing Your Hands
oneLiner: Wash your hands at the sink and photograph the lather.
details: Dry a spot on the window ledge or the back of the sink, well away from the splash, and stand the phone there. Start the timer, then soap both hands under a gentle flow so the lather covers the palms. The picture should be all hands, water and basin.
tips: Lather reads better against a dark basin than a white one.
If the phone is close to the tap, angle it so a splash cannot reach the lens.

title: Zipping the Pouch
oneLiner: Zip a pouch shut and frame the pinch of the pull.
details: Use a toiletry bag, a pencil case or a small backpack on a table. Prop the phone at one end, start the timer, and use one hand to hold the fabric while the other draws the zipper. Stop halfway so the pull and the pinching fingers are both clear.
tips: A light-coloured zip on dark fabric is easier to focus on.
Get low, level with the pouch, rather than shooting down.
constraint: The zipper is half closed.

title: Watering the Pot
oneLiner: Pour water from a jug onto a houseplant with your hands showing.
details: Set a houseplant in the sink or on a tray, or a mug if you have no plant. Prop the phone to the side and use the timer so one hand can tilt a jug or a cup while the other steadies the pot or the mug. A small pour is enough; you want the grip and the water, not a flood.
tips: Focus on the hand at the pot rim rather than the leaves.
A slow pour keeps the water from splashing the lens.

title: Rolling a Sock Pair
oneLiner: Roll two socks together and show the press of your palms.
details: Pair two socks on a table and start rolling them into each other. With the phone propped overhead on a stack of books and the timer running, pause when both palms are pressing the roll. Crop wide enough to show the wrists and the table, and no wider.
tips: Odd socks with different colours make the roll easier to read.
Overhead light can flatten the hands; use a window to the side instead.
constraint: Both palms must be in the frame.

title: Polishing a Glass
oneLiner: Polish a drinking glass with a cloth in your hands.
details: Hold a clean glass in a dish towel. Rest the phone on the counter against a can, start the timer, and polish with both hands for a moment before the shutter goes. The cloth should wrap the glass so your fingers dent the fabric.
tips: A coloured glass or a coloured cloth separates the shapes.
Turn the glass so a finger shows through the cloth, not just a lump of fabric.

title: Pouring Cereal
oneLiner: Pour cereal into a bowl and catch the stream from your hand.
details: Hold the phone in one hand beside a bowl and pour cereal, oats or rice with the other. Shoot while the stream is still falling, not after it has landed. Your pouring hand should be in frame, with the box or jar cropped however it needs to be.
tips: Pour from lower down so the stream is short and easier to freeze.
Tap focus on your fingers, then pour.
constraint: The pour is visibly mid-flow.

title: Spreading on Toast
oneLiner: Spread butter on toast and keep the spreader in your hand.
details: Use a butter spreader or the back of a spoon on a slice of toast or bread. Hold the phone with your free hand, just above table height, and shoot as the spreader moves. The working fingers and the toast surface should both be sharp.
tips: A thin layer shows the gesture better than a loaded heap.
Keep the phone's shadow off the toast by standing to the window side.

title: Tying the Garbage Bag
oneLiner: Tie a garbage bag and photograph the knot in your fingers.
details: Lift the edges of a garbage bag, or a grocery bag, onto a clear table if the garbage can is too deep to see into. Prop the phone at the table edge, start the timer, and tie the bag with both hands. The knot, or the moment the two handles meet, should be the sharpest point.
tips: A light bag against a dark table, or the reverse, outlines the fingers.
Stop just as the knot tightens rather than after your hands have left.
constraint: The knot is the sharpest point.

title: Can Opener Twist
oneLiner: Turn a can opener with one hand braced on the can.
details: Set a can on the counter and fit a can opener, keeping the can on the surface rather than in the air. If you have no opener, twist a pepper mill while your other hand steadies it, and frame that grip instead. Prop the phone at counter height, use the timer, and show one hand turning while the other steadies.
tips: Come in from the side so both hands and the can top are visible.
A dish towel under the can stops it skating and adds a plain base.

title: Cream on the Palms
oneLiner: Rub hand cream between your palms and shoot from above.
details: If you have no hand cream, a drop of lotion or a little soap lather works the same way. Prop the phone on a shelf or a stack of books looking down at the table, start the timer, and rub your palms together in the frame. The sheen on the skin and the overlap of the fingers are what you are after.
tips: A dark tabletop makes pale hands easier to see.
Rub slowly so the fingers do not smear.
constraint: Shoot from above your hands.

title: Placing the Fork
oneLiner: Set a fork on a plate and show the hand that places it.
details: Hold the phone in one hand and lower a fork onto a plate with the other. Shoot just before the fork touches, so the hand is still carrying the weight. A plain plate and a bare table keep the gesture obvious.
tips: Come from the side so the fork points across the frame.
Focus on the fingertips, then lower the fork.

title: Tape Along the Table
oneLiner: Run a tape measure along the table with your fingers on the case.
details: If you have no tape measure, straighten a charger cable or a piece of string across the table instead. Prop the phone at one end, use the timer, and let one hand pin the end while the other holds the case or the coil. The line should cross the frame, with your hands at either end or grouped on the case.
tips: A low viewpoint along the tape makes the hand on the case look larger.
Lock focus on the hand, not the far end of the table.
constraint: The tape or cable runs across the frame.

title: Fastening a Watch
oneLiner: Fasten a watch or a bracelet on your own wrist.
details: Prop the phone on a table pointing at a clear patch of surface and start the timer. Bring your own wrist into the frame and fasten a watch, a bracelet or a hair tie with the other hand. Crop so the clasp and the fastening fingers fill the picture.
tips: A metal clasp catches window light better than a dark strap.
Rest the wrist on the table so it does not drift during the timer.

title: Scrubbing the Basin
oneLiner: Scrub the bathroom basin and show the cloth in your hand.
details: Hold the phone above the basin with one hand and scrub with the other, using a cloth, a sponge or a brush. Work along the rim or around the plug so the hand has a clear edge to follow. Keep your head out of the top of the frame.
tips: A dry cloth shows the grip; a soapy one shows the work. Pick one.
The wide lens will distort a hand very close to the corner, so keep the hand nearer the middle.
constraint: Only the basin, the cloth and your hand.

title: Folding a Paper Note
oneLiner: Fold a blank sheet in half and catch the crease under your fingers.
details: Use a blank sheet so no writing shows. Prop the phone overhead, start the timer, and fold the paper with both hands, pausing as your fingers press the crease. The crease line and the fingertips should be the sharpest things in the frame.
tips: A coloured sheet on a pale table gives the fingers an edge.
Press the crease towards the camera so the fold catches light.

title: Pinching a Herb Leaf
oneLiner: Pinch a herb leaf from a pot and show the pinch.
details: Hold the phone in one hand and pinch a herb leaf with the other. If you have no herbs, pinch a tired leaf from any houseplant, or the corner of a lettuce leaf over the sink. Shoot while the leaf is still attached, so the pinch is doing the work.
tips: Get close enough to see the fingerprint ridges if the light allows.
A window behind the leaf will outline the fingers.
constraint: The leaf is still attached when you shoot.

title: Tying a Shoelace
oneLiner: Tie a shoelace while seated and frame both hands.
details: Sit on a chair indoors and prop the phone against a book or a box pointing at your shoe. If your shoes have no laces, tie a cord or a spare lace around your ankle. Start the timer and tie the bow so both hands are in the knot.
tips: A light lace on a dark shoe is easier for the phone to grab.
Sit so a plain stretch of floor fills the background.
constraint: Both hands are in the knot.

title: Wiping the Handle
oneLiner: Wipe the outside door handle with a cloth in your hand.
details: Stand at your own front door and hold the phone in one hand. With the other, wipe the outside handle or mail slot flap with a dry cloth. Come in close so the cloth, the fingers and the handle fill the frame.
tips: Wipe slowly or the cloth will blur and hide the grip.
Shoot from slightly below the handle so your arm does not block it.

title: Shaking the Mat
oneLiner: Shake a mat with both hands and catch the grip.
