details: Prop the phone low against a wall and start the timer. Use a bath mat, or a doormat you have brought inside, and give it one short shake with both hands on the edge. Keep the shake small so the mat stays clear of the phone.
tips: One shake is enough; several will only blur the hands.
A low phone position shows the hands against a wall rather than the ceiling.
constraint: Both hands hold the mat.

title: Filling the Kettle
oneLiner: Fill the kettle at the tap and show the hand on the handle.
details: Hold the phone in one hand, off to the side of the sink. With the other, hold the kettle under a gentle flow, or hold a mug if the kettle is too heavy to lift one-handed. The picture is your grip and the water, so keep your face and most of the kitchen out.
tips: A short pour is easier to hold sharp than a full blast.
Tap focus on your knuckles before you turn the tap.

title: Brushing a Shoe
oneLiner: Brush dust off a shoe indoors and keep your hand on the brush.
details: Set a shoe on a sheet of newspaper or a cloth on the floor. Hold the phone in one hand and brush the upper with a shoe brush, an old toothbrush or a dry cloth. The bristles or the cloth should meet the shoe while your fingers stay visible.
tips: Brush across the window light so any dust shows against the shoe.
Focus on the point where the brush meets the leather or cloth.
constraint: The shoe stays on the cloth.

title: Sweeping the Kitchen Floor
oneLiner: Sweep the kitchen floor and show your hands on the broom.
details: Prop the phone on the floor against a can or a heavy mug, pointing along the floor, and start the timer. Put both hands on a broom, or on a hand brush if that is what you have, and sweep once. The grip on the handle is the subject, with the floor as the setting.
tips: Hands stacked on the handle make a stronger shape than one hand alone.
Sweep towards the phone so the bristles and the hands share the frame.

title: Scooping into the Dustpan
oneLiner: Hold a dustpan to the floor and show the steadying hand.
details: Crouch by a bit of floor you can tidy, with the phone in one hand. Press a dustpan, or a piece of card, flat to the floor with the other hand. The picture is the hand pinning that edge down, with the floor filling the rest.
tips: Get the phone down near floor level so the hand is seen from the side.
A bright pan against a dark floor, or the reverse, separates the shape.
constraint: The dustpan or card touches the floor.

title: Pulling on a Glove
oneLiner: Pull on a glove in the hallway and catch the tug.
details: Prop the phone on a chair or against the wall indoors and start the timer. Pull a glove, a mitten or a clean sock onto one hand with the other, and pause mid-tug. Both the pulling fingers and the hand being covered should be in frame.
tips: A snug glove shows the tug better than a loose one.
Face the phone so the cuff of the glove is visible.

title: Wringing the Cloth
oneLiner: Wring a damp cloth over the sink with both hands.
details: Dampen a cloth, prop the phone on the window ledge or the back of the sink, and start the timer. Wring the cloth over the empty basin so the twist and the opposing grip of your hands fill the frame. A bowl in the sink works if the basin is full of dishes.
tips: Wring slowly so the fingers stay sharp.
A coloured cloth shows the twist more clearly than a white one.
constraint: Both hands are on the cloth.

title: Lifting a Shopping Bag
oneLiner: Lift a shopping bag from the floor and show the grip.
details: Set a shopping bag or a tote on the kitchen floor. Hold the phone in one hand and grip the handles with the other, shooting as the bag leaves the floor. The fingers around the handle are the subject.
tips: A side view shows the gap between the bag and the floor.
Keep your face behind the phone so only the hand and the bag show.
constraint: The bag is off the floor.

title: Hanging Up a Shirt
oneLiner: Hang a shirt on a hanger and show both hands.
details: Prop the phone on a shelf or a box at about chest height and start the timer. With both hands, settle a shirt, a blouse or a dish towel onto a hanger. Pause while your fingers are still pinching the fabric at the shoulders or the corners.
tips: A pale shirt on a dark hanger, or the reverse, outlines the fingers.
Wait for the timer rather than reaching back for the phone.

title: Tearing Kitchen Paper
oneLiner: Tear a sheet of kitchen paper and show both hands.
details: Prop the phone on the counter and start the timer. Hold a roll of kitchen paper, or a paper napkin, and tear one sheet with both hands. Pause while the tear is still opening so the fingers on either side stay sharp.
tips: Tear slowly or the rip will hide the grip.
A white sheet on a dark counter gives the fingers an edge.
constraint: Both hands stay on the paper.

title: Cracking an Egg
oneLiner: Crack an egg into a bowl and catch the moment in your hands.
details: Hold the phone in one hand beside a bowl, or prop it and use the timer if you want both hands on the egg. Crack the egg on the bowl rim and shoot as the shell opens. If you have no egg, snap a bread roll in half over a plate with the same grip.
tips: Shoot a short burst so one frame catches the shell just opening.
A plain bowl keeps the focus on your fingers rather than a pattern.

title: Steam Over the Kettle
oneLiner: Catch steam rising from a kettle that has just boiled.
details: Switch it off and leave it where it is, on its base or the counter. Stand at arm's length and look for wisps above the spout, with a dark cupboard or wall behind them. Do not touch the kettle, and do not move it while it is hot.
tips: Stand side-on to a window so the wisps catch the light.
Tap focus on the spout rather than the wall behind.
Take a short burst; the shape changes while you watch.
constraint: Stay at least an arm's length from the kettle.

title: Spice Jar Labels
oneLiner: Line up spice jars so their labels and lids tell a small colour story.
details: Pull a few jars from the rack and arrange them by colour or height on the counter. Look for repeating shapes, round lids and rectangular labels, and leave a little breathing room between jars. The goal is a tidy portrait of an everyday pantry.
tips: Wipe the glass so the labels stay readable.
Try a slightly high angle so every lid reads as a circle.
Turn the phone upright if you want the row to feel stacked.

title: Board After Prep
oneLiner: Show a board with bread, citrus peel, and a resting spoon.
details: Pull a strip of citrus peel off by hand, tear a piece of bread, and set both on the board with a spoon. Use only those three things, and keep the rest of the counter out of the frame. Let the board edges act as a border so the scatter feels chosen.
tips: Shoot from counter height so it feels like cooking, not a map.
Let the spoon handle point towards a corner.
Keep the counter beyond the board out of the picture.
constraint: Exactly three objects: peel, bread, and spoon.

title: Dish Rack Geometry
oneLiner: Find repeating lines and circles in the drying rack.
details: Walk up to the dish rack and study how plates, glasses, and utensils repeat. Look for circles nested inside rectangles and the gaps between items. A single strong angle can turn an ordinary chore into a clean composition.
tips: Move in close so the rack fills the picture.
Align one rack edge with the side of the frame.
Switch to mono if the mixed colours fight each other.
constraint: Step closer rather than pinching to zoom.

title: Morning Coffee Ring
oneLiner: Capture a dried mug ring on a saucer or the counter.
details: Find a dried ring left by a mug, on a saucer, a napkin, or the counter. Treat it like a tiny landscape: notice how sharp the rim is and how pale the middle looks. Move the phone until the ring sits calmly in the middle of the frame.
tips: Shoot straight down so the ring stays a true circle.
Use soft window light and skip the flash.
Tap focus on the darkest part of the ring.

title: Refrigerator Shelf Portrait
oneLiner: Open the fridge and frame one shelf as a still life.
details: Pick the shelf that looks most interesting, whether that is condiments, fruit, or leftovers in tubs. Hold the door steady and compose before cold air clouds the lens. Let the shelf edge lead across the frame.
tips: Turn the flash off and rely on the fridge lamp.
Brace the phone on the door so labels stay sharp.
Crop until neighbouring shelves disappear.
constraint: Keep every item on a single shelf.

title: Whisk and Bowl
oneLiner: Pair a mixing bowl with a whisk or wooden spoon.
details: Set a bowl on the counter and lean a whisk or wooden spoon across the rim. Notice how the curve of the tool echoes the circle of the bowl. A plain wall or a run of tile is enough behind it.
tips: Choose one dominant colour and let the rest stay quiet.
Shoot from slightly above so the inside of the bowl shows.
Leave a patch of empty counter on one side.
constraint: Nothing in frame except the bowl and the tool.

title: Salt and Pepper Pair
oneLiner: Pose salt and pepper as a small matched pair.
details: Place the shakers side by side on a clear patch of table or counter. Look for symmetry, or a deliberate mismatch, in their shapes and wear. A plain surface behind them keeps the pair as the whole story.
tips: Line their tops up so neither looks as if it leans.
Step back a little so the phone does not bend their shapes.
Try a low angle so the pair feels larger than it is.

title: Tea Bloom in Glass
oneLiner: Watch colour leave a tea bag in a clear mug.
details: Use a clear glass mug if you have one, or a glass jar. Pour, set the mug down, and lower the bag in with a spoon so you are not holding hot glass, then wait for a plume of colour to sink. Shoot from the side so the pale water and the dark plume share the frame. A white sheet of paper behind the glass will show the colour cleanly.
tips: Tap to focus on the glass wall, not the paper behind it.
Keep the flash off so the plume is not blown white.
Hold the phone level with the middle of the mug.
constraint: Keep your hands out of the frame.

title: After the Toast
oneLiner: Record the crumbs and crust left once the toast is gone.
details: Once the toast has cooled, move it to another plate and look at what remains: a crust edge, a smear of butter, a scatter of crumbs. Walk around the plate until the leftovers suggest a meal that just ended. Side light from a window will give each crumb a small shadow.
tips: Get low so the crumbs rise against the plate.
Wipe the lens if you have just been near steam.
Lock focus on the largest crumb.

title: Ladle in the Pot
oneLiner: Lean a ladle inside a saucepan and study the two curves.
details: Choose any pot, empty or holding cool water, and rest the ladle, or a large spoon, so its bowl touches the pot's curve. Look for the echo between the two rounded shapes. A dark stovetop behind them will separate the metal from the background.
tips: Shoot from a three-quarter angle rather than straight above.
Catch a window highlight along one metal edge.
Let the handle run towards a corner of the frame.
constraint: Show both the pot rim and the ladle head.

title: Jar of Dry Pasta
oneLiner: Show a jar of dry pasta as a pantry portrait.
details: Fill a clear jar with spaghetti, penne, or whatever shape you have, and set it on the counter. Turn the jar until the shapes stack in a rhythm. Leave the lid off or on, but keep any loud label away from the lens.
tips: Stand a sheet of coloured paper behind the jar if the kitchen is busy.
Focus on the pasta just inside the glass.
Crop in so the frame trims both the top and the base.

title: Papery Onion Skins
oneLiner: Stack dry onion skins so their copper layers overlap.
details: Pull only the dry outer skins off an onion by hand, and lay them on a pale plate. Overlap two or three so light comes through the thin parts. The thicker ribs of the skin can act as lines across the frame.
tips: Backlight the plate from a nearby window.
Tap focus on the thinnest, brightest patch of skin.
Keep the onion itself out of the picture.
constraint: Use no more than three skins.

title: Rings Before Cooking
oneLiner: Frame the empty stovetop as a quiet set of circles.
details: Before you cook, look down or along the stovetop at the rings. Notice stains, shine, and the way the circles overlap. Include one utensil at the edge if the rings alone feel too bare, or leave them empty.
tips: Make sure the stovetop is off and cool before you lean in.
Place one ring near the middle of the frame.
Lower the exposure if the metal glare turns pure white.

title: Spoon in the Jam
oneLiner: Rest a spoon in an open jar of jam or honey.
details: Open a jar of jam, marmalade, or honey and lay a spoon so it rests in the jar and against the rim. Look at the line where the spoon meets the surface. A window to one side will gloss the jam without hiding its colour.
tips: Wipe drips off the outside of the jar first.
Focus where the spoon enters the jam.
Shoot slightly downward so the jar mouth becomes an oval.
constraint: The jar must touch the bottom edge of the frame.

title: A Line in Flour
oneLiner: Drag one line through a dusting of flour on the counter.
details: Sprinkle a little flour on a dark board or the counter. Draw a single line with a dry spoon handle or a fingertip. Photograph the path so the loose powder and the darker line share the frame.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the counter.
Side light makes the flour look thicker.
Tap focus on the edge of the line.
constraint: Only one line, and no letters or numbers.

title: Mugs on Their Hooks
oneLiner: Gather hanging mugs into a row of handles and rims.
details: Find the hooks, a mug tree, or a shelf where mugs live. Slide them so the handles repeat, or leave a gap where one mug is missing. That gap can matter as much as the mugs themselves.
tips: Stand so the hooks make a level line.
Focus on the nearest handle.
A plain wall behind the mugs keeps the shapes clear.

title: Spent Coffee Grounds
oneLiner: Look into used coffee grounds in a filter or French press.
details: After a brew, wait until the grounds are cool and any steam has cleared. Leave them in the paper filter, the French press, or a small bowl, and move close until the damp clumps look like dark soil. If you have no coffee grounds, use damp loose tea in that same filter. A bright rim of paper or metal around them gives the picture an edge.
tips: Skip the flash, which flattens the clumps.
Focus on a highlight where the grounds are still wet.
Crop tight so the container nearly disappears.

title: Oil Beside Vinegar
oneLiner: Set oil beside vinegar and compare their colour and height.
details: Place a bottle of oil and a bottle of vinegar on the counter with a small gap between them. Turn any labels away so the liquids and the glass do the talking. Notice which one looks thicker, greener, or more lit.
tips: Shoot from a low angle so the bottles rise in the frame.
Hang a pale cloth behind them if the kitchen is busy.
Focus on the line where liquid meets glass.
constraint: Only the two bottles are in the frame.

title: Milk Meets Cereal
oneLiner: Pause as milk first swirls into a bowl of cereal.
details: Pour slowly into flakes, oats, or puffed rice in a plain bowl. Stop when the milk has made one visible swirl and has not yet covered everything. Shoot from above or from the side, whichever shows the dry pieces against the wet.
tips: Use burst mode and keep pouring so you can choose the frame later.
Tap focus on the bowl rim before you pour.
A matte bowl will not throw a white glare back at you.
constraint: The pour must still be visible in the picture.

title: Clove and Papery Shell
oneLiner: Separate one garlic clove from its loose papery shell.
details: Break a clove free with your hands and set it next to the skin you pulled off. The contrast between the smooth clove and the crinkled shell is the picture. A dark plate will make the pale skin glow.
tips: Use window light from the side to trace the wrinkles.
Focus on the shell, which is thinner and easier to lose.
Keep the rest of the bulb out of the frame.

title: Apron on a Hook
oneLiner: Tuck a wooden spoon into an apron pocket and hang it up.
details: Hang an apron on a hook, the back of a door, or a cupboard handle. If you have no apron, hang a dish towel over a handle and tuck the spoon into a fold. The cloth and the spoon should suggest that cooking is about to start.
tips: Stand square to the cloth so it does not slant by accident.
Include the hook or handle at the top of the frame.
Move closer if the room behind it is busy.

title: Cans Turned Away
oneLiner: Crop a stack of cans with every label turned out of sight.
details: Stack three or four cans from the cupboard on the counter. Rotate each one so printed labels face away and you see plain metal, rings, and rims. The stack should feel like a small tower from the pantry.
tips: Shoot from slightly below so the tower gains height.
Align the cans so their rims make parallel ovals.
A plain wall beats an open cupboard as a background.
constraint: No readable words anywhere in the frame.

title: Butter on the Dish
oneLiner: Show a block or pat of butter with a spoon beside it.
details: Set the butter on its dish, a plate, or the opened corner of its wrapper. Lay a teaspoon next to it. Look for ridge marks and the way the butter takes warm light.
tips: Side light from a window picks out the ridges.
Keep the wrapper only if the lettering is small.
Focus on the butter rather than the spoon handle.

title: A Scoop of Rice
oneLiner: Heap uncooked rice in a measuring cup or a small bowl.
details: Fill a metal or plastic measuring cup, or a little bowl, until the rice mounds above the rim. Tap the side once so a few grains slide. Those loose grains at the base keep the picture from looking too neat.
tips: Shoot from a low side angle to show the mound.
Focus on the grains at the front edge.
Slip a dark cloth under the cup if the counter is busy.
constraint: Leave a few grains outside the cup.

title: One Glass Draining
oneLiner: Turn one glass upside down on the dish rack or the counter.
details: Rinse one glass and set it upside down on the dish rack, or on the counter beside the sink if you have no rack. Clear a space so it is the only object. The ring of the rim and the droplets can say the dishes have just been washed.
tips: Get down to the height of the rack or the counter.
Focus on a droplet near the rim.
Leave the flash off so the highlights stay small.
constraint: Only one glass in the frame.

title: Herbs Standing in Water
oneLiner: Place herb stems in a jar of water on the counter.
details: Parsley, mint, basil, or green onion tops will do, even a short bunch you already have. If there are no herbs, stand a few salad leaves in the jar instead. Put the jar where the kitchen window lights the leaves from the side.
tips: Shoot through the side so stems show in the water.
Focus on one leaf and let the others soften.
Keep packets and labels out of the frame.

title: The Oven Dial
oneLiner: Move close to the oven dial, timer, or temperature knob.
details: Choose the dial you actually turn when you cook. If the oven has no dial, use the knob on a toaster or a kettle instead. Fill the frame with numbers, a marker, and the surface around it. Tilt until a reflection does not wipe the markings out.
tips: Wipe fingerprints off the panel first.
Tap focus on the pointer rather than any logo.
Angle the phone so the window is not mirrored over the numbers.
constraint: Crop out any brand name.

title: The Used Strainer
oneLiner: Rest a damp tea strainer on a saucer after a brew.
details: Leave a few leaves in a tea strainer or a small sieve so it looks used, not stored. Set it on a saucer or a small plate that gives it a stage. Side light will sparkle in the mesh and darken the leaves.
tips: Shoot from above at a slight tilt so the mesh stays a circle.
Focus on the leaves rather than the saucer pattern.
A plain saucer is kinder than a busy one.

title: Bowl After Oats
oneLiner: Tilt an emptied bowl towards the light to show what remains.
details: After oats, yoghurt, or soup, wait before you rinse. Angle the bowl so a smear, a spoon track, or a last streak catches the window. The picture is the end of a meal, told by the marks inside.
tips: Fill the frame with the inside of the bowl.
Expose for the pale smear, not the dark rim.
Keep the table out of the picture.
constraint: No food still heaped in the bowl, only traces.

title: Sponge by the Tap
oneLiner: Leave the dish sponge where it lives, by the tap.
details: Set it on the sink, in its holder, or on the rim of a bowl, still a little damp from the last wash. Include a little of the tap or the sink so the sponge has a job, not just a texture. Keep bottles and cloths out of the cluster.
tips: Squeeze it once so it holds a shape, then leave it.
Focus on the sponge rather than the chrome of the tap.
A damp sponge shows more texture than a dripping one.
constraint: The sponge and part of the tap both show.

title: Toaster Crumb Tray
oneLiner: Pull out the toaster tray and photograph what it has caught.
details: Slide the crumb tray open and look at the burnt specks and seeds before you tip them away. If there is no tray, unplug the toaster, check that it is cool, and photograph the crumbs in the slot without putting your fingers inside. The tray or the slot is the frame for all those breakfasts.
tips: Shoot from above so the whole tray is included.
Add a little exposure if the crumbs disappear into a dark tray.
Tap the largest speck, which is easier to lock onto.

title: Fridge Door Pocket
oneLiner: Open the fridge door and frame the bottles in the pocket.
details: Use the door shelves, not the main interior you might already have framed. Bottles, jars, and cartons crowded into that narrow pocket are the story. Turn the loudest label away and shoot before the glass mists over.
tips: Brace the phone on the door so the rows stay sharp.
Let the pocket rail run across the frame.
Leave the flash off and use the fridge lamp.

title: Rice Rinse Cloud
oneLiner: Pour cloudy water off rinsed rice into the sink.
details: Rinse a handful of rice in a bowl until the water turns milky, then pour. Catch the pale stream and the grains left in the bowl. It is an ordinary bit of prep, seen from the side at the sink.
tips: Stand to the side of the pour so the stream is a clean line.
Focus on the bowl rim before you tip.
Use burst mode and choose the frame where the cloud still holds together.
constraint: The pour must be visible.

title: Lemon and a Juicer
oneLiner: Set a whole lemon beside a hand juicer on the counter.
details: A lemon, a lime, or an orange, still whole, next to a juicer or a fork is enough. You do not need to juice it. The fruit and the tool together suggest the job without starting it.
tips: Shoot from a low side so both objects have weight.
Put a plain board under them if the counter is busy.
Focus where the fruit nearly touches the juicer.
constraint: The fruit stays whole.

title: Eggs in a Bowl
oneLiner: Gather a few eggs into a bowl and shoot from the side.
details: Three or four eggs in a bowl on the counter are enough. Look for the way the shells touch and the shadow pooled inside the bowl. Keep the carton out of the frame.
tips: Get down to the rim so the eggs stack against each other.
Window light from one side will model the shells.
Focus on the nearest shell.

title: The Pepper Mill
oneLiner: Grind a few specks of pepper onto a board and include the mill.
details: Do this on the counter, on a pale board or a light plate. Grind or shake a short scatter of pepper and leave the mill or the shaker beside it. Leave most of the surface bare so the specks have room.
tips: Shoot from slightly above and to the side.
Focus on the specks rather than the mill's logo.
Turn any branded face of the mill away.

title: Suds in the Sink
oneLiner: Run a little water and soap until suds gather around one mug.
details: Keep this in the sink. Let the suds climb the side of a single mug, the start of the dishes. Move the rest of the dirty dishes out of the picture so the mug and the foam can be read clearly.
tips: Get low enough to see the foam's surface.
Turn the mug handle towards the side of the frame.
Watch that your reflection does not cover the suds.
constraint: Only one mug in the sink.

title: Cold Bottle Beads
oneLiner: Take a bottle from the fridge and photograph the beads on the glass.
details: A milk bottle, a water bottle, or any cold jar will sweat once it sits in the warm kitchen. Set it by the window and give it a minute. The beads are the subject, so turn the label away.
tips: Focus on a bead rather than the whole bottle.
Side light makes the droplets glint.
Shoot before they merge into a sheet.

title: Loaf in the Box
oneLiner: Open the bread box and frame the loaf sitting in its shadow.
details: If you have no bread box, open the bag the bread lives in on the counter and crop the printed side away. The crust in that darker opening is the picture. Shoot before you lift the loaf out.
tips: Include the rim of the box or the mouth of the bag.
Expose for the crust so the shadow stays dark.
Focus on the nearest end of the loaf.

title: Sieve on a Bowl
oneLiner: Rest a sieve or a colander on a bowl in the sink.
details: An empty sieve is enough, or one holding a few leaves you are actually rinsing. The overlap of mesh and bowl rim is the subject. Stay at the sink, where this job belongs.
tips: Shoot from a three-quarter angle so both rims read.
Focus on the mesh where it crosses the bowl.
Clear bottles from the background.

title: A Thread of Honey
oneLiner: Lift a spoon of honey until a thread stretches back to the jar.
details: Do this over the jar on the counter so any drip stays put. Honey or syrup will stretch into a thread. Lift slowly and shoot while the thread between spoon and jar is still intact.
tips: Stand the jar by the window so the honey glows.
Focus on the thread, not the jar label.
Take several frames; the thread thins quickly.
constraint: The thread of honey must be visible.

title: Ring Pull Ready
oneLiner: Frame the ring pull on a can you have not opened.
details: Choose an unopened can with a ring pull and set it on the counter. The picture is the pause before it is opened, so leave the ring flat. If you have no ring-pull can, photograph the sealed lid of a jar instead, and keep any tool out of frame.
tips: Turn the loudest lettering away from the lens.
Focus on the ring rather than the whole can.
Come in close enough that the lid fills the frame.
constraint: Whatever you photograph stays sealed.

title: Stopper in the Drain
oneLiner: Seat the stopper in an empty sink and shoot from above.
details: Use the sink stopper or the metal strainer basket, and leave the sink empty. Wipe it so the metal reads clearly, and clear bottles and cloths away. This is the pause before the dishes, told by the drain alone.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the sink.
Focus on the stopper or the holes in the basket.
Shift a little if your reflection covers the drain.
constraint: No dishes in the sink.

title: Light Leaking the Seam
oneLiner: Find the bright seam where a shade joins and fill the frame with that leak.
details: Switch on a table lamp or a ceiling shade and look for the line where two parts of the shade meet. Move close until that bright seam crosses the frame. The cloth or metal on either side should fall darker than the leak.
tips: Tap the bright line so the shade around it keeps some detail.
Turn the shade until the seam runs diagonally.
constraint: The seam must cross the frame from edge to edge.

title: Edge of the Pool
oneLiner: Show where a lamp's pool of light ends on a table or a wall.
details: Switch on one lamp and find the boundary where its light gives way to the dimmer room. Frame that edge on a tabletop or a plain wall, with no other object sitting in it. Daylight can be present; stand close enough that the fade is still obvious.
tips: Lock exposure on the bright side, then recompose so the dark side stays dark.
A plain surface shows the edge more clearly than a patterned cloth.
constraint: Leave the lamp itself outside the frame.

title: Warm Against Cool Day
oneLiner: Place a lit lamp beside a window so warm light meets cooler daylight.
details: Set a switched-on lamp next to a window in the daytime, without closing the room completely. Put a mug, a book, or a jug where the warm pool and the cooler window light both reach it. The picture is the meeting of those two lights on one object.
tips: Turn off the ceiling light so only the lamp and the window remain.
Walk around the object until both lights are visible on it at once.

title: Wash Up the Wall
oneLiner: Aim a lamp at a bare wall and photograph the wash of light.
details: Point a lamp, or a floor lamp aimed upward, at a clear piece of wall. A separate flashlight propped on a book can take the lamp's place if you have no shade to tilt. Step back until you see the whole wash, brightest near the source and softer as it rises, and keep furniture out so the light has an empty wall to cross.
tips: A cream wall shows the fade better than a very dark one.
Include the lamp at the bottom edge if the wash needs an origin.
constraint: The wall should be clear of pictures and hooks.

title: Circle on the Page
oneLiner: Open a book under a lamp and frame the circle of light on the paper.
details: Open any book under a desk lamp or a bedside lamp. Lower or tilt the shade until a bounded patch of light sits on the page. Shoot so the bright paper is the subject and the words fall soft.
tips: Focus on the page, not the shade above it.
Angle the phone to avoid a white flare in the middle of the patch.

title: Colander Cast Light
oneLiner: Hold a colander between a lamp and the table so dots of light fall.
details: In a room dimmer than the lamp, hold a colander, a sieve, or a slotted spoon between the bulb and a plain table. Let the holes throw dots across the surface. Move the colander until the dots are distinct circles rather than one blob.
tips: Keep your fingers at the rim so they do not block the pattern.
The closer the colander sits to the lamp, the larger the dots become.
constraint: The dots, not the colander, fill the frame.

title: Dim Room Bulb
oneLiner: Darken one room, switch on a single bulb, and move in close.
details: Draw a curtain or shut a door so one room is dimmer than the lamp, even at midday. Switch on a single bulb, shaded or bare. If the bulb is bare, do not touch it. Move close until the glow and the dark around it share the frame.
tips: Lower the exposure so the bulb keeps a core instead of a white smear.
Switch the lamp off again once you have the picture.
constraint: Only one light source in the room.

title: Pillow Gradient
oneLiner: Light a bedside lamp and follow the fade across the pillow.
details: Switch on the bedside lamp and leave the rest of the bedroom quieter. Lay the pillow so the light crosses it from one side to the other. Shoot along that fade, from the bright edge of the fabric into the dimmer fold.
tips: Smooth the pillow, then leave one crease to catch the light.
Stand at the head of the bed so the gradient runs across the frame.

title: Desk Lamp Cone
oneLiner: Include the shade and the bright patch so the lamp's cone is implied.
details: Sit at a desk or table with an adjustable lamp. Frame the shade near the top and the bright patch on the desk below, in one side-on view. The beam itself may be invisible; the two ends should still describe the cone.
tips: Put a pale sheet of paper on the desk so the patch has a clean floor.
Come from the side, level with the shade, rather than from above.
constraint: Both the shade and the patch must appear.

title: Up Into the Shade
oneLiner: Look up into a lit shade and show the glowing interior.
details: Stand under a lit pendant or tip a table lamp so you can see inside the shade. The interior should glow while the outside rim stays darker. Include the bulb only if it does not wipe out the cloth around it, and do not touch a hot bulb.
tips: Drop the exposure until the inside of the shade shows its colour and seams.
Brace an elbow on the table while you look up into the shade.

title: Closet Cave
oneLiner: Set a lamp inside the closet and shoot the glow between the clothes.
details: Place a cool lamp on the floor of the closet or on a high shelf, with fabric well clear of the bulb, and leave the door open. Shoot from outside so the glow sits between hanging clothes. Take the lamp out again as soon as you are done.
tips: Prefer a lamp that stays cool, and do not shut the door on it.
Expose for the clothes nearest the light so they keep their folds.
constraint: The lamp must not touch any cloth.

title: Split Across the Corner
oneLiner: Put a lamp in a corner so the glow fades differently on each wall.
details: Set a lamp on the floor or a low stool in a corner, aimed so both walls catch some light. One wall should be brighter because it faces the lamp more directly. Shoot the corner where the two fades meet.
tips: Move the lamp closer to one wall to widen the difference.
Keep the horizon of the baseboard low in the frame.

title: Cloth Beside the Lamp
oneLiner: Hold a dish towel near a lamp, clear of the bulb, and shoot the glow through it.
details: Switch on a shaded lamp and hold a dish towel or a thin shirt in front of the shade, not on the bulb. Stretch the cloth so light comes through the weave. The picture is the cloth becoming luminous, with your fingers at the edge.
tips: Keep a gap between cloth and bulb at all times.
A pale cloth glows more readily than a thick dark one.
constraint: The cloth must not touch the bulb.

title: Glass Jug Glow
oneLiner: Set a glass jug or bowl in front of a lamp and photograph the lit glass.
details: Place a clear jug, a drinking glass, or a glass bowl between you and a lit lamp. Let the lamp light the rim and the thickness of the glass. Water in the jug is optional; the glow in the glass is the subject.
tips: Shift left or right until the lamp sits just behind the rim.
Tap the glass edge so the lamp behind it can stay soft.

title: Fingers Before the Shade
oneLiner: Hold your fingers just in front of a lit fabric shade and catch the glow around them.
details: Switch on a lamp with a fabric shade and hold one hand a few centimetres in front of it, without touching the cloth. Your fingers turn into dark shapes edged with warm light. Spread or curl them until the gaps between them glow evenly.
tips: Focus on the nearest fingertip.
Turn other lights off so the shade is the only bright thing.
constraint: Your hand must not touch the shade.

title: Crooked Shade
oneLiner: Tilt a shade slightly and show the uneven pool it throws.
details: Tip a table-lamp shade a little off level, or use one that already sits crooked. Look at the pool on the table: one side should stretch farther than the other. Include enough of the shade to explain why the pool is lopsided.
tips: Put the lamp on a plain cloth so the uneven edge is easy to see.
Shoot from table height rather than from above.

title: Source and Bounce
oneLiner: Include both the lamp and the fainter patch where its light bounces.
details: Switch on a lamp near a pale wall. Frame the lamp and, farther along the wall, the softer patch where the light has bounced. Those two brightnesses in one picture are the point.
tips: A white or cream wall bounces more than a dark painted one.
Step back until both the lamp and the faint patch fit.
constraint: Do not add a second lamp.

title: The Faint Pool
oneLiner: Use a low setting, or move the lamp back, and shoot the faint pool.
details: Turn the lamp down, or slide it farther from the wall, until the pool is only just brighter than the room. Photograph that weak patch with darkness around it. You are after the glow at the edge of disappearing.
tips: Brace the phone on a table because the scene is dim.
Lift the exposure slightly, but stop before the pool becomes ordinary.
constraint: The pool should be subtle, not a hard spotlight.

title: Under the Cabinet
oneLiner: Push a lamp against the counter wall and shoot the strip of glow.
details: If you have an under-cabinet light, switch it on and leave the ceiling dark. If you do not, push a small lamp to the back of the counter so it grazes the wall. Photograph the strip of light along the counter, with jars allowed only at the edge.
tips: Crouch to counter height so the strip runs horizontally.
Switch off the overhead so it does not flatten the strip.

title: Glowing Sheet
oneLiner: Drape a sheet over chairs with a lamp inside and photograph the glowing cloth.
details: Drape a pale sheet over two chairs like a loose tent and set a lamp underneath on the floor. Leave plenty of air around the bulb and do not let the sheet touch it. From outside the tent, photograph the cloth where it glows and where it falls into shadow.
tips: Use a cool lamp and check with a hand near, not on, the bulb that the cloth stays clear.
Shoot the brightest panel and one darker fold in the same frame.
constraint: The sheet must not touch the bulb.

title: Ceiling and Table
oneLiner: Switch on a ceiling light and a table lamp and include both glows.
details: Turn on the overhead light and a table lamp together. Stand where you can see the ceiling glow and the warmer pool on the table in one frame. The difference in spread and brightness is the subject.
tips: Let the lamp occupy the lower third and the ceiling light the upper third.
If one source dominates, move until both still read as lit.

title: Half-Lit Mug
oneLiner: Set a mug where the lamp lights only one side and leave the other dim.
details: Place a mug, a jug, or a bottle at the edge of a lamp's pool. One side should be warmly lit and the other should fall into the dimmer room. Shoot from the side so the dividing line runs down the object.
tips: Rotate the handle to the shadow side so it still has a readable shape.
A matte mug shows the divide more clearly than a shiny one.
constraint: The divide between lit and dim must be visible on the mug.

title: Weave of the Shade
oneLiner: Move close to a fabric shade so the light comes through the threads.
details: Switch the lamp on and move close to a fabric, paper, or woven shade. Fill the frame with threads or fibres lit from behind. You should see the material itself, not the whole lamp.
tips: Rest the phone against your other hand, which can brace on the table.
If the weave blows out, back off a few centimetres and lower the exposure.
constraint: No top knob, no stand, only the lit material.

title: Oval on the Boards
oneLiner: Tilt a lamp towards the floor and photograph the oval of light.
details: Aim a lamp down towards bare boards, a rug, or vinyl flooring. The pool will land as an oval. Photograph that oval from standing height and crop the lamp out, unless a small part of the stand explains the shape.
tips: A wooden floor shows the edge of the oval better than a busy rug.
Darken the exposure if the centre of the oval is pure white.

title: Glow in the Pan
oneLiner: Set a small lamp in a cold pan or bowl and photograph the contained glow.
details: Set a cool lamp in a cold saucepan or a large bowl, with the bulb clear of the metal. A separate flashlight standing upright can take the lamp's place. Dim the room by drawing a curtain, then photograph into the pan so the glow is held by the rim.
tips: Do not use a hot stovetop, and do not cover the bulb.
Include the rim as a dark frame around the light.
constraint: The bulb must not touch the pan.

title: Slit of the Door
oneLiner: Leave the door ajar on a lit lamp and photograph the slit of warm light.
details: With a lamp on in the hall or the living room, pull the door until only a slit of that light escapes. Stand on the other side of that door, in the hall, the corridor, or just outside, and photograph the slit rather than the whole room. The warm line against the darker door is the picture.
tips: Focus on the edge of the door where the light leaks.
If the slit is too wide, it becomes a view; narrow it until it is a line.

title: Drum Circle
oneLiner: Frame a round machine door, or a bowl of water, as a porthole.
details: If you have a machine, open the door and fill the frame with the round glass or the ring of holes in the drum. If you have no machine, fill a large bowl with water and shoot straight down so the rim makes the circle. Move until the round shape feels like a porthole rather than a chore.
tips: Turn a nearby lamp off if it glares in the glass.
Tap the rim, not the dark holes, so the circle stays sharp.
constraint: The circle must dominate the frame.

title: Rack of Pegs
oneLiner: Line up the pegs on a drying rack until they make a repeated row.
details: Clip pegs, binder clips, or hair clips along a drying rack, a coat hanger, or a string tied between two chair backs. Keep the spacing uneven in one place if you can, so the row is not perfect. Shoot from clip height and let the repeats run across the frame.
tips: A plain wall behind the row keeps it readable.
Focus on the second clip, not the nearest one.
constraint: At least five clips must appear.

title: Heel to Heel
oneLiner: Pair two socks heel to heel so they mirror one another.
details: Take a matching pair from the clean pile and set them on a bed or table with heels touching. Toes can point in opposite directions. The picture is the small satisfaction of a pair found, so leave the rest of the laundry out.
tips: Smooth the cuffs so both socks share the same outline.
Shoot from directly above and keep the heels at the centre.

title: The Odd Sock
oneLiner: Set a single sock alone on a wide expanse of sheet or floor.
details: Choose one sock whose pair you cannot see, or hide the pair out of frame. Place it on a plain bedsheet, a bare table, or a clear patch of floor. Give it a lot of empty space so the missing match is the subject.
tips: Put the sock well off the middle so the empty area feels deliberate.
Use the same light across the whole surface. A hotspot looks like a stain.
constraint: Only one sock in the frame.

title: Towel Layers
oneLiner: Shoot the side of a towel stack so the folds read as layers.
details: Stack three or more folded towels, dish towels, or pillowcases on a chair or a shelf. Get level with the stack and photograph the striped edges rather than the top. Each fold should read as a separate band.
tips: Push the stack against a wall so it cannot slump mid-shot.
Side light from a window picks out every edge.

title: Hook Thicket
oneLiner: Gather hanger hooks into a tangle and fill the frame with wire.
details: Bunch several hangers on a rail, a door, or a cupboard hook so the metal hooks cross. Move close until the hooks become a thicket and the clothes, if any, drop out of frame. A single hook sitting apart can be the way in.
tips: A dark shirt behind the hooks makes thin wire easier to see.
Shoot slightly from the side so the hooks do not stack into one line.
constraint: At least three hooks must overlap.

title: Basket Gap
oneLiner: Move close to a laundry basket until colour shows through the weave.
details: Put at least one coloured garment in a basket, hamper, or even a colander if that is all you have. Bring the phone close to the holes or the weave. Let one patch of colour sit in a gap and let the basket material frame it.
tips: Focus on the near weave, with the cloth behind a little softer.
Turn the basket until the strongest colour finds a hole.

title: The Fresh Fold
oneLiner: Fold one shirt into a clean rectangle and give it room around it.
details: Fold a t-shirt, a pillowcase, or a dish towel into a tidy rectangle and set it on the bed. Leave empty sheet or tabletop on every side. Shoot from above so the corners and the collar, if there is one, are calm and exact.
tips: Align the rectangle with the edges of the frame, then turn it slightly if that feels stiff.
Pull loose threads off the bed before you shoot.
constraint: Empty surface must show on all four sides.

title: Inside Out Sleeve
oneLiner: Turn a sleeve inside out and photograph the seam you usually hide.
details: Pull a shirt sleeve inside out and lay it on a table near the window. Look for the seam, the hem stitch, and the way the cloth puckers. If a label shows, turn it so the words cannot be read.
tips: Stretch the seam gently with books on either side, out of frame.
Raking light shows stitches that flat light swallows.

title: Washer Dial
oneLiner: Crop in on the machine dial until it becomes an abstract gauge.
details: Use the washing machine dial, or a round kitchen timer you use while washing, and get close to the markings. Crop out the brand name and any full words. An arc of lines and numbers is enough, as long as the circle still feels like a control.
tips: Tilt to dodge the reflection of the window in the plastic.
Tap a single tick mark so the arc stays crisp.
constraint: No brand name in the frame.

title: Door Gasket
oneLiner: Trace the rubber seal around the washing machine door.
details: Open the machine and photograph the rubber ring that seals the door, following its curve. Include a little of the metal or glass so the soft black band meets a hard edge. If you have no machine, use the rubber lip of a bucket or a sink stopper in the same close way.
tips: Wipe beads of water off the rubber so the texture is the seal, not droplets.
A lamp, or a separate flashlight set to the side, deepens the folds in the rubber.

title: Lint Cloud
oneLiner: Pull a little lint or towel fluff and treat it as a soft cloud.
details: Take lint from the machine filter, or rub a dry towel with a damp hand until fluff comes off. Set that fluff on a dark cloth. Get close and low so it rises like a small cloud on a flat ground.
tips: Shoot quickly. A breath will move it.
Lock exposure on the dark cloth so the fluff stays bright.
constraint: The fluff must be the only subject.

title: Crumple and Fold
oneLiner: Lay a crumpled shirt beside a folded one of a similar size.
details: Use two t-shirts, two dish towels, or two pillowcases. Leave one in a loose crumple and fold the other into a tidy shape. Put them side by side on the bed so the undone and the done share one picture.
tips: Keep the colours close so shape, not dye, is the difference.
Shoot from the foot of the bed, looking slightly down.
constraint: Both versions must be fully in the frame.

title: Wash Bag Net
oneLiner: Press a coloured garment against a mesh bag and shoot the net.
details: Use a mesh wash bag, a string bag, or a piece of net curtain over a bright shirt. Press the colour against the mesh and photograph the grid lying on top of it. The net should be sharper than the cloth behind.
tips: Stretch the mesh with one hand outside the frame.
Fill the picture so the grid runs off every edge.

title: Cool Sole
oneLiner: Photograph the cool sole of an unplugged iron at rest.
details: Unplug the iron and touch the sole only when it is fully cool. Set it so the metal point aims toward a corner of the frame and leave the cord out. If you have no iron, photograph the pointed end of an ironing board or a sleeve board instead.
tips: A window reflection on the metal is welcome if it does not hide the shape.
Get low, level with the sole, rather than looking down on it.

title: Board Cover
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the cloth cover of the ironing board.
details: Look at the ironing board cover for its grid, stripes, scuffs, or a faded patch where the iron usually sits. Move close and let that pattern run edge to edge. If you have no board, stretch a striped dish towel flat and shoot the weave the same way.
tips: Include one stain or scuff if the cover has one. It gives the pattern a place.
Hold the phone parallel to the board so the grid stays rectangular.

title: Measure Cap
oneLiner: Look straight down into a capful of detergent or clothes soap.
details: Fill the cap, scoop, or a small lid with liquid detergent, powder, or a little dissolved soap. Set it on the machine or the table and shoot from above. Crop out the bottle and any brand name so the circle of soap is the whole picture.
tips: A spoon can stir powder flat before you shoot, then leave the spoon out.
Lower the exposure if the soap is white and the cap is pale.
constraint: Shoot from above, with the cap fully visible.

title: Drying Map
oneLiner: Hang a just-washed shirt indoors and map the patches that are still damp.
details: After a wash, or after wetting a shirt at the sink and wringing it, hang it on a hanger indoors near a window. Look for darker damp regions against lighter dry ones. Photograph the cloth so those patches read as a map, not as a portrait of a shirt.
tips: Backlight from the window makes damp cloth look deeper.
Crop the hanger out if it distracts from the patches.

title: Hung to Dry
oneLiner: Hang one shirt indoors and photograph it from the side.
details: Peg or hang a shirt on a door, a radiator, a hanger, or a drying rack. Stay indoors. Photograph the whole shirt from the side so a sleeve and whatever holds it are both clear.
tips: Wait until the shirt stops swinging.
A plain wall behind it keeps the shape easy to read.
constraint: Whatever is holding the shirt must be visible.

title: The Pinch
oneLiner: Show several clips gripping real cloth, close enough to see the pinch.
details: Clip pegs, binder clips, or hair clips along a towel on a drying rack or the back of a chair. Move in so you can see the fabric bunch under the pressure. Three or four clips are enough, ideally on different colours.
tips: Focus on the cloth just under one clip.
Leave a little towel visible between the clips.

title: Basket Heap
oneLiner: Stand over the laundry basket and shoot down into the jumble.
details: Leave the basket, hamper, or bag of washing where it usually sits. Stand over it and photograph the heap contained by the rim. Do not tidy the clothes. The jumble is the true state of the wash.
tips: Lean aside until your shadow leaves the clothes.
Include the whole rim so the heap has a container.
constraint: The rim must be fully in the frame.

title: Chair as a Line
oneLiner: Drape a towel over a chair back and let the chair do the drying.
details: Use any sturdy chair indoors. Drape a towel or a shirt over the back as if the chair were a drying rack. Photograph the drape from the side, including the chair, and do not stand on the chair.
tips: Leave one corner of the towel longer than the other.
Move back far enough to show the whole back of the chair.

title: Sock on a Chair
oneLiner: Balance one sock on a chair back or a radiator.
details: Hang a single sock over the back of a chair, a radiator rail, or a drying rack. It should look briefly parked, not styled. Shoot from sock height so the support runs horizontally through the frame.
tips: A slight sag in the sock is better than a stiff fold.
Keep the background to a plain wall.

title: Along the Pegs
oneLiner: Look along a row of pegs so the line runs away from you.
details: Clip a row of pegs or binder clips along a drying rack, a hanger, or a string between two chairs. Lower the phone to clip height and look along the row. Near clips should feel large and far ones small.
tips: The nearest clip can be soft if the third one is sharp.
Keep the line entering from a bottom corner.
constraint: The row must recede into the frame.

title: Colour on the Wall
oneLiner: Hang one bright garment against a dull indoor wall.
details: Peg, tuck, or drape a strongly coloured shirt or towel against a grey, brown, or plain wall or door. Let the dull surface show around the cloth. The wash should look like a block of colour set on the wall.
tips: Hide your fingers behind the cloth or under a clip.
Stand square to the wall so the garment does not skew.
constraint: The wall must remain visible around the cloth.

title: The Empty Rack
oneLiner: Clear the drying spot and photograph the rack with nothing on it.
details: Take the cloth off a drying rack, a radiator, or the back of a chair, then photograph that bare support. The picture is the place washing hangs, seen empty. If you have no rack, the empty back of a chair is enough.
tips: Include the bars, hooks, or clips if they are still there.
A plain wall stops the empty rack getting lost.
constraint: No clothes in the frame.

title: Floorboard Vanishing Point
oneLiner: Follow the floorboards until they meet at the far end of the room.
details: Stand at one end of a room or hallway where floorboards run away from you. If the floor is covered, use tile joints or the long grain of a wooden table instead. Lower the phone so the nearest lines are wide and the far ones crowd together. Include the point where they meet a wall, a door or a piece of furniture.
tips: Hold the phone level so the lines do not lean sideways.
Tap a line a little way in, then lower exposure if the floor is bright.
constraint: Keep the far meeting point inside the frame.

title: Charge Cable Pointer
oneLiner: Let a charging cable point from the outlet toward a lamp.
details: Find a cable already running from an outlet to a lamp, a router or a charger you are not holding. Stand so the outlet sits at one edge of the frame and the thing it powers sits at the other. Tuck spare loops aside until a single line remains.
tips: Wipe the lens if you come in close to the cable.
Turn on the grid and let the cable follow one of the thirds.

title: Edge Toward the Mug
oneLiner: Use the near edge of a table to lead the eye to a mug.
details: Sit at the side of a table, desk or counter. Set a mug, glass or jar at the far end of the edge you want to use. Frame that edge so it enters from a near corner and finishes at the mug.
tips: Focus on the mug and let the near edge soften slightly.
A low viewpoint stretches the edge.
constraint: The mug must sit where the edge ends.

title: Shelf to the Last Object
oneLiner: Run your eye along a shelf until it stops on one object.
details: Choose a shelf, a mantel or the top of a cabinet that already holds a few things. Stand at one end and look along the front edge so it becomes a line. Let that line finish on one object, or on a clear gap at the far end.
tips: Shift sideways until the front edge is a single straight stroke.
Leave out the shelf above if it cuts across the line.

title: Grout Line to the Faucet
oneLiner: Trace one grout line from the edge of the frame to the faucet.
details: In the bathroom or kitchen, find a grout line that runs toward the faucet. Stand so that line starts at the near edge of the picture and ends at the faucet or its base. If you have no tiles, use the junction where a counter meets the wall, heading toward a jar or the kettle.
tips: Focus on the line about halfway along its run.
If the surface is shiny, shift until a bright reflection does not wipe the line out.
constraint: One line should do the leading, not the whole tile grid.

title: Baseboard Into the Corner
oneLiner: Show the baseboard running unbroken into a corner.
details: Pick a stretch of baseboard, or the junction of wall and floor, that reaches a corner without furniture blocking it. Crouch so the line runs from a near corner of the frame toward that far corner. Let the floor occupy the lower part of the picture so the line stays easy to read.
tips: Use the grid to keep the near end level.
Slide a garbage can or a bag aside if it snaps the line.

title: Banister Diagonal
oneLiner: Frame a handrail as a diagonal that arrives at the landing.
details: Use the handrail of indoor stairs if you have them. Stand at the bottom and let the rail run from a lower corner until the eye arrives at the landing above. If you have no stairs, use the sloping back of a chair or a diagonal bar on a drying rack, and let that line arrive at the top of the chair or the top of the rack.
tips: Show a little of whatever the rail leads toward, not the rail in isolation.
Brace an elbow on a wall so the diagonal stays crisp.
constraint: The landing, the chair top or the rack top must sit in the frame.

title: Slats Across the Frame
oneLiner: Aim blind slats so they arrive at a plant or a latch.
details: Tilt a venetian blind, or use a vent, a grille or the fins of a radiator. Stand to one side so the slats run from the near edge toward the far one, rather than lying flat across the picture. A plant, a latch or the far end of the vent gives the lines somewhere to arrive.
tips: Move closer if the slats are thin, so each edge stays clear.
Light from a window or a lamp at the side will pick out every rib.

title: Rug Border Invitation
oneLiner: Catch a rug border leading inward toward a chair.
details: Use a rug, a runner or a doormat with a border you can see. Stand at a corner of it so one border travels from the bottom of the frame into the room. That line should head toward a chair, a doorway or the far edge of the rug, even if the destination is only partly shown.
tips: Crouch, rather than pointing the phone straight down.
Sweep loose bits off the border before you shoot.
constraint: Show where the border enters the frame and where it is heading.

title: Counter to the Kettle
oneLiner: Stand at one end of the counter and follow it to the kettle.
details: Stand at one end of the kitchen counter, or of the longest table you have. Look along the front edge, or along the edge where it meets the wall. A kettle, a toaster or a bowl at the far end is the stop. Keep that edge stronger than any other line in the picture.
tips: A small crouch makes the counter feel longer.
Check the far object is fully inside the frame.

title: Drawer Handle Path
oneLiner: Line up drawer handles so the row ends on the last one.
details: Find a chest, a cabinet or a kitchen unit with two or more handles or knobs in a row. If you only have one, use the top edges of a run of cupboard doors instead. Stand almost square to them, then shift a little sideways so the row recedes. The eye should travel along that row and arrive at the last handle, or at the end panel of the unit.
tips: Focus on a handle in the middle of the row.
If the fronts are dark, bring a lamp in from the side.
constraint: The row must recede and end on the last handle or the end panel.

title: Pipes in the Cupboard
oneLiner: Follow an under-sink pipe until it reaches a valve.
details: Open the cupboard under the sink and look for a water pipe or a drain pipe. Frame the clearest one so it runs from an edge toward the back or toward a valve. You do not need to touch the plumbing. If the pipes are boxed in, use a visible radiator pipe along a wall instead.
tips: Rest the phone on the cupboard base so it stays steady in the low light.
Aim a lamp in from the side and leave the flash off.

title: Curtain Fold Drop
oneLiner: Drop a curtain fold from the top of the frame to the floor.
details: Pull a curtain so one deep fold stands apart from the rest. Frame that fold as a line from the top of the cloth down to the floor. If you have no curtain, hang a towel or a shirt over a door and use one long fold in the same way. The eye should travel down that fold and arrive at the hem on the floor.
tips: Light from the side makes the fold brighter than the cloth next to it.
Keep neighbouring folds out if they start a second path.
constraint: The fold must run from the top edge of the frame to the bottom.

title: Page Edges Receding
oneLiner: Look along page edges until they arrive at a bookend.
details: Stand at the end of a bookshelf and look along the page blocks, not the spines. The pale edges should stack into lines that narrow as they go and arrive at a bookend, a wall or a gap. With only a few books, stack notebooks or magazines and look along those page edges until they arrive at the end of the stack.
tips: Lower the exposure a little if the pale page edges turn pure white.
Shoot from just above the shelf rather than from underneath it.

title: Radiator Fin Climb
oneLiner: Climb a radiator's fins until they arrive at the valve.
details: Stand close to a radiator and let its fins fill the picture as parallel lines. Angle the phone so the fins run from the bottom edge toward the top and arrive at the valve or a wall bracket. If you have no radiator, set a cold grill pan on the counter and look along its ridges until they arrive at the handle or the far rim.
tips: Focus on a fin a short way in so the nearest metal stays recognisable.
A lamp from the side gives each fin a thin bright edge.
constraint: The valve, bracket, handle or far rim must sit in the frame.

title: Bath Rim to the Faucet
oneLiner: Sight along the bathtub rim until it reaches the faucet.
details: If you have a bathtub, crouch at the end opposite the faucet and look along the rim. The rim is the leading line and the faucet is where it ends. With no bathtub, use the raised edge of a shower tray, or the rim of a large tray on a table, and stand a cup where the faucet would be.
tips: Tap the middle of the rim so it stays sharp along its length.
Dry the rim if drops break the line.

title: Towel Rail Horizon
oneLiner: Run a towel rail across the frame until it meets a bracket.
details: Find a towel rail, a curtain rod or a closet rail that runs across the wall. Stand so it crosses the frame from side to side and the eye travels along it. Let the line arrive at a single towel, one curtain ring, or the bracket at the far end.
tips: Set the rail on the upper or lower third using the grid.
Step back if being too close makes the rail bow.

title: Headboard or Chair Slats
oneLiner: Let headboard slats recede toward the end of the board.
details: Look for a row of vertical slats on a headboard, the back of a wooden chair, a vent or a radiator cover. Stand a little to one side so the slats are not all the same width and they step away from you. Let them lead toward the end of the headboard, a chair leg or the end of the vent.
tips: A plain wall behind the slats keeps the rhythm clear.
Turn the phone upright if the slats need more room to repeat.
constraint: Stand to the side so the slats are visibly unequal in width.

title: Notebook Lines to a Pen
oneLiner: Point the ruled lines of a notebook toward a pen.
details: Open a notebook, a pad or a sheet of ruled paper on a table. Lay a pen, a pencil or a spoon at the far end so the printed lines aim at it. Shoot from the near end of the page, low enough that the lines converge a little.
tips: Fill the frame with paper so the table does not compete.
Focus on the pen rather than the near edge of the page.

title: Coat Hook Queue
oneLiner: Queue the coat hooks so the row arrives at the last one.
details: Use a row of coat hooks, pegs or wall knobs. Stand at one end so the hooks recede and the eye arrives at the farthest hook. You may hang one item on that last hook, or leave the row empty. If you have no hooks, a row of cupboard knobs works the same way, ending on the last knob.
tips: Get close to the first hook so it feels larger than the rest.
A plain stretch of wall behind the row helps the line read.
constraint: The farthest hook or knob must be in frame, and the row must recede.

title: Windowsill from One End
oneLiner: Shoot along a windowsill toward a plant or its far end.
details: Go to a window and set the phone at one end of the sill, looking along it. A plant, a jar or any small object already there can be the destination. If the sill is empty, the far end of the ledge is enough. A narrow shelf can stand in if the window has no sill.
tips: Rest the phone on the sill and lift the near end a fraction so the line climbs.
Shift until your reflection in the glass leaves the line.

title: Fridge Shelf Depth
oneLiner: Peer along a fridge shelf until it reaches the back.
details: Open the fridge and look along one shelf from the front edge toward the back. Let jars, tubs or a carton mark where that shelf ends. Close the door as soon as you have the picture. With no fridge, use a bookshelf and one row of books in the same way.
tips: For the fridge, switch other lights off and use only the lamp inside.
Hold the door with an elbow and keep your fingers out of the frame.
constraint: The shelf edge must run from the front of the frame toward the back.

title: Open Drawer Rails
oneLiner: Slide a drawer open and follow one side to the back.
details: Open a drawer halfway and look along one side toward the back. A metal rail, or the top edge of the drawer side, should enter at a near corner and arrive at the back corner or at one item sitting there. Leave the other contents quiet so that single stop is easy to see.
tips: Light the drawer with a lamp from above so the rail does not vanish.
Focus on the rail, not on whatever is stored inside.

title: Broom Handle Diagonal
oneLiner: Lean a broom so the handle arrives at the head or the wall.
details: Lean a broom, a mop, a brush or a closed umbrella in a corner. The handle should run from low on one side to high on the other, and the eye should arrive at the head of the brush or where the handle meets the wall. Step around until that handle is the clearest line in the picture.
tips: Give the handle a plain wall so the diagonal is obvious.
Focus on the handle rather than the wall behind it.
constraint: The brush head, or where the handle meets the wall, must be in frame.

title: Shoes Toward the Mat
oneLiner: Let shoes already by the door form a line toward the mat.
details: Use the shoes where you normally leave them, inside by the door. Nudge them only if they need to share one direction along the floor. Frame low so the row leads toward a mat, the door or the baseboard.
tips: Brace the phone on your knee so the low angle stays steady.
The nearest shoe can be cut off by the frame.

title: Duvet Edge to the Pillow
oneLiner: Fold the duvet so one edge runs toward the pillow.
details: On the bed, smooth a duvet, sheet or blanket so one edge runs from the foot or the side toward a pillow. Stand at the foot and let that edge do the leading. The pillow is where the line arrives.
tips: Flatten creases that fight the main edge.
Shoot from the foot of the bed rather than from overhead.
constraint: Keep the pillow at the end of the line.

title: Hangers Down the Rail
oneLiner: Step to the end of a rail and follow hangers to the last one.
details: Open a closet or find a rail with several hangers. If you have no rail, hook several hangers over the top of a door. Stand at one end and look along the rail so the hangers shrink as they go. The eye should arrive at the last hanger, with or without a garment on it.
tips: Light from the room, or a lamp beside you, keeps the rail from turning black.
Place the rail along a third of the frame.

title: Stripes Leading to a Cup
oneLiner: Lay stripes of a towel so they lead to a cup.
details: Use a striped towel, dish towel or shirt. Lay it on a table so the stripes run away from you toward a cup, a glass or a piece of fruit. If nothing is striped, pleat a plain dish towel into parallel ridges and use those ridges as the lines. The stripes, or the ridges, are many versions of the same path.
tips: Pull the cloth tight so the stripes or ridges stay straight.
Lower the phone until those lines converge a little.
constraint: The cup, glass or fruit must sit on the stripes or ridges, not beside them.

title: Door Moulding Inward
oneLiner: Follow door moulding inward until it reaches the handle.
details: Close a panelled door and stand a little off to one side. Use the moulding around a panel as lines that lead toward the handle or the centre of the door. If the door has no raised panels, use the inner edge of the frame instead, running toward the handle.
tips: Square the phone so the panel lines do not lean by accident.
Let the handle be the sharpest point in the picture.

title: Ceiling Line to the Corner
oneLiner: Trace the trim where wall meets ceiling into a corner.
details: Look up to where the wall meets the ceiling. Follow the crown moulding, a picture rail, or that plain junction as it runs into a corner. The line should start large at one edge and arrive at the corner. A lamp held low can lift a pale line off a pale ceiling.
tips: Keep the phone level so the line does not tip the wrong way.
Expose for the ceiling so it keeps a little tone instead of burning out.
constraint: The corner where the line ends must be in frame.

title: Hallway Convergence
oneLiner: Stand in a hallway and let the walls meet a far door.
details: Stand at one end of a hallway, a corridor or your longest room. Hold the phone level and include the floor, both walls and the far end. The joins between wall and floor should run toward that far end, which should be a door, a cupboard or a turn.
tips: Keep door frames upright by holding the phone level with the floor.
Stand near the middle so the two wall lines agree.

title: Long Edges Converging
oneLiner: Use the long edges of a board so they converge at the far end.
details: Open an ironing board with the iron unplugged and out of frame, or use a tray, a shelf or a narrow table. Stand at the near end and look along it so the two long edges converge. A pointed end, or a small object you set there, is where the eye arrives.
tips: Get low so the two edges separate widely at the near end.
Choose a plain floor or wall so other lines stay quiet.
constraint: Both long edges must be visible.

title: Cloth Down the Table
oneLiner: Run a cloth down the middle of the table toward a bowl.
details: Lay a table runner, a scarf or a dish towel along a table so it runs away from you. Set a bowl, a plate or a mug at the far end. The cloth is the path and the vessel is why the path is there.
tips: Smooth the cloth so its long edges stay parallel.
Shoot from table height rather than from overhead.

title: Rack Bars Across
oneLiner: Run rack bars across the counter toward a cup.
details: Use a cooling rack, a dish rack, an oven shelf or the grate of a cold stovetop. Set it so the bars run from the near edge and arrive at a piece of fruit, a cup or the far end of the rack. Make sure the stovetop is cold and the oven is off before you pull a shelf out.
tips: Get close and focus on the nearest bar.
A lamp at the side adds a bright edge to each bar.
constraint: The bars must run from the front of the frame toward the back.

title: Bristles Along the Frame
oneLiner: Hold a hairbrush so the bristles lead toward the handle.
details: Hold a hairbrush or a comb close to the phone. Turn it so the bristles or teeth run from one side of the picture and arrive at the handle, or at the far end of the brush head. A plain wall or a sheet of paper behind it keeps the lines clear. Brace your hands on a table because this is a tight shot.
tips: Clean the lens first, because you will be very close.
Tap a bristle near the middle of the row.

title: Paving Joints Recede
oneLiner: Crouch so paving joints run toward a wall or a bend.
details: On the sidewalk outside your home, find joints between slabs, or a seam in concrete, that run away from you. Crouch and let two or three of those lines leave the bottom of the frame and narrow until they arrive at a wall, a doorway or a bend.
tips: The lowest comfortable crouch gives the strongest convergence.
Focus on a joint a metre or two ahead.
constraint: Keep your feet out of the frame.

title: Under the Cabinets
oneLiner: Follow the strip beneath the cabinets to the end of the run.
details: Crouch and use the strip along the bottom of the kitchen cabinets, a bookcase or a dresser, or the line where that piece meets the floor. Let it run from a near corner of the frame toward the end of the run or the tall thing it stops against. That end is where the eye should arrive.
tips: Get low so the strip reads as one long stroke.
Keep the countertop out if it starts a second, stronger line.
constraint: The line must reach the end of the cabinets, bookcase or dresser.

title: Brick Courses to a Door
oneLiner: Read the brick courses across a wall toward a door.
details: From the sidewalk, stand before a brick, block or stone wall of your own building and choose the horizontal courses as your lines. A smooth painted wall with a clear trim line can stand in. Shift until those lines run toward a doorway, a vent or a corner, and leave the glass of any window out of the picture.
tips: Fill the frame with wall so the courses have room to travel.
Focus where the courses are busiest, about halfway along.
constraint: A doorway, vent or corner must sit at the end of the lines.

title: Rings Along the Rod
oneLiner: Look along shower rings until they arrive at the last one.
details: Use the rings on a shower curtain rod, a closet rod or a curtain rod. Stand at one end so the rings shrink as they go and the eye arrives at the last ring or the bracket. If you have no rings, clip several binder clips along a taut string between two chairs and look along those instead.
tips: Let the nearest ring be partly cut off by the frame.
Focus on a ring a short way along, not the nearest metal.
constraint: The rings or clips must get smaller as they recede.

title: Frames Along the Wall
oneLiner: Let a row of frames lead the eye to the last one.
details: Hang or lean two or more picture frames, book covers or notebooks in a row along a wall or a shelf. Stand at one end so the row recedes and finishes on the last frame. You are following the frames, not reading anything inside them, so turn printed pages away.
tips: Get close to the first frame so it feels larger than the rest.
Leave wall visible above the row so the line stays easy to follow.

title: Drainpipe Down the Wall
oneLiner: Take a vertical pipe down the wall until it meets a bracket.
details: Find a vertical pipe fixed to an outside wall you can see from the sidewalk. Frame it so it travels from the top of the picture and arrives at a bracket or the ground. If no pipe is visible, use the outer edge of your own door frame in the same way, from the top of the frame down to the threshold. Stay at ground level.
tips: Stand square to the wall so the pipe stays vertical.
Include a little wall on both sides so the pipe is not a bare stripe.

title: Hem Across the Window
oneLiner: Run a curtain hem sideways until it meets the frame.
details: Draw a curtain, a sheet or a towel so its lower hem crosses the picture. Let that hem travel from one side and arrive at the window frame, a door edge or the end of the cloth. If the hem is uneven, smooth only the part you want to use as the line.
tips: Set the hem on the lower third using the grid.
Light from the side will brighten the hem against a darker wall.
constraint: The hem must meet a frame, a door edge or the end of the cloth.

title: Cable on the Outside Wall
oneLiner: Trace an outside cable until it arrives at a clip or a box.
details: Look for a cable already clipped along the outside of your building. Stand on the sidewalk so it travels from one edge of the frame and arrives at a clip, a box or a corner. Do not pull at it, and do not add a cable of your own. If you cannot see a cable, use a horizontal trim line on the same wall and let it arrive at a corner.
tips: Daylight from the side shows the clips as beats along the line.
Move in until the cable is thick enough to read clearly.

title: Keys Toward the Corner
oneLiner: Angle a keyboard so its rows run toward the far corner.
details: Set a laptop or a desk keyboard on a table and keep the screen out of the picture. Stand at one corner so the rows of keys run away from you and arrive at the far corner of the keyboard. The letters can fall soft. The rows are the lines.
tips: Get low beside the near corner so the rows start to converge.
Turn the keyboard until a bright window does not glare off the keys.

title: Cord to the Blind
oneLiner: Follow a blind cord down until it reaches the toggle.
details: Find the cord of a blind, a curtain pull or a lamp pull that hangs in a straight drop. Frame it from the top of the cord down to the toggle, the tassel or the end. Move loose loops aside so one clear line remains. A string with a spoon tied on the end can stand in if you have no cord.
tips: Stand square to the wall so the cord stays vertical.
A plain stretch of wall beside the cord keeps the line easy to read.
constraint: The toggle, tassel or end must sit in the frame.

title: Wire Down the Spine
oneLiner: Follow a spiral binding until it reaches the bottom of the page.
details: Open a spiral notebook or a wire-bound calendar and stand it so the wire runs vertically. Let the coils form a line from the top of the frame down toward the bottom of the notebook. A pen laid at the bottom gives that line a place to stop.
tips: Focus on a coil near the middle of the wire.
Turn the page so any handwriting faces away.

title: Tread Edges Stacked
oneLiner: Stack the edges of indoor steps so they reach the top.
details: Use indoor stairs if you have them. Stand at the bottom and frame the front edge of each tread so the edges stack and lead up to the landing. If you have no stairs, set three or more books on the floor, each one a little farther back and higher than the last, and use those front edges as the climb.
tips: Hold the phone near the height of the lowest edge.
Stop the frame where the landing or the top book closes the lines.
constraint: The edges must arrive at a landing or the top book.

title: A Row of Spoons
oneLiner: Lay spoons in a row so the handles lead to the last bowl.
details: Set three or more spoons on a table, handles aiming the same way, each one a little farther from you. The handles should form a line that arrives at the bowl of the farthest spoon. A row of pencils works the same way if the spoons are in the wash.
tips: Shoot from the handle end, low, so the bowls grow smaller.
A plain cloth underneath keeps the table grain from competing.
constraint: At least three spoons or pencils must recede.

title: Shelf Brackets Recede
oneLiner: Let shelf brackets shrink until the eye reaches the last one.
details: Use the brackets under a shelf, or the hooks under a rack, if you can see two or more. Stand at one end so the nearest bracket is large and the others grow smaller toward the last one. A shelf with no brackets can be replaced by a row of matching mugs, ending on the last mug.
tips: Include the shelf edge so it ties the brackets together.
Focus a couple of brackets in, rather than on the bare wall.
constraint: The brackets, hooks or mugs must get smaller as they recede.

title: One Bold Letter
oneLiner: Find a single large letter in your home and make it the whole subject.
details: Look on book covers, posters, or large type on packaging, and choose a letter that is not part of a logo. Crop tight so one letter dominates. Background clutter should fall away so the shape of the character matters more than the word.
tips: Rotate the phone for vertical letters.
Tap focus on the ink edge.
Watch for glare on glossy packaging.
constraint: Only one letter visible, with no full word.

title: Calendar Date Detail
oneLiner: Photograph today's date on a wall calendar, planner, or paper diary.
details: Open a paper calendar or planner on today. If you have none, write today's date large on a scrap and photograph that. Frame the numeral large, leave a little of the page around it, and crop out any other notes.
tips: Shoot parallel to the page to avoid skew.
Use soft light to keep the paper even.
Crop square on the date cell if it helps.

title: Book Spine Type
oneLiner: Stack or line up book spines and celebrate the typography on their edges.
details: Pull a few books from a shelf and arrange spines facing the camera. Mix colours and font styles if you like. Move close enough that one title or author name is legible while others blur softly.
tips: Align spines vertically for a clean column.
Use window light so the foil titles do not flare.
Vary the book heights for a staggered edge.
constraint: At least three book spines must appear.

title: Keyboard Key Portrait
