oneLiner: Move close on one keyboard key until its letter feels oversized.
details: Choose a key with meaning to you, such as an initial, a shortcut you use often, or the escape key, on a laptop or any keyboard that is not the phone in your hand. Photograph it at an angle so surrounding keys fall out of focus. If you have no separate keyboard, write one large letter on paper and shoot that instead. The single character should feel like a sign seen from very near.
tips: Wipe the key so dust does not sit on the letter.
Rake a desk lamp across the key for texture.
Keep any note with a password outside the frame.
constraint: One key sharp, with the others blurred or cropped out.

title: Clock Face Numbers
oneLiner: Photograph a clock and let one numeral or marker anchor the frame.
details: Use a wall clock, a watch face, or a stove timer. Crop so a single number or tick mark is prominent while the rest of the dial curves away. Hands may appear, but they do not need to show a particular time.
tips: Shoot straight on to limit distortion of the dial.
Shift until a glass cover stops reflecting the phone.
Try a mono filter if the dial colour fights the numerals.

title: Nutrition Label Digits
oneLiner: Crop into a food label until a cluster of numbers becomes abstract art.
details: Grab any packaged food from the pantry and move close on the nutrition panel. Let serving sizes and percentages fill the frame as shapes. You are hunting for graphic rhythm in ordinary printed data.
tips: Flatten the package so the rows stay readable.
Align the rows with the phone edge for a calm crop.
Leave the barcode outside the frame.
constraint: Numbers must occupy most of the frame.

title: Magazine Letter Cutout
oneLiner: Find a bold letter on a magazine page and isolate it tightly.
details: Flip through a magazine, a flyer, or a book until a large initial catches your eye. Photograph the page flat with even light and crop to the letter alone. Leave out any name, address, or logo, and you can leave the page intact.
tips: Weight the page corners with mugs outside the frame.
Shoot from directly above to keep the letter square.
Add a little exposure if the ink looks muddy.
constraint: The letter must fill at least half the frame.

title: Page Number Corner
oneLiner: Open any book to a page and feature its printed page number prominently.
details: Choose a book and compose so the page numeral sits near a third with the text softly blurred around it. The number can be Arabic or Roman, whatever you find. Keep the shot about the type, not the story on the page.
tips: Press the page gently so the numeral lies flat.
Use indirect light to avoid shine on the paper.
Either phone orientation works if the number stays large.

title: Microwave Clock Glow
oneLiner: Dim the room and fill the frame with a microwave or oven clock.
details: Turn the kitchen lights down until the display is the brightest thing you can see. Move close so the digits sit in the middle and the rest of the appliance falls away. A toaster or stovetop clock works the same way if the microwave has no lit display.
tips: Lower the exposure so the glowing digits keep their edges.
Tap focus on the display, not the dark door.
constraint: Show no more than four digits.

title: Remote Button Rows
oneLiner: Angle in on a remote until one row of buttons reads as type.
details: Any remote with numerals will do, or a calculator if you have no remote. Rest it on a table and shoot along one row so those numbers are sharp and the next row softens. Dust in the gaps can stay if it does not hide a digit.
tips: Light the remote from the side with a lamp so the printed numbers catch.
Brace your wrist on the table for this close angle.

title: Dial Arc Letters
oneLiner: Follow the printed arc around a washing machine dial.
details: Open the laundry space and find the cycle dial or the printed panel beside it. Fill the frame with the curve of words and temperatures rather than the whole machine. A dishwasher or dryer panel is a fair stand-in.
tips: Move a little to the side so the panel glass does not mirror your phone.
Wipe fingerprints off the words you want sharp.
constraint: The type must follow a curve through the frame.

title: Jar Label Depth
oneLiner: Line up two labelled jars and let the front label stay sharp.
details: Spice jars, jam, or any labelled cupboard jars will do. Set them on the counter so a descriptive word or a weight faces you, with the brand and any logo turned away. If a label is stained or peeling, keep that wear in the picture.
tips: Tap focus on the front label and let the rear jar soften.
Stand a sheet of paper behind the jars if the cupboard is busy.

title: Cup Measurement Ticks
oneLiner: Move close until the measurement ticks on a cup become the pattern.
details: A measuring cup, a medicine cup, or a bottle printed with volume lines all work. Hold it near a window so the marks read as dark ticks. Crop close enough that the numbers matter more than the container.
tips: Put a little water in an empty cup so the marks have something pale behind them.
Lock exposure on the printed ticks before you reframe.
constraint: At least three measurement marks must be visible.

title: Magnet Letter Heap
oneLiner: Scatter letter magnets, or paper stand-ins, into a small heap.
details: If you have alphabet magnets, slide a handful onto the fridge without spelling a tidy word. Shoot close so the letters overlap and tilt. If you have none, cut four letters from a cereal box and lean them in a heap against the fridge.
tips: Turn the room light off if the fridge lamp adds a green cast.
Place the heap away from the middle using the grid.
constraint: No complete word may be readable.

title: Insole Size Mark
oneLiner: Look inside a shoe and enlarge the printed size mark.
details: Check the tongue, the insole, or the heel of any sneaker or boot for a size stamp. Angle the phone so that number is sharp and any brand mark falls outside the frame. The scuffs around the stamp are welcome.
tips: Switch on a lamp beside you if the shoe interior is a cave.
Tap the printed size, then lean a little closer without refocusing on cloth.
constraint: The size number must be the sharpest mark in the frame.

title: Dial in the Hall
oneLiner: Creep in on a thermostat, heater, or radiator dial.
details: Let the numerals curve or stack, and include the little pointer if there is one. If the display is backlit, dim the room so the type glows on its own. An oven knob with temperatures printed around it is a fine substitute.
tips: Angle off a glossy panel until your reflection leaves the digits.
Expose for the numbers when they are brighter than the wall.

title: Percent in the Dark
oneLiner: Darken the room and crop a battery percent on a blank screen.
details: On a laptop, a tablet, or any screen other than the phone in your hand, open the battery page after you have cleared banners, and hide every name. Crop so the percent number sits large against a dark ground. If that phone is your only screen, crop the digits on a microwave or oven clock the same way, with no other text.
tips: Drop the screen brightness a notch so the digits do not bloom.
Clean the glass and focus on the number, not the room reflected in it.
constraint: No names or message text may be readable.

title: Barcode Stripes
oneLiner: Treat a barcode and the digits under it as a striped print.
details: Any box or tin from the cupboard has a barcode. Move close so the bars and the small numbers beneath them fill the frame. Hide the product name so the picture stays about rhythm rather than a brand.
tips: Press the package flat with a hand that stays outside the frame.
Line the bars up with the long edge of the phone.
constraint: The brand name must sit outside the frame.

title: Margin Date Sharp
oneLiner: Open a notebook and give the margin date the sharpest focus.
details: A diary, a planner, or a scrap of paper you date yourself will do. Compose so the date sits near a corner and any other writing falls too soft to read. If the page is blank, write today's date large and photograph that.
tips: Shade a glossy page with your body rather than adding a hard lamp.
Hold the book open with a mug kept outside the frame.

title: Digits Through Glass
oneLiner: Catch glowing temperature digits through the oven door glass.
details: Switch on the oven lamp if it has one, with no need to heat anything. Shoot through the door so the digits sit among faint reflections of the kitchen. A toaster or air fryer display seen through its window is the stand-in.
tips: Shift sideways until a reflection slides off the digits.
Focus on the display, not on a smudge on the outer glass.
constraint: The digits must be seen through glass.

title: Door Numeral Close
oneLiner: Approach your own door and let one numeral fill the frame.
details: Stand at your own door and move close to the house number on the door, the frame, or the wall beside it. Choose a single digit and keep the screw, the paint edge, or the shadow under the character. If there is no number, write one digit on a scrap, tape it to your own door, and take it down afterwards. Never include a street name.
tips: Stand to the side so your shadow does not cover the digit.
Tap focus along the edge of the numeral.
constraint: Only one digit may be fully inside the frame.

title: Can Lid Digit
oneLiner: Crouch by a garbage can and frame the number on its lid.
details: Your own garbage can, kept indoors or just beside your door, often carries a short painted or moulded number. Crouch so the digit sits against the scuffed plastic. If it has no number, use a capacity mark on a kitchen pail or a storage tub you already own.
tips: Wipe grit off the digit before you focus.
Shoot in open shade so the plastic does not glare.

title: Chalk Digit on Paper
oneLiner: Draw one large numeral on paper and photograph it on the fridge.
details: With chalk, a crayon, or a thick pen, draw a single number big enough to fill a photo. Tape the paper to the fridge or a plain cupboard door and include a margin around the digit. Take the paper down when you are finished.
tips: Stand square to the paper so the digit does not lean.
Leave the rough strokes visible rather than tidying them.
constraint: The numeral must be one you made for the picture.

title: Expiry in the Cupboard
oneLiner: Crop a printed date on a packet and leave the brand outside.
details: Open a cupboard and find a box, tin, or bottle with a printed date. Move close to the date where the packet already sits, in the shade of the shelf. Keep the brand name and any logo out of the picture.
tips: Turn the packet until the date faces the light from the room.
Steady your wrist against the shelf for this tight crop.
constraint: The date must be the only readable text.

title: Card Corner Rank
oneLiner: Crop the corner of a playing card so the rank fills the frame.
details: Any playing card will do, or a square of paper with a rank you write yourself if you have no cards. Lay it on a table and move close so the corner character is large and the rest of the card falls away. Leave the box, and any other cards, out of the picture.
tips: Shoot from above so the card corner stays square.
Tap the rank itself so the rest of the card can soften.

title: Windowsill Plant Tag
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the letters on a houseplant tag.
details: A herb on the kitchen sill, or any indoor pot with a nursery tag, will do. If the pot has no tag, use a small printed label on a bottle or a box and leave the brand out. Crop so the letters fill the frame and the soil or the surface is only a soft band. If the tag names a shop, leave that line and any logo out.
tips: Pinch the tag flat with a finger that stays outside the picture.
Focus on the printed letters rather than the shiny plastic.
constraint: The shop name must not be readable.

title: Sink-Side Recycling Code
oneLiner: Crowd the frame with the recycling mark on a rinsed tub.
details: Turn a rinsed tub in the sink so the small triangle and number face upward. Lean over it and crop tight, letting the basin fall soft. Any brand name or logo should stay outside the frame.
tips: Shift away from window glare so a moulded number stays visible.
Rest your wrist on the counter before you take the shot.
constraint: The code number must be legible.

title: Mat Letter Close
oneLiner: Bend close to a mat or towel and let one worn letter take over.
details: Look at a doormat, a bathmat, or a dish towel, and if none has a letter, write one on a scrap and lay it on the cloth. Move close so that single letter fills the frame with the fibre around it. Crop out any address, name, or logo.
tips: Shoot from above and a little to one side.
Brush loose grit off the letter you are featuring.
constraint: Hide any address completely.

title: Masking Tape Digit
oneLiner: Form one numeral from masking tape on the table, then photograph it.
details: Tear short strips of masking tape or paper and lay them into a single digit on a table or the kitchen floor. Shoot from standing height so the whole digit and a margin of surface are included. Peel the strips up when you finish.
tips: Use the grid and settle the digit away from the exact middle.
Include the torn ends of the tape so the making stays visible.
constraint: Use only one numeral.

title: Care Label Codes
oneLiner: Open a care label and enlarge the letters and numbers on it.
details: Look inside the seam of a shirt, a towel, or a sheet for the printed care label. Lay the cloth flat and move close so a short run of letters and numbers fills the frame. Fold any brand name out of the picture.
tips: Pull the label gently so it lies flat, then take your fingers away.
Light it with a lamp from the side if the cloth is dark.

title: Suitcase Dial Crop
oneLiner: Crop a suitcase dial so the numbers show and the code does not.
details: A suitcase, a briefcase, or a padlock indoors is enough, and three handwritten digits on paper scraps work if you have no dial. Move close until the numbers cross the picture. Turn or crop them so a full code cannot be read from the photo.
tips: Use a lamp from the side to pick out the engraved numbers.
Wipe fingerprints off the dials before you shoot.
constraint: The full code must not be readable.

title: Window Sticker Digits
oneLiner: Crop the tiny print in the corner of a window or a frame.
details: Look at the corner of a window in your home, or of a picture frame, for a year mark or a tiny code. Crop tight so those characters sit against a soft background. Skip any mark that shows a logo, a phone number, a name, or an address.
tips: Focus on the sticker, not the room beyond the glass.
Angle the phone so the sky does not wash out the print.

title: Charger Print Crop
oneLiner: Crop the tiny ratings printed on a charger or a plug.
details: A phone charger, a lamp plug, or an adaptor is covered in small ratings. Set it on a table and move close until a short run of letters and numbers fills the frame. Leave the brand and any logo off to the side.
tips: Roll the plug until the print faces a lamp.
Brace your wrist on the table so the tiny type stays sharp.

title: Tub Volume Marks
oneLiner: Lean in until the volume marks on a tub or bottle fill the frame.
details: A bucket, a large bottle, or a mixing bowl stored indoors is enough. Lean in until the printed amounts fill the frame, and leave the container where it already lives. If there are no marks, use the capacity number moulded on a storage tub.
tips: Fill the lower third with the curve of the container.
Stand away from a bright window so white plastic does not burn out.

title: Faded Price Digits
oneLiner: Find a leftover price sticker and crop it down to the numbers.
details: Look under a pot, on a book, or on the base of a lamp for a faded sticker. Move close so the price numbers and the curl of the sticker fill the frame. Keep the shop name and any logo outside the picture.
tips: Include the peeling corner of the sticker.
Focus on the ink even if the sticker is wrinkled.

title: Cupboard Note Digit
oneLiner: Stick one handwritten numeral inside a cupboard door.
details: Write a single large number on a sticky note or any small scrap. Press it onto the inside of a cupboard door and shoot straight on so the paper stays square. The ink, the paper edge, and the door colour are the whole picture.
tips: Stand square to the door so the note does not become a trapezoid.
Use room light from the side so the paper does not glare.

title: One Word on the Counter
oneLiner: Write three plain words and let only one of them stay sharp.
details: On a scrap, write three ordinary grocery words yourself, with no names and no addresses. Lay it on the counter, weight it with a mug, and focus on a single short word so the other lines go soft. Put the paper away when you are done.
tips: Tap the word you want sharp.
Shoot from above so the paper stays rectangular.
constraint: Exactly one word should be readable.

title: Bulb Rating Digits
oneLiner: Read the tiny rating on a cool bulb or a lamp cord.
details: Switch a lamp off and let the bulb cool before you touch it. Unscrew it, or read the rating printed on the lamp base or the cord, and fill the frame with those digits. Leave any brand outside the picture.
tips: Lay the plug on a pale cloth so the digit has a plain ground.
Light it from a window, or from another lamp that is still on.

title: Ruler Along the Desk
oneLiner: Lay a ruler along the desk so the numbers recede.
details: A school ruler or a tape measure on a desk or a table is the subject. Lay it so the numerals march from the near edge towards the far side. Include a little of the desktop on both sides so the numbers have a place to travel.
tips: Hold the phone close to the desktop at the near end of the ruler.
Tap focus on the nearest numerals and let the far ones soften.

title: Single Die on the Table
oneLiner: Set one die on the table and enlarge the number facing up.
details: One die is enough, or a handwritten number on a square of paper if you have no die. Place it on the table and shoot from above so the number is large and the table surface frames it. Leave any box or pack out of the picture.
tips: Shoot from directly above so the die stays square.
Use a lamp to the side so the pips cast a small shadow.
constraint: Only one number may be readable.

title: Letters on the Table
oneLiner: Drop handmade letter squares on the table and shoot where they fall.
details: Write four different letters on scraps of paper, or use game tiles if you already have them. Drop them on the table and leave the overlaps and the upside-down ones. Shoot from above before you tidy them away.
tips: Use even room light so every scrap is readable.
Crop out anything that is not paper, table, or letter.

title: Pot Base Digits
oneLiner: Tip a plant pot onto a towel and photograph the marks on its base.
details: Many pots have a diameter or a code moulded into the bottom. Tip one carefully onto a towel on the floor, shoot the marks, and set it upright again. If the base is blank, use any moulded number on a plastic tub in the kitchen.
tips: Brush soil off the digits before you tip the pot.
Focus on the moulded edge, not the dirt around it.

title: Digit in the Flour
oneLiner: Write one digit in a dusting of flour and photograph it from above.
details: Scatter a little flour, salt, or cocoa on a plate. A dusty indoor windowsill works if you would rather not use food. Write a single number with a finger and shoot it from above, then wipe it away.
tips: Get close enough that the finger strokes are clear.
Include a little of the dusted surface around the digit.

title: Speaker Volume Digits
oneLiner: Move close on the numbered scale beside a volume knob.
details: A speaker, a stereo, or a heater often has a short run of numbers beside a knob. Fill the frame with those digits and the pointer if there is one. Leave any brand mark outside, and leave the appliance as you found it.
tips: Angle a lamp so the printed numbers catch the light.
Tap the pointer, then crop until the brand falls away.

title: Ceiling Fixture Portrait
oneLiner: Look straight up at a ceiling light, fan, or medallion and make it the symmetrical hero.
details: Stand beneath a ceiling light, a fan, or a plain medallion and point the phone straight up. Place the fitting in the middle, with a margin of ceiling around it. If the ceiling is bare, let the paint be a quiet surround for whatever hangs there.
tips: Switch the fitting on only if the glow stays contained.
Take one step aside rather than tipping the phone at a steep slant.

title: Tree Canopy Tunnel
oneLiner: From the sidewalk, look up into branches that frame a patch of sky.
details: Stand on the sidewalk under a street tree, or close to a trunk you can reach while staying there. Point the phone up so branches reach in from the edges and hold a patch of sky. Thick or thin leaves both work, and the upward view is the picture.
tips: Turn until the brightest opening sits near the middle.
Tap the sky, then ease exposure down if you still want detail in the branches.
constraint: Include a branch or a slice of trunk at one edge.

title: Building Crown From Below
oneLiner: Shoot upward at a building top so edges and cornices converge toward the sky.
details: From the sidewalk by your own entrance, tilt up the face of the building. Let edges, window tops, or the top trim run towards the sky.
tips: Leave a band of sky so the top edge has somewhere to arrive.
Use the grid and keep the nearest corner as upright as you can.

title: Floating Bright Rectangle
oneLiner: Frame a bright ceiling opening, or a high window, as a floating rectangle.
details: Use a skylight, a fanlight over a door, or any high window, and stay on the floor of the room. Stand so the glass becomes a bright rectangle in a darker surround. Any daylight will do, and a little of the frame should remain so the rectangle feels suspended.
tips: Tap the bright glass, then lower exposure a notch so the surround survives.
Hold the phone close to vertical.
constraint: The bright rectangle should not touch the picture edges.

title: Pendant Glass Glints
oneLiner: Catch glints in a pendant lamp by looking straight into it from below.
details: A glass pendant, a beaded shade, or a simple metal fitting overhead will do, and a chandelier works if you have one. Stand beneath it and shift until small highlights sit on the glossy parts. Let most of the frame belong to the lamp, with only a rim of ceiling.
tips: Lower the exposure slightly so the bright specks keep a shape.
Rest a shoulder against a door frame if your neck tires.

title: Power Lines Against Sky
oneLiner: Frame wires crossing the sky while you stand on the sidewalk.
details: From the sidewalk by your entrance, look up at wires crossing whatever sky you have today. Let them slice the frame. Use the cable fixed to your own wall if no other lines are in view.
tips: Include a short run of wall so the lines have an anchor.
Tap the sky and darken the exposure if the wires vanish.
constraint: Let the wires or the cable cross most of the frame.

title: Stairwell Skywell
oneLiner: Tilt up through stacked frames, using stairs, a doorway, or a tall hall.
details: If you have stairs, stand on a lower tread against the wall and shoot upward so rails and landings stack towards the top. If you have only a doorway, stand in it and tilt up so the frame, the wall, and the ceiling line stack in one view. Keep a hand on a rail or the door frame, with your weight over the tread you are on.
tips: Let the phone tilt while your feet stay planted.
Include at least two horizontal edges that lead upward.

title: Under the Shelf
oneLiner: Point the phone up beneath a shelf and photograph the hidden underside.
details: Choose a wall shelf, a mantel, or the underside of a wall cupboard. Tilt up from standing height so the hidden face fills the frame. Look for screw heads, a faded label, a bracket, or the shadow line where the shelf meets the wall.
tips: Switch on a lamp below the shelf if the underside is too dark to read.
Get close enough that the brackets feel large.

title: Beneath the Table
oneLiner: Get under a table and shoot the underside above you.
details: Sit or kneel under the kitchen or dining table and point the phone at the board overhead. The picture can be the grain, the screws, a folded flap, or the cross-brace. Include one table leg at the edge so the view still makes sense as 'under'.
tips: Prop your elbows on your knees to keep the phone steady.
A lamp on the floor beside you will open up a dark underside.
constraint: Include one leg or brace so the surface reads as a table.

title: The Alarm Disc
oneLiner: Make a round study of the smoke alarm by standing directly under it.
details: Stand under a smoke alarm, a ceiling sensor, or a round vent. Point the phone straight up and place the disc near the middle. Let a ring of ceiling remain so the circle has a setting.
tips: If the disc is white on white, underexpose slightly to keep its slots.
Shoot before you are perfectly underneath, then take one step to centre it.

title: A Crack Overhead
oneLiner: Find a crack, seam, or stain on the ceiling and follow it upward.
details: Scan the ceiling for a hairline crack, a plaster seam, a water mark that is long dry, or the joint between boards. You are not inspecting damage; you are using the line as a path. Fill the frame with that line and the ceiling texture around it.
tips: Side-on light from a lamp rakes the crack into relief.
Rotate the phone so the line runs diagonally.
constraint: Nothing but ceiling in the frame.

title: Three Planes Meeting
oneLiner: Aim into the corner where two walls meet the ceiling.
details: Stand in a corner and tilt up so both walls and the ceiling occupy the frame. The three planes should meet at one point. A cobweb-free paint corner is enough; a band of trim or a change of colour makes the meeting clearer.
tips: Keep the meeting point away from the exact middle for a less static picture.
Turn off mixed lamps so each plane has one tone.
constraint: All three planes must appear.

title: Along the Curtain Track
oneLiner: Tilt up to the curtain track and follow it towards a corner.
details: From the floor side of the curtains, raise the phone to the track, the pole, or the fabric valance. Let it run from one edge of the frame towards a corner or a bracket. Gliders, rings, or a single break in the spacing give the line a beat.
tips: Include a little curtain top so the track has something to hold.
Focus on the nearest bracket and let the far end soften.

title: Top of the Door Frame
oneLiner: From close to a shut door, raise the view to the top of the frame.
details: Stand near a closed door and tilt up until the top rail and the lintel area become the subject. Include the corner where the upright meets the top. The ceiling can take the upper third.
tips: Step in close so the frame feels tall.
Keep the uprights as vertical as the tilt allows.

title: Up Through the Leaves
oneLiner: Shoot through the leaves of a houseplant from underneath.
details: Use a trailing plant on a shelf, or hold a leafy stem above a phone propped on the table. Point up so leaves overlap against the ceiling or a bright window. Look for one gap where light comes through.
tips: Prop the phone in a mug so both hands can lift the plant.
Tap a leaf, not the bright gap, if you want the greens sharp.
constraint: Leaves must occupy most of the frame.

title: Pages Above the Lens
oneLiner: Hold an open book above the phone so daylight comes through the pages.
details: Prop the phone on a table, pointing up, near a window. Hold an open book or a thin magazine between the lens and the glass. Move the pages until printed type softens and the paper glows, with the inner fold of the book as a dark spine.
tips: A thinner page glows more than a thick cover, so use an inside leaf.
Set the timer if holding the book and the shutter at once is awkward.

title: Blanket Above You
oneLiner: Lie back under a raised blanket and photograph that cloth ceiling.
details: Drape a blanket or duvet over the backs of two chairs, or over a table, so you can lie underneath. Point the phone at the cloth above you. Folds, a seam, or a thin patch where light seeps through should structure the frame.
tips: Wait until the cloth stops swinging before you shoot.
A lamp beside the cloth will show the weave without flattening the folds.
constraint: Show only the cloth overhead, not the chairs.

title: Shower Head Above
oneLiner: Point up at a shower head or a colander and centre the circle.
details: Stand in the shower or the bath and aim straight up at the head. If you have neither, hold a colander or a slotted spoon above the phone in the kitchen and treat it the same way. Place the round fitting in the middle, with its holes or arms readable.
tips: Dry the fitting first if drops are not the subject you want.
A small step back keeps the whole circle in the frame.

title: Hooks From Under
oneLiner: Stand beneath a row of hooks and let them hang into the top of the frame.
details: Coat hooks, mug hooks, or a rail under a shelf all work. Stand directly beneath them and tilt up so the hooks and whatever hangs there enter from the top. The ceiling or the shelf underside is the background.
tips: Empty hooks are fine; a single mug or hat gives scale.
Line the phone up so the rail runs level.
constraint: At least three hooks must appear.

title: Blind Roller Tube
oneLiner: Raise the phone to the roller at the top of a blind and show its curve.
details: Tilt up to the barrel of a roller blind, a Roman blind headrail, or a curtain pole. Let the curve or the straight rail cross the frame. Include the bracket at one end and a little of the fabric falling away.
tips: Shoot from slightly below and to one side so the tube reads as round.
Focus on the bracket, which is usually the sharpest small detail.

title: Box Held Overhead
oneLiner: Hold a cardboard box overhead and shoot up through the open flaps.
details: Open a light cardboard box and hold it above a propped phone, flaps outward. The picture is the square opening and the flaps against the ceiling. Shift the box until the opening sits askew rather than perfectly square.
tips: Use a box you can hold with one hand.
Daylight from a window beside you keeps the inside of the flaps visible.
constraint: The opening must show ceiling or light beyond it.

title: Fan Guard Above
oneLiner: Look up into a fan guard or a round ceiling grille.
details: Hold a desk fan above the phone, or stand under a ceiling vent or an exhaust fan. Point up so the bars or the ring dominate. A glimpse of ceiling or blade through the guard gives the metal some depth.
tips: Keep fingers off the guard so they do not block the ring.
If the fan can spin, leave it still so the bars stay sharp.

title: Where the Ceiling Turns
oneLiner: Frame the trim, or the plain ceiling edge, where it turns a corner.
details: Tilt up to the decorative trim, the picture rail, or simply the line where wall meets ceiling. Choose a corner so that line changes direction. Let the turn sit in the upper part of the frame.
tips: Include a short run of both directions, not only the corner point.
A lamp bounced off the ceiling can separate white trim from white paint.

title: Through a Colander
oneLiner: Hold a colander above the lens and shoot up through the holes.
details: Prop the phone on the floor or a low stool, pointing up, and hold a colander, a sieve, or a slotted spoon over it. Aim towards a ceiling light or a bright window. The holes should reveal fragments of that brightness.
tips: Move the colander until one hole contains the lamp or the window.
Focus on the metal, not on the ceiling beyond.
constraint: The colander fills the frame.

title: Under the Wall Cupboards
oneLiner: Stand under wall cupboards and photograph the undersides and the light there.
details: In the kitchen, stand at the counter and tilt up to the bottoms of the wall cupboards. Look for the strip of light, the underside seams, and any hooks or marks. Let the cupboard bottoms occupy the top half and the counter shadow the lower edge.
tips: Take one step back if the cupboards crop too tight.
Include a mug hook or a small seam so the surface is not blank.

title: Cord to the Ceiling
oneLiner: Follow a light pull or a blind cord from below up to the ceiling.
details: Find a light pull, a blind cord, or a string of a hanging planter. Start the frame near the lower part of the cord and let it rise to the fitting or the ceiling. The cord should be the clearest line in the picture.
tips: A plain wall behind the cord makes the line easy to see.
Tap the cord itself so it stays sharp against a brighter ceiling.
constraint: The cord must reach the top edge of the frame.

title: Up the Bookcase
oneLiner: Stand at the base of a tall bookcase or closet and tilt up the front.
details: Stand close to a bookcase, a closet, or a tall cupboard and tilt the phone up its face. Let the sides angle inward as they rise. Shelves, handles, or the top edge against the ceiling give the rise a finish.
tips: Include the floor at the bottom so the height has a start.
Keep the phone's tilt steady by tucking your elbows in.

title: Pipe Across the Ceiling
oneLiner: Trace a pipe, a conduit, or a beam where it crosses the ceiling.
details: In a kitchen, bathroom, or hall, look up for a pipe, a plastic conduit, a beam, or the edge of a bulkhead running overhead. Follow it with the phone so it crosses the frame. A bracket, a joint, or a change of direction is the detail to include.
tips: Shoot along the pipe rather than from directly below it.
Let it enter at a corner and leave by the far edge.

title: Where the Ceiling Drops
oneLiner: Stand where the ceiling drops and shoot along that overhead step.
details: Many homes have a place the ceiling steps down: a bulkhead, a boxed-in pipe, or a lower section over a hallway. Stand so that step runs across the upper frame. The contrast between the higher and lower planes is the subject.
tips: Include both levels, not only the vertical face of the drop.
If both planes are white, use side light to separate them.
constraint: Both ceiling heights must be visible.

title: Umbrella Canopy
oneLiner: Open an umbrella indoors, hold it overhead, and shoot into the canopy.
details: Open a dry umbrella inside and hold it above you. Point the phone up into the panels. Ribs, a seam, and the bright or dark centre where they meet should organise the picture.
tips: Stand clear of lamps so you do not catch a rib on a shade.
Focus where the ribs meet, then recompose a little.

title: Bunting Overhead
oneLiner: String a short line of bunting and photograph it from underneath.
details: Hang a short string of bunting, or make one from folded paper and cotton, across a doorway or between two chairs. Stand underneath and shoot up so the flags repeat against the ceiling. Let the string rise diagonally through the frame.
tips: A plain ceiling behind the flags keeps their shapes clear.
Wait until the paper stops spinning.
constraint: At least four flags should appear.

title: Slats of the Bed
oneLiner: Lie on the floor and shoot up at the bed slats above you.
details: Lie beside the bed and point the phone at the underside. Slats, a fabric base, or the shadow under the mattress can fill the frame. If the bed sits flush to the floor, use the underside of a chair or a stool in the same way. Include one leg so the view still reads as underneath.
tips: Rest your elbows on the floor so the phone stays steady.
A lamp to one side will show slats that would otherwise sink into dark.
constraint: Include one leg or edge so the surface reads as furniture.

title: The Door Overhang
oneLiner: From the sidewalk, tilt up to the lip above the entrance.
details: Stand on the sidewalk and tilt up to the lip above the door, the lintel, or the top of the door frame. Let that edge cut against the sky.
tips: Expose for the edge if the sky is much brighter.
Include a little of the door top so the lip has a home.
constraint: Keep the sky in the upper half only.

title: Drainpipe Rising
oneLiner: Follow a drainpipe upward from the sidewalk to a bend or the sky.
details: From the sidewalk by the entrance, point the phone up a drainpipe or a vertical cable cover. Let it rise through the frame and end at a bracket, a bend, or the sky.
tips: Leave a margin of wall so the pipe reads as attached.
Tap the pipe, not the bright sky, if you want its clips sharp.

title: Antenna Against Sky
oneLiner: From the sidewalk by your door, frame the antenna against the sky.
details: Look up from the sidewalk at your entrance at a television antenna, a vertical pipe, or a tall post. Place that shape against the sky, with a little wall or bracket at the edge.
tips: Give the antenna room so its arms do not crop.
Darken the sky slightly if the metal silhouette fills in.
constraint: The antenna, pipe, or post must stand against open sky.

title: A Crossing Branch
oneLiner: From the sidewalk, isolate one branch crossing the open sky.
details: From the sidewalk, find one branch or a long shrub stem that crosses open sky. You do not need the trunk. Let that one line travel diagonally, with a few twigs as smaller echoes.
tips: Move until the branch is separate from other clutter.
Tap the branch so it stays crisp against the bright background.

title: Leaves With Sky Behind
oneLiner: From the sidewalk, fill the frame with leaves that have sky behind them.
details: From the sidewalk, look up at leaves on a low branch or a shrub beside you. A bright sky behind the leaf is enough to show the structure. Fill the frame with two or three leaves so the veins read as pale lines.
tips: Expose for the leaf if the sky turns it into a flat silhouette.
Hold the twig steady by bracing your wrist against your shoulder.
constraint: Veins must be visible, not only the outline.

title: Rack Overhead
oneLiner: Hold a cooling rack overhead and shoot up through its bars.
details: Stand indoors and hold a cooling rack or a slatted tray above the phone. Point up so the bars cross the ceiling or a bright window. Keep your grip at the frame edge so the grid stays readable.
tips: Place one crossing of the bars near a third of the frame.
Focus on the nearest bar.

title: Pot From Below
oneLiner: Lift a light pot above the phone and shoot into its base.
details: Stand indoors and lift an empty, light pot just above the phone. Shoot up into the base so the circle and any marks on it fill the view. A saucepan, a plant pot, or a plastic bowl all work.
tips: Include a fingertip at the rim so the base has some scale.
Tap the darkest part of the base so it does not turn pure black.
constraint: Show the whole circle of the base.

title: Strings Overhead
oneLiner: Hold keys or spoons overhead and let the strings rise.
details: Tie a few keys or spoons onto short lengths of cotton or string, or use a wind chime if you already have one indoors. Hold the bundle overhead. Shoot up so the strings run through the frame and the metal sits toward the bottom.
tips: Wait for a still moment so the metal does not smear.
A plain ceiling behind the strings keeps them separate.

title: Leaf From Below
oneLiner: Hold a broad leaf overhead and photograph its pale underside.
details: Use a houseplant leaf, a cabbage leaf, or a piece of lettuce. Hold it above the phone with the pale underside facing the lens and a window behind it. Veins, ribs, and small holes are the detail.
tips: Pinch the stem at the frame edge.
If the leaf is thin and glaring, turn a little away from the window.
constraint: The underside fills at least three quarters of the frame.

title: Into the Bloom
oneLiner: Come up under a houseplant flower and fill the frame with petals.
details: Use an open flower on a houseplant or in a jar. If nothing indoors is flowering, hold a cabbage leaf or a succulent overhead and tilt up into the layered centre. Fill the frame with petals, leaves, or florets radiating above the lens.
tips: Focus on the nearest petal or leaf edge.
Shade the subject with your body if the highlights blow out.

title: Ribs of the Shade
oneLiner: Frame the ribs inside a lampshade by looking straight up.
details: Use a hanging shade, or hold a table lamp shade above a phone propped on the table, with the lamp switched off. Point up so the ribs or the wire frame cross the bright opening. A plain ceiling or a window beyond the shade keeps that structure easy to read.
tips: Focus on the nearest rib so the far ones can soften.
Keep your fingers on the outer rim, out of the opening.
constraint: At least two ribs or wires must show.

title: Upright Tips Overhead
oneLiner: Tilt up so a row of upright tips meets sky or ceiling.
details: If railings stand by your entrance, tilt up from the sidewalk so the tops of the uprights touch the sky. If you have none, use the uprights of a chair back or a stair rail indoors and tilt up so their tips meet the ceiling. The tips should form a rhythm along the upper frame.
tips: Keep the tips just inside the frame rather than cropping them.
Expose for the uprights if they turn into featureless black.

title: Window Beam Still Life
oneLiner: Place one everyday object where morning light cuts a shape across it.
details: Find a window and a plain surface near it. Set a single object, such as a mug, book or piece of fruit, where the morning light meets the dimmer part of the table. If the light is a hard strip, let it graze one edge; if it is a soft wash, let the brightest part of that wash fall across the object. Move until the divide between bright and dim feels deliberate.
tips: Expose for the bright patch and let the dim side stay dark.
Turn the object until one edge meets the brightest light.
constraint: Shoot from table height only.

title: Desk at First Light
oneLiner: Capture your desk or table as the first soft light of the day arrives.
details: Before you turn on any lamps, photograph the surface where you work or eat. Let the cool early glow reveal clutter, texture or empty space. You are documenting a quiet transition, not staging a perfect setup. Include only objects already there.
tips: Steady the phone against the table edge so the dim light stays sharp.
Let a window frame or a notebook edge give you one diagonal.

title: Building Edge Glow
oneLiner: Find where the early light picks out one edge of a wall or fence near you.
details: Step just outside your door and look for a corner, railing or wall panel that is brighter than the surface beside it. Fill most of the frame with the dimmer side and let the lit edge stay a thin highlight. A flat morning still works if one plane faces open sky and the other turns away. Stay on the path beside the building.
tips: Stand so the bright edge does not flood the whole frame.
Turn the grid on and set that glowing edge near a third.
constraint: Use your default lens with no zoom.

title: Warm Spoon Moment
oneLiner: Catch morning light on a spoon or other metal utensil on the counter.
details: Rest a metal spoon where the morning light reaches the counter, whether that light is warm or cool. Watch the handle, the bowl and the counter each take a different tone. You are chasing a small highlight, not a full breakfast. Keep the background simple so the gleam stays obvious.
tips: Tilt the spoon until one clean highlight appears on the metal.
Tap focus on the brightest curve of the spoon.
constraint: Only one utensil may appear in frame.

title: Ground Lines at Dawn
oneLiner: Trace the brighter and dimmer bands of morning light across the ground by your door.
details: Look down at the path or paving just outside. Let one boundary between a brighter patch and a dimmer one cut across the frame. If the light is hard, a long shadow may give you that line; if it is soft, use the gentle falloff beside a wall. Stay on familiar ground by the entrance.
tips: Lower the phone to about hip height so the ground fills the view.
Wait until the boundary crosses a crack or a change in texture.

title: Houseplant Halo
oneLiner: Backlight a houseplant so leaves glow around the edges.
details: Set a houseplant between you and a bright window so the light comes through the leaves. Some leaves will turn translucent while others fall dark. Shift the pot until a clear glow outlines the edges. Move closer until those edges dominate the frame.
tips: Tap the brightest leaf edge so the glow does not blow out.
Fill the frame with a single leaf if the whole plant feels busy.
constraint: Spend no more than ten minutes finding the angle.

title: Curtain in the Light
oneLiner: Let morning light filter through a curtain and become the subject.
details: Find a window with a sheer or thin curtain and photograph the fabric itself. Notice folds, seams and any dust catching the soft light. You do not need a view outside, because the curtain is enough. Move until the brightest area sits away from the middle.
tips: Keep the window behind the curtain rather than off to one side.
Lower the exposure a touch so the folds keep their detail.

title: Quiet Door Corner
oneLiner: Frame an empty corner of your building as the morning light arrives.
details: Step outside your door and choose a corner where two walls meet, or where the wall meets the path. Let the pale morning light soften the surfaces and keep the frame still. Include a drainpipe, a door frame or a wall fixture as an anchor, and keep the shot at the entrance.
tips: Shoot from the path, with your back close to the door.
Include both a lit plane and a dimmer one so the light has a scale.
constraint: Keep every face and figure out of the frame.

title: Light Pool on the Floor
oneLiner: Photograph a rectangle of morning light lying on your floor.
details: Open or close curtains until one brighter patch of morning light sits on the floor. Place nothing in it, or let one shoe or the edge of a book touch the border. The patch itself is the subject. Step back until the bright shape reads clearly against the dimmer flooring.
tips: Point the phone straight down if you want the patch to look graphic.
Take a second frame a minute later and keep the one where the shape is clearest.
constraint: Use only the daylight already in the room.

title: White Wall Colour
oneLiner: Show the colour of this morning's light on a plain white wall or sheet of paper.
details: Pin or hold a white sheet, or find a patch of white wall near a window, with no lamp mixed in. The picture should be about the tint of the light, cool blue or soft grey, rather than about an object. Include a small darker edge, such as a door frame or the border of the paper, so the tint has something to sit against. If the wall is cream, the paper will tell the truth more clearly.
tips: Fill the frame with the paper first so the phone reads its tint, then ease back a little.
Lock exposure on the white, then reframe so a dark edge sits at one side.
constraint: No switched-on lamp may light the surface.

title: Kettle Shoulder Highlight
oneLiner: Let morning light draw a single highlight along the curve of a kettle or pan.
details: Set a kettle, saucepan or metal jug on the counter where window light reaches it. Ignore any miniature room in the metal and look only for the bright line running along the shoulder. Roll the kettle until that line is long and clean. A matt pan still works if you catch the rim.
tips: Shade the lens with your free hand if the window flares into the glass.
Focus on the metal, then lower exposure until the highlight is a line and not a white blob.

title: Mug Ellipse
oneLiner: Look down into a mug and photograph the shape of the light inside it.
details: Use an empty mug, glass or jar and stand it where morning light can fall in. Look straight down so the bright area becomes an oval or a crescent on the inner wall. Turn the mug until that shape is simple. A dark mug will show the light more clearly than a white one.
tips: Rest your wrist on the table so the phone stays steady above the mug.
Tap the inner wall, not the table, so the oval stays sharp.
constraint: The rim must be fully inside the frame.

title: Dim Room Bright Door
oneLiner: Stand in a dim room and frame the brighter morning beyond an open door.
details: Open an interior or exterior door and stand on the darker side. Let the bright opening occupy less than half the frame, with the dim room around it. You are comparing two strengths of morning, not documenting the view. If every room is equally bright, close a curtain behind you to make a darker foreground.
tips: Expose for the bright opening so the near room falls into tone.
Hold the phone against the door frame to keep the edges straight.

title: Motes in Morning Air
oneLiner: Catch specks drifting in a bright patch of morning light against a dark background.
details: Stand so a dark cupboard, a bookshelf or a coat makes a blackish background, with bright window light passing in front of it. Look for specks in that bright air. If the air looks clear, photograph the soft column of brightness against the dark furniture instead. Move an inch and the column will shift.
tips: Turn night mode off so the phone does not smear the bright air.
Focus on the dark edge where the brightness begins.
constraint: The dark background must fill at least half the frame.

title: Cupboard Front Row
oneLiner: Open a cupboard and photograph how far the morning light reaches inside.
details: Choose a cupboard, closet or drawer near a window and open it just enough for light to touch the front items. The things at the back should fall dim. Arrange nothing new; the story is the reach of the light. A kitchen cupboard, a bookshelf or a bedside cabinet all work.
tips: Stand to the side so your own shadow does not block the opening.
Lock focus on the last object the light still touches.

title: Linen Light Gradient
oneLiner: Spread a pale sheet or shirt and show morning light fading across the cloth.
details: Lay a pale sheet, pillowcase or shirt fairly smooth on a bed or table near the window. You want a gentle change from brighter cloth to dimmer cloth, so quiet the folds rather than featuring them. If the light is even, move the cloth so one side tucks into the shade of the bed or a chair. The gradient is the subject.
tips: Shoot along the cloth, not straight down, so the fade has distance.
Tap a mid-tone area so both the bright end and the dim end keep detail.
constraint: Keep the cloth free of patterns that shout louder than the light.

title: Paper Caustics
oneLiner: Set a glass of water in morning light and photograph the pattern it throws.
details: Fill a clear glass or jar with water and place it on pale paper or a light table near the window. Look for the wiggling bright patch the glass throws beside it, and photograph that patch rather than the glass. If the morning is soft, slide the glass closer to the window until a faint pattern appears. A bottle will do if you have no glass.
tips: Focus on the paper where the pattern lands, not on the glass rim.
Lift the glass a centimetre if you want the pattern to sharpen.
constraint: The glass itself may occupy no more than a third of the frame.

title: Fruit Side Light
oneLiner: Turn one piece of fruit until morning light models its roundness.
details: Place an apple, orange, onion or egg near a window and turn it until a bright side and a darker side both show. One is enough. Move the camera until the background is a plain wall or cloth. The roundness should come from the light, not from a busy table.
tips: A slight side angle shows the shadow edge better than a flat-on view.
Wipe the lens if the highlight on the skin looks smeared.

title: Unlit Lamp at Dawn
oneLiner: Include a switched-off lamp in the frame, sitting only in morning light.
details: Find a lamp that is off and place it, or leave it, where the window light falls across the shade. The unlit bulb and the daylight on the shade should share the picture. Do not switch it on, even to test. A small desk lamp or a bedside lamp is enough.
tips: Expose for the shade so the window behind does not become a white hole.
Step left or right until the shade has both a lit face and a quieter one.
constraint: The lamp must stay switched off.

title: Sink Steel Gleam
oneLiner: Find the small gleam of morning light on a faucet, sink or steel pot.
details: In the kitchen, look for a tiny morning highlight on the faucet, the sink rim or a steel pot. Move the camera until that gleam sits against a duller metal surface. You are not polishing the room, only noticing one spark. If the kitchen is dim, open the blind a little rather than adding a lamp.
tips: Get close enough that the gleam is larger than a pinprick.
Tap and hold on the highlight to lock the exposure.

title: Page Rake
oneLiner: Rake morning light across an open page so the paper texture appears.
details: Open a notebook, a printed page or an envelope on a table and turn it until the light skims along the paper. The texture of the sheet should rise, and the words can fall soft. A blank page is fine. If the light is coming from above, tilt the page up toward the window.
tips: Focus near the front of the page and let the far edge soften.
Lower the phone until it almost touches the table.
constraint: Do not include your hands.

title: Hands in the Patch
oneLiner: Hold your hands in a patch of morning light and photograph only the light on the skin.
details: Find a patch of morning light on a table or floor and rest your own hands in it. The picture is the light on the skin, the brighter knuckles and the dimmer palms, not a task you are doing. Keep the background to the patch and a little of the surrounding shade. Either hand is enough if holding the phone is awkward; prop the phone and use the timer.
tips: Use the three-second timer if you need both hands in the patch.
Expose for the skin so the patch does not burn out to white.
constraint: Only your own hands may appear.

title: Bathroom Cool
oneLiner: Record the cool morning light in a bathroom, on tile, mirror edge or tub.
details: Leave the bathroom lamp off and let the small window, or the light from the hall, do the work. Choose one surface, a tile, the rim of the tub, a mirror edge or a pale sink, and show how cool the morning looks there. Include a darker corner so the pale tone has weight. Steam is optional and not required.
tips: Wipe a clear spot if you are shooting near the mirror.
Lean on the door frame so the low light does not blur.

title: Shelf Lip Light
oneLiner: Show morning light catching only the front lip of a shelf or mantel.
details: Look along a shelf, mantel or the top of a headboard where morning light touches the front edge and leaves the objects behind in quieter light. Line the bright lip up so it runs across the frame. What the shelf holds can stay secondary. A windowsill edge counts if you have no shelf.
tips: Shoot from one end of the shelf so the lip becomes a line.
Drop the exposure slightly until the lip is bright but still has colour.
constraint: The lit edge should cross the full width of the frame.

title: Threshold Stripe
oneLiner: Let a narrow band of morning light fall across whatever waits by the door.
details: Near the front door, inside, find or make a narrow band of morning light by almost closing the door or leaving a gap in a curtain. Let that band cross a shoe, a bag, a box or the bare floor. The band matters more than the object. If the light is a wide wash, narrow the opening until it becomes a stripe.
tips: Get down to the height of the stripe rather than shooting from standing.
Focus on the point where the stripe crosses the object.

title: Bread Crust Glow
oneLiner: Skim the crust of bread or toast with morning light until the surface shows.
details: Set a piece of bread, a roll or a slice of toast on a board near the window. Turn it until the light skims the crust and the bumps catch small highlights. The crumb or the board can fill the rest. If you have no bread, a cracker or a rough cookie works the same way.
tips: Get close enough to see the crust texture, then tap the nearest bump.
A side view shows the skim of light better than a top-down shot.
constraint: Fill at least half the frame with the crust.

title: Two Window Tones
oneLiner: Compare the light from two windows, or a window and a door, in one frame.
details: Stand where you can see light from two openings at once, or from one window and an open door. Let each light fall on a different wall or on two halves of the same floor. The difference in brightness or tint is the picture. If you have only one window, compare the lit wall with the wall that faces away from it.
tips: Do not use flash or a lamp, or the comparison collapses.
Include a little of both areas rather than cropping to the prettier one.

title: Bowl of Bright
oneLiner: Fill a pale bowl with morning light and shoot into it from above.
details: Set an empty pale bowl, plate or colander where the window light falls inside it. Shoot from above so the interior holds a pool of light and the near rim stays a little darker. Shift the bowl until the bright area is a clean shape. A white cereal bowl is ideal, though a light pan will do.
tips: Hold the phone just above the rim so the ellipse stays wide.
Tap the bright interior, then nudge exposure down if the bowl clips.
constraint: Nothing may sit inside the bowl.

title: Curtain Gap Patch
oneLiner: Leave a narrow gap in the curtains and photograph the patch of light it throws.
details: Part the curtains, or almost close a door, until a narrow gap throws a shaped patch on the floor, a sofa or a wall. Photograph the patch, not the gap. Move a cushion or leave the floor bare, but do not fill the patch with a collection of objects. If the patch is faint, darken the rest of the room.
tips: Wait half a minute and shoot when the edge of the patch looks sharpest.
Include a sliver of the darker room so the patch has a boundary.

title: Jam Jar Glow
oneLiner: Backlight a jar of jam, honey or dish soap so the contents glow.
details: Stand a jar of jam or honey, or a translucent bottle of dish soap, on the windowsill with the morning coming through it toward you. The translucent colour should light up, and the glass edge can stay darker. Turn any label away so the glow is clear. An empty jar is the wrong subject, so pick something the light can pass through.
tips: Tap the glowing contents, then lower the exposure until the colour holds.
Come close enough that the jar or bottle fills most of the frame.
constraint: Only one jar or bottle.

title: Bedroom Corner Wash
oneLiner: Visit the bedroom before any lamp is on and record the window's light there.
details: Go to the bedroom while it is still lit only by the window. Choose a corner where the light thins out across the bed, a closet or the floor. Do not tidy beyond moving one thing that blocks the view. The wash of light, and where it gives up, is the subject.
tips: Brace the phone on the mattress if the room is dimmer than you expected.
Keep the window itself small in the frame, or leave it out, so the light on surfaces leads.

title: Door Paint Rake
oneLiner: Skim morning light along the paint or grain of your front door.
details: Stand close to your front door, outside, and look along the paint, the grain or the panels. The morning light should rake across that surface so small bumps catch it. If the door faces away from the light, try the frame or the wall immediately beside it. You only need to stand at the door.
tips: Shoot almost parallel to the door so the texture stretches.
Focus a third of the way into the frame.
constraint: Stay within arm's reach of the door.

title: Paving in Low Light
oneLiner: Get low and show how morning light reveals the texture of paving by your door.
details: Crouch or kneel on the paving or concrete just outside and aim along the ground. Low morning light, even when soft, will show grain that you miss from standing. Include a join, a crack or a change of material. If the ground is smooth, the doormat edge can supply texture.
tips: Rest your elbow on your knee to keep the low angle steady.
Turn the grid on and let the ground line run to a corner.

title: Broad Outdoor Sheen
oneLiner: Show the morning sheen on a railing or metal box already outside.
details: Just outside, look for a railing, a metal meter box or a painted post that is already part of the entrance. Find a broad highlight and a duller area on the same surface, and fill the frame with that surface. If the metal is dull, the painted top of a low wall will still show a quieter sheen. Leave the view beyond your entrance out of the picture.
tips: Crouch so the highlight stretches toward you.
Expose for the sheen, allowing the surroundings to darken.
constraint: Keep the frame on that one surface.

title: Wall Plane Brighter
oneLiner: Choose the brighter face of an outside wall and set it against a darker recess.
details: From the path by your entrance, pick one outside wall that faces the light more than the recess beside it, a doorway, a corner or the shadow side of a drainpipe. Fill the frame with the brighter plane and let the darker notch sit at one edge. This is about a broad field of light, not a thin glowing line. A flat morning still gives you a quieter version of the same comparison.
tips: Step sideways until the darker recess is only a slim vertical band.
Lock exposure on the bright wall before you reframe.

title: Leaf in the Light
oneLiner: Hold one outdoor leaf up to the daylight and photograph its glow.
details: Find a leaf you can reach from your own entrance: a weed in a crack, a low branch, or one already on the ground. Hold it between you and the bright sky and shoot through it so the leaf glows and the edges go darker. A flat day still backlights a thin leaf. Keep your fingers at the edge or out of the frame.
tips: Tap the glowing middle of the leaf, then reduce exposure a little.
Fill the frame with the leaf so the sky is only a rim.
constraint: Use one leaf, not a handful.

title: Stripe on the Page
oneLiner: Lay a band of morning light across a page so it reads like a highlighter.
details: Open a notebook or a printed page on a table near the window. Narrow the curtains or shift the page until one band of morning light crosses the lines, brighter than the rest of the sheet. The band is the subject, so let the words stay secondary. A blank page with faint lines works as well as a printed one.
tips: Tap the bright band so the paper keeps its texture.
Turn the page until the band runs on a diagonal.
constraint: The band of light must cross the page.

title: Light on the Tea
oneLiner: Catch morning light as a bright patch on a cup of tea, milk or water.
details: Pour tea, milk or plain water into a mug and set it where morning light reaches it. Come down to rim height so a bright patch sits on the surface, and wait until the liquid is still. The patch is the subject, so the table can fall away. Plain water is enough if you are not making a drink.
tips: Hold the phone almost level with the rim.
Tap the bright patch, then nudge exposure down if it clips to white.

title: Handle Highlight
oneLiner: Find a door handle, knocker or mail slot flap catching the morning.
details: Look at the handle, knocker, bell or mail slot on your own door and find the small highlight the morning puts there. Come close so the metal or plastic gleam is clear against the door. If the fitting is matt, the edge of the mail slot flap or a hinge may still catch a line. Stay on your side of the threshold.
tips: Angle yourself until the highlight is a small shape, not a smear.
Tap the metal, then pull exposure down until the door keeps its colour.

title: Ceiling Wash
oneLiner: Photograph the wash of morning light on the ceiling near a window.
details: Stand under the ceiling beside a window and look up at the pale wash of morning light, ignoring the rest of the room. Include the corner where the ceiling meets the wall so the wash has an edge. If the ceiling is evenly lit, move until the brightness fades before the far wall. A plain ceiling shows the light more clearly than a busy one.
tips: Press the phone lightly to your brow so the upward shot stays steady.
Expose for the ceiling so a white ceiling does not clip to a blank.
constraint: Leave the window itself out of the frame.

title: Row of Tumblers
oneLiner: Line up glasses so each one catches its own point of morning light.
details: Stand two or more clear glasses, jars or tumblers in a row on the counter where morning light reaches them. Turn the row until each glass holds a small highlight in a different place. You are after the repeated glints, not a portrait of the glasses. A glass and a jar side by side are enough if you have only one of each.
tips: Get down to the height of the highlights rather than shooting from above.
Tap the nearest glint, then check the farther ones are still bright.
constraint: At least two glasses or jars.

title: Morning on Steel
oneLiner: Let the morning tint a wide steel surface such as a tray or the sink.
details: Find a wide steel surface in the kitchen, a baking tray, the side of the sink or a wide pan. Let morning light from the window fall across it and show both a brighter area and a duller one. Fill the frame with the metal. If the only steel is small, a saucepan lid laid flat will give you a round field of the same tint.
tips: Shoot at a low angle so the tint stretches toward you.
Drop the exposure slightly so the steel keeps a colour rather than going white.

title: Cloth at the Window
oneLiner: Hold a pale cloth against the window and photograph the light coming through.
details: Hold a dish towel, a shirt or a pale pillowcase against the window from inside the room. Shoot toward the glass so the cloth glows. Folds can show, but the light through the fabric is the point. A darker cloth will only give you a rim, so choose something pale, and keep your fingers at the edges.
tips: Expose for the glowing cloth, not the bright gap around it.
Pinch one corner flat if a fold is hiding the glow.

title: Sugar Spark
oneLiner: Skim morning light across sugar, salt or coffee so the grains spark.
details: Spread a spoonful of sugar, salt or ground coffee on a dark plate near the window. Lower your angle until the morning light skims the grains and the nearest ones spark. The dark plate should stay quiet underneath. Brush the pile thinner if it looks like a mound rather than a field of specks.
tips: Get as close as the phone will focus, then tap a grain in the front.
Shade the lens with a hand if the window flares across the plate.
constraint: The grains must fill the frame.

title: First Light on the Bed
oneLiner: Show the unmade bed in whatever light the morning gives.
details: Look at the pillows, the folds, and the blanket before you tidy any of them. Use the light you actually have, whether that is a bright patch or a cool even wash. The rumpled cloth should suggest the start of the day, and your face stays out of it.
tips: Expose for the brightest part of the bedding so the folds keep detail.
Shoot before you straighten anything.
Stay low, level with the mattress.
constraint: Shoot from bed height only.

title: Steam on the Bathroom Mirror
oneLiner: Record a fogged mirror after a shower, before it clears.
details: Look for soft changes where the steam thins and a sliver of the room returns. If the mirror is clear, run hot water in the sink or breathe on the glass until it clouds. Wipe a small arc with one finger if you want contrast, or leave the glass fully clouded.
tips: Keep your face out of the reflection.
Focus on the texture of the condensation rather than the room.
Make the wiped mark small so the clouded glass still dominates.

title: Breakfast Waiting
oneLiner: Arrange breakfast things and pause before you sit to eat.
details: Set out a bowl, a mug, a spoon, and a napkin as a place waiting to be used. Step back and check that the group is not crowded. The meal should still be ahead of you, with the chair empty and the food not yet started.
tips: Use the window beside the table and leave the ceiling light off.
Clear anything that is not part of breakfast.
Let the place setting run on a diagonal.
constraint: Include exactly four items on the table.

title: Alarm Clock Glow
oneLiner: Frame a clock or a watch with the morning time visible.
details: Use a bedside clock, a watch, or the clock on the stove. Notice the glow or the pale face, and one nearby object such as glasses or a book. Keep the mood quiet, as if the day has only just been announced, and leave the phone you are shooting with out of the picture.
tips: Switch off the overhead light so the display can glow.
Steady the phone against the table for a sharp readout.
Include the clock and only one other object.
constraint: No flash allowed.

title: Slippers by the Door
oneLiner: Show the slippers or shoes you reach for when you get up.
details: Find where your morning footwear lives, by the bed, the closet, or the entry mat. Photograph the pair as they are, a little worn and recently used. The angle should feel as if you have just stepped out of them.
tips: Put the phone on the floor and tilt the screen up to see the pair.
Point both shoes the same way.
Leave a strip of floor in the frame for context.

title: Kettle Before the Pour
oneLiner: Frame your kettle, French press, or mug before the first pour of the day.
details: Set the vessel on a clear counter with nothing competing behind it. Look for a waiting mug or a cool lid, and if a wisp is rising leave the kettle where it is and do not touch it. This is the pause before the drink exists.
tips: Place the mug off to one side rather than dead centre.
Catch a thin highlight along the kettle's curve.
Keep the background darker than the vessel.
constraint: Use only one colour besides white or grey.

title: Notebook and Pen
oneLiner: Set an open notebook and a pen in the light you have now.
details: Open a journal or any notebook to a blank page, or to writing that will not be legible in the picture. Let light from the window graze the paper. Point the pen towards that light or off the edge of the page.
tips: Angle the page so private words fall out of focus.
Expose for the paper so the window does not become a white hole.
Include the pen's shadow on the page.
constraint: Keep any writing too soft to read.

title: The Unplugged Cord
oneLiner: Coil the cord where your phone was charging overnight.
details: Use the bedside table or the kitchen counter, wherever the phone charged. Unplug the spare length and leave it in a loose coil, with the phone itself in your hand and out of the picture. Include the outlet or the edge of the table so the coil has a place.
tips: Shoot from above so the coil reads as a loop.
Include a little of the table so the cord has a place.
Move a glass aside if it crowds the coil.

title: Half-Drawn Curtains
oneLiner: Part the curtains halfway and photograph the gap.
details: Draw the curtains or tilt a blind only part of the way, as they look before the room is fully open. Stand inside and frame the gap, the cloth or the slats, and a little of the glass. The picture is the moment the day is let in, not the view beyond.
tips: Focus on the curtain edge closest to you.
Let the gap run vertically through the frame.
Underexpose a touch if the glass is much brighter than the cloth.

title: Stripe on the Brush
oneLiner: Lay a stripe of toothpaste along a dry brush.
details: Put the toothpaste on before the bristles are wet, so the stripe stays neat. Rest the brush on the edge of the sink or on a clean glass. The small ribbon of paste is the whole story of getting ready.
tips: Shoot from above, close enough that the paste fills a third of the frame.
Wipe splashes off the porcelain first.
Tap focus on the paste, not the handle.
constraint: The stripe of paste must be unbroken.

title: Clothes Laid Out
oneLiner: Spread today's outfit on the bed before dressing.
details: Choose what you will wear and lay the pieces on the bed in the order you think of them. A shirt, trousers or a skirt, and socks are enough; add a sweater if that is the day. Shoot from the foot of the bed so the outfit reads as a plan.
tips: Smooth one garment and leave another slightly creased.
Keep pillows in the top of the frame as a clue to the room.
If the bed is wide, shoot from the foot rather than climbing up.

title: The Sleep Dent
oneLiner: Find the dent your head left in the pillow.
details: Before you shake the pillow, look for the hollow from the night. Angle the phone so the dip is a soft bowl and the surrounding cloth rises around it. This is the last trace of sleep.
tips: Use light from the side so the hollow gets a shadow.
Fill the frame with the one pillow.
Do not fluff it until after the picture.

title: Gown on the Door
oneLiner: Hang the robe or dressing gown where it waits each morning.
details: Use a dressing gown, a robe, or the hoodie you pull on indoors. Hang it on the bedroom or bathroom door, sleeves as they naturally fall. Photograph it as a stand-in for the minute between bed and getting dressed.
tips: Include the hook or the door top so it is clearly hanging.
Stand straight in front so the door edges stay vertical.
Let one sleeve come closer to the camera than the other.

title: Water Before Tea
oneLiner: Fill a plain glass with water before tea or coffee.
details: The first drink can be water. Fill a tumbler at the kitchen faucet and set it where you would usually put the kettle on. Leave the glass alone in the frame so it feels like a small start.
tips: Shoot through the side so the water line is clear.
A sheet of white paper behind the glass will show the rim.
Dry the outside if drips confuse the shape.
constraint: The glass is the only object.

title: Today's Socks
oneLiner: Place today's socks side by side with heels touching.
details: Pick the pair you mean to wear and set them on the bed, a chair, or the floor where you dress. Heels together and toes apart makes a small butterfly shape; both straight is fine too. They should look chosen, not lost.
tips: Shoot from above so both socks are the same size in frame.
Use a plain bit of sheet or floor behind them.
Focus on the ribbing at the cuffs.
constraint: Exactly two socks, and they must match.

title: Towel Before Washing
oneLiner: Hang the towel you will use and leave the shower empty.
details: Hang a bath towel over the rail, the door, or a hook before you wash. Leave the shower floor or the edge of the bath empty, with no bottles crowding the picture. It should feel like the wash is about to happen.
tips: Stand so the towel's lower edge and the empty floor both show.
Focus on the towel rather than the tiles.
Turn the brightest bathroom light off and use the window if there is one.

title: Glasses on the Book
oneLiner: Rest folded glasses on the book from last night.
details: Use the glasses you wear, sunglasses, or an empty case if you have no glasses. Set them on the closed book, magazine, or notebook that lives by the bed. The pair and the closed cover together say the night is finished.
tips: Shoot at a low angle across the cover.
Watch for a reflection that hides the frames.
Keep the stack to those two things.
constraint: The glasses or their case, and the book, must both show.

title: Night Clothes Heap
oneLiner: Leave night clothes heaped where you changed.
details: After you dress, leave the pyjamas or the t-shirt you slept in where they fell, on the bed or a chair. Do not fold them for this picture. The heap is the handover from night to day.
tips: Shoot from the side so the heap has height.
Include a corner of the made or unmade bed for context.
Move jewellery and pocket contents out of the pile.

title: Lunch Box Started
oneLiner: Pack a lunch box with only one piece of food.
details: Open a lunch box, a food tub, or a clean paper bag and put in one thing: a roll, an apple, or a wrapped cheese. Stop there. A single item and a lot of empty box show that packing has only just started.
tips: Shoot from above into the open box.
Push the food towards one corner.
Turn any printed wrapper away from the lens.
constraint: Only one piece of food in the box.

title: A Stripe Across the Floor
oneLiner: Let one stripe of morning light cross the floor.
details: Tilt a blind until a single band of light falls across the floor. If you have no blinds, open a door a little so light comes through the gap as one stripe. The stripe is what you made by opening the room.
tips: Stand so the stripe runs from one edge of the frame to another.
Expose for the bright band and let the rest go dim.
Keep your feet out of the stripe.
constraint: Only one stripe of light.

title: Coat on the Peg
oneLiner: Hang the coat you will put on to go out, alone on its peg.
details: Choose the coat or jacket for going out and hang it on its usual peg or hook. Move the other coats aside for a minute so this one is alone. Photograph it before you put it on.
tips: Include the hook and the shoulders.
Close the door behind it if the background is cluttered.
Focus on a button, zip, or collar.

title: Keys in the Dish
oneLiner: Leave your keys in their dish, still untouched.
details: Find the bowl, tray, or hook where keys wait near the door. Leave them there, before the moment you pocket them. If they usually sit loose on a shelf, gather them into a cup for the picture.
tips: Shoot from slightly above so the keys sit inside the dish.
Avoid a glare on a glossy bowl by moving to the side.
Keep letters and name tags turned over.
constraint: The dish and the keys only.

title: Brush and Hair Tie
oneLiner: Put a hairbrush and a hair tie side by side.
details: Set a brush or a comb beside a hair tie or a scrunchie. If you do not use a hair tie, put a hair clip beside the comb instead. Use the shelf, the sink edge, or the top of a chest of drawers.
tips: Lay both objects on a plain surface.
Let the brush handle point out of the frame.
Focus on the teeth or bristles.

title: Shelf Before the Mirror
oneLiner: Line up the bottles you reach for at the sink.
details: Choose two or three things you actually use in the morning, such as soap, toothpaste, and moisturiser. Line them along the shelf or the sink rim and turn loud labels away. The row should feel like a routine, not a shop display.
tips: Hold the phone level with the tops of the bottles.
Leave a gap between them so each silhouette is clear.
Wipe the shelf so dried splashes do not distract.

title: Kettle Under the Stream
oneLiner: Fill the kettle under the faucet and include the stream.
details: Hold the kettle or a saucepan under a gentle stream and photograph from the side. The water entering the metal is the start of the hot drink. Keep the stream modest so it does not splash the phone.
tips: Stand to the side, not behind the falling water.
Focus on the end of the spout.
A faster shutter, if your phone offers it, will bead the stream.
constraint: The running water must be visible.

title: The Open Latch
oneLiner: Unlatch one window and frame the open catch.
details: Open a window you can reach safely from the floor, just enough to swing the handle or loosen the catch. Photograph the hardware and a little of the frame, from inside. This is the first air of the day, shown by metal rather than by the outdoors.
tips: Get close so the handle fills half the picture.
Include both the handle and the frame it meets.
Wipe the glass only if a smear crosses the handle.

title: Duvet Pulled Aside
oneLiner: Pull the duvet aside so the sheet takes half the frame.
details: Draw the duvet or the blanket to one side of the bed and leave the sheet exposed on the other. The line between covered and bare is the moment of getting up. Shoot from above the middle of the bed, or from the side if the bed is against a wall.
