tips: Make the boundary between duvet and sheet a strong diagonal or a clean vertical.
Smooth the sheet once so the contrast reads.
Keep pillows out if they confuse the divide.
constraint: Both the cover and the sheet must show.

title: Cloth on the Sink
oneLiner: Drape a face cloth over the rim of the sink.
details: Use a face cloth or a small hand towel. Drape it over the rim so one end hangs down and the other stays in the bowl. It should look ready for a wash, not stored away.
tips: Shoot from the side at rim height.
Include the faucet only if it does not crowd the cloth.
Focus on the fold that goes over the rim.

title: Feet on the Mat
oneLiner: Stand barefoot on the mat where the morning starts.
details: Stand on the bathroom mat or the rug beside the bed, whichever you touch first. Point the camera down at your own feet. The picture is simply that you are up.
tips: Hold the phone out and angle it down, or prop it against a bottle and use the timer.
Include the edge of the mat and a little bare floor.
Use the timer if you cannot see the screen.
constraint: Both feet must be in the frame.

title: Closet Door Open
oneLiner: Open a closet or rail and frame the hanging clothes.
details: Open the closet, a clothes rail, or the door that hides your hooks, just wide enough to see a row of shoulders. Choose the section you actually hesitate over in the morning. The open edge of the door can cut the frame like a curtain.
tips: Stand so hanging garments overlap a little.
Focus on the nearest sleeve.
Leave the ceiling light off if a window lights the clothes more softly.

title: Shoes as You Leave
oneLiner: Look down at both shoes once you have put them on.
details: Put them on where you always do, and stay indoors on the mat or by the door. Point the camera down so the pair and a little of the floor show. This is you about to leave, not a pair arranged for a picture.
tips: Angle the phone down from about chest height.
Include the edge of the mat or the bottom of the door.
Keep the laces as you would actually wear them.
constraint: Both shoes are on your feet.

title: One Sleeve On
oneLiner: Put one arm in a sleeve and leave the other hanging.
details: Use the shirt or sweater you are about to wear. One arm is through a sleeve and the other sleeve hangs empty. Prop the phone or use the timer, and keep your face above the frame.
tips: Use the timer so you can stand still for the shot.
Let the empty sleeve fall towards the bottom of the frame.
A plain wall behind you keeps the sleeve easy to read.
constraint: Crop below the chin so your face stays out.

title: Bag by the Door
oneLiner: Set today's bag on the floor just inside the door.
details: Use the bag you would actually leave with, and keep the door shut. Look down so the bag, the floor, and a little of the door are all in frame. If you carry nothing, lay the jacket you have put on in the same spot.
tips: Shoot from chest height, looking down.
Let the bag or jacket touch the door.
Keep your face and your hands out of the picture.
constraint: The bag or the jacket touches the bottom of the frame.

title: Mail Face Down
oneLiner: Leave the morning mail face down on the indoor mat.
details: If letters have arrived, turn them so names and addresses cannot be read. If none came, use a plain envelope or a note you have turned over. The small pile on the mat is the morning's arrival, still inside.
tips: Shoot from above so the mat's edge shows.
Check the screen for any readable name before you finish.
Keep shoes out of this picture.
constraint: No readable name or address.

title: Lanyard on the Chair
oneLiner: Coil the lanyard or strap you leave with on a chair.
details: Use the hall chair, the bed, or the table where you actually pick it up. Turn any badge so the blank side shows. If you have no lanyard, coil the belt you put on in the morning in the same place.
tips: Shoot from slightly above the coil.
Hide any printed name against the chair.
Let the chair seat be the whole background.
constraint: No readable name.

title: Where the Kettle Sits
oneLiner: Slide a cool kettle aside and photograph the mark beneath.
details: Make sure the kettle is cool, then slide it just far enough to show the ring, the mat, or the clean circle underneath. If you have no kettle, do the same with a teapot or a coffee jug. Put it back when you have the picture.
tips: Include a sliver of the kettle at the edge so the gap has a cause.
Shoot from above, parallel to the counter.
Wipe loose crumbs away only if they hide the ring.
constraint: The vessel is cool before you move it.

title: Scarf on the Coat
oneLiner: Loop a scarf or a tie over the coat you will wear.
details: Use the indoor peg, the banister, or the back of a chair, wherever the coat already lives. If you have no scarf, loop a tie or a cardigan over the coat instead. Let the two ends fall differently so this reads as getting ready.
tips: Fill the frame with the looped cloth and the coat's shoulder.
Focus on the loop where the scarf turns.
Step closer if the hallway behind is busy.

title: Yesterday's Mug
oneLiner: Find last night's mug and leave the dregs as they are.
details: Look in the sink or on the bedside table for the mug you finished yesterday. Leave any stain or cold dregs, and do not rinse it for this picture. If there is no dirty mug, set an empty one in the sink as it would look before washing.
tips: Shoot from the side so any dregs show as a line.
Leave the flash off so the stain keeps its colour.
Crop out taps and bottles if they crowd the mug.
constraint: Do not rinse the mug before you shoot.

title: The First Drawer
oneLiner: Open the drawer you reach into first and frame the inside.
details: Socks, shirts, or whatever you actually take out in the morning will do. Leave the contents as they are and turn printed labels away. Let the drawer front make a bar along the bottom of the picture.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the open drawer.
Focus on the nearest folded edge.
Push the drawer in a little if the room behind is busy.

title: The Door Chain
oneLiner: Slide the indoor chain or bolt and fill the frame with it.
details: Use the chain or bolt on the inside of your door, the one you touch when you get up. If you have neither, crop in on the lock you turn from the hall. This is the hardware of leaving, seen from inside.
tips: Keep the phone parallel to the door.
Include a little paint or wood around the metal.
Focus on the chain or the bolt, not the whole door.
constraint: Shoot from inside the home.

title: Brush in the Cup
oneLiner: Stand your dry toothbrush in its cup before you use it.
details: Use the cup, glass, or holder by the sink, and leave the brush dry, before any paste. If you have no cup, lay the dry brush across the rim and include a little of the sink. This is the minute before washing, not the stripe of paste.
tips: Shoot from the side so the bristles and the cup both read.
Wipe splashes off the porcelain first.
Focus on the bristles rather than the handle.
constraint: The brush is still dry.

title: One Sock On
oneLiner: Photograph your own feet with one sock on and one bare.
details: Sit where you dress, on the bed or a chair. The uneven pair is the moment halfway through getting ready. Both feet should show, and your face should not.
tips: Point the camera down and use the timer if you cannot see the screen well.
Use the bed or the floor as a plain ground.
Focus on the sock cuff.
constraint: One foot in a sock and one foot bare.

title: Dab on the Hand
oneLiner: Put a dab of cream on the back of your hand and shoot that.
details: Put a small pale patch of moisturiser or hand cream on the back of your own hand. Rest the hand on the sink edge or a towel. The dab is the moment of getting ready, and your face stays out.
tips: Fill most of the frame with the back of the hand.
Side light will show the cream sitting on the skin.
Wipe the lens if you have just had wet hands.
constraint: Your face stays out of the frame.

title: Print on the Mat
oneLiner: Step once on the bath mat and photograph the damp print.
details: After washing, the mat often holds a faint darker shape. Shoot it before it fades. If the mat is dry, wet the sole of your foot, step once, and then photograph that mark.
tips: Shoot from above, parallel to the mat.
Expose for the damp patch so it does not turn black.
Keep bottles and the sink out of the frame.

title: Spoon in a Circle
oneLiner: Spin a wooden spoon, a spatula or a whisk and catch the circular blur.
details: Hold the handle and turn a wooden spoon, a spatula or a whisk in a small circle in front of a plain wall, well clear of lamps and shelves. The moving end should trace soft arcs. A quick, even spin blurs in an ordinary photo. If the shape freezes, switch on a motion photo and spin again.
tips: Keep your feet planted and let only the object turn.
A plain cupboard door is enough background if the wall is busy.
constraint: Use a plain background.

title: Fan Blades as Smears
oneLiner: Run a household fan, or spin a saucepan lid, so the moving part smears.
details: Aim a desk fan or a pedestal fan towards a plain wall and shoot straight at the spin. If you have no fan, set a saucepan lid on a smooth table and spin it with a finger. Never push a finger through a guard, and keep clear of the lid's edge. A fast spin smears in an ordinary photo.
tips: Shoot from the side if the front of the fan hides the blades.
Dim one lamp if the spin looks frozen in a very bright room.

title: Cloth You Set Moving
oneLiner: Flick a dish towel or scarf and keep the frame where the hem streaks.
details: Hold a dish towel or scarf indoors and snap it with your free hand in front of a plain wall. Shoot as the hem travels. Use a motion photo if an ordinary frame freezes the cloth into a sharp fold. The soft streak is the picture.
tips: Snap from the wrist so the hem travels farther than your arm.
Review the motion photo and keep the frame with the longest streak.

title: Pouring Water Stream
oneLiner: Pour water from a jug and let the stream blur into one strand.
details: Set a clear glass on the table or by the sink, and prop the phone so it cannot wobble. Draw a curtain if the window is glaring, then pour steadily while night mode or a live photo's long-exposure effect runs. The stream should turn into one soft strand rather than a row of frozen drops. A towel on the counter saves a spill.
tips: Pour from just above the glass first, then try a slightly higher stream.
Focus on the rim so the bright strand above it stays the subject.
constraint: The stream runs from the jug to the glass.

title: Pan Around an Anchor
oneLiner: Turn your body around a still chair so the room streaks and the chair holds.
details: Dim the room until the picture starts to look a little slow. Choose a chair, a lamp or a tall bottle as the still point and turn around it while you shoot. Begin the turn before you press the shutter and keep that object in the middle. If the chair smears as much as the room, turn more slowly and darken the room a little more.
tips: Bend your knees so the turn stays smooth rather than jerky.
Try the turn once before you press the shutter.
constraint: The still object stays in the middle of the frame.

title: Drawer Slide Sequence
oneLiner: Pull a drawer open while you shoot so the contents streak sideways.
details: Use a kitchen or desk drawer, and take anything fragile out first. Dim the room, keep the phone steady, and pull smoothly while night mode or a live photo's long-exposure effect is running. The contents should streak sideways and the front of the cabinet should stay still.
tips: Stand square to the drawer so the streak runs left to right.
A slower pull gives a longer streak than a quick yank.
constraint: The phone stays still while the drawer moves.

title: The Running Tap
oneLiner: Open a tap and photograph the falling water as a soft continuous strand.
details: Use the kitchen or bathroom tap over an empty sink, set to a steady stream rather than a wide spray. Brace the phone on the edge of the sink. Use night mode, or a live photo's long-exposure effect, so the flow silks into one strand. If you still see separate drops, lower the lights or close the blind and try again.
tips: Shoot from the side against a plain sink back.
Wipe the lens if the sink edge has splashed it.
constraint: The stream runs from the tap to the basin.

title: Coin in a Spin
oneLiner: Spin a coin, a button or a bottle cap on a table and catch the wobble.
details: Use a smooth table and spin the coin so it travels a little as it slows. Get low and shoot the edge from the side, with bare table around it. A fast spin blurs that edge in an ordinary photo, especially once the coin starts to wander.
tips: Start shooting as the spin begins to wobble, not only while it is upright.
A coin with a ridged edge shows the turn more clearly than a smooth button.

title: Marble Round the Bowl
oneLiner: Swirl a bowl so a grape or a bottle cap circles inside it.
details: Set a mixing bowl on a towel in the middle of the table. Put in one grape, a marble or a bottle cap, then swirl the bowl gently so it runs around the inside. Shoot from above while it circles. A moderate swirl makes a soft ring in an ordinary photo, and the bowl keeps everything contained.
tips: Keep one hand on the bowl so it cannot walk off the towel.
A pale bowl shows a dark grape more clearly.
constraint: The bowl stays on the table.

title: Flipped Pages
oneLiner: Fan the pages of a book or notebook so they blur as they fall.
details: Hold a paperback, a notebook or a magazine by the spine. Let the pages flip from one hand towards the other and shoot from the side so you see the edges. Bend the book so the pages fan instead of dropping as one block. Use a motion photo if they freeze sharp.
tips: Stand side-on so the cover is not square to the lens.
A desk lamp from the side puts a bright line on the moving paper.

title: Water Sloshes Across
oneLiner: Tilt a tray of water so a wave runs across it while you shoot.
details: Pour a shallow layer of water into a baking tray or a large mixing bowl, with a towel underneath. Brace the phone level with the rim. Tilt the tray so the water rushes sideways during a live photo's long-exposure effect. You want the surface to smear, not a sharp picture of still water.
tips: A drop of milk makes the moving surface easier to see.
Get level with the rim so the rush reads as a line.

title: Vortex in a Glass
oneLiner: Stir a glass of water, pull the spoon out, and shoot the spinning hollow.
details: Use a clear glass on a pale surface. Stir quickly, lift the spoon out, and shoot from above in the first second, with a crumb or a tea leaf in the water so the spin shows. A live long-exposure, started as the spoon leaves, lets that speck draw a circle.
tips: Shoot before the hollow flattens and the crumb stops.
A white plate under the glass keeps the water easy to read.

title: The Turning Plate
oneLiner: Spin a plate on the table and catch the rim as a circular blur.
details: Set an empty plate or a lid on a smooth table and spin it from the rim. Shoot from above while it turns quickly, and keep your hands out of the finished frame. A fast spin blurs the pattern around a steadier middle. If it looks frozen, spin harder or switch on a motion photo.
tips: Keep the spinning finger at the rim, then take it away.
A plain plate with one stripe of tape shows the turn more clearly.
constraint: Keep your hands out of the finished frame.

title: A Lamp Draws a Line
oneLiner: Prop the phone, darken the room, and move a lamp so its light draws a line.
details: Close the curtains and prop the phone facing a plain wall. Switch on night mode or a live photo's long-exposure effect. Then move a lit lamp slowly across the view, or a separate flashlight if that is the light you can carry, so the light streaks and the room stays still. Point the lamp at the wall, not back into the lens.
tips: Move the lamp in one direction only, about as fast as a slow walk.
Switch other lights off so a single line is easy to see.
constraint: The phone stays still while the lamp moves.

title: Whisk Mid-Stir
oneLiner: Stir fast with a whisk, fork or spoon and photograph the blur in the bowl.
details: Put a little water in a bowl. Stir in quick circles and shoot from above so the utensil becomes a soft arc. The rim of the bowl can stay sharper as a still reference. Ordinary room light is enough when the stir is fast and close.
tips: Brace the bowl against a wall so it does not travel with the whisk.
Overhead light on the water helps the arc catch a highlight.

title: Follow the Tin
oneLiner: Roll a tin across the table and pan with it so the kitchen streaks behind.
details: Dim the kitchen first, or a bright shutter will freeze everything. Use a drinks can, a tin or a lidded jar and roll it slowly along the middle of the table. Follow it with the phone and press the shutter only once you are already moving. The tin should stay clearer than the cupboards behind it.
tips: Roll the tin along a book edge so it keeps a straight line.
If both tin and cupboards are sharp, darken the room and pan again.
constraint: The tin stays near the middle while the background smears.

title: Card Slides Past
oneLiner: Slide a card across the table and let it streak past a still phone.
details: Prop the phone at table height, facing along the surface, and set a book at the far end as a stop. Dim the room and start night mode or a live photo's long-exposure effect. Slide a postcard, a coaster or a playing card gently along that lane so it records as a soft streak. A sharp card sitting still means the exposure was too brief.
tips: Slide it level so the streak crosses the middle of the frame.
Stand to the side of the phone so you are not in the frame.

title: The Door in Motion
oneLiner: Swing an interior door and shoot the moving edge against the still frame.
details: Stand to the side of a room door so you see the edge travel, not a slab coming at the lens. Keep the phone still. Swing the door steadily during night mode or a live long-exposure, so the doorway stays put and the door itself smears.
tips: Include the hinge side so the pivot reads as the still point.
A slower swing makes a thicker blur along the edge.

title: Feet Walk Through
oneLiner: Prop the phone at ankle height and walk past so your shoes blur through.
details: Dim a hall or kitchen and lean the phone against a wall or a book at ankle height, aimed along the floor. Start night mode or a live long-exposure, use a short timer, then walk through at an easy pace. The shoes should streak and the floor should stay clearer. Keep your face well above the frame.
tips: Aim sideways, not up the leg.
Slippers or shoes with a clear outline give the streak a shape.
constraint: No face in the frame.

title: A Stream of Pasta
oneLiner: Pour dry pasta, rice or oats from one bowl to another and catch the stream.
details: Do this over a table with a cloth underneath. Prop the phone at the side, use night mode or a live long-exposure, and pour in a steady ribbon. The pieces should streak as they fall. A sharp scatter of grains means you need a longer effect or a dimmer corner.
tips: Pour from about a hand's span above the lower bowl.
A dark cloth behind pale oats separates them from the room.

title: Curtain Pulled Fast
oneLiner: Pull a curtain or a hung towel quickly across and shoot during the pull.
details: Prop the phone on a chair facing a curtain, or a towel hung over a door or a rail. Start night mode or a live long-exposure, then pull the cloth across in one smooth move. The fabric should smear and the wall or window behind it should stay sharper.
tips: Pull parallel to the window so the smear runs straight across.
Use both hands on the cloth once the phone is propped.
constraint: The phone does not move during the pull.

title: Sock Ball Bounce
oneLiner: Bounce rolled socks in a dim room and let the path smear.
details: Roll socks into a ball. Dim the room, prop the phone at floor level, and bounce the socks in front of a plain wall during night mode or a live long-exposure. You want a soft vertical smear, not a sharp ball frozen in the air.
tips: Bounce straight down so the smear stays in one vertical line.
A plain baseboard gives the streak a quiet backdrop.

title: Falling Leaf
oneLiner: Drop a leaf indoors and let it streak on the way down.
details: Use a herb leaf or a fallen leaf you already have inside, and stand in front of a plain wall. Hold the phone very still or prop it, start a live long-exposure, and let the leaf go. Keep a result where it streaks in the air and has not yet landed.
tips: Drop it against a mid-tone wall so a dark leaf does not vanish.
Hold the phone out to the side, clear of the falling path.
constraint: The falling leaf does not touch the ground in the picture.

title: Shaken Houseplant
oneLiner: Shake a houseplant gently and let only the leaves blur.
details: Brace the phone so it stays put. Shake a houseplant gently, or a leafy stem standing in a jug if the pots are sparse. Use a motion photo or a live long-exposure so the leaves smear and the pot or the stem stays sharper. Keep the shake small so nothing nearby gets knocked.
tips: Shake once and let go, rather than rattling the plant the whole time.
Focus on a still stem so the moving leaves have something sharp beside them.

title: Rolling Pin Blur
oneLiner: Spin a rolling pin or a bottle between your hands and catch the blur.
details: Hold a rolling pin, a jar or an empty bottle with the lid on, horizontally over a towel on the table. Spin it with your fingers so it turns in place and does not travel. Shoot from the side. A fast turn blurs the ends in an ordinary photo while your hands stay at the edges.
tips: Spin at a steady speed so the blur stays round.
Keep the object over the table, not out in the room.

title: Lights You Sweep
oneLiner: Sweep the phone across a lamp or fairy lights so they draw lines.
details: Darken the room and leave one lamp switched on, or a separate flashlight or a short string of fairy lights if that is what you have. Use night mode, or a live photo's long-exposure effect, and sweep the phone sideways while that exposure runs. The lights should become lines. If the picture is sharp, the shutter was too quick, so darken the room and sweep again.
tips: Sweep parallel to the lights rather than towards them.
One lamp is enough if you have no fairy lights.
constraint: The phone moves and the lights stay put.

title: Wiping the Pane
oneLiner: Wipe a window in circles and let the cloth smear against the glass.
details: Prop the phone facing the inside of a window. Wipe a small circle on the indoor glass with a dry or slightly damp cloth while a motion photo or a live long-exposure runs. The cloth should smear and the frame should stay still. Stay inside for the whole picture.
tips: Keep the circle small so the cloth stays inside the frame.
Focus on the glass rather than on the view through it.

title: Spin a Still Wheel
oneLiner: Spin a wheel that stays in place, such as a tape roll or a suitcase wheel.
details: Indoors, spin a roll of tape on a pencil, a chair caster or a suitcase wheel, while the chair or case itself does not travel. The edge should smear around a steady middle. Shoot from the side with your free hand.
tips: A small tab of tape on the roll gives the blur a visible mark.
Spin with one hand and take that hand out before you shoot.
constraint: The wheel does not travel across the frame.

title: Bottle Along the Floor
oneLiner: Lay the phone low indoors and let a bottle roll past it.
details: Use an empty bottle with the lid on. Set the phone on an indoor floor, start night mode or a live long-exposure, and roll the bottle slowly across the view, with a book ready to stop it. The bottle should blur while the floor close to the lens stays clearer.
tips: Roll the bottle across the frame, not straight at the lens.
A book under one edge of the phone can aim it up a fraction.
constraint: The phone stays on the floor.

title: Towel in a Shake
oneLiner: Shake a large towel indoors so the cloth smears and the room stays.
details: Prop the phone first in a hall or bathroom with space around you. Hold a clean towel or a light blanket by the hem and give it one strong shake. Use a live photo or a motion photo, and the long-exposure effect if it appears, so the cloth smears and the wall stays put. Keep the shake in open floor space, away from lamps and shelves.
tips: Give one strong shake rather than a string of little flaps.
Grip a hem if a corner keeps twisting the cloth.

title: Salad Spinner Whirl
oneLiner: Pump a salad spinner, or turn a lazy Susan, and shoot the whirl.
details: If you have a salad spinner, pump it and shoot down through the lid while it turns. A lazy Susan, a turntable or the base of an empty swivel chair works if you have no spinner. The circle should smear and the outer rim stay still. A fast turn does this in an ordinary photo.
tips: Shoot from above so the circle stays round.
A single leaf inside the spinner makes the whirl easier to see.

title: Blinds in a Flick
oneLiner: Flick a blind, a hanging cord or a belt and let it blur.
details: Use venetian blinds if you have them. If not, hang a belt, a necklace or a string of beads from a rail and flick that instead. Prop the phone, then flick once during a motion photo so the slats or the cord streak and the window frame stays still.
tips: Flick across the frame rather than straight at the lens.
A slower follow-through makes a longer streak than a tiny twitch.

title: Broom Sweep
oneLiner: Sweep an indoor floor with a broom or brush and let the bristles blur.
details: Use a broom, a mop or a hand brush on a kitchen or hall floor. Prop the phone low and still, start a motion photo or night mode, and sweep once across the frame. The bristles should blur and the floor remain readable.
tips: Set the phone against a baseboard at brush height.
Sweep away from the lens so dust does not hit it.

title: Lid in a Swing
oneLiner: Lift a lid indoors and let it smear as it swings open.
details: Use a saucepan lid or a box lid you can open at table height. Prop the phone to the side and lift the lid during a live long-exposure. The lid should smear through the swing, not sit frozen halfway. Keep your free hand away from the hinge.
tips: A slower lift is easier for the long-exposure effect to record.
Shoot from the side so the changing angle is visible.
constraint: The lid is blurred rather than frozen sharp.

title: Stem Springs Back
oneLiner: Bend a soft stem or a spatula, let it go, and catch the return as a blur.
details: Use a long houseplant stem or a silicone spatula held at one end, over a clear table. Pull it aside gently, let go, and shoot with a motion photo while the phone stays still. The return should blur across a plain wall. Leave stiff sticks out of this one so nothing gets knocked.
tips: Let the stem move across the frame, not straight at the lens.
Take your fingers away before it springs.

title: Shower Streaks
oneLiner: Photograph the shower spray as soft streaks, and keep the phone dry.
details: Turn a shower to a steady spray, switch off the brightest ceiling light, and stand outside the water. Brace the phone and use night mode or a live long-exposure so the spray becomes streaks. If you have no shower, fan the kitchen tap against the back of a spoon over the sink and photograph that spread of water the same way.
tips: Keep the phone behind a glass screen or well back from the spray.
A dimmer bathroom lets the streaks build instead of freezing.
constraint: The phone stays out of the water.

title: Toothbrush Buzz
oneLiner: Switch on an electric toothbrush or mixer and catch the buzzing blur.
details: Hold an electric toothbrush or a hand mixer in front of a plain wall and switch it on. If you have neither, spin a fork quickly between your fingers, close to the lens. The moving end should smear in an ordinary photo while the handle stays sharper. Keep your fingers clear of the blades or the brush head.
tips: Come closer if the head looks sharp, then shoot again.
A mid-tone wall stops a white brush disappearing.

title: Zip in Motion
oneLiner: Pull a zip so the slider streaks along the teeth.
details: Use a jacket, a bag or a cushion with a zip. If nothing has a zip, pull a drawstring through its channel instead. Prop the phone close, dim that corner, and use a motion photo or night mode while you pull smoothly. The slider should blur along the line and the fabric stay still.
tips: Pull towards the side of the frame so the streak has length.
Rest your wrist on the table so the phone does not follow the pull.

title: Slats Streak Past
oneLiner: Pan indoors along slats or a bookshelf so the uprights streak.
details: Dim the room. Pan the phone slowly along a radiator, a banister, a bookshelf or the back of a slatted chair while night mode or a live long-exposure runs. The uprights should smear sideways. Keep the phone moving for the whole exposure.
tips: Move the phone parallel to the row, already moving as you shoot.
Hold the phone upright if the slats are vertical.
constraint: The uprights smear sideways.

title: Spoon in the Mug
oneLiner: Stir a mug of water and photograph the spoon as a soft arc.
details: Set a mug of water on the table and prop the phone at rim height. Stir in a steady circle during night mode or a live long-exposure. The spoon should smear in an arc above the rim and the mug stay still. Ordinary stirring is enough, and nothing needs to swing free.
tips: Keep the spoon inside the mug so the water stays put.
A light wall behind a dark spoon makes the smear readable.
constraint: The mug stays still on the table.

title: Sweep the Shelf
oneLiner: Move the phone along a shelf so the objects streak sideways.
details: Dim the room and face a shelf, a row of books or a spice rack. Use night mode or a live long-exposure and move the phone sideways during the exposure, parallel to the shelf. The row should become horizontal streaks. If everything is sharp, darken the room further and sweep more slowly.
tips: Keep the phone the same distance from the shelf all the way along.
A short string of three or four objects is enough to streak.
constraint: You move the phone, not the objects.

title: Book as a Fan
oneLiner: Fan the air with a book or magazine and catch the repeated blur.
details: Hold a paperback or a magazine and fan it quickly in front of a plain wall. Shoot from the side with your other hand. The pages should become a soft repeated shape. Use a motion photo if a single frame freezes the book.
tips: Fan close to the wall so the background stays simple.
A faster fan, nearer the lens, blurs more than a slow wave.

title: Tape Pulls Out
oneLiner: Extend a tape measure or a ribbon and let it streak as it lengthens.
details: Set a tape measure on a table, or use a roll of ribbon if you have no tape. Prop the phone to the side, dim the room, and start night mode or a live long-exposure. Pull the tape or ribbon out smoothly so it streaks while the case stays still. Stop before it runs off the table.
tips: Pull parallel to the table so the streak stays in frame.
A slow pull gives a longer blur than a snap.

title: A Slow Ribbon
oneLiner: Pour honey, syrup or shampoo so it blurs into a thick ribbon.
details: Tip a jar and pour honey, syrup or shampoo down the inside of a glass in a steady ribbon. Brace the phone and use night mode or a live long-exposure while it runs, with the room a little dim. The ribbon should soften as it moves. A sharp still line means the room was too bright or the pour had already stopped.
tips: Put the jar on a pale plate so the dark ribbon stands out.
Start the exposure once the ribbon is already moving.

title: Keys on the Counter
oneLiner: Lay your keys out and tell a small story about where your day might go.
details: Empty your pocket or bag and arrange your keys on a clean surface. Shoot from above or at a slight angle so rings, tags, and wear marks are visible. You do not need every key, just an honest slice of what you carry.
tips: Wipe the surface to avoid crumbs in frame.
Overlap keys slightly for depth.
Use window light for soft shadows.
constraint: Include your key ring or fob in the shot.

title: Wallet Flat Lay
oneLiner: Open your wallet or card holder and photograph what you reach for daily.
details: Spread cards, cash, or transit passes in a tidy flat lay. Keep numbers and personal details turned away or out of frame. The photo should feel like a map of your routines, not a document dump.
tips: Shoot overhead with parallel edges to the frame.
Group items by colour or size.
Leave a little empty space for breathing room.
constraint: No visible full card numbers or names.

title: Earphone Coil
oneLiner: Coil the earphones you carry and choose a tangle or a tidy loop.
details: Take the wired earphones or the case of buds you actually bring out with you. If they have a cable, coil it loosely or leave the real tangle. Set them on a table and crop the rest of the room away so the coil is the whole story.
tips: A mid-grey cloth stops black buds disappearing.
Tap focus on the earpiece mesh, not the table.
constraint: Keep screens and other devices out of the frame.

title: Pen Meets Notebook
oneLiner: Photograph the pen and whatever page you actually write on.
details: Open a notebook, a planner, or the back of an envelope, and rest a pen or pencil on it. Shoot from above or from just beside the page. Leave a hint of handwriting if you like, but nothing private needs to appear.
tips: Align the pen pointing into the frame.
Use soft light to avoid harsh page glare.
Crop tight on the corner of the page.
constraint: The pen or pencil and the page must both appear.

title: Pocket Miscellany
oneLiner: Gather the small odds and ends from your bag and arrange them in one frame.
details: Think mints, lip balm, a tissue, a hair tie, or a spare charger you actually keep with you. If the bag is nearly empty, add a coin and the keys you carry so the group still feels like a day out. Lay them on a flat surface so each object reads clearly.
tips: Odd numbers of items often look more natural.
Keep similar sizes separated for clarity.
Shoot from directly above for a catalogue feel.
constraint: At least four different object types in frame.

title: Lenses at Rest
oneLiner: Set sunglasses or everyday glasses down where you usually leave them.
details: Place sunglasses or the glasses you wear on a table, a book, or your bag near a window. Let the lenses reflect the ceiling or a wall. Keep your face out of that reflection. The frame should feel casual, like a paused moment.
tips: Wipe lenses to control smudges.
Shoot slightly off-angle to reduce self-reflection.
Fold one arm of the glasses so it points into the frame.
constraint: No faces visible in lens reflections.

title: Sanitiser and Tissue
oneLiner: Photograph the sanitiser, tissues, or wipes you keep within reach.
details: Set hand sanitiser, tissues, or wipes together on a clean surface. Keep labels turned if you prefer privacy. Leave the background bare so the small containers are clearly the habit you carry.
tips: Group bottles upright with caps visible.
Use neutral background colours.
Soft light keeps plastic from blowing out.

title: Change and Receipt
oneLiner: Spread loose change beside a crumpled slip from your pocket or bag.
details: Lay coins beside a folded receipt or ticket. If you have no paper, a crumpled tissue from the same pocket still gives you something soft against the metal. Turn any names and numbers away from the camera.
tips: Mix coin sizes for visual rhythm.
Leave one corner of the receipt curled.
Shoot close so texture shows.
constraint: Include at least three coins and one soft paper item.

title: Waterline
oneLiner: Show the waterline inside the bottle you carry today.
details: Stand your water bottle on a table near a window and get level with the water inside. The line where liquid meets air should cross the frame. If the bottle is empty, pour in a little water so the line appears.
tips: Focus on the line, not the lettering on the bottle.
Stand the bottle in front of a dark cupboard so the line stays easy to see.
constraint: The waterline must run clearly across the frame.

title: Pocket Map
oneLiner: Open your bag flat and diagram the pockets you actually use.
details: Empty the main compartment enough to see the inner pockets, then lay the bag open on a bed or table. Leave one everyday item in the pocket it really lives in. Shoot from above so the bag reads as a map of where things go.
tips: Kneel beside the bed or table so the phone points straight down.
Tug the lining smooth so each pocket mouth is visible.

title: Strap Curl
oneLiner: Take off your watch or bag strap and photograph the curl it keeps.
details: Set a watch strap, fitness band, or the loose end of a bag strap on the table and let it keep the curve it learned from being worn or packed. Shoot from the side so the curl becomes a loop or a wave. The buckle can sit at one end as an anchor.
tips: Side light along the curve shows creases in leather or weave.
Slide a pale sheet under a dark strap so the curl separates from the table.
constraint: The curled shape must be the subject, not a time display.

title: Balm and Cap
oneLiner: Uncap the lip balm you carry and set the cap beside the stick.
details: Find the balm, glue stick, or small care tube that lives in your bag. Take the cap off and lay it next to the open stick on a plain surface. Get close enough to see the texture of the product and the scuffs on the cap.
tips: Roll the product up a little so the tip catches light.
Keep brand lettering turned toward the edge you will crop.

title: Umbrella Spiral
oneLiner: Look into the end of a closed umbrella and find the fabric spiral.
details: Take the umbrella you carry, or a reusable bag rolled tight if you have no umbrella. Point the folded end at the window and look straight into the cloth. The wrapped panels should read as a spiral or a tightly furled bloom.
tips: Lean the folded umbrella in a corner so both hands can hold the phone.
Tap the nearest fold. The deeper ones can fall soft.
constraint: Fill the frame with the folded end.

title: Lid from Above
oneLiner: Photograph the lid of the cup you take out, straight from above.
details: Set a reusable cup, travel mug, or the bottle lid you carry on a table. Shoot straight down so the sipping hole, slider, or screw ridges sit in the middle. The lid should look like a small machine, not a product advert.
tips: Turn off any overhead glare by shifting the cup toward the window.
Align the drinking hole with a corner of the grid.

title: Lunch Latch
oneLiner: Frame the latch or seal on the box that carries your food.
details: Use a lunch box, a food tub, or any lidded container you take with you. Close it properly and photograph the clip, seal, or locking tab. A side angle shows whether the lid sits tight or has a familiar warp.
tips: Wipe crumbs off the seal so the mechanism reads clearly.
Include a thumb's width of the box so the latch has context.
constraint: The latch or seal must be the sharpest point.

title: Hanging Keys
oneLiner: Leave your keys on their hook and shoot the hanging cluster.
details: Use the hook, knob, or bowl by the door where the keys actually live. Step to the side so the keys overlap in a vertical bunch rather than spreading flat. Let the wall or door behind them stay simple.
tips: Focus on the nearest key and let the ones behind soften.
A lamp to one side throws each key a separate shadow on the wall.

title: Wallet Corner
oneLiner: Move in on the worn corner of the wallet you carry every day.
details: Take the wallet, card sleeve, or purse you use and find the corner that has softened, frayed, or faded. Fill the frame with stitching, scuffs, or peeling layers. The rest of the wallet can fall out of focus.
tips: Rake light across the corner so loose threads lift.
Shoot along the edge rather than flat onto the face.
constraint: The worn corner must touch two edges of the frame.

title: Seated Buds
oneLiner: Open the case and show the buds sitting in their nests.
details: If your earphones live in a case, open it and photograph the buds in their slots. If you only have wired earphones, nest the two earpieces side by side in a small dish. The picture is about the pair waiting, not about a screen.
tips: Get slightly above the case so both nests are visible.
Clean fingerprints off the case lid before it reflects the window.

title: Cord Spiral
oneLiner: Coil a cord you carry into a flat spiral on the table.
details: Use a lanyard, a glasses cord, a badge strap, or the tie from a hood you take with you. Wind it into a flat spiral and set the clip or end at the centre. Shoot from above so the loops stay even and readable.
tips: Start the coil from the outside and keep each loop touching the last.
A plain table is enough. A busy cloth fights the spiral.
constraint: The spiral must be seen from directly above.

title: Dented Tube
oneLiner: Photograph the dents in a tube of cream or balm from your bag.
details: Find a hand cream, toothpaste, or balm tube that rides along in your bag. Lay it on its side so the squeezed dents face the window. The tube should look used, because those dents show you really carry it.
tips: Side light makes each dent a small valley.
Cap the tube so the frame stays about the dents, not an open top.

title: Handle Stitch
oneLiner: Find the stitch where your bag handle joins the body.
details: Set the bag on a chair and bring the phone close to one handle attachment. Look for the bar tack, rivet, or reinforced patch that takes the weight. Fill the frame with that joint and a little of the cloth around it.
tips: Pull the handle gently upright so the stitch is not folded under.
If the cloth is dark, add a lamp low and to the side.
constraint: Show one join only.

title: Card Backs
oneLiner: Fan the cards you carry so only the plain backs are visible.
details: Slide out the cards you keep in a wallet and fan them with the blank or magnetic backs upward. Names, photos, and long numbers stay face down. Shoot from a low angle so the fan opens toward the camera like a hand of plain rectangles.
tips: Four to six cards are enough. A thick fan hides the backs.
Check the screen for a reflected number before you keep the frame.
constraint: No names, photos, or full numbers visible.

title: Banded Cable
oneLiner: Show the short cable you keep in your bag, held by its own band.
details: Take the charging cable or headphone cable that lives in the bag, unplugged from everything. Leave it in the wrap, strap, or knot you actually use to keep it tidy. Photograph that bound bundle on a table so the band is as important as the cable.
tips: Choose a table tone that differs from the cable.
Include the connector at the edge so it reads as a cable, not a random cord.

title: After Unpacking
oneLiner: Empty the bag and photograph the lining it leaves behind.
details: Unpack onto a chair, then look inside the bag you carry. Dust, a loose thread, a crumb, or a faded patch will be in there. Crop to the lining so the picture is about the marks of daily use, not the objects.
tips: Hold the bag open toward a window so the lining is lit.
Tap focus on a speck of dust or a seam, not the dark middle.
constraint: No carried objects left in the compartment you show.

title: Zip Pull
oneLiner: Isolate the zip pull on the bag you take out each day.
details: Lay the bag so one zip runs across the frame and the pull sits near the middle. Leave the zip partly open if that is how you usually drop it. The pull, the tape, and a little of the bag cloth are enough.
tips: Angle the pull so it does not reflect a bright window as a white blob.
Focus on the pull's hole or knot.

title: Side Pocket Bulge
oneLiner: Slide your bottle into a side pocket and shoot the bulge it makes.
details: Put the bottle, a slim case, or a folded umbrella into the pocket that usually holds it. Do not tidy the rest of the bag. Photograph the stretched fabric from the side so you can tell what is hiding there by shape alone.
tips: Stretch is clearer in side light than in flat light from the front.
Leave the pocket unzipped a little if a rim or cap peeks out.
constraint: The object stays mostly inside the pocket.

title: Pen Standing
oneLiner: Stand the pen you carry upright in a glass and shoot its height.
details: Use the pen from your bag or pocket. Drop it into a clear glass or mug so it stands, cap on. Get low and let the pen rise through the frame against a plain bit of wall or cupboard.
tips: A clear glass shows the pen. A coloured mug hides it, so choose clear.
Focus on the pen about halfway up.

title: Cover Elastic
oneLiner: Photograph the band that holds a notebook or a small book shut.
details: Close the notebook, journal, or planner from your bag and find the band that keeps it shut. If there is no band, wrap a hair tie once around a small book or a card holder you carry. Photograph the band where it lies, including the place your thumb usually pulls.
tips: Shoot at a slant so the band casts a thin shadow.
Keep bookmarks and loose notes tucked out of sight.
constraint: The band must cross most of the frame.

title: Coin Pocket
oneLiner: Open the coin pocket of your wallet and show what stays in it.
details: Use the small pocket of a wallet or purse, still attached, not emptied onto the table. Let it gape enough to see a few coins or the empty lining if that is the truth today. Shoot from slightly above so the mouth of the pocket frames the coins.
tips: One finger can hold the pocket open from behind, out of frame.
Tilt coins so they do not mirror the window as blank discs.

title: Ring Charm
oneLiner: Single out the charm, bead, or tag that is not a key.
details: Look at your key ring for the extra thing: a charm, a coloured tag, a shop token, or a short ribbon. Set the ring down so that extra object sits in front and the keys fall behind. The picture is about the one item you did not strictly need.
tips: If every item is a key, use the most worn tag as the extra.
Open up to a wider view only after the charm is sharp.
constraint: The non-key item must be the closest object.

title: Case Scuffs
oneLiner: Close the case you carry and study the scuffs on its shell.
details: Use a glasses case, an earphone case, or a small hard pouch from your bag. Shut it and find the scratches from other objects. Fill the frame with that worn patch and ignore the logo if there is one.
tips: A lamp at a steep angle reveals fine scratches on smooth plastic.
Crop lettering out rather than trying to hide it with a finger.

title: Grab and Go
oneLiner: Line up the three things you would grab if you left right now.
details: On the table nearest the door, set only the three objects you would actually pick up: often keys, wallet, and a bottle, glasses, or a bag. Keep them in a simple row. Shoot from a slight angle so each one is fully visible and none is staged as a shop display.
tips: Leave a gap between objects about as wide as a finger.
Use the light already in the room. A flash will kill the quiet mood.
constraint: Exactly three objects.

title: Key in the Lock
oneLiner: Put your key in a door at home and photograph it there.
details: Use any door you can lock from the inside. Turn the key just far enough that it stays put, then stand to the side and frame the key against the door. The door colour and the metal together are the picture.
tips: Focus on the key head, where your fingers usually pinch.
Hold the phone square to the door so the key does not look bent.
constraint: The door must fill the background.

title: Slumped Bag
oneLiner: Drop your everyday bag on a chair and show how it slumps.
details: Set the bag you carry on a chair or the floor, packed as it is right now. Do not pose the handles. Photograph from the side so the sag, the bulge, and the way it leans are honest.
tips: Include the whole bag with a little of the chair or floor around it.
Use the light already in the room.

title: Bottle Daylight
oneLiner: Stand your bottle by a window or a lamp and shoot the glow inside.
details: Set a clear bottle where a window or a lamp can shine through the liquid. Get close to the side so the water glows. If your bottle is solid metal, pour a little water into a clear glass you carry and use that instead.
tips: Tap the near edge, then lower the exposure if the glow turns white.
Let any lettering fall soft. The light in the liquid is the subject.
constraint: The glow inside the bottle or glass must be obvious.

title: Hidden Coin
oneLiner: Find the coin caught in a seam of your bag and show it there.
details: Run a finger along the lining and the pocket seams of the bag you carry. A coin or a token is often trapped there. If the seams are empty, tuck a coin you carry halfway under the lining. Photograph it still half hidden.
tips: Hold the lining open with one finger kept at the frame edge.
Tap the coin's rim so the cloth around it can soften.
constraint: The coin must stay half hidden in the lining.

title: Leaning Umbrella
oneLiner: Lean a closed umbrella in the hall and frame that slim shape.
details: Use the umbrella you carry, or a rolled reusable bag if you have no umbrella. Lean it where you would actually leave it, against the inside of the door or in a corner by the coats. The long shape against a plain surface is the picture, with the strap visible.
tips: Place the handle at the bottom and include all of it.
Move sideways so the umbrella separates from the door edge.

title: Bag Feet
oneLiner: Turn the bag over and photograph the feet or the worn base.
details: Look at the bottom of the bag, backpack, or case you carry. Studs, a scuffed panel, or a ring of dirt will be there. Set it on a chair so you can see the base without lying on the floor, and fill the frame with that underside.
tips: Leave most of the dirt. One wiped patch can sit beside the rest.
A lamp to the side shows scuffs that overhead light flattens.

title: Plug Face
oneLiner: Show the scuffed end of the charging cable you carry.
details: Unplug the short charging cable from your bag and set the connector on a plain cloth. Fill the frame with the metal end, the contacts or the oval opening, and the scuffs around it. The rest of the cable can trail out of the picture.
tips: A cloth lighter or darker than the connector keeps the shape clear.
Tap the metal end so the cable behind it falls soft.
constraint: The connector must be the sharpest thing in the frame.

title: Handle Arch
oneLiner: Lift your bag handles into an arch and photograph the curve.
details: Set a tote, shopper, or backpack on a chair. Raise the handles or the top loop so they make an arch. Shoot through that arch toward a plain bit of wall.
tips: Hook the handles on a cupboard knob, or hold them outside the frame.
Focus on the nearest handle so the wall behind softens.
constraint: The arch must frame a plain bit of wall.

title: Trailing End
oneLiner: Let a scarf or sleeve trail from the bag and photograph that end.
details: Leave one soft thing partly out of the bag you carry: a scarf, a handkerchief, a sweater sleeve, or a folded tote. Set the bag on a chair and photograph only the trailing end against the seat or the floor. The bag itself can be mostly out of frame.
tips: A twist in the cloth is more alive than a straight drop.
Expose for the cloth if it is lighter than the chair.

title: Pass Half Out
oneLiner: Slide a travel pass halfway out of a pocket and stop there.
details: Use a transit card, a library card, or any pass you carry. Push it halfway out of a wallet pocket or a bag slot while the bag sits on a chair. Turn it so the name and photo, if any, face away. The picture is the card caught mid-reach.
tips: Shoot from close to the slot, as if your hand were about to pull the card.
Check the screen twice for a readable name before keeping it.
constraint: Hide names, photos, and long numbers.

title: Spout Close-Up
oneLiner: Get close to the drinking spout of the cup you carry.
details: Take the reusable cup or bottle you leave with and set it on the table. Open the spout if it has a lid. Fill the frame with the opening you actually drink from, including a stain or a chip if one is there.
tips: Angle the opening so a window does not turn it into a blank white hole.
Focus on the rim.

title: Hooked Glasses
oneLiner: Hook your glasses over the rim of your bag and shoot that perch.
details: Hang sunglasses or everyday glasses from the edge of your bag or from a handle, with the bag on a chair. Let the arms do the holding. Frame the place they hook, with the bag as a simple mass behind them.
tips: Angle the lenses toward a wall so they do not mirror your face.
Include both the hook point and one lens.
constraint: The glasses must be supported by the bag, not by your hand.

title: Single Chair, Empty Room
oneLiner: Frame one chair surrounded by open floor or wall space.
details: Move furniture aside if needed so the chair sits in generous empty space. The emptiness should feel intentional, not accidental. Let walls and floor create a simple stage around the seat.
tips: Stand back to show more empty space than chair.
Keep vertical lines straight in the frame.
Use soft daylight for even tones.
constraint: At least sixty percent of the frame must be empty.

title: Lone Mug on Counter
oneLiner: Place one mug on a wide counter and leave most of the frame bare.
details: Clear the counter except for a single mug placed off to one side. The bare surface becomes the subject as much as the cup. Look for subtle texture in laminate, stone, or wood.
tips: Push the mug towards a corner of the frame.
Avoid reflections of clutter in shiny counters.
Expose for the empty surface, not the mug.

title: Corner Where Walls Meet
oneLiner: Photograph an empty room corner where two walls and the ceiling meet.
details: Find a clean corner and align your phone so lines converge calmly. Shadows along the seam add depth without needing objects. The image should feel quiet and architectural.
tips: Hold the phone level to keep lines true.
Include a slice of floor for grounding.
Try monochrome for a graphic look.
constraint: No objects larger than a light switch.

title: Shadow on Blank Wall
oneLiner: Catch one object's shadow stretching across an otherwise empty wall.
details: Hold or place something simple, such as a plant, your own hand or a chair, between a light source and a blank wall. The shadow becomes the subject; the object may sit outside the frame. Move until the shadow shape feels crisp or softly blurred.
tips: Side light from a window makes longer shadows.
Keep the wall free of frames and switches if possible.
Tap exposure on the wall, not the window.
constraint: The object casting the shadow stays out of frame.

title: Sky Slice Above the Fence
oneLiner: Tilt up just outside and let the sky fill the frame.
details: Stand on the ground just outside your door and tilt up until sky fills the picture and a wall, a fence or the doorframe sits along one border. Clouds or a clear stretch both work. Keep your feet planted beside the door.
tips: Keep the horizon line low in the frame.
Do not stare into bright sun through the lens.
Use grid lines to keep the edge level.

title: Open Drawer, Empty Gap
oneLiner: Pull open a drawer and photograph the empty space inside it.
details: Remove contents temporarily so the drawer cavity reads as a rectangle of space. Include the front edge for context. The goal is to make ordinary furniture feel like a geometric study.
tips: Shoot straight on to square the rectangle.
Use daylight to avoid yellow indoor cast.
Close surrounding drawers to reduce clutter.
constraint: Leave the drawer completely empty.

title: Hanger on Bare Rod
oneLiner: Hang one empty hanger on a closet rail with space around it.
details: Clear neighbouring clothes if needed so one hanger floats in calm space. The hook and shoulders make a small mark against the back of the closet. Soft light from the room keeps the mood gentle.
tips: Centre the hanger, or sit it on a third of the frame.
Avoid showing identifiable clothing elsewhere.
Use a tall crop so the empty rail feels longer.
constraint: Only one hanger visible.

title: Window Bright, Room Dark
oneLiner: Expose for a bright window so the interior falls into silhouette.
details: Stand inside and aim towards the window without including your reflection. Let the frame glow while furniture or walls become simple dark shapes. The contrast tells a story of inside versus out.
tips: Tap the window to set exposure, then recompose.
Hide mirrors that might show you.
Shoot during daytime for a strong glow.

title: Sock on the Sheet
oneLiner: Leave one sock on a wide stretch of bed sheet.
details: Pull the sheet or duvet smooth and drop a single sock near a corner of the frame. The fabric around it should be almost empty. Shoot from the side of the bed so the sock stays small and the sheet fills the rest.
tips: Smooth wrinkles with your hand, then take the hand away.
Stand at the bedside rather than climbing onto the mattress.
constraint: The sock touches nothing else.

title: Apple on Bare Boards
oneLiner: Set one apple on the floor and let the boards surround it.
details: Clear a patch of floor and place a single apple, orange or small fruit where the boards or carpet are plain. Move back until the fruit is only a small mark in the picture. Keep your own feet out of the frame.
tips: Crouch, do not shoot from full standing height, so the floor has some perspective.
If the floor is very dark, tap the boards to lift the exposure.

title: Spoon on a White Plate
oneLiner: Put one teaspoon on a large plain plate.
details: Choose the biggest pale plate you have and lay a single teaspoon slightly away from the middle. The plate should read as a field of empty china. Shoot from above and crop so the plate nearly fills the frame.
tips: A pale plate on a pale table needs a little side light to show the rim.
Rotate the spoon so the handle aims at a corner.
constraint: Only the spoon and the plate.

title: One Cushion, Wide Sofa
oneLiner: Clear a sofa down to one cushion and frame the spare space.
details: Move extra cushions and throws out of shot, leaving a single cushion on a sofa, a bed or a bench. Stand back so most of the frame is the empty seat and back. Sit the cushion to one side rather than in the middle.
tips: Shoot from the arm of the sofa looking along the seat.
A portrait crop makes the empty back feel taller.

title: Soap in the Empty Bath
oneLiner: Place a bar of soap alone in a dry, empty bath.
details: Dry the bath if it is wet, or use a dry shower tray or a wide empty sink if you have no bath. Lift bottles down so the surface is a blank curve. Set one bar of soap, or a small sponge, near the far end, and shoot along the length so the empty surface surrounds it.
tips: Wipe water spots or they become extra subjects.
Hold the phone high and point along the length of the tub.
constraint: No bottles along the edge.

title: Ring on Bare Wood
oneLiner: Lay a ring or a coin on a wide bare table.
details: Clear the table completely. Place one ring, a coin or a button well inside the area you will frame. Stand over it and check that most of the picture is empty surface before you take the shot.
tips: Focus on the ring; the table grain can stay slightly soft.
A window from the side will lift the metal without a flash.

title: Pencil on Blank Paper
oneLiner: Rest a pencil on a large blank sheet.
details: Use printer paper, the back of a poster or an open notebook page with no writing. Lay the pencil near one corner of the sheet. Shoot from above so the paper's emptiness is the point of the picture.
tips: Tape the corners down just outside the crop, or smooth the sheet and take your hand away.
Turn on the grid and keep the pencil off the exact middle.
constraint: The paper must show no writing.

title: Magnet on a Wide Door
oneLiner: Frame one magnet on a fridge door that is otherwise clear.
details: Move other magnets out of the patch you will photograph, or use the side of the fridge if the front is busy. Leave a single magnet. Stand back so it is small against a wide field of the door.
tips: If the door is glossy, shoot at an angle that hides your reflection.
A landscape frame gives the door more width to feel empty.

title: Tea Bag on a Saucer
oneLiner: Set a dry tea bag on an empty saucer.
details: Use a saucer, a small plate or a lid. Place one dry tea bag, or a single sugar cube, off to the side. Come close enough to see the paper texture, but keep plenty of bare saucer around it.
tips: A dry bag lies flatter than a used one and keeps the saucer clean.
Expose for the pale saucer so it does not turn grey.
constraint: Leave the saucer otherwise empty.

title: Hook on the Closet
oneLiner: Photograph one empty hook on a large closet door.
details: Choose a closet or cupboard door that can fill the frame, with a single hook or a small handle visible. If clothes cover it, use the inside of the door instead. The hook should stay small and the door a wide plain field.
tips: Close the door fully so the gap does not become a second subject.
Stand square to the door to keep it rectangular.
constraint: No clothes in the frame.

title: One Grape on the Board
oneLiner: Place a single grape on a long empty board.
details: Use a cutting board, a tray or a baking sheet. Set one grape, a blueberry or a pea near an end. Shoot along the board from a low angle so the empty length stretches away from that one small thing.
tips: Rest the phone on the table at board height.
A dark board and a pale grape, or the reverse, will separate the subject.

title: Small Clock, Wide Wall
oneLiner: Frame a wall clock so the blank wall dominates.
details: Stand well back from a clock, a round timer or, if you have neither, a small round tin leaned on a shelf against the wall. Let the object sit high or to one side, with plain wall around it. Keep the shelf, if you need one, as a thin line at the bottom.
tips: Walk further back once you think the clock is small enough.
Tap the wall to set exposure so the clock does not turn into a black blob.
constraint: The clock or tin fills less than a quarter of the frame.

title: Empty Shelf, One Bowl
oneLiner: Leave a single bowl on an otherwise empty shelf.
details: Clear a shelf, a mantel or a windowsill and put back one bowl, cup or small pot near one end. Shoot straight on so the shelf is a long empty line. Keep busier shelves above or below out of the frame.
tips: A bowl with a strong rim reads clearly at a distance.
Level the phone so the shelf does not slope.

title: Cap on an Empty Desk
oneLiner: Set a bottle cap alone on a cleared desk.
details: Clear the desk or a table and place one cap, an eraser or a coin near a corner. Move back, and only come closer if the cap vanishes. Most of the frame should be bare desktop.
tips: Shoot across the desk from the front edge, not from directly above.
A cap with a coloured top helps it survive in a wide frame.
constraint: Nothing else on the desktop.

title: Switch on a Bare Wall
oneLiner: Photograph a light switch as a small mark on a big wall.
details: Find the plainest wall and frame the switch plate so it sits low or to one side. Stand back until the wall is most of the picture. Keep frames, posters and cables out.
tips: Portrait orientation gives the wall more empty height.
If the switch is white on a white wall, underexpose a touch so the plate edge appears.
constraint: Nothing else on the wall in frame.

title: One Shoe, Long Hall
oneLiner: Place one shoe in a hallway and leave the rest clear.
details: Move the other shoes out of sight. Set a single shoe near the baseboard and stand at the far end of the hall. If the hall is very short, use the longest clear floor in one room and keep the shoe small in the frame.
tips: Put the shoe against the baseboard so it has a clear edge to sit on.
Hold the phone at waist height rather than pointing steeply down.

title: Lid on a Wide Pan
oneLiner: Set a lid to one side of a large empty pan.
details: Place a frying pan or a wide saucepan on the stovetop or a table, empty and dry. Rest the lid inside it, off to one side, so most of the pan is bare metal. Shoot from above.
tips: Dry the pan or water beads will clutter the empty metal.
Turn off the overhead light if it glares, and use a window instead.
constraint: The pan stays empty of food.

title: Plant Against the Pane
oneLiner: Stand a small plant in front of a window and leave the sill empty.
details: Use a small pot, or a sprig in a glass. Place it in the lower corner of the frame and keep the rest of the windowsill clear. Shoot along the sill so the bare sill and the glass make a wide quiet field around the pot.
tips: Expose for the sill, not the brightest part of the glass.
Shift the pot until it sits on a third, then stop moving it.

title: One Dish in the Oven
oneLiner: Slide one empty bowl onto an otherwise clear oven shelf.
details: Make sure the oven is off and cool before you open the door. Place a metal bowl or a small tin on the middle shelf and take out trays that crowd it. If you have no oven, open a cool microwave and use one bowl the same way. Shoot so the dark interior surrounds that single dish.
tips: Turn on the room light behind you rather than using flash inside the cavity.
Include the door frame as a border around the dark space.
constraint: The oven or microwave must be off and cool.

title: One Book, Wide Desk
oneLiner: Leave a single closed book on a desk and stand well back.
details: Clear the desk first. Place the book off to one side, closed, so the cover is a small rectangle. Shoot from the front edge of the desk and include the empty surface.
tips: A dark cover on a light desk, or the reverse, keeps the book visible.
Do not open the book; the closed cover is the small shape you want.

title: Small Glow, Dark Room
oneLiner: Let one small glow sit in a room you have darkened.
details: Close the curtains and switch off the main lights. Open the fridge a crack, or switch on a small lamp in the far corner. Stand well back so the glow is a small bright patch and the dark room fills the frame.
tips: Tap the bright patch, then pull exposure down until the room goes deep.
Lean on a doorframe so the long exposure of a dim room stays sharper.
constraint: No other lights visible.

title: Sponge in a Wide Sink
oneLiner: Leave one sponge in a cleared, empty sink.
details: Move bottles and brushes out of the sink and dry the worst of the water. Set a sponge or a folded cloth near one corner. Shoot from above so the basin is a wide pale field and the sponge stays small.
tips: A coloured sponge survives better on a white basin.
Include the rim so the empty basin has an edge.

title: Remote on the Long Unit
oneLiner: Place the remote at one end of a cleared TV unit.
details: Clear the top of a TV unit, a sideboard or a long shelf. Set one remote, or a single coaster if you have no remote, at the far end. Stand back so the empty surface runs across the frame and the object stays small.
tips: Shoot along the surface from the near end, not from above.
A dark remote on a pale top will still read at a distance.
constraint: Nothing else may sit on that surface.

title: Spool on the Duvet
oneLiner: Set a spool of thread near the corner of a wide bed.
details: Smooth the duvet or a bedsheet and place one small object near a corner: a spool of thread, a ring box or an eraser. Stand at the foot of the bed so the bed fills the frame. The object should feel almost lost in the cloth.
tips: A spool with a coloured core stays visible on a pale duvet.
Move further back after you think you are far enough.

title: Knocker on a Broad Door
oneLiner: Frame the door knocker as a small shape on a large door.
details: Stand back from your own front door until the knocker or handle is small, and fill the frame with the door. If there is no knocker, use the handle or a hook the same way. If the door is glazed and shows the room, shift so a plain panel is what you see.
tips: Square your shoulders to the door before you lift the phone.
Stay by your own door rather than walking off down a path.
constraint: The door fills the whole frame.

title: Aerial Against Open Sky
oneLiner: Catch a small aerial or dish in a wide stretch of sky.
details: From the ground outside your door, tilt up until the sky is almost the whole picture and one aerial, satellite dish or chimney pot sits near an edge. Keep your feet planted. If nothing like that is visible, use only the top edge of your doorframe along the bottom and let sky do the rest.
tips: Tap the sky so it keeps detail instead of washing out.
A tiny object in the corner is enough; do not zoom it larger.

title: One Fork, Long Table
oneLiner: Lay a single fork on a long, cleared table.
details: Clear the table or a long counter. Place one fork well to the side, with the handle pointing along the surface. Stand at the near end so the empty table stretches away and the fork stays a small mark.
tips: Rest the phone on the near edge so the low view stays steady.
A fork on a pale table needs a little side light to show the handle.
constraint: Only one piece of cutlery in the frame.

title: One Hairpin, Wide Shelf
oneLiner: Leave a single hairpin on an otherwise empty shelf.
details: Clear a bathroom shelf or a windowsill. Set down one hairpin, a clip or a spare button, close to an end. Shoot straight on so the shelf is a long empty line and the small object does not sit in the middle.
tips: A dark pin on a pale shelf is easier to find in a wide frame.
Level the phone so the shelf runs flat across the picture.
constraint: The hairpin or button is the only object.

title: One Peg on the Rack
oneLiner: Clip a single peg on an otherwise empty drying rack.
details: Leave a drying rack bare and clip one peg near an end. If you have no rack, hang one peg on a coat hook and stand well back so the door fills the frame. The peg should be a small mark in a large quiet surface.
tips: A wooden peg on a pale door reads more clearly than a white peg on a white rack.
Stand further back than feels natural, then shoot.

title: Egg Cup on a Wide Tray
oneLiner: Stand one egg cup at the far end of a large tray.
details: Use a tray, a baking sheet or a large cutting board. Stand an egg cup, a small glass or an espresso cup at the far end and leave the rest bare. Get the phone down at tray height so the empty surface leads to that one small shape.
tips: A cup with a coloured rim survives better than clear glass at this distance.
Keep the near edge of the tray in the frame so the surface has a start.
constraint: Include no other objects.

title: Key on the Bare Table
oneLiner: Lay one key on a wide, cleared table.
details: Take one key off the bunch if it will come free, or lay the whole bunch if it will not. Place it well inside a cleared table. Stand back until the key is small and the tabletop is most of the picture.
tips: A key with a coloured fob stays visible when you stand back.
Shoot across the table from the front edge, not from overhead.

title: Mat in a Wide Frame
oneLiner: Shoot a doormat small, with bare floor around it.
details: Use the mat by your door, whether it lives inside or just outside. Stand so the mat is a modest patch, not the whole picture, and let the surrounding floor do the rest. If you are on a shared landing, keep the frame on your own mat and your own door.
tips: Include the mat fully, with space on at least three sides.
A higher angle makes the mat a small rectangle; a low angle makes it a thin band. Choose the higher one.

title: Orange in the Empty Fridge
oneLiner: Leave one orange on an otherwise cleared fridge shelf.
details: Move other food aside on one shelf, or use the door shelf if that is easier to clear. Place a single orange, a lemon or a small jar at one end. Shoot from the open door so the lit shelf is a wide field and the fruit stays small, then close the door so the fridge does not warm.
tips: The fridge light is enough. Leave the phone flash off.
A round fruit reads faster than a jar when the shelf is mostly empty.
constraint: Only one piece of fruit or one jar.

title: Matchbox on a Long Shelf
oneLiner: Stand a matchbox at one end of a long empty shelf.
details: Clear a shelf, a mantel or a windowsill. Stand one small box at the far end: a matchbox, a small tin or a bandage box. Shoot from the other end so the shelf runs across the frame and the box stays small.
tips: A box stood on its end has a clearer shape than one lying flat.
Keep busier shelves above and below out of the picture.

title: Cup on the Wide Stovetop
oneLiner: Set one cup on a cold stovetop and leave the rings bare.
details: Check the stovetop is off and cold before you put anything on it. Place a single cup or a small bowl away from the middle. Shoot from the front edge so the stovetop is a broad empty surface around that one cup.
tips: A cup with a handle gives the small shape a direction.
Turn the overhead light off if it glares on the stovetop, and use the window.
constraint: The stovetop must be off and cold.

title: Coaster on the Bare Table
oneLiner: Clear a table and leave one coaster in the corner.
details: Clear the dining table or a desk completely, then put back a single coaster, a lid or a small dish near a corner. Stand at the opposite corner. The picture is the empty surface, and the coaster only stops it feeling unfinished.
tips: A round coaster reads more clearly than a clear glass lid.
Check the corners of the frame for a second object before you shoot.
constraint: Move other objects out of the frame.

title: Lamp Pool at Night
oneLiner: Photograph a single lamp casting a warm circle of light in an otherwise dark room.
details: Turn off the other lights and let one lamp define the scene. Include the edge of a table, a book, or a wall where the brightness falls away into shadow. You are tracing how far that one source reaches. Do not look straight into the bulb.
tips: Drag the exposure down after you tap so the room stays mostly dark.
Include the lamp base if it explains where the pool comes from.
constraint: Only one light source may be on.

title: String Light Bokeh
oneLiner: Turn small string or fairy lights into soft glowing orbs in the background.
details: Drape fairy lights or a short string of small bulbs far behind a mug, a plant, or your hand at the frame edge. Focus on the near subject so the lights behind melt into circles. A shelf, a headboard, or the far side of a table all work. If you own no string, use the small bulbs around a bathroom mirror and stand back until those bulbs can blur.
tips: Move farther from the lights if you want the glowing circles to grow.
Switch night mode off if it tries to sharpen the background bulbs.

title: Screen Glow in Dark
oneLiner: Let a TV, monitor, or tablet be the only light on one nearby object.
details: In a dim room, pause a bright image on a television, a monitor, a laptop, or a tablet, and place a mug, a plant, or your hands where the glow lands. Colours from the screen become the lamp. You are not photographing what is on the screen, you are borrowing its light. Keep the screen content generic.
tips: Pause on a bright frame so the colour on the object stays steady.
Turn the room lights fully off before you frame the object.
constraint: No readable text from the screen may appear in frame.

title: Streetlamp Cone
oneLiner: From your doorway, tilt up at a lamp you can already see.
details: After dark, stand in the doorway or just outside it, close enough to touch the frame. Tilt the camera up at a lamp that is already in view, and let the bright cone sit against the dark. A door frame, a wire, or a branch may cross the light. Do not walk away from the door to get closer to the lamp.
tips: Tap the bright cone, then lower the exposure so the surroundings stay deep.
Lean the phone against the door frame to keep the lamp sharp.
constraint: The camera must point upward, with no horizon in the frame.

title: A Warm Rim
oneLiner: Light one nearby edge with a candle, or with a low lamp instead.
details: If you are happy to use a flame, light one candle or tea light and set a cup, a book, or a piece of fruit close enough that only a warm rim is lit. If you would rather not use a flame, tilt a small lamp low so it lights that same rim. If you do light a flame, stay beside it the whole time and put it out before you leave the room. Keep the bright edge sharp and let the rest of the object fall softer.
tips: Brace both elbows on the table so the rim does not wander.
Shoot a short burst and choose the frame where the edge is cleanest.
constraint: Only an edge of the object may be lit.

title: Fridge Light Drama
oneLiner: Use the brief glow of an open fridge to illuminate one shelf scene.
details: Open the refrigerator in a dark kitchen and choose the shelf with the strongest colour, such as fruit, jars, or bottles. Photograph that shelf before the glow starts to feel ordinary, and let a label go soft if you have to move. Close the door as soon as you have the frame. The door itself can enter the picture only to show where the light begins.
tips: Work in one short burst, then shut the door to keep the cold in.
Tap a colourful jar so the white interior does not fool the exposure.

title: Oven Door Glow
oneLiner: Show the oven lamp glowing through the dark glass of the door.
details: Turn the kitchen lights off and switch on the oven lamp, keeping the heat off. Move close so the glass holds that glow and the kitchen around it stays dark. If the lamp will not come on by itself, open the door of the cold oven and let a hood light or a lamp in the doorway fall into the cavity.
tips: Tap the glass, not the dark room around the oven.
Wipe the door if a smear is brighter than the lamp inside.
constraint: The oven heat must stay off.

title: Bedside Reading Glow
oneLiner: Show a book or notebook lit by a bedside lamp in an otherwise dim room.
details: Build a small night scene from a pillow, a blanket, and one lamp. Let the warm light fall across an open page or a closed cover, whichever you prefer. The rest of the room can disappear into shadow. Keep the picture to that intimate patch, not a tour of the whole bedroom.
tips: Angle the shade so the page is lit and the bulb does not flare the lens.
Leave a corner of blanket in frame so the light has texture to land on.
constraint: Use only the warm bedside lamp, with overhead lights off.

title: Keyboard Backlight Mood
oneLiner: Let a laptop's small lights be the only colour in a dark desk scene.
details: Open a laptop in a dim room and look for the keys glowing. If they stay dark, angle the screen so a little of its light falls across the keyboard deck instead. Include one object that picks up the spill, such as a mug or a notebook, and leave the screen free of passwords, messages, or anything private.
tips: Lower the screen brightness if it washes the keys out.
Shoot from a low side angle so the rows of keys recede.

title: Inside the Microwave
oneLiner: Open the microwave in the dark and use only its interior lamp.
details: In a dark kitchen, open the microwave and let its lamp light the glass plate or a plain mug set inside. If the cavity stays dark, set a small lamp on the counter so light falls through the opening. Do not start a cycle, and close the door once the picture is done.
tips: Stand a little to the side so the lamp does not flare straight out at you.
Use a mug with a plain surface so the glow has a simple shape.
constraint: Do not start the microwave.

title: Rim of the Shade
oneLiner: Crop in on the glowing rim of a lampshade in a dark room.
