details: Switch off every light except one lamp with a shade. Move close to the rim where the glow escapes, and let the rest of the room fall black. The bright oval of the shade is the subject, not the furniture around it. If the shade is opaque, photograph the bright gap between the shade and the stand instead.
tips: Stand to the side so the bulb does not flare straight into the lens.
Tap the rim, then lower the exposure until the glow has an edge.
constraint: Only one lamp may be switched on.

title: Router Constellation
oneLiner: Treat the tiny lamps on a router or modem as a small constellation.
details: Find a router, a modem, a power strip, or a charger block with status lights. Turn the room lights off and move close until those points are the subject. A cable curve can lead the eye, but hide any network name printed on the box. A dark shelf or a floor corner is setting enough.
tips: Tap the brightest LED, then reduce exposure so the dots stay separate.
Wipe the lens first, because haze blooms around small lights.
constraint: No readable words or network names in the frame.

title: Slit Under the Door
oneLiner: Photograph the bright slit leaking from under a closed door.
details: Turn a light on in one room and close the door. From the darker side, get low and frame the glowing gap along the floor. A rug edge or the shadow of the door bottom can give scale. If the door sits flush, open it a finger's width and shoot that narrow bright line instead.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor so the slit stays level.
Expose for the bright gap and let the surrounding floor go dark.

title: Arc from the Night Light
oneLiner: Find the small arc a night light throws on a nearby wall.
details: Plug in a night light, or set a very small lamp on the floor against a wall if you have none. Turn every other light off and photograph the arc on the wall or the floor. Let the baseboard show how low the source sits. Slide the fitting until the glow has a readable edge.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor and use the timer so your hand is clear.
Nudge the fitting sideways until the arc reads as a half-moon.

title: Glow on the Desk
oneLiner: Use a laptop screen as the only light falling across the desk.
details: Open a laptop in a dark room and angle the screen so its light falls across the desk rather than into the lens. A notebook, a mug, or the bare wood can carry that glow, and the page on screen should stay blank or generic. Keep the laptop at the edge of the frame, because the lit desk is the subject. Dim any keyboard lights if they start to compete.
tips: Turn the screen until the pool on the desk has a firm edge.
Tap the lit wood, then ease the exposure down a little.

title: Curtain Takes the Amber
oneLiner: Let a street lamp colour the curtain while the room stays dark.
details: Turn the room lights off and find a curtain or a blind that faces a street lamp. Photograph the warm colour on the cloth, and leave most of the window out of the frame. A fold, a hem, or a woven stripe will give that colour texture. If no lamp reaches the glass, switch a warm lamp on in the room and shoot the colour it throws on the same cloth.
tips: Include a fold so the colour has something uneven to land on.
Lock the exposure on the cloth rather than on the bright gap outside.

title: Light on the Threshold
oneLiner: Frame the patch of doorway light on the floor just outside.
details: After dark, stand just outside your door, close enough to touch it, and frame the mat or the bare floor where a lamp by the door falls off into the dark. If there is no lamp outside, open the door and use the indoor light that spills onto that same patch. Include both the lit area and the darker ground beside it, and do not walk farther out for a wider view.
tips: Turn the flash off so it does not flatten the fade.
Crouch so the phone looks across the mat rather than straight down.

title: Blind Stripe Light
oneLiner: Let an outside lamp stripe the ceiling through slatted blinds.
details: After dark, switch the room lights off and tilt slatted blinds until an outside lamp draws lines on the ceiling, the bed, or the floor. Those stripes are the subject, so leave most of the window out of the frame. If no lamp reaches the glass, put a bright lamp in the doorway and close the blinds until similar lines appear. Nudge one slat at a time until the spacing feels even.
tips: Focus on the surface the stripes land on, not the blinds.
Wait a moment after you touch the slats so they stop trembling.

title: One Charging Dot
oneLiner: Make one charging LED the brightest point in a dark frame.
details: Plug in a charger, a toothbrush base, or a small appliance so a single indicator glows, and do not use the phone you are shooting with as that light. Turn everything else off and move close, then ease back until the dot anchors a mostly black picture. Show just enough of the plug or the base to explain the dot.
tips: Tap the dark area beside the LED so the phone does not brighten the whole scene.
Cover any second indicator with a bit of tape for this one shot.

title: Mirror Bulb Row
oneLiner: Switch on a bathroom mirror light and crop in on the bulbs.
details: Leave the ceiling light off and use the mirror lights, a light over the sink, or a single bulb beside the mirror. Frame the fittings so they repeat, or let one bulb dominate a dark mirror. Wipe the glass first if you want a clean edge of light rather than a smear. If you only have a ceiling bulb, shoot it from the doorway with the rest of the room dark.
tips: Stand to the side so your reflection stays out of the glass.
Lock focus on the fitting, not on the mirror surface.
constraint: Keep your own reflection out of the mirror.

title: Cloth Tint on the Wall
oneLiner: Hold thin coloured cloth in front of a cool lamp to tint the wall.
details: Use a cool lamp, and keep cloth well away from a hot bulb. Hold a shirt, a scarf, or a thin dish towel between the lamp and a pale wall so the wall changes colour. Photograph the coloured wall, with a fold of cloth at the edge if you want to show the cause. Never rest the fabric on the shade or the bulb.
tips: Stretch the cloth tight for an even tint, or leave a fold for a streak.
Set the lamp close to the wall if the colour looks too weak.
constraint: Do not lay fabric on a hot shade or bulb.

title: Dark Cupboard, Bright Side
oneLiner: Open a cupboard and let one room lamp fall on a single object.
details: Open a cupboard or a closet and leave the room dark except for one lamp. Let that lamp reach one mug, one shoe, one box, or a folded towel inside. Shoot from outside so the cupboard frame stays black around the object. Swing the door until the object has a bright side and a dark side.
tips: Tap the lit side of the object and let the shelves drop away.
Open the door only far enough to keep the surround dark.
constraint: The room outside the cupboard must stay dark.

title: Digits in the Dark
oneLiner: Let a clock display be the only glow on a nearby surface.
details: In a dark bedroom or kitchen, wake a digital clock, a microwave display, or an oven clock and leave larger lamps off. Photograph the glow on the table, the counter, or the pillow beside it. You do not need the whole appliance, only the digits and the light they spill. If nothing shows digits, a small night light in that same spot will do.
tips: Tap the digits, then ease exposure down so they stay crisp.
Include a little of the surface so the glow has somewhere to fall.
constraint: No other lamp in the room may be on.

title: Standby Skyline
oneLiner: Gather tiny standby lights from a few devices onto one dark shelf.
details: At night, look along a media shelf, a desk, or a bedside table for LEDs that stay on. Turn the main lights off and photograph the row of small glows. Cover a light that is too fierce with a scrap of tape for the length of the shot. The picture should feel like a quiet skyline of dots.
tips: Shoot along the shelf so the dots recede from the camera.
Turn screens off so only the little indicators remain.
constraint: No screens may be lit, only small indicator lamps.

title: Colour on the Door Wall
oneLiner: From the doorway, show the colour a street lamp casts on the wall.
details: Stand in the doorway, close enough to touch the frame, and look at the wall beside the door. Photograph the amber or cool patch a street lamp already casts on the brick, the paint, or the door. Keep that lamp out of the frame if the colour is strong enough, and do not walk out towards it. If no outside lamp reaches, open the door and use the indoor light falling on that same wall.
tips: Fill most of the frame with the coloured surface.
Stay within arm's reach of the door for the whole shot.

title: Patch on the Ceiling
oneLiner: Frame the soft patch a bedside lamp throws on the ceiling.
details: Angle a bedside lamp, or any small lamp, so it throws a patch on the ceiling or the wall high above the bed. Turn the other lights off and frame the place where that glow fades into the dark. A ceiling corner or the top of a headboard can give the patch a boundary. Keep the lamp at the bottom edge or leave it out.
tips: Tilt the shade in small moves until the patch has an edge.
Focus on the ceiling where the light thins, not on the lamp.
constraint: The patch must reach a corner or the top of the wall.

title: Kettle Indicator
oneLiner: Catch the indicator glow on a kettle, toaster, or coffee machine.
details: In a dark kitchen, wake the small lamp on a kettle, a toaster, a coffee machine, or a similar counter appliance. You do not need a full boil. Photograph the glow where it meets the counter, and let a nearby cup catch a little of the spill. If nothing has an indicator, use the microwave display or the oven clock as that small source.
tips: Get close enough that the indicator is larger than a speck.
Turn the overhead kitchen light off before you press the switch.

title: Through the Frosted Door
oneLiner: Leave a light on behind frosted glass and shoot from the dark side.
details: Switch on the light behind a frosted, reeded, or patterned bathroom door, and stand on the dark side. The glass should read as a soft glowing panel, with the frame around it darker. If your door is clear, use a frosted shower screen or a textured cabinet door with a lamp switched on beyond it.
tips: Focus on the glass itself so the frame stays crisp around the glow.
Shift until the panel is brighter than the frame around it.

title: Bathroom Left On
oneLiner: From the dark hall, frame the bathroom glowing through its doorway.
details: Switch on the bathroom light and leave every other room dark. From the hall, frame the cooler glow on the tiles, the sink, or the mirror's edge, and let the doorway crop the view. This picture is the bathroom after dark, so resist showing the rest of the home. If there is no door, shoot from the darkest nearby corner so the foreground falls away.
tips: Expose for the tiles so the pale surfaces keep a little detail.
Include the door frame as a dark border around the glow.
constraint: Only the bathroom light may be on.

title: Warm Door Rectangle
oneLiner: Look back from the doorway at the warm shape of your own door.
details: Turn one indoor lamp on, stand just outside the open door, and look back at the glass or the gap of light. The goal is that warm rectangle against the darker outside, not a tour of the room. Shift until the bright shape sits cleanly in the frame. If the door has no glass, open it a little and shoot the gap.
tips: Expose for the warm interior so the outside stays dark.
Move a little sideways if your reflection shows in the glass.
constraint: Your reflection must not be visible in the glass.

title: Laptop Wall Wash
oneLiner: Bounce a blank laptop screen onto a nearby wall in the dark.
details: Open a laptop or a tablet on a plain bright page and turn the room lights off. Angle the screen so it washes a wall, a curtain, or the side of a desk. Hide icons by using an empty document or a white page. Photograph the soft edge where the glow fades into the dark.
tips: Tilt the screen slowly until the wash has a visible boundary.
Lock exposure on the fading edge, not on the screen itself.
constraint: No icons, words, or pictures may be readable.

title: Bent Glow in Water
oneLiner: Look through a water glass at a lamp and frame the bent light.
details: Fill a clear glass with water and set it on a table in a dark room, with a lamp a short distance behind it. Look through the glass so the lamp bends into a bright patch with a soft odd edge. Move the glass until that patch is the clearest thing in the frame. Keep the lamp itself outside the picture.
tips: Move the glass a finger's width at a time, because the bend jumps.
Tap the bright patch in the glass so the table stays dark.
constraint: The lamp must stay outside the frame.

title: Warm Lamp, Cool Screen
oneLiner: Include a warm lamp and a cool screen glow in the same frame.
details: In a dark room, switch on one warm lamp and open a laptop or a monitor on a blank, cool page. Arrange them so both glows land together, on a wall, a desk, or a bedspread. The picture is the meeting of those two colours, warm to one side and cool to the other. Keep writing off the screen.
tips: Underexpose a little so the two colours stay distinct.
Seat the lamp to one side and the screen glow to the other.
constraint: Both the warm glow and the cool glow must be visible.

title: Circle from Above
oneLiner: Use only a ceiling light and frame the pool it drops on the table.
details: At night, switch the lamps off and leave one ceiling light on over a table or a counter. Frame the pool on the surface and keep the fitting out of the picture. A plate, a seam in the wood, or the rim of a mat can sit inside that pool. If the bare bulb is too fierce, use a shaded pendant, or a lamp aimed down from a high shelf.
tips: Tap the rim of the pool so the fade stays visible.
Clear spare objects until the circle reads as one shape.
constraint: The ceiling fitting must stay out of the frame.

title: Hood Above the Stovetop
oneLiner: Use only the stove hood lamp and shoot the empty stovetop beneath it.
details: At night, leave the kitchen dark except for the hood lamp or the light fitted just above the stovetop. Photograph the pool on the empty stovetop or the bare counter beneath it. Leave the heat off, because the falling light is the subject. If you have no hood lamp, stand a lamp at the back of the counter and aim it down onto that same surface.
tips: Shoot from chest height and angle down towards the pool on the stovetop.
Wipe the stovetop so you are photographing light, not crumbs.
constraint: Overhead ceiling lights must stay off.

title: Far Points of Light
oneLiner: Frame distant lamps as small dots from a dark window.
details: Switch the room lights off and stand at a window that faces other lights. Keep those lamps as small dots, with a curtain edge for scale, and do not open the window or lean out. If the outdoors is completely dark, switch on a lamp in a far room and shoot those distant points down the hall instead. The points should stay small against a large dark area.
tips: Hold the phone against the window frame to cut shake.
Lower the exposure until the dots stop blooming into blobs.

title: Leaves Against the Lamp
oneLiner: Set a small lamp behind a plant and frame the glowing leaves.
details: In a dark room, set a small lamp behind a houseplant, a bunch of herbs, or leafy greens standing in a jar. The leaves should glow at the edges while the room stays dark. Move the lamp until a few leaves are bright and the rest fall into shadow. Keep the lamp hidden behind the foliage.
tips: Expose for the bright leaf edges so they keep their colour.
Slide the lamp until the glow has a crisp outline.
constraint: The lamp must stay hidden behind the foliage.

title: Page Light on the Quilt
oneLiner: Rest a lit tablet on the bed and photograph the spill on the quilt.
details: Rest a tablet or an e-reader on the bed with a bright blank page, and keep your phone in hand for the shot. Let that cool rectangle light the quilt or the sheet around it, with the rest of the room dark. A fold in the bedding will show the fade more clearly than a smooth patch. Hide any writing by staying on an empty page.
tips: Tap the lit cloth, not the bright page.
Prop the tablet so the spill reaches a fold.

title: The Slow Blink
oneLiner: Catch the tiny blink of a smoke alarm or a ceiling sensor.
details: Find a smoke alarm, a ceiling sensor, or another fitting that blinks a small light, and give it a few moments if the blink is slow. Turn the room lights off, aim up, and take a short burst so one frame holds the blink at its brightest. Include a little ceiling around the dot so it has a place to sit. If nothing overhead blinks, use the blink on a charger or a toothbrush base on a shelf.
tips: Use burst and keep the frame where the point is brightest.
Lean on a door frame so the dot does not drift.

title: The Hall Left On
oneLiner: From a dark room, frame the light spilling through the doorway.
details: Turn a light on in the hall, the kitchen, or the next room, and leave the room you are standing in dark. Frame the doorway so the bright space is a clear shape inside the dark frame. A rug edge or the line of the floor can lead into the light. If every room opens into the same space, shoot from behind a sofa so the foreground stays dark.
tips: Expose for the lit room so the doorway frame stays dark.
Stand far enough back that the whole doorway fits.

title: Lamp in the Dark Glass
oneLiner: Catch your lamp reflected in the dark window glass.
details: At night, leave one lamp on and stand so a window shows that lamp in the glass. Distant lights outside may sit in the same pane, and you can include them if they are already there. Shift until the reflection is readable, and do not open the window or lean out. If the glass shows nothing, move the lamp until its shape appears.
tips: Turn other lamps off so only one reflection appears.
Wipe the glass if dust breaks the reflection into specks.
constraint: Stay on the indoor side of the glass.

title: Amber Through the Glass
oneLiner: Find the warm colour an outside lamp throws on an indoor wall.
details: Turn the indoor lights off and look for a warm cast on a wall or the ceiling, coming through the window. Photograph that amber patch on the paint, and leave the window mostly out of the frame. A corner or the edge of a door frame will give the patch a boundary. If the windows stay dark, bring a warm lamp close to a pale wall and photograph the colour it leaves, with the lamp out of frame.
tips: Leave white balance warm if a cool setting washes the cast away.
Include a straight edge so the patch has a clear stop.

title: Strip Along the Counter
oneLiner: Paint the counter with under-cabinet lights and leave the ceiling dark.
details: At night, switch on the lights fixed under the cabinets and leave the ceiling off. Clear a short run of counter and leave one or two things, such as a kettle and a jar, standing in that strip. Let the brightness fade before the front edge of the counter if you can. If you have no strip, set a lamp at the back of the counter and aim it along the surface.
tips: Shoot along the counter so the strip of light recedes.
Lift any object that blocks the strip and casts a muddled shadow.

title: One Window Opposite
oneLiner: From your own window, frame a single lit window across the way.
details: Switch your own lights off and stand at the window. Choose one lit window far enough away that it is only a bright rectangle, with no interior visible. Leave the glass closed, and do not lean out. If you can see into that room, or nothing outside is lit, switch on a lamp in another room of your home and frame that distant opening instead.
tips: Hold the phone against the frame so the rectangle stays still.
Lower the exposure if the window swells into a white block.
constraint: Only one window may be the subject.

title: Hot Meets Cold
oneLiner: Place something warm beside something cold and capture both in one frame.
details: Set a mug of just-boiled water beside a glass or bottle you have just taken from the fridge. Shoot quickly, while steam shows above the mug and droplets show on the cold glass. Stand them against something dark so the steam has a shape.
tips: Backlight steam against a dark background.
Condensation on the cold item adds story.
Shoot within a minute, before the steam thins out.
constraint: Both the steam and the cold droplets must be visible.

title: Rough Versus Smooth
oneLiner: Find two textures, one rough and one smooth, and split them in one frame.
details: Pair a scourer with a glazed plate, a rough towel with a smooth mug, or unfinished wood with a metal spoon. Arrange so each texture occupies roughly half the frame. Move close enough that the difference is obvious without a caption.
tips: Use side light to exaggerate rough texture.
Keep colours simple so texture carries the idea.
Place the join between the two textures about a third of the way across.

title: Big Beside Small
oneLiner: Put a large everyday object next to a tiny one and play with scale.
details: Try a mug beside a coin, a shoe beside a button, or a book beside a paperclip. Place them on the same surface so the size contrast is honest. Shoot from an angle that keeps both fully visible and clearly different in scale.
tips: Leave space between objects so they do not merge.
Eye-level often reads scale best.
A plain tea towel under both objects keeps the scale easy to read.
constraint: One object must be at least four times larger.

title: Light Against Dark
oneLiner: Compose one brightly lit object against a deeply shadowed background.
details: Place a pale item in a beam from a window or lamp and let the surroundings fall dark. Expose for the bright subject and let shadows go black if needed. The opposite tones should feel deliberate, not accidental.
tips: Close curtains behind the subject to darken the room.
Use a white or pale object for maximum contrast.
Tap exposure on the lit subject before recomposing.
constraint: Half the frame or more must read as shadow.

title: Old Next to New
oneLiner: Pair something worn with something fresh and let the contrast tell the story.
details: Match an aged book with a new one, a scuffed shoe with a clean one, or a faded towel with a bright one. Keep both items in sharp focus and similar size in frame. The wear should be visible without needing words.
tips: Place the newer item on the side you read first.
Use even light so wear shows in detail.
Avoid logos that dominate the story.

title: Full Versus Empty
oneLiner: Photograph a full container beside an empty one of the same kind.
details: Use two glasses, bowls, or bottles, one filled with water, snacks, or coins, one bare. Align them side by side on a flat surface. The emptiness should feel as intentional as the fullness.
tips: Matching pairs make the idea instant.
Shoot straight-on for a clear comparison.
Leave the empty container truly empty.
constraint: Both containers must be the same shape and size.

title: Soft and Hard
oneLiner: Combine something soft with something hard in one playful still life.
details: Try a cushion against a wooden chair leg, a sponge on a plate, or a folded cloth wrapped partly around a metal spoon. Let the materials contrast through texture and the sharpness of their edges. Leave your hands out so the soft thing and the hard thing meet on their own.
tips: Rumple soft items so they look touchable.
Side light reveals texture on both surfaces.
Put the place where the two materials meet about a third of the way across the frame.
constraint: The soft material and the hard material must touch.

title: Order Versus Chaos
oneLiner: Split the frame between neat rows and a messy pile of the same stuff.
details: Use coins, pens, or buttons. Line half of them in tidy rows and heap the rest loosely. Shoot from above so the split reads instantly. The opposites should share the same objects so the joke lands.
tips: Use a contrasting background under the messy side.
Keep the dividing line roughly vertical or horizontal.
Fill the frame edge to edge.

title: Open and Shut
oneLiner: Stand an open jar beside a closed one of the same kind.
details: Use two jam jars, spice jars, or storage jars you can match for size. Leave one lid off and screw the other on. Place them side by side so the only real difference is open and shut.
tips: Get the rims at the same height in the frame.
A spoon of dry rice in the open jar makes the inside readable.
constraint: Both jars must match in size and shape.

title: Damp Beside Dry
oneLiner: Lay a damp cloth against a dry one and show both states.
details: Wet one dish towel, wring it, and set it beside a dry towel of a similar size. The damp cloth will look darker and will cling to itself. Shoot from above so the boundary between them is a clean line.
tips: Wring hard so water does not pool and reflect the ceiling.
Use two cloths of the same colour so dampness, not dye, is the difference.

title: Matte Meets Gloss
oneLiner: Pair a matte surface with a glossy one in a single close frame.
details: Try a wooden spoon on a glazed plate, or a sheet of paper next to a shiny tile. Give each material about half the picture. Move close until the two surfaces could be judged by touch.
tips: Tilt the glossy half until a window reflection sits in it.
Keep the matte half free of that same reflection.
constraint: The two surfaces should meet near the middle.

title: Curve and Line
oneLiner: Set a curved object against a hard straight edge.
details: Place a mug, a banana, or a coiled cable so it touches the straight edge of a book, a tray, or a table rim. The curve should push against the line. Shoot from above so both shapes stay fully readable.
tips: Leave the straight edge parallel to the frame.
One point of contact is clearer than a long overlap.

title: Warm Beside Cool
oneLiner: Bring a warm-toned material next to a cool-toned one.
details: Set a wooden board, a brown loaf, or a cork beside a steel spoon, a fork, or a pale tin. Ordinary window light is enough. Let the warm object and the cool one touch so neither needs a label.
tips: Avoid mixed lamp light, which can paint both objects the same yellow.
Fill the frame with the two materials and little else.
constraint: The warm object and the cool object must touch.

title: Clear and Solid
oneLiner: Place a clear glass against an opaque mug and compare them.
details: Use an empty drinking glass and a ceramic mug, or a clear bottle and a tin. Stand them so they overlap slightly. You should see the room through only one of them.
tips: A plain wall behind the glass keeps the transparency obvious.
Focus on the rim that crosses in front.

title: Sharp and Soft
oneLiner: Focus hard on one object and let the other fall completely soft.
details: Set two similar things in a line away from you, such as two mugs or two bottles. Get close to the near one and tap it so focus locks there. The far one should stay recognisable but blurry, so sharp and soft share the frame.
tips: The closer you are to the near object, the softer the far one becomes.
Rest the phone on the table so the near edge stays crisp.
constraint: Both objects must still be identifiable.

title: Tall and Short
oneLiner: Stand a tall bottle beside a short jar on the same surface.
details: Choose two containers, one clearly taller, and stand them close together. A bottle and a jam jar, or a vinegar bottle and a spice pot, both work. A plain wall behind them stops other shapes joining the comparison.
tips: Shoot from halfway up the taller object.
Keep both bases visible so the heights are fair.

title: Dust and Polish
oneLiner: Wipe one patch of a dusty surface and leave the rest untouched.
details: Find dust on a baseboard, a fridge top, or a windowsill. Clean a sharp patch with a dry cloth and stop at a straight edge. Photograph the boundary between the wiped area and the dust you left.
tips: Side light shows dust that looks invisible face-on.
Make the boundary a vertical or horizontal line.
constraint: The cleaned patch must meet the dusty patch inside the frame.

title: Heavy and Light
oneLiner: Set something heavy beside something you could blow away.
details: Pair a book, a pan, or a full bottle with a tissue, a cotton pad, or a scrap of tissue paper. Put them on the same surface so they almost touch. The heavy object should look planted and the light one ready to lift.
tips: Shoot from low so the heavy object has weight in the frame.
Do not use a fan. Still air keeps the light object where you placed it.

title: Round on Square
oneLiner: Rest a round object on a square one and keep both shapes clear.
details: Try a plate on a book, an orange on a square coaster, or a roll of tape on a tin. Shoot from above so the circle reads against the square. Crop loosely enough that neither shape is reduced to an arc or a corner.
tips: Centre the circle on the square for the clearest contrast.
A small gap of table around the square helps the outer shape.
constraint: Both the full circle and the full square must be visible.

title: Vivid and Faded
oneLiner: Match a bright cloth with a faded one of a similar size.
details: Use two towels, two shirts, or two bags, one still strong in colour and one washed pale. Fold them into similar rectangles and lay them edge to edge. Even light stops a shadow pretending to be the fade.
tips: Shoot in window light with the lamp off.
Align the folds so the eye compares colour, not shape.

title: Knot and Tail
oneLiner: Tie a knot in a cord and leave the other end loose.
details: Use a shoelace, an earphone cable, or a length of string. Knot one half tightly and let the other half sprawl. Shoot from above so the tight side and the loose side split the frame.
tips: A pale table under a dark cord keeps every loop visible.
Push the knot toward one third and let the tail occupy the rest.
constraint: Use only one cord.

title: Upright and Tipped
oneLiner: Stand one mug up and lay a matching mug on its side.
details: If you do not have two mugs, use two cups, bottles, or glasses that match. The upright one stays composed. The one on its side should show its opening, so the same object tells two postures.
tips: Stop the tipped mug with a finger while it settles, then remove your hand.
Get low enough to see into the opening.

title: One and Many
oneLiner: Set one coin apart from a heap of matching coins.
details: Make a tight heap of coins on one side of a table and place a single coin of the same type alone on the other. Leave clear space between the heap and the single. Shoot from above so many and one read at a glance.
tips: Use coins of one size so the lone one matches the heap.
A dark cloth stops silver coins melting into a pale table.
constraint: The single coin must not touch the heap.

title: Whole and Cracked
oneLiner: Show a whole cookie beside pieces broken from the same packet.
details: Snap a plain cookie, cracker, or square of chocolate with your fingers. Place the intact one next to the broken pieces so a jagged edge faces a smooth edge. Keep the crumbs. They belong to the broken side.
tips: Shoot from above on a plain board.
Put the intact cookie on the left and the pieces on the right.

title: Peeled and Whole
oneLiner: Set a peeled clove or segment beside one that is still whole.
details: Peel a garlic clove or an orange segment with your fingers, and leave a matching one unpeeled. Place them side by side on a board. The bare surface and the papery or dimpled skin are the opposites.
tips: Shoot from above so both pieces are fully visible.
A plain board stops the skins blending into the background.

title: Paint Meets Wood
oneLiner: Find the line where paint gives way to bare wood.
details: Look on a door, a window frame, a wooden spoon, or a chair for a chip, a worn corner, or an unpainted edge. Fill the frame with the boundary between coating and wood. Do not peel anything that is still firmly attached.
tips: Rake a lamp along the surface so the paint edge stands proud.
Crop tight. A whole door makes the boundary too small.

title: Cold Handle
oneLiner: Frame a metal handle against the warmer face of a door.
details: Choose any door in the home and photograph the handle where it meets the wood or the paint. Let metal take one side of the frame and the door the other. The contrast is material, so both need to be sharp.
tips: Angle off the shiny metal so your own reflection stays out.
Include the screws or the base so the handle is attached, not floating.
constraint: Metal and door surface must each occupy about half the frame.

title: Leaf on Tile
oneLiner: Lay a soft leaf against a hard tile or coaster.
details: Pick a lettuce leaf, a herb sprig or a houseplant leaf and lay it on a ceramic tile, a stone coaster or an upside-down plate. Get close so the soft leaf spreads across the hard surface and both occupy the frame. The join between leaf and tile is the picture.
tips: Shoot from a low angle so the leaf has height against the hard surface.
Focus where the leaf edge meets the tile.

title: Two Leaves
oneLiner: Lay a green leaf beside a dry brown one.
details: Take a green leaf from a lettuce, a herb or a houseplant, and a dry one from a used tea bag, a bay leaf or a plant that has dropped a leaf. Lay them side by side on a plate. Shoot from above so colour and condition are the only story.
tips: Overlap them by a finger's width so they read as a pair.
Use the same light on both so one is not simply sitting in shadow.
constraint: Only two leaves in the frame.

title: Buttoned and Open
oneLiner: Show a fastened button beside a buttonhole left open.
details: On a shirt, a coat, or a cushion cover, fasten one button and leave the next one undone. Photograph the pair so the closed button and the empty hole sit in the same frame. The cloth behind them can fall soft.
tips: Get close enough to see the stitches around the hole.
Smooth the cloth so the two states are easy to compare.

title: Half in Shade
oneLiner: Let a book shade half of a plain surface.
details: At a table, prop a book or a folder so it shades one half of a sheet of paper or the table itself. Put a small object, such as a mug or a key, on the lit half. The bright side and the shaded side should meet in a clean line.
tips: Use one lamp and switch the other lights off.
Expose for the lit half so the shade stays deep.
constraint: The boundary between light and shade must be sharp.

title: Sweet and Sharp
oneLiner: Place two spoons so one reads sweet and the other sharp.
details: Put honey, jam, or syrup in one teaspoon and pickle, mustard, or a lemon slice in the other. Set the spoons parallel on a plate so the sweet and the sharp sit in matching shapes. Leave the jars out of the frame.
tips: Shoot from above and keep the spoon handles out of the frame.
A white plate makes both colours easier to judge.

title: Front and Back
oneLiner: Show the hollow of one spoon and the back of another.
details: Lay two spoons on a cloth. Turn one so the bowl faces up and the other so the back faces up. The hollow and the dome should be obvious at a glance.
tips: Side light puts a shadow in the hollow spoon.
Keep the handles parallel so the heads are what differ.
constraint: Both spoon heads must be fully visible.

title: Raw and Toasted
oneLiner: Set an untoasted slice beside a toasted one.
details: Toast one slice of bread and leave another untoasted. If you cannot toast, use a pale cracker beside a darker rye or brown crispbread. Place them side by side on a board so colour and surface are the story.
tips: Shoot from above in even window light.
Line the crusts up so both pieces read as the same kind of food.

title: Post Meets Rail
oneLiner: Include one upright and the horizontal bar where they join.
details: Find a stair rail indoors, the joint where a chair leg meets a rung, or the bar a hand towel hangs from, where that bar meets the wall. Fill the frame with that joint so one piece runs up and down and the other runs side to side. A door edge meeting the top of a table makes the same two directions if you have no rail.
tips: Stand so the two pieces make a clear T or L.
Focus on the joint, including a bolt or a tie if one is there.
constraint: Both directions must touch inside the frame.

title: Round Knob
oneLiner: Set a round knob against a rectangular door panel.
details: Use any interior door. Frame a round handle or knob against a rectangular panel, or against the rectangle of the door itself. Get close enough that the circle is large, and keep a corner so the straight edges still read.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the door so the rectangle stays square.
Let the knob sit off the middle so the rectangle has room.

title: Flake and Intact
oneLiner: Photograph flaking paint right beside a still intact patch.
details: On a door, a windowsill, a radiator, or a tin, find paint that has cracked next to paint that is still smooth. Fill the frame with that change. Do not lift the flakes. The contrast is already there.
tips: Side light picks out raised edges that flat light hides.
Tap focus on the first broken edge.
constraint: Both conditions must be in focus.

title: Loose and Tight
oneLiner: Leave one lace loose and tie the other into a firm bow.
details: Use a pair of shoes or sneakers. Tie one lace into a normal bow and leave the other lace undone and spread out. Photograph both shoes from above so tight and loose are the whole story.
tips: Push the shoes together so the laces nearly meet.
A plain floor keeps the laces easy to follow.

title: Upside and Upright
oneLiner: Stand one cup the right way up and turn another upside down.
details: Use two matching cups, mugs, or glasses. Leave one standing normally and turn the other fully upside down beside it. Shoot from the side so the opening of one and the base of the other are both clear.
tips: A low angle shows the rim of the upright cup.
If the upside-down cup rocks, settle it before you take your hand away.

title: Ink and Blank
oneLiner: Show a written line beside a blank stretch of the same page.
details: Open a notebook or the back of an envelope. Write one short line that is not private, such as the word today, and leave the rest of the page empty. Photograph the written mark against the blank paper so both feel deliberate.
tips: Shoot from above and keep the pen out of the frame.
Angle the page if the ink reflects the window.
constraint: The writing must be your own and must not include a name.

title: Bent and Straight
oneLiner: Hold a glass of water over a straight line and show the bend.
details: Fill a clear glass with water and hold it in front of a ruled notebook, a tile line, or the straight edge of a book. The line should be visible both through the glass and beside it. Focus on the line as the water bends it.
tips: Keep your fingers at the base of the glass, out of the frame.
A plain background behind the glass makes the bend easier to see.
constraint: The bent line and the straight line must both appear.

title: Coarse and Fine
oneLiner: Put a heap of coarse grains beside a heap of fine powder.
details: On a dark plate, make one small heap of sugar, salt, or rice and another of flour or cocoa. Push them close without mixing. Shoot from a low angle so the coarse grains and the fine powder read as two different grounds.
tips: Side light shows the grains and leaves the powder softer.
Use a dry spoon for each so the heaps stay separate.

title: Thick Book, Thin Book
oneLiner: Stand a thick book beside a thin one and compare their spines.
details: Choose two books, magazines, or notebooks, one much thicker than the other. Stand them so the spines face you, or lay them so the page edges show. The difference in bulk should be obvious, with nothing else in the picture.
tips: Keep the tops level so the thickness is the only change.
Even window light stops a shadow adding a false edge.
constraint: No other objects in the frame.

title: Dim Hall, Bright Door
oneLiner: From inside, frame the darker hall against the brighter opening.
details: Open a door between a dimmer room and a brighter one, and stay on the dim side. If the rooms match, switch a lamp on beyond the door. Include a slice of the dim interior and a slice of the brighter opening, and let one side fall much darker.
tips: Expose for the bright side if you want the hall to fall into shadow.
Keep your body out of the doorway so you do not block the light.

title: Flat Light Through Glass
oneLiner: Soften an outdoor view by shooting through a sheer curtain.
details: Stay indoors and cover a window with a sheer curtain, a thin white cloth, or baking paper taped at the corners. The cloth should quiet whatever is outside, whether that is a wall, a tree, or another building. You do not need a particular kind of sky for this. Keep a little of the window frame so the softness has a border.
tips: Focus on the curtain threads, then focus past them and keep the softer frame.
Tape baking paper flat if no sheer curtain is available.
constraint: Keep the sky itself out of the frame.

title: Muted Still Life Trio
oneLiner: Arrange three grey or neutral objects into a quiet tabletop composition.
details: Choose things you already have, such as cups, a folded cloth, or a plain box, in similar tones. Space them so each shape can be read on its own. Light the group from a north-facing window, through a sheer curtain, or with bounce from a white wall. Move back until the three feel balanced.
tips: Clear brightly coloured clutter out of the background first.
Shoot from a little above the table so the gaps between objects stay clear.
constraint: Use no more than three objects.

title: Frosted Window Wash
oneLiner: Light a small bathroom object with the even glow of frosted glass.
details: Use a frosted bathroom window, a shower screen, or baking paper taped over any window. Set a cup, a bottle, or a folded white towel where that light falls and look for almost no hard shadow. If the glass is clear, hold a white shirt between the window and the object. Slide the object until its shadow nearly disappears.
tips: Turn off the bathroom bulb so it does not cut a second, harder shadow.
Move the object farther from the glass if the shadow is still sharp.
constraint: No hard-edged shadow may fall across the object.

title: Shadowless Painted Wall
oneLiner: Photograph the shaded outside wall where the light stays even.
details: Stand just outside your door and face a wall that is not in direct sun. If every wall you can see from there is bright, hold a white sheet or a shirt to block the sun and shoot in that shade. Fill the frame with the even tone of the wall. A small fixture or a hairline crack may stay, but the flat light is the subject.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the wall so the surface stays rectangular.
Tap the paint so the focus does not slip past it.
constraint: No hard shadow may cross the wall.

title: Pale Cloth Diffuser
oneLiner: Hang a pale cloth in a window and photograph the even light it makes.
details: Drape a white or light grey sheet, shirt, or dish towel over a window so the room light softens. Place one plain object, such as a bowl or a closed book, in that light and notice how little shadow it casts. Smooth the cloth if a fold tries to become the subject. You can also hold the cloth between the window and the object if you cannot hang it.
tips: Stand the object a short way in front of the cloth, not against it.
Check the shadow on the table and move the object until that shadow pales.
constraint: The cloth must be plain, with no bold pattern.

title: Bounced Desk Light
oneLiner: Bounce one lamp off a white wall so the desk light stays soft.
details: Turn the overhead lights off. Aim a desk lamp, or a separate flashlight if you have one, at a white wall, a large sheet of paper, or the ceiling, and let only the bounced light reach a notebook. The page should be readable without a hard shadow from a pen. If the shadow is still sharp, move the light farther from the wall so the source gets broader.
tips: Keep the lamp itself out of the frame so only the bounced light shows.
Use cream paper, which shows a gentle falloff more clearly than glossy paper.
constraint: The lamp must point at the wall, not at the paper.

title: Shade Past the Curtain
oneLiner: Find the soft shade just beside a window and photograph that patch.
details: Draw a sheer curtain, or tape baking paper over part of a window, and look at the floor or a chair where the light is even. That quiet shade is the subject. If a hard-edged patch of sun remains, cover more of the glass until it softens. You can set one pale object there if it helps you judge how gentle the light is.
tips: Include the boundary of the shade only if the edge stays soft.
Turn any ceiling lamp off so it does not add a second shadow.
constraint: No direct sunlit patch in the frame.

title: Veil of Baking Paper
oneLiner: Shoot a familiar object through baking paper so the tones go quiet.
details: Hold or tape a sheet of baking paper, tissue, or a thin white bag between the camera and a mug, a bottle, or a plant. The layer should lower contrast without hiding the shape. Window light or a bounced lamp can sit behind the object. If you would rather use glass, breathe on a mirror and shoot while the veil is still even.
tips: Touch the paper to the lens only if you want the veil at its strongest.
Choose a simple shape, because fine detail will not survive the paper.

title: Where the Bounce Fades
oneLiner: Photograph the soft boundary where bounced daylight fades on a wall.
details: Find a wall lit by daylight that has bounced off another wall, a sheet, or a sheer curtain. Look for the place where that light gently fades, with no hard edge. Frame the fade so both the brighter and the quieter parts show. If the edge is crisp, you are still in a direct beam, so move until it melts.
tips: Lock exposure on the middle of the fade so neither side blocks up.
Include a baseboard line so the fade has a straight reference.
constraint: The change in tone must be gradual, with no hard edge.

title: Shelf in Soft Light
oneLiner: Line up muted objects on one shelf and light them evenly.
details: Pick books, boxes, or jars in dusty blue, grey, or brown. Stand them on one shelf with small gaps and shoot straight on. Use a north window, a sheer curtain, or bounce from a white wall, and avoid glossy highlights. If a hard shadow appears, move the objects farther from the window until the light flattens.
tips: Hold the phone level with the middle of the shelf.
Remove one object if its brightness breaks the calm.
constraint: All objects must sit on one shelf level.

title: Inside a White Bowl
oneLiner: Fill a white bowl with bounced light until the shadow inside fades.
details: Set a white or cream bowl near a window, but not in a direct beam. Hold a sheet of white paper opposite the window so light bounces into the bowl. Watch the shadow inside shrink as you angle the paper. Photograph down into the bowl when the interior looks almost even.
tips: Use a matte bowl, because a glossy one will throw a hard glint.
Brace the phone on the rim only if the rim stays out of focus.
constraint: The inside of the bowl must show no black shadow.

title: Light on the Sill
oneLiner: Photograph the bare windowsill where indirect daylight falls evenly.
details: Clear a windowsill that does not get a direct beam, or draw a sheer curtain across one that does. The subject is the light lying on the sill, so leave the sill empty. Include the line where the sill meets the frame if it helps, and stop before the view outside takes over. If the light pools in a hard patch, cover more of the glass.
tips: Shoot along the sill so the tone can fade gently with distance.
Dust the sill first, or the specks will become the subject.

title: Detail in a Dark Mug
oneLiner: Show the surface of a dark mug that soft light still manages to describe.
details: Place a dark mug, a black remote, or a dark notebook by a north-facing window or behind a sheer curtain. The task is to keep the object dark and still show its rim, seam, or texture. If it turns into a flat black shape, add bounce from a white card on the shadow side. Direct sun will make this harder, so stay out of it.
tips: Tap the dark surface and raise the exposure a fraction if the detail vanishes.
Leave a pale background so the mug separates without a hard rim light.
constraint: The dark object must not become a silhouette.

title: Plane of the Bed
oneLiner: Shoot the flat plane of a made bed in indirect daylight.
details: Smooth a duvet or a sheet until it is as flat as it will go, and stand where the window light reaches it indirectly. You are photographing the even tone across that plane, so avoid a sculpted fold. A pillow edge may stay at the border for scale. If a window square of sun falls on the bed, close the curtain until the patch softens.
tips: Shoot from the foot of the bed, looking along the surface.
Smooth with your hand, then wait a second so the fabric settles.

title: Cupboard Left Ajar
oneLiner: Open a white cupboard a crack and photograph the soft light inside.
details: Choose a pale cupboard or closet near a window. Open the door only a little, so daylight leaks in and fades before the back wall. Photograph that gentle falloff on the empty interior or on one plain box. A wide-open door will look like ordinary room light, so keep the gap narrow.
tips: Put the phone partly inside the gap and shoot towards the side wall.
Empty one shelf so the falloff has a clear surface to cross.
constraint: The cupboard door must stay nearly closed.

title: Sink in Indirect Light
oneLiner: Clear the sink and photograph it in light that casts almost no shadow.
details: Empty the sink and switch the room light off. Use whatever daylight arrives through a frosted window, a net curtain, or an open door around the corner. Look at the basin and the metal for soft shading rather than bright spots. If the tap throws a hard shadow, shift until that shadow leaves the frame.
tips: Wipe droplets away so they do not sparkle harder than the basin.
Include the curve of the basin and little else.

title: Stack of Pale Plates
oneLiner: Stack pale plates near a north window and shoot the quiet rims.
details: Stack three or four white or cream plates, bowls, or saucers where the light is indirect. If the window is bright, hang a sheer cloth or baking paper over it first. Shoot from the side so the rims make soft repeated lines. The light should describe each rim without a hard shadow between them.
tips: Nudge the stack until the rims are parallel to the frame.
A side position shows the gaps better than a view from above.

title: Paper as a Bounce
oneLiner: Use a sheet of white paper to lift the shadow side of a mug.
details: Set a mug near a window so one side is brighter. Hold white paper, a napkin, or a pale book on the darker side, just out of frame, and angle it until detail returns there. You should still see which side the window is on, but the dark side should not go black. Photograph the mug once the two sides are close in tone.
tips: Move the paper in and out to watch the shadow side lift.
Keep your bouncing hand outside the frame.
constraint: The paper must stay out of the frame.

title: Milky Shower Curtain
oneLiner: Place a bottle behind a white shower curtain so the light turns milky.
details: Hang a white or pale shower curtain, or a white shirt, between a window and a bottle of shampoo or a cup. The fabric should knock the contrast down so the object looks softened rather than dramatised. Stand on the dimmer side and focus on the object through the cloth. If the cloth is patterned, fold it until a plain area covers the lens view.
tips: Pin the cloth so it stays still while you focus through it.
Focus on the bottle, not on the weave, unless the weave is all you can see.

title: Even Grey Lid
oneLiner: Photograph a closed laptop, a tin, or a grey folder in soft window light.
details: Choose a flat grey or silver surface: a closed laptop, a cookie tin, or a plain folder. Set it where daylight arrives through a curtain or from across the room, not as a direct beam. The surface should show a gentle tone from one side to the other, without a blown highlight. Angle it until any reflection of the window is broad and dull.
tips: Tilt the lid until the highlight becomes a wide soft patch.
Clean fingerprints first or they will read louder than the light.

title: Flour in Flat Light
oneLiner: Spread a little flour or rice in a dish and light it as evenly as you can.
details: Scatter flour, oats, or dry rice in a shallow dish or on a pale plate. Carry it to a spot of indirect window light, or bounce a lamp off a white wall onto it. Smooth the surface with a spoon or a card so there is no ridge throwing a shadow. The picture should look quiet and almost textureless from a short distance.
tips: Shoot from above so the surface reads as one field.
Wipe the rim of the dish so stray grains do not pull the eye.

title: Corner with Lamps Off
oneLiner: Turn every lamp off and photograph a room corner in daylight only.
details: Pick a corner that receives daylight from another part of the room rather than a direct beam. Switch every lamp off and look at how the two walls meet. The seam should be visible, but neither wall should fall into a black shadow. If one wall is much darker, bounce light into it with a white sheet held out of frame.
tips: Include equal amounts of both walls.
Stand far enough back that the corner line is straight.
constraint: No lamp may be switched on.

title: Sweater as a Tone
oneLiner: Fill the frame with a pale sweater so the picture is mostly one quiet tone.
details: Lay a light grey or cream sweater, a towel, or a pillowcase flat on the bed. Light it from a window with a sheer curtain, or with daylight bounced off a white wall. Smooth the cloth until no fold makes a dark valley. Move close so the tone fills the picture edge to edge.
tips: If a crease keeps a shadow, turn that area out of the frame.
Tap the cloth and lower the exposure if the pale tone blows out.

title: Eggs in Soft Light
oneLiner: Set eggs in a carton by a sheer curtain and keep the shadows pale.
details: Place a few eggs in a carton, or use white buttons or cotton pads in a small box if you have no eggs. Set them beside a window covered with a sheer curtain or baking paper. The shells should be separated by pale shadows, not black ones. Shoot from a low side angle so each curve gets the same soft light.
tips: A side angle shows the roundness without a hard highlight on top.
Keep the carton flap down so it does not cast a lid shadow.
constraint: The container must appear in the frame.

title: Two Mugs, One Tone
oneLiner: Place two similar mugs so flat light makes them almost merge.
details: Choose two mugs, jars, or bowls of nearly the same pale colour. Set them touching in indirect window light or in light bounced off a white wall. The aim is a picture where the gap between them is only a faint line. If a hard shadow splits them, move farther from the window or add more bounce.
tips: Match the heights by shooting from the side, not from above.
Push them until they touch, then frame out the handles if they distract.
constraint: The two objects must touch.

title: Jug in Soft Light
oneLiner: Set a pale jug by a sheer curtain and catch its dull highlight.
details: Place a pale jug, a bottle, or a vase on a table where daylight comes through a sheer curtain, or where it is bounced off a white wall. Look for a wide, dull highlight rather than a sharp white spot. If the highlight is a tiny spark, turn the jug or draw the curtain farther across. The background can be a plain wall.
tips: Turn it until the highlight is wide and soft.
Crouch to the height of the jug so the table edge stays quiet.

title: Where Wall Meets Ground
oneLiner: Find the outdoor corner where wall and ground share almost the same tone.
details: Stand just outside your door and look for open shade where the wall and the ground are similarly light or similarly dark. Shoot that meeting line so the two surfaces nearly blend. If sun hits one of them, shade both with a held sheet rather than walking away from the door. A pipe or a crack may stay, as long as the tones stay close.
tips: Expose for the lighter surface so the darker one does not block up.
Keep the meeting line near the middle so both surfaces get room.
constraint: Both the wall and the ground must appear.

title: Shirt by the Window
oneLiner: Hang a pale shirt indoors and photograph it in diffused light.
details: Hang a white or light grey shirt, a dish towel, or a pillowcase on the inside of a door or on a hanger near a window. Draw a sheer curtain, or bounce the light off a white wall, so the cloth has no hard edge of sun. Smooth it enough that the tone stays even, with only a gentle sleeve or hem for shape. Shoot straight at the cloth.
tips: Wait until the cloth stops swinging.
Fill most of the frame with fabric and keep the window frame thin.

title: Bricks Without Shadow
oneLiner: Frame outside bricks only where the mortar lines cast no hard shadow.
details: Stand just outside your door and move close to brick, concrete block, or a painted wall that sits in open shade. The mortar lines can show, but they should not throw crisp dark grooves. If the sun is raking across them, shade the patch with a sheet rather than walking off. The flatness of the light is the point, so stop when the grooves stay soft.
tips: Hold the phone square to the wall.
Tap a mortar line so the focus sits on the surface.

title: Leaves in Soft Light
oneLiner: Photograph a houseplant where the leaves throw no hard shadows.
details: Set a houseplant, a herb pot, or a leafy vegetable from the kitchen by a window covered with a sheer curtain or baking paper. The test is whether you can see the leaves clearly without black leaf-shaped shadows on the wall or on other leaves. If a hard shadow remains, move the plant farther from the glass or add another layer of cloth. Shoot a small cluster.
tips: Get close to three or four leaves rather than the whole plant.
Hold a white sheet out of frame if one edge is still harsh.
constraint: No hard-edged leaf shadow in the frame.

title: Cutlery in Soft Light
oneLiner: Lay a few spoons in soft light and keep the shadows between them pale.
details: Lay three spoons on a pale cloth where light comes through a sheer curtain or off a white card. The spoons should be readable without black gaps between them. If the shadows are hard, hold baking paper between the window and the spoons. Shoot from above so the arrangement reads at once.
tips: Separate the spoons a little so each one stays distinct.
A white card beside them will lift the darker side.
constraint: No black shadow may sit between the spoons.

title: Only Bounced Light
oneLiner: Light a plain wall with bounce alone and photograph the even tone.
details: Turn the lamps off. Let the window light a white wall, a hanging sheet, or a large piece of paper, and point the camera at a different surface that receives only that reflected light. The window itself should stay out of the frame. If the surface is too dark, move the white sheet closer until the tone lifts without a hard shadow.
tips: Lock exposure on the wall so the phone does not hunt for the window.
Move a chair out of the way if it throws a hard shadow on the wall.
constraint: The window must stay outside the frame.

title: Cushion in Soft Light
oneLiner: Smooth a plain cushion and light it so the folds stay pale.
details: Set a cushion or a pillow where daylight is diffused by a sheer curtain or bounced off a white wall. Plump it, then smooth the front so any remaining fold is gentle. The light should describe the curve without a dark valley. If a fold goes black, turn that side away or soften the light further.
tips: Shoot from slightly to the side so the curve of the cushion shows.
Lower the exposure a touch if the pale cloth starts to blow out.

title: Kettle in Soft Light
oneLiner: Photograph the kettle where a soft highlight follows its curve.
details: Set the kettle on the counter in light from a sheer curtain, a north-facing window, or a white wall used as bounce. You want a dull, wide highlight that shows the curve, not a tiny white spark. If the window is sparking off the metal, draw the curtain farther across. Fill the frame with the kettle and a little of the counter.
tips: Wipe the metal so the highlight belongs to the shape, not to a fingerprint.
Turn the kettle until the highlight wraps the curve instead of sitting in one spot.

title: Lenses in Soft Light
oneLiner: Lay a pair of glasses down and light both lenses evenly.
details: Set a pair of glasses, sunglasses, or a clear lid on a pale cloth. Use a sheer curtain or light bounced off a white wall so both lenses are easy to see. You want the frames described without a black shadow underneath. If one lens flares, tilt them until the flare becomes a dull patch.
tips: Shoot from a low side angle so the two lenses read as separate shapes.
Wipe the lenses first, or the dust will be louder than the light.
constraint: Both lenses, or the whole lid, must be in the frame.

title: Slats in Soft Light
oneLiner: Close the blinds until the slats sit in even, quiet light.
details: Use slatted blinds, a vent, or a radiator grille. Choose a patch where daylight on the slats is even, with no hard stripes of sun. Fill the frame with the repeated lines. If the sun cuts through, close the slats more or shade them with a sheer curtain.
tips: Hold the phone square to the slats so the lines stay parallel.
Wait until the slats stop moving before you shoot.
constraint: No hard stripe of sun may cross the slats.

title: Light from the Next Room
oneLiner: Open a door a little and photograph the soft light that leaks through.
details: Choose an interior door between a brighter room and a dimmer one. Open it only slightly, so daylight from the far room washes the nearer wall without a hard beam. Photograph that even glow on the wall or the floor. If a stripe of sun crosses it, close the door a little more or draw a curtain in the far room.
tips: Include the door edge only as a thin border.
Switch lamps off in both rooms so the daylight stays soft.

title: Water Without Glitter
oneLiner: Fill a bowl with water in soft light and keep hard glints out.
details: Set a bowl of water on a table lit by a sheer curtain, a north-facing window, or bounce from a white wall. Look at the surface and move until you see no sharp sparkles, only a soft dull reflection of the room. A bright spark means a direct beam is still reaching the water, so draw the curtain or shift the bowl. Angle the bowl towards a wall if the window itself appears in the reflection.
tips: Wait for the water to go still.
Shoot from a slight angle so the surface shows, rather than only the bowl's side.
constraint: The window must not appear in the reflection.

title: Colour Goes Quiet
oneLiner: Move a bright cloth into diffused light and show how the colour calms.
details: Choose something strongly coloured, such as a rubber glove, a dish towel, or a sock. Photograph it where daylight comes through a sheer curtain, baking paper, or a bounce off a white wall. The colour should still be recognisable, but quieter, with no hard shadow slicing it. If a hard edge remains, add another layer of cloth between the window and the object.
tips: Fill the frame with the coloured cloth so the calm tone is obvious.
Keep the background quiet, or the soft light will look muddy.

title: White Cup, Soft Edge
oneLiner: Place a white cup in diffused light and leave its shadow out of frame.
details: Set a white cup, a mug, or a small bowl on a table by a sheer curtain or in light bounced off white paper. Move it until the shadow falls outside the frame. A sheet of baking paper over the window will help if the light is still hard. The cup should look fully described by soft light.
tips: Get the lens near the table so the background is a plain wall.
A white cup against a mid-tone wall shows the soft edge more clearly.
constraint: The cup's shadow must fall outside the frame.

title: Ground in Even Shade
oneLiner: Look along a stretch of ground that sits in open shade.
details: Stand in your doorway and look along the floor just inside, a shared hall, or the sidewalk you can see without stepping down. Choose a stretch where the light is even, and hold the phone low so the surface recedes. Do not walk off to find a better patch. If sun covers everything within reach, shade a small area with a sheet and shoot inside that shade.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor for a steady low view.
Keep the frame on the ground and leave the far distance out.

title: Coil in Soft Light
oneLiner: Coil a scarf or a cable on the bed and keep the edges gentle.
details: Coil a scarf, a belt, or a cable on a bed or a sofa in light from a sheer curtain or bounced off a white wall. The loops should have soft edges rather than black contact shadows. If the coils cut hard shadows, move them farther from the window or diffuse the light with another cloth. Fill the frame with two or three loops.
tips: Shoot from above so the loops read clearly.
Separate the loops a little if they clump into one dark mass.

title: Even Light on a Door
oneLiner: Move close to your door and shoot the even light on one panel.
details: Use your own door, inside or just outside, and find a panel where the light is even. Move close until the surface fills the frame, and keep one hinge, panel edge or handle so it still reads as a door. The colour should be true, without a hard diagonal shadow. If sun falls across the outside of the door, shade a patch with a sheet, or move to an interior door instead.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the panel.
Crop out house numbers if they pull attention from the tone.

title: Page in Soft Light
oneLiner: Hold a printed page in diffused window light and keep the tone even.
details: Open a book, a notebook, or a printed page near a window with a sheer curtain, or in light bounced off a white wall. Photograph the paper so the tone is even from edge to edge. Words may be visible if you are content to show them. If one side of the page is brighter, turn it until both sides match.
tips: Hold the page square to the camera, or lay it on the table.
Draw the curtain farther if a bright edge creeps onto the paper.
constraint: The page must fill most of the frame.

title: Wall Leaf Shadow
oneLiner: Cast one houseplant's shadow on a plain wall and photograph the shadow.
details: Set any houseplant, or a leafy stem in a jar, a hand's width from a plain wall. Place a lamp to the side and a little below the leaves, and switch the other lights off. Move the lamp until the shadow is larger than the plant, then frame the shadow and leave most of the plant out.
tips: Expose for the wall so the shadow stays deep.
Tap the wall, not the leaves, if both are in frame.
constraint: The shadow must be larger in the frame than the plant itself.

title: Curtain Leaf Theatre
oneLiner: Shine a lamp so a plant throws its shape onto a curtain.
details: Stand a plant between a lamp and a light curtain or a sheet hung over a door. The cloth should be pale enough for the shadow to read. Move to the side and photograph the curtain, not a portrait of the plant.
tips: Pull the cloth smooth where the shadow falls.
Dim the lamp if the cloth blows out to white.

title: Herb Shadow on Tile
oneLiner: Stand a herb sprig in front of a tile and shoot only the shadow.
details: A sprig of herb, a houseplant leaf, or a weed stem from a pot will do. Lean it in a glass near the kitchen tiles and light it from the side with a lamp. Crop so the tile and the shadow fill the frame.
tips: Choose a plain tile rather than a busy pattern if you can.
Focus on the tile surface where the shadow edge is sharpest.
constraint: The sprig itself stays out of frame.

title: Shadow Across the Page
oneLiner: Let a leafy stem throw a shadow across an open book.
details: Open any book or notebook on a table under a single lamp. Hold a stem, or prop it in a jar, so the shadow falls over the page. You are photographing the shadow on the paper, so the words can go soft.
tips: Angle the page until the paper is evenly lit around the shadow.
Focus on the paper, not the stem.

title: Long Shadow on the Floor
oneLiner: Aim a low lamp so a plant draws a long shadow over the floor.
details: Put the lamp on the floor beside a plant, close to the ground, and turn the ceiling light off. The shadow should stretch away across the boards or the rug. Get down and shoot along the shadow so it runs from the plant towards the far side of the frame.
tips: Include the plant only as a small shape at one end.
Use the floorboards or the rug edge as a line beside the shadow.
constraint: The shadow must cross at least half the frame.

title: Mug in Leaf Shade
oneLiner: Place a mug where a leaf shadow breaks across the cup.
details: Set a mug, a glass, or a jar on a table and aim a lamp through a plant so the shadow stripes the cup. Turn the mug until the shadow crosses the handle or the rim. The drink inside can be anything pale, or the mug can be empty.
tips: Focus on the rim where the shadow crosses it.
Shift the lamp a little if the shadow misses the mug.

title: Crossed Plant Shadows
oneLiner: Cross two plant shadows on one wall and shoot the overlap.
details: If you have two plants, set them so their shadows meet on a wall, using one lamp. A second stem in a jar beside the main plant works if you only have one pot. Look for the darker patch where the shadows overlap, and make that the centre.
tips: Switch off every light except the lamp.
Place the overlap away from the middle of the frame.
constraint: Both shadows must be visible, and they must touch.

title: Ceiling Leaf Map
oneLiner: Set a lamp on the floor and throw a plant shadow onto the ceiling.
details: Put a lamp low, just beyond a plant, and aim it upward so the leaves map onto the ceiling. Close the curtains if the ceiling is too bright for the shadow to show. Rest the phone on a table aimed up, or hold it high, and frame the ceiling shadow with only a hint of the plant at the bottom.
tips: Expose for the ceiling, or the shadow will look washed out.
A portrait frame gives a long leaf room to stretch.

title: Bright Dot in the Shadow
oneLiner: Choose a leaf with a hole and catch the bright dot inside its shadow.
details: Look for a leaf that already has a small hole or a torn edge. Cast its shadow on a pale wall with a lamp close to the leaf so the hole becomes a bright dot in the dark shape. If every leaf is whole, overlap two leaves and leave a small gap that lights up in the shadow.
tips: Move the lamp closer to make the dot sharper.
Focus on the wall at the bright dot.
constraint: The bright gap must sit inside the shadow.

title: Stem Shadow Lines
oneLiner: Crop a plant shadow until only thin stems cross the frame.
details: Use a plant with visible stems, or a few twigs standing in a jar. Aim a lamp from the side, or stand them in daylight from a window, so the stems throw lines onto a plain wall or a sheet of paper. Crop tight so the picture is lines, not a full leafy shape. The lamp or the window supplies the light, so you are not waiting on sunshine.
tips: A sheet of white paper taped to the wall makes a clean ground.
Keep the stems themselves just outside the frame.

title: Shadow on a Shirt
oneLiner: Drape a plain shirt and cast a plant shadow over the cloth.
details: Hang a pale shirt, a dish towel, or a pillowcase over a chair back. Place a lamp to the side, or stand the chair near a bright window, so the shadow falls on the cloth rather than the wall. Folds in the fabric can bend the shadow, and that bend is worth keeping.
tips: Use a pale cloth so the shadow does not disappear.
Focus on the cloth where a leaf edge crosses a fold.
constraint: The plant stays outside the frame.

title: Keyboard in Leaf Shade
oneLiner: Let a plant shadow fall across a keyboard in a dim room.
details: Set a lamp to one side of a small plant on the desk and aim the shadow over the keys. Turn the screen away or switch it off so it does not compete. The letters on the keys can show through the shadow.
tips: Lower the lamp until the shadow edges look crisp on the keys.
Tap a key that sits under a leaf edge.

title: Shadow Down the Spines
oneLiner: Send a leaf shadow down a short stack of books.
details: Stack three or four books, or stand them in a row, on a table against a wall. Place a stem so its shadow falls down the spines like a vine. One lamp from above and to the side will do the throwing.
tips: Line the books up so the shadow has a clear path.
Expose for the book edges, which are often brighter than the shadow.
constraint: The shadow must touch at least two books.

title: Shadow on Its Pot
oneLiner: Light a plant so its leaves shadow the outside of their pot.
details: Move a lamp low and to the side until the leaves throw shapes onto their own pot. A pale pot shows this best, so slip a sheet of paper around a dark pot if you need to. Shoot close, with the soil only a thin band at the top.
tips: Rotate the pot until a strong leaf shape lands on the near side.
Focus on the pot, not the leaf above it.

title: Pillow Under Leaf Shade
oneLiner: Lay a pillow flat and cover it with the shadow of a ferny leaf.
details: A pillow, a cushion, or a folded pale towel on the bed will hold the shadow. Use a feathery leaf if you have one, or any leaf with a strong outline. Light it with a lamp from the side of the bed, or set the pillow near a window and let the daylight cast the shadow, then shoot from above.
tips: Smooth the pillow so the shadow is not lost in creases.
Fill the frame with the pillow and the shadow.
constraint: Shoot from above, with the pillow filling the frame.

title: Fridge Door Shadow
oneLiner: Throw a houseplant shadow onto the fridge door.
details: Stand a plant on the counter beside the fridge, or hold a stem just out of frame. Use a lamp from the kitchen side so the shadow lands on the door. Move notes aside if they break the shape, and hide any name.
tips: The fridge surface is shiny, so angle the lamp until the glare leaves the shadow.
Focus on the door at the sharpest leaf tip.

title: Spoon in Leaf Shade
oneLiner: Rest a spoon where a leaf shadow can stripe it.
details: Lay a spoon on a pale plate or the table. With a lamp, or with the spoon placed in window light, cast a leaf shadow across the metal so part of the spoon is in shade and part is bright. The curve of the spoon will bend the shadow a little.
tips: Watch the highlight on the metal and move until it does not eat the shadow.
Get close enough to see the shadow edge on the metal.
constraint: The spoon and the shadow must both be in the frame.

title: Grout Breaks the Shadow
oneLiner: Break a leaf shadow across bathroom tiles so the grout interrupts it.
details: Take a small plant or a stem into the bathroom and light it with a lamp against the wall tiles, or hold the stem in window light if the tiles face a window. Find a spot where the shadow crosses a grout line and the line slices the leaf shape. A kitchen tile wall works if the bathroom is too tight.
tips: Turn off the bright mirror lights if they flatten the shadow.
Square the phone to the tiles so the grout stays straight.

title: Fruit Under a Leaf
oneLiner: Set an apple or a tomato where a leaf shadow crosses the fruit.
details: Any single fruit or vegetable with a smooth skin will do. Put it on a plate and cast a leaf shadow over the top so the shape wraps the curve. A lamp from the side, close to the leaf, keeps the edge sharp.
tips: Focus on the fruit skin where the shadow bends.
Use a plain plate so the shadow has somewhere to continue.
constraint: Only one piece of fruit or vegetable.

title: Laptop Lid Shadow
oneLiner: Close a laptop and cast a plant shadow on the lid.
details: A closed laptop, a tin, or a pale box lid gives you a plain panel. Set a plant beside it and use a lamp, or daylight from a window, so the shadow falls on that panel. Keep the screen shut so no words join the picture.
tips: Angle the lid until reflections slide off the shadow.
Crop tight to the lid.

title: Bent Shadow in Water
oneLiner: Stand a glass of water in a plant shadow and shoot the bent shape.
details: Cast a clear leaf shadow across the table with one lamp. Set a glass of water in the path of that shadow and look for the place where the shadow kinks. Photograph the table and the glass together so the bend is obvious.
tips: Focus on the table where the shadow changes direction.
Wipe the glass if drips confuse the shape.
constraint: The bent part of the shadow must be visible.

title: Giant Close Shadow
oneLiner: Bring the lamp close so a small sprig throws a giant shadow.
details: A single small leaf or a herb sprig is enough. Put it very near a pale wall and bring the lamp close to the leaf, on the side away from the wall. The shadow should grow much bigger than the sprig.
tips: Start with the lamp close to the leaf, then ease back until the shape is sharp.
Leave a little of the sprig in a corner so the scale is clear.

title: Slat-Broken Shadow
oneLiner: Cast a leaf shadow through blind slats or a slatted chair.
details: Venetian blinds, a slatted chair, or a colander held between a lamp and the wall will slice a plant shadow into bands. A bright window works if you have no lamp to hand. Put the slats between the plant and a pale wall or the floor, and photograph the broken shadow.
tips: Line the slats so they run across the leaf shape, not along it.
Expose for the bright bands between the slices.
constraint: The shadow must be broken into at least three pieces.

title: Softened Leaf Shadow
oneLiner: Soften a plant shadow by hanging thin cloth between the lamp and the plant.
details: A dish towel, a tissue, or a thin sock stretched over the lamp will do, as long as it cannot touch a hot bulb. Leave a gap so the cloth never rests on the lamp. The shadow on the wall should have a fuzzy edge rather than a hard one.
tips: Move the cloth until the shadow edge looks fuzzy, then take the picture.
Keep the cloth out of the frame.
constraint: The cloth must not touch the bulb.

title: Shadow on Your Arm
oneLiner: Lay your forearm down and let a leaf shadow fall across the skin.
details: Rest your forearm on a table, prop a leaf in a jar beside it, and cast the shadow with a lamp. Use your other hand for the phone, or the timer. Keep your face out, and let the shadow be the subject rather than a picture of an arm.
tips: Focus on the skin where the leaf edge is sharpest.
A side lamp will show the shadow better than a ceiling light.

title: Sink Basin Shadow
oneLiner: Direct a plant shadow into the basin of a sink.
details: A kitchen or bathroom sink is a pale bowl that can hold a shadow. Prop a stem at the edge and light it with a lamp, or with daylight from a window, so the shape falls down the inside of the basin. Shoot from above, including the rim as a frame.
tips: Dry the basin so water highlights do not cut the shadow.
Turn off the overhead light so it does not wash the shadow out.
constraint: The shadow must fall inside the basin, not only on the rim.

title: Milled Coin Edge
oneLiner: Stand a coin on its rim and photograph the milled edge.
details: Empty a pocket onto a table and pick one coin. Prop it in a fold of paper so the ridged rim faces you. Move until those ridges become a rhythm across the frame.
tips: Rest your wrist on the table before you shoot.
Tap the nearest ridge rather than the tabletop.
constraint: The coin must fill at least half the frame.

title: Receipt in a Spiral
