oneLiner: Let a receipt curl into a spiral and shoot along that curl.
details: Thermal paper from a pocket often bends into a tube. Place it on a plain surface and look down the spiral so the layers repeat. Turn printed words inward so the paper shape leads and any name stays hidden.
tips: Side light from a window will separate each layer.
Leave the curl as it wants to sit.

title: Lint Nest
oneLiner: Gather the lint from one pocket and light it from the side.
details: Turn a pocket out over a dark plate or a dark cloth. Pile the fluff so it has a little height. Get close and low until fibres catch the light and the pile has a small horizon.
tips: A desk lamp from the side is enough for this pile.
Tap the brightest fibre, not the dark cloth.
constraint: Use a dark background so the lint stays readable.

title: Elastic Loop
oneLiner: Place a hair tie or rubber band on a plain surface and square it.
details: A hair tie, a rubber band, or a loop of string will do. Lay it so the loop is nearly a circle, with the knot or the metal join at the top. Come close enough that the band has thickness, not just an outline.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the table.
Put the knot near a grid intersection.

title: Button Face
oneLiner: Find a loose button and fill the frame with its face and holes.
details: Check pocket corners, a drawer, or the tin where spare buttons end up. Any spare button works. Light it from one side so the holes sink a little and the rim catches a line.
tips: Prop the phone on a mug if your hand wobbles this close.
Focus on the near rim of one hole.
constraint: Crop so the button dominates a plain field.

title: Bent Clip
oneLiner: Give a paperclip one bend, then photograph the crooked shape.
details: A paperclip from a pocket or a junk drawer is enough. Give it one gentle bend so it is no longer a plain loop, or choose one that is already crooked. Lay it on pale paper and shoot from above so the wire reads as a single line.
tips: Lift a corner of the paper if you want a cleaner ground.
Focus on the bend itself.

title: Tissue Peak
oneLiner: Crush a clean pocket tissue into a peak and shoot the ridges.
details: An unused tissue is kinder to the lens than a used one. Crush it lightly, then open it just enough to leave one sharp ridge. Low side light will turn the folds into a small range of slopes.
tips: Come down to the height of the tissue.
Lock exposure on the brightest ridge so the hollows stay dark.
constraint: One tissue only, with the packet kept out.

title: Foil Wrapper Map
oneLiner: Smooth a candy wrapper just enough to keep the creases.
details: A foil or plastic wrapper from a pocket holds a map of creases. Flatten it with one palm, not perfectly, and lay it under window light. Look for a highlight that runs along a fold and place that highlight near the middle.
tips: Shift the wrapper until glare sits on one crease only.
Tap that lit crease to focus.

title: Knotted Band
oneLiner: Twist a rubber band into a knot and photograph the knot close up.
details: If you have no rubber band, a hair tie or a loop of string will knot the same way. Tighten it until the knot is dense. Fill the frame with the crossing strands and the tiny dark gaps inside them.
tips: Weigh a loose end with a coin so the knot sits still.
Come closer instead of using digital zoom.
constraint: Sit the knot in the middle third of the frame.

title: Pocket Grit
oneLiner: Tip a pocket onto dark paper and keep only the grit and dust.
details: Brush the larger objects aside. What remains is sand, crumbs, thread, and grey dust. Spread it thinly so the specks have space, then get close. The picture is the scatter, not a single grain.
tips: Shoot from directly above so the specks stay a similar size.
Tap the screen on a larger crumb.

title: Pin Spring
oneLiner: Close a safety pin and photograph the tight coil at one end.
details: A safety pin is a common pocket find, and a hair pin will also do. Lay it on paper and move in until the coil or the bend fills the frame. You want metal thickness and the little gap, not the whole pin as a distant line.
tips: Tilt the pin if a blob of glare sits on the coil.
Brace both elbows on the table.
constraint: Metal and the plain paper beneath, nothing else.

title: Lonely Pen Cap
oneLiner: Stand a pen cap on its clip and shoot that small upright shape.
details: Pen caps detach and live in pockets. Stand the cap on its clip, or lay it so the clip makes a strong curve if it will not balance. Use a plain book or a wall behind it and leave open space on one side.
tips: Get down to the height of the cap.
Focus where the clip meets the plastic.

title: Turned-Away List
oneLiner: Fold a pocket note so the writing faces down and shoot the paper.
details: A shopping list or a crumpled reminder works. Fold it so the words are hidden and the outside shows creases, fibre, and a soft edge. Place it near a window and photograph the stack of folds.
tips: Check the screen for any readable line and refold if you see one.
Hold the phone square to the paper.
constraint: No readable writing in the picture.

title: Cap Ridges
oneLiner: Turn a bottle cap upside down and fill the frame with the ridges.
details: A metal cap from a pocket shows a ring of ridges around a printed disc. Shoot from above, slightly off vertical, so the ridges catch light on one side. Let the printed middle go soft so any branding falls out of importance.
tips: Try portrait mode only if the ridges stay crisp.
Wipe the cap if it is sticky.

title: Screw Thread
oneLiner: Lay a small screw so the thread becomes a repeating pattern.
details: Small hardware often rides home in a pocket. If you have no screw, a bolt or the threaded neck of a jar will show the same grooves. Light it from the side and shoot along the thread so the ridges repeat.
tips: Roll it until a highlight runs along the top.
Tap the nearest groove.
constraint: The thread must run from edge to edge.

title: Uneven Stack
oneLiner: Stack two or three coins so each one sticks out a little.
details: Use whatever coins were in the pocket, even if the sizes differ. Offset each coin so a rim and a sliver of face still show. Shoot from a low side angle so the stack has height and the table is only a line.
tips: Steady the stack with a fingertip kept out of frame.
If the coins go dark, tap a bright rim and ease exposure only a touch.

title: Tangled Pair
oneLiner: Leave a button and an elastic tangled, and shoot them as found.
details: Do not tidy the knot. Drop them on a plain cloth and move around until both objects are readable. The point is that they shared a pocket, so neither one may hide completely.
tips: Circle the pair and choose the side with the least overlap.
Focus where the elastic crosses the button.
constraint: Do not rearrange the tangle before you shoot.

title: Found Order
oneLiner: Line up one pocket's contents in the order you pulled them out.
details: Reach in and place each item in a row as it appears. Slip any card or folded note that shows a name back into the pocket before you shoot. If the pocket is nearly empty, two honest items are enough. Shoot from above so each object sits separate.
tips: Keep the phone parallel to the table so sizes stay honest.
Leave a little bare table at both ends of the row.

title: Crumb and Thread
oneLiner: Choose the two smallest things from the pocket and pair them.
details: A crumb, a seed, a bit of thread, or a speck of grit will do. Pick the two tiniest and set them close, but not touching, on a dark surface. Come near until they feel large, with empty surface around them.
tips: Brace the phone on a short stack of books.
Use the window and switch the overhead light off so the colour stays even.
constraint: Both objects sharp, with nothing else in the frame.

title: Bobby Pin Curve
oneLiner: Lay a hair pin on pale paper and let its curve cross the frame.
details: A bobby pin or any small bent wire from a pocket will do. Place it on a diagonal. Move close so the metal has width and the open end stays fully inside the picture.
tips: A diagonal gives the curve room to travel.
Tilt the paper until a bright reflection leaves the metal.

title: Bag Clip Teeth
oneLiner: Photograph the teeth of a bread-bag clip from very close.
details: These clips hide in pockets after shopping. If yours has a hinge, open it so the teeth face you. Any small plastic clip with ridges will do if you cannot find one. Side light and a plain background will separate tooth from tooth.
tips: Fill the view with the toothed edge.
Tap the tooth nearest the lens.
constraint: Crop out any printed logo.

title: Worn Eraser
oneLiner: Shoot the worn face of a pencil eraser that lived in a pocket.
details: The worn face is often shiny, stained, or rounded. Stand the pencil so that face points towards you, or lay a loose eraser on paper. Come close until the scuffs fill the view.
tips: Light from the side to show the shine on the rubber.
If the pencil rolls, nest it in a fold of paper.

title: Stuck Sticker
oneLiner: Find a sticker that has folded onto itself and shoot the curl.
details: Pocket stickers glue themselves shut. Place the curl on a dark notebook and look for the glossy lip. You are after the loop of paper and the sticky edge, so turn any printed face away.
tips: Set a lamp low beside it so the curl gets a bright rim.
Focus on the outermost edge of the loop.
constraint: No readable print and no brand mark.

title: Seam Fluff
oneLiner: Pull the wisp that gathers in a pocket seam and photograph it.
details: Turn a pocket inside out and look along the seam. A little cotton usually sits there. Leave it attached if you can, and shoot the wisp against the pocket cloth. If the pocket is bare, use a loose thread from the same clothing.
tips: Stretch the cloth with your free hand kept outside the frame.
Tap the thread, not the weave behind it.

title: Twisted Wrapper Ends
oneLiner: Keep a wrapped candy whole and frame the two twisted ends.
details: The wrapper ends are the picture: two twists and the barrel between them. Set the candy on a plain plate. Turn it until both twists catch a little light and the printed middle matters least.
tips: Get down to the height of the plate.
Focus on the nearer twist.
constraint: Both twists must sit fully inside the frame.

title: Paper Grain
oneLiner: Move in on the fibres of a blank stretch of receipt.
details: Lay the receipt flat under a window. Choose a faded patch or a blank margin so the paper fibres lead, and let any words fall at the edge of the picture. Crop out barcodes and anything that looks like a name.
tips: Skim the light across the paper so the fibres stand up.
Hold the phone parallel so the grain stays even.

title: Nothing Along the Sidewalk
oneLiner: Look along the sidewalk and show a stretch with nothing moving.
details: Stand on the sidewalk near home and aim along it so the slabs run between the fronts. The picture is that stillness: a street that has gone quiet, whether the buildings are houses, apartments, or shops. Keep the picture on the sidewalk and the fronts beside it. If a walker enters, pause for a moment or shorten the frame to the clear part nearer you.
tips: Hold the phone level with the line of the fronts so the view does not tilt.
Early or late helps, but a short clear run is enough at any hour.
constraint: The sidewalk and the fronts should fill the picture.

title: Shutter on the Corner
oneLiner: Find a closed shopfront and photograph the stillness in front of it.
details: From the sidewalk, frame a shop with the shutter down, the hatch shut, or the door closed and the display dark. Include the clear slabs in front so the picture is a place at rest, not a study of the lock. If no shop is near, use a row of unopened front doors and the empty sidewalk along them, which carries the same pause.
tips: Stand a little aside so any glass does not give you back your own face.
Let the sidewalk in front take as much room as the closed front.

title: Bench with No One
oneLiner: Show an empty bench as a small pause in the street.
details: On the sidewalk near home, or on a shared path you may use, find a bench with a clear seat. Frame it from the side or from behind so the empty seat is the point, with sidewalk or path around it. If you have no bench, use a low wall that is already used as a seat, or a chair left outside a shop.
tips: Crouch until the seat sits against a plain stretch of paving.
If anyone nears the seat, let them move on before you shoot.
constraint: The seat must be empty.

title: Quiet Between Buildings
oneLiner: Stand at the mouth of a gap and frame the stillness inside it.
details: From the sidewalk, look into the space between two buildings, or between a block and a wall, without stepping in if you cannot see the ground. Let the two sides hold a quiet slot, and include only the depth you can already see. If your home has no such gap, frame the open interval between your entrance and the next front.
tips: A vertical hold suits a tall narrow slot.
Expose for the shade in the gap so it keeps a little detail.
constraint: The near mouth of the gap must stay in the frame.

title: Street Through Glass
oneLiner: From indoors, photograph the quiet street and keep the glass in the picture.
details: Stand inside at a window that faces the sidewalk or the path outside your building. Include a trace of frame, sill, or faint reflection so the pane is part of the picture, a layer between you and the calm outside. Choose a patch that is already still. If a walker crosses that patch, wait a moment instead of hunting a longer clear view.
tips: Tap the scene outside, then look again to see whether the pane adds a second layer.
Switch the room lamp off if your reflection swallows the street.

title: Bicycle Left Behind
oneLiner: Frame a parked bicycle as the only thing waiting on the sidewalk.
details: From the sidewalk, find a bicycle left against a railing, a stand, or a wall near home. Give it room so it reads as something left in a quiet patch, not a close look at the lock. If none is parked within a short walk on the sidewalk, a scooter left in the same way can take its place.
tips: Shoot from the side so both wheels and the frame make one clear shape.
Step sideways if your shadow falls across the bicycle.
constraint: Include the empty sidewalk around the bicycle.

title: Sidewalk Running On
oneLiner: Let an empty sidewalk lead the eye away from where you stand.
details: Stand on the sidewalk and lower the phone toward your waist so the near slabs grow large and the sidewalk runs on. This is the empty way itself, seen as a long quiet surface. End the frame on the sidewalk itself, before the view opens past the fronts, and if the distance is full, stop the picture at the nearest corner where the slabs are clear.
tips: Turn the grid on and set the sidewalk edges along two of the lines.
A slight crouch makes the near ground feel wider and calmer.

title: Fronts All Shut
oneLiner: Line up a row of closed entrances along a hushed stretch of sidewalk.
details: From the sidewalk, look along doors that repeat: a short row, a block of apartments, or two or three houses. A slight angle lets them recede while the sidewalk stays along the bottom. You only need a few. Stop before the row runs into a part of the street that will not settle.
tips: Shift sideways so your shadow misses the nearest door.
Match the phone to the verticals so the door heads stay level.

title: The Long Window View
oneLiner: Catch a long view down the street from inside, with nothing in motion.
details: From a window, aim along the sidewalk so it runs into the distance between the fronts. A house, an apartment, or a landing window all work, as long as the phone stays in the room. The calm comes from watching the street rather than standing in it. If the far end will not clear, keep only the nearer half, where the slabs and walls are already still.
tips: Rest the top edge of the phone against the frame to steady the long view.
A horizontal hold gives the street room to run.
constraint: The phone stays inside the room.

title: Across the Fronts
oneLiner: Stand on the sidewalk and show light laid across a row of fronts.
details: Face the buildings from the sidewalk and look for light resting on walls, doors, or upper windows. Houses, apartments, and a mixed row all count, and you do not need bright sun. Keep a band of sidewalk at the bottom so the lit fronts belong to a quiet street. Crop in until the bit you can see is still.
tips: Turn until the light skims along the wall and gives it a little shape.
Shoot toward the light, or step aside, so your shadow stays out.

title: Shelter at Ease
oneLiner: Photograph an empty bus shelter from the sidewalk beside it.
details: If a shelter stands on your way from home, frame the empty seat, the pale interior, and the clear sidewalk around it. Stay beside it on the sidewalk, and aim along the shelter so the picture is the waiting place at rest. If there is no shelter, use a doorway recess or a covered entrance that is empty in the same way.
tips: Include the seat or ledge so the emptiness has a place to belong.
Step under the shelter only when it sits fully on the sidewalk and is clear.
constraint: The shelter or recess must be empty.

title: One Quieter Window
oneLiner: Pick out one window that sits quieter than the rest of the row.
details: From inside, look across at the fronts you can see. Choose one window that is lit, curtained, or simply darker than the others, and let that single note sit in a larger still front. Photograph the glass, not the room behind it. Keep any movement on the sidewalk below out of the frame.
tips: Turn your own lamp off so the pane does not mirror the room.
If the chosen window is bright, lower the exposure until the glow keeps its shape.
constraint: Only one window should feel like the subject.

title: The Quiet Way Through
oneLiner: Follow a quiet path near home and show it empty from end to end.
details: Use the sidewalk along your building, or a shared path you are allowed to be on. Stand there and let it lead through the quiet stretch, with doors or walls at the sides. A way through a block works the same if that is the path you can use. End the frame where the path is clear.
tips: Chest height keeps this as a calm walk rather than a steep view of the ground.
If anyone comes along the path, let them go and then shoot.

title: Paused in the Doorway
oneLiner: Stay in your doorway and frame the still street beyond the threshold.
details: Stand in the open doorway of your house or apartment and look out along the sidewalk. The door frame can edge the picture, a held view of the quiet outside. Keep the frame on the sidewalk and the fronts. If the distance will not settle, stop at the first clear stretch.
tips: Lean a shoulder on the frame so the hold stays steady.
Try a vertical frame so the doorway borders a narrow quiet view.
constraint: Keep your feet at the threshold.

title: The Street in a Lull
oneLiner: From your window, catch the sidewalk in a brief quiet lull.
details: Look out from inside and watch for a gap in the walking on the sidewalk below, which usually comes if you give it a moment. Frame that cleared stretch with a door, a corner, or the line of the front. A higher window looks down; a lower one looks along. You stay in the room.
tips: Pre-focus on the sidewalk so you can shoot as soon as the lull arrives.
Include one closed entrance so the empty stretch has a scale.

title: Knee Height, Empty Way
oneLiner: Get low and let the empty slabs fill the foreground.
details: From the sidewalk, drop to about knee height and aim along the sidewalk so the nearest slabs become a wide quiet plane. The low view hides a lively distance and keeps the picture on the ground beside you. Stay crouched on the sidewalk, and leave your shoes just outside the frame.
tips: Rest an elbow on your knee so the low angle does not wander.
Focus on the near slabs and let the far end soften.
constraint: Shoot from about knee height or lower.

title: Light on Opposite Fronts
oneLiner: Watch light fall across the fronts opposite and leave the street still.
details: From inside, find light on the outside of the walls and doors across the way, and keep the sidewalk in the frame beneath them. Stay with those fronts, and do not include a view into any room. The light can be soft or hard, and you are not waiting on sunshine. Frame that quiet row and crop away any movement at the edges.
tips: Put the band of light on a grid line so the fronts stack cleanly.
If the pane reflects the room, move to the other side of the window.

title: Around the Quiet Turn
oneLiner: Frame the corner where the sidewalk turns and nothing comes back.
details: Walk only as far as the next corner you can reach on the sidewalk. Stand so the sidewalk runs out of sight, and shoot when that turn is clear. The quiet is the fact that nothing comes around it. If a walker appears, the corner usually empties again after a short pause.
tips: Place the turn slightly off the middle so the near sidewalk leads into it.
Keep the phone upright so the walls stay vertical.

title: Path from the Window
oneLiner: Look down from indoors onto a shared path with no one on it.
details: From a window, frame the sidewalk below or a shared path beside the building, without going out. Let that path be the quiet line through the view. Whatever you look onto, a short clear stretch is enough.
tips: A higher window can hold the whole path; a lower one can hold a short clear run.
Tap the path itself so the near frame does not steal the focus.
constraint: The path should run from the near edge toward a bend or an end.

title: Looking Back Home
oneLiner: Walk a short way along and look back at your entrance across empty sidewalk.
details: Walk a few paces along the sidewalk and turn toward your own door or block entrance. The sidewalk between you and home is the quiet part of the picture. Apartments, houses, and a shop-fronted block all work. If a walker fills that gap, wait until it clears.
tips: Eye height makes the look back feel like a natural glance.
Give the empty sidewalk a generous share of the frame.
constraint: Your own entrance must appear in the frame.

title: Shutter Across the Way
oneLiner: Frame a closed shutter on the far side, seen from your room.
details: From inside, find a shop shutter, a garage door, or a closed hatch across the way or along the block. The closed face and the empty sidewalk in front of it should read as one quiet fact. Keep to that closed surface, with no room visible through the glass. If nothing like that faces you, use a run of shut entrance doors and the clear sidewalk beneath the window.
tips: Move closer to the glass if you want the shutter larger, rather than pinching the view.
Keep a strip of sidewalk under the shutter so it sits in the street.

title: The Side Turning
oneLiner: From the main sidewalk, frame a quieter side turning with no one in it.
details: Stand on the sidewalk you started from and look into a narrower side sidewalk, without stepping off. The picture is that quieter branch: fronts closer, ground empty. If you have no side turning, frame the recess of your own entrance from a few paces away, a small pocket of the same calm.
tips: Hold the phone at chest height so the side way reads as a path.
End the frame before the side way opens onto a busier stretch.
constraint: The side way in the frame must be empty.

title: Slot from the Sill
oneLiner: Use the window to frame the quiet gap between two buildings.
details: From inside, find the narrow opening between two blocks, two houses, or a house and a wall. Let the window edges echo that slot, so the picture is the quiet held between solid sides. If your view has no gap, frame the space between two shut doors or two dark windows on the front you can see.
tips: Turn the phone upright so the slot can run tall.
Focus on the far end of the gap and let the near frame go soft.
constraint: Both sides of the gap must appear.

title: Glass Door, Quiet Lobby
oneLiner: Through your block's glass entrance, show a lobby with nobody in it.
details: If you live in a block with a glass entrance, stand on the sidewalk outside and frame the quiet lobby: the floor, an inner door, a light left on. Do not go in for the picture, and wait if anyone is in there. If your door is solid, open it and frame the empty hall from the threshold, then close it again.
tips: Angle the phone so your reflection is not the brightest shape in the glass.
Focus a little beyond the pane so the lobby reads more clearly than the door.

title: Lamp Off, Street Clear
oneLiner: Switch off the lamp and let the quiet outside show through the glass.
details: Stand at the window and turn off the lights behind you so the street shows more clearly than your reflection. Frame a still stretch of sidewalk and front, at whatever hour it is. A small clear patch is enough, even in the middle of the day. If a walker crosses it, shoot the gap after they leave.
tips: Lean the phone on the sill if the room is dim and the hold needs help.
Tap the sidewalk, then lift the exposure a touch if the street looks sunk.
constraint: The room lights stay off.

title: Walkway of Shut Doors
oneLiner: Along an outdoor walkway, frame a run of shut apartment doors and clear floor.
details: If your building has an open walkway or a shared landing you may use, stand there and look along the closed doors. The clear floor and the repeated shut doors are the quiet. If you live in a house, do the same from the sidewalk with the nearest run of closed front doors. Stay where the footing is level, and keep well back from any rail.
tips: A slight angle gives the doors depth without losing the floor.
A brief pause is usually enough for the walkway to clear.
constraint: Every door in the frame should be shut.

title: Curtain and the Street
oneLiner: Part a curtain and let it border a still view of the sidewalk.
details: Draw a curtain or blind aside just enough to see the sidewalk outside. The cloth becomes the near edge of a quiet street picture. Keep the view simple: sidewalk, a front, and the calm between them. If the outside will not settle, narrow the gap until only a clear slice remains.
tips: Focus beyond the cloth so the street is the sharp part.
A sheer curtain can stay in the picture if the sidewalk is still readable through it.
constraint: The curtain or blind must touch one edge of the frame.

title: One Window Apart
oneLiner: Find one window that feels apart from the quiet row around it.
details: From the sidewalk, look at a block or a run of homes and choose a single window that is lit, curtained, or darker than the others. Frame enough of the front that the one window feels like a small event in a still street. Keep to the glow or the curtain, not a view into the room. The sidewalk along the bottom shows where you stood.
tips: Daylight is fine if the odd window is curtained rather than lit.
Tap that window, then check the rest of the front has not gone muddy.
constraint: Do not show the inside of the room.

title: Straight Down to Empty
oneLiner: Aim steeply down from the window onto a clear patch of sidewalk.
details: From inside, point the phone down at the sidewalk directly outside, as an upper window allows. The joints, the empty slabs, and perhaps the corner of an entrance are the whole quiet map. A lower window can tilt down more gently. This patch is enough; you do not need the length of the street to clear.
tips: Touch the phone lightly to the glass if your hands will not settle.
Fill the frame with paving so the picture stays on that quiet ground.

title: A Clear Stretch
oneLiner: Take the next clear stretch of sidewalk and make that the whole picture.
details: On the sidewalk near home, find a few metres that are already empty and photograph just that, with your building alongside. Early or late makes it easier, and so does ending the frame at a wall. If a walker comes into the frame, let them leave and use the lull that follows.
tips: Stand side-on to the building so the clear stretch runs across the frame.
Include one shut door so the emptiness has something to be next to.

title: Where It Bends Away
oneLiner: From inside, follow the sidewalk until it bends out of sight.
details: Look for the place where the sidewalk turns a corner and disappears, seen from your window. Nothing needs to come around that bend; the stillness is the point. Frame the turn with the near sidewalk leading in. If your street is straight, use the point where it vanishes behind a building, and keep the phone indoors.
tips: Set the bend near a third so the eye has somewhere to travel.
If something rounds the corner, wait for the empty turn to return.

title: Light on the Upper Fronts
oneLiner: Show brightness resting on the upper fronts above a quiet sidewalk.
details: From the sidewalk, frame the upper walls where the light sits, and the sidewalk below in relative shade. Any hour works, and the sky is not the subject. The still fronts over the empty slabs are the picture, so aim up from where you stand.
tips: Expose for the brighter wall so the shaded sidewalk keeps some tone.
Give the sidewalk at least the lower third.

title: Bench in the View
oneLiner: Include an empty bench as a small still note in the view from home.
details: From your window, find a bench or a shelter seat along the sidewalk. Leave it small inside a wider quiet view, a pause in the street rather than a portrait of the seat. If none is visible, a single bicycle or a shut entrance can be that small note instead. Stay indoors.
tips: Step back from the glass so more of the surrounding sidewalk can enter.
Check the seat is clear, then shoot before the view changes.
constraint: That bench, bicycle, or entrance stays under a third of the frame.

title: Only Your Shoes
oneLiner: Set your shoes at the frame edge and the empty sidewalk beyond them.
details: Stand on the sidewalk and tilt the phone just enough to catch the toes of your own shoes at the bottom, with the clear sidewalk running away. The shoes mark where you stopped; the stillness beyond them is the subject. If the distance fills, raise the angle so the frame ends on the empty slabs nearer your feet.
tips: A short timer lets you settle the angle and then look along the sidewalk.
Wipe the lens if the near ground looks hazy.
constraint: Your shoes may occupy only the bottom edge.

title: Pane as a Border
oneLiner: Hold the window frame around a quiet piece of street.
details: Stay inside and let the window frame sit on at least three sides. Inside that border, place a still bit of sidewalk and frontage, so the street feels held and a little distant. Choose the stillest part of the view rather than waiting for every direction to clear. The frame is the edge; the quiet outside is the picture.
tips: Tap the outside scene so the frame itself falls slightly soft.
If the frame is pale, expose for the street so the border does not burn out.
constraint: The window frame must show on at least three sides.

title: Where the Street Rests
oneLiner: Find the place the sidewalk seems to stop and let that be the stillness.
details: Look for the point where the sidewalk finishes at a wall, a fence, or the corner of your building. Stand on the sidewalk and frame that stop, with the quiet fronts around it. You are showing a street that has come to rest. If that end is not a place you can stand, frame the same stop from your window.
tips: Stand so the stop sits ahead of you, with sidewalk leading up to it.
Keep the fronts and the slabs, and let the stop sit inside the frame.

title: Both Sidewalks Clear
oneLiner: At a meeting of sidewalks, show both directions empty at once.
details: Where two sidewalks meet near home, stand on the corner slabs and frame both ways. This is the sidewalk corner, so keep the picture on the paving and the fronts. A low angle lets you end the frame before a distant walker matters. If one way will not clear, let a wall hide it and photograph the clear arm.
tips: Let the corner slab lead into the two empty directions.
Level the phone against the line of the nearest front.
constraint: At least one full direction of sidewalk must be empty.

title: Set Back and Still
oneLiner: Frame fronts that sit back from the sidewalk, with quiet ground in between.
details: Where buildings stand back behind a front paved area, a railing, or a strip of ground, stay on the public sidewalk and look across that quiet gap toward the shut fronts. Do not go in. Houses, apartments, and small blocks all do this in different ways. If your fronts open straight onto the sidewalk, stand against the wall and shoot along that nearer line of wall and sidewalk instead.
tips: Include the near sidewalk so the gap in front of the buildings has depth.
Focus on the fronts and let the nearest slabs fall a little soft.

title: A Slice Beside You
oneLiner: Use a near wall to crop the street down to one still slice.
details: Stand on the sidewalk close to a wall, a pillar, or the side of your doorway, and let that surface block most of the view. What remains is a narrow slice of quiet sidewalk and front. This is a way to catch a calm street without waiting for the whole of it to empty. A walker who enters the slice leaves it again quickly.
tips: Let the near wall fill almost half the picture.
Focus on the slice of street, not on the wall that hides the rest.
constraint: A near wall or pier must hide at least half the view.

title: Glow Behind the Door
oneLiner: Shut the door, leave a light on inside, and shoot it from just outside.
details: Switch on a light inside, close your own door, and photograph it from just outside, on the sidewalk if the door opens there or in the corridor if you live upstairs. Frame the closed door with that glow and the empty floor in front, a home shut against a quiet stretch. If the door is solid, leave a narrow opening so a strip of light shows, or use a glazed panel. A shop already shut with a light on works too, from the sidewalk in front.
tips: Stand to the side so you are not mirrored in the brightest pane.
Expose for the sidewalk, then check the glow has not blown to white.
constraint: The entrance stays closed, or open only a narrow strip.

title: Garages in a Line
oneLiner: Follow a line of shut garage doors with clear sidewalk in front.
details: Some side paths near home have a run of garage doors or storage doors. From the sidewalk, look along the shut faces so they repeat, with empty ground in front. If you have none, a row of shed doors on a shared path, or outdoor cupboard doors on a block, can repeat in the same quiet way.
tips: Get a little lower so the doors overlap into a rhythm.
Three or four doors are enough; you do not need a long clear run.

title: Balconies at Rest
oneLiner: From the paving by your entrance, show a stack of still balconies.
details: Stand on the paving outside your entrance, or on the sidewalk in front of the building, and look at the balconies as a quiet stack of rails and shut doors. Shoot from the ground only, and do not lean on a rail. If there are no balconies, or you live in a house, frame the repeated windows of the nearest block in that same calm stack. Keep a strip of empty paving at the bottom.
tips: The paving strip shows that you were standing on the ground.
Hold the phone level so the balcony lines do not slope.
constraint: Shoot from ground level only.

title: Mostly Empty Ground
oneLiner: Give the empty sidewalk three quarters of the frame and the fronts the rest.
details: Stand on the sidewalk and tilt slightly down so the slabs dominate and the buildings are only a band along the top. The amount of empty ground is the whole idea. Crop before the sidewalk reaches a busy point, or use a lull and shoot in the gap.
tips: Set the fronts along the top grid line and let the slabs take the rest.
Focus a couple of metres ahead so the near ground is crisp.
constraint: Sidewalk must fill at least three quarters of the frame.

title: Bars and Quiet Ground
oneLiner: Look through bars or a fence at the still ground on the far side.
details: From the sidewalk, frame a fence, a railing, or your own shut gate, and show the quiet paving beyond. Leave it closed, and stay on the public side. If none of those is near, use the narrow gap beside your entrance and the empty ground you can already see.
tips: Focus past the bars so the ground beyond is clearer than the metal.
Keep the fence or the railing large enough that the picture shows you stayed outside.
constraint: Leave the fence, railing, or gate closed.

title: Spoon World Upside Down
oneLiner: Photograph a room reflected upside down inside a spoon or shiny ladle.
details: Hold a spoon so it fills part of the frame and mirrors your surroundings. The curve distorts furniture and windows into a tiny planet. Move your hand until the reflection sits in the middle and stays readable. A ladle or a large serving spoon gives you a bigger world than a teaspoon.
tips: Wipe the spoon dry so the reflection is not broken by droplets.
Tap focus on the reflected window, not on the metal rim.
constraint: The reflection must fill at least half the frame.

title: Mirror Double Room
oneLiner: Use a wall mirror to show the same space twice in one frame.
details: Stand at an angle to a mirror so you capture both a real corner and its reflection. Step aside, or keep the phone in front of your face, so your face stays out of both views. The goal is a calm duplicate of the room. Adjust until the seam between the real corner and the reflected one feels quiet.
tips: Clean one patch of the mirror so the seam is not a smear.
Include one object that appears in both the real view and the mirror.

title: Window Glass Reversal
oneLiner: Shoot through a window so the reflection and the view beyond overlap.
details: Stand inside and aim at a window where you can see both the outside scene and the room reflected in the glass. Move until a tree, a wall or the sky merges with a lamp or a ceiling line. You are composing on a transparent layer. If the outside is much brighter, step to a shallower angle until the room appears in the glass.
tips: Angle your stance so your own face drops out of the glass.
Wipe one clear patch and shoot through that.

title: Screen on the Table
oneLiner: Capture a tablet, laptop or spare screen reflecting the room on a tabletop.
details: Use a tablet, a laptop or any screen you are not shooting with. Turn it off, or open a black page, so the glass acts as a mirror. Place it flat or propped on a table and shoot from above or from the side. If you have no second screen, lay a picture frame glass-up on the table and use that rectangle.
tips: Tilt the device until one reflection dominates the dark glass.
Use a plain table so the screen has a quiet border.

title: Countertop Sky
oneLiner: Find a glossy counter or appliance top mirroring light from above.
details: Look at kitchen counters, a fridge top or polished furniture for a soft reflection of the ceiling or a bright window. Move until the highlight forms a shape you like. You do not need a literal sky, because any bright patch overhead will do. Treat the surface as a dark, still pool.
tips: Lower the phone close to the surface so the reflection opens up.
Expose for the highlight and let the surrounding surface go deep.
constraint: Shoot within arm's reach of the surface.

title: Bent in the Tumbler
oneLiner: Bend a window or a lamp in the curve of a drinking glass.
details: Fill a clear tumbler, a glass jug or a jar with water and set it where it can see a window or a lamp. Look through the side, not down into the water, until the window frame bends into a curve. The distortion is the picture. Turn the glass until that curve sits simply in the middle.
tips: Focus on the bent frame inside the glass, not on the near rim.
Put a dark cloth behind the glass if the curve is hard to see.
constraint: The bend must be obvious in the glass.

title: Glasses World Miniature
oneLiner: Photograph the tiny room reflected in one lens of eyeglasses.
details: Rest glasses on a table, or hold them steady, with the lenses facing a bright part of the room. Move in until one lens fills the view. The room bends into a bubble. Sunglasses or reading glasses you already own will do, and a small hand mirror is a fair stand-in if you have no glasses.
tips: Get as close as the phone can focus, or switch on the closest focus mode.
Hold a hand above the lens to block a bright overhead smear.

title: Floor Tile Mirror
oneLiner: Shoot a polished floor tile reflecting ceiling lights or a window.
details: Find a glossy tile, a shiny patch of flooring or a waxed board in your home. Crouch low so a light or a window flips into the lower half of the frame. The symmetry can be tidy or broken. If the floor is matte, a single glazed tile propped on it will stand in.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor, lens toward the glossy patch, for a steadier low view.
Draw a sheer curtain partway if a window reflection is harshly bright.
constraint: Keep the camera below knee height.

title: Door Glass Layers
oneLiner: Layer the room and the daylight together in a door or a window pane.
details: Stand inside and aim at a glazed door or a window until the room and the daylight outside occupy the same glass. A lamp shape might sit on top of a wall, or a ceiling line might cross what is outside. If the door is solid, use any window and shoot the pane rather than only the view through it. Move until the two layers are both readable.
tips: Shift a few centimetres left or right until one interior shape locks onto one outdoor shape.
Wipe a hand-sized patch of glass and compose inside it.

title: Kettle Window Strip
oneLiner: Find a window reflected as a bent strip in the side of a kettle or pot.
details: Set the kettle or a steel pot where it can see the window, and look for a bent bright strip in the metal rather than a whole tiny room. Roll the kettle until that strip is long and placed where you want it. A stainless teapot or a mixing bowl works if the kettle is busy. Come close enough that the strip is a real shape.
tips: Focus on the strip, then drop exposure until it is bright metal and not pure white.
Turn other clutter away so the strip has dull metal around it.
constraint: The window's reflection should be a strip, not the whole frame.

title: Ceiling in the Bowl
oneLiner: Fill a bowl with water and photograph the ceiling reflected in it.
details: Fill a bowl, a wide pan or the kitchen sink with still water and set it under a light or a bright bit of ceiling. Shoot from above, slightly off vertical, so the ceiling appears in the water. Wait a moment for ripples to die. A dark bowl shows the reflection more clearly than a white one.
tips: Do not bump the table, or the ceiling will break into rings.
Include the rim so the reflection has a round frame.

title: Switched Off Screen
oneLiner: Use a switched-off television or monitor as a dark mirror for the room.
details: Turn a television, a monitor or a laptop screen fully off so it becomes a dark mirror. Stand so the screen holds a simple reflection of a lamp, a window or a doorway. The black rectangle should frame that reflection. If you have no such screen, a large black baking tray propped up will do a smaller version.
tips: Stand to the side so your face stays out of the dark glass.
Dim a nearby lamp if the reflection is a white glare with no shape.
constraint: The screen fills most of the frame.

title: Lid as Mirror
oneLiner: Hold a saucepan lid so the room sits in the middle of the metal.
details: Hold a saucepan lid, a round tin lid or a metal plate up at chest height and tilt it until a window or a lamp sits in the middle of the circle. The curve will bend straight lines. Keep your fingers at the rim. A glass lid can work too if it has a reflective backing.
tips: Wipe the lid first, then tilt until the reflection stops sliding off the edge.
Come close so the circle of metal nearly fills the frame.

title: Chrome Tap Bubble
oneLiner: Move in on a chrome tap or faucet until it mirrors a tiny piece of the kitchen.
details: Find a chrome tap or faucet, a metal mixer or a shiny spout and move close until the curved surface holds a tiny piece of the kitchen, a window, a tile or the opposite cupboard. You want that miniature, not a portrait of the fitting. If the metal is matte, try the curve of a steel soap dispenser or the kettle spout.
tips: Brace a finger on the sink so the close focus does not wander.
Tap the tiny reflected window, not the highlight beside it.
constraint: The reflected scrap of room must be recognisable.

title: Surface of a Drink
oneLiner: Photograph the window or a lamp reflected in the surface of a drink.
details: Pour water, tea or milk into a mug or a glass and look into the surface from a low angle. A window or a lamp should appear as a bright shape on the liquid. Still the cup so the shape holds. Do not shoot straight down, or you will mostly see the bottom of the mug.
tips: Get the phone almost level with the rim and aim slightly down.
Wait for the surface to settle after you set the mug down.

title: Oven Door Dark
oneLiner: Treat the oven door as a mirror and frame one reflected object in the glass.
details: With the oven off and cool, use the door glass as a dark mirror. Place yourself so one thing, a kettle, a chair back or a doorway, sits clearly in the reflection. If you have no oven, a microwave door or a dark picture frame will stand in. Keep your face out of the glass.
tips: Switch off the room's brightest overhead light if it veils the glass.
Stand at an angle until the chosen object separates from the glare.
constraint: Only one reflected object should be the point of the picture.

title: Picture under Glass
oneLiner: Shoot the glass of a framed picture so the room floats over the image.
details: Find a framed picture, a postcard in a plastic sleeve or a glossy cover behind glass. Angle the phone so the room, a window or a lamp, floats over the image. You are not copying the picture; you are using it as a background for the reflection. If nothing is framed, slide a magazine into a clear sleeve.
tips: A shallower angle usually strengthens the reflection over the picture.
Focus on the glass, not on the print behind it.

title: Sink Curve
oneLiner: Catch a bright window in the curve of a stainless sink or a metal bowl.
details: Look into the curve of a stainless sink, or set a metal bowl in it, and find the window as a bright bent patch. Place that patch where the curve is simplest. You are not trying to see the whole kitchen, only the window's shape in the metal. A steel mixing bowl on the counter works if the sink is dull.
tips: Dry the metal so water spots do not chop the reflection.
Move a few centimetres until the window patch is a single shape.
constraint: Keep the phone out of the brightest part of the reflection.

title: Shower Screen Layer
oneLiner: Stand so a shower screen or a glass door layers the room with itself.
details: Stand near a shower screen, a glass cupboard door or a glazed internal door. Find an angle where you see the room both through the glass and reflected in it. A towel, a bottle or a door handle can be the thing that doubles. If every screen is frosted, use the frosted glass only where it still mirrors a bright window.
tips: Shift your head until a reflected edge lines up with a real one.
Wipe a small clear circle and compose through that.

title: Repeating Tunnel
oneLiner: Face a small mirror at a larger one and photograph the repeating tunnel.
details: Hold a hand mirror or a makeup compact so it faces a wall mirror. Look into one of them for the tunnel of repeating frames. Photograph that tunnel, not your face, and aim so the frames repeat into the distance. If you have only one mirror, angle a dark picture frame or a switched-off tablet toward it.
tips: A small tilt stops your face sitting in the middle of the tunnel.
Tap the second or third repeat, which is where the effect reads.
constraint: Your face must not be the subject.

title: Glossy Page Mirror
oneLiner: Lay a glossy magazine or plastic sleeve flat and shoot the reflection on it.
details: Lay a glossy magazine, a laminated card or a plastic sleeve flat on a table near a window. Shoot across it from a low angle so the page mirrors the window or a lamp. The print can show through the reflection. If nothing glossy is nearby, lay a picture frame glass-side up and shoot across that pane.
tips: Get the lens almost on the table so the reflection stretches.
Roll the page flat with a mug out of frame if it curls.

title: Bottle Shoulder
oneLiner: Turn a glass bottle until a lamp or window appears on its shoulder.
details: Stand a glass bottle, a jar or a vase on the table and turn it until a lamp or a window appears as a bright patch on the shoulder. The highlight should sit on the curve, small and deliberate. Clear glass and dark glass both work. Move the lamp if the window is not cooperating.
tips: Focus on the bright patch on the glass, not the label.
A dark background behind the bottle makes the reflection easier to see.
constraint: One bottle only.

title: Mirror toward the Ceiling
oneLiner: Angle a hand mirror, or a wall mirror, so it delivers the ceiling.
details: Angle a hand mirror upward, or stand close under a wall mirror and aim into it, until the ceiling appears in the glass. A ceiling light, a crack or a plain expanse is enough. If you have no hand mirror, the wall mirror in a bathroom or hall will still show the ceiling when you tilt the phone. Keep your face below the frame.
tips: Include the mirror's edge so it is clear you are looking into glass.
Tap the reflected ceiling rather than the mirror frame.

title: Microwave Strip
oneLiner: Find a thin reflection of the kitchen in the dark glass of a microwave.
details: With the microwave off, look into the dark door for a thin reflection of the kitchen, a window line or the opposite cabinets. Come close so that band is strong. If you have no microwave, any dark appliance window or the black glass of an oven will do. Angle past your own reflection.
tips: Stand left or right until the reflection is a band and your face is gone.
Lower the exposure if the glass looks muddy grey.
constraint: Shoot the door, not the food inside.

title: Plate Pond
oneLiner: Pour a shallow pool of water on a plate and photograph what it reflects.
details: Pour a thin layer of water onto a dinner plate or a shallow tray and set it under a window or a lamp. The reflection will be a disc, thinner and more fragile than a deep bowl. Shoot from a low angle so the disc mirrors something above. Dry the table around it so the only shine is the water.
tips: Wait for the water to stop shivering after you pour.
A low side view gives you more reflection than a straight top-down view.

title: Fridge Door Soft
oneLiner: Use a glossy fridge door or cabinet to mirror a soft shape from the room.
details: If the fridge door is glossy, stand so it mirrors a soft shape, a curtain, a shirt or a bunch of utensils, rather than a hard grid of windows. If the door is matte, use a glossy cupboard, the tiles behind the counter or the side of the kettle. The reflection can be blurry, as long as the shape is there. Keep your face out.
tips: Step back until the reflected shape is large and simple.
Focus on the door surface.
constraint: Choose a soft reflected shape, not a cluttered one.

title: Dark Mug Rim
oneLiner: Look into a dark empty mug and catch a reflection near the rim.
details: Take a dark empty mug, a black bowl or a deep cup and look just inside the rim for a reflection of a window or a lamp. The glaze near the lip often mirrors a small bright shape. Angle the mug until that shape sits on the inner curve. A pale mug will fight you, so choose the darkest cup you have.
tips: Light from the window, and keep the phone from blocking it.
Focus on the inner rim where the bright shape sits.

title: Lamp in the Metal
oneLiner: Switch on a lamp and find its reflection in a kettle, toaster or pot.
details: Switch on a lamp and move a kettle, a toaster or a steel pot until the lamp appears in the metal. You want the lamp's shape, shade and all, not just a white dot. Turn the appliance until the reflection is whole. Daylight can stay; the lamp is the thing being reflected.
tips: Place the lamp farther away if its reflection is a blown-out blob.
Come close enough to see the shade's outline in the metal.
constraint: The reflected lamp must be identifiable as a lamp.

title: Counter Tile Gleam
oneLiner: Take the reflection in the tiles behind the counter, or in a shiny tray.
details: Look at the tiles behind the counter, a single glazed tile or a shiny tray propped up. Find a reflection of the window or a tap in that surface. One tile is enough if you come close. If every tile is matte, the tray or a metal baking sheet will carry the reflection instead.
tips: Shoot along the tile at a shallow angle to strengthen the reflection.
Wipe the tile so a single smear does not become the subject.

title: Shine on the Apple
oneLiner: Catch a window in the shiny skin of an apple or a pepper.
details: Choose a shiny apple, a pepper or a tomato and set it where the window can reflect in the skin. Turn it until a small bright shape of the window sits on the curve. The fruit or vegetable is only the mirror here. A dull potato will not help, so pick the shiniest one you have.
tips: Wipe the skin if a fingerprint breaks the reflection.
Come close and tap the bright patch on the skin.
constraint: The reflected window must be visible on the skin.

title: Holes of the Colander
oneLiner: Look into a metal colander and photograph the broken reflections.
details: Hold a metal colander or a perforated spoon up toward a window or a lamp. Each hole should carry a tiny bright reflection, and the metal between the holes stays darker. Fill the frame with that pattern. A slotted spoon gives you fewer holes and the same idea if you have no colander.
tips: Angle the metal until several holes light up together.
Focus on the nearest holes and let the far rim soften.

title: Inside the Shade
oneLiner: Look into a switched-on lampshade and photograph the room mirrored there.
details: Switch on a lamp with a shade and look into the shade from the side, away from a direct view of the bulb. The inner surface often mirrors a window, a wall or the bulb itself as a soft shape. Keep your face out of that reflection. If the shade is very dark inside, tilt the lamp until a pale wall appears in it.
tips: Stand to the side so the bulb is not a blank glare in the middle.
Tap the reflected shape inside the shade, not the bulb.
constraint: The lamp stays on.

title: Doorknob Fisheye
oneLiner: Find the whole room curved into the shine of a round metal doorknob.
details: A round metal doorknob, a cabinet knob or a shiny bottle cap works like a tiny fisheye mirror. Bring the phone close and look for the window or a lamp bent into a bright arc across the metal. Shift your angle until your own reflection is small and off to one side.
tips: Tap the knob so the phone focuses on the reflection, not the door.
Brushed metal blurs the room; polished metal keeps it readable.
constraint: The knob must fill at least half the frame.

title: Night Window Mirror
oneLiner: Let a dark window mirror one lamp back into the room.
details: Switch on a lamp and stand where the window already looks darker than the room, which is easy after dusk or with a curtain partly drawn. Aim at the glass so the lamp, a chair or a doorway appears in the pane and the view outside falls away. Move until that reflected shape is simple. Leave your own reflection outside the frame.
tips: If the outdoors is still brighter, switch on a second lamp and stand closer to the pane.
Tap the reflected lamp, not the window frame.
constraint: The reflected lamp must be recognisable.

title: Handles in a Row
oneLiner: Find the same window repeated in a row of cupboard handles.
details: Leave the cupboards shut and look along a row of metal handles, drawer pulls or taps. Each one should hold a tiny repeat of the window or a lamp. Come close enough that two or three repeats share the frame. If the handles are matte, a row of glasses will repeat the highlight instead.
tips: Shoot along the row so the repeats shrink away from you.
Focus on the second handle, where the tiny window is clearest.
constraint: At least two handles or glasses must show the repeat.

title: Glaze as Mirror
oneLiner: Find a window sitting in the glaze of a vase, pot or mug.
details: Choose a glazed vase, a plant pot or a shiny mug and set it near the window. Look into the glaze, not the soil or anything growing in it, until a patch of window appears on the curve. Turn the pot until that patch is a simple shape. A matte terracotta pot will not reflect, so pick a glossy one.
tips: Focus on the glaze, not on anything standing in the pot.
Shift a few centimetres until the bright patch becomes one shape.

title: Cookie Tin Bend
oneLiner: Turn a metal tin until the window bends along its side.
details: Find a cylindrical tin, a tea caddy or a steel flask and set it where a window or a lamp can reflect in the side. Roll it until the reflection stretches into a long bent band. You want that band, not a label. If every tin is matte, lay a stainless bottle on its side and use the same stretch.
tips: Come close so the band of reflection is wider than any label.
Focus on the metal, then lower exposure until the window is a shape.

title: Key as Mirror
oneLiner: Find a tiny window in the round head of a key or a keyring.
details: Take a key, a keyring or a small metal charm and look for a window or a lamp in the shiniest curve. The reflection will be a small bent patch, so come as close as the phone will focus. Turn a dull key until one polished edge catches the light. The miniature is the subject, so the jagged end of the key can fall out of frame.
tips: Brace both hands together so the close view stays sharp.
Tap the bright speck, not the darker metal around it.

title: Gloss of a Leaf
oneLiner: Use a glossy houseplant leaf as a small mirror for the window.
details: Find the glossiest leaf on a houseplant, the kind that looks wet even when it is dry. Move the plant, or yourself, until a window or a lamp sits on that leaf. Let the leaf fill the frame. If every leaf is matte, wipe one with a damp cloth and shoot while it is still wet.
tips: Tap the bright patch on the leaf.
Turn the leaf slowly until the window sits in the middle of it.

title: Black Glass Stovetop
oneLiner: Treat a black glass stovetop, or a black tray, as a mirror for the pans.
details: If you have a black glass stovetop, leave it off and cold, and look for a pan, the tiles or the window reflected in it. Shoot from a low angle across the glass so the reflection is a broad field. If you have no stovetop, prop a black baking tray on the counter and reflect a kettle or a jar in it. Keep your face out of the glass.
tips: Wipe the glass so crumbs do not become the subject.
Lower the phone until it almost touches the counter.
constraint: Keep the surface unlit and cool.

title: Inside the Mixing Bowl
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the room bent inside a metal mixing bowl.
details: Hold a metal mixing bowl, or set it on the table, and look into the curve. The window and a piece of the kitchen should bend inside it, a wider world than a spoon gives you. Turn the bowl until a window or a door frame sits in the middle. Keep your fingers on the rim.
tips: Wipe the bowl so old spots do not chop the room apart.
Come close enough that the metal fills the frame.
constraint: Use only one bowl.

title: Close to the Glaze
oneLiner: Move close to a glazed door and fill the frame with layered reflections.
details: Move close to a glazed door or a window pane until you no longer need to recognise the room. Fill the frame with layered bands of reflection, bright sky against a darker interior shape, or two tones overlapping. Abstract is the aim. If the door has no glass, use any window in the home and do the same on that pane.
tips: Focus on the glass surface itself.
Shift a centimetre at a time until two bands overlap cleanly.

title: Cup over the Mirror
oneLiner: Lay a hand mirror flat and stand a cup on it so the cup doubles.
details: Lay a hand mirror, a picture frame's glass or a switched-off tablet flat on the table. Stand a cup, a bottle or a small vase on the glass. Shoot from low so you see the object and its reflection as a pair. Keep your face out of the glass, and do not use the phone you are shooting with as the mirror.
tips: Get the lens down to table height.
Wipe the glass so the doubled edge stays sharp.
constraint: The object and its reflection must both be in the frame.

title: Crumpled Foil
oneLiner: Crumple foil lightly and photograph the broken reflections indoors.
details: Crumple a sheet of foil, a silver cake board or a shiny wrapper, then open it partway so it is wrinkled but not a ball. Hold it near a window or a lamp and photograph the broken reflections in the facets. Each crease should hold a different brightness. If you have no foil, smooth a shiny snack bag and wrinkle it again.
tips: Let the foil fill the frame so the facets become the whole picture.
Focus on the nearest crease and let farther ones soften.

title: Blind Stripes on the Wall
oneLiner: Capture parallel shadow stripes from blinds or slats on a plain wall.
details: Adjust blinds, a slatted chair back or a rack so bars of shadow repeat across a wall, floor or sheet of paper. Fill the frame with the pattern and let it go slightly crooked if that gives it energy. You are making a graphic study from something ordinary. If daylight is too soft to cut a hard edge, light the slats from the side with a lamp.
tips: A lamp close to the slats will crisp the bars when the window light is mushy.
Tilt the phone a little so the stripes run on a diagonal.
constraint: Fill at least eighty percent of the frame with stripes.

title: Object Shadow Portrait
oneLiner: Make the shadow of a single object more important than the object itself.
details: Place a cup, a bottle or a wooden spoon near a wall or a sheet of paper, with light coming from the side. Compose so the shadow is large while the object stays small or partly out of frame. The shadow tells the shape. Shift the shadow by moving the object or a lamp, rather than waiting on the weather.
tips: A desk lamp from the side beats a soft window when you want a definite edge.
Focus on the shadow edge, where it meets the paper or the wall.

title: Layered Lamp Shadows
oneLiner: Use two light sources to stack soft shadows from one small object.
details: Turn on two lamps at different angles near a table, or use one lamp and a bright window from the other side. Set one simple object, a bottle, a box or your own hand, in the middle. Notice how the shadows overlap and blur into a double edge. Photograph the place where the layers look richest.
tips: Move the nearer lamp closer if you want its shadow to go softer.
Raise the exposure a little so the overlapped tones do not block up.

title: Hand Shadow Play
oneLiner: Cast a playful shadow shape from your hand onto a wall or door.
details: Shine a lamp at your hand, or stand so window light throws the shadow, with a pale wall or door behind it. Twist your fingers until the shadow looks like something else, a beak shape, a crown or an abstract creature. Shoot the wall, not your hand. Keep it quick and a little silly.
tips: Bring the hand nearer the wall if you want the shadow sharp.
Dim the room so the shadow has more contrast.
constraint: Your hand must not appear in the photo.

title: Slatted Shadow Grid
oneLiner: Catch repeating shadow bars from a rack, a chair back or blinds.
details: Set a dish rack, a slatted chair or a blind where a lamp or a side window throws bars of shadow onto a wall, the floor or a sheet of paper. Fill the frame with the repeat, and tuck one small interruption, a crumb, a cord or a fold, inside a single dark bar. An indoor stair rail can do the same job if you have one.
tips: Crouch so the repeats travel from the bottom of the frame toward a corner.
Come closer until one dark bar is wide enough to read.

title: Sill Shadow Reach
oneLiner: Set a small object on a bright sill and photograph the shadow it lays down.
details: Choose a bottle, mug or remote with a clear outline and stand it on a windowsill or a table pulled to the window. Aim at the shadow on the sill, and let the object sit at the edge of the frame. If the daylight is too soft to cast a hard shape, bring a lamp in from the side. The shadow should be readable in one glance.
tips: Wipe the sill first so crumbs do not compete with the shadow.
Lower the phone to sill height and shoot along the shadow.
constraint: Keep the object to less than a third of the frame.

title: Corner Shadow Triangle
oneLiner: Find a sharp triangular shadow where two walls or planes meet.
details: Look at room corners, the side of a cabinet or the gap beside a fridge, anywhere light leaves a wedge of darkness. Fill the frame with the triangle and a sliver of lit surface. This is abstract geometry hiding in the home. If you have stairs, a tread can supply the wedge, but a cupboard corner is enough.
tips: Turn the phone upright if the wedge is taller than it is wide.
Step back until the whole triangle fits with a little lit wall around it.

title: Your Shadow Leading
oneLiner: Place your own shadow in the frame as a leading line toward something ahead.
details: Stand so your shadow stretches along a hallway floor toward a door, a plant pot or a mark on the floor. Keep your body out of the shot and let the shadow lead the eye. If the light is too soft, set a lamp low behind you so the shadow runs ahead. This is a picture made only of shadow.
tips: Hold the phone at chest height and point it down the shadow.
Wait until the frame holds only your shadow.
constraint: Use the rear camera and do not zoom.

title: Paper Cut Shadow
oneLiner: Cut or tear a simple shape from paper and photograph its crisp shadow.
details: Use scrap paper and scissors, or just tear, to make a basic form such as a circle, a star or a blocky letter. Hold it near a lamp so the shadow lands on a flat surface. Shoot the surface, not the paper. Small moves change the shadow size a great deal.
tips: Move the paper closer to the surface for a sharper edge.
White paper and patterned paper throw the same darkness, so pick whichever you can see against the lamp.
constraint: The cut shape must be visible only as a shadow.

title: Sieve Dot Shadow
oneLiner: Throw the dotted shadow of a sieve, rack or perforated spoon onto the counter.
details: Hold a sieve, a cooling rack or a perforated spoon between a lamp and the counter. The holes become dots of light and the rest becomes shadow. Move the sieve nearer the counter for harder dots, or nearer the lamp for bigger ones. Photograph the counter, with the sieve mostly out of frame.
tips: Switch off other lights so only one set of dots appears.
Tap focus on a single dot's edge.
constraint: The sieve itself stays out of the picture.

title: Cable Loops
oneLiner: Arrange a charging cable so its shadow loops across a plain surface.
details: Coil a charging cable or an earphone lead loosely on a pale table or a sheet of paper. Light it from a low side angle so the loops throw a second, darker drawing. Move the lamp until the shadow loops are as interesting as the cable. A plain wall behind a dangling cable works too.
tips: Keep the lamp close to table height so the loops stretch.
Focus on the shadow, even if the cable goes a little soft.

title: Two Mug Shadows
oneLiner: Overlap the shadows of two mugs until a new shape appears between them.
details: Set two mugs, glasses or jars on a table with a lamp to one side. Slide them until their shadows overlap and make a shape that belongs to neither mug alone. Photograph the overlap, letting the mugs sit at the edge or partly out. If you have only one mug, a glass and a bottle will pair just as well.
tips: Raise the lamp a little if the shadows are running off the table.
Expose for the table so the overlapped region stays a separate tone.
constraint: The new overlapped shape must sit fully in the frame.

title: Door Wedge Dark
oneLiner: Open a door partway and photograph the wedge of shadow it casts.
details: Open an interior door halfway and look at the shadow it throws on the floor or across the next room. The wedge should be the subject, with the door itself only a slim edge. A lamp in the room you are leaving will sharpen the wedge if daylight is flat. Shoot from low so the wedge feels large.
tips: Kneel so the floor shadow occupies the lower half of the picture.
Include the bright gap under the door if there is one.

title: Key Cluster Shadow
oneLiner: Cast the shadow of your keys and let the shadow be larger than the keys.
details: Hold your keys between a lamp and a plain wall or a sheet of paper, close to the light so the shadow grows. The teeth and rings should read clearly in the shadow. Let the real keys stay small at the edge of the frame, or hide them just outside it. A single key is enough if that is all you carry.
tips: The closer the keys are to the lamp, the larger the shadow becomes.
Steady the keys on the edge of a book if they keep swinging.
constraint: The shadow must be at least twice as wide as the keys.

title: Comb Teeth Shadow
oneLiner: Hold a comb or fork in front of a lamp and shoot the striped shadow.
details: Hold a comb, a fork or a slotted spatula in front of a lamp so the teeth throw stripes on a wall or paper. Turn it until the stripes are even. This is a small, made pattern, different from blinds across a room. A wide-toothed comb gives bolder bars.
tips: Rest your wrist on a table so the stripes do not wobble.
Move the comb away from the wall to widen the bars.

title: Hanger Outline
oneLiner: Project a coat hanger's shadow onto a door or a bare wall.
details: Hang a wire or plastic hanger on a door hook, or hold it, and light it so the hook and shoulders read clearly as a shadow. An empty hanger is better than one with a coat, because the outline stays simple. If you have no hanger, a looped scarf will throw a softer cousin of the same shape. Shoot the wall.
tips: Place the lamp farther back if the shadow looks blobbed.
Turn the hanger until the hook is unmistakable.
constraint: The hanger may appear, but the shadow must be larger.

title: Hard and Soft Edge
oneLiner: Show one hard shadow edge and one soft shadow edge from the same object.
details: Put a bottle or mug close to a large lamp and let its shadow travel across the table. Near the object the edge should be fairly crisp, and farther along it should soften. Frame both parts of that single shadow. If the whole edge looks equally sharp, use a broader lamp or a shade, which softens the far end.
tips: Shoot along the shadow so near and far edges share the frame.
Tap the crisp end first, then check the soft end is still visible.

title: Foot on the Floor
oneLiner: Set a lamp low and photograph the long shadow of your own foot.
details: Place a lamp on the floor to one side of you, or on a low stack of books if it will not sit flat, and aim it across your foot. Bare foot or sock, either is fine. Keep your face out and let the shadow stretch away from the toes. Prop the phone on a chair and use the timer if you want the foot and the shadow without a hand in the way.
tips: The lower the light, the longer the foot shadow.
Include a floorboard line or a rug edge so the shadow has a map.
constraint: Only your own foot or its shadow may suggest a body.

title: Box Flap Geometry
oneLiner: Fold a cardboard box flap so it throws a triangle or stripe of shadow.
details: Open a cardboard box, a cereal carton or a delivery box and bend one flap until its shadow on the table is a triangle or a hard stripe. Light it with a lamp from the side. You are building a little piece of geometry, then photographing the shadow it makes. The printed side of the carton can face away.
tips: Crease the flap firmly so it holds still while you shoot.
Come close enough that the shadow shape fills half the frame.
constraint: No more than one flap may cast the shadow.

title: Rim Loop Shadow
oneLiner: Lay eyeglasses on a table and frame the looping shadows of the rims.
details: If you have glasses, lay them on a pale table with a low side light so the rims throw two loops. Frame the loops. If you have no glasses, a hair tie, a bangle or a cup handle will throw a cousin of the same loop. The thinness of the shadow is the point.
tips: A lamp at table height beats a ceiling light here.
Focus on the sharpest bit of the loop and let the frames go soft if they must.

title: Ceiling Dot Pattern
oneLiner: Aim a lamp up through a rack or sieve and photograph the pattern on the ceiling.
details: Set a lamp on a table, or a separate flashlight if that is the light you have, and hold a sieve, rack or colander above it. Look up at the dotted pattern on the ceiling and photograph that. Prop the phone on a shelf aimed upward, or use the timer, if you need both hands for the sieve. Any pale ceiling will take the pattern.
tips: Darken other lights so the dots stay crisp.
Hold the sieve still for a beat before the shutter.
constraint: The ceiling pattern is the whole picture.

title: Inside the Drawer
oneLiner: Pull a drawer open a little and catch the shadow inside it.
details: Open a drawer a few centimetres and look at the shadow lying across the things inside, or across the empty bottom. The drawer front should cut that shadow. A kitchen drawer, a desk drawer or a bedside drawer all work. If the room is bright and the shadow vanishes, stand so your body blocks the extra light.
tips: Shoot from above the open gap, not from across the room.
Tap the shadow line where it crosses a spoon, a sock or the bare drawer.

title: Fork Lattice
oneLiner: Cross two forks or two spoons and photograph the lattice of their shadows.
details: Lay two forks or two spoons so they cross on a pale board, and light them from the side. Their shadows should cross too, making a small lattice. Shift the angle until the shadows are as clear as the metal. A pair of chopsticks or two pencils will do if the cutlery is busy.
tips: Keep the light low and to one side so the shadows fall cleanly beside the metal.
Fill the frame with the crossing point.
constraint: Exactly two utensils, or two sticks, in the setup.

title: Coat on a Hook
oneLiner: Photograph the shadow of a coat, scarf or bag hanging from a hook.
details: Hang a coat, scarf or bag on a hook where a lamp or a side window can throw its shadow on the door. Stand so the shadow is larger in the frame than the garment. A scarf gives a softer edge, a coat a heavier shape. If the shadow is faint, move a lamp closer to the hook.
tips: Turn the lamp until a sleeve or a strap is obvious in the shadow.
Step to the side so you do not cast a second shadow over the first.

title: Broken on Cloth
oneLiner: Let a hard shadow fall across a textured cloth so the edge breaks up.
details: Drape a knitted sweater, a towel or a rumpled blanket and cast a hard shadow across it from a bottle, a book or your hand held out of frame. On the cloth the straight edge should break into little steps. A smooth table would be the wrong surface here. Use a small lamp so the edge starts out crisp.
tips: Focus on the spot where the shadow first hits the texture.
Come close enough to see the knit or the pile interrupt the line.
constraint: The shadow edge must cross the cloth, not stop before it.

title: Frame on the Floor
oneLiner: Find the shadow of a window frame lying on the floor or a sofa.
details: Look for the shadow of a window frame, a cross of mullions or a door frame, lying on the floor, a bed or a sofa. If the day is too flat to cast it, tape two strips of paper into a cross, hold them in front of a lamp, and cast that cross instead. Either way the picture is the cross-shaped shadow on a surface. Keep the real window out of frame if you can.
tips: Shoot from above so the cross sits flat and readable.
Include one object the shadow falls across, a cushion corner or a book.

title: Handle Loop
oneLiner: Isolate the looped shadow of a cup handle on a bright wall or paper.
details: Stand a cup or mug so its handle throws a loop of shadow on a wall or a propped sheet of paper. Hide most of the cup at the edge of the frame. Turn the handle until the loop is a clean oval. A jug handle works the same way.
tips: A hard lamp to the side beats diffuse window light for this loop.
Focus on the far side of the loop, where the shadow is thinnest.
constraint: The loop must be fully visible.

title: Bottle Stretch
oneLiner: Dim the room, then stretch one bottle's shadow across the table with a low lamp.
details: Close the curtains or switch off the overhead light, then set a lamp low behind a bottle, or a separate flashlight if that is what you have, so the shadow stretches a long way. Photograph the length of it, knowing a tall bottle gives a cleaner shape than a wide jar. This works in the daytime as long as the room is dim.
tips: The nearer the lamp is to the table, the longer the stretch.
Include the bottle at one edge so the shadow has a source.

title: Palm Edge Line
oneLiner: Cast only the shadow of your palm's edge, a thin dark line on paper.
details: Hold your hand sideways, palm toward you, between a lamp and a sheet of paper, so the shadow is a thin line rather than a hand shape. Tilt the palm until the line is as narrow as you can make it. Your hand stays out of the picture. A book held on its edge will substitute if you would rather not use a hand.
tips: Move the palm closer to the paper to keep the line sharp.
Shoot straight down onto the paper.
constraint: The shadow should read as a line, not a hand.

title: Remote Steps
oneLiner: Stand a remote or a small box so its shadow becomes a row of steps.
details: Stand a remote, a small box or a charger brick on its side and rake light across the buttons or the edges. The shadow should turn those bumps into a row of little steps. A plain rectangular box with a ridge will do if you have no remote. Photograph the shadow more than the object.
tips: Light from slightly above and to the side so each bump casts a tread.
Get close and focus on the first step of the shadow.

title: Shadow on the Door
oneLiner: Cast your shadow onto a door and fill the frame with that shape.
details: Stand between a lamp and a room door so your shadow falls on the door, and fill the frame with that shape. You can raise an arm so the shadow gains a gesture. The inside of the door is enough. Keep your body out of the picture.
tips: Step closer to the door for a sharper shadow, farther for a larger one.
Expose for the door so the shadow stays dark and the paint keeps colour.
constraint: Your body stays outside the frame.

title: Pot Shadow Oval
oneLiner: Photograph the round shadow of a pot, a basket or a lampshade.
details: Use a plant pot, a round basket or a lampshade, and light it from the side with a lamp so a clear oval falls on the floor or a wall. Come low so that shape is easy to read. If the light is soft, frame the dark side of the object against a lighter surface. Do not carry something outdoors just to cast the shadow.
tips: Get the phone down near the ground and tilt up slightly at the oval.
Include the base of the object so the dark shape connects to it.

title: Small Hardware Shadow
oneLiner: Catch the small shadow thrown by a hinge, a handle or a hook.
details: On your own door, find the small shadow of a hinge, a handle, a hook or a mail slot flap. Come close enough that the little shadow is obvious.
