If daylight draws no shadow, light the fitting from the side with a lamp and frame its darker edge against the door. A plain door and a small shadow are enough.
tips: Stand to the side so your own shadow does not swallow the small one.
Tap the shadow edge and lock exposure there.
constraint: Shoot only fittings on your own door.

title: Diagonal Door Shadow
oneLiner: Let one diagonal shadow, from a door or a leaning frame, cross the picture.
details: Open an interior door a little, or lean a picture frame or a book against a wall, and light it from the side with a lamp. Look for the diagonal shadow it throws across the floor or the wall. Let that diagonal run from one corner of the picture toward the opposite corner. A door indoors is enough.
tips: Use the grid and let the shadow run corner to corner.
Kneel so the line feels longer.

title: Whisk Fan
oneLiner: Cast the fan-shaped shadow of a whisk or a slotted spoon.
details: Hold a whisk, a slotted spoon or a fork in front of a lamp so the wires throw a fan of shadow on a pale wall or a sheet of paper. Turn it until the wires separate instead of merging into one blob. Photograph the wall, with the whisk mostly out of frame. A wide whisk gives a clearer fan than a tight one.
tips: Rest your wrist on the table so the fan stays still.
Move the whisk away from the wall to widen the wires.
constraint: The utensil stays out of the picture.

title: Shadow Reaches
oneLiner: Pose your shadow so it appears to touch a pot, the handle or the frame.
details: Arrange your shadow so the arm or the head of it seems to touch a plant pot, a door handle or a door frame. Set a lamp low behind you so the shadow is easy to aim. Look at the shadow, not at yourself, and adjust until the gesture reads. It should feel like a small joke.
tips: Watch the shadow on the door while you move, and shoot when the touch happens.
A lower light makes the arm of the shadow longer and easier to aim.
constraint: You appear only as a shadow.

title: Long Shadow Band
oneLiner: Find a long band of shadow from a door frame, a stand or a pipe.
details: Look for the long shadow of an interior door frame, a slim lamp stand or a wardrobe edge falling across a wall or the floor. If the light is soft, the darker side of that upright against the wall can stand in. Let the band run the full height of the picture. You can do this in a hallway.
tips: Stand so the band is a vertical third, with wall on both sides.
Expose for the wall so the dark band stays clearly separate.

title: Toward the Doorway
oneLiner: Let one object throw its shadow toward a doorway, and follow that line.
details: Choose one object indoors, a chair, a pot or a tall bottle, and light it so its shadow points across the floor toward a doorway. Follow that line with the camera, object at the near end and shadow leading off. Stop the frame at the doorway. If the shadow is faint, move a lamp behind the object until the line is clear.
tips: Hold the phone low, near the object's base, and aim along the shadow.
Keep the far end of the frame at the doorway.
constraint: One object only.

title: Page Cut by Shadow
oneLiner: Divide an open page with one hard shadow from a mug or bottle.
details: Open a printed page or a notebook and cast a hard shadow across it from a mug, a bottle or your hand held out of frame. The shadow edge should slice the page so one part stays readable and the other falls dark. Use a small lamp so the edge is crisp. The cut through the lines is the picture, so a blank page is the weaker choice.
tips: Focus on the shadow edge where it crosses a line of type.
Angle the lamp until that edge is nearly straight.
constraint: The shadow edge must cross the page.

title: Rough Wall Edge
oneLiner: Break a hard shadow edge across the roughest surface in the house.
details: Use a small lamp close to a bottle, a book or your hand held out of frame, and cast a hard shadow onto a rough surface. Bare brick, textured plaster, a woven basket or a coarse mat will break the edge into jags. Come close enough to see that break. A smooth painted door is the wrong surface for this one.
tips: Focus on the jagged boundary, not on the object casting it.
A small lamp close to the object gives a harder edge than a ceiling light.
constraint: The rough surface must fill the frame.

title: Rectangle on the Wall
oneLiner: Cast the rectangular shadow of a picture frame or a book onto the wall.
details: Hold a picture frame, a hardcover book or a small tray between a lamp and a plain wall. Tilt it until the shadow is a clean rectangle, larger than the object. Let the object sit at the edge of the frame or just outside it. A slightly crooked rectangle is fine if the corners stay readable.
tips: Move the frame closer to the lamp if you want a larger shadow.
Face the wall squarely so the rectangle keeps its corners.
constraint: The shadow must read as a four-sided shape.

title: Circle on the Wall
oneLiner: Hold a plate or lid up to a lamp until its shadow is a clean circle.
details: Hold a plate, a round lid or a hoop between a lamp and a pale wall. Tilt it until the shadow is as circular as you can manage. Your hand can stay out of frame behind the plate. If the shadow is egg-shaped, tilt a little more toward the wall.
tips: Move the plate closer to the wall for a tighter, rounder shadow.
Face the wall squarely so the circle does not turn into an oval.
constraint: Aim for a shadow that reads as a circle.

title: Light between Bars
oneLiner: Frame a thin strip of light between the dark bars of a rack or chair.
details: Look for a thin bright gap between darker bars: a dish rack, a slatted chair, blinds or a radiator. Frame that trapped strip of light. A lamp or soft daylight still works, because the bright slit between dark bars is the subject. Come close until the slit is a bold vertical or a diagonal.
tips: Expose for the bright slit so it does not blow out.
Rest an elbow on a table if you are close to the bars.

title: Block against the Wall
oneLiner: Use a basket, a box or a large pot as a block of shadow on a wall.
details: Set a laundry basket, a storage box or a large plant pot near a plain wall, and light it from the side with a lamp. Frame the heavy dark shape it lays on the wall or the floor. The shape should be a simple mass, almost a rectangle. If the light is soft, use the unlit side of that object against the brighter wall.
tips: Move until the block of shadow has one clean edge.
Include a little of the object so the dark mass has a cause.
constraint: The shadow mass should be the largest shape in the frame.

title: The Widest Gap
oneLiner: Find the widest empty gap on a shelf and make that space the subject.
details: Look along a bookcase, cupboard or spice shelf until you find a stretch with nothing in it. Stand so the gap sits between two groups of objects and the bare board reads as a deliberate pause. Shift until the things on either side frame that pause cleanly.
tips: Turn the grid on and keep the shelf line level.
Step back if the gap is getting cropped at the sides.
constraint: The empty gap must be wider than any single object beside it.

title: The Odd One Out
oneLiner: Isolate the single item that refuses to match the row around it.
details: Scan a shelf of similar things, such as mugs, jars or paperbacks, and choose the one that breaks the set. Ease it a fingertip forward if it is yours to move, or leave it and shoot from a slight angle. Keep the matching row in frame so the mismatch is obvious.
tips: Focus on the mismatched item, then recompose.
A half-step sideways will lift it off the row behind.

title: Where Spines Shift
oneLiner: Follow book spines until a colour change becomes the picture.
details: Stand before a shelf of books, notebooks or magazines and look for a short run where the spine colours shift. The change might be pale to dark, or one hue giving way to another. Frame that transition in the middle of the picture rather than at the edge.
tips: Face the shelf square on so the spines stay upright.
If pale spines glare, drop the exposure a little.
constraint: Show spines on both sides of the colour change.

title: Lid Rhythm
oneLiner: Line spice-jar lids into a rhythm that runs across the frame.
details: Open a cupboard or look at a rack of spice jars, small tins or vitamin bottles with similar lids. Nudge them into a tidy row if you are free to move them. Shoot from one end so the lids shrink away, or face them square if the caps themselves are the better story.
tips: Wipe fingerprints off the lids before you shoot.
Get the phone down to lid height so the tops share one line.

title: The Top Shelf
oneLiner: Tilt up toward the highest shelf and whatever has settled there.
details: Find the highest shelf in a cupboard, bookcase or closet, the one you rarely study. From a normal standing position, tilt up and let the underside of the shelf share the frame with whatever sits on it. If that shelf is bare, photograph the empty board and the shadow beneath it.
tips: Switch on a nearby lamp if the top shelf falls into gloom.
Hold the phone with both hands so the upward tilt stays steady.
constraint: The shelf edge must cross the frame while you look upward.

title: Under the Lowest
oneLiner: Crouch into the dim band beneath the lowest shelf in the room.
details: Kneel by a bookcase, a low cupboard or a TV stand and look into the space under the bottom shelf. That band is usually darker than the floor beyond it. Let the dim strip fill the lower half of the picture, with a brighter rug or floorboard showing past it.
tips: Brace an elbow on your knee before you press the shutter.
Expose for the brighter floor, then darken slightly if the underside goes grey.

title: Mug Alone
oneLiner: Set one mug alone on a shelf and let the bareness surround it.
details: Clear a short stretch of kitchen shelf, or use a shelf that is already nearly empty, and place a single mug near the middle. Step back until the shelf runs from edge to edge of the picture and the mug is the only object. A plain cupboard door or wall behind it keeps the scene quiet.
tips: Shoot from mug height rather than looking down.
Leave portrait mode off if it smears the shelf line.
constraint: No other object may touch the mug.

title: The Gentle Lean
oneLiner: Lean a short stack until the diagonal fills the picture.
details: On a shelf you may rearrange, lean a few books, magazines or notebooks so they rest against a vertical book or the shelf end. The lean should look gentle, not like a collapse in progress. Come in close enough that the diagonal of the stack is the main line in the picture.
tips: Focus on the nearest spine in the leaning stack.
Keep the phone parallel to the front of the shelf.

title: Label Stripe
oneLiner: Catch a band of labels so they form one thin horizon line.
details: Choose tins, jars or boxes on a pantry shelf whose labels sit at roughly the same height. Crouch or rise until that band runs straight across the middle of the picture. Crop away most of the shelf above and below so the labels become a stripe.
tips: Match the label band to the middle line of the grid.
Tap the nearest label so the stripe stays sharp.
constraint: The label band must cross the frame from edge to edge.

title: Just Straightened
oneLiner: Record a shelf in the minute after you finish straightening it.
details: Spend a moment nudging books, bottles or folded clothes into a neater line, then stop. Photograph the result before you walk away, and leave one small imperfection on purpose. Everything should face forward, as if the shelf has just been touched.
tips: Include the full width of the shelf, with a little wall at each end.
Lock exposure on a mid-tone spine or bottle.

title: The Ignored End
oneLiner: Frame the crowded corner of a shelf you usually walk past.
details: Look at the far end of a closet shelf, the back of a cupboard, or the corner behind a stack. Bring the phone close to that neglected pocket of objects. Include the place where the shelf walls meet, so the corner itself is part of the picture.
tips: Clean the lens first so any dust in the photo belongs to the shelf.
If you need a lamp, keep it off to the side rather than blasting the corner flat.
constraint: Leave the tidy middle of the shelf out of the frame.

title: Floating on Glass
oneLiner: Use a glass shelf so objects seem to hover over their reflections.
details: Find a glass or clear plastic shelf in a bathroom cabinet, a dresser or the fridge. Choose two or three light objects that already sit there, or set a glass and a small bottle on it for a minute. Shoot from slightly below so you see the objects and the faint reflection under them. If no shelf is clear, set a transparent box lid on an ordinary shelf, stand a cup on the lid, and shoot that.
tips: Angle the phone until your own reflection leaves the glass.
Focus on the object, not the softer reflection beneath it.

title: Folded Edge Stack
oneLiner: Show the layered edges of a towel stack as a set of stripes.
details: Find a bathroom shelf, a linen shelf or a towel pile where towels, dish towels or pillowcases are folded. Turn the stack so the layered edges face you and the folds read as stripes. A single stack is enough, and napkins work if you have no towels to hand.
tips: Let doorway light come from the side so each fold picks up a line.
Move in until the stripes run the full width of the picture.
constraint: Show the folded edges and leave the rest of the room out.

title: One Shelf Lit
oneLiner: Light a single shelf with a lamp and leave the others dark.
details: With the curtains closed or after dusk, switch on a lamp near a bookcase and aim it so only one shelf is bright. Turn the ceiling light off if you can. Photograph the lit shelf between darker ones so the glow feels like a small stage.
tips: Lock exposure on the lit shelf so the darker shelves stay dark.
Rest the phone on a lower shelf or a stack of books.
constraint: Only one shelf may be clearly lit.

title: Lids from Above
oneLiner: Look straight down onto a cluster of round lids.
details: Stand over a spice shelf, a coffee shelf or a bathroom shelf and point the camera down at the lids. Leave them as they are unless one lid is lying on its side and you want it upright. Circles of metal, plastic or cork against the board are the whole picture.
tips: Hold the phone flat so it is parallel to the shelf.
Fill the frame until the board edges barely show.

title: Past the Lip
oneLiner: Show one object jutting past the front lip of its shelf.
details: Find something that already sticks forward, such as a pulled-out book, a wooden spoon or a small frame. If everything is pushed back, ease one unbreakable object a few centimetres forward. Shoot from the side so the overhang and the empty air in front of it are both obvious.
tips: Focus on the point where the object crosses the lip.
A side angle tells this story better than a head-on view.
constraint: The object must cross the front edge of the shelf.

title: Shelf to Shelf
oneLiner: Include two shelves whose contents seem to answer each other.
details: Frame a pair of shelves, one above the other, in a bookcase or cupboard. Choose a view where the upper shelf is crowded and the lower one is sparse, or the other way round. Keep both horizontal lines parallel to the frame so the pair reads as a set.
tips: Step back until both shelves fit with a margin of wall.
Check the grid before you shoot so neither shelf slopes.

title: Fridge Shelf Glow
oneLiner: Open the fridge and frame one shelf in its own pale light.
details: Open the fridge and let its interior light be the illumination you use. Choose one shelf of bottles, jars or leftovers and crop out the room behind you. A middle shelf usually has the clearest line. Work quickly and close the door when the picture is done.
tips: Tap a jar near the front so the shelf stays sharp.
Steady the phone against the door edge without blocking the lamp inside.
constraint: Use the fridge light only, and switch the room lights off if you can.

title: Resting on the Spines
oneLiner: Find a small object lying on the tops of upright books.
details: Look along a bookcase for something resting on the books rather than on the shelf board: a glasses case, a postcard, a small box or another book laid flat. That horizontal shape against the vertical spines is the picture. If nothing sits there, lay a postcard or an envelope across the tops for a minute and shoot from the side.
tips: Move to the side so the object is seen in profile on the spines.
Focus on the object and let the spines beneath it soften a little.
constraint: The object must rest on the books, not on the shelf board.

title: Bottle Skyline
oneLiner: Group bathroom bottles by height and shoot the skyline they make.
details: On a bathroom shelf, gather the bottles and tubes you already keep there. Order them roughly from short to tall if you can do it in a moment. Photograph the row from the side so the tops rise and fall like a low skyline against the wall.
tips: Wipe any water spots off the bottles so the highlights stay clear.
Crouch until the lens sits at shelf height.

title: The Pulled Volume
oneLiner: Pull one book forward and photograph the slot it leaves behind.
details: On a shelf of books, notebooks or magazines, draw one volume forward a few centimetres so a dark slot opens behind it. The slot is the subject, not the cover. Shoot straight at the shelf so the gap reads as a narrow vertical shadow between the spines.
tips: Expose for the spines, letting the slot stay dark.
Keep the phone square so the slot does not turn into a wedge.

title: Along the Shelf
oneLiner: Sight along a shelf so it narrows like a short corridor.
details: Stand at one end of a bookcase, a kitchen shelf or a closet shelf and look along its length. Let the front lip run from the near corner into the distance. Objects along the way should shrink, and the far end should be a small bright or dark stop.
tips: Focus a third of the way along, not on the nearest corner.
Rest the phone on the shelf end if your hands wobble.
constraint: The near end of the shelf must be larger than the far end.

title: Hooks Beneath
oneLiner: Look up at what hangs from hooks under a shelf or along a rail.
details: Kitchen shelves, mug trees and the backs of cupboard doors often carry hooks. Point the camera up so the hooks and whatever hangs from them share the frame. A closet rail with hangers, or pegs on the back of a door, works if the kitchen has none. Hang two mugs or two hangers for a minute if the hooks are empty, then put them back.
tips: Hold the phone with both hands for the upward angle.
Include the underside of the shelf so the hooks have a place.
constraint: At least two hanging things must be in the picture.

title: The Indoor Sill
oneLiner: Treat the indoor windowsill as a shelf of things that already live there.
details: Stand inside and look along a windowsill. It may hold a bottle, a plant, a stone or a small dish, or it may be almost bare. Photograph the flat board running across the frame, the things that belong there, and the light behind them. Leave the arrangement as you found it.
tips: Shoot from sill height so the board reads as a shelf.
Tap the nearest object, not the bright glass behind it.

title: Behind the Front Row
oneLiner: Focus through the front row onto something at the back of the shelf.
details: Open a cupboard or face a bookcase where objects stand in front of other objects. Bring the phone close to the front lip and aim through a gap. Let one jar, box or book at the back be sharp, with the front row falling soft.
tips: Tap the back object, then hold still so the focus does not jump forward.
A slight side angle opens a gap if the front row is packed tight.
constraint: The sharpest object must sit behind another object.

title: What Holds It Up
oneLiner: Photograph the bracket, peg or panel that carries a shelf.
details: Look under a bookcase shelf, a kitchen shelf or a floating shelf for the piece that holds it: a bracket, a peg, a pin or the side of the cupboard. Come close so that support and the underside of the board share the frame. If the shelf is a solid box, photograph the vertical divider where two sections meet.
tips: Bring a lamp in from the side so the bracket separates from the dark underside.
Brace your wrist on a lower shelf if there is one to lean on.

title: Toes in Line
oneLiner: Align a pair so both toes point the same way and almost touch.
details: Set a pair of your own shoes on the floor just inside the door, toes aimed the same direction and nearly meeting. The small gap between the toes is part of the picture. Shoot from above and slightly in front so both shoes are fully in frame and the pair feels deliberate.
tips: Turn the grid on and put the gap near the middle.
Wipe the toes if dried mud hides the shape.
constraint: The toes must nearly meet but must not touch.

title: Sole Map
oneLiner: Flip one shoe and photograph the wear written on the sole.
details: Turn one shoe sole-up on a plain patch of floor. Look for the polished patches, the grit in the tread, or the place the heel has worn smooth. Come close enough that the sole fills the frame and the upper barely shows.
tips: Tap the most worn patch so the tread stays sharp.
Angle the phone slightly if the sole throws a white glare.

title: Lace Tangle
oneLiner: Fill the frame with laces left in a loose tangle.
details: Leave the laces of one shoe in a loose heap, or pile the lace loosely on the tongue if they are short. Bring the camera close so the cord, the plastic tips and the knots become the whole picture. A plain floor or the shoe leather can sit underneath as a quiet background.
tips: Use burst and pick the frame where the loops stay separate.
Focus on the highest loop, not the floor beneath.
constraint: Laces must occupy more than half the frame.

title: One on Its Side
oneLiner: Set one shoe upright and lay the other on its side.
details: On the floor by the door, stand one shoe up as usual and tip the other onto its side so the opening faces you. The contrast between the tidy shoe and the fallen one is the story. Step back until both are fully visible with a little floor around them.
tips: Get down to floor level rather than shooting from standing height.
Focus on the opening of the fallen shoe.

title: Heel Chorus
oneLiner: Line up heels under a bench, rack or cupboard so they repeat.
details: Set out the shoes you own, counting slippers or sandals, and turn them so the heels face the camera in a row. A shoe rack, the space under a bench, or the floor of a cupboard all work. Shoot from low so the heels repeat across the frame and the toes point away.
tips: Keep the phone parallel to the row of heels.
If the cupboard is dark, open the door wider before you expose.
constraint: At least two heels must face the camera.

title: Slipper and Shade
oneLiner: Place a soft shoe where a shadow can sit beside it.
details: Set a slipper, sneaker or other soft shoe on the floor near a lamp or a bright window. Move the shoe until a shadow falls to one side and is long enough to notice. Photograph shoe and shadow together, with the floor as an empty background.
tips: Lock exposure on the floor so the shadow does not fill in.
Switch the lamp off and on to see which version has the clearer shape.
constraint: The shadow must be fully inside the frame.

title: Inside the Shoe
oneLiner: Look down into a shoe and photograph the pattern of the insole.
details: Hold a shoe under a window or lamp and point the camera straight into it. Look for stitching, a printed pattern, a worn heel cup, or the ridges where your foot has pressed. Crop tightly so the opening becomes the frame around the insole.
tips: Rest the shoe on a table so you can hold the phone with both hands.
Tap the insole, because the rim is closer and will steal the focus.

title: From the Floor
oneLiner: Lower the phone to the floor and shoot a pair from ankle height.
details: Place a pair just inside the door and lie the phone almost on the floor in front of them, lens aimed at the shoes. The toes will look larger and the heels smaller. Keep both shoes fully in the picture, with the floor stretching toward them.
tips: Use the self-timer so you are not jabbing a phone that sits on the floor.
Clean the lens after it has been near the floor.
constraint: The phone must be no higher than the top of the shoes.

title: Odd Pair
oneLiner: Pair two shoes that do not match and let the clash be the story.
details: Choose two shoes from different pairs: a boot and a slipper, a dark shoe and a pale one, a lace-up and a strap. Set them side by side as if they belonged together. Photograph them from the front so the differences are easy to compare.
tips: Stand the mismatched shoes on a plain floor so nothing else competes.
Shoot straight on, at the height of the shorter shoe.

title: Undone Bow
oneLiner: Undo a bow and photograph the laces before you retie them.
details: Untie one shoe and let the lace fall in a natural droop across the tongue and onto the floor. Do not rearrange every loop. Come close so the loose bow, the eyelets and a little of the shoe leather share the frame.
tips: A side light from a window will separate the lace from the leather.
Focus on the knot, even if the ends fall soft.
constraint: The bow must be untied.

title: The Shoe Pile
oneLiner: Open a shoe cupboard and frame the pile exactly as it fell.
details: Open the cupboard, rack or corner where shoes land in a heap, and do not tidy it first. Look for overlaps, a sole facing out, a tongue folded under. Frame the pile so it fills the picture, including the shelf or floor that holds it.
tips: If the interior is dim, shoot from the lit side of the open door.
Tap the nearest sole so the heap has a sharp anchor.

title: Worn Creases
oneLiner: Move close to the creases and scuffs on a shoe you wear often.
details: Pick the shoe with the most lived-in surface and bring the camera close to the toe or the flex point. Look for creases, pale scuffs, or a place where the colour has rubbed thin. Let that worn patch fill the frame, with the shape of the toe only suggested.
tips: Brace the phone against your knee so the close view does not blur.
Try a slight side angle to throw a line of light along each crease.
constraint: The worn patch must fill at least half the frame.

title: Eyelet Rhythm
oneLiner: Treat a row of eyelets and the lace through them as a pattern.
details: Choose a lace-up shoe and photograph along the row of eyelets from the toe toward the tongue. The metal or plastic rings and the lace weaving through them should repeat. If your shoes have straps rather than laces, shoot the row of holes or the buckle hardware instead.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the tongue so the row stays straight.
Focus on the middle eyelet.

title: The Dark Opening
oneLiner: Frame the dark oval opening of a shoe as the main shape.
details: Set a shoe on a table or the floor with the opening facing the camera, and let the inside fall into shadow. The oval of that opening is the subject. A window behind you, not behind the shoe, will keep the interior dark.
tips: Expose for the rim so the inside stays a deep tone.
Crop until the opening dominates and the background falls away.
constraint: The opening must be the largest shape in the picture.

title: The Lone Shoe
oneLiner: Set out three shoes so one of them is clearly without a mate.
details: Arrange three shoes on the floor: a true pair close together, and a third shoe off to one side. Slippers and sandals count if you are short of pairs. Photograph the group from above so the single shoe reads at once as the one without a mate.
tips: Include enough floor to show the gap as empty space.
Hold the phone above the shoes and angle the lens down.

title: The Quiet Pair
oneLiner: Find a pair you rarely wear and photograph the dust on it.
details: Look at the back of a closet, a high shelf or a box for a pair that has been left alone. Dust, a faded cloth shoe bag, or tissue paper around them all help the story. Photograph the pair where you found it, or set it in the light without wiping it first.
tips: Side light will show dust that a frontal lamp would hide.
Do not blow the dust away before the shutter fires.
constraint: Do not clean the shoes before you photograph them.

title: Under the Bed
oneLiner: Slide a pair out from a dark corner and shoot it in that dim light.
details: Find shoes under the bed or in the darkest part of a closet. Pull them just far enough into the light that their shape appears, and leave the background dark. Photograph them half in that shadow so the hiding place is still obvious.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor and use the timer.
Lift the exposure if the shoes turn into a black blob.

title: On Your Feet
oneLiner: Point the camera down at the shoes you are already wearing.
details: Stand in the hall or the bedroom and look straight down. Photograph the shoes still on your feet, with the floor around the toes. Crop at the ankles if you would rather not include skin. Slippers count if you are not wearing shoes.
tips: Angle the screen so you can judge the preview while looking down.
Shift a foot until the pair sits clear of the rug edge.

title: Heels Touching
oneLiner: Set a pair with the heels touching and the toes spread apart.
details: Place a pair on the floor the way they land when you kick them off, heels together and toes pointing away from each other. Shoot from above so the two shoes make a wide V. The floor should be plain enough that the shape of the pair is obvious.
tips: Put the touching heels near the middle of the frame.
Hold the phone overhead with both hands so the pair stays level.
constraint: The heels must touch, and the toes must not.

title: Side Profile
oneLiner: Stand one shoe side-on against a plain background.
details: Set a single shoe on a table or the floor with its side facing you and a plain wall or cupboard behind it. Step back until the whole shoe is in frame, from toe to heel. The outline is the subject, so keep other shoes out.
tips: Get the lens level with the middle of the shoe.
Let a window to one side trace the outline with a thin light.
constraint: Only one shoe may be in the picture.

title: The Heel Tab
oneLiner: Come close to the little tab at the back of a heel.
details: Find the pull tab, the loop or the stitched seam at the back of a heel. Fill the frame with that small part and the curve of the heel around it. If your shoes have no tab, photograph the back seam where the two sides of the heel meet.
tips: Brace the phone against your knee at this distance.
Skim a lamp across the tab so the stitching lifts off the surface.

title: Under the Chair
oneLiner: Find shoes pushed under a chair and shoot them from the floor.
details: Look under a kitchen chair, a desk chair or a bedside stool for shoes that have been kicked there. Rest the phone near the floor and aim into that shadow. Include the chair legs so the hiding place is part of the picture. If nothing is under a chair, set a pair there for a minute.
tips: Use the timer so the phone can rest on the floor without a jab.
Raise the exposure a little if the shoes sink into the dark.
constraint: The chair legs must stay in the frame.

title: Crossed Pair
oneLiner: Rest one shoe across the other and show where they overlap.
details: On the floor, lay one shoe on its side across the other, the way a pair lands when you drop them. Do not tidy the overlap. Photograph from above so both shoes are recognisable and the crossing is obvious.
tips: Leave a margin of floor around the pair.
Focus on the point where the two shoes cross.

title: Padded Collar
oneLiner: Photograph the padded collar that rolls around a shoe opening.
details: Look at the soft rim around the opening of a sneaker, boot or slipper. Come close until that padded roll fills the frame, with a little of the darker inside showing. A crease, a line of stitching or a worn shine on the collar is what you want.
tips: Tap the collar rather than the deeper inside of the shoe.
Turn the shoe until the collar catches light from the side.
constraint: The collar must run across the frame.

title: Waiting on the Mat
oneLiner: Frame the shoes that already wait on the mat inside the door.
details: Look at the indoor mat, or the patch of floor just inside the door, where shoes tend to land. Leave them as they are. Photograph the pair or the small pile where it sits, with enough of the mat to show this is the place they live.
tips: Take one pace back so the whole group fits in the frame.
Crouch, rather than shooting the mat from full standing height.

title: The Long Seam
oneLiner: Follow a line of stitching along the side of a shoe.
details: Choose a shoe with a visible seam running from the toe toward the heel, or around the side. Fill the frame with that line so it travels across the picture. The panels on either side can stay, but the seam is the subject. If the side looks seamless, follow the seam around the heel instead.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the side of the shoe.
Skim a lamp across the seam if the room light is flat.
constraint: The seam must cross the frame from edge to edge.

title: Bent Through Water
oneLiner: Set a glass of water between you and a houseplant.
details: Fill a clear drinking glass and hold it a short distance in front of a houseplant, a herb pot, or leafy stems in a jar. Move the glass until those stems bend and swell in the water. Tap the glass where the bend is strongest, so the phone locks on the refraction and not on the leaves behind it.
tips: Wipe wet fingers off the outside of the glass before you shoot.
A bright window behind the plant makes the bend easier to see.
constraint: The plant must stay recognisable through the water.

title: Mesh Over the Fruit
oneLiner: Cover a piece of fruit with a sieve and shoot through the mesh.
details: Set an apple, a lemon or a tomato on the table. Hold a sieve or a tea strainer between the phone and the fruit, with a clear gap so the mesh is not pressed to the lens. Very close mesh goes soft and the fruit turns to colour with no holes, so keep the sieve nearer the fruit and tap the fruit itself.
tips: Stand near a window so the holes do not collapse into a dark block.
Shift the sieve until the fruit sits near the middle of the mesh.

title: Behind the Sheer
oneLiner: Stand behind a sheer curtain and frame the mug beyond it.
details: Use a net curtain that hangs between you and the window, and set a mug or a small plant on the sill beyond the cloth. If you have no net curtain, hold a thin white handkerchief between the phone and that mug, a little off the lens. Stand on the room side and tap the mug or the plant, not the threads. Too close, you only get weave, and the subject beyond the cloth disappears.
tips: Expose for the mug or the plant, or the cloth blows out and the subject vanishes.
If only thread is sharp, you are too close: ease back and focus on the mug again.
constraint: The cloth stays between the lens and the subject.

title: Tunnel to the Lamp
oneLiner: Look through a cardboard tube and place a lamp at the far end.
details: A paper towel tube, or a sheet of paper rolled and taped into a short tube, makes the tunnel. Switch a lamp on and look down the tube so that light sits in the round opening. Rest the near end close to the phone without touching the lens, then tap the lamp so the bright circle is what locks, while the cardboard falls dark.
tips: Lock exposure on the lamp, or the cardboard turns the picture muddy grey.
If the circle goes black, pull the phone back until the lamp reappears.
constraint: The tube opening must touch the edges of the frame.

title: Through the Porthole
oneLiner: Frame a coloured towel through the washing machine door.
details: Put a coloured towel or a shirt in the drum if it is empty, close the door, and leave the machine off. The round glass is what you shoot through, and the cloth is what should read on the other side. If you have no machine, hold a round glass saucepan lid in front of a folded towel and use the rim the same way. Tap the cloth, not a smear on the glass.
tips: Wipe streaks off the glass so you are seeing cloth, not dried soap.
Stay far enough back that the phone can still lock on the towel.
constraint: The machine stays off, or the lid stays between you and the towel.

title: Bristles Across the Mug
oneLiner: Hold toothbrush bristles between the phone and a coloured mug.
details: Stand a bright mug by the window. Hold a dry toothbrush so the bristles cross the mug, about a palm's width from the phone, and focus on the mug behind them. Pressed against the lens, the bristles melt into a grey smear and the mug disappears, so keep that gap and let the bristles read as soft streaks over a clear cup.
tips: Use a plain coloured mug so the streaks have something simple to cross.
Turn the brush until the bristles run the way you want, level or steep.

title: Bubble Wrap Veil
oneLiner: Lay bubble wrap over a coloured cup and shoot through the bubbles.
details: Any coloured cup or bottle will do. Lay bubble wrap, or a blistered piece of clear packaging, over it with the bubbles toward you. The cup is the thing on the far side and should still read as one object, broken into rounded cells. Tap the cup, and keep the phone a little above the wrap: jammed against the lens, the cells go soft and the colour flattens.
tips: Daylight from the side helps each bubble pick up an edge.
Shift the wrap until the cup sits under the clearest patch of bubbles.
constraint: The cup colour has to read through the wrap.

title: Lace in the Way
oneLiner: Hang a piece of lace between the phone and a plain mug.
details: Use a piece of lace, a paper doily, or an eyelet hem from a thin shirt. Hang it over a chair back, or hold it taut, with a plain mug on the far side. The open pattern should lie across the mug like a second drawing. Keep the cloth off the lens, leave a gap so the holes do not blur shut, and focus on the mug until the rim is clear under the pattern.
tips: A plain mug beats a busy one, because the lace is already busy.
Stretch the cloth from the edges so the middle stays open.

title: Grid of the Rack
oneLiner: Aim through one hole of a cooling rack at a mug behind it.
details: Stand a mug behind a cooling rack. An oven shelf is fair too, if the oven is off and cool and you can lift the shelf out safely. Line one opening up with the mug so the metal grid cuts the picture and the mug is clearly the thing beyond it. Hold the phone a little back from the bars, or the metal softens into blur, and tap the mug.
tips: Shoot from rack height so the bars stay square.
Move sideways until the mug sits cleanly in a single rectangle.
constraint: One opening should frame the mug.

title: Frosted Shower Shape
oneLiner: Find a bottle's shape through frosted bathroom glass.
details: Set a tall, brightly coloured bottle on the far side of a closed frosted screen, or behind a frosted bathroom window. Stand on the dull side and move until the bottle becomes a soft upright shape. If that glass is clear rather than frosted, smear a little lotion on your side, keep the bottle on the far side, shoot through the smear, then wipe the glass. Tap the textured glass so the frost stays crisp, and let the bottle remain a soft shape rather than opening the screen for a clearer view.
tips: Switch the bathroom light on if the shape is too faint.
A few centimetres of movement changes the shape, so shift slowly.

title: Wobble of a Water Bag
oneLiner: Fill a clear food bag with water and look through it at fruit.
details: Part-fill a clear food bag, push out the extra air and seal it. Hold it over the sink, in front of a mug or a piece of fruit on the counter by the sink, and tilt it until that object stretches. Tap the bag where the stretch is strongest, and keep the mug or fruit recognisable on the far side.
tips: Keep the bag over the sink for the whole shot.
Dry your fingers so the phone does not slip while the bag wobbles.
constraint: Hold the bag over a sink in case it leaks.

title: Softened by Paper
oneLiner: Lay one sheet of parchment over a dark mug and shoot through it.
details: Set a dark mug or a bright lemon on the table and lay a single sheet of parchment over it. Baking paper or one sheet of tissue works if you have no parchment. Shoot through the paper so the shape softens but stays recognisable, and tap the mug or the lemon rather than a crease in the paper.
tips: One layer is enough, because a second sheet kills the shape.
Lift the phone a little if the paper looks like a blank field.

title: Stripes from a Comb
oneLiner: Hold a comb in front of the phone so a lamp breaks into stripes.
details: Switch on a lamp with a simple shade. Hold a comb, teeth across, about a palm's width in front of the phone, with the lamp well beyond it. A comb held against the lens goes soft and the gaps vanish, so keep that distance, tap the lamp, and turn the comb until the stripes run level or steep.
tips: Do not let the comb touch the lens.
Expose for the lamp, or the stripes blow out to white.
constraint: The comb stays off the lens, with the lamp still reading as stripes.

title: Whisk in Between
oneLiner: Place a whisk between you and a strongly coloured bowl.
details: Set a bright bowl, or a white bowl with a lemon in it, on the counter. Hold a whisk in the foreground so the wires cross the bowl, and turn it until they make a loose drawing rather than a solid clump. Keep the whisk a palm's width from the phone and tap the bowl, so the colour on the far side stays clear while the wires cross it.
tips: Daylight from the side keeps the metal from becoming a black tangle.
If the wires clump, twist the handle a quarter turn and try again.

title: A Drop for a Lens
oneLiner: Put one fat drop of water on the window and find the tiny picture.
details: Touch a wet finger to the inside of a window so a single large drop sits on the glass. Brace a knuckle on the pane and move in until the drop fills a good part of the frame, then tap the drop and hold still. You are looking for a tiny flipped picture of the bright window or the room, sitting inside the drop. If the phone will not lock, ease back a little, because closer than it can focus only gives you a shiny bead.
tips: One fat drop works better than a scatter of small ones.
Clean the pane around the drop so specks do not steal the focus.
constraint: Only one drop, large enough to hold a tiny picture.

title: Mesh in the Door
oneLiner: Set a cup inside the microwave and shoot it through the door mesh.
details: Put a ceramic or plastic cup of water inside, close the door and leave the microwave switched off. The fine mesh is what you shoot through, and the cup is what should stay recognisable on the other side. The mesh is finer than it looks, and too close it turns into a flat grey wash, so move back until the cup is easy to read, then tap the cup.
tips: Use a plain cup so the mesh is what complicates it.
Disable the flash, which will bounce off the door and hide the cup.
constraint: The microwave stays off, with a non-metal cup inside.

title: Racks Behind Glass
oneLiner: Look through the oven door at the racks while the oven stays off.
details: Check the oven is off and cool and shut the door on the racks, or use a glass cupboard door with one mug on the shelf if the oven door is solid. Shoot through that glass so a rack wire or the mug crosses the frame as the thing beyond it. Reflections will compete, so shift until a dark gap lets the far object show, then tap the wire or the mug rather than a mark on the glass.
tips: Stand to one side of the window light to calm the reflection.
Look for one strong line crossing the frame, a rack wire or the edge of the mug.

title: Ribs in the Tumbler
oneLiner: Turn a ribbed glass until a lamp splits into vertical bands.
details: Hold an empty ribbed glass, or any glass with vertical ridges, a short distance from the phone. Put a lamp, a plant or the window farther away, and turn the glass until that far thing splits into repeating bands. Ridges pressed to the lens become a smear, so keep them just far enough to stay separate, tap the lamp or the plant, and hold the glass upright.
tips: Rotate in small turns, because the bands change quickly.
Keep your fingers at the rim so they do not stripe the picture twice.

title: Colour in the Bottle
oneLiner: Look through coloured liquid in a bottle at a lemon behind it.
details: Use dish soap, juice or cooking oil in a clear bottle, and turn any label away. Hold the bottle close and look through the liquid at a lemon, a spoon or the edge of the counter. The colour should stain that far object. Tap the lemon or the spoon, not the label, and keep the background plain.
tips: A plain counter behind the lemon keeps the stain readable.
Turn the bottle until the deepest colour crosses the lemon.
constraint: No label text may be readable.

title: Plastic Wrap Haze
oneLiner: Loosen plastic wrap in front of the lens and frame a mug beyond.
details: Stretch a small sheet of plastic wrap and hold it a palm's width in front of the lens, never stuck to the glass. Let it wrinkle, and frame a mug through those wrinkles so the outline of the mug warps, with the focus locked on the mug. Against the lens the film is only a smear, so that gap is what lets the warp show.
tips: Pinch the film at the sides so fingerprints stay out of the middle.
If the warp is too wild, pull the film a little tighter.

title: Leaf Near the Lens
oneLiner: Bring one leaf close and frame a lamp through a gap.
details: Use a houseplant leaf or a herb leaf, and switch a lamp on behind it. Hold the leaf about a palm's width from the phone, close enough to feel large, and move until the lamp shows through a gap or a thin patch. Almost on the lens, the leaf goes soft and the gap closes up, so keep that distance and tap the leaf beside the opening. The lamp is the brightness on the other side, and it can stay a glow.
tips: Keep the leaf off the glass of the lens.
Pinch the stem at the corner so your fingers stay out of the gap.
constraint: The leaf sits closer to the phone than the lamp does.

title: Spoon Under Ice
oneLiner: Find a spoon through ice cubes in a glass of water.
details: Put a spoon in a clear glass, add water, then a few ice cubes or a little crushed ice from the freezer. Look through the side of the glass and hunt for the spoon where a cube shifts it. Wipe the outside as it cools, or the phone will lock on droplets, and tap the spoon itself.
tips: Shoot while the cubes still have edges.
A plain background behind the glass keeps the shifted spoon readable.

title: Fruit in the Net
oneLiner: Leave a piece of fruit in a mesh bag and shoot through the net.
details: Keep an orange, an apple or a lemon inside a produce net, or slip it into a clean string bag, and set it on a plain plate. Look through the knots at the fruit so the colour still reads. Come close enough to see the knots, but not so close that the net blurs, and tap the fruit where the net crosses the brightest part.
tips: Spread the net so the holes stay even across the fruit.
A pale plate stops the background arguing with the net.
constraint: The fruit stays inside the bag.

title: Spoon in the Honey
oneLiner: Sink a teaspoon into honey and shoot through the side of the jar.
details: Use a jar of honey, syrup or clear jam, and lower a teaspoon in. Photograph through the glass so the spoon thickens and shifts in the liquid, with a plain background beyond the jar. Turn the label away, wipe drips off the outside, and tap the spoon through the glass.
tips: Warm daylight through the jar makes the colour glow.
If the spoon vanishes, move it closer to the glass you are facing.
constraint: The spoon must be visible through the jar wall.

title: Film Across the Cup
oneLiner: Span a cup with soapy film and look through it at the light.
details: Stir a drop of dish soap into a bowl of water. Dip the rim of a small cup or a ramekin and lift it out flat so a thin film spans the opening, then hold that film up to a window or a lamp. The film is what you focus on, and the light beyond it is what wakes the coloured bands. Keep the cup a comfortable distance from the phone, tap the film, and work over the bowl so drips stay put.
tips: Shoot while the bands are vivid, before the film pops.
A gentle tilt moves the colours without breaking the surface.

title: Thicket of Spaghetti
oneLiner: Stand dry spaghetti in a jar against the window and shoot through it.
details: Put uncooked spaghetti, noodles or any long dry pasta into a clear jar. Stand the jar against a window and shoot through the glass so the bright window splinters between the strands. Tap the nearest strands and let the back of the jar soften. The picture is those strands against the light, so let the pasta fill the frame.
tips: A thin jar works better than a very deep one.
Turn the jar until a bright gap sits between two strands.

title: Grater as a Screen
oneLiner: Hold a grater between the phone and a brightly coloured cloth.
details: Lay a bright dish towel or a coloured shirt flat, and hold a grater by its frame so the small round holes face the phone. The cloth is the colour on the other side of the holes. A palm's width from the lens is about right, because closer than that the holes go soft and stop being holes. Tap the cloth through an opening, and keep your fingers off the punched face.
tips: Use the face with small round holes so the cloth reads as dots of colour.
Rest your forearm on the table if the grater starts to wander.
constraint: The holes cross the whole frame and the cloth shows through them.

title: Weave of the Basket
oneLiner: Shoot through the weave of a basket at the cloth inside.
details: Line a wicker basket, a woven shopping basket or a wicker chair seat with a bright cloth. Shoot through the weave so the cloth colour comes through the gaps. Hold the phone far enough back that the strands stay separate, and tap the cloth rather than the nearest wicker. Pressed into the basket, the weave turns to a brown blur and the cloth behind it disappears.
tips: Turn the basket toward the window so the gaps light up.
Fill the frame with weave, not with the handle or the rim.

title: Spiral in Front
oneLiner: Let a notebook's spiral sit in front of a coloured mug.
details: Hold the spiral binding of a notebook about a palm's width in front of the phone, with a coloured mug beyond the loops. Focus on the mug, which should stay readable through the curls. If the loops disappear into softness, the binding is too close, so ease it forward toward the mug until the curls read again.
tips: A plain mug keeps the loops from fighting a busy pattern.
Turn the notebook until the spiral runs down the middle of the cup.
constraint: The spiral crosses the mug.

title: Glowing Segments
oneLiner: Lift a slice of citrus to the window so the segments glow.
details: Take a slice of lemon, orange or cucumber and hold it up to a window. You are shooting through the slice, and the window is only the light on the other side. Keep the slice a short distance off both the phone and the glass, then tap the slice so the segments stay sharp. Against the lens it becomes a flat wash of colour, with no segments at all.
tips: Choose a thin slice so the light can get through the segments.
Shade the phone with your free hand if the window glares on the glass.

title: Softened by Nylon
oneLiner: Stretch thin nylon in front of a lamp until the lamp becomes an orb.
details: Stretch sheer tights, pantyhose or a hairnet a short distance in front of the phone, and point it at a switched-on lamp so the lamp sits behind the cloth. This close to the phone the knit will not be sharp, and that softness is the point, so tap the lamp and let it swell into a hazy orb. Do not lay the nylon on the lens, or you only get a dark smudge.
tips: A darker nylon makes a rounder, quieter orb than a pale one.
Move the cloth a fraction until the orb has a clean edge.
constraint: The lamp is the only bright thing in the frame.

title: Down the Sleeve
oneLiner: Look down a sleeve toward a bright window at the far cuff.
details: Pull a sweater sleeve or a shirt sleeve straight and look down the inside of it toward a bright window or a lamp. The sleeve is the tunnel and the light at the cuff is the subject on the far side. Rest the phone at the shoulder end without touching the cloth to the lens, and tap the bright opening. If the tunnel goes black, you are too far inside the sleeve, so ease back until the light returns.
tips: A pale sleeve keeps the tunnel from swallowing the light.
Hold the cuff open with your free hand, kept at the edge of the frame.

title: Under the Canopy
oneLiner: Open an umbrella indoors and shoot through the cloth at a lamp.
details: Open an umbrella where you have room to stand clear of shelves and lamps. Point the canopy at a window or a switched-on lamp and shoot up through the cloth, so the light on the other side glows through the fabric and the ribs show as dark lines. Tap the cloth, because you want that glow, not a picture of the room around the umbrella.
tips: A pale canopy lets more of the lamp through than a black one.
Stand fully under the rim so the frame is only cloth and ribs.
constraint: The canopy fills the frame.

title: Slit Beneath the Door
oneLiner: Lie at floor level and look through the gap under a door.
details: Choose an internal door that shows a thin line of light underneath, from a lamp or a window in the next room. Lie so the phone is level with that gap, and shoot through it at the brighter floor beyond. Tap the light in the gap, not the door edge. If the door meets the floor with no gap, pick another door, because without a slit of light there is nothing to shoot through.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor, or on a book, so it stays level.
Switch the far room's lamp on if the line of light is too thin to see.

title: Fan of Paper
oneLiner: Fold a sheet of paper into a fan and slice a lamp through the gaps.
details: Fold a sheet of paper back and forth, pinch one end, and look through the slits so they slice a lamp into stripes. A venetian blind you already have is the same picture: stand on the room side and let the lamp, or the bright window, show between the slats. Tap that far brightness, and keep the phone back from the paper or the blind so the slits stay open instead of blurring shut.
tips: Narrower folds make more stripes, as long as you can still see the lamp.
Turn the fan until the stripes run the way you want.
constraint: The slits cross the whole frame.

title: A Gap in the Fingers
oneLiner: Curl your hand and frame a lamp through the opening.
details: Curl your free hand until a small opening remains, and look through that opening at a switched-on lamp, so the lamp sits in the hole and your fingers make the border. Hold the hand about a palm's width from the phone. Closer than that, the fingers melt together and the hole disappears, so tap the lamp and keep the opening a clear shape.
tips: Try a round opening, then a narrow one, and keep the clearer of the two.
Expose for the lamp so your hand falls into a dark border.
constraint: Only your own hand and the lamp are in the frame.

title: Centre of the Roll
oneLiner: Peer through the hole in a tape roll at a button beyond.
details: Lay a button or a coin on a plain cloth. Hold a roll of tape a short distance above it so the button sits in the hole, which is what you shoot through. Tap the button. If the roll is against the lens you only get a dark blur, so keep the round edge visible and the button sharp on the far side.
tips: A light cloth under the button stops the hole reading as a black well.
Lower the roll until the button almost fills the opening.
constraint: The button or coin sits inside the hole.

title: Neck of the Bottle
oneLiner: Sight through the neck of an empty bottle at a lamp.
details: Take a clear empty bottle, turn any label away, and point the neck toward a lamp a little farther off. Bring the phone close to the mouth without touching it, so the glass neck becomes a tunnel with the lamp at the far end. Tap the lamp, and if the neck fills the lens and goes black, pull the phone back until the lamp reappears as a bright disc.
tips: A paler bottle keeps the tunnel from going too dark.
Wipe the mouth of the bottle so dried drops do not sit on the disc of light.

title: Loops of Cable
oneLiner: Coil a cable in front of a mug and shoot through the loops.
details: Coil a headphone lead or a charging cable into a loose handful of loops and hold the loops between the phone and a coloured mug. The mug should stay recognisable through the gaps. Keep the coil about a palm's width off the lens, or the loops fuse into a dark blob, and focus on the mug.
tips: Three or four loops are enough, because a tight handful of cable hides the mug.
Let the cable catch a little window light so it does not turn pure black.
constraint: At least two loops cross the mug.

title: Bottle Behind Plastic
oneLiner: Close a pale shower curtain and find a bottle through it.
details: Set a coloured bottle on the far side of a clear or pale shower curtain, or on the rim of the bath where the curtain can fall in front of it. The plastic is the screen and the bottle is the shape on the other side, so tap the bottle and keep the plastic off the phone. If the curtain is too thick to see through, hold a pale plastic tablecloth a little off the lens with the bottle beyond it, still tapping the bottle so the plastic does not smear into a blank sheet.
tips: A brightly coloured bottle survives the veil better than a clear one.
Close the curtain fully so the plastic, not the room beside it, fills the frame.

title: Crate Over Colour
oneLiner: Hold a crate or lattice basket over a coloured cloth on the table.
details: Lay a bright dish towel or a coloured shirt flat on a table. Hold a plastic crate, a lattice basket or a rigid open basket above it and shoot down through the openings, focusing on the cloth colour in the holes. Keep the grid off the lens and parallel with the phone, or the holes skew and go soft.
tips: Weigh a corner of the cloth with a spoon if it curls up.
Fill the frame with the grid rather than the table around it.
constraint: The grid crosses the whole frame.

title: Through Dark Glass
oneLiner: Hold a sunglass lens close and simplify a chair and a lamp.
details: Hold one lens from a pair of sunglasses a short distance in front of the phone, and look through it at a chair with a lamp on behind it. The chair and the lamp should fall into broad dark masses behind the lens. Tap the lamp, and tilt the lens until its own reflection is not the whole picture. If you have no sunglasses, look through the glass of an empty green or brown bottle, label turned away, at the same chair and lamp.
tips: Keep the dark lens closer than the chair so the shapes simplify.
A lamp behind the chair gives the dark glass something bright to hold.
constraint: The dark lens stays between you and the chair.

title: Cotton Ball Blush
oneLiner: Thin out a cotton ball and let a mug blush through it.
details: Set a bright mug on the table and pull a cotton ball into a thin veil between the phone and the mug. The cotton is what you shoot through and the mug is the colour on the other side, so tap the mug. A dense lump blocks the colour, so thin the cotton until the mug shape returns, and keep it off the lens.
tips: Stretch the cotton over your fingers at the edge of the frame.
Stop thinning it once the mug colour just appears.

title: Mug Between the Books
oneLiner: Part two books and frame a mug through the narrow gap.
details: Stand two books upright on the table with a narrow gap between them, and place a bright mug just behind that gap. Come close so the pages make a dark border and the mug sits in the slit you are shooting through, then focus on the mug. If the phone only sees the book edges, open the gap a fraction and tap the coloured side of the mug again.
tips: Plain covers keep the border quiet so the mug can read.
A strongly coloured mug shows up in a thin slit better than a white one.
constraint: The mug must be recognisable through the gap.

title: Links in the Way
oneLiner: Raise a short chain and let a lamp show through the links.
details: Use a necklace, a key chain, or four paperclips linked into a short chain. Hold it up so a switched-on lamp glints through the openings in the links. Keep the chain about a palm's width off the lens, or the links fuse into one dark shape, and tap the lamp.
tips: A few links across the frame read more clearly than a tangled bunch.
Let the lamp sit in one opening rather than behind a knot of metal.

title: A Parted Zip
oneLiner: Open a zip part way and shoot the lining through the gap.
details: On a jacket, a cushion cover or a bag, open the zip a few centimetres. Shoot through that opening at the lining or the cloth underneath, with the teeth as the border. Hold the phone far enough back that the teeth stay separate shapes, and tap the cloth in the gap. Pressed against the zip, the teeth melt together and the lining goes dark.
tips: A lighter lining is easier to focus on than a black one.
Open the zip just wide enough for the cloth to read.
constraint: The teeth stay in frame around the cloth.

title: Stitches Over the Lamp
oneLiner: Hold a chunky knit against a lamp so the stitches glow.
details: Hold a single layer of a chunky sweater, or a thick knitted scarf, in front of a switched-on lamp. The knit is what you shoot through and the lamp is the glow on the other side. Keep the wool about a palm's width from the phone, close enough for the stitches to look large, but not on the lens. Tap the glow coming through one hole so the light stays the subject and the stitches still read.
tips: One layer only, because a folded sweater blocks the lamp.
Switch other lights off so the glow is clearly coming through the stitches.

title: Slats in the Doorway
oneLiner: Use chair slats or a banister to frame the room beyond.
details: Stand a slatted chair in a doorway, or use banister spindles, or hold two wooden spoons a little apart if you have no slats. Put a lamp or a bright towel beyond them so there is something definite on the far side. Tap that far object, and hold the phone a little back from the nearest bar so the bars stay separate instead of turning soft.
tips: Line one gap up with the lamp before you worry about the other gaps.
Shoot level so the slats stay parallel.
constraint: The far object must be readable between the slats.

title: Kink Under the Ruler
oneLiner: Lay a clear ruler over a bold ink line and shoot the kink.
details: Draw one thick line on a scrap of paper with a pen, and nothing else, then lay a clear plastic ruler across it. Shoot through the plastic so the line kinks or shifts, with the ruler as the thing you look through and the line as the subject underneath. Tap the line under the plastic, and skip any metal ruler, because you cannot see through it.
tips: Tilt the ruler until a reflection slides off the line.
A thicker line shows the kink more clearly than a hairline.
constraint: The line must visibly shift where it passes under the ruler.

title: Dark Leaves, Bright Pane
oneLiner: Set a houseplant against the brightest window and let the glass go white.
details: Turn room lamps off and stand the plant between you and the window. Move until several leaves join into one dark shape, or until a single leaf reads on its own. Step sideways if a window bar cuts the shape in a way you dislike.
tips: Tap the bright glass, then drag exposure down until the plant turns solid.
Shift a leaf if it merges with the window frame.
constraint: Hide the pot unless it truly belongs to the shape.

title: Open Palm
oneLiner: Raise your open hand against a bright window and keep every finger separate.
details: Hold the hand near the glass, palm towards you or away, whichever gives cleaner gaps. Spread the fingers so light shows between them. If the pane will not go bright, stand the hand in front of a switched-on lampshade and turn the other lights off.
tips: Focus on a fingertip.
Hold still, because a small shake doubles each finger.

title: Mug Handle Hook
oneLiner: Silhouette a mug so the handle reads as a clear hook.
details: Put the mug on the sill or hold it up, and turn it until the handle is a full loop against the bright pane. The body can be a simple block. Check that the handle does not merge with the mug or with the window frame.
tips: Come closer than a normal mug photo so the handle has thickness.
Expose for the window, not for the ceramic.
constraint: The handle hole must show bright background through it.

title: Spoon in Outline
oneLiner: Hold a spoon against a bright pane so only its curve remains.
details: A teaspoon or a wooden spoon both work. Turn the spoon until the bowl makes one clean curve and the handle is a slim bar or leaves the frame. Hide your fingers behind the handle, or let two fingertips show if they clarify the shape.
tips: Wipe the spoon if a highlight punches a hole in the shape.
Tap the edge of the spoon, not the window.

title: Kettle Spout Profile
oneLiner: Place the kettle against a bright background and keep the spout crisp.
details: A kettle, or a large jug with a spout, can sit on a table in front of a bright window or an open doorway. Move until the spout is a clear beak and the handle does not tangle with it. A pale wall lit by the window works if the object itself stays darker.
tips: Focus on the tip of the spout.
Step until the spout sits free of the body in the outline.
constraint: The spout must be fully inside the frame.

title: Chair in the Door
oneLiner: Place a chair in a bright doorway and reduce it to a solid shape.
details: Daylight through an open door is the background. Put a chair or a stool in that light, stand where the room is darker, and shift it if the legs tangle. If the space beyond the door is dim, set the chair in front of your brightest window instead.
tips: Expose for the doorway so the chair falls dark.
Shoot from chest height so the seat stays a clear line.

title: Bottle Neck Contour
oneLiner: Backlight a bottle so the shoulder and neck become one dark contour.
details: A water bottle, a sauce bottle, or a vase will do. Empty or full, it should sit against the window. Turn it until the shoulder curves smoothly into the neck, and let the label area fall black.
tips: Tap the bright background and lower exposure until the glass stops glowing.
Rotate the bottle until the contour is smooth.
constraint: No label readable anywhere in the picture.

title: Shirt on a Hanger
oneLiner: Hang a shirt on a hanger in front of the window and shoot the outline.
details: Use a hook near the window, or hold the hanger up. A sleeve that sticks out makes a better silhouette than a shirt pressed flat. Smooth one side and leave the other slightly crumpled so the outline is not a plain rectangle.
tips: Stand so the shirt covers the brightest part of the pane.
Focus on the shoulder of the outline.

title: Leaf at Arm's Length
oneLiner: Hold one leaf up to the light until the shape stays and the veins go.
details: Use a leaf from a houseplant, or one already loose, and hold it against the window. Move it closer to the lens for a large shape, or farther if you want it small in the pane. Stop when the leaf is a solid dark form.
tips: Hide most of your fingers behind the stem.
If the leaf glows, drop the exposure until it turns black.
constraint: One leaf only.

title: Pages in a Fan
oneLiner: Open a book towards the light and photograph the fanned page block.
details: A book or a notebook will do. Stand near a window and open it so the page block is a wedge of darkness, and let the covers fall out of frame if you like. Turn it until the curve of the page edges is the clear shape.
tips: Focus on the page edges, not the bright pane.
Angle the pages so any readable text falls away.

title: Round Fruit Mass
oneLiner: Backlight an apple or an orange so it becomes a simple round mass.
details: Set the fruit on the sill or hold it up with two fingertips. The outline should be almost a circle, with a stalk only if it helps the shape. Let the window go bright white behind it.
tips: Place the fruit in the middle, then check the outline is not cut off.
Lower exposure if the fruit looks grey instead of dark.
constraint: The fruit must not touch the edge of the frame.

title: Loop of Cable
oneLiner: Drape a charging cable into one loop against a bright screen or window.
details: A phone charger is enough. Make one loop, not a tangle, and hold it against a window or a laptop screen set to a blank white page. The loop should be a single dark oval with a tail leaving the frame.
tips: Switch the screen to a blank page before you raise the cable.
Tap the cable, then darken the exposure.

title: Circle of Fingers
oneLiner: Make a circle with finger and thumb against the light and photograph the hole.
details: Hold the circle up to the window so the bright pane shows through the middle. The fingers should be dark and the hole clean. Try both a small pinch and a wider ring, and keep the rounder hole.
tips: Focus on the finger edge closest to you.
Pause before the shutter so the circle stays round.
constraint: The bright hole must be fully enclosed.

title: Shoe in the Doorway
oneLiner: Set a shoe in a bright doorway and shoot its outline from low down.
details: Place one shoe on the floor just inside an open door, with daylight behind it. Get low so the shoe becomes a dark profile and the bright doorway fills the background. Point the toe sideways so you see a profile rather than a blob from the front.
tips: Rest the phone on the floor if that keeps it steady.
Expose for the doorway, not the shoe.

title: Whisk Against the Pane
oneLiner: Hold a whisk against the window so the wires bloom into a fan.
details: A balloon whisk is ideal. If you have none, a fork held so the tines spread against the glass is a fair stand-in. You want each wire or tine separate, with bright gaps between them.
tips: Tap a wire near the middle of the fan.
If two wires merge, rotate the whisk a fraction.
constraint: At least four separate wires or tines must be readable.

title: Faucet in Outline
oneLiner: Shoot the bathroom faucet against a bright window or a white lampshade.
details: If the bathroom has a window, stand so the faucet sits in front of it. If not, shoot the faucet towards a brighter doorway, or hold a switched-on lamp behind it at a safe distance from the water. The spout and the handles should read as one dark mechanism.
tips: Turn the bathroom light off so the faucet does not pick up pale edges.
Focus on the end of the spout.

title: Bare Wire Hanger
oneLiner: Hang an empty hanger against a brighter room and trace its hook.
details: A wire hanger or a plastic one will do. Hang it on a door that opens onto a brighter space, and stand on the dimmer side. The hook should be a clear curve, and the shoulders a simple triangle or bar.
tips: Wait until the hanger stops swinging.
Expose for the brighter room so the hanger stays black.
constraint: The hook must be complete, not cut off.

title: Fingers and a Leaf
oneLiner: Pinch a leaf in front of the window so your fingers and the leaf merge.
details: This time the fingers are part of the silhouette. Pinch the stem so two fingers and the leaf make one combined shape. Move until you can still tell which part is leaf and which is finger.
tips: Spread the unused fingers out of frame.
Focus on the pinch point.

title: Two Mugs Crossed
oneLiner: Place two mugs against the light so their outlines cross.
details: Set them on the sill or hold one in each hand. Slide them until the outlines overlap and you can still see two handles or two rims. A gap of light between the bodies helps the crossing read.
tips: Line the pair up with the brightest part of the window.
Darken exposure until both mugs go solid.
constraint: Both mugs must be identifiable in the outline.

title: Comb at the Window
oneLiner: Hold a comb to the light and let the teeth break the bright background.
details: A fine comb or a wide one both work. Hold it so the teeth point across the frame and light shows in the gaps. Crop in until the teeth are large, with the spine of the comb along one edge.
tips: Keep the comb parallel to the phone so the teeth stay a similar width.
Tap the nearest tooth.

title: Jug Handle Loop
oneLiner: Backlight a jug so the handle makes a bright hole inside a dark loop.
details: A jug, a measuring cup, or a large mug will do. Turn the handle towards the window until you see a bright oval through it. The body can fall partly out of frame if the loop is the better shape.
tips: Focus on the inner edge of the handle.
Shift until the hole is a clean oval rather than a squashed slit.
constraint: The hole in the handle must be bright from edge to edge.

title: Glasses as Outline
oneLiner: Set a pair of glasses against the window and keep both rims intact.
details: If you do not wear glasses, a bangle, a roll of tape, or a jar lid gives a similar thin loop. Lay the glasses on the sill, or hold them up by one arm. Both rims should be complete, with the bridge joining them.
tips: Tilt slightly if a reflection punches a white hole in a rim.
Focus on the nearer rim.

title: Spaghetti Fan
oneLiner: Stand spaghetti in a jar against the light and fan the sticks a little.
details: A handful of dry spaghetti, breadsticks, or rosemary sprigs in a mug is enough. Set it on the sill and spread the sticks so they are not one dense block. The fan of lines is the subject, so the jar can sit along the bottom.
tips: Nudge sticks apart until most of them have light between them.
Focus on the sticks, not the glass.
constraint: The sticks must reach the top edge of the frame.

title: Key Teeth Horizon
oneLiner: Hold a key against a lamp so the teeth become a jagged edge.
details: Hold one key by the bow so the teeth sit in profile. A switched-on lampshade behind it works at any hour, and a bright window works in the daytime. Crop until the teeth are the main event and the bow is only a lump at one end.
tips: Turn the key until each tooth separates.
If the lamp flares, move the key a little off the brightest spot.

title: Torn Paper Outline
oneLiner: Tear a simple shape from paper and hold it up to a lamp.
details: Tear the paper rather than hunting for tools. A hill, a rough circle, or a blunt star is enough. Hold the scrap in front of a switched-on lampshade so the paper goes dark and the shade glows around it.
tips: Keep your fingers at the edge so they do not eat the shape.
Move the paper until the shade is an even field behind it.
constraint: The torn shape must sit fully inside the bright area.

title: Stripes Across a Plant
oneLiner: Close the blinds part way so stripes cut across a plant silhouette.
details: Put a houseplant between you and a bright window. Close venetian blinds until dark bars cross the shape without hiding what it is. If you have no blinds, tape three strips of paper on the pane, shoot, and take them down after.
tips: Expose for the bright gaps so the plant and the bars both go dark.
Focus on the plant, not on the blind or the paper.

title: Onion on the Sill
oneLiner: Set an onion or a garlic bulb against the glass and let the pane go white.
details: The bulb should become a dark globe, with a dried stem only if it adds a clear spike. Place it on the sill so the window is directly behind it. A lemon works if you have no onion or garlic.
tips: Get low so the bulb rises into the bright pane.
Darken exposure until the skin stops glowing.
constraint: The bulb must not be cut off by the frame.

title: Hand in the Sky
oneLiner: Lift your open hand into the sky and keep every finger separate.
details: From the sidewalk just outside your door, lift a hand into a patch of sky and spread the fingers so gaps show between them. The sky can be grey or bright, as long as it is brighter than your hand.
tips: Tap the sky, then drag exposure down until the hand is solid black.
Keep the fingertips inside the frame.

title: Headphone Arc
oneLiner: Backlight a pair of headphones so the band becomes one dark arch.
details: Hold them or hang them against the brightest window. The band should be a clean arch, with an ear cup at each end. If you have no headphones, a curved bag handle held at the same window will give a similar arch.
tips: Wait until the band stops swinging.
Darken the exposure until the ear cups lose their highlights.
constraint: The arch must be unbroken from one end to the other.

title: Plants Against Sky
oneLiner: Tilt up so a tree or a branch reads dark against the sky.
details: From a window, or from the sidewalk just outside your door, look up at a tree or any leaves already in sight. Do not lean out of the window. The leaves should be dark shapes rather than a study of green. If no leaves are outside, set a houseplant against the bright window and tilt up into the leaves so they read as a dark canopy.
tips: Drop exposure until the leaves lose their colour.
Include a little of the building only if it stays darker than the sky.

title: Pipe Against Sky
oneLiner: Tilt up at a pipe or a cable until it is a dark line on the sky.
details: From a window, or from the sidewalk by your door, find a vertical pipe, a cable, or a fence post that breaks the sky. Do not lean out. Let it run through the frame as a simple dark bar. If none of those lines is visible, hang a charging cable against the window and use that dark line the same way.
tips: Keep the line off-centre so the bright background has room.
Tap the line where it meets the sky or the pane.
constraint: Sky or the bright pane must show directly behind the line.

title: Plate in Profile
oneLiner: Stand a plate on its edge and backlight it into a thin disc.
details: A dinner plate, a saucer, or a lid will do. Stand it on the sill or hold it so the window is behind it, and shoot from the side. You want a slim dark oval, not the decorated face. A mug kept out of the outline can stop it rolling.
tips: Focus on the near rim of the plate.
Lower the exposure if the plate looks grey instead of dark.
constraint: The whole disc must sit inside the frame.

title: Sleeve Against Glass
oneLiner: Hold a sleeve against the window and keep the cuff a clear shape.
details: Use a coat or a shirt you already have indoors. Extend one sleeve so it hangs against the bright pane, and let the rest of the garment fall out of frame. The cuff and the bend matter more than the whole garment.
tips: Wait for the sleeve to hang still.
Expose for the pane behind the cuff.
constraint: The sleeve must sit against the bright pane, not a wall.

title: Open Scissors
oneLiner: Open a pair of scissors at the window so the blades make a clean V.
details: Open them part way and hold them so light shows between the blades and through the finger holes. The pivot should read as a small dark knot. If you have no scissors, a pair of tongs or two pencils spread in a V will do.
tips: Tap the pivot so both arms stay equally sharp.
Rotate them if the two arms merge into one mass.
constraint: Light must show between the two arms.

title: Edge Against the Sky
oneLiner: Frame a dark edge, a railing or the open door against the sky.
details: From just inside the open door, or from the sidewalk beside it, tilt up to the top edge of the door, a railing, or a fence if one is already there. That edge should be a dark line with sky above it and solid structure below. The door edge is enough if you have no railing or fence.
tips: Decide whether the line is level or diagonal, and hold that choice.
Tap the sky just above the line.
constraint: Sky must occupy the upper half of the frame.

title: Clothes Peg
