oneLiner: Pinch a clothes peg against the window so the two legs stay separate.
details: A peg, a hair clip, or a bulldog clip will do. Hold it so the spring end is a lump and the legs are two dark bars with light between them. Crop in until the peg is the whole story.
tips: Focus on the gap between the legs.
Ease the spring if the legs close into one shape.
constraint: Light must show between the legs.

title: Glove Fingers
oneLiner: Spread a glove against the window until the fingers become a dark fan.
details: A wool glove, a rubber glove, or a mitten will do. Slip your hand inside or pinch it at the cuff, and spread the fingers so light shows between them. A mitten can be a single solid shape if that is all you have.
tips: Hide the holding fingers behind the cuff.
Drop the exposure if the fabric stays grey.

title: Colander Disc
oneLiner: Hold a colander or a slotted spoon to the window so it becomes a dark disc.
details: The round body is the subject. Holes may sparkle, but let the disc read first. Hold it against the window and hide your hand on the handle. A slotted spoon is a smaller version of the same disc.
tips: Fill most of the frame with the disc.
Drop exposure so the metal stops reflecting the pane.

title: Layered Hands
oneLiner: Overlap your two hands against the window and leave a gap of light between them.
details: Raise both hands at the brightest pane and cross them so they are not one lump. A gap of light between the palms, or between the fingers, keeps them readable. Spread or curl the fingers until the combined outline feels deliberate.
tips: Tap the bright gap between the hands.
Settle the pose, then shoot, rather than shooting while you adjust.
constraint: A gap of light must show between the hands.

title: Curved Fruit
oneLiner: Hold a banana or a pepper against the window and follow the curve.
details: Choose a fruit with a bend. Pinch it at one end so the curve runs across the bright pane. The shape should be one smooth dark arc, with the stem only if it adds a small spike. A zucchini works if you have no banana or pepper.
tips: Turn the fruit until the curve is at its widest.
Darken exposure if the skin stays coloured.

title: Chain Curve
oneLiner: Hang a chain against the light and let it fall in one curve.
details: A necklace, a keyring chain, or a bag strap will do. Hold one end and let the rest drop against the window in a single curve, not a knot. The links can merge into one dark line.
tips: Wait until the chain stops spinning.
Focus on the middle of the curve.
constraint: The curve must be one continuous line.

title: Hat Brim
oneLiner: Backlight a hat so the brim reads as a dark wing.
details: A cap, a sun hat, or a wool hat will do. Set it on the sill or hold it so the window sits behind the brim. You want the brim's outline, with the crown as a simple lump. If you have no hat, a shallow bowl held at the same angle gives a similar brim.
tips: Turn the hat until the brim is at its widest.
Expose for the window so the crown goes black.

title: Sieve Mesh
oneLiner: Hold a sieve to the window until the rim is a dark ring.
details: A sieve, a tea strainer, or a skimmer will do. Let the mesh go dark and the round rim stay the clear shape. Hide your fingers on the handle. If the mesh glows, lower the exposure until it turns solid.
tips: Fill most of the frame with the rim.
Tap the near edge of the rim, not the bright pane.
constraint: The rim must be a complete ring.

title: Stemmed Glass
oneLiner: Backlight a stemmed glass so bowl, stem, and foot stay distinct.
details: Any stemmed glass or a candlestick will do. Set it on the sill against the bright pane. Move until the bowl, the thin stem, and the foot are all separate parts of one dark outline. Empty is better, so the glass stays a shape rather than a glow.
tips: Tap the stem so the thin part stays sharp.
Lower the exposure if the bowl starts to glow.
constraint: The stem must be visible between bowl and foot.

title: Weed Stem Dark
oneLiner: Set a thin stem or a pencil against the sky or a bright pane.
details: Look for one stem already growing in a crack by the entrance. Get the phone down low and aim upward so the stem crosses open sky, rather than sitting against a wall. If no stem is there, hold a pencil or a chopstick up to the window and aim along it so the thin line crosses the bright pane.
tips: Leave more sky or pane than subject, with the shape off to one side.
Focus where the shape is thinnest.
constraint: The bright pane or the sky must show behind the thin shape.

title: Towel Against Glass
oneLiner: Drape a towel over your forearm and hang it against the window.
details: Stand at a bright window and raise your forearm so the towel hangs against the pane. One hanging end is clearer than two even ends. The folds can merge. You want the outer outline.
tips: Keep the wall out from behind the towel.
Focus on the lowest corner of the cloth.

title: Spoon and Mullion
oneLiner: Line a wooden spoon up with a window bar and put the bowl in the light.
details: Stand indoors and raise the spoon so the handle continues a vertical window bar, or crosses it on purpose. The bowl should sit in the bright pane. Keep whichever version, lined up or crossing, makes the stronger shape.
tips: Close one eye to judge the line, then shoot with both open.
Tap the edge of the spoon bowl.
constraint: The spoon bowl must sit fully in the bright pane.

title: Umbrella Hook
oneLiner: Silhouette a closed umbrella so the handle reads as a hook.
details: Keep the umbrella closed. Hold it against the window and turn the handle until the curve is a clear hook, with the shaft as a straight bar. If you have no umbrella, a bag handle held at the same window will give you the hook.
tips: Wait until the handle stops swinging.
Focus on the inner curve of the hook.
constraint: The hook must be fully inside the frame.

title: Jar as a Ring
oneLiner: Raise an empty jar to a lamp and shoot the rim as a dark ring.
details: Hold the jar up to a switched-on lampshade, or to the window, and look so the lip becomes a circle with brightness inside it. The body may fall dark around that ring. A mug rim works if you have no jar. Turn other lights off if you are using a lamp, so the rim stays dark.
tips: Tilt until the ring is as round as you can make it.
Focus on the near lip.
constraint: The ring must be complete.

title: One Shape Overhead
oneLiner: Isolate one overhead shape, or the even field if the sky is plain.
details: From a window, or from the sidewalk just outside your door, look toward the open sky overhead. If one soft mass or a distinct outline is there, keep only that shape and leave the buildings out. If the sky is an even colour, let the whole frame be that quiet field. Move aside if the sun is high, and never look straight at it.
tips: Lock the exposure on sky beside the shape so a pale edge does not burn out.
Take a sideways step if a cable slices the shape you meant to keep.
constraint: If a distinct shape is there, include only that one.

title: Sky in Slatted Bands
oneLiner: Break the sky into bands with blinds or with bars the window already shows.
details: Stay in the room and tilt venetian blinds so the gaps show sky while the slats stay dark stripes. If you have no blinds, use the bars that divide the glass, or a railing visible from the window, to slice the sky in the same way. The colour in the bright bands is the note for today. Keep your head inside and do not lean out.
tips: Focus on the nearest slat or bar so the dark stripes stay crisp.
Shift the blind angle, or your stance, until the bright bands feel evenly spaced.

title: A Diagonal in the Air
oneLiner: Let one long line cut the sky on a diagonal.
details: From the sidewalk, or just outside your door, look up for a wire, a clothesline or a pale streak already lying across the sky. Turn the phone so that line runs from one corner toward the opposite side. If nothing crosses the open sky, use the edge where the top of a building meets it, still on a diagonal, and keep the sky as the larger area.
tips: Tap the line itself so the focus does not hunt in empty distance.
Turn the phone in both hands before you commit to the slope.
constraint: Sky fills more of the frame than the line does.

title: Where the Sky Changes
oneLiner: Frame the place where the sky shifts from lighter to darker.
details: Walk onto the sidewalk and look for a lighter stretch beside a darker one, however slight, with the sun itself kept out of view. Give both tones room and sit the change near the middle. If the sky is one even tone, bring the dark top of a nearby building in along one side so the frame still moves from sky to something heavier. Leave the ground out.
tips: Set exposure on the lighter side, then check the darker side still has detail.
Move a pace if a wire lies exactly on the change you want.
constraint: Keep the ground out of the frame.

title: Sky Held in a Window
oneLiner: Catch today's sky as a reflection in glass or on a dark surface.
details: Stay inside and look for today's sky reflected in a turned-off screen, a glossy door, or the glass of a picture frame near the window. If the window pane itself is mirroring the sky back into the room, use that pane instead of another surface. Move until the reflection reads as sky rather than the room, and keep your own shape smaller than that sky. An even colour is as useful here as a broken one.
tips: Focus on the glass or the glossy surface so the reflected sky stays sharp.
Sidestep until your own shape slips toward the edge of the shine.
constraint: The reflected sky is larger than your own reflection.

title: The Brightest Safe Patch
oneLiner: Find the brightest patch of sky that is still comfortable to view.
details: Stand outside your door and look for the brightest area you can glance at without narrowing your eyes. If the sun itself is glaring there, hide it behind a building edge or a branch, or leave it just outside the frame. Never look straight at the sun, and never aim the phone at a bare sun. You want a glow with a colour you can name.
tips: Ease the exposure down until the glow keeps a colour instead of a white hole.
Let a building edge cover the brightest core as soon as your eyes tighten.
constraint: No bare sun in the frame.

title: From the Sill Upward
oneLiner: Show how the tone of the sky changes from low in the window to high.
details: Stay inside and let the sky occupy most of the glass, with a sliver of frame as a border. Watch for any change between the lower part of the view and the higher part, including a very slight one. If the sky looks perfectly even, keep that thin frame so one edge is darker than the colour beyond it. Do not tilt up into the sun hoping for a deeper blue.
tips: Wipe the inside of the glass before you decide what the tone really is.
Rest the phone on the frame so the change from low to high stays smooth.
constraint: Sky occupies at least three quarters of the picture.

title: The Darker Reach
oneLiner: Photograph the darkest reach of sky you can see without facing the sun.
details: Just outside the door, turn through the directions you can safely face and choose the part of the sky that looks heaviest. If every direction is the same tone, that even darkness is the picture and it should fill the frame. A thin rim of building may sit at the border so the sky reads as lighter than the solid, but the sky stays the subject.
tips: Lift the exposure a little if the heavy area collapses into a black block.
Put the sun behind you while you decide which way is darkest.

title: Straight Up, One Colour
oneLiner: Reduce the calmest patch of sky to one even colour.
details: From the sidewalk just outside your door, or through a window if you stay indoors, point the phone at the calmest area of sky. Blue, grey or nearly white all count, because you are recording the field as it is. If patches interrupt it, tighten onto the even part. Keep the sun out.
tips: Stop the exposure slider once you can name the colour you see.
Tuck your elbows against your sides so the overhead aim does not drift.

title: Colour Just Outside
oneLiner: Step out of the door and record the colour the sky has right now.
details: Pause just beyond the doorway and point at open sky. This entry is the colour of this hour, whether you have only just got up or the day is already busy. Let that colour take most of the picture, and allow a slim edge of door or wall only if the colour needs a border. If the sun sits in front of you, aim to one side of it.
tips: Trust your eyes for the colour, then nudge the preview until it agrees.
Keep the door edge in the picture only when the colour looks lost without it.
constraint: The sky's colour fills at least three quarters of the frame.

title: The Middle Hours
oneLiner: Note the sky above the buildings around midday, or at the hour you have.
details: If you are out near the middle of the day, stand on the sidewalk and frame the sky over the buildings so you can see how light or deep it is. If it is earlier or later, use that same framing for the colour actually overhead. Keep the tops of the buildings as a thin base. Leave the sun out of the upper area.
tips: Hold the phone so the building tops make a level base.
Darken the exposure a notch if the upper sky turns blank white.

title: After the Light Goes
oneLiner: Record the cool dim colour after sunset, or the overhead colour if day remains.
details: When the sun has left, stand just outside the door and fill the frame with whatever dim colour remains, blue or grey. When it is still full daylight, photograph the overhead colour instead and do not wait around for evening. Either picture is the sky at the moment you came out. If the doorway faces a wall, use the nearest window that shows open sky.
tips: Brighten the exposure a little if a dim evening sky looks muddy.
Stay close to the door rather than wandering once the light has dropped.
constraint: No sun disk in the frame.

title: Moon or Plain Sky
oneLiner: Include the moon when it is visible, and the plain sky when it is not.
details: From the sidewalk just outside your door, or from a window if you stay in, look up and see whether the moon is showing. If it is, keep it small in a wide area of sky and stop zooming before the picture turns gritty. If it is not there, fill the frame with the plain sky in the direction you checked, and let that empty colour stand as the entry. If the sun is up, keep it behind you while you look.
tips: Lower the exposure a touch if the moon is only a blank white disc.
Lean the phone against a wall if that small bright mark is hard to hold still.

title: The Doorway Again
oneLiner: Frame the sky over your door so the same view can be repeated.
details: Stand just outside and lay a fixed edge along the bottom, either the door frame or the top of the building opposite. Sky fills everything above that edge. If you already looked from here earlier today, match the edge and the amount of sky so the two would agree. If this is the first look, keep the framing simple enough that you could find it again.
tips: Remember which edge you used, so a later picture can line up with this one.
Plant your feet in the same relation to the door if you come back.
constraint: Use one fixed edge along the bottom.

title: Sky Between Blocks
oneLiner: Photograph the sky caught between nearby buildings.
details: From the sidewalk just outside your door, find a gap of sky between two buildings, or between a building and a tree. Fill the picture with that gap and keep the windows of nearby homes out of it. If the view is wide open, let your doorway and a nearby wall act as the two sides. The sky inside the gap is enough, in whatever state you find it.
tips: Raise the aim until only sky sits between the two dark sides.
Move back along the sidewalk until both sides of the gap fit.
constraint: The sky is bordered on two sides.

title: One Limb on the Sky
oneLiner: Let a single branch lie across a much larger stretch of sky.
details: Just outside, find one branch that stands cleanly against the sky and keep the sky as the main area. Focus on the branch so the colour behind it stays readable. If no tree is near the door, a wire or an antenna can take the same role. Do not point along that line toward the sun.
tips: Shift until the branch crosses near the upper third of the picture.
Turn a little so a clump of leaves does not swallow the thin line.
constraint: The thin line fills less than a quarter of the frame.

title: The Cable's Sag
oneLiner: Follow one cable as it sags against the sky.
details: On the sidewalk, choose a single cable and let the curve of its sag be the line you keep. Sky should sit around it on most sides. If you cannot see a cable, follow the long edge where the top of a building meets the sky, running as it really runs. Crop extra wires away until one line is clearly the subject.
tips: Tap the cable, or the building edge, so it stays sharp against the bright background.
Close in until competing wires leave the picture.

title: Above the Building Line
oneLiner: Show the sky resting on the line where the buildings end.
details: Stand on the sidewalk and include the tops of the buildings, or the skyline, as a dark band low in the frame. Everything above that band is sky, in the state you find it today. The band is only there to show where the open sky begins. If the sun is sitting on the line, hide it behind the buildings.
tips: Level the phone so the building line does not slope by accident.
Expose for the sky and allow the buildings to fall dark.
constraint: The building line stays in the lower third.

title: An Edge Worth Keeping
oneLiner: Photograph an edge in the sky, or the edge where sky meets a building.
details: Look up from just outside the door. If the sky itself has a boundary where one area meets another, put that soft edge in the frame and let it travel clearly. If the sky is perfectly even, photograph the hard line where it meets the top of a building or a tree instead. The edge you can actually see is the subject, and the sun stays outside it.
tips: Place the edge off centre so the two sides are unequal.
Glance along the line and retake it if one end goes soft.

title: The Long Overhead Strip
oneLiner: Look along the row and keep the long strip of sky between buildings.
details: From the sidewalk outside, or from a window that looks along the buildings, find a length of sky running away above them. Let that strip lead through the picture. If there is no row to follow, use the longest open stretch of sky you can see from the door or the window. Take the sky as it is, even or broken up.
tips: Turn the phone upright when the strip of sky is narrow.
Shuffle until a single tall edge is not blocking the middle of the strip.
constraint: The strip of sky must lead through the picture.

title: Sky Boxed by Walls
oneLiner: Let a doorway, a window or nearby walls box a patch of sky.
details: Stay in the doorway or at a window, and point upward so the frame and a nearby wall hold a patch of sky. The building opposite can make another side, as long as you keep its windows out. The sky inside that box is the entry for today. Keep the sun outside the picture.
tips: Move until the box of sky is not pinched on one side.
Include enough wall or frame to explain the box, then stop adding more of it.

title: Inside One Pane
oneLiner: Fill one window pane with nothing but today's sky.
details: Pick a single pane and let the sky run to the edges of that rectangle. If the window is one sheet of glass, crop until only sky and a thin border of frame remain. Blue, grey or a pale near-white are all honest notes of the colour in that opening. Stand square to the glass so the pane keeps its corners.
tips: Expose for the sky and let the indoor frame go dark if it must.
Shift your head if a reflection of the room is sitting in the pane.
constraint: Sky fills the chosen pane.

title: A Curtain Across Sky
oneLiner: Draw a curtain edge, or use the frame, so it cuts into the sky.
details: Pull a curtain or a blind part of the way across the glass so the edge slices into open sky. Stay inside and include both that edge and the sky beyond it. If you have neither curtain nor blind, the window frame itself can make the cut. The open side should still show the colour the sky has now.
tips: Focus on the fabric or the frame, since it is nearer than the sky.
Try the cut on the left third, then the right, and keep the clearer one.

title: The Opposite Opening
oneLiner: Frame the gap of sky between the buildings you see from the window.
details: From your usual window, look for the shape of sky between the blocks, houses or trees opposite. Aim above their windows so the picture holds the gap and not the rooms. If nothing interrupts a wide view, let your own frame sit along the bottom of a large sky. Whatever sits in that opening today is the right subject.
tips: Raise the phone until the rooms opposite slip out of the bottom.
Use a small amount of zoom if the gap is only a slice of the view.
constraint: Aim above the windows opposite.

title: A Crack of Sky
oneLiner: Open a window a crack and photograph the sky in that slit.
details: From inside, open the window just wide enough to leave a slit of sky between the frame and the part that moves. If it does not open, use the gap beside a curtain, or crop to the narrow sky still visible along one upright of the frame. Those edges should read as dark borders. Keep your hands in the room.
tips: Bring the phone close to the opening so a reflection does not cover the slit.
Keep your fingers off the border you want to stay clean.

title: Sill as the Floor of Sky
oneLiner: Anchor a wide sky on the dark line of the windowsill.
details: Rest the lower edge of the phone on the windowsill and point it outward, so a dark line of sill runs along the bottom and sky fills the rest. You remain indoors, and that sill line is the foreground under the sky. If the sun falls in the outward view, slide the phone until a building outside covers it. The line should feel like a base, not a shelf of objects.
tips: Press the phone gently so the sill line stays level across the bottom.
Clean the lower glass, which sits closest to the lens in this position.
constraint: The sill runs along the bottom edge.

title: Today's Flat Colour
oneLiner: Turn the even part of the window sky into one field of colour.
details: Point at the calmest part of the sky in the glass and set the exposure there. The field may be blue, grey or nearly white, and that flat colour is the whole record. Let the room around the window go dark if it must. Shut out wires, leaves and the sun so nothing breaks the field.
tips: Finish adjusting as soon as the colour has a name you would say aloud.
Lean closer to the glass if the frame keeps creeping into a corner.

title: Lamps Off for the Sky
oneLiner: Darken the room and let the window show the sky's real colour.
details: Turn off lamps and screens that throw a warm cast toward the glass, then stand at the window. The sky's own colour, pale, grey or blue, should sit in the glass without that indoor warmth mixed in. If the preview looks blank, ease the exposure down until a colour comes back. Keep the sun outside the frame while you judge it.
tips: Dim the phone screen so its light does not fall back onto the glass.
Look past the phone at the real sky before you accept the colour on screen.

title: A Slim Line on Sky
oneLiner: Cross the sky in the window with one slim branch, wire or bar.
details: From the glass, find a twig or a wire that already crosses the sky and keep it thin against a large background. If neither is in the view, a slim bar of the frame can be the line. Focus on that line so the colour behind it stays clean. Do not follow the line toward the sun.
tips: Place the crossing near the upper third rather than through the middle.
If leaves thicken the twig, turn until only a slim stem remains.

title: A Column of Open Sky
oneLiner: Find a tall column of sky between two dark edges.
details: From the window, find a tall notch of sky between two buildings and let that notch run off the top of the picture. The buildings are only the dark sides. If there is no notch, use a tall gap between a tree and a wall, or the window frame as one dark side with sky running off the top. Stay back from the glass and do not lean out.
tips: Move back until both edges fit while the sky still leaves the top.
Hold the phone upright so the column has height to travel.
constraint: The sky column runs off the top of the frame.

title: Under a Hard Line
oneLiner: Underline a large sky with the tops of the buildings opposite.
details: From the window, take in only the top edge of the buildings across the way, or of a wall, along the bottom. The rest of the picture is sky as it looks at this moment. The edge gives a sense of scale, then it stays quiet. When glare sits on that edge, drop it behind the buildings rather than including it.
tips: Rest the phone on the sill so the lower edge does not wobble.
Crop tighter if anything below the top edge starts to compete with the sky.

title: Bright, But Not the Sun
oneLiner: Seek the brightest sky in the window that you can still look at.
details: Find the brightest part of the sky the glass will show while your eyes stay relaxed. If the light is too hard, let the frame or a curtain cover the core, or aim beside it. Never point the phone at a bare sun. You are after a brightness that still has a colour once the exposure comes down.
tips: Drop exposure until the bright area keeps a hint of blue, grey or cream.
Use the window frame as a shield the moment your eyes want to narrow.
constraint: Do not aim at an unobscured sun.

title: Zoomed Into Today
oneLiner: Use a little zoom and move in on the sky's texture or its smoothness.
details: Through the window, put a modest zoom on sky alone. Where the sky has a faint texture, record that texture. Where it is smooth, stay with the smoothness and let it become a flat field. Stop before the image goes fuzzy, and keep every edge, wire, leaf and the sun outside the crop.
tips: Brace the phone on the window frame, because zoom makes any shake obvious.
Back the zoom off as soon as the picture turns noisy or soft.

title: Diagonal at the Frame
oneLiner: Rotate the phone until frame and sky meet on a diagonal.
details: Choose the place where the window frame, a wall edge or the top of a building meets the sky. Turn the phone until that line runs from one corner of the picture to the opposite corner. Sky should still cover more of the picture than the solid side. Any sky will do, provided the sun sits outside the frame.
tips: Rotate the phone itself, not only your head, so the line truly hits both corners.
Take the exposure from the sky on the open side of the line.
constraint: The meeting line runs from corner to corner.

title: The Less Warm Half
oneLiner: Pick the cooler side of the window and leave the warmer side out.
details: Compare the sky on the left of the glass with the sky on the right, using your eyes rather than the screen. Keep the side that looks bluer, greyer or simply less warm. If both sides agree, fill the frame with that shared colour and leave lamps out of it. The sun does not belong in the half you choose.
tips: Judge cool and warm by eye, because the screen adds a cast of its own.
Step nearer the glass so the chosen side can fill the frame alone.

title: The Middle Division
oneLiner: Place the buildings' upper edge halfway up and give the rest to sky.
details: From the window, find where a wall or the buildings opposite give way to sky, and set that line about halfway up the picture. The top half is sky in whatever state you find. If the view is short, a wall top is enough to make the division. If the sun sits on the line, lower the frame until the sun is gone.
tips: Turn the grid on and park the dividing line on the middle horizontal.
Level the phone unless you have decided the line should slope.
constraint: The dividing line sits near the middle.

title: As Wide as the Glass
oneLiner: Take the widest view of sky your window can give.
details: Aim at the most open part of the glass and let sky run from one side of the picture to the other. Keep only a thin strip of frame if you cannot lose it. Even, pale or broken into soft masses, the sky you have is the one to use. Do not wait for a clearer spell, and leave the sun outside the picture.
tips: Hold the phone level so the wide view does not lean to one side.
Move along the glass if a bar is blocking the middle of the view.

title: Two Areas of Sky
oneLiner: Include two areas of sky and notice whether they match.
details: Frame two panes that both hold sky, with the bar between them visible. If you have only one opening, use the higher sky and the lower sky in that same glass as the two areas. They may agree or differ, and either result is worth keeping as today's comparison. Keep the sun out of both.
tips: Put the dividing edge near the middle so each area has room.
Expose for the sky and let the bar or frame fall dark.
constraint: Both areas show sky.

title: Only the High Band
oneLiner: Crop to the highest band of sky in the window and leave the lower view out.
details: From inside, raise the phone until only the highest band of sky in the window remains and the lower buildings drop away. You are noting the colour up there, not the whole outlook. If the top of the glass is blocked, use the highest open patch the window still gives you. Keep the sun out of that band.
tips: Lift the phone rather than zooming, so the band stays broad.
Check the bottom of the picture is still sky, with the lower view gone.
constraint: Only sky from the upper part of the window is included.

title: Early Colour at the Glass
oneLiner: Note the colour in the window, especially if the day has only just started.
details: If it is first thing, fill the frame with the colour the sky has before the day warms, seen from a window you can reach without going out. If the morning has already gone, photograph the colour in the glass now and let that later colour be the entry. A thin line of frame may remain so you remember which window it was. Even when the sun is low, keep it out of the picture.
tips: Face the window before you raise the phone, so low glare does not surprise you.
Darken the exposure if the early sky looks washed out to white.

title: Same Window, Later
oneLiner: Fix the window corners so this view of sky can be matched later.
details: Include two corners of the frame so the crop is easy to find again, and let sky fill the middle. If you already photographed this pane earlier today, stand in the same place and match those corners. If this is the only look, keep the sill clear so the record is just frame and sky. The picture you make now is the sky at this moment, ready to sit beside a later one.
tips: Stand on the same floorboard or rug edge so your height will match later.
Keep the same two corners in, and leave objects off the sill.
constraint: Two corners of the window frame are visible.

title: If the Moon Shows
oneLiner: Look for the moon in the glass, and settle for the plain sky if it is absent.
details: Check the window for the moon before you arrange anything, because nothing should be held up in front of the glass. If you can see it, leave it small in a large area of sky. If you cannot, photograph the plain sky in the pane where you looked and let the empty colour be the note. Do not hunt for it by looking straight at the sun.
tips: Steady the phone on the sill when the moon is only a small bright mark.
Reduce the exposure slightly so a visible moon keeps a clean edge.
constraint: Nothing is held up in front of the glass.

title: The Heaviest Tone
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the heaviest tone of sky the window shows.
details: Compare the patches the glass allows and choose the one that looks heaviest. When they all match, that even tone is still the right picture. Let it fill the frame, with at most a thin border of the window frame. Turn away from hard glare so you are choosing the dark part, not squinting toward the sun.
tips: Raise the exposure slightly if the heavy tone loses every trace of detail.
Keep the frame on sky, with at most a thin border of your own window.

title: Sky in the Tree
oneLiner: Gather the scraps of sky between branches, or one gap if the view is bare.
details: If a tree stands outside the window, frame the separate scraps of sky caught among the branches, and let the trunk stay secondary. If no tree is there, use one clean gap of sky between buildings instead. Expose for the openings so they keep the colour of the moment. The dark growth, or the building edge, is only the border.
tips: Focus on the nearest twigs, or on the building edge if you are using a gap.
Shift sideways until the openings show sky and not the wall behind the tree.

title: Spill on the Lowest
oneLiner: Let light from an open doorway fall across the lowest step.
details: Open a door onto the stairs at home, or onto the lowest steps of the stairwell in your building, and watch where the brighter space lights the first tread. If you cannot use a flight, light a single indoor step or the raised lip between two rooms from the brighter side. Make that lit patch the subject, and let the darker surface around it stay in frame.
tips: Expose for the lit patch so it keeps a little detail.
Step to the side until the door edge does not slice the middle of the step.
constraint: The brightest area must sit on the tread or the raised lip, not on the door.

title: The Bright Nosing
oneLiner: Catch the front edge of one step as a thin bright line.
details: Choose one tread on the stairs at home or in your building, and find its rounded front edge. Move until that edge, the nosing, picks up a highlight and the rest of the surface falls quieter. With no flight at all, use the raised lip between two rooms and let that bright line run from side to side across the frame.
tips: Crouch so the highlight runs level through the middle third.
Tap the highlight, then lower exposure a touch if it blows out.

title: Up from the Floor
oneLiner: Stand at floor level and look up into the light above.
details: Stand at the bottom of the stairs at home, or on the lowest landing of the stairwell in your building, and look up. Do not climb onto the rail or lean over an open side. Let the steps rise toward whatever is brighter above, a window or an open landing. If no flight is available, stand in a dimmer room and look through a doorway toward a brighter one, with the floor line along the bottom of the frame.
tips: Hold the phone with both hands and keep your heels on the floor.
Include the nearest step edge so the rise has a starting point.
constraint: Stay on the floor at the bottom, or inside the doorway.

title: Rail Shadow Stripes
oneLiner: Show the repeated stripes a rail throws across the treads.
details: Look for a handrail whose bars throw repeated stripes onto the treads, at home or in the stairwell of your building. Photograph the stripes on the steps, not the rail itself, and stand to the side of the flight. If you have no rail, set a slatted chair so it casts bars across a single indoor step, then move the chair afterwards.
tips: Turn off extra lamps so the stripes stay hard.
Focus on the stripe that crosses the nearest tread.
constraint: At least three dark stripes must cross the step.

title: Landing Pool
oneLiner: Frame the landing as a bright pool between darker steps.
details: If your stairs turn on a landing, stand at the bottom or on a lower step with a hand on the rail and frame that landing as the bright pause. The shared landing in an apartment building works too, as long as you stay on it and keep the steps below darker. If you have no landing at all, photograph a bright room floor from a dimmer hall, with the doorway holding that bright patch.
tips: Lock exposure on the bright floor so the darker steps stay deep.
Keep verticals upright by holding the phone level.

title: Dark Riser
oneLiner: Keep the vertical face of a step dark and the top of it bright.
details: Find one step where the upright face sits in shade and the top surface catches the light. The stairs at home, a step in your building, or a single step between rooms will all do. Shoot from low and to the side so the dark face and the bright top are both clear.
tips: Get the lens near tread height so the top becomes a wedge of light.
Tap the bright top, not the black riser.
constraint: Both the dark riser and the lit tread must be in the frame.

title: One Lamp After Dark
oneLiner: After dark, light the stairs with one lamp and no ceiling light.
details: When it is dark, switch off the ceiling light and place one lamp on the floor at the bottom of your own stairs. If you have no flight, set that lamp beside a single indoor step or the raised lip between two rooms. Let that single pool describe the change of level. Photograph from a few paces back so the fade into darkness is visible.
tips: Set the lamp slightly to one side so each edge gets a highlight.
Rest the phone on a book so the low light stays sharp.
constraint: Only one lamp may be on.

title: Raking the Steps
oneLiner: Rake a lamp across the steps so every edge throws a small shadow.
details: Set a lamp low and to the side of the steps in your home, or beside a single indoor step if that is all you have. A separate flashlight propped on a book can take the place of the lamp. The light should skim the surface so each edge throws a little shadow. Shoot along the light so those small shadows are easy to see.
tips: Lower the lamp until the shadows grow, then leave it still.
Use the timer so a finger on the screen does not nudge the phone.

title: Nap of the Stair
oneLiner: Use side light to reveal the nap of a carpeted step.
details: If a step at home is carpeted, stand so window light or a lamp skims the pile and shows which way the nap lies. A carpeted tread in your building works the same way if you can shoot it without blocking the flight. Come close until the texture fills the frame and the step edge is only a boundary. On a bare step, or on a hall carpet if you have no step, use that side light to show grain, paint, concrete or the pile meeting a hard floor.
tips: Switch the ceiling light off and skim a lamp in from the side.
Tap the carpet, then hold still for a slower shutter.
constraint: The surface texture must fill more than half the frame.

title: Only Two Treads
oneLiner: Limit the picture to two treads and the light that splits them.
details: Pick two treads and show how the light treats them differently, one brighter and one quieter. Two treads near the bottom of a building stairwell are enough, and you do not need the whole flight. If you only have a single step, pair it with the floor directly below and treat those two surfaces as the pair.
tips: Crop tight so a third step does not sneak in.
Align the horizontal edges with the grid.
constraint: No more than two horizontal surfaces may appear.

title: Cloth on the Step
oneLiner: Lay a pale cloth on a step so you can see the shape of the light.
details: Spread a dish towel, a sheet of paper or a pale pillowcase over one tread inside your home, or over a single indoor step if you have no flight. Do not leave cloth on a shared stairwell. The cloth shows the shape of the light better than a dark carpet does. Photograph the bright patch and include the edge of the tread so the place is still obvious.
tips: Smooth the worst wrinkles so they do not pretend to be shadows.
Expose for the cloth, not for a bright window behind it.

title: Where Step Meets Wall
oneLiner: Photograph the corner where a step meets the wall, and the light there.
details: Find the inside corner where a tread meets a wall, on the stairs at home or in the stairwell of your building. Notice whether the light dies in that corner or pools there. If you have no flight, use the corner where a doorway meets the frame and the floor. Fill the frame with that corner so the two planes and the light on them are the whole story.
tips: Turn the phone so the corner sits on a third, not dead middle, if that feels stronger.
Tap the corner join so both planes stay acceptably sharp.
constraint: The join of the two planes must be inside the frame.

title: Rim Under the Stairs
oneLiner: Find the dark space under the stairs and the rim of light at its edge.
details: If there is open space under the stairs at home, photograph from the room side so the interior stays dark and a rim of light outlines the opening. Do not crawl into a tight space. If you only have a shared flight, stay on the landing and photograph the shadow under the front lip of one tread, where the top overhangs the face below.
tips: Let the dark area stay dark by locking exposure on the rim.
Brace the phone against a wall rather than reaching into the opening.

title: Sheen on the Tread
oneLiner: Look for a soft sheen on a worn tread and photograph only that glow.
details: Look for the dull shine where feet have polished a wooden, painted or vinyl tread, at home or on the stairs in your building. Angle the phone until that sheen appears, usually when the step reflects a window or a lamp. Crop close so the glow is the subject. With no step anywhere, use the same dull polish on a well-walked wooden floor.
tips: Shift a few centimetres up or down until the sheen switches on.
If the shine is faint, turn off a competing ceiling light.
constraint: The shiny patch must sit fully inside the frame.

title: Along the Rail
oneLiner: Follow a highlight as it runs along the handrail.
details: Stand with both feet on the floor at the bottom of your stairs, or on the lowest landing in your building, and look along the handrail. A window or a lamp should lay a bright line on the rail as it rises. If you have no rail, follow a bright door frame from close to the phone toward the far end of the room.
tips: Focus partway along the rail so the near end is slightly soft.
Switch off a ceiling light if it flattens the highlight.
constraint: The rail, or the diagonal corner, must run from the foreground into the picture.

title: Even Across the Flight
oneLiner: Photograph the flight in soft light with almost no hard shadow.
details: Look for stairs washed in even light, from a window over your own flight, the landing light in your building, or a lamp bounced off a wall. You want the treads quiet and readable, not sliced by a hard shadow. On your own stairs you can close a curtain or switch off a harsh lamp until the light softens. With no flight to use, photograph a short hall and include the change of level at a doorway.
tips: Leave the flash off so it does not paint a hard edge.
Fill the frame with treads and keep your feet out of it.
constraint: Leave your own shadow out of the picture.

title: The Sawtooth
oneLiner: From the side, show the repeating profile of treads and risers.
details: Move to the side so you can see the zigzag of treads and upright faces. A home flight works, and so does a building stairwell when that profile is visible from a landing. If the stairs are enclosed, shoot from the bottom corner until the edges stack, staying on the floor and keeping off the rail. If you cannot see a profile, set two thick books or two low boxes in a stack and light them from the side so the climb still reads.
tips: Line the nearest edge up with the grid.
Tap the nearest edge and let the farther ones soften.
constraint: At least two changes of level must show in profile.

title: One Tread Lit
oneLiner: Find a patch of light that lands on only one tread.
details: Watch for a window, an open door or a lamp that brightens a single tread and leaves the ones beside it quieter. Try this on your own stairs or on a flight in your building, and frame the bright tread among darker ones. If the light on your own stairs is even, close a door until a narrower band falls on just one. With no flight, use a single indoor step and keep the bright patch on only one side.
tips: Expose for the bright patch so the rest stays deep.
Move sideways if your body is blocking the light.
constraint: The brightest patch must sit on only one tread, or on only one side of a single step.

title: The Newel
oneLiner: Let the post at the foot of the stairs take the light.
details: The newel is the thicker post where a handrail begins. Stand close, at the foot of your own stairs or at the bottom of the stairs in your building, and photograph that post where it meets the lowest tread, light on one side and shade on the other. If there is no post, use the wall corner at the start of the stairs, or a hall corner with a lamp if you have no stairs at all.
tips: Get the lens near the middle height of the post.
Include a little of the lowest tread so the post has a place.

title: Shadow Beside the Flight
oneLiner: Catch the rail's shadow where it falls on the side wall.
details: Study the wall that runs beside the stairs, not the treads themselves. At home a rail may stripe that wall, and a building stairwell often does the same in the light from above. On your own stairs, turn off extra lamps so the pattern stays clear. If you have no flight, set a lamp low beside a slatted chair so the bars fall on a plain wall, then put the chair back.
tips: Lock exposure on the wall so the shadow does not fill in.
Move the lamp until the bars are separate, then leave it still.
constraint: The shadow must fall on the wall.

title: The Darkest Tread
oneLiner: Choose the darkest tread and set it between brighter ones.
details: Scan for the tread sitting in the deepest shade, without leaning over the rail. Your own stairs will do, or the lower flight in the building if you keep one hand on the wall. Photograph it from the floor or from the tread just below, and include one brighter tread so the darkness has something to compare with. With no flight, photograph the darker side of a single indoor step and include the brighter floor next to it.
tips: Expose for the brighter tread beside it so the dark one keeps a little detail.
Leave the flash off, or the dark tread will turn flat grey.
constraint: The darkest area must be fully inside the frame.

title: Between the Balusters
oneLiner: Frame a bright gap between two uprights in the railing.
details: Look through the gaps in a railing from the floor at the bottom. One gap should hold a bright wall, a window or a landing, pinched between two uprights. Metal bars in a building stairwell are ideal, and if the side is solid, or you have no stairs, frame a bright doorway between the darker edges of the door instead.
tips: Focus on the uprights and let the bright gap stay a little soft.
Step sideways until the gap is a clean slot.
constraint: The bright opening must sit between two darker uprights.

title: Baseboard Diagonal
oneLiner: Follow the diagonal where the flight runs against the wall.
details: Follow the baseboard, or the painted line, as it climbs beside the steps. Side light should pull that diagonal off the wall, whether the wall is beside your stairs or along the building flight. If there is no baseboard, follow the shadow where each tread meets the wall. With no flight, use the diagonal where a door frame meets the floor.
tips: Hold the phone so the diagonal is the strongest line.
Tap the line itself, about halfway along.

title: Light Falling Away
oneLiner: From a low tread, look down at the light on the tread below.
details: Stand no higher than the second tread, at home or on the lowest flight in your building, with one hand on the rail or the wall. Point the camera down at the tread below and the floor, so you are photographing light falling away from you. Do not climb higher, and do not lean out. If you have no stairs, stand in a doorway and look down at the floor beyond it.
tips: Bend your knees rather than leaning out over the rail.
Include both the lower tread and a piece of floor.
constraint: Stay no higher than the second tread, or stay in the doorway.

title: Where the Light Enters
oneLiner: Include the window or doorway that actually lights the flight.
details: Find what actually lights the flight: a window beside your stairs, a small window over a door, or the bright opening at the top of a building stairwell. Put that bright opening in the frame with at least two treads, and let the steps fall softer than the source. If you have no stairs, use a hall and the doorway that lights it, with the floor included.
tips: Expose for the treads, even if the window goes bright.
Keep the phone level so the doorway stays upright.
constraint: The bright opening and the floor or treads it lights must both appear.

title: Divided Tread
oneLiner: Find one tread split between light and shade.
details: Look for one tread split between light and shade by a door edge, a rail or a wall corner. Try your own stairs or a flight in your building, and keep the front edge of that tread in the picture. If your own stairs are evenly lit, switch a lamp on to one side until a soft split appears. A single indoor step crossed by the shadow of a door works if you have no flight.
tips: Put the dividing line near the middle of the lit surface.
Lock exposure on the lit half so the shade stays dark.
constraint: Light and shade must share one tread or one single step.

title: Column at the Window
oneLiner: Backlight a kettle plume against a bright window and show its column.
details: Boil the kettle, switch it off, and leave it on the counter. Stand at arm's length and place the plume between the phone and a bright window. Do not touch the body or the spout. Wait until the steam holds a column, then take the picture.
tips: Expose for the window so the plume stays bright at the edges.
Turn the kettle base slightly until the column sits free of the window frame.
constraint: The plume must be between the camera and the window.

title: Ribbon by the Lamp
oneLiner: Set a steaming mug in front of a lamp and catch the ribbon it makes.
details: Pour a hot drink, set the mug on a table, and step back. Place a lamp behind it so the steam crosses the light. Look for a ribbon, a hook or a leaning thread rather than a vague haze. Keep your hands off the mug while you shoot.
tips: Switch off the ceiling light so the lamp defines the ribbon.
Use burst and keep the frame where the ribbon has a clear edge.

title: Doorway After a Shower
oneLiner: From the bathroom doorway, frame the vapour after a warm shower.
details: Run a warm shower for a minute with the door nearly shut, then turn the water off. Step fully out of the room and photograph the vapour from the doorway. Keep your body out of the picture. A lamp or the room window behind the vapour will show its shape.
tips: Wipe the phone lens, which will bloom if you have been near the warm room.
Lock exposure on the brightest part of the vapour.
constraint: The picture must show the empty room, with no part of you in it.

title: Patch on the Mirror
oneLiner: Breathe on a mirror and photograph the soft patch before it fades.
details: Stand close to a bathroom mirror and breathe once so a soft patch appears. Step to the side and shoot the patch while its edges are still visible. The shape of that patch is the subject, so include a little of the clear mirror around it.
tips: Focus on the glass, not on the room reflected in it.
Take two frames quickly, because the patch thins within seconds.

title: The Chilled Glass
oneLiner: Breathe on a glass you have chilled and catch the bloom that appears.
details: Put a clean drinking glass in the fridge for a few minutes, then set it on the table. Breathe gently toward it and photograph the milky bloom that forms and fades. If the glass will not bloom, use a mirror that has been held against a cold fridge door for a moment, then breathe on that.
tips: Shoot from a low side angle so the bloom reads against a dark background.
Tap the near rim of the glass to set focus.
constraint: The bloom must still be visible when you press the shutter.

title: Heat Already Off
oneLiner: Turn the stovetop off, step back, and photograph steam from plain water.
details: Heat a pan of plain water, then switch the stovetop off before you pick up the phone. Stand well back and let a window or lamp sit behind the rising steam. Do not lean over the pan, and do not use oil. A mug of hot water on the counter is a fair stand-in if you would rather not use the stovetop.
tips: Include the pan rim so the cloud has an anchor.
Drop the exposure until the white vapour keeps an outline.
constraint: If you use a pan, the heat must be off before you frame the picture.

title: Only One Steams
oneLiner: Place two mugs together and let only one of them steam.
details: Set a mug of hot water beside a mug of cold water on a dark surface. Step back and photograph them together so the steam rises from one and not the other. The difference is the picture. Leave both mugs on the table.
tips: Put a dark tray or cloth under the pair if the table is pale.
Focus on the rim of the steaming mug.

title: Through the Curtain Gap
oneLiner: Send kettle steam through a narrow gap of window light.
details: Close the curtains until only a narrow band of window light remains. Once the kettle has boiled and clicked off, set it so the plume crosses that band. Stand to the side, not over the spout, and photograph the piece of steam that the band lights up.
tips: Hold the phone just outside the bright band so the lens does not flare.
Wait for a thicker puff before you shoot.
constraint: Only a narrow band of window light may fall on the steam.

title: A Curl, Caught
oneLiner: Use burst mode to freeze one curl of steam in mid-air.
details: Set a hot mug, or a kettle that has just boiled, where a window or lamp sits behind the steam. Hold the phone steady and fire a burst as a curl forms. Choose the frame where that curl has a definite hook. Discard the frames that are only a soft smear.
tips: Brace your elbows on the counter, well away from the hot vessel.
Swipe through the burst at full size before you pick the curl.

title: Against the Cabinet
oneLiner: Put the plume in front of a dark cupboard so the shape reads clearly.
details: After the kettle has boiled, or once a mug of hot water is on the counter, move it until a dark cupboard or appliance sits behind the steam. The dark ground will show the outline. Stand to the side and include just enough of the vessel to show where the plume begins.
tips: Turn a room lamp toward the steam, not toward the cupboard.
Tap the plume's brightest point, then lock focus.
constraint: The background directly behind the steam must be dark.

title: Through the Handle
oneLiner: Frame the steam so it rises inside the handle of the mug.
details: Set a steaming mug on the table and crouch until the handle makes a small window. Wait until a wisp climbs through that opening. Keep the mug on the table and your hands off it. A plain wall behind will help the wisp show.
tips: Focus on the handle so the steam in the opening stays readable.
Lower the exposure a little if the wall behind is very pale.
constraint: The steam must pass through the handle opening.

title: Curve from the Side
oneLiner: Shoot a mug from the side so the steam makes a curve, not a blob.
details: Place a steaming mug at eye level by crouching beside the table. Look for a moment when the vapour leans into a curve or an S. Take that, rather than a front view that turns the steam into a vague puff. Keep your face and hands clear of the mug.
tips: Raise or lower yourself a few centimetres until the curve separates from the rim.
A plain wall behind the mug will help the curve read.
constraint: The steam must show a curve with a visible direction.

title: The Last Wisp
oneLiner: Wait until the steam is almost gone, then catch the last thin wisp.
details: After a kettle has clicked off or a mug has been standing, watch the plume shrink. The picture you want is the last thin wisp, not the first thick cloud. Have the framing ready so you can shoot as that thread disappears.
tips: Pre-focus on the rim before the wisp thins.
Shoot a short burst across the final seconds.

title: Vapour on the Screen
oneLiner: Include both the vapour in the air and the beads on the shower screen.
details: After a warm shower has been turned off, look at the screen or curtain from outside the shower. You want two shapes at once: beads on the surface, and softer vapour in the air beyond. Stay on the dry side of the screen and keep yourself out of the reflection.
tips: Focus on the beads, and let the air vapour stay a little softer.
Angle the phone so a window or lamp lights the droplets.
constraint: Both beads and airborne vapour must be visible.

title: Steam Past the Spout
oneLiner: Let the spout stay dark and make the steam the brightest shape.
details: With the kettle off, place it against a bright window or lamp and expose so the spout falls into silhouette. The steam leaving it should be the light shape. Stand to the side of the spout and do not reach over it.
tips: Tap the bright background, then reduce exposure until the spout is a clean dark shape.
Crop tight so the spout and the first hand-span of steam fill the frame.

title: A Sheet from the Lid
oneLiner: Lift a pan lid a little and catch the sheet of steam that escapes.
details: Heat plain water in a pan, then switch the stovetop off. With a cloth around your hand, lift the lid only a crack, step back, and photograph the sheet that rolls out. If you have no stovetop, ease up the lid of a kettle that has just boiled, using the same cloth. Close the lid again as soon as you have the picture.
tips: Pre-frame the gap so you are ready as the steam rolls out.
Keep the phone well to the side of the rising steam.
constraint: The heat must be off before you lift the lid.

title: Glass of Rising Vapour
oneLiner: Use a clear glass so you can see the surface and the steam together.
details: Pour hot water into a clear glass or jug, set it down, and wait a moment. Crouch until you can see both the surface of the water and the steam leaving it. Do not wrap your hands around the glass. A dark background will separate the vapour from the room.
tips: Focus on the water line, not on the far rim.
Wipe any drip off the outside only after the glass is cool enough to touch, or leave the drip out of frame.

title: Leaves Behind the Plume
oneLiner: Set a houseplant behind backlit steam so the leaves show through.
details: Place a mug of hot water, or a kettle that has just boiled, in front of a window, with a houseplant, a herb or a salad leaf behind the plume. You want the steam bright and a leaf or two readable through it or beside it. Step back and keep your hands off the mug. A single stem in a jar is enough if you have no larger plant.
tips: Expose for the window so the steam keeps a bright edge.
Move the plant until a leaf sits in the plume, then take your hand away.
constraint: At least one leaf must be visible with the steam.

title: Drift to the Side
oneLiner: Open a door a crack so the plume drifts sideways, and stay indoors.
details: Set a hot mug, or a kettle that has just boiled, on a counter near a door. Open the door a crack so the steam leans sideways, then stay on the indoor side to photograph that drift. The sideways shape is the point. Do not carry the kettle to the door.
tips: Include a vertical door edge so the lean of the steam is obvious.
Shoot when the plume is a clear diagonal rather than a puff.

title: Low Under the Column
oneLiner: Get below the plume and let it rise through the frame.
details: Crouch beside a table where a mug of hot water is already standing. Point the phone upward so the steam rises through the picture and leaves at the top. Keep the mug at the bottom edge. Do not put the phone into the plume.
tips: Rest your elbow on your knee for the upward angle.
A ceiling or cupboard in the background should be darker than the steam.
constraint: The plume must travel from the lower part of the frame toward the top.

title: From Behind the Kettle
oneLiner: Stand behind a kettle that has just boiled and watch the plume leave.
details: Once the kettle clicks off, move to the side opposite the spout so you look past the body toward the steam going into the room. A window or pale wall beyond the plume will show its shape. Do not lift the kettle, and do not put the phone over the spout. Include the spout at the edge of the frame so the plume has a source.
tips: Crouch to spout height so the plume reads as a trail.
Pre-focus on the spout before the plume thins.

title: Just Switched Off
oneLiner: Shoot in the moment the kettle switches off, when the plume is tallest.
details: Stand ready, at arm's length, with the kettle between you and a window or a pale wall. As soon as it clicks off, photograph the tall plume before it slackens. Do not lift the kettle. If your kettle is quiet, use the moment you take a pan of water off the heat and set it back on a cold burner.
tips: Pre-frame the spout so you are not hunting for it after the click.
Fire a burst through the first few seconds.
constraint: Take the picture within a few seconds of the kettle switching off.

title: The Fogged Window
oneLiner: After a shower, photograph the bloom across the bathroom window.
details: Once the shower is off, look at the bathroom window from the dry floor, or at the mirror if there is no window. The glass should carry a soft bloom, perhaps with a drip just starting. Photograph that bloom and the light coming through it, and include the frame. If the glass stays clear, breathe close to it and shoot the patch before it fades.
tips: Focus on the glass, not on whatever is beyond it.
Include the window frame so the bloom has a boundary.
constraint: The bloom on the glass must be visible.

title: Line in the Patch
oneLiner: Wipe one line through a breath patch and photograph the soft edges.
details: Breathe on a mirror so a patch appears, then pull one fingertip through it to leave a clear line. Photograph before the patch heals over. The soft edges against the clear stroke are the subject.
tips: Stand at a slight angle to avoid your own reflection in the middle.
Focus on the wiped line.
constraint: A single clear stroke must cross the breath patch.

title: Jets from the Lid
oneLiner: Photograph the small jets of steam leaving the kettle lid.
details: After the kettle boils and switches itself off, look at the lid rather than the spout. Many lids let out a thin jet from a hole or along a loose rim. Come close enough to see that jet, while staying to the side. If your lid stays sealed, crop tight on the first vapour at the spout so it reads as a small jet instead.
tips: A dark cupboard behind the lid will show a thin jet.
Use a short burst and keep the frame with the clearest thread.
constraint: Stay to the side of the kettle, not over the lid.

title: Fridge Light Behind
oneLiner: Use the open fridge as a backlight for a mug of steam.
details: Set a mug of hot water on the counter, then open the fridge so its light sits behind the steam. Turn the room light off if the fridge glow is too weak. Photograph from the side, with the mug still on the counter, and close the fridge when you are done.
tips: Do not rest the mug on the fridge door.
Expose for the fridge glow so the steam keeps a bright rim.
constraint: The fridge light must be the backlight.

title: Three Objects, One Surface
oneLiner: Arrange any three household objects into a balanced still life.
details: Choose items with different heights and shapes—a cup, book, and candle, for example. Place them on a plain table and move around until the spacing feels even. Negative space between objects matters as much as the objects themselves.
tips: Odd numbers often compose more naturally.
Use one window as your only light source.
Remove everything else from the table.
constraint: Exactly three objects, no more.

title: Keys on the Entry Tray
oneLiner: Photograph your keys resting where you drop them each day.
details: Find the bowl, hook, or tray that holds your keys. Include the surface texture beneath them—wood, ceramic, or fabric. The jumble of metal shapes can feel sculptural when lit from one side.
tips: Add one non-key object for scale if needed.
Avoid showing legible personal tags.
Shoot at a slight angle, not flat overhead.

title: Fruit Bowl Portrait
oneLiner: Arrange a few pieces of fruit in a bowl and photograph the cluster.
details: Use whatever fruit you have—apples, bananas, citrus. Stack or overlap pieces so the colours talk to each other. Watch for bruises and decide whether to hide or highlight them.
tips: Place the brightest fruit on a rule-of-thirds point.
Remove price stickers before shooting.
Try a dark cloth so the fruit stands out.
constraint: Use no more than five pieces of fruit.

title: Reading Glasses Rest
oneLiner: Capture glasses, or a glasses case, beside a book or a lamp.
details: Set the glasses where you left them last, on a side table, desk or nightstand. If you wear none, use sunglasses or a glasses case in the same spot. Let the arms, the lenses or the case make a quiet line, with one nearby object for context.
tips: Avoid reflections of yourself in the lenses.
Use soft light to prevent glare.
Focus on the hinge or temple curve.
constraint: Shoot from tabletop height.

title: Candle and Matchbook
oneLiner: Pair an unlit candle with matches or a lighter as a quiet still life.
details: Place an unlit candle and a matchbook or lighter on a stable surface, with space between them so the eye travels across the gap. If you have no candle, use a small bottle and its cap in the same pairing. Notice the texture of wax or glass, and the paper grain if you have a matchbook. Do not light anything; this is composition only.
tips: Align objects on a diagonal for energy.
Keep backgrounds plain and uncluttered.
Expose for the nearer object, not the window.

title: Umbrella by the Door
oneLiner: Photograph a closed umbrella standing where you keep it.
details: Find the stand, hook or corner that holds a folded umbrella. If you have none, hang a folded scarf or a tote on the same hook. Frame the handle or the straps against the fabric, and let the hallway sit quietly behind so the object reads as a small arranged scene.
tips: Crouch beside it rather than shooting down the hall.
Tap focus on the handle or the straps, then recompose.
Leave the flash off so the fabric keeps its real colour.
constraint: Keep the object closed or folded.

title: Desk Lamp Still
oneLiner: Arrange one small object in a desk lamp's pool of light.
details: Choose a pen, a cup or a small tin and set it where a lamp's light falls, with the shade partly in frame. Any lamp you can aim at the table will do. Shift the object until the bright pool and the dark table feel deliberate, and clear every other item off the table before you shoot.
tips: Lower phone exposure slightly to hold highlights.
Avoid pointing the lamp into the lens.
Crop so the lit object is the clear subject.
constraint: Only one artificial light source allowed.

title: Spoon, Whisk and Spatula
oneLiner: Fan a wooden spoon, a whisk and a spatula on the counter.
details: Clear a patch of counter and lay out a wooden spoon, a whisk and a spatula, or any three different kitchen tools you already own. Overlap the handles slightly so they read as one group. Use the window side of the counter and leave the rest bare.
tips: Point the longest handle towards the bottom corner.
A pale counter needs side light or the tools will look flat.
Wipe flour or water off the counter before you frame.

title: Marmalade and Toast
oneLiner: Build a small breakfast still life with toast and a jar.
details: Set a plate of toast or plain bread, a jar of marmalade or jam, and a butter spreader on a clear table. Leave the lid off the jar so the surface inside catches the light. Walk around the table until the three heights make a tidy triangle.
tips: Wipe smears off the plate rim before you frame.
Stand the jar on the far side so it rises behind the toast.
constraint: Include exactly three items.

title: Window Sill Bottles
oneLiner: Line up three bottles on a windowsill and compose them.
details: Gather any three bottles, jars or flasks from the kitchen or bathroom and stand them on a windowsill. Mix the heights so the row rises and falls instead of marching in a flat line. Shoot along the sill so the glass overlaps and the window sits behind as a bright backdrop.
tips: Lock exposure on the glass, not the bright pane.
Rotate one bottle so its label faces away.
constraint: Use only the bottles and the sill.

title: Spice Jar Triangle
oneLiner: Group three spice jars into a tight triangle on the counter.
details: Take three spice jars, or any three small jars from a cupboard, with different lids or heights. Set them close together on a clear patch of counter and turn noisy labels away. Crouch to counter height so the lids read as a little skyline.
tips: A sheet of baking paper under them calms a busy counter.
Focus on the middle lid and let the back jar soften.

title: Pot, Cup, Spoon
oneLiner: Arrange a teapot or mug, a cup and a spoon as a trio.
details: Set a teapot, or a second mug if you have no pot, beside a cup and a spoon. Point the spoon handle towards a corner of the frame so the eye travels. Use the window side of the table and leave the rest of the surface bare.
tips: Fill the cup so the liquid line shows.
Shoot from seated height rather than standing over the table.
constraint: The spoon handle must point towards a corner.

title: Soap, Brush, Cloth
oneLiner: Compose a bar of soap, a brush and a folded cloth.
details: In the bathroom or by the kitchen sink, set a bar of soap, a nail brush or dish brush, and a small folded cloth on a dry surface. Slip the cloth partly under the soap so the group feels joined. Shoot from slightly above and to one side.
tips: Dry the surface first so water spots do not compete.
Turn the brush so the bristles face the soap.

title: Coiled on a Notebook
oneLiner: Coil your earphones on a closed notebook and frame the spiral.
details: Place a closed notebook or paperback on the desk and coil wired earphones on top. If you have no earphones, loop a charging cable in the same spiral. Tuck the plug so it sits like a small accent, and keep the background to the bare desk.
tips: Shoot straight down so the coil stays a circle.
Tap focus on the plug, which is the sharpest small shape.
constraint: Nothing else may sit on the notebook.

title: Egg in an Egg Cup
oneLiner: Stand one egg in a cup and photograph that simple pair.
details: Use an egg cup if you have one, or a small glass or an espresso cup. An egg is ideal, though a small tomato or a round shallot will stand in. Set the cup on a plain cloth or a bare table and come in close so the rim and the round top fill the frame.
tips: A window to the side will trace the curve of the shell.
Hide the cloth edges so the background stays quiet.

title: Onions on a Cloth
oneLiner: Rest two onions on a crumpled cloth and study the arrangement.
details: Take two onions, or one onion and a lemon if that is all you have, and set them on a dish towel you have crumpled on purpose. Let the cloth make soft hills under the round shapes. Light them from the side with a window or a lamp.
tips: Pull one loose onion skin forward if it adds a curl.
Expose for the cloth, then check the onion skins are not blown out.
constraint: Use no more than two round vegetables or fruit.

title: Buttons in a Saucer
oneLiner: Scatter a handful of buttons in a saucer and tidy the pile.
details: Find spare buttons in a tin or a sewing kit, or use coins or beads if you have none, and drop a few into a saucer or a small dish. Nudge them until the colours sit in a loose cluster rather than a flat heap. Shoot from above and let the rim of the dish hold the picture.
tips: Remove one button if the pile looks jammed.
A plain wooden table under the saucer keeps the colours clear.

title: Envelopes Under a Weight
oneLiner: Stack unopened envelopes under a small weight and photograph the pile.
details: Use two or three envelopes or junk flyers, face down so no names show. Set a stone, a spoon or a small jar on top as the weight. Place the pile near the edge of a table and shoot from a low side angle.
tips: Let one envelope corner stick out so the stack has a ledge.
Turn the phone sideways if the pile is wider than it is tall.
constraint: No readable names or addresses.

title: Jug Beside a Glass
oneLiner: Set a jug of water next to an empty glass.
details: Fill a jug or a bottle with water and place an empty drinking glass beside it. Choose the gap between them on purpose, either tight or a full hand apart. Stand them on a windowsill or a pale counter and shoot so the waterline is clear.
tips: Wipe fingerprints off the glass first.
Get low enough to see the waterline as a straight mark.

title: Stem in a Bottle
oneLiner: Put a single stem or twig in a narrow bottle.
details: Pick one stem from a houseplant, or bring in a short twig from just outside the door, and stand it in a narrow bottle or jar with a little water. Place the bottle on a bare table against a plain wall. Leave the wall uncluttered so the stem reads clearly.
tips: Turn the stem until its best leaf faces the window.
Focus on the leaf, not the bottle rim.
constraint: Only one stem in the bottle.

title: Three Face-down Cards
oneLiner: Lay three playing cards face down in a loose fan.
details: If you have no cards, use three identical coasters, postcards or envelopes, also face down. Overlap them slightly so each edge shows. Shoot from above on a plain table and keep your hands out of the picture.
tips: A fan that is too neat looks printed; leave a small uneven gap.
Use the grid and keep the table edges out.

title: Pencil, Tape, Ruler
oneLiner: Group a pencil, a roll of tape and a ruler on the desk.
details: Clear a patch of desk and set the three tools down. Keep two of them parallel and turn the long one so it breaks the line. If you have no ruler, a postcard or a chopstick can be the long piece. Shoot from one end so the objects point into the frame.
tips: Sharpen nothing; a stubby pencil has more character.
Rest your elbows on the desk so the low angle stays steady.
constraint: Two objects parallel, one deliberately turned.

title: Compact and Lipstick
oneLiner: Pair a makeup compact with a lipstick on a bare surface.
details: If you do not use makeup, a lip balm and a small tin of cream, or a glasses case and a hair tie, can take their place. Keep both items closed so this stays an arrangement of two objects. Place them on a bare shelf or the dry edge of the sink.
tips: Put the taller item slightly behind the shorter one.
A towel just outside the frame can block a cluttered background.
constraint: Only two objects in the frame.

title: Tin of Cookies
oneLiner: Open a tin of cookies and arrange a few on the lid.
details: Use a cookie tin, a box of crackers or any closed tin of dry snacks. Set the lid beside the tin and place three or four cookies on the lid, leaving the rest inside. Shoot from a low side angle so the open tin and the lid both show.
tips: Turn the tin so a bright label does not face the lens.
Break nothing: whole cookies keep a cleaner shape.

title: Glass, Book, Clock
oneLiner: Arrange a water glass, a book and a clock on the bedside table.
details: Use whatever timepiece you have, or a wristwatch if there is no clock. Stand the glass, lean the book, and set the watch or clock so the three heights differ. Clear tissues and cables out of the frame, and keep any screen face down so no names show.
tips: Shoot from the pillow side so the table edge leads in.
Switch a lamp on only if the room is dim, and keep it out of frame.
constraint: Show no readable notifications or names.

title: Spools and a Thimble
oneLiner: Stack two thread spools and set a thimble beside them.
details: From a sewing kit, stand two spools of different colours and place a thimble, a button or a safety pin alongside. If you have no spools, two rolls of tape will do the same job. Shoot close, with a plain cloth underneath.
tips: Stack the spools only if they will not roll; otherwise stand them.
Come close enough that the cloth texture shows under them.

title: Jar Beside the Mug
oneLiner: Stand a jar of coffee or tea beside the mug you use.
details: Fill the frame with a jar of coffee, tea or sugar and the mug that usually sits near it. Add a spoon only if the pair feels unfinished without it. Place them where you actually make the drink and clear the counter behind.
tips: Take the spoon out if it crosses the mug handle.
Shoot before steam or a pour starts, so the objects stay still.
constraint: No hands in the frame.

title: Plates with a Napkin
oneLiner: Stack two plates and tuck a napkin between them.
details: Use dinner plates, side plates or shallow bowls. Slip a folded cloth napkin or a clean dish towel between them so a band of fabric shows. Shoot from the side at table height and let the stack sit left or right of centre.
tips: Align the plate rims or offset them on purpose, then commit.
A dark wall behind the stack will separate the pale china.

title: Shakers on a Bare Table
oneLiner: Stand salt and pepper together on a bare table.
details: Use the shakers, mills or little dishes you actually cook with. If you only have salt, pair it with a small dish of sugar or a second empty shaker. Give them space and shoot from a low angle so you see the sides of both shakers.
tips: Get below the tops of the shakers so you see their sides.
A plain wall behind them beats a busy kitchen shelf.
constraint: Shoot from below the height of the shakers.

title: Toothbrush and Tumbler
oneLiner: Stand a toothbrush in a glass on the bathroom shelf.
details: Clear a small patch of shelf or the edge of the sink. Stand one toothbrush in a glass or a mug, and lay the toothpaste tube beside it. Shoot from the side so the handle rises out of the glass.
tips: Dry the glass rim so toothpaste smears do not steal the frame.
A darker tile behind the glass will separate the pale handle.
constraint: Only the glass and what is in or beside it.

title: Nested Measuring Spoons
oneLiner: Unclip a set of measuring spoons and fan them on a cloth.
details: Use measuring spoons, or three ordinary teaspoons if that is what the drawer holds. Lay them on a plain dish towel so the bowls overlap and the handles spread. Shoot from above and keep the cloth in the frame as a quiet border.
tips: Unclip the ring so the spoons can lie flat.
A dark towel under pale spoons makes the fan easier to read.

title: Comb and Two Clips
oneLiner: Lay a comb beside two hair clips on a bare shelf.
details: Set a comb or a brush on a dry shelf, or on the closed lid of the toilet tank. Add two clips, ties or pins beside it so the group has one long shape and two small ones. Come in close and leave the rest of the shelf out of the picture.
tips: If you have no clips, a hair tie and a spare button will do.
Turn the comb so the teeth face the smaller items.
constraint: Only three items in the frame.

title: Oil, Vinegar, Dish
oneLiner: Stand oil and vinegar behind a small empty dish.
details: Choose two bottles of different heights, such as oil, vinegar or soy sauce, and set a little dish or a lid in front of them. Turn noisy labels away. Shoot at counter height so the dish sits low and the bottles rise behind it.
tips: Wipe drips off the bottle shoulders before you shoot.
Leave a finger's width between the bottles so they stay two shapes.

title: French Press and a Cup
oneLiner: Set a French press or a teapot beside an empty cup.
