details: Use a French press, a teapot or a second mug as the tall piece, and an empty cup as the short one. Leave the plunger up or the lid off so the top has a shape. Place them on a bare table with a window to one side.
tips: Empty the pot first so you are arranging objects, not pouring.
Get low enough to see the cup's rim as an ellipse.
constraint: Only the two vessels.

title: Garlic and a Small Dish
oneLiner: Break a garlic bulb into cloves and set them in a dish.
details: Use a whole garlic bulb, or a small onion if you have no garlic. Separate a few cloves with your fingers and leave the rest of the bulb whole beside the dish. Shoot from slightly above so the papery skins catch the light.
tips: Keep the loose skins in the dish if they curl.
A dark plate under a pale bulb gives the skins an edge.

title: Broom in the Corner
oneLiner: Lean a broom and a dustpan in the corner where you store them.
details: Use the broom, a mop or a long-handled brush, and the dustpan or a small bucket that lives with it. Stand them in their usual indoor corner and shift them until the handles make two separate lines. Include a little of the floor so they have a place to stand.
tips: Move sideways until the doorway is only a slice of the frame.
Tap focus on the nearer handle.
constraint: Both handles must be fully in frame.

title: Walnuts in a Bowl
oneLiner: Fill a small bowl with walnuts, corks or smooth stones.
details: Use small rounds you already have in the kitchen, such as walnuts, corks or a few stones from a plant pot. Set them in a bowl on the table, not piled above the rim. Shoot from above so the bowl holds the cluster and the table stays quiet around it.
tips: Leave one piece touching the rim so the circle feels anchored.
A window to the side picks out the ridges in the shells.

title: Lunchbox Still Life
oneLiner: Pack a lunchbox with three plain items and leave it open.
details: Use a lunchbox, a food container or a sandwich box. Put in three simple things you would actually eat later, such as an apple, a roll and a small bottle, and leave the lid open beside it. Shoot from above and turn any labels away.
tips: If you have no box, a shallow bowl with the same three things works.
Keep the lid touching the box so the group stays one arrangement.
constraint: Exactly three items inside the box.

title: Dice on a Dark Cloth
oneLiner: Roll two dice onto a dark cloth and leave them where they land.
details: Use dice if you have them. If not, two sugar cubes or two large buttons will sit the same way. Drop them on a dark dish towel and do not tidy where they land, then shoot from above with the cloth filling the background.
tips: A second drop is allowed if the first pair touches and merges.
Come close enough to see the pips, the sugar grain or the button holes.
constraint: Nothing else on the cloth in frame.

title: Honey Jar and Spoon
oneLiner: Set an open jar of honey beside a spoon on a saucer.
details: Use honey, jam or any slow spoonable spread. Keep the jar open, rest a spoon on a saucer beside it, and wipe the table around them. Side light from a window should catch the surface inside the jar.
tips: Wipe the jar lip so a drip does not become a second subject.
Rest the spoon so the handle runs off the saucer and stays easy to see.
constraint: Shoot from table height, not from above.

title: Plant, Pot and Saucer
oneLiner: Group a plant pot, its saucer and one fallen leaf.
details: Set a houseplant on the table with its saucer, and place one leaf from that plant on the saucer. If there is no loose leaf, set a small cup beside the pot, and if you have no plant, use a mug, a saucer and a spoon. Shoot from the side so the three shapes all read clearly.
tips: A plate works under the pot if you have no saucer.
Turn the fullest leaves away from the window so they do not turn black.

title: Folded Sweater on the Bed
oneLiner: Fold a sweater into a tidy block and set it on the bed.
details: Use a sweater, a cardigan or a shirt. Fold it so a collar, a cuff or a hem shows, and place it on a smooth bit of bed with the pillows out of frame. Shoot from the side of the bed so the folded block has a soft background.
tips: Tuck dangling sleeves in so the shape stays one block.
Stand beside the bed rather than leaning over the middle.
constraint: The sweater is the only object.

title: Herb Pot on the Counter
oneLiner: Set a herb pot beside the mug you drink from.
details: Use a herb pot or a tiny houseplant, and set your usual drinking mug beside it on the counter so the two openings echo each other. If you have no plant, use two mugs of different heights instead. Shoot from slightly above so the counter frames the pair and the wall behind stays simple.
tips: Rotate the plant so its fullest side faces the mug.
Shift bottles behind them out of the frame before you shoot.

title: Shoe Brush by the Door
oneLiner: Lay a shoe brush on the floor just inside the door.
details: Pair a shoe brush with a folded cloth, or an old toothbrush with a cotton pad if that is what you have. Set them on the indoor mat or a bare bit of floor by the door. Shoot from low so both items and a little of the floor fill the frame.
tips: Lay the brush across the cloth so the two shapes cross.
Focus on the bristles, which are the busiest texture.
constraint: Leave shoes out of the frame.

title: Mirror Twin
oneLiner: Stand a small object against a mirror so the reflection completes the pair.
details: Use a bathroom mirror, a small mirror stood on a table, or a switched-off television. Place a mug, a bottle or a piece of fruit against the glass so the reflection supplies the other half. Stand square to the mirror's edge, not face-on to the glass, level the phone, and put that edge on the vertical centre line of the grid. The join between the object and its reflection should read as one clean vertical line.
tips: Wipe the glass so the join stays a sharp line.
Tap the real object so the phone does not hunt for the reflection.
A handle turned outward makes the doubled shape easy to read.
constraint: The mirror edge must run through the middle of the frame.

title: Open Spread
oneLiner: Open a book flat so the two pages mirror each other.
details: Any book, magazine or notebook will do. Lay it open under a window or a lamp and hold the phone square above the pages, level the phone, and run the fold between the pages down the vertical centre line of the grid. The pages mirror each other in shape even when the words do not. A bookmark, a pencil or a turned corner on only one page is the break.
tips: Keep the page edges parallel with the sides of the frame.
Shade a glossy page with your body if the lamp glares.
Tap along the fold so both pages share the same focus.

title: The Middle Tine
oneLiner: Set a fork face up with its middle on the midline.
details: A fork mirrors left and right through the middle of its head. If it has an even number of tines, that middle is the gap between the centre pair, and if it has an odd number, it is the centre tine. Lay it face up on a plain table, hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put that middle on the vertical centre line of the grid so the tines match. Let the handle drift a little off the line so one side refuses the mirror.
tips: Rest a wrist on the table so the tines stay crisp.
Brush crumbs away before they look like a third subject.
Move closer instead of using digital zoom.
constraint: Keep every tine in focus, and keep part of the handle in frame.

title: One Side Plugged
oneLiner: Show a double outlet with a cord in only one side.
details: Find a double outlet on a wall you can reach. Fit a cord into one side and leave the other empty. Stand square to the plate, level the phone so the sides stay upright, and put the line between the two outlets on the vertical centre line of the grid. If you only have single outlets, centre one plate on that line and let the cord spoil the balance.
tips: Switch a nearby lamp on if the plate is sitting in gloom.
Include a short run of cord, not only the end at the outlet.
Tap the screws on the plate so the plastic stays detailed.

title: One Shoe Turned
oneLiner: Lay a pair of shoes so one of them breaks the mirror.
details: Use sneakers, boots or any pair already by the door. Set them side by side with the toes the same way until they mirror, then rotate one. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put the gap between the shoes on the vertical centre line of the grid. Keep both shoes complete.
tips: Point the unturned shoe at the top of the frame.
Window light from one side is enough to separate the pair from the floor.
Shift stray socks out of the picture first.
constraint: Both shoes must be fully inside the frame.

title: Spoons Across A Plate
oneLiner: Set two matching spoons so they mirror across a plate.
details: Set a plain plate in the middle of a table or counter. Place two identical spoons, one each side, bowls pointing away from the plate and both handles pointing down towards you, so the pair mirrors. Stand square to the near edge of the table, level the phone, and put the middle of the plate where the grid lines cross. Keep the background to the bare table or a single mat.
tips: Match the gap from each spoon to the rim before you shoot.
A tighter overhead crop drops chair backs out of the picture.
Tap one spoon so the plate does not steal the focus.

title: Yolk Off Axis
oneLiner: Centre a round pan or cookie, and keep the yolk or jam off the middle.
details: Cook one egg gently, then let the pan cool before you lean over it. The white settles into a rough circle and the yolk rarely lands in the middle. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone so the pan stays round, and centre the pan where the grid lines cross. If you would rather not cook, set a spoonful of jam or a pat of butter off to one side of a round cookie or an English muffin, with that round centred the same way.
tips: A dark stovetop makes the pale white easier to see.
Wait until the white has stopped spreading.
Raise the exposure a little if the metal has gone muddy.
constraint: The yolk, jam or butter must sit clearly away from the middle.

title: Basin Midline
oneLiner: Look straight down into a sink with the faucet on the midline.
details: A bathroom sink or a kitchen sink works. Stand square over the middle of the bowl, not over a corner, level the phone so the rim is not an oval, and put the faucet on the vertical centre line of the grid. The left curve of the bowl should match the right. Dry splashes on the chrome first, or they pull the eye off the line.
tips: Tap the faucet itself so the drain does not take the focus.
A tissue on the chrome softens a hard glare.
Lean in from the middle if a deep bowl hides the far rim.
constraint: The faucet must sit on the vertical midline of the picture.

title: One Door Ajar
oneLiner: Face two cupboard doors and leave only one of them ajar.
details: Kitchen or closet doors that meet in the middle are the subject. Close them, stand square on, level the phone, and put the seam on the vertical centre line of the grid. Open one door just a hand's width so the pair is no longer a mirror. Include both doors and a little of the wall around them.
tips: Step back until both doors fit without cutting a corner.
Matching handles make the small gap easy to read.
Focus on the seam, then check the handles are still sharp.

title: Collar Off The Line
oneLiner: Spread a shirt flat and turn one collar point out of line.
details: Use a buttoned shirt, a blouse or a jacket with a clear front opening. Lay it on a bed, front up, and smooth it so the buttons or the zip run down the middle. Stand over the shoulders, hold the phone square to them, level the phone, and put that fastening line on the vertical centre line of the grid. Flip one collar point, or turn one cuff back, so the mirror fails on one side only.
tips: Smooth the half you want to read as the matching side.
Light from one window is enough to show the collar fold.
Crop above the hem so the shoulders carry the picture.
constraint: The button line or zip must run vertically through the middle.

title: Headphone Wings
oneLiner: Place headphones so the two cups mirror across the headband.
details: Set over-ear headphones on a table. Slide them until the headband arches evenly, then hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put the top of the band on the vertical centre line of the grid so both cups match in size. If you only have earbuds, open their case flat, centre the hinge on that line, and let the cable be the break. A plain table stops the band merging with clutter.
tips: Drop the phone lower if one cup still looks larger.
Tap the nearer cup, not the table.
Turn the cable towards a corner so it reads as the one flaw.

title: Twelve And Six
oneLiner: Frame a clock or round dial so the top and bottom share one line.
details: Use a wall clock, a wristwatch or a kitchen timer with hands. Stand square to the face, level the phone, and put twelve and six on the vertical centre line of the grid. The hands rarely share that line, so the picture is how far they stray from it. If you have no clock with hands, use a round dial on an appliance and treat its top marker and its bottom edge the same way.
tips: Wipe the glass so a smear does not become a numeral.
Tap the hands or the pointer rather than the rim.
Step closer until the face fills the frame.
constraint: Twelve and six, or the top and bottom of the dial, must sit on the vertical midline.

title: One Tie Undone
oneLiner: Draw both curtains even, then loosen the tie on one side.
details: Close or half-close a pair of curtains so they meet near the middle of the window. Stand square, level the phone so the rail sits on a horizontal grid line, and put the meeting place on the vertical centre line. Undo one tie and leave the other fastened, so one side billows. If there are no ties, pull one panel a little off the middle, or hang two dish towels at the same height and drop one lower.
tips: Expose for the cloth if the glass behind is bright.
Stand far enough back that both panels fit.
Check the rail is horizontal before you take the picture.

title: Rug Corner Up
oneLiner: Square a patterned rug in the frame, then turn one corner back.
details: A rug, a bath mat or any rectangular mat can mirror left and right, even when the printed design does not. Photograph it from above, stand square to its edges, level the phone, and put the middle of the mat on the vertical centre line of the grid. Turn one corner over so the underside shows. Brush fluff off first so it does not become a second subject.
tips: Line a seam or a long edge up with a grid line.
Crouch and keep the phone parallel to the floor.
Fill the frame with the mat rather than the whole room.
constraint: One corner must be folded back.

title: One Space Empty
oneLiner: Leave one gap in a grid of eggs, muffins or ice cubes.
details: An egg carton with several eggs, a muffin tin or an ice-cube tray gives you a ready-made grid. Empty a single space, not a corner, so the eye expects a full set and misses one. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and centre the tray where the grid lines cross rather than centring the hole. Fill the frame with the tray, not the whole counter.
tips: Line the outer edge of the tray up with the frame.
Even window light stops one hole falling into black.
Tap the near rim so the far cells stay acceptably sharp.

title: Citrus Star
oneLiner: Look down on a fruit so its middle sits in the middle.
details: A clementine, an apple seen from the stem end, or a citrus you have already halved will show a centre you can aim at. Put the fruit on a plain plate or board. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone so the fruit stays round, and put the stem or the cut centre where the grid lines cross.
tips: Brace an elbow on the table so the phone does not tilt.
Tap the fruit, then hold the shutter to lock focus if your phone offers it.
A white plate separates the fruit from a busy cloth.
constraint: The stem or the centre of the fruit must sit in the middle of the frame.

title: Ribs To The Middle
oneLiner: Centre the hub where a shade's ribs, or an umbrella's, all meet.
details: A lampshade with visible ribs, or a dry umbrella opened indoors, is a wheel of spokes. Leave a shade where it hangs, or support an umbrella by hooking the handle on a sturdy chair back. Point the phone squarely at the hub, level the phone, and put the meeting point where the grid lines cross. Close an umbrella once you have the picture.
tips: A plain ceiling keeps umbrella ribs easy to pick out.
Expose for the fabric if a window behind the shade is bright.
Turn the shade until one rib points at a corner of the frame.

title: Cloth On One End
oneLiner: Centre a radiator, then let one object spoil one end.
details: A radiator is a row of repeated columns, symmetric until something interrupts one end. Drape a cloth, hang a sock or stick a magnet at one end only. Stand square to the wall, level the phone so the top runs along a horizontal grid line, and put the middle column on the vertical centre line. If you have no radiator, line up matching books, centre the middle book the same way, and lean one extra object against an end book.
tips: Take a few paces back so the whole row fits.
Side light from a window picks out each column.
Keep the extra object inside the frame, not cropped away.
constraint: Only one end may carry the extra object.

title: The Shifted Cushion
oneLiner: Match two cushions, then slide one so the pair no longer mirrors.
details: On a bed or a sofa, use two cushions or pillows that already match and sit them so they mirror. Stand square to the seat, level the phone, put the seat line on a horizontal grid line, and put the midpoint between them on the vertical centre line. Then shift or rotate just one, a little, and take the picture. Clear other clutter off the seat so the almost-match is the whole story.
tips: Crouch to cushion height rather than shooting steeply down.
Plump both before you shift one, or the match never existed.
A level seat line makes a small slide obvious.

title: Bridge Of The Frames
oneLiner: Set a pair of glasses so the bridge sits on the midline.
details: Lay glasses or sunglasses flat, lenses up. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and nudge the frames until the bridge sits on the vertical centre line of the grid and the two rims match. If a window flares in a lens, take a small step sideways and level the phone again. If you have no glasses, set two identical jar lids so they touch at one point on that same line.
tips: Tap a lens, not the table, so the rims stay crisp.
A dark cloth makes thin metal frames easier to see.
Include both rims whole, temples and all.
constraint: The bridge, or the point where the two lids touch, must sit on the vertical midline.

title: The Button That Breaks
oneLiner: Press one rocker of a double switch so the pair no longer matches.
details: Find a double light switch, the plate with two rockers side by side. Stand square to it, level the phone, and put the gap between the rockers on the vertical centre line of the grid. Press one rocker so it sits out of line with the other, then return it when you are done. If you have no double switch, lay a game controller face up, centre its body on the grid, and show how the controls refuse to mirror.
tips: Flip a rocker you can return, or use a lamp you can switch.
Come in close so the two rockers fill the frame.
Tap the plate rather than the wall around it.

title: The Handle Decides
oneLiner: Include the whole handle of a round pan so the circle is broken.
details: Set an empty frying pan or saucepan on the stovetop or a table. From above, the body is a circle and the handle is the piece that refuses to mirror. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone so the body stays round, and centre that circle where the grid lines cross, with the handle running towards a corner. Keep the tip of the handle inside the picture, and shift so your own shape does not appear in the metal.
tips: Lift the exposure a touch if the pan is dark metal.
A slightly higher stance still reads as overhead.
Wipe water spots so they do not look like a second handle.
constraint: The full handle must be visible.

title: Colander Crown
oneLiner: Shoot a colander from above so the holes ring a clear centre.
details: A colander, a sieve or a showerhead has holes arranged around a middle. Set the colander or sieve on a plain surface with the handle towards a corner, or stay on dry flooring and point the phone at the showerhead without stepping into the tray. Hold the phone square to the ring, level the phone so it stays round, and put the centre where the grid lines cross. The handle, the shower arm or a small chip is enough to stop the picture being perfect.
tips: Let a bright surface show through the holes.
Focus on the near rim so the ring stays crisp.
For a showerhead, shoot from outside the tray and keep the phone dry.

title: Thumbs Out
oneLiner: Lay two gloves thumbs outward so they mirror like a pair of wings.
details: Gloves are a true pair, one left and one right. Lay them flat, thumbs outward and cuffs level with each other, on a plain table or floor. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put the gap between the gloves on the vertical centre line of the grid. If you have no gloves, lay two matching socks toes outward and cuffs together, and centre that gap the same way.
tips: Match the cuffs so one is not sitting higher.
A contrasting cloth helps if the gloves are dark.
Include both shapes whole, cuffs and fingertips.
constraint: The two gloves, or the two socks, must mirror each other left and right.

title: Even Bow
oneLiner: Tie a bow and photograph it so the two loops match.
details: A shoelace still in the shoe, a bathrobe belt or a bit of gift ribbon will all tie. Make the two loops as even as you can and leave the tails a little uneven, so the bow almost mirrors and then does not. Put the knot where the grid lines cross, level the phone, and shoot straight down onto a table or square-on to a bow still in a shoe. Fill the frame with the knot and both loops.
tips: Tap the knot rather than a tail.
Soft window light shows the fold in each loop.
Tuck a frayed end in if it looks like a third loop.

title: The Leaf Midrib
oneLiner: Let a single leaf show its veins mirrored about the midrib.
details: Use a leaf from a herb, a cabbage or a lettuce, or one a houseplant can spare. Lay it flat and hold it up to a window so light comes through the veins. Square the phone to the leaf, level the phone, and put the midrib on the vertical centre line of the grid so it runs from the top of the frame to the bottom. A small tear on one side is a welcome break, not a reason to change leaves.
tips: Weigh a curling edge down with a clean spoon.
Tap along the midrib so the side veins stay readable.
A plain bright window is better than a busy view behind the leaf.
constraint: The midrib must run from the top of the frame to the bottom.

title: Rosette From Above
oneLiner: Look down into a lettuce, cabbage or succulent and find its centre.
details: The heart of a lettuce or a cabbage, the root end of an onion, or a succulent on the windowsill is a spiral around a centre. Set it on the counter or leave the plant in its pot. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone so the subject stays round, and put that centre where the grid lines cross. Outer leaves can run off the edges.
tips: Move closer until the centre is large in the frame, and check it is sharp.
Turn the subject until a natural gap faces a corner.
Stand so your body blocks glare on a shiny counter.

title: Broken Ring
oneLiner: Coil a cable into a circle and let one end break the ring.
details: Use a charging cable or earphones on a pale table. Shape a loose circle, as round as it will sit, and leave the connector or the free end sticking out. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and centre the circle where the grid lines cross, not the stray end. The ring should feel deliberate and the end should feel like the one mistake.
tips: A light tabletop makes a dark cable easy to follow.
Nudge the coil with one finger until it holds its shape.
Keep the whole ring, including the break, inside the frame.
constraint: The coil must read as a circle, with one end breaking it.

title: Faucet As Wings
oneLiner: Line the phone up with the faucet and balance both sides.
details: At a bathroom or kitchen sink, look straight at the faucet rather than down into the bowl. Stand square, level the phone so any tiles stay upright, and put the gap between two faucets, or the body of a single faucet, on the vertical centre line of the grid. Equal amounts of the sink should show on both sides. Wipe water spots off the chrome before you frame.
tips: Lower the exposure a touch if the chrome turns pure white.
Include the base of the faucet, not a crop through the middle of it.
Move back a little if the faucet still looks skewed.

title: Single Slat
oneLiner: Find a set of parallel bars and shift only one of them out of line.
details: Venetian blinds are the easy version: set the slats even, then twist one with a finger if it will move. A cooling rack or a fixed vent gives you the same lines; if a bar will not move, lay a teaspoon across one gap so a single line is interrupted. Square the phone to the bars, level the phone, and let the matched slats run parallel to the horizontal lines of the grid. The picture only works if every other line still agrees.
tips: Side light throws a thin shadow that shows which line is wrong.
Fill the frame with the bars and leave the surrounding wall out.
Count the lines on the screen before you shoot.
constraint: Only one slat, bar or spoon may sit out of line.

title: One Foot Out
oneLiner: Stand in socks and turn one foot so the pair no longer matches.
details: In socks or bare feet, point the phone down and keep your face out of the frame. Line both feet up as a mirror, then angle one foot outward. Hold the phone square so the straight foot points at the top of the frame, level the phone so both feet look the same size, and put the gap between the heels on the vertical centre line of the grid. A plain bit of floor is plenty of background.
tips: Watch the screen while you aim, and shuffle until both feet fit.
A plain floor reads more clearly than a busy rug.
Heels on one horizontal grid line make the turned foot obvious.

title: Odd One In The Middle
oneLiner: Pair two matching items on a shelf with a different one between them.
details: On a fridge shelf or a cupboard shelf, set two matching pots, cartons or bottles with a clearly different item between them. The outer two should agree in height and colour. Stand square, level the phone, and put the middle item on the vertical centre line of the grid, with the shelf along a horizontal grid line. Turn printed faces away if a logo would dominate.
tips: A straight-on stance stops one pot looking taller than its twin.
Clear nearby leftovers so they do not join the group.
Leave a little shelf visible above and below the trio.
constraint: The two outer items must match and the middle one must not.

title: Shelf Seesaw
oneLiner: Balance a shelf so the left side weighs the same as the right, visually.
details: Choose a shelf and put one object in the middle to be the axis: a clock, a vase or a tall book. Stand square, level the phone, put the shelf on a horizontal grid line and that object on the vertical centre line. Using things you already own, match the height of the group on the left to the group on the right. If one side still shouts, move a single object and shoot again.
tips: Squint at the screen: the louder side is the heavy one.
Leave a little empty shelf so the objects can breathe.
Step back until the whole shelf fits, including both ends.

title: Handle Aside
oneLiner: Square up to an interior door and let the handle be the only break.
details: Close an interior door and stand in front of its middle. Level the phone, stand square so the door edges run parallel to the picture edges, and put the door's midpoint on the vertical centre line of the grid. Panels, if there are any, should mirror left and right. The handle sits off to one side, and that is the point; a plain door still works if you centre it cleanly.
tips: Take one step back so a little of the surround shows.
Check the top edge against a horizontal grid line.
Focus on the handle so the break is sharp.
constraint: The door edges must stay parallel to the edges of the picture.

title: Off The Centre Hook
oneLiner: Hang one thing just off the middle of a row of hooks.
details: Coat hooks, mug hooks or a rail of identical hangers will do. If you have none, use a row of matching mugs or jars on a shelf. Stand square, level the phone so the rail or shelf sits on a horizontal grid line, and put the middle of the row on the vertical centre line. Hang or place one thing just off that middle, and leave the other places empty so the row is the mirror and the object is the break.
tips: Include the whole rail or shelf, not a cropped section.
A plain wall behind the hooks keeps the shapes clear.
The object should miss the centre line, not sit on it.

title: Entrance On Axis
oneLiner: Centre a front, or just the door, so the two halves really match.
details: Your own front door, or the shared entrance of your building, often splits into matching halves when the door sits in the middle of its wall. If the door is off to one side, centre the door itself: matching panels are the halves, and on a plain door the handle is the break. Stand square to it, in the hallway or on the sidewalk, level the phone, and put the door on the vertical centre line of the grid. Frame the door and its surround, and if there is glass, let it stay dark rather than showing a room.
tips: Shuffle left or right until the entrance sits on the centre line.
Hold the phone upright so the uprights do not lean.
Include the top of the doorway and matching width on both sides.
constraint: The entrance or the door must sit on the vertical midline.

title: Panel On Axis
oneLiner: Centre a control panel and see whether the buttons mirror.
details: Use the button panel on a stove, a washing machine or a microwave, or an intercom plate beside your building door. Stand square, level the phone, and put the middle of the panel on the vertical centre line of the grid. Crop away any readable names so the picture stays about shape. A knob, a display or a button that sits off the mirror is the break, and if every control matches, that match is the picture.
tips: Shift until the panel edges run parallel with the frame.
Tap the panel so a bright display does not blow out.
Crop a logo if it shouts louder than the buttons.
constraint: Readable names and numbers must stay out of the frame.

title: Panes Either Side
oneLiner: Centre the bar that divides a window into matching panes.
details: Use a window in your home, or one on your own building seen from the sidewalk, and find the upright bar that divides it into matching panes. Stand square to the glass, level the phone, and put that bar on the vertical centre line of the grid so the two sides agree in width. Keep the picture on the bar and the frame, with the glass as an even tone rather than a view into a room. A latch or a curtain on one side can be the break, and if your window has no centre bar, centre a picture frame on the wall in the same way.
tips: Use a horizontal grid line to keep the frame level.
Come closer so the bar and both panes fill the width.
A small move sideways will square a bar that still leans.
constraint: The bar, or the middle of the frame, must sit on the vertical midline.

title: Cover Underfoot
oneLiner: Centre a round metal cover and whatever pattern sits on it.
details: Look for a round or square metal cover set into the sidewalk near home. Hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put the middle of the cover where the grid lines cross, with the sides of a square cover parallel to the frame. Bolts usually ring that middle, and one scuff is enough to keep it from being perfect. If you cannot find one, centre a round metal lid on the floor at home in the same way.
tips: Keep your shoes out of the corners.
Tap the metal so it does not turn into a black disc.
Take a small step aside if your shadow covers the pattern.

title: The Wall Between
oneLiner: Frame two matching windows with the wall between them as the axis.
details: Many buildings near home have two similar windows with a stretch of wall between them. Stand on the sidewalk, square to that wall, level the phone so the uprights stay upright, and put the middle of the wall on the vertical centre line of the grid. Choose a pair that matches in size, and keep the picture on the frames and the wall between them. Let the glass stay an even tone so no room shows through, and mismatched curtains can be the break.
tips: Move back so both frames are complete.
Focus on the frames, not whatever sits on the sill.
If one window is a different size, keep looking for a pair that agrees.
constraint: The strip of wall between the windows must fall in the middle of the frame.

title: Pipe To One Side
oneLiner: Use a downspout as the break in an otherwise even stretch of wall.
details: Find a downspout on an outside wall near home. The repeating lines of siding, tile, brick or an even stretch of stucco are the pattern, and the downspout is what interrupts it. Stand square, level the phone, put a horizontal joint on a grid line, and set the pipe clearly to one side of the vertical centre line so one half of the frame stays quieter. If there is no downspout, use a vertical cable or a strip of trim on an even wall in the same way.
tips: Include the pipe from near the ground to as high as the frame allows.
Keep the pipe vertical against a grid line.
Daylight as it is right now is enough to separate pipe and wall.

title: Post In The Rail
oneLiner: Put a post or a middle bar on the midline and see if the bars agree.
details: Railings along a sidewalk, or metal bars across a window, will give you a thicker post or a middle bar, and the picture is of the bars rather than anything behind them. Stand square, level the phone so the top line is horizontal, and put that post or middle bar on the vertical centre line of the grid, with several bars on both sides. If a bar is bent or missing, include that unevenness. Where the bars cross glass, let the glass stay dark so no room shows through.
tips: A small move left or right is what centres the post.
Focus where the post meets the top rail.
Let the bars run parallel to the vertical grid lines.
constraint: The post or the middle bar must sit on the vertical midline.

title: Ring Around The Trunk
oneLiner: Point the camera down and centre the trunk or the plant.
details: Some trees near home sit in a circular or square grille. Stand at the edge of it on the sidewalk, hold the phone square overhead, level the phone, and put the trunk where the grid lines cross so the grille repeats around it. If there is no grille, use the circle of soil or stones at the foot of the tree. If you cannot find a tree, centre a round pot and the plant in it on the floor at home.
tips: Keep your shoes outside the frame.
Tap the grille so the metal is not too dark.
A small shift around the tree changes which gap faces you.

title: The Grate's Middle Bar
oneLiner: Centre the middle bar of a sidewalk grate and square the rest.
details: Find a drain grate set into the sidewalk near home, one you can photograph without leaving the sidewalk. Stand over it so the bars run straight up the frame or straight across it, level the phone, and put the middle bar, or the gap between an even pair, on the centre line of the grid. The other bars should agree in spacing. One blocked slot or a bent bar can be the break.
tips: Square the phone until the bars are parallel with the frame.
Tap the metal if the slots have turned pure black.
Brush loose grit only if it hides the bar you are centring.
constraint: The middle bar, or the middle gap, must sit on the centre line of the frame.

title: Rail Down The Middle
oneLiner: Use a central rail or a long seam as a line of symmetry.
details: Some stairs have a rail running down the middle, which splits the flight into two halves. If you have no rail like that, use a straight seam running away from you down a hallway floor or a paved path. Stand square at the near end, level the phone, and put the rail or the seam on the vertical centre line of the grid. The line should start near the bottom of the frame and run toward the middle.
tips: Include both halves, even if one side is more worn.
Tap focus part of the way along the rail or the seam.
The horizontal grid lines will show if the phone is tilting.

title: The Middle Slat
oneLiner: Face a slatted chair or bench and centre its middle.
details: A chair back, a slatted headboard or an empty bench is a row of repeated lines. Stand square to it, level the phone, put the top line of the slats on a horizontal grid line, and put the middle slat, or the gap between an even pair, on the vertical centre line. The lines should repeat evenly to the left and right. If a bench is in use, use a chair at home instead, and leave bags out of the picture.
tips: Step until the two ends feel even in the frame.
Keep the top rail of the back horizontal.
A plain wall behind the chair makes the slats easier to count.
constraint: The middle slat, or the middle gap, must sit on the vertical midline.

title: Band On The Post
oneLiner: Level a post so a band or a seam runs across the middle.
details: A sidewalk bollard, a sign pole or a lamp post is a column, and from the front it mirrors left and right. Stand square to it, level the phone so any band, seam or sticker is horizontal, and put that band on the horizontal centre line of the grid with the column on the vertical line. A dent or a missing patch is the break. If you cannot find a post, stand square to a floor lamp at home and centre the shade the same way.
tips: Come close enough that the column fills the width.
Tap the band so it does not blow out to white.
Keep your feet out of the bottom of the frame.

title: Gap In The Pair
oneLiner: Stand square to two similar cans and centre the gap.
details: Two recycling bins, garbage cans, laundry baskets or large boxes side by side make an everyday near-mirror. Use a pair you already have, indoors or where they already stand outside. Stand square, level the phone, and put the gap between them on the vertical centre line of the grid. A sticker, a crooked lid or a different colour is the break.
tips: Close the lids so the shapes can agree.
Turn a label away if it would dominate the pair.
Include both of them whole, from top to base.
constraint: The gap between the pair must sit on the vertical midline.

title: Circle Overhead
oneLiner: Aim upward at a round ceiling fitting and centre it.
details: A smoke alarm, a round ceiling light or a round vent is a circle you already live under. Stand directly beneath it so you are square to the fitting, level the phone so the circle stays a circle and not an oval, and put the middle where the grid lines cross. A test button, a tiny lamp or a moulded petal usually stops it being perfect, and if every mark is centred the symmetry itself is the picture. Stay on the floor.
tips: If the circle turns into an oval, you are not underneath it yet.
Tap the fitting, not the ceiling around it.
Turn a light on if the fitting is sitting in shade.

title: Along the Edge
oneLiner: Sight along a table edge until it narrows into the distance.
details: Stand at one end of a dining table, desk or console and lower the phone to the height of the top. Let the front edge run from the near corner toward the far end. Anything already on the table can stay, but the narrowing line is the subject.
tips: Focus a third of the way down the edge.
Keep the phone upright so the edge does not bow.
constraint: The near end of the edge must look larger than the far end.

title: Handle Over the Brink
oneLiner: Rest a spoon so the handle crosses the edge and the bowl stays put.
details: Lay a spoon, a wooden server or a pencil on the table so most of its weight is on the top and only the handle crosses the edge. It must be stable. Photograph from the side so the crossing point is obvious and the empty space below the handle shows.
tips: Tap the point where the handle leaves the table.
A side lamp will separate the handle from the dark floor.

title: The Drop Beyond
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the table edge and the empty drop beyond it.
details: Choose a clear stretch of table or counter and bring the camera close to the edge. Let the top surface occupy the upper half and the empty drop the lower half. The line between them should be sharp. No need to include the whole room.
tips: Hold the phone so the edge runs straight across.
Focus on the edge itself, not the floor below.
constraint: The edge must cross the frame from side to side.

title: Near and Far
oneLiner: Place one object near the edge and another well back on the table.
details: Set two ordinary objects on the table, such as a cup and a small book. Put one close to the edge, fully supported, and the other near the middle. Shoot from a low angle along the top so the gap between them feels like a decision.
tips: Get the lens just above the tabletop.
Focus on the object nearer the edge.
constraint: Both objects must be fully on the table.

title: Cloth Over the Edge
oneLiner: Drape a cloth so it breaks over the edge and hangs a short way.
details: Use a dish towel, a shirt or a tablecloth and drape it so the fold breaks exactly at the table edge. Let a short length hang. Photograph the break, showing both the cloth on the top and the cloth falling away.
tips: Side light will mark the fold with a thin shadow.
Smooth only the worst lump, and leave the break itself alone.

title: At Edge Height
oneLiner: Hold the phone level with the edge so the tabletop becomes a thin band.
details: Crouch until the lens is level with the thickness of the table or counter. The top should shrink to a thin band, and the vertical face of the edge should fill more of the picture. A plain object on the top can peek into that band.
tips: Brace a hand on your knee, not on a wobbly leaf of the table.
Tap the vertical face so the thin top stays a clean line.
constraint: The tabletop must appear as a thin band, not a broad surface.

title: The Table Corner
oneLiner: Frame the corner where two edges meet and the planes fall away.
details: Find a corner of a table, desk or counter. Stand so the corner points toward you and both edges leave the frame. The top plane and the two vertical faces can all be visible. Empty the corner of clutter for a minute if you need the shape to read.
tips: Get slightly above the corner so you see the top plane.
Use the grid to keep the corner from tilting by accident.

title: Spaced Along the Lip
oneLiner: Line small objects along the edge with even gaps between them.
details: Choose three to six small things, such as teaspoons, bottle caps, coins or buttons. Space them along the table edge with similar gaps, each one fully on the table. Shoot from above or from a low side so the rhythm and the edge share the picture.
tips: Check the gaps in the preview and nudge one object before the final frame.
Keep the phone parallel to the edge.
constraint: Use at least three objects, none of them hanging off.

title: Dark Line at the Window
oneLiner: Put the table edge against a bright window so it reads as a dark line.
details: Pull a table or stand at a counter that has a window behind it. Crouch until the edge becomes a dark line against the brighter glass. Expose for the window light and let the table fall into tone. The line should stay recognisable as an edge.
tips: Turn the room lamp off so it does not fill the silhouette.
Include a short length of the line rather than the whole room.
constraint: The edge must be darker than the window behind it.

title: Plate and the Cut
oneLiner: Angle the phone so the table edge appears to cut across a plate.
details: Set a plate or a shallow bowl fully on the table, a little in from the edge. Lower the camera until the edge visually crosses the plate, even though the plate is safe and supported. The crossing is the picture, so keep other dishes out.
tips: Move an inch at a time until the edge bisects the plate in the preview.
Focus on the rim where the edge crosses it.

title: Notebook at the Brink
oneLiner: Slide a notebook until its far side sits just inside the desk edge.
details: On a desk or table, slide a notebook, a magazine or a stack of paper until it stops just short of the edge. The slim gap between paper and drop is the subject. Shoot from above so that gap is a clean line.
tips: Include the corner of the notebook and a length of the edge.
Tap the paper edge nearest the drop.
constraint: A visible gap must remain between the paper and the drop.

title: Chips in the Paint
oneLiner: Come close to chips and worn paint along the edge of a table.
details: Run your eye along a table, desk or counter for chips, dents or rubbed colour. Choose the most honest patch and fill the frame with it. Include the corner where the top turns into the vertical face, so it is clearly an edge. If the edge is unmarked, photograph that same corner where the top material meets the side.
tips: Rake a lamp from the side to lift the chips.
Steady the phone against your free hand, cupped underneath.

title: Lamp Along the Lip
oneLiner: At night, send a lamp along the edge so it becomes a highlight.
details: After dark, or with the curtains closed, set a lamp so its light skims the table edge and turns it into a bright line. Switch off stronger overhead lights. Photograph that highlight, including where it fades along the edge.
tips: Place the lamp near one end rather than above the middle.
Lock exposure on the highlight and let the room go dark.
constraint: The edge must carry a visible highlight.

title: The Bare Edge
oneLiner: Clear a long stretch of table edge and photograph it empty.
details: Move objects aside until a long run of table or counter edge is bare. Stand so that empty line crosses the picture with nothing sitting on it. The wood, laminate or paint of the edge is enough.
tips: Include both a near and a far portion so the line has length.
Check the preview for a single crumb and leave it only if you want it.

title: Fork Beside Spoon
oneLiner: Lay a fork and a spoon parallel to the edge, close but stable.
details: Place a fork and a spoon parallel to the table edge, handles pointing the same way, both fully supported. The edge should run just beyond them. Photograph from above so the two pieces echo the line of the table.
tips: Align the handles with the grid.
Wipe water spots off the metal before you shoot.
constraint: Both pieces must be parallel to the edge.

title: Tangent Fruit
oneLiner: Bring a round fruit up to the edge and stop it before it can roll.
details: Set an orange, an apple or another round fruit fully on the table, a finger's width back from the edge. If the table slopes, wedge it gently against a folded napkin. Photograph the near-miss from a low angle, with the drop visible beyond. The fruit should look close to the edge and still be completely stable.
tips: Put a hand near, but not in frame, until you are sure it will not roll.
Focus on the point of the fruit closest to the edge.
constraint: The fruit must be stable and fully supported.

title: Cable Over the Side
oneLiner: Let a cable run off the desk edge and photograph the drop it makes.
details: Use a charging lead, a headphone cord or a length of string. Let it travel across the desk and fall over the edge in a simple curve. Photograph the moment it leaves the surface. Keep the plug or loose end on the floor, out of the way of your feet.
tips: Shoot from the side so the curve is a clear hook.
Tap the cable where it bends over the edge.

title: Flush with the Books
oneLiner: Align a stack of books so one face sits flush with the table edge.
details: Stack two or more books, notebooks or magazines and push them until one vertical face lines up with the table edge. Look from the side: the book face and the table face should feel continuous, then stop. Photograph that alignment.
tips: Get to edge height so you can see whether the faces truly line up.
Nudge the stack before shooting if a corner sticks out.
constraint: The book face and the table edge must line up.

title: Shadow Off the Table
oneLiner: Place an object at the edge so its shadow falls off the table.
details: Set a glass, a bottle or a small vase fully on the table near the edge. Use a lamp or window so the shadow leaves the tabletop and continues onto the floor or a chair. Photograph both parts of the shadow, on the table and beyond it.
tips: Lower the lamp until the shadow stretches.
Include the object and both parts of its shadow.

title: Where the Sink Cuts In
oneLiner: Photograph the curve where the counter gives way to the sink.
details: Look at the edge where the counter drops toward the sink, or the rim where the basin meets the counter. That curve is different from the long straight lip. Include a little of the basin so the edge has a reason, and leave the water switched off. A bathroom basin and the ledge around it work the same way.
tips: Wipe splashes off the rim only if they hide the line.
Get slightly above the rim so the curve reads clearly.
constraint: The curve where the basin meets the top must be in the frame.

title: Edge Meets Wall
oneLiner: Photograph the point where a table or counter edge runs into a wall.
details: Find the place a table, desk or counter actually meets a wall, or stops just short of it. That junction is the subject. Include a little of the wall and a length of the edge, and keep the meeting point inside the frame.
tips: Square the phone to the wall so the vertical is upright.
Tap the junction rather than the middle of the table.

title: The Overhang
oneLiner: Show the lip of the counter and the shadow on the cupboard below.
details: Stand at the kitchen counter and find where the top juts past the cupboard door. The horizontal lip and the darker recess beneath it are the subject. Include a little of the door or drawer front so the overhang has a scale. A desk with a drawer underneath works if the kitchen counter sits flush.
tips: Crouch until you can see both the lip and the door front.
Bring a lamp to the side if you want a deeper shadow under the lip.
constraint: The overhang and the face below it must both appear.

title: The Leaf Seam
oneLiner: Follow the seam of a table leaf until it meets the outer edge.
details: If your table extends, look at the seam where the leaves meet, whether it is open or closed. Follow that line to the point where it hits the outer edge. If the table does not extend, use the join between two counters, or the line down the middle of a drop-leaf. The meeting of seam and edge is the picture.
tips: Shoot from slightly above so both lines are readable.
Tap the point where the seam meets the edge.
constraint: The seam must touch the outer edge inside the frame.

title: Chair Under the Lip
oneLiner: Look along the narrow gap between a chair and the table edge.
details: Push a chair in until it nearly touches the table or desk. Crouch and look along the dark slot between the chair and the underside of the top. That line, with the edge above it, is the subject. A stool tucked under a counter works if you have no chair.
tips: Get the lens down to the height of the gap.
Focus on the nearest part of the gap and let it narrow away.

title: Two Parallel Edges
oneLiner: Lay a mat so its near edge runs parallel to the table edge.
details: Put a placemat, a folded dish towel or a large book on the table, squared so its near side echoes the table edge. Leave a clear gap between the two lines. Photograph from above, including a corner of the mat and a good length of the table edge.
tips: Use the grid to check that the two lines really are parallel.
Nudge the mat before you shoot if the gap widens at one end.
constraint: The gap between the mat and the table edge must be visible.

title: Edge in Section
oneLiner: Come close until the thickness of the tabletop is the subject.
details: Look at the edge in profile, close enough to see how the top is made: a thin skin over a core, a wooden lip, or a smooth curve from top to side. Fill the frame with that band. If the edge is perfectly plain, skim a lamp along it so the curve still reads.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the edge so the band stays even.
Rest a knuckle lightly on the top to keep this close view steady.
constraint: The thickness of the top must be visible.

title: Towel Weave Close-Up
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the weave of a bath or kitchen towel.
details: Hold the fabric near a window and move in until the threads become a landscape. Look for loops, a grid of fibres, or a frayed edge. A small change of angle makes the texture feel deeper.
tips: Focus on the threads nearest the lens.
Turn the towel if a hard highlight wipes the loops out.
Skip portrait mode if it smears the fine edges.
constraint: Fill at least eighty percent of the frame with texture.

title: Wood Grain Table
oneLiner: Follow the grain across a wooden table or board.
details: Move the phone slowly over the surface until a line of grain travels through the frame. Notice knots, scratches, and shifts from pale to dark. Treat the table as a map you are reading from very near.
tips: Use a low slant so the grain throws tiny shadows.
Keep cups and hands out of the picture.
Switch to mono if the wood stain is the only thing you notice.

title: Citrus Peel Landscape
oneLiner: Pull citrus rind off by hand and photograph the pitted skin up close.
details: Pull a strip of rind off an orange or a lemon with your fingers, and hold it near the light until the dimples take over the frame. Let the colour stay bright and clearly from a fruit. Rotate the peel until a highlight runs through the pits.
tips: Blot juice so the skin does not glare.
Rest the peel on a plain plate for a quiet background.
Focus on the bump closest to the lens.
constraint: No zoom; move your body closer instead.

title: Knit Stitch Pattern
oneLiner: Capture the repeating stitches of a sweater, blanket, or sock.
details: Lay the knit flat or drape it so the stitches catch light from the side. Follow one row of loops across the frame like a line of writing. A slight tilt makes some loops stand proud of the others.
tips: Take the light from a window at the side of the fabric.
Keep the background from showing through holes in the knit.
Hold the phone parallel to the cloth.
constraint: Use black and white only.

title: Sponge Pores
oneLiner: Move in on the holes of a sponge or loofah.
details: Get close enough that the pores feel like small caves. A damp sponge catches sharper highlights, while a dry one looks softer. Keep the background simple so the holes stay clear.
tips: Angle a lamp or the window so the holes hold shadow.
Focus in the middle of the sponge, on a hole.
A square crop suits this if your camera offers one.

title: Book Page Fibres
oneLiner: Open a book and photograph the rough edge or paper texture.
details: Fan the pages slightly, or shoot the cut edge where the fibres show. Bring the phone close until separate lines of paper appear. Cream or off-white paper will feel warmer than bright white.
tips: Let any printed words fall too soft to read.
Keep the paper out of hard glare from the window.
Support the pages so they do not spring shut.
constraint: Paper texture fills the frame edge to edge.

title: Tile Grout Lines
oneLiner: Crop until grout grit and the pits in the tile are all you see.
details: Choose a kitchen or bathroom tile and move in until the sandy grout and the speckled glaze fill the picture. Chips and worn shiny patches are welcome. You are after the surface itself, not a plan of the room.
tips: Rake light from the side to lift the grit.
Wipe water spots if they flash white.
Focus on the grout, which is rougher than the glaze.
constraint: Stay close enough that no more than two tiles appear.

title: Outside the Door
oneLiner: Move in on your own front door until the surface fills the frame.
details: Stand just outside your own door and move close to the outer face. Wood grain, brush marks, dents, or the fine grain of a metal skin are all worth having. If the door is mostly glass, use the frame, or the wall within arm's reach, and keep the wider view out.
tips: Hold the phone flat to the surface.
Focus on a dent or a raised grain of paint.
Shade the lens with your hand if a bright patch flares.
constraint: The surface touches all four edges of the frame.

title: Bread Crust Terrain
oneLiner: Tear a piece of bread and fill the frame with crust.
details: Tear rather than slice, so the crust cracks in a natural line. Hold that edge towards the window until the blisters and the scorched spots show. The soft interior can appear only as a thin strip.
tips: Tap focus on a raised blister.
A dark plate under the bread makes the crust stand out.
Get close enough that the crust feels like ground.
constraint: The crust covers at least three quarters of the picture.

title: Potato Skin
oneLiner: Hold a potato close until the skin becomes a landscape.
details: A potato, a carrot, or a piece of ginger will do. Turn it until eyes, scars, or earthy specks give the surface something to look at. Daylight from the side will show how rough it really is.
tips: Rest it on a board so your fingers can stay out.
Brush loose soil off only if it hides the skin.
Focus on the nearest eye or scar.

title: Sugar Crystals
oneLiner: Spill a little sugar and photograph the crystals up close.
details: Scatter white or brown sugar on a dark plate or a sheet of black paper. Look until single crystals catch the light like grit. Leave them as they fell, with clumps and bare gaps.
tips: Shoot from a low angle rather than straight down.
Focus on the nearest crystal and let the rest soften.
A lamp at the side helps if the window is dull.
constraint: No spoon or jar in the frame.

title: Cork Surface
oneLiner: Get close to a cork board, a coaster, or a cork lid.
details: Find cork on a corkboard, a coaster, a mat, or a jar lid. If all you have is a bottle cork, hold it in the light and fill the frame with its cut face. The pits and the tan flecks are the subject.
tips: Light it from the side to deepen the pits.
Keep pins and notes out of the corkboard crop.
Hold steady, because this close the phone shakes easily.

title: Wicker Close
oneLiner: Move across a basket until the weave fills the picture.
details: Use a basket, a wicker tray, a woven placemat, or a laundry basket. Follow one strand as it ducks over and under the others. The crossings should feel like a textile seen from a hand's breadth away.
tips: Focus where two strands cross.
Let a little of the hole between strands go dark.
Turn the basket until the weave runs diagonally.
constraint: The weave touches all four edges.

title: Rug Pile
oneLiner: Lower the phone onto a rug until the pile fills the frame.
details: Use a rug, the carpet, or a bath mat. Get low enough to see separate tufts, not the pattern of the whole rug. A side light will make the pile look taller.
tips: Rest your elbows on the floor to keep steady.
Brush the pile one way with your hand, then shoot.
Focus on the tufts in the front.

title: Brushed Steel
oneLiner: Graze the brushed metal of a sink, faucet, or fridge door.
details: Look for the fine lines of brushed steel on a sink, a faucet, the fridge, or a toaster side. Move until those lines run across the frame like hair. A smudge or a faint scratch gives the metal a place to rest the eye.
tips: Tilt to avoid a white blob of reflected window.
Focus on a scratch, which is easier than the smooth grain.
Include no objects, only the metal.
constraint: Only the metal surface, nothing standing on it.

title: Soap Surface
oneLiner: Study the worn surface of a bar of soap up close.
details: Use a bar that has already been handled, so there are ridges, cracks, or a softened edge. Set it on a dry dish or a plate. The creamy cuts and the duller wet-dry patches are the texture.
tips: Dry your hands so you do not smear the lens.
Side light from a window marks the ridges.
Fill the frame with the top of the bar.

title: Cardboard Flutes
oneLiner: Open a cardboard flap and photograph the corrugated ribs.
details: Tear or unfold a flap so the wavy inner layer shows. Brown shipping boxes are ideal. Move in until the ridges become a repeating relief and the printed outside is gone.
tips: Light along the ridges so each wave has a shadow.
Focus on the torn edge where the layers separate.
Keep logos and addresses out of the crop.
constraint: Show the inner corrugation, not the printed outside.

title: Leather Grain
oneLiner: Find the grain on a belt, bag, shoe, or jacket.
details: Look for real leather or a convincingly grained synthetic on something you already own. Creases at a fold, pores, and scuffs are better than a brand-new patch. Fill the frame with that skin.
tips: Bend the item slightly so the grain rises.
Avoid a flash, which flattens leather.
Focus on a crease rather than a smooth area.

title: Bristle Ends
oneLiner: Come close to toothbrush bristles until they look like a thicket.
details: A toothbrush is enough, dry or damp. Shoot along the bristles rather than down onto the head, so they stand like a crowd. The cut ends and the tiny gaps are the texture.
tips: Prop the brush on the sink edge so you can use both hands on the phone.
Focus on the first row of bristles.
A dark towel behind them separates the pale tips.
constraint: The handle stays out of frame.

title: Bubble Sheet
oneLiner: Lay bubble wrap flat and fill the frame with the bumps.
details: Use bubble wrap if you have it, or the dimpled lid of a plastic tub. Lay it flat near a window so each bump gets a small highlight. Popped bubbles are useful; they break the sameness.
tips: Shoot at a slant so the bumps become ovals.
Focus on the nearest blister.
Keep the print on the plastic from becoming the subject.

title: Paint Stipple
oneLiner: Find stippled paint on a wall and crop in tight.
details: Any painted wall works, even one that looks smooth from across the room. Move in until the roller marks, the orange-peel bumps, or the tiny craters show. A scuff can stay, but the paint surface is the point.
tips: Take the light from the side, not from a ceiling lamp overhead.
Hold the phone parallel to the wall.
Focus a hand's breadth in from the edge of the frame.
constraint: No switches, hooks, or frames in the picture.

title: Fine Mesh
oneLiner: Cover the frame with the mesh of earphones or a speaker.
details: Use earphone mesh, a speaker grille, a hairdryer intake, or a fine sieve. Get close until the holes become a field. The dust in some of the holes is part of the texture, so do not clean it all away.
tips: Light from the side to shadow the holes.
Focus on the mesh, not the room behind it.
A mono treatment can help if the object is a loud colour.

title: Freezer Ice
oneLiner: Take an ice cube from the freezer and shoot its crystals.
details: Set one cube on a dark plate by the window. Look into the fractures, the clouded core, and the clear edges before they round off. A second cube is allowed only if it stays in the background softness.
tips: Shoot quickly, then put the ice back.
Focus on an internal crack.
Wipe the plate if meltwater floods the texture.
constraint: The cube must still have hard edges.

title: Denim Twill
oneLiner: Stretch a jeans leg so the twill runs across the frame.
details: Use jeans, a denim jacket, or any cloth with a diagonal weave. Stretch it a little so the ridges stand up, and move in until the twill is the whole picture. A seam can cross the frame, but the weave is the subject.
tips: Take the light from the side so each ridge has a shadow.
Hold the phone parallel to the cloth.
Focus on the weave nearest the lens.

title: Creased Foil Sheet
oneLiner: Crumple a sheet of foil and fill the frame with the creases.
details: Use kitchen foil, or a candy wrapper if that is what you have. Crumple it, open it once, and lay it near a window so the creases catch light. Crop out any printed words on a wrapper.
tips: Tilt the foil until the highlights are small, not a white sheet.
Focus on a sharp crease.
Rest it on a dark board so the edges do not vanish.
constraint: No readable words on the foil.

title: Cupboard Hinge
oneLiner: Close in on a cupboard hinge until the metal fills the view.
details: Open a cupboard, a closet, or a door in the home and move in on the hinge. Paint flecks, screw slots, and dull metal are the texture, whether or not any of it is rusty. You only need the hardware, not the room beyond.
tips: Keep the phone parallel to the hinge plate.
Focus on a screw slot or a chip of paint.
Open the door only wide enough to see the metal.

title: Lettuce Ribs
oneLiner: Hold a lettuce leaf so the pale ribs cross the frame.
details: Use a lettuce leaf, a cabbage leaf, or the green top of a green onion. Hold it up to a window so the ribs show through, and pinch the stem at the edge of the frame. The back of the leaf is often clearer than the front.
tips: Let the window light the leaf from behind.
Focus on the thickest rib.
Wait until the leaf stops trembling.

title: Dust at the Baseboard
oneLiner: Photograph the dust where the baseboard meets the floor.
details: Look along the baseboard, behind a door, or in a corner nobody has swept. Move in until the specks, hairs, and scuffs become the picture. This is the texture of that corner, not a view of the room.
tips: Rest the phone near the floor and tilt the screen so you can still see.
Focus on the largest speck.
Leave the dust where it is until after the picture.

title: Crazed Eggshell
oneLiner: Tap an egg until the shell crazes, then move in close.
details: Tap an egg gently on the rim of a bowl until the shell crazes, and do not peel it yet. Hold the cracked shell up to the window so the breaks catch the light. Tip the egg into the bowl afterwards if you want to keep it.
tips: Focus on a crack, not the smooth shell.
Side light shows the lifted edges of the shell.
Keep your fingers at the edge of the frame.

title: Lid Ridges
oneLiner: Turn a jar lid sideways and fill the frame with its ridges.
details: Use the ridged edge of a jar lid, a bottle cap, or a spice lid. Turn it so the ridges run across the frame and the printed top stays out. Wear on the ridges is welcome.
tips: Light from the side so each ridge throws a line of shadow.
Focus on the nearest ridge.
Brace your hand on the counter.
constraint: The printed face of the lid stays out.

title: Worn Spoon Bowl
oneLiner: Find the worn bowl of a wooden or metal spoon.
details: Choose a spoon that has stains, scratches, or a softened edge from use. Lay it on a plain board and move in until the bowl fills the frame and the handle leaves. Those marks are the texture.
tips: Side light picks out scratches better than light from above.
Focus on the roughest patch in the bowl.
Turn any bright reflection off the metal by tilting the spoon.
constraint: The handle stays out of frame.

title: Embossed Tissue
oneLiner: Spread a paper towel so its pressed pattern fills the frame.
details: Use a paper towel, a tissue, or a paper napkin, and choose a patch where the pressed pattern shows. Lay it flat and move in until the dimples replace the sheet. A torn edge can stay at the border, but the pattern is the subject.
tips: Graze the light across the sheet so the pattern rises.
Hold the phone parallel to the paper.
Focus on a raised dot in the pattern.

title: Split Teabag
oneLiner: Split a dry teabag and move in on the paper and the leaf.
details: Use a dry teabag, a coffee filter, or the paper sleeve from a cookie packet. Tear a small opening so both the paper and the leaves or the fibres show. Move in until that torn edge fills the frame, and keep any printed brand out.
tips: Lay it on a dark plate so the pale paper reads.
Focus on the tear, where the layers separate.
Side light shows the fibres in the paper.
constraint: No readable brand in the frame.

title: Cookie Snap
oneLiner: Snap a cookie and fill the frame with the rough inside.
details: Break a plain cookie, a cracker, or a piece of shortbread with your hands. Turn the rough face to the light and move in until crumbs and air holes replace the tidy top. A dark plate underneath will show the pale interior.
tips: Focus on a crumb still clinging to the break.
Shoot from a low angle so the broken face has height.
Brush loose crumbs off the lens afterwards.

title: Banana Peel
oneLiner: Peel a banana by hand and move in on the pale inner skin.
details: Pull a banana peel back with your fingers and look at the stringy pale inside, not the yellow outside. If you have no banana, use the dry skin of a garlic clove and fill the frame with its wrinkles instead. Lay it towards the window so the strings or the wrinkles catch the light.
tips: Blot any wet patch so it does not glare.
Focus on a string still clinging to the peel.
Keep the fruit itself at the edge or out.

title: Net Bag Knots
oneLiner: Bunch a net bag so the knots and holes fill the frame.
details: Use the net bag fruit or onions come in, a laundry mesh bag, or a loose-weave dishcloth held up to the light. Bunch it near a window so the knots or the holes overlap and the gaps go dark. Crop out any label so the mesh itself is the texture.
tips: Focus where two strands knot together.
Let the holes fall darker than the string.
Pinch the net at the edge of the frame so it stays still.
constraint: No label in the frame.

title: Coin Milling
oneLiner: Lay a coin flat and move along the milled edge.
details: Use any coin and set it on a dark surface. Come in from the side until the little ridges of the edge fill the frame and the face of the coin drops away. The wear on those ridges is the texture.
tips: Rest the phone on the table so the edge stays sharp.
Focus on the milling, not the face.
Turn the coin if a highlight wipes the ridges out.
constraint: The face of the coin stays out of frame.

title: Rubber Strip
oneLiner: Track a rubber seal so the worn patches cross the frame.
details: Open a door or a window from inside and look at the rubber or foam strip. Dust, cracks, and shiny compressed patches are all useful. If there is no seal, use the rubber ring from a jar or the gasket in a lunch box.
tips: Shoot along the strip so it leaves the frame on two sides.
Focus on a crack or a shiny worn patch.
Open the door only wide enough to see the rubber.

title: Pilled Fleece
oneLiner: Find a pilled fleece and let the bobbles fill the frame.
details: Use a fleece, a pilled sweater, or the bobbled inside of a coat. Stretch it slightly so the little balls stand off the cloth. Move in until the pills, not the garment, are the picture.
tips: Side light lifts the bobbles off the cloth.
Focus on the pill nearest the lens.
Keep zips and labels out of the crop.

title: Glove Wrinkles
oneLiner: Lay a rubber glove so the wrinkles fill the frame.
details: Use a rubber dish glove or, if you have none, a crumpled piece of a clean plastic bag. Bunch the wrist, or the bag, and lay it on the counter. The creases and the slight shine are the texture.
tips: Side light marks each wrinkle.
Focus on the tightest crease.
Keep the fingers out if they look like a hand.
constraint: Only the glove or the bag, with the sink out of frame.

title: Tomato Star
oneLiner: Frame the star-shaped scar on top of a tomato.
details: Use a tomato, a pepper, or an apple, and leave it whole. Move in on the scar where the stalk was, until that mark and the skin around it fill the frame. The smooth skin and the rougher scar should share the picture.
tips: Rest it on a board so your fingers stay out.
Focus on the scar, which is rougher than the skin.
Turn it if a window reflection wipes the detail.
constraint: The fruit stays whole.

title: Zip Teeth
oneLiner: Run the frame along a zip until the teeth become a ridge.
details: Use a zip on a jacket, a bag, or a cushion cover. Come in from the side so the teeth make a ridge and the cloth falls away. If you cannot find a zip, use the teeth of a comb in the same tight crop.
tips: Light along the teeth so each one throws a shadow.
Focus on the nearest tooth.
Keep the pull tab at the edge or out.
constraint: The teeth cross the frame from side to side.

title: Sole Facing Up
oneLiner: Turn a shoe over on the floor indoors and crop into the tread.
details: On the kitchen floor or beside the bed, turn a shoe sole-up and move in on the tread. Worn patches, nicks, and dust packed in the grooves are the texture. Any shoe you own will do.
tips: Use window light from the side so the grooves hold shadow.
Focus on dust caught in the tread, or on a worn patch.
Keep the upper of the shoe out of frame.
constraint: Only the sole.

title: Newsprint Dots
oneLiner: Move close to printed packaging until the letters fall into dots.
details: Use a cereal box, a newspaper, or a plain printed carton. Move in until the words break into dots and shapes and can no longer be read. Crop out any logo that still reads as a picture.
tips: Keep the carton flat so the dots stay even.
Focus on a cluster of dots, not a headline.
If the words are still readable, move closer.
constraint: No word in the frame should be readable.

title: Grout Takes Over
oneLiner: Let the grout lines, not the tiles, be what the picture is about.
details: Find a tiled wall or floor in the bathroom, kitchen or hall. Move close until the grout lines are as strong as the tiles, or stronger. Shoot straight on so the grid stays square and the lines look deliberate.
tips: Match the phone grid to the grout if you want the lines dead level.
Tap a grout crossing so the joints stay sharp.
constraint: Grout lines must be easy to see without zooming in later.

title: The Broken Tile
oneLiner: Find one chipped, stained or odd tile and let it break the grid.
details: Scan the tiles for a chip, a stain, a different colour, or a replacement that does not quite match. Stand so that odd tile sits among correct ones. The repeat should still be obvious, with the break inside the frame.
tips: Include at least one full surrounding tile on every side if you can.
Focus on the flaw, not on the perfect tile beside it.

title: Wall Meets Floor
oneLiner: Photograph the corner where wall tiles meet a different floor grid.
details: In a bathroom or kitchen, crouch at the join between wall tiles and floor tiles. The two grids rarely share the same scale. Include both, and the line where they meet, so the collision of patterns is clear.
tips: Put the join near the lower third of the frame.
Hold the phone upright so the wall stays vertical.
constraint: Both wall grid and floor grid must appear.

title: Along the Joints
oneLiner: Look along floor tiles so the grout lines converge.
details: Stand at the edge of a tiled floor and lower the phone close to the ground. Aim along a grout line so the joints narrow into the distance. A hall, a kitchen or a bathroom floor will do. The convergence is the subject.
tips: Rest the phone on a book if your hands will not stay low and still.
Focus on the second or third joint, not the one touching the lens.

title: Grout Up Close
oneLiner: Come close enough that one grout line shows its own texture.
details: Pick a single grout line with crumbs, a stain, a crack or a change of width. Fill the frame with that line and the tile edges beside it. You are photographing the joint, not the whole wall.
tips: Brace a knuckle on the tile to keep this close view steady.
Side light from a window will deepen the groove.
constraint: One grout line must run through the frame from edge to edge.

title: Squares to Diamonds
oneLiner: Turn the phone so square tiles read as diamonds.
details: Face a regular grid of square tiles on a wall or floor. Rotate the phone about forty-five degrees until the squares stand on their corners. Keep the rotation honest in the preview, and let the diamonds fill the picture.
tips: Hide the edges of the tiled area so nothing gives the true horizontal away.
Tap the nearest grout cross.

title: Where the Grid Stops
oneLiner: Show the place where the tiled grid gives way to another floor.
details: Find the boundary where tile meets wood, vinyl, carpet or a bare threshold. Photograph that ending so several tiles are visible and then the grid simply stops. The material on the other side should be recognisable.
tips: Stand square to the boundary so it runs cleanly across.
Include three or four tiles so the grid is established before it ends.
constraint: The boundary must cross the frame.

title: Two Tile Colours
oneLiner: Frame the seam where two colours of tile meet.
details: Look for a backsplash, a bathroom border or a floor where one tile colour gives way to another. If every tile matches, use the seam between the tiles and a baseboard, a metal trim or a painted wall. Photograph the seam as a firm line through the grid.
tips: Get close enough that the colour change is the event.
Turn off a warm lamp if it muddies the two tones.

title: Gloss and the Window
oneLiner: Catch a window reflected in glossy tiles and keep the grid visible.
details: On a glossy bathroom or kitchen wall, move until a window or a bright doorway reflects in the tiles. You should still see the grout, so the reflection is broken into a grid. Shoot at a slight angle rather than straight into the shine.
tips: Shift your stance until your own reflection leaves the tiles.
Expose for the reflection, then brighten if the grout vanishes.
constraint: The reflection must be split by grout lines.

title: Raking the Matte
oneLiner: Rake a lamp across matte tiles until the surface texture appears.
details: If your tiles are matte, set a lamp to the side and low so the light skims the surface. Texture, pits and uneven glaze should wake up. Photograph a small group of tiles with that raking light, and turn the ceiling light off while you do it.
tips: Move the lamp lower until tiny shadows appear in the texture.
Keep the lamp itself out of the frame.

title: One Tile, Framed
oneLiner: Frame a single tile so its grout border holds it like a picture.
details: Choose one complete tile and crop so its grout border is the frame around it. The tile can be plain. What matters is that the border is complete on all four sides and the tile sits alone as a picture.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the wall or floor.
Leave a sliver of the next tiles outside the grout if the crop allows.
constraint: All four grout borders of that tile must be visible.

title: The Interrupted Grid
oneLiner: Show a drain, faucet or pipe breaking an otherwise regular grid.
details: Find the place a drain, a faucet, a pipe or an outlet interrupts the tiles. The fixture is there to break the pattern, so include enough grid around it that the interruption is obvious. A kitchen backsplash or a shower wall both work.
tips: Wipe splash marks only if they hide the grid.
Stand a little off-axis so the fixture has a slight side.

title: The Cut Tile
oneLiner: Find a tile that was cut to fit and photograph the incomplete piece.
details: At the edge of a tiled area, look for a tile sliced to fit against a wall, a cupboard or a door frame. That partial piece is the subject. Include one full tile beside it so the missing portion is easy to imagine.
tips: Get close so the cut edge is sharp.
Include the obstacle the tile was cut against.
constraint: A partial tile and at least one whole tile must both appear.
