title: Where Four Meet
oneLiner: Centre on the cross where four tiles and their grout lines meet.
details: Find a tidy crossing where four tile corners come together. Put that cross in the middle of the picture and let the four tiles share the frame. Small errors in the grout will show themselves, and you can keep them.
tips: Use the grid overlay and park the cross on the centre lines.
Step in until the four tiles fill the picture.

title: Half Covered
oneLiner: Lay a towel or rug so it hides part of the tile grid.
details: On a tiled floor, lay a towel, a bath mat or a small rug so it covers some tiles and leaves others bare. Straighten it loosely, not perfectly. Photograph the meeting of cloth edge and grid from above.
tips: Stand so you can angle the phone down without stepping on the cloth.
Include both covered tiles and at least two fully visible tiles.
constraint: The cloth edge must cross several grout lines.

title: Small Tiles, Tight
oneLiner: Crop in on the smallest tiles you have until the grid feels dense.
details: If you have mosaic, hexagonal or other small tiles, fill the frame with them until the repeat feels dense. If your tiles are large, move in until four of them become a tight field with almost no wall around them. Either way, the rhythm should feel packed.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the surface so the shapes stay even.
Tap the centre of the group.

title: Lamp on Gloss
oneLiner: At night, let one lamp repeat as highlights on glossy tiles.
details: After dark, turn off the ceiling light and aim one lamp at a glossy tiled wall. Each tile may catch the lamp as its own small highlight. Photograph the repeat of those highlights across the grid. Matte tiles can instead catch the lamp along their grout.
tips: Move the lamp until the highlights sit in a row.
Lock exposure on a highlight so the tiles around it stay deep.
constraint: Only one lamp may light the tiles.

title: The Crooked One
oneLiner: Choose a tile that sits slightly off true and make that the subject.
details: Look along a grout line for a tile that tilts a little, sits proud, or breaks the spacing. You may have to get close to notice it. Photograph along the line so the small error is visible against the straighter joints.
tips: Use the edge of the phone grid as a ruler against the grout.
Take one wider frame and one tighter frame, and keep the tighter story.

title: Beside the Mirror
oneLiner: Photograph the line where the bathroom mirror meets the tiles.
details: Stand in front of the bathroom mirror and look at the edge where the glass, or its frame, meets the tiled wall. That boundary is the subject. Include a few tiles so the grid is clear, and shift until your own reflection stays out of the glass. A mirrored cabinet door works the same way.
tips: Focus on the mirror edge rather than on tiles farther along.
Angle the phone so a ceiling light does not glare on the glass.
constraint: The edge of the mirror and at least two tiles must appear.

title: Tiles Around the Reveal
oneLiner: Show tiles turning the corner into a window or door recess.
details: Find a window, a door or a shower opening where the tiles leave the flat wall and turn into the recess. The grid has to bend around that corner. Photograph the turn so you see both the wall tiles and the tiles inside the recess. If nothing is recessed, use the corner where wall tiles meet the side of a cabinet.
tips: Stand a little to one side so the corner has some depth.
Tap the corner so both planes stay acceptably sharp.
constraint: The tiles must be seen changing direction.

title: Where Two Walls Meet
oneLiner: Photograph the vertical corner where two tiled walls come together.
details: In the bathroom or kitchen, find an inside corner where tiled walls meet. The grout there is often a different line from the regular grid. Fill the frame with that corner and the tiles leaving it on both sides. Hold the phone upright so the corner stays vertical.
tips: Put the corner near the middle, with tiles on both sides.
A lamp from the side will mark the corner with a thin shadow.

title: The Bottom Course
oneLiner: Frame the lowest row of wall tiles as a band above the floor.
details: Crouch at the foot of a tiled wall and let the bottom row run across the picture. These tiles are often cut shorter than the ones above, which is part of the story. Include the floor or the baseboard they sit on, and one row of full tiles above. The rim of a bath can stand in for the floor if it hides the very bottom.
tips: Keep the row level with the grid overlay.
Include the cut edge if the bottom tiles are shorter than the rest.
constraint: The lowest row must cross the frame.

title: Backsplash and Bare Wall
oneLiner: Show the line where the backsplash ends and the plain wall begins.
details: On a kitchen or bathroom wall, find the top of the tiled area, where tile gives way to paint. Photograph that horizontal stop so several tiles sit below it and plain wall sits above. The line should run cleanly across the frame. A tiled panel beside the stove works as well as the backsplash by the sink.
tips: Square the phone to the wall so the stop stays level.
Get close enough that the change of surface is obvious.
constraint: Both tile and plain wall must be in the frame.

title: The Finishing Strip
oneLiner: Come close to the trim that closes the edge of a tiled area.
details: Look for the metal, plastic or wooden strip that finishes a run of tiles, often where tile meets a counter, a carpet or a door frame. Fill the frame with that strip and the tile edge beside it. Let the trim cross the picture as a line in its own right. If there is no separate strip, photograph the frame or the counter edge where it meets the tile.
tips: Skim a lamp along a metal edge if you want a thin highlight.
Tap the trim and let the tile beside it fall slightly soft.
constraint: That finishing line must cross the frame.

title: The Soft Joint
oneLiner: Photograph the soft seal where tiles meet the bath or the basin.
details: Find the sealant line where tiles meet a bath, a shower tray or a basin. It is usually smoother and rounder than the grout. Come close so that soft bead and the hard tile grid share the frame. A seal along the counter works if you have no bath.
tips: Side light will show the roundness of the seal.
Include a few grout lines so the grid is still present.
constraint: The seal and the tiles must both be visible.

title: A Rail Across the Tiles
oneLiner: Let a towel rail or shelf cross the tile grid in one line.
details: Find a towel rail, a glass shelf or a shower screen that crosses a tiled wall. The crossing should interrupt the grid in a clean line. Photograph it so tiles remain visible on both sides. If nothing is fixed to the wall, use the rim of the bath where it cuts across the lowest tiles.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the wall.
Include at least two full tiles above or below the crossing.
constraint: The crossing line must run over more than one tile.

title: Salt Crystal Close-Up
oneLiner: Pour a pinch of salt and explore its tiny crystal landscape with your phone.
details: Scatter salt on a dark plate or counter and move in as close as your phone allows. Crop tighter afterward if needed. Look for glittering facets and irregular peaks that feel like a miniature mountain range.
tips: Use bright side light to make crystals sparkle.
Tap focus on the sharpest grains in front.
A dark background makes white salt pop.
constraint: Shoot from no farther than a hand's length away.

title: Button on Fabric
oneLiner: Make a single shirt button look like a monument in a cloth landscape.
details: Button up a shirt or jacket and photograph one button surrounded by fabric weave. Get close, then crop so threads look like fields and the button like a round building. Keep the scene still and evenly lit.
tips: Use indirect daylight or a soft lamp.
Align the button slightly off-centre.
Rest both wrists on the table so the weave stays sharp.

title: Fork Tine Forest
oneLiner: Turn fork tines into a strange metal forest seen from ground level.
details: Lay a fork on its side and shoot along the tines toward the tips. Move in close so the spaces between tines feel like alleys or trees. A plain surface behind the fork keeps the tiny world believable.
tips: Place a sheet of paper behind for a clean backdrop.
Shoot from table height, not overhead.
Wipe the fork to avoid greasy smudges in macro.
constraint: Show only the fork—no food in frame.

title: Pencil Tip Horizon
oneLiner: Fill the frame with a sharpened pencil tip like a lone peak on the horizon.
details: Prop a sharpened pencil so the tip points upward against a plain wall or a sheet of paper. Fill most of the frame with the wood and the graphite point. Let the empty background read as sky and the tip as a lone peak.
tips: Use a neutral background behind the pencil.
Tap focus precisely on the graphite point.
Try rotating the pencil for different leading lines.
constraint: The pencil tip must touch the top third of the frame.

title: Droplets on a Leaf
oneLiner: Find water droplets on a houseplant leaf and treat each bead as a tiny world.
details: Dampen a leaf with a few drops from a glass, or use a plant you have just watered, then move close until the beads are obvious. Shoot so one bead is sharp while others blur softly. The curve of the leaf can feel like rolling hills beneath glass spheres.
tips: Backlight droplets with a window for sparkle.
Hold the phone with both hands for stability.
Shoot many frames—focus is tricky up close.

title: Coin Stack Canyon
oneLiner: Stack a few coins and photograph them like a canyon wall of metal.
details: Stack three to six coins and shoot from the side at coin height. Crop tight so rims and stamped detail feel monumental. A dark surface below can read as shadowed ground in your miniature scene.
tips: Use coins of one size for cleaner lines.
Soft window light shows engraved detail.
Prop the stack against a book if it wobbles.
constraint: Use at least three coins in the stack.

title: Spice Label Texture
oneLiner: Move in on a spice jar label until the print becomes an abstract tiny landscape.
details: Choose any jar from your kitchen and photograph the label as close as possible. Let letters blur into colour blocks and texture. Rotate the jar to find a patch of type or pattern that feels like terrain on a map.
tips: Avoid glare by tilting the jar slightly.
Wipe the glass before shooting.
Crop square afterward for a graphic look.
constraint: No readable full words—abstract crop only.

title: Desk Pebble Planet
oneLiner: Make one small sphere on your desk look planet-sized.
details: Use a pebble, a marble, a large bead, or a round mint. Set it on a plain surface and shoot from its own height, with empty background around it. Move closer until the sphere dominates and the table falls away.
tips: Use side light to show surface pits and shine.
Blur the background by moving closer to the stone.
Try a dark desk mat for a space-like feel.

title: Rice Grain Desert
oneLiner: Scatter uncooked rice on a dark plate and treat the grains as dunes.
details: Pour a small handful of dry rice onto a dark plate or tray. Get down to grain height and look along the surface so the rice rises like a low desert. A darker grain or a gap can sit in the middle as a landmark.
tips: Rest your elbows on the table so the phone stays steady.
Lock focus on the nearest grains, then recompose slightly.
constraint: Keep the plate rim out of the frame.

title: Bristle Forest
oneLiner: Shoot along toothbrush bristles so they read as a dense little forest.
details: Rest a dry toothbrush on its side on the bathroom counter. Bring the phone close and look between the bristles toward the far tips. A towel or plain tile behind them stops the miniature woodland looking cluttered.
tips: Tap the nearest bristle tips so the far ones soften.
A lamp from the side separates each bristle with a highlight.
constraint: Leave the handle out and keep the tips in frame.

title: Sponge Crater Field
oneLiner: Crowd the frame with a kitchen sponge until the holes look like craters.
details: Wet a clean sponge and squeeze it so the surface stays open and uneven. Move in until holes and ridges are all you can see. Side light from a window or a lamp will sink a shadow into each hollow.
tips: If the sponge is very wet, dab it so highlights do not blow out.
Turn the sponge until the largest hole sits near a third.

title: Breadcrumb Range
oneLiner: Push fresh breadcrumbs into a ridge and photograph them as a mountain chain.
details: Crumble a bit of bread onto a board and sweep it into one low ridge with a finger. Shoot from crumb height so the ridge crosses the frame like a range. A dark cloth under the board lets the pale crumbs stand forward.
tips: Focus on the crest, where the crumbs are thinnest.
Lower the exposure a touch if the bread turns pure white.
constraint: Keep your finger out of the finished shot.

title: Citrus Peel Moon
oneLiner: Turn a piece of citrus peel into a pitted moon surface.
details: Peel a small piece from an orange, lemon, or any citrus you have, and lay the outer face upward near a window. Get close enough that the dimples become craters. Let a strip of white pith sit at the edge like a pale shore.
tips: Rake the light across the peel rather than from above.
Wipe juice off the phone lens if you handled the fruit.

title: Grounds Coastline
oneLiner: Spread coffee, cocoa, or tea and find a coastline in the pile.
details: Spoon a little dry coffee, cocoa, or loose tea onto a pale plate and shape one edge into a curve. Shoot from above so the dark grounds meet the empty plate like land beside still water. A few larger specks on the empty side can stand in as offshore rocks.
tips: Use the grid and set the boundary near a third.
Tap focus on the boundary where single grains separate.

title: Pasta Boulder Field
oneLiner: Drop a few pieces of dry pasta and make them look like scattered boulders.
details: Use any small pasta you have. Shells and short tubes both work. Set three to seven pieces on a plain cloth and shoot from a low angle so each one reads as a separate rock.
tips: Leave uneven gaps so the pieces do not look like a pattern.
A sheet of grey or brown paper makes a believable ground.

title: Foil Ridge Line
oneLiner: Crumple a strip of foil and follow its shiny ridge like a tiny range.
details: Tear a short strip of kitchen foil, crumple it once, then open it partway. Lean it against a cup so the crest stands up. Look along that crest until highlights jump from fold to fold.
tips: Expose for the bright foil or the highlights will vanish to white.
A dark mug behind the strip keeps the ridge readable.

title: Bubble Moons
oneLiner: Move in on bubble wrap until each bubble feels like a small moon.
details: Lay a scrap of bubble wrap on a dark surface. If you have none, the dimpled side of a plastic berry box works the same way. Focus on one bubble and let the others soften, with a lamp to the side putting a bright curve on the plastic.
tips: Shoot slightly off the perpendicular to dodge reflections of the room.
Pinch to check sharpness, then reshoot if the plastic looks smeared.
constraint: One bubble must be sharper than the rest.

title: Lentil Shore
oneLiner: Arrange dry lentils so they read as pebbles along a pale shore.
details: Scatter a spoon of lentils, peppercorns, or other small seeds on a light plate and sweep most of them to one side. Leave a few stragglers on the empty half. Shoot from a low angle so the heap becomes a bank of stones.
tips: Get the lens almost on the plate, braced on a folded towel.
Focus on a lone seed in front of the heap.

title: Paperclip Bridge
oneLiner: Stand a paperclip on its side and frame it as a bridge over cloth.
details: Bend a paperclip gently into an arch, or open a safety pin if that is what you have, and rest it on a folded dish towel. Get down to wire height so the arch makes a span. A plain fold underneath can pass for the ground it crosses.
tips: A pale towel under a dark clip keeps the arch visible.
Tap to focus on the highest point of the wire.
constraint: The arch must reach from one side of the frame toward the other.

title: Soap Bar Quarry
oneLiner: Study the worn face of a bar of soap as if it were cut stone.
details: Choose a used bar with nicks, ridges, or a hollow where the stamp has worn. Set it on a dry dish and move in until the surface fills the frame. Raking light from the side will show every scrape as a terrace.
tips: Dry the bar first so suds do not hide the cuts.
Turn printed lettering to the side you crop away.

title: Zipper Teeth Fence
oneLiner: Close in on a zipper until the teeth look like a metal fence.
details: Lay a jacket, cushion cover, or pencil case flat and run the zipper only partway. Photograph where the teeth meet. A shallow angle along the tape makes the row recede like a long fence.
tips: Wipe fingerprints off metal teeth before you shoot.
Include the slider at the far end as a gatehouse.

title: Sugar Cube Mesa
oneLiner: Set one sugar cube on a saucer and give it the scale of a mesa.
details: Place a sugar cube, or a stock or bouillon cube if that is what you have, alone on a pale saucer. Shoot from cube height with empty saucer around it. The hard edges should feel huge against the soft blur of the dish.
tips: Side light shows the grain of the cube without flattening it.
If the cube is white on white, slip a grey napkin under the saucer.
constraint: Only one cube in the frame.

title: Tissue Fibre Drift
oneLiner: Tear a tissue and photograph the frayed edge as a stand of pale grass.
details: Gently tear a plain tissue and look at the fuzzy edge against a dark book or cloth. Get close enough that single fibres separate from the mass. Lift the tissue slightly so a few strands catch the light and stand apart.
tips: Backlight the fibres with a window behind the dark book.
Take a short burst. Loose fibres shift as you breathe.

title: Tap Mesh Stars
oneLiner: Look into the holes of a tap or faucet mesh and find a star field.
details: Lean over the kitchen or bathroom tap, or a faucet, and frame the little mesh where the water comes out. If there is no mesh, use the face of a shower head instead. Angle a lamp so the holes glint, and wipe the metal first.
tips: Turn the water fully off so the mesh stays dry and sharp.
Fill the frame, then tap the brightest hole to set focus.
constraint: Show the mesh or shower face alone.

title: Comb Tooth Skyline
oneLiner: Lay a comb flat and shoot its teeth as a skyline of identical towers.
details: Set a clean comb on a table with plain paper or a bare wall behind it. Get level with the teeth and look through the gaps. One missing or bent tooth, if you have one, becomes the landmark in an otherwise even row.
tips: Brace the phone on the table so the gaps stay crisp.
A coloured sheet of paper behind the comb gives the skyline a sky.
constraint: Shoot from comb height, not from above.

title: Sill Dust Land
oneLiner: Frame the dust on a windowsill so it reads as barren ground.
details: Do not clean first. Look along a windowsill for the pale film, fluff, and grit that has settled there. Get low and crop tight until the sill edge disappears and the dust becomes open land.
tips: Skim a lamp along the sill, or a separate flashlight if you have one, so the dust lifts into relief.
Focus on one larger speck and let the rest fall soft.

title: Onion Skin Map
oneLiner: Peel one dry onion skin and read its veins as a map.
details: Take a papery outer skin from an onion, or a garlic skin if you have no onion, and lay it on a dark plate. Hold it near a window so light comes through the veins. Move until the lines look like paths across a chart.
tips: Stick the skin flat with a tiny drop of water if it curls.
Overexpose slightly so the thin skin does not turn muddy.
constraint: Light must pass through the skin.

title: Ice Cube Berg
oneLiner: Set one ice cube on a dark plate and catch it while the edges stay sharp.
details: Take a single cube from the freezer and set it on a dark plate near a window. Shoot from the side within a minute so the edges are still sharp. A thin pool of melt around the base can read as a moat.
tips: Wipe condensation off the plate outside the cube so it stays matte.
Lock exposure on the dark plate, not on the ice.

title: Colander Caves
oneLiner: Look through colander holes until one of them feels like a cave.
details: Hold a colander, a sieve, or a perforated spoon up near a window. Move close to the metal so the holes become dark mouths with bright rims. One hole, sharper than the rest, can be the cave you are facing.
tips: Tap the nearest hole so the farther ones fall soft.
Angle the metal so the rims catch the window and not your face.
constraint: Keep your fingers outside the frame.

title: Thread Trail
oneLiner: Lay a short thread on dark cloth and follow it like a path.
details: Pull a loose thread from a hem, or take a short length from a spare spool of thread. Drop it in a gentle curve on a dark sweater or a book. Get down to cloth level so the thread rises like a pale track across open ground.
tips: A lamp from the side gives the thread a bright edge.
Focus on the nearest bit of thread and let the far end soften.

title: Hook and Loop Scrub
oneLiner: Photograph a hook-and-loop patch so the hooks look like scrub.
details: Find a hook-and-loop fastener on a jacket, a sneaker, a bag, or a strap. Photograph the hooked side, not the soft side, as close as the phone allows. Side light should catch the tips so each hook stands up like a tiny shrub.
tips: Pick loose fluff off the hooks before you shoot.
Brace both elbows on a table so the hooks stay separate.

title: Grille City
oneLiner: Read a speaker grille as a city made of tiny holes.
details: Use a radio speaker, a headphone earcup, or the mesh on a hairdryer. Get close enough that the holes or the weave fill the frame. A few larger openings, if they exist, can stand in as squares among the smaller ones.
tips: Tilt the grille until you lose the reflection of your face.
Tap one hole near the middle and let the edges soften.
constraint: The mesh or grille must run off every edge.

title: Flour Drift
oneLiner: Dust a little flour on a dark board and find a drift in it.
details: Shake a pinch of flour or powdered (icing) sugar onto a dark chopping board or a plate. Tip the board slightly so the powder slides into a low bank. Shoot along that bank from table height, and let a few lumps sit as boulders.
tips: Lock exposure on the dark board so the powder stays bright.
Breathe to the side so you do not blow the drift away.

title: Vein Chart
oneLiner: Hold a leaf to the window and map its veins as paths.
details: Use a leaf from a houseplant, a herb, or a bit of salad. Hold it against a window, or lay it on a glass with a lamp behind, so light comes through. Move close until the veins branch like routes across a chart.
tips: Pinch the stem outside the frame so your fingers stay hidden.
If the leaf is thick, choose a herb leaf that lets the light through.
constraint: The leaf must fill the frame edge to edge.

title: Screw Head Plaza
oneLiner: Make a single screw head look like a round plaza.
details: Find a screw you can see indoors, on a hinge, a shelf bracket, an outlet plate, or the back of a cupboard. Fill the frame with the head and its slot. The paint or wood around it becomes the district around the plaza.
tips: A slight angle shows the rim as a low wall.
Wipe dust out of the slot with a dry finger.

title: English Muffin Craters
oneLiner: Turn the holes in an English muffin into craters.
details: Take an English muffin, toasted or fresh, or any bread with an open crumb. Set it on a board and move in until the holes fill the frame. Rake a lamp across the surface so each hole drops into shadow.
tips: Focus on the near rim of the largest hole.
If the crumb is very pale, lower the exposure a touch.

title: Stalk and Sky
oneLiner: Photograph a slim plant so it towers against sky or a bright window.
details: Find a grass stalk, a dry seed head, or a slim weed in a pot by the entrance or in a crack you can reach from a shared path. Get below it and let the sky, or a plain wall if the sky is dark, sit behind. If you have no outdoor plant, hold a houseplant stem against the brightest window and shoot from below.
tips: Tap the stalk to focus, then drag exposure down if the sky or window burns out.
Leave a little stalk entering from the bottom so it has a base.
constraint: The plant must be sharp against sky, a plain wall, or a bright window.

title: Rust Islands
oneLiner: Find rust on a tin and read the spots as islands on a grey map.
details: Look at a baking tin, a metal tray, a radiator, or an old utensil for freckles of rust or dark worn spots. Crop tight so the marks sit apart on the metal. Side light helps the orange or brown rise off the grey.
tips: If the metal is shiny, tilt until the window leaves the frame.
Fill the picture with metal only.

title: Bobble Hills
oneLiner: Move close to a bumpy surface until each nub becomes a hill.
details: Use a rubber bath mat, the bumpy sole of a slipper, a pebbled phone case, or any surface covered in small bumps. Fill the frame with the nubs. One bump sharper than the rest can be the summit.
tips: Hold the phone square to the surface so the hills do not lean.
A lamp to the side gives every nub a dark face.

title: Mug Cavern
oneLiner: Shoot into a mug so the dark middle reads as a cavern.
details: Set a mug, a bottle, or a cardboard tube on a table with the opening toward you. Frame the bright rim and let the inside fall black. A highlight on the rim can read as sunlit rock around the mouth.
tips: Expose for the rim so the hole stays truly dark.
Rest the phone on the table to keep the circle even.
constraint: Keep your hands out of the opening.

title: Cut Wood Rings
oneLiner: Read the end grain of a board as the rings of a giant log.
details: Find end grain on a chopping board, a wooden spoon, a rolling pin, or the cut edge of a shelf. Fill the frame with the rings and cracks. If you only have side grain, follow one dark line as a path through the fibres.
tips: A slight side angle deepens the cracks.
Wipe crumbs away so the grain stays the subject.

title: Rind Map
oneLiner: Crop a cheese rind or a dry peel until it looks like a map.
details: Use the rind of a piece of cheese, a citrus peel you have already taken, or the dry skin of a pumpkin. Lay it on a board and get close. Cracks, spots, and changes of colour can mark borders between regions.
tips: Include one darker speck as a town on the map.
Rake the light so the rind is not one flat block of colour.

title: Leaf in a Cap
oneLiner: Float one small leaf in a bottle cap of water and shoot the voyage.
details: On the table, set a bottle cap or a small lid and add a little water. Float a tiny herb leaf, a petal, or a flake of spice. Shoot from the side so it sits like a boat in a round harbour.
tips: Wait a few seconds so the surface settles before you shoot.
Get low enough to see the leaf reflected in the water.
constraint: The cap must be fully in frame.

title: Rubber Ridges
oneLiner: Get low along a ribbed rubber surface and read the ridges as hills.
details: Use a doorstop, the sole of a slipper, or the grip ridges around a jar lid. Get the phone almost on the table and look along the ridges. A scuff, a crumb, or a speck of dust can be a boulder on the slope.
tips: Brace the phone on the table so the ridges stay sharp.
A lamp to one side gives each ridge a dark face.

title: Chair Rail Scuff
oneLiner: Find the rub where a chair meets the wall and fill the frame with it.
details: Walk the rooms until you see a dull patch or grey rub at the height of a chair back or sofa. Move in so the mark sits large and the cleaner paint around it becomes a border. Side light from a window will show the difference in sheen.
tips: Stand so the light skims the wall rather than hitting it flat.
Tap the dullest part of the rub so the sheen stays in focus.
constraint: Keep the mark larger than your fist in the frame.

title: Switch Plate Rectangle
oneLiner: Treat a light switch plate as a small picture hung on a plain wall.
details: Choose a switch on a fairly clear stretch of wall. Step back until the plate sits small and square, with paint around it on every side. Look for grime, a hairline crack in the plastic, or screw heads that sit slightly off true.
tips: Turn the grid on and square the plate to it.
Lock exposure on the wall so the plate does not become a black slab.

title: Nail Hole Cluster
oneLiner: Gather several old nail holes into one tight frame.
details: Search the wall behind where a picture used to hang, or along a hallway. Include three or more holes so they read as a group rather than a single speck. A lamp raked across the plaster will drop a tiny dark pit into each hole.
tips: Slide the lamp until each hole darkens inside.
Steady the phone by resting a knuckle on the wall.
constraint: Nothing but wall and holes may enter the frame.

title: Paint Layer Reveal
oneLiner: Locate a chip where an older colour shows through the top coat.
details: Check corners, door frames, and places a bag bumps the wall. Frame the chip so both colours sit clearly, with the edge of the flake sharp. If you only find a scuff, use the boundary between clean paint and worn paint instead.
tips: Tap the edge of the chip, not the plain wall beside it.
Move closer rather than pinching to zoom.

title: Faded Rectangle
oneLiner: Hunt the pale ghost left after a frame or poster came down.
details: Look for a rectangle of slightly different paint, often above a shelf or behind a sofa. Stand square-on so the shape does not lean. Include one full corner of the ghost so the edge is obvious.
tips: Expose for the wall, not for a bright window nearby.
Step back until the whole rectangle fits with room to spare.
constraint: The whole faded shape must sit inside the frame.

title: Sofa Rub Band
oneLiner: Show the horizontal band a sofa or bed has polished into the wall.
details: Look behind furniture that sits close to the wall. The mark is often a soft stripe, shinier than the paint around it. Shoot over the back, or ease the furniture forward if you can do that safely, and let the stripe run from edge to edge.
tips: Place the stripe near the middle so it reads as a horizon.
Wipe the lens if you are close to dusty paint.

title: Outlet Grime Halo
oneLiner: Frame the dirty halo that collects around a well-used outlet.
details: Find an outlet that sees plugs often, usually near a lamp. Come close enough that the plate, the screws, and the grey dust ring all read clearly. Leave every plug as you found it.
tips: Angle a little so the outlet face is evenly lit.
If a lamp reflects in the plastic, shift your feet until that reflection leaves.
constraint: Crop tight so only wall and outlet remain.

title: Baseboard Dust Tide
oneLiner: Photograph the dust line where the wall meets the board at its base.
details: Crouch beside the baseboard, the board that runs along the bottom of the wall. Look for a soft grey band, a hairline gap, or a brush mark in the dust. Let that joint cross the frame, with wall above and board below.
tips: Rest your forearm on your shin so the low angle stays steady.
Use the window as side light rather than the bulb overhead.

title: Adhesive Ghost
oneLiner: Find a sticky patch left by tape, a hook, or a poster.
details: Bathroom doors, kitchen walls, and the insides of cupboards often keep a dull oval of old adhesive. Tilt until the patch catches light and turns shinier than the paint. Include the edge where the sticky area meets clean wall.
tips: Hold a lamp to the side and skim its light across the patch.
Tap the shiny boundary so it, not the surrounding paint, is sharp.
constraint: Place the patch near the centre of the frame.

title: Corner Colour Join
oneLiner: Stand in a corner where two wall colours meet and make the seam the subject.
details: Find an inside corner, perhaps where a hall meets a room. If your walls are one colour, use a patched area meeting the original paint, or the corner where the light simply changes. Place the seam near the middle and look for a wobbly line or one side more scuffed than the other.
tips: Hold the phone level so the corner stays vertical.
Step back if the wide view bows the walls.

title: Plaster Crack Path
oneLiner: Follow a crack in plaster or paint until it makes a strong line.
details: Check above door frames and along walls, only as high as you can see without climbing. Let the crack enter from one edge of the picture and leave through another. If your walls are smooth, use a hairline in the paint or a seam in the wallpaper.
tips: Rake a lamp along the wall to deepen the crack.
Focus on the sharpest split, not the broad wall.
constraint: The crack must touch two edges of the frame.

title: Handle Strike
oneLiner: Catch the dent where a door handle has bumped the wall.
details: Open a door slowly and look at the wall it swings towards. There is often a chip, a small cup mark, or a rubber stop, with bruised paint around it. Come close and let the dent sit large, including the stop if one is there.
tips: Hold the door still with your foot so it does not creep into the picture.
Focus on the chipped rim of the dent.

title: Cleaner Patch
oneLiner: Show the cleaner patch left when a shelf, mirror, or clock left the wall.
details: The clue is a sharper rectangle or circle of cleaner paint, sometimes with a hook still in it. Photograph it straight on so the shape stays true. Include a border of the dirtier wall so the difference reads.
tips: Stand centred and square so the shape does not skew.
Lock exposure on the clean area, then check the surrounding wall still shows.
constraint: Include the entire clean shape plus a border of ordinary wall.

title: Cable Clip Scars
oneLiner: Trace the little scars left by cable clips along a wall.
details: Follow a run where a cable used to go, often beside a desk. The marks may be pinholes, sticky dots, or tiny chips in a line. Let that line lead through the frame, and include one clip if it is still stuck there.
tips: Get low and look along the row rather than straight at the wall.
Tap the nearest hole to set focus.

title: Chipped Outer Corner
oneLiner: Photograph an outside corner of wall where paint has chipped off the edge.
details: Outside corners, window reveals, and the edges of a boxed-in pipe take the most knocks. Choose one chipped edge and shoot along it so the damage comes towards you. Show the raw plaster or the older paint inside the chip.
tips: Use light from the side to pick out the rough edge.
Brace an elbow on the wall before you shoot.
constraint: Let the chipped edge run from the near foreground into the picture.

title: Heat Tide
oneLiner: Look above a radiator or heater for the dusty tide left on the wall.
details: Many radiators and heaters leave a faint brown or grey band on the wall above them. Frame that band with the top of the heater just in shot, or crop to the stain if it is clearer on its own. If you have neither, use the dusty band above a garbage can, a headboard, or a storage cupboard.
tips: Expose for the wall, not for shiny metal.
If the metal glares, shift so less of it shows.

title: Coat Hook Wear
oneLiner: Include a wall hook and the scrape or shine directly beneath it.
details: By the front door or in a bedroom, hooks leave a vertical rub from coats and bags. Frame the hook near the top and let the worn trail fall downward. If the paint is unmarked, keep the hook and the screw that holds it, which is mark enough.
tips: Leave a little wall above the hook so it is not cut off.
Focus on the hook, then glance to see the rub is still readable.
constraint: The hook and the mark under it must both be visible.

title: Splashback Speckle
oneLiner: Move in on the speckles and wipe marks on the wall behind a sink.
details: The wall beside a stove, a kettle, or a bathroom basin collects tiny marks and wiped arcs. Fill the frame with that surface. Look for one arc that reads clearly among the speckles.
tips: Wipe your lens first, because splash zones film it quickly.
Angle off glossy paint so the glare slides away.

title: Shelf Screw Holes
oneLiner: Count the screw holes left when a shelf or bracket left the wall.
details: You want the group of holes and any torn paint around them, not a view of the room. Four holes in a rectangle are ideal, and two will do. Rake light from the side so each hole reads as a small pit.
tips: A lamp from the side is enough to sink the holes.
Check the grid so the row of holes stays level.
constraint: Only the holed patch of wall, with none of the wider room.

title: Hidden Pen Tick
oneLiner: Search for a pen mark on a wall and let that speck be the subject.
details: Check a door jamb, the inside of a cupboard, and the wall beside where a phone usually sits. A pen dot, a short line, or a faint scratch all count. If the walls are spotless, use a painted-over screw head or a tiny chip, and come close until that mark is the only event.
tips: Rest a finger on the wall beside the mark to steady the phone.
Hold the phone square to the wall so the speck stays a dot.

title: New Paint Island
oneLiner: Frame a repair where newer paint does not quite match the rest.
details: Look for a roller patch, a filled hole with a different sheen, or a square that is smoother than the wall around it. Stand close enough that the patch is clearly the subject and far enough that the mismatch still shows. The interest is the almost-match.
tips: Use one light only so the sheen difference can appear.
Hold the phone parallel to the wall.
constraint: Keep the whole patch inside the frame with older paint around it.

title: Doorstop Bruise
oneLiner: Photograph the scuffed wall where a door rests when it is open.
details: Low on the wall a door swings into, look for a rubber stop, chipped baseboard, or a grey bruise. Get down so you meet the mark at its own height. Include a little of the stop or the chip that explains it.
tips: Rest your elbows on your knees.
Focus on the point where the stop meets the wall.

title: Wallpaper Lip
oneLiner: Catch a lifting seam, a bubble, or a peeled corner of wall covering.
details: Look for a lifting seam, a bubble, or a peeled corner of wallpaper. If you have none, use a poster corner or paint peeling along a seam. Come close and let the lifted lip make a thin dark line. Show both the lifted piece and the wall under it, and do not pull it further.
tips: Side light makes the raised lip stand proud of the wall.
Focus on the outermost lip.
constraint: The lifted edge should cross the frame.

title: Cupboard Rub
oneLiner: Open a cupboard and find the rub where the door meets the inside.
details: Kitchen and bathroom cupboards often have a shiny patch or a chip where the door or a shelf hits. Use the room light, or aim a lamp into that small space. Fill the frame with the worn spot and the edge that causes it.
tips: Brace your wrist on a shelf.
Bring the lamp in from the side rather than from above.

title: Picture Hook Alone
oneLiner: Photograph a single picture hook still waiting on an empty wall.
details: The hook is small, so move close and let it sit in a broad field of paint. Notice the nail, the bent metal, and any flake of plaster at the hole. Square yourself to the wall so the hook reads clearly.
tips: Tap the hook itself to focus.
Lock exposure on the wall so the metal does not drop to black.
constraint: The hook is the only object, with empty wall doing the rest.

title: Frame Gap
oneLiner: Photograph the dark gap where a door frame has left the wall.
details: Look along the side of a door frame for a hairline split between timber and plaster. That gap is often filled with dust or a bead of old paint. Let the split run through the picture, and include both the timber and the wall so the separation reads.
tips: Rake a lamp along the split so the gap darkens.
Tap the split rather than the flat timber.
constraint: The gap must run from one edge of the picture to another.

title: Knit Sweater Weave
oneLiner: Fill the frame with the repeating weave of a knit sweater, blanket, or scarf.
details: Lay a knit sweater, blanket, or scarf on a bed, or drape it over a chair by a window. Move close until the stitches become a field of repeated loops. Find the spot where a cable, a mend, or a change of stitch breaks that rhythm.
tips: Let window light skim sideways so each loop throws a tiny shadow.
Tap the nearest stitches and allow the farther ones to soften.

title: Peeling Paint Layers
oneLiner: Find chipped or peeling paint on wood or metal and photograph the layered edges abstractly.
details: Search a door edge, a windowsill, or a painted chair for paint that has cracked into repeating flakes. Move close until the curled edges read as stacked contour lines. Include one flake that has lifted higher than the rest so the rhythm has a single break.
tips: Tilt until the curled rims catch a thin bright line.
Steady the phone by resting a finger on the wood beside the flakes.
constraint: Fill the frame with paint and the surface under it.

title: Citrus Segment Ring
oneLiner: Arrange citrus segments in a circle on a plain plate.
details: Pull an orange or a lemon into segments with your fingers, or use tomato pieces if you already have them, and set them on a plain plate radiating from the centre. Shoot from above on the counter. Nudge one piece just outside the ring so the circle has a deliberate flaw. A few segments are enough if the plate is small.
tips: Blot juice so it does not merge the segments into one shine.
A pale plate keeps the fruit edges easy to separate.

title: Grate and Shadow Grid
oneLiner: Photograph a metal grate, vent, or sieve so its holes cast a tight dot pattern.
details: A colander, a sieve, or a vent cover will do. Hold it in window light so the holes throw dots on a counter, or fill the frame with the holes themselves. Let the dots repeat until a dent, a larger hole, or the rim interrupts them.
tips: Keep the metal parallel to the phone so the holes stay round.
Step in until the pattern nearly touches every edge.
constraint: Let the repeating holes cover almost the whole frame.

title: Book Page Edge Forest
oneLiner: Stack old books and shoot their page edges so they look like a striped paper forest.
details: Stack a few books of different thicknesses on a table, or use the ones already on a shelf. Photograph from the side so the page edges become fine vertical stripes. A bookmark, a darker page block, or a thinner volume should break the stripe.
tips: Stand close to the nearest book so later edges fall a little soft.
Wipe the lens if the pale page edges look fogged.

title: Oil on Water Swirls
oneLiner: Float a drop of cooking oil in a shallow dish of water and photograph the rainbow swirls.
details: Pour a shallow pool of water into a white bowl and add one drop of cooking oil near a window. Swirl once with the handle of a spoon until bands of sheen repeat. Photograph them just as the pattern starts to split.
tips: Shoot from directly above before the oil gathers into a blob.
Plant your elbows on the counter for the close view.
constraint: Keep the bowl rim outside the frame.

title: Fence Shadow Lattice
oneLiner: Capture repeating stripes cast by a fence, a rack, or a slatted chair.
details: Stand a drying rack, a slatted chair, or a grate in front of a lamp so the bars throw stripes on a plain wall. Photograph the stripes, and include one gap where the beat breaks. A cloth hung over one bar, or a dent in the rack, can be that gap if the bars are perfectly even.
tips: Leave only one lamp on so the stripes do not double.
Slide the rack until the stripes are distinct, not a grey mush.

title: Bubble Wrap Landscape
oneLiner: Turn bubble wrap or packing material into an alien terrain by shooting it extremely close.
details: Lay a piece of bubble wrap or similar packing on a table in soft indoor light. Move very close so each dome becomes a hill in a repeating field. Press one dome flat so a single break sits among the rounds.
tips: A lamp from the side gives every dome its own highlight.
Put a plain cloth under the wrap if the table pattern shows through.
constraint: Show only the wrap, with no tape, label, or box edge.

title: The Slanted Slat
oneLiner: Tilt one blind slat the wrong way and photograph the broken rhythm.
details: Close a venetian blind, then twist a single slat so it leans against the repeat. Stand where the slats read as parallel bands and that one rebel cuts across them. The bright gap is useful, but the slanted slat is the subject.
tips: Focus on the twisted slat rather than the glass behind it.
Shift sideways until the closed slats look evenly spaced.
constraint: Place the odd slat in the left or right third.

title: Bent Comb Tooth
oneLiner: Move close on a comb until the teeth repeat, then find one that bends.
details: Lay a hair comb on a pale surface and fill the frame with the teeth. If every tooth is straight, ease one sideways with a fingertip so the comb has a fault. Shoot along the row so the bent tooth is obvious without hiding the repeat.
tips: Use the window as a side light so each tooth gains a bright edge.
Rest the phone on the table if the teeth start to blur.

title: Vacant Egg Cup
oneLiner: Leave one hollow in an egg carton empty and shoot the repeating cups.
details: Set an egg carton on the kitchen table, cardboard or plastic. Leave one cup empty and let eggs fill the others, or drop a bottle cap or a cork into every cup but one if the carton is bare. Shoot from above, or from a low angle along the row, so the empty hollow reads as a pause.
tips: If the carton is dark, expose for the shells so they stay round.
A low angle turns the cups into a receding line.

title: Missing Square
oneLiner: Break a bar of chocolate so one square is gone, then photograph the grid.
details: Any scored chocolate, cracker, or cookie with a repeating grid will do. Remove one piece from an edge so the absence is obvious. Shoot from above on a plain board and keep the grooves running true to the frame.
tips: Focus on the broken edge where the gap begins.
A cool window keeps brown chocolate from going muddy.

title: Pencil Row Intruder
oneLiner: Line up pencils and slip one pen into the row as the odd one out.
details: On a desk or table, lay at least six pencils with their tips pointing the same way. Swap one for a pen, a brush, or a crayon. Shoot from above so the intruder shows by its clip, colour, or thickness.
tips: Include both tips and ends so the mismatch runs the full length.
Slide a plain sheet under the row if the table is busy.
constraint: Shoot straight down and run the row horizontally.

title: One Card Facing Up
oneLiner: Spread a deck of cards face down and turn a single card over.
details: A pack of cards, index cards, or matching coasters will do. Lay them in a fan or a grid so the backs repeat. Flip one card and shoot from above, letting that single face break the pattern.
tips: Overlap the cards slightly if the table is small.
Stand between the cards and the window to keep glare off the faces.

title: Gingham Break
oneLiner: Lay a checked cloth flat and let one object sit on a single square.
details: Smooth a gingham dish towel, a checked shirt, or a windowpane cloth on a bed or table. Let the squares run evenly to the edges. Place a button, a berry, or a coin on one square only, so the check continues and the object interrupts it.
tips: Tug a corner so the squares sit square to the frame.
Focus on the small object and keep the surrounding checks sharp too.
constraint: Align the check with the edges of the frame.

title: Gap in the Hangers
oneLiner: Open the closet and frame a row of hangers with one gap left bare.
details: Slide the hangers along the rail until their hooks repeat, then leave one empty space. Step back so at least three hangers show and the gap reads as a pause. If the rail is crowded, a garment on only one hanger can be the break instead.
tips: Focus on the hooks, where the repeat is clearest.
Open the door fully so the door edge does not slice the row.

title: Zip Slider Break
oneLiner: Run a zip nearly shut and let the slider interrupt the teeth.
details: A jacket, a cushion cover, or a small zip pouch gives you a zip. Lay the fabric flat and fill the frame with the teeth. Keep the slider in view so the repeating teeth stop or bunch against it.
tips: Side light puts a bright edge on each tooth.
Smooth the cloth so the zip runs in a clean line.

title: Odd Note on the Pad
oneLiner: Stick notes in a neat grid and rotate one so it will not match.
details: Use sticky notes or small squares of paper on a wall, a fridge, or a table. Align at least nine of them in rows. Turn one, or choose a different colour for a single sheet, and shoot the grid straight on.
tips: Stand square to the notes so the rows do not lean.
Put pale notes on a darker ground if their edges vanish.
constraint: Only one note may break the grid.

title: Pasta in Ranks
oneLiner: Arrange dried pasta into parallel ranks and lay one piece across them.
details: Spaghetti, another straight noodle, or a row of coffee stirrers works on a dark tray. Line them so they run together like a comb. Lay one piece across them, or set one short piece the other way, and shoot from above.
tips: A dark tray turns pale pasta into clear stripes.
Nudge the pieces until the gaps look even.

title: Fork Tine Cadence
oneLiner: Place four forks side by side so the tines become a repeating comb.
details: Line the forks on a dish towel with the tines pointing the same way. Let the metal points set up a rhythm, and crop most of the handles away. Turn one fork over or shift it down so a single set of tines breaks step.
tips: Take the highlight from a window at your side, not overhead.
Tap the nearest tine and keep the row in one plane.
constraint: Leave the handles out so tines and necks remain.

title: Speaker Mesh Field
oneLiner: Move close on speaker mesh until one hole breaks the field.
details: A radio, a laptop speaker, or a headphone earcup all have a mesh or a field of holes. Move close until that field covers the picture. A screw, a seam, or a slightly larger port should be the one break.
tips: Brush crumbs off the mesh before they become extra dots.
A lamp to one side shows the depth of each small hole.

title: Slipped Wallpaper
oneLiner: Find a wallpaper repeat and stand where one seam fails to line up.
details: Patterned wallpaper is ideal, but wrapping paper or a notebook cover carries the same idea. Let one motif appear at least twice. Include the seam or the cut where the print drifts, so the repeat visibly fails.
tips: Face the pattern straight on so the lines stay parallel.
Focus on the failed join rather than the middle of a motif.
constraint: Show the motif at least twice, plus the place it breaks.

title: Woven Basket Break
oneLiner: Crop in on a basket, placemat, or wicker edge where the weave changes.
details: Find a basket, a cane chair seat, a woven bag, or a rattan placemat. Fill the frame with the over-under rhythm of the strands. Use the border, a repair, a handle join, or a colour change as the place the regular weave ends.
tips: A lamp from the side picks out the strands that cross on top.
Brace a knuckle on the rim so the close view stays still.

title: Corrugated Ridges
oneLiner: Stand a piece of corrugated card so the ridges run and one is crushed.
details: Peel the outer paper from a box flap until the wavy inner layer shows. Lay that layer on a table in side light. Press one ridge flat so a single valley collapses while the others keep their wave.
tips: Skim the light across the ridges to reveal the crushed one.
Crop tight enough that the waves reach every edge.
constraint: No printed box face, only the bare ridges.

title: A Pleat Apart
oneLiner: Draw one curtain pleat out of line and photograph the gather that rebels.
details: Close a curtain or a shower curtain so the folds repeat. Tug one pleat forward, or flatten it, so it refuses the rhythm. Shoot along the row of folds with the rebel pleat easy to find.
tips: Stand to the side so the pleats overlap as a run of edges.
Focus on the loose pleat and let farther folds soften.

title: Bead on a String
oneLiner: Lay a beaded necklace in a curve and turn one bead the other way.
details: A necklace, a bracelet, or buttons threaded on cotton will do, and dried beans in an arc work if you have no beads. Photograph along the repeat. Include one bead, button, or bean that is a different colour or flipped.
tips: A soft shadow under each bead stops them merging.
Coil the string loosely so several repeats fit on the table.
constraint: Let the repeat cross the frame from edge to edge.

title: The Darker Brick
oneLiner: Face a brick wall and find the one unit that fails to match.
details: From outside your entrance, face a brick or block wall you can reach. Let the courses repeat across the frame. Find one unit that is darker, cracked, repaired, or turned, and place that difference off to one side.
tips: Stand square to the wall so the mortar stays straight.
Include several courses so the odd brick is clearly the exception.
constraint: Let the wall fill the frame.

title: Torn Leaflet
oneLiner: Follow a houseplant stem and frame the leaflet that breaks the repeat.
details: Use a fern, a herb sprig, or any houseplant with leaflets along a stem. Compose so the leaflets repeat. Let one torn, folded, or missing leaflet break that sequence.
tips: Hold the stem at the frame edge so your fingers barely show.
A plain wall behind the leaf keeps the pairs clear.

title: One Bent Blade
oneLiner: Fill a frame with parallel leaves and catch the blade that bends.
details: Use chives, a spider plant, the long leaves of a houseplant, or green onion tops. Move close so the blades run in parallel. Catch one blade that bends, crosses, or is a different width.
tips: Lower the phone near the pot so the blades rise through the frame.
If the window behind them burns out, tap a blade and let the background darken.

title: The Odd Bean
oneLiner: Cluster beans or buttons and set one paler piece among them.
details: Scatter dried beans, lentils, or buttons on a plain plate so size and tone repeat. Set one paler or darker piece in the group. Shoot from above and let that single tone be the break.
tips: A dark plate separates pale beans more clearly than a white one.
Fill the frame with the cluster and leave the table out.
constraint: Only one piece may clearly differ in tone.

title: Slipped Cable Clip
oneLiner: Follow the clips along a baseboard and stop where one has slipped.
details: Look along a baseboard, a desk edge, or the back of a shelf for clips holding a cable. Frame the repeated fasteners. Include the one that has opened, slipped, or lost its cable so the spacing breaks. If you have no clips, use the hooks under a shelf and include the one that sits out of line.
tips: Get close enough that the clips, not the whole wall, fill the picture.
Keep the line of clips running from corner to corner.

title: Ribbed Mat
oneLiner: Frame the ribs of a mat and lay one object across the grooves.
details: Use the mat inside the door, a ribbed bath mat, or the slotted base of a dish rack. Let the ribs run from edge to edge of the frame. Lay a button, a teaspoon, or a houseplant leaf across them so one line cuts the repeat.
tips: Shoot from low and to the side so the ribs pick up small shadows.
Align the ribs with the short side of the frame.
constraint: The crossing object should cover only a few ridges.

title: One Handle Turned
oneLiner: Line mugs up on the counter and turn a single handle the other way.
details: Set three or more mugs, cups, or jars in a row on the counter or a shelf. Turn them so the handles repeat. Twist one handle the opposite way and shoot along the row from one end.
tips: Drop to rim height so the openings stack in perspective.
A plain bit of wall behind the row keeps each handle readable.

title: Radiator Gap
oneLiner: Crop in on radiator fins and show the one gap that changes.
details: A radiator, a baseboard heater, or the bars of a drying rack gives you a run of repeated metal. Fill the frame with those bars. If none is bent, hang a sock or thread a strip of paper through one gap so a single interval changes.
tips: Let the bars run diagonally for a stronger rhythm.
Rest the phone against a nearby chair if you shoot along the row.
constraint: Nothing but the bars and the one interruption.

title: Kinked Coil
oneLiner: Coil a cord on the floor so the loops repeat, then kink one.
details: A vacuum tube, an extension cord, or a thick charging cable will coil into repeated loops. Lay the coil on a rug or a bare floor. Pull one loop out of round so it kinks, and shoot from above.
tips: Choose a coil that separates in tone from the floor.
Stand over the coil so the loops read as circles rather than ovals.

title: Floret Field
oneLiner: Move close on broccoli, cauliflower, or a pine cone and find one odd floret.
details: Set broccoli, cauliflower, a pineapple, or a pine cone on a board. Fill the frame with the repeating florets or scales. Find one piece that is darker, missing, or a different size, and let that be the break.
tips: Turn the head until window light from the side skims the tips.
Tap a single floret if your phone has a close-focus option.
constraint: Use a plain cloth or the board as the background.

title: Blocked Cell
oneLiner: Frame a dish rack or basket grid and block a single opening.
details: A dish rack, a grid laundry basket, or an ice-cube tray gives you a lattice at home. Shoot from above or a little off axis. Block one opening with a sponge, a sock, or a fingertip so a single cell drops out of the repeat.
tips: Line the phone up with the grid so the holes stay rectangular.
Tilt shiny plastic until the glare leaves the bars.
constraint: Only one opening may be blocked.

title: Flat Tuft
oneLiner: Press one toothbrush tuft flat so it breaks the field of bristles.
details: Lay a toothbrush on a pale cloth and fill the frame with the bristle tufts. They should read as a tight repeated field. Press one tuft sideways with a dry finger so a single clump breaks the grid.
tips: Window light from the side gives each tuft a bright edge.
Rest the phone on the table so the close view stays sharp.

title: Bent Spiral
oneLiner: Follow a notebook spiral and include the loop that sits out of line.
details: Open a spiral notebook, a calendar, or a bound pad on the table. Fill the frame with the repeated loops of wire. Bend one loop slightly, or include the place the wire already sits out of line.
tips: Let the loops run from one edge of the frame to the other.
A lamp from the side puts a highlight on the wire that has slipped.

title: Jar Turned Away
oneLiner: Line up similar jars and turn one so its back faces you.
details: Stand three or more similar jars, cans, or glasses in a row on the counter. Let the lids or rims repeat. Turn one so you see its back or base, and shoot along the row from a low angle.
tips: Hold the phone near the counter and look along the line.
Let the row enter from a bottom corner.
constraint: Keep the row as the subject, with only a strip of counter beside it.

title: Fan Guard Rhythm
oneLiner: Frame a fan guard so the bars repeat, then break the rhythm once.
details: Use a desk fan, the round guard of a bathroom fan, or a bicycle wheel stored indoors. Fill the frame with the radiating bars. Break the pattern with the cable, a clip, or a fingertip at the rim.
tips: Put the hub near the middle so the bars radiate evenly.
Turn the guard until a window highlight sits on only one bar.
constraint: Keep the hub inside the frame.

title: Flipped Bowl
oneLiner: Set bowls in a row indoors and flip one of them upside down.
details: Three similar bowls, mugs, or pot saucers are enough. Place them in a line on the counter. Flip one so its base faces you while the others show their rims, and shoot from a low side angle.
tips: Keep the row tight so the flipped one still belongs to the group.
Use a plain section of wall as the background.

title: Odd Keycap
oneLiner: Photograph a run of keys and let one different key break the grid.
details: Fill the frame with a stretch of keyboard keys, a remote control, or the buttons on a calculator. The grid should feel regular. Include one key that is a different tone, a blank, or a wider bar so the repeat fails.
tips: Stand square to the keys so the rows do not lean.
Wipe dust from the tops so the odd key is the only surprise.

title: Pale Underside
oneLiner: Lay leaves in a row indoors and flip one to show the underside.
details: Take a few leaves from a houseplant, a herb, or a cabbage. Line them up on the table with the tips pointing the same way. Flip one so the underside breaks the row, and shoot from above.
tips: Match the leaves in size so the flip is the only surprise.
Turn the table if the leaves are shiny and throwing glare.

title: Curtain Gap Light
oneLiner: Frame the bright slit of daylight between partly drawn curtains.
details: Close the curtains until a narrow beam cuts through. Include fabric folds on one side and the glowing window on the other. The slit itself should feel like the subject.
tips: Expose for the bright gap to deepen room shadow.
Use a steady two-handed grip.
Try vertical orientation to emphasize the beam.

title: Door Handle Portrait
oneLiner: Photograph an interior door handle at an angle that shows wear and shine.
details: Pick the handle you use daily and move close enough to see scratches or polish in the metal. Include part of the door panel for context, but keep the handle dominant. Side light helps model the shape, and a lamp will do if the daylight is dull.
tips: Wipe fingerprints if you want a cleaner look.
Avoid showing keys with readable codes.
Try a low angle looking slightly upward.
constraint: Fill at least half the frame with the handle.

title: Blinds and Shadow Bars
oneLiner: Capture striped shadows cast by blinds across a wall or floor.
details: Adjust the blinds so parallel bars of light and dark repeat across a wall or the floor. If you have no blinds, stand a comb in the window light so it throws bars on the wall. Move until the stripes lead into the frame rather than cutting it awkwardly. The pattern should feel rhythmic and calm.
tips: A lamp at the side can sharpen the bars if the daylight is too even.
Include a corner for depth if it helps.
A mono filter helps if the stripes fight the room colour.
constraint: Use black and white only.

title: The Window Arm
oneLiner: Photograph the arm or hinge that holds a window open.
details: Open a window a little and find the metal arm, the hinge, or the bar that holds it. Frame that hardware against the frame, with the narrow gap beside it. If the window only slides, use the latch that locks it, and keep the phone inside.
tips: Tap the arm or latch so the glass beyond falls softer.
A vertical frame suits a long arm.
Rest a knuckle on the frame to steady the phone.
constraint: The phone must stay fully inside the room.

title: Frosted Bathroom Window
oneLiner: Photograph diffused light through a frosted or textured bathroom window.
details: Close the door for privacy and frame the glowing panel. If the glass is clear, tape thin white paper over part of it and shoot that instead. Notice how shapes outside become soft and unreadable. Keep fixtures minimal so the glass, or the paper, stays the canvas.
tips: Turn off harsh overhead bulbs.
Do not include reflections of yourself.
Tap focus on the glass texture.
constraint: No recognisable shapes beyond the glass.

title: Key at a Half Turn
oneLiner: Show your key partly turned in an entry lock from the outside.
details: At your own front door, insert the key and pause before turning it fully. Frame the cylinder, the bow of the key, and a hint of door paint. Stay on the path or the landing, and do not block a shared hallway.
tips: Shoot in shade to avoid metallic glare.
Crop tight on lock hardware.
Check that no address numbers are readable.
constraint: Shoot from outside the door only.

title: Mail Slot from Inside
oneLiner: Catch the slot of light where mail arrives, from the indoor side of the door.
details: Sit on the indoor side of your front door and frame the mail slot flap. Lift the flap with a finger if you can, so outside brightness sits inside that small rectangle. If the door has no mail slot, use the bright gap under the door instead.
tips: Tap the bright slot so the door around it falls darker.
Brace a knuckle against the door to keep the phone still.
constraint: Keep the flap or the gap inside the middle third of the frame.

title: Chain on the Latch
oneLiner: Show a door held open only as far as its chain or latch allows.
details: Open the front door a little and let a chain or a swing bar stop it. If the door has neither, leave it barely open and photograph the latch in the gap. Stand inside so only a thin slice of outside shows, because that limit is the idea.
tips: Focus on the metal link or the latch tongue, not the view beyond.
If the outside is much brighter, tap the hardware so it keeps detail.

title: Sill Against the Glass
oneLiner: Arrange one or two small objects on a windowsill and shoot along the glass.
details: Clear the sill until a mug, a jar, or a small bottle remains. Put the phone near sill height so the glass rises behind the object like a pale wall. Shift left or right until the object separates from the frame.
tips: A slight angle keeps your own reflection off the pane.
Lock focus on the object, then reframe a little lower.
constraint: Use no more than two objects.

title: Door Left Ajar
oneLiner: Let an interior door stand ajar and photograph the wedge of the next room.
details: Open a door halfway so you see a slice of the room beyond: a chair leg, a rug edge, or a patch of floor. Keep the door edge as a strong vertical. The picture is about the invitation of that gap, not a full view of the room.
tips: Expose for the room beyond if you want the near door to go dark.
Step sideways until the door edge is truly vertical.

title: Through a Sheer Curtain
oneLiner: Soften the outside view by shooting it through a sheer curtain.
details: Stand close to a sheer, lace, or net curtain and focus on the weave, letting the outside fall gently behind it. If you have none, hold a thin dish towel against the glass. Choose a simple shape out there, such as a wall or the bright part of the window. The cloth should visibly veil the view.
tips: Tap the fabric so the threads stay crisp.
If the weave is faint, move a hand's width closer.
constraint: The cloth must cover the whole frame.

title: Hinge in Close-Up
oneLiner: Fill the frame with a door hinge, its screws, and the gap it makes.
details: Open the door enough to see the barrel of the hinge and the dark gap beside it. Move close until the metal and the paint edge are the whole subject. Look for a scrape, a drip of paint, or the shine on the pin.
tips: Use the phone's closest focus and pull back if the hinge goes soft.
A lamp from the hinge side picks out the round barrel.

title: Brightness Under the Door
oneLiner: Photograph the bright line leaking under a closed interior door.
details: Shut a door onto a brighter room, or leave a lamp on beyond it. Lay the phone near the floor and frame the glowing slit with floor in the foreground. The line should be thin and deliberate.
tips: Underexpose a touch so the slit stays a line, not a white blob.
Rest the phone on the floor and use the timer so you are not in the way.
constraint: Shoot from floor level.

title: The Meeting Rail
oneLiner: Find where two panels or a pair of doors meet, and shoot that seam.
details: Look for the horizontal or vertical meeting of a window, a pair of cupboard doors, or a folding door. Frame the seam so it runs cleanly through the picture, with a handle or latch as a small accent. The join is the subject.
tips: Align the seam with a grid line before you take the shot.
Tap the seam itself if the phone wants to focus on the room.

title: Blind Stopped Halfway
oneLiner: Stop a roller blind or a shade halfway and photograph the divided window.
details: Leave a roller blind or shade covering about half the glass, so the frame holds both cloth and view. If you have only curtains, draw one panel across half the glass. Include the bottom bar, or the curtain hem, as a clean horizontal. The split between hidden and open is the picture.
tips: Level the phone so the dividing edge does not slope.
Tap that edge if you want it sharper than the view.
constraint: Cloth must cover roughly half the window in frame.

title: Held with a Tie-Back
oneLiner: Show a curtain pulled aside by a tie-back, hook, or band.
details: Gather one curtain and fasten it with a tie, a band, or a hook. If you have none, tuck the fabric over the window handle or a nearby hook. Frame the fastener, the bunch of cloth, and the opening beside it.
tips: Side light from the window will trace the folds better than a ceiling bulb.
Come closer so the fastener is large, not a speck.

title: Glazing Bars
oneLiner: Treat the bars that divide a window into panes as the main subject.
details: Move close to a window with glazing bars, or to a grille over glass. Fill the frame with the cross or the grid so the outside view becomes only filler. If your windows are one plain sheet, use the frame corners where the side meets the top.
tips: Shoot straight at the bars so they stay rectangular.
Lower the exposure if the glass behind them blows out.
constraint: Bars or frame edges must reach all four sides of the picture.

title: A Fully Shut Door
oneLiner: Make a closed interior door a flat plane, with its handle small and exact.
details: Stand square to a shut door and include the whole door if you can, or a calm crop of panels. Let the handle sit off to one side so the door reads as a coloured surface. Avoid opening it; the refusal is the point.
tips: Even lighting from the room keeps the panels visible.
Turn the grid on and line the door edges with it.

title: Along the Slider Track
oneLiner: Follow the track of a sliding door, closet, or shower screen.
details: Get low or close and look along the metal or plastic track so it runs into the frame. Include a wheel, a stop, or the edge of the door where it sits in the groove. Dust in the channel is welcome if it shows the route.
tips: Focus on the near groove, and let the far end soften.
Wipe only your lens; leave the track as it is.
constraint: The track must lead from one edge of the frame to another.

title: Mitred Corner of the Frame
oneLiner: Isolate the diagonal joint where two pieces of a window frame meet.
details: Pick an upper or lower corner of a window or door frame. Come close enough to see the diagonal joint, the paint line, and maybe a small gap. Fill the picture with that joint so the corner reads as a shape.
tips: Tap the joint, because the glass nearby will steal focus.
Rotate the phone so the diagonal runs corner to corner.

title: Open a Hand's Width
oneLiner: Open a window just a hand's width and photograph the narrow gap.
details: From inside, open a window a little and frame the dark or bright slot between the window and its frame. Stay well inside the room; do not lean out. Include the hardware that holds it, if you can see an arm or a latch.
tips: Hold the phone back from the gap so you do not reach outside.
Focus on the near frame edge.
constraint: The phone must stay fully inside the room.

title: Coat on the Door
oneLiner: Hang a coat, scarf, or bag on a door and shoot the door as a quiet hook.
details: Use the back of a door or a hook beside the frame. Let one garment hang so its shape breaks the plain door. Step back until you see the handle or the frame as well, so the door is part of the picture.
tips: A plain door colour makes the garment easier to read.
Stand square so the door edges stay upright.

title: The Peephole Disc
oneLiner: Treat the door peephole as a small metal subject, not a view through it.
details: On the inside of your front door, find the round viewer. Photograph the ring, the glass dot, and the paint around it. Do not put your eye to it and do not shoot whatever is outside.
tips: Use the closest focus your phone allows, then ease back until the ring is sharp.
A flashlight from the side, or a lamp, will catch the metal rim.
constraint: The peephole must sit near the middle of the frame.

title: Wedge in the Gap
oneLiner: Prop a door with a wedge, a book, or a shoe and photograph the prop.
details: Open a door and stop it with whatever you safely use as a stop. Get down and frame the wedge in the triangle of space under the door. Include a little of the floor so the weight of the door feels present.
tips: Shoot from floor height so the gap reads clearly.
Tap the prop, not the floor beyond it.

title: The Highest Small Pane
oneLiner: Aim at the top pane of a door or the small window above a door.
details: From inside, look up at the highest glass in a door, or the little window over it if you have one. Fill the frame with that pane and its immediate frame. If your doors are solid, use the top corner of the tallest window in the home.
tips: Raise the phone rather than climbing on anything.
A vertical crop suits a tall top pane.
constraint: Include the frame around the pane, not glass alone.

title: Hem Resting on the Sill
oneLiner: Show the lower hem of a curtain where it meets the windowsill.
details: Frame the last few centimetres of curtain, the sill, and the line where cloth piles or stops. Look for dust in the light, a frayed thread, or the shadow the hem throws. This is the quiet bottom edge of the window, not the view.
tips: Turn the phone sideways and let the sill run across the frame.
Expose for the cloth if the window behind is bright.

title: One Door Beyond Another
oneLiner: Line up two doorways so one opening sits inside the other.
details: Stand where an open doorway frames a second door or doorway farther on. Move until the inner frame is fully visible inside the outer one. A hall, a kitchen door, or a cupboard seen through a room door all work.
tips: Focus on the farther frame so the near one is a border.
A small step left or right will square the two openings.
constraint: Both frames must be fully visible.

title: Cord and Toggle
oneLiner: Photograph the cord, chain, or toggle that works a blind.
details: Find the pull for a roller blind, a shade, or a set of slats. If there is no blind, use the ring or hook that holds a curtain. Let the pull hang against the window or the wall beside the frame. Come close enough that the toggle, tassel, or hook is a clear object.
tips: A plain bit of wall behind the pull keeps it readable.
Focus on the pull and let the cord or fabric fall slightly soft.

title: The Strike Plate
oneLiner: Close in on the metal plate a door latch meets.
details: Open the door and find the small plate set into the frame, with its rectangular hole. Photograph the scratches around the hole and the screws that hold the plate. That worn target is the subject.
tips: Use close focus and fill the frame with the plate.
Angle the phone so the hole shows a little depth.
constraint: The plate should occupy most of the picture.

title: Bathroom Door Barely Open
oneLiner: Leave the bathroom door barely open and shoot the slit of light.
details: Turn the bathroom light on, leave the hall darker, and open the door just enough to leak a vertical strip of light. Frame the door edge and that strip. Keep towels and clutter out so the light stays the subject.
tips: Tap the bright strip, then lower exposure if the edges bloom.
Shoot in portrait so the strip can run tall.

title: Lever from the Side
oneLiner: Shoot a lever handle from the side so the gap under it shows.
details: Instead of a straight-on portrait, stand at the door's edge and look along the lever, or along a round knob if that is what you have. The space between handle and door should be visible. Include a little paint so the metal has a home.
tips: A low side light, from a window or a lamp, separates handle from door.
Do not let a keyring with a readable tag hang in frame.
constraint: The handle must be seen in profile.

title: Where Frame Meets Door
oneLiner: Photograph the painted seam between a door and its frame.
details: Choose a spot where the door closes against the frame and layers of paint have built up. Fill the frame with that vertical seam, including a chip, a drip, or a change of colour if you can find one. The shut line is the whole story.
tips: Rake a lamp across the seam so the paint ridges show.
Keep the seam parallel to the long edge of the photo.

title: Door Squared to the Phone
oneLiner: From the sidewalk or landing, square your front door to the frame.
details: Face your own closed door from the sidewalk, path, or landing outside it, and hold the phone level so the door does not lean. Include the frame and a little wall, but let the door dominate.
tips: Use the grid and match the top of the door to a horizontal line.
Move back along the sidewalk if you cannot fit the whole door.
constraint: The door must look rectangular, not skewed.

title: Bell, Knocker, or Plate
oneLiner: Choose the thing visitors touch first: a bell, a knocker, or a push-plate.
details: On your own entrance, frame that piece of hardware and a small field of door or wall around it. Look for tarnish, a finger-worn shine, or a screw that sits slightly off. If you have none of these, use an outside hinge on the same door.
tips: Shade the metal with your body if the highlight is blank white.
Come close enough that the fitting is larger than the door around it.

title: The Metal Threshold
oneLiner: Look down at the metal or rubber bar under your outer door.
details: Open the door and, from the indoor side, point the phone at the bar where your floor meets the landing or the ground outside. Include the scuffs and the line it makes across the opening. Keep your feet out of the picture.
tips: Hold the phone parallel to the bar so it stays straight.
Tap the worn metal, not the brighter floor beyond.
constraint: The bar must run from edge to edge.

title: Just Outside the Door
oneLiner: From inside the doorway, photograph the floor just outside.
details: Stand on the indoor side of the doorway and shoot the floor immediately outside. If there is a single step, include its edge and a little of the surface beyond. If the way out is level, use the hallway floor or the first slab of the landing.
tips: A downward angle shows the edge better than a straight-on view.
Shift until your shadow is not covering the whole surface.
constraint: Shoot from the indoor side only.

title: Latch on the Outer Door
oneLiner: Make the outside latch of your own door the subject.
details: Frame the latch or catch on the outside of your own front door, and include a little of the wood or metal around it. A gate latch is fine only if you have a gate on your own path; otherwise the door is enough. Stay on the path or the landing while you shoot.
tips: Stand close, on the path or the landing.
Focus on the catch rather than the wall behind it.
constraint: Stay on the path or the landing.

title: Pane Above the Door
oneLiner: Frame the glass that sits directly above your front door.
details: From the sidewalk or the landing, look up at the glass set above the door. Include the curve or the bars, and the top of the door beneath. If there is no glass above the door, photograph the top edge of the door and the wall just over it.
tips: Hold the phone at chest height and tilt up from where you already stand.
Vertical framing fits a tall top light.

title: Mail Slot from Outside
oneLiner: Shoot the outside of the mail slot, flap closed, on your own door.
details: Stand on the path or the landing and fill much of the frame with the outer flap, the slot, and the surrounding paint or panel. Notice polish from letters, a thin gap, or a hinge pin. If the door has no mail slot, frame a horizontal moulding on that same door instead.
tips: A slight side angle shows the thickness of the flap.
Check the frame for a readable name and shift if one shows.
constraint: Shoot only your own door.

title: Door in its Recess
oneLiner: Move back and show the door set into the wall.
details: If your door sits in a recess, stand outside it, on the path or in the hallway, and include the side walls of that niche. Let the door be smaller in the frame so the depth around it matters. If the door is flush with the wall, include wall on both sides so it still sits in a wider frame.
tips: Expose for the door if the recess is darker than the space in front.
Include both side walls if you can.

title: Wheel at the Frame
oneLiner: Find the little wheel, cover, or runner at the side of a window.
details: At the side of a window, find a small wheel, a cover over a cord, or the plastic runner of a sliding pane. Fill the frame with that fitting and the painted wood or plastic around it. Stay inside while you shoot.
tips: Use the closest focus, then ease back until the wheel or runner is sharp.
A lamp from the side picks out the round edge of a pulley.
constraint: Keep the phone inside the room.

title: Your Window from Outside
oneLiner: From outside, photograph one window of your own home.
details: Go outside and turn back to a window you can see from the path or the sidewalk. Include the frame and whatever curtain or blind is really there. Keep to your own window rather than moving in on another home.
tips: Stand so your reflection is not the brightest thing in the pane.
Include a little wall so the window has a place.

title: Handle on the Outside
oneLiner: Make the exterior door handle the subject, seen from outside.
details: This is the handle on the outside of the door, not the one indoors. Frame it with a portion of panel, and look for worn shine or a dull patch where hands fall. Remain on the path or the landing while you shoot.
tips: Shoot slightly from the hinge side so the handle lifts off the door.
Wipe the lens if the metal looks falsely hazy.
constraint: Keep the handle larger than anything else in the frame.

title: Looking into the Hall
oneLiner: With the door open, frame the hall from the path or landing.
details: Open your own door and stand just outside, on the path or the landing. Photograph the rectangle of interior the doorway offers: floor, a wall, or a mat already there. The frame of the door should contain that view.
tips: Tap the interior if you want the outside frame to fall darker.
Hold the phone level so the top of the door stays horizontal.
